before: The old chapel of the Varadouros, so called because of where it stood, was demolished around 1682 and rebuilt in 1689, when the well-known Varadouros Gate was built there. The gate became the main entrance to the city, through which bishops and governors made their solemn and ceremonious entry into Funchal. The chapel had been rebuilt over the arch of this gate, which bore at its top a stone with a curious Latin inscription, transcribed on page 628 of the annotations to the *Saudades da Terra*.

The chapel had been rebuilt over the arch of this gate, which bore at its top a stone with a curious Latin inscription, transcribed on page 628 of the annotations to the ‘Longing for the Homeland’.

before: The church of São Tiago Menor (St James the Less), now the parish church of the parish of Santa Maria Maior, preserves on its façade a stone with a Latin inscription recording the grant made in 1803 by the Municipal Council (*Câmara Municipal*) of Funchal to the State, so that the church might serve as a parish church. This was because the great flash flood (*aluvião*) of that year had destroyed the original church, which then stood between the Largo dos Lavradores and the public fountain known as the Poço de Nossa Senhora do Calhau (Well of Our Lady of Calhau).

before: The British warship, the frigate *Howe*, anchored in our harbour on the morning of 2 November 1847, carrying Queen Adelaide. She came ashore at two o’clock in the afternoon to visit the house prepared for her lodging, returning on board the same day; only on the following day did she disembark and settle at the Quinta Vigia, temporarily transformed into a royal palace. The queen landed at the Pontinha, where she received the homage of all the local authorities, who accompanied her to her residence.

before: He was a colonel of the militia (*milícias*) and died in Funchal in 1810. We know nothing about him that would make him worthy of mention, but the horrible death he met at the bottom of a tomb deserves special record here. In an official document we came across the following information: ‘Francisco Anacleto de Figueiroa, colonel of the militia, was taken for dead in Funchal, where he lived. He was carried to the burial vault (*carneiro*) of João Gonçalves Zarco in the convent (*convento*) of Santa Clara (St Clare of Assisi). Years later, another death in the family made it necessary to open the vault, and there, beside the heavy iron grille at the entrance, at the gloomy foot of the stairway, lay the skeleton of Figueiroa, clutching the bars in a last despair of atrocious agony.’

before: This is the street that runs directly from Rua Direita to the small square (*largo*) of the church of Carmo (Carmelite church); Rua dos Medinas and Rua do Monteiro lead into it. Its name comes from the old city gaol (*cadeia*) that once stood there, at the corner formed by this street and Rua Direita, on the right as one walks from the church of Carmo towards the latter street. In Rua da Cadeia Velha stands the house that belonged to the Oliveira family, whose members included João Francisco de Oliveira, Joaquim de Oliveira Alvares and Benjamim de Oliveira (see those entries), among others. Paulo Perestrelo da Câmara states that it was one of the largest town houses in Funchal, and its construction must date from the beginning of the 18th century.

before: Campo Grande, on the Paul da Serra, is one of the places chosen for the gatherings of the sorceresses, over which the devil presides, often taking the form of a goat. The sign of the cross, made with devotion, is enough, they say, to drive off the king of hell should we have the misfortune to meet him on our way, whatever form he may take. The words ‘tosca, marrosca, olhos na cara e freio na bôca’ [TN: a charm; roughly ‘tosca, marrosca, eyes in the face and bit in the mouth’], spoken aloud, are said to be extraordinarily effective in warding off any sorceress or sorceresses who seek to harm us or amuse themselves at our expense.

before: The will-o’-the-wisps that appear over ground containing rotting matter are, the people say, the work of sorceresses, who have no fear of revealing their presence anywhere, especially at night. Sorceresses are as a rule old and ugly women, and it is believed in Madeira, as in Portugal, that their power lies chiefly in a ball of thread that the devil gives each of them at her initiation. The case of the prophets of Porto Santo, related in all seriousness on p. 55 of Gaspar Frutuoso’s *Saudades da Terra*, is attributed by that writer to ‘deceptions or wiles of Satan’. On p. 180 of the same work we read the account of a struggle that a cleric had with the devil near the chapel of Nossa Senhora das Neves (Our Lady of the Snows), a struggle from which the devil would have emerged victorious had the cleric not crossed himself or invoked the name of Jesus on realising that his life was in danger.

before: He was born on 19 April 1844 at the Quinta do Descanso, in the parish (*freguesia*) of Santa Luzia, which belonged to his paternal grandfather, the holder of the entail (*morgado*) Tristão Joaquim Bettencourt da Câmara. He died in the parish of Câmara de Lobos on 19 October 1875, while travelling from Estreito da Calheta to this city, aged only 31. He contributed valuably to several newspapers and showed a remarkable talent for letters. He devoted himself above all to genealogical and heraldic studies and had a wide knowledge of the lineages of the old Madeiran families. Some of the notes in the *Saudades da Terra* dealing with genealogical subjects are his. He was preparing a valuable work on this subject, which he never completed.

before: A European member of the Rosaceae-Pomoideae, widely cultivated in Madeira and also found on the island of Porto Santo. Its fruits vary greatly in both shape and flavour. The best known are those usually called by the following names: *bergamotas*, *caniças*, *condes*, *flamengas*, *francesas*, *carvalhais*, *de São João*, *marmelas*, *formigas*, *brancas* and *saramanhas*. These last two pears and the *caniças* are the most sought after for preserves. On Porto Santo only the *caniça* pear exists.

before: Opinions vary on the discovery of the Canary Islands archipelago. Some authors state that these islands were discovered three times, the last at the end of the 14th century or the beginning of the 15th. Father António Cordeiro says in the *Historia Insulana* that they were discovered ‘for the third time in the year 1417 by their Betencor kings; and the island of Madeira having been discovered and settled in 1420, and great fame of it spreading at once, this finally moved the aforesaid second king of the Canaries to sell the four over which he reigned to our Lusitanian and Most Serene Henry the Navigator..., and indeed he sold them to him for certain estates which the Infante gave him on the said island of Madeira, to which (and near which) the said king of the Canaries moved, now at last without a kingdom, and on Madeira he remained, and the descendants of the Betencores endure there even today...’.
after: Opinions vary on the discovery of the Canary Islands archipelago. Some authors state that these islands were discovered three times, the last at the end of the 14th century or the beginning of the 15th. Father António Cordeiro says in the ‘Island History’ (*Historia Insulana*) that they were discovered ‘for the third time in the year 1417 by their Betencor kings; and the island of Madeira having been discovered and settled in 1420, and great fame of it spreading at once, this finally moved the aforesaid second king of the Canaries to sell the four over which he reigned to our Lusitanian and Most Serene Henry the Navigator..., and indeed he sold them to him for certain estates which the Infante gave him on the said island of Madeira, to which (and near which) the said king of the Canaries moved, now at last without a kingdom, and on Madeira he remained, and the descendants of the Betencores endure there even today...’.

before: ‘And there, on another *lombada* (long ridge between valleys) belonging to the same daughter (Beatriz Gonçalves), on a high spot with a fine view of the sea and the land, the same captain (Zarco) traced with his own hand a church of Nossa Senhora da Estrela, and said that he would leave this church strongly commended to his children, because he had long wished to build it in a place of his liking.’ Such, as Gaspar Frutuoso describes it, is the origin of this chapel’s foundation. It was Diogo Cabral (see Cabral), husband of Dona Beatriz Gonçalves da Câmara, daughter of João Gonçalves Zarco, who fulfilled the discoverer’s wishes by having this chapel built; it was the head of the entailed estate (*morgadio*) he founded. Diogo Cabral died on 15 December 1486 and was buried in the chapel he had founded. When it was already in an advanced state of ruin, some decades ago, the tombstone covering Diogo Cabral’s mortal remains was moved to the parish cemetery and placed over an ordinary grave. On that occasion the epitaph and Cabral’s coats of arms were either scratched out of the slab, or else it was laid face down, hiding the inscription from visitors. The founder’s bones, however, remained among the rubble of the chapel, and today not even traces of those ruins can be found.

before: Grasshoppers or locusts are orthopteran insects known in Madeira by the name of *cigarros*. The common green grasshopper (Madeiran *cigarro*) is *Phaneroptera-4-punctata*; the grey *cigarro*, frequent in the fields, is *Pachytilus danicus*. It was *Dectycus albifrons* that caused great devastation to the crops of Madeira and Porto Santo in 1844. It appears from time to time on the first of these islands, carried by winds from the coast of Africa, but since that year it has never again caused significant damage to crops.

before: From the *Diário do Governo* of 29 October 1903: Directorate-General of Health and Public Welfare – 2nd Department. Informed by this knowledge, and after His Majesty’s Government had granted authorisation to build sanatoria there, the Prince of Hohenlohe organised a mission. Its medical side was represented by Professor Frankel of the Berlin Faculty, where his scientific authority is respected and enjoys the most glorious renown, and by Dr Pannwitz, secretary-general of the International Tuberculosis Bureau, who has so distinguished himself in directing various works in the fight against tuberculosis and in organising countless sanatoria. The mission’s aim was to choose sites on the island suitable for building sanatoria, some for those predisposed to tuberculosis, others for those infected with it. As the Prince wished a Portuguese physician to accompany the mission, Your Excellency’s generous goodwill saw fit to choose me, and it is with pleasure, and with the assurance of my gratitude, that I now report on my modest discharge of the honourable task I accepted.

before: The immediate construction of sanatoria for rich and poor, run as closed establishments where the most meticulous disinfection is guaranteed, will surely transform the results that the immigration of consumptives has so far brought the island. The very grave drawback of the consumptive’s passage through the island disappears entirely, so that the benefit the patient seeks and obtains there brings it nothing but prosperity. In other words, building sanatoria prevents future invasions of Koch’s bacillus. But what of the present evil? Part of it can be remedied by creating establishments for the poor; the rest will be met by enforcing the decree of 30 August 1902, which Your Excellency, with your lofty judgement, will know how to put into practice, providing Madeira with the equipment and staff indispensable for its defence. The law is certainly excellent, but ineffective and inapplicable without disinfection stations, etc., etc.

before: On the advice of the medical mission, as soon as the company begins its work two meteorological stations will be set up, one on the Arieiro at 1,700 metres and another on the Paul da Serra at 1,500 metres, to judge reliably the winter weather conditions. The existing data, above all those presented by Mr João Tierno on the Paul, and the limited use made of the Arieiro for a few patients, admirable though they are, are not enough to form a scientific opinion.

before: At the locality (*sítio*) of Estanquinhos, at an altitude of 1450 metres, there is a house that shelters travellers. The mountain shelter known as Meio Paul, which the Englishman Roberto Page had built towards the end of the first quarter of the 19th century, disappeared long ago through the action of time. This latter house stood at Campo Grande, a spot almost entirely bare of vegetation and the most inhospitable part of the Paul da Serra plateau.

before: The former Agricultural Board (*Junta Agrícola*) planned a road that would cross the Paul plateau along its greatest length, running from the Encumeada de São Vicente to the landing place of the parish of Porto do Moniz, about 38 kilometres long. The sections of this road were to be: from the Encumeada to the locality of Lombo do Mouro, a distance of 4,200 metres; from there to Pico da Urze, a stretch of 8,300 metres; a third section from Pico da Urze to Lamaceiros (Porto do Moniz), 23 kilometres long; and the last from Lamaceiros to the seaport, measuring 3,000 metres. Work on the road began in 1914 at both ends, but only a few kilometres of it were built.

before: Three years later, at the urgent request of the inhabitants of Funchal, King Sebastian founded a college of the Society in this city by the royal decree (alvará régio) of 20 August 1569, which is transcribed in full on p. 738 of the *Saudades da Terra*. This document fixed the annual endowment at 600$00 *réis* (old Portuguese money of account; 1$000 = 1,000 réis, 1:000$000 = one conto = 1,000,000 réis), ‘paid in produce of the best quality and that with which the Rector and fathers of the said College are most content’. This endowment, for the year 1569, that is, three and a half centuries ago, was not small, but it grew considerably through many private donations and various privileges granted by the monarchs.

before: The Jesuits then moved their residence to the hospice (*albergaria*) of São Bartolomeu, founded by Gonçalo Anes Velosa (see vol. 1, pp. 30 and 70), and remained there for some years. before: Besides the church of the College of São João Evangelista (St John the Evangelist) (*Colégio de São João Evangelista*), the Jesuits owned the residences of Pico dos Frias, near the Pico fortress (*Fortaleza do Pico*), of Pico do Cardo, in Santo António, of Nossa Senhora do Socorro (Our Lady of Succour), in Caniço, and of Fundoa, in São Roque, on the right bank of the Ribeira de Santa Luzia. before: When the Marquis of Pombal ordered the expulsion of the Jesuits throughout the country, the members of the Society living on this island had to abandon their College, after being held there as prisoners, cut off from all contact, for more than a year. On 29 May 1759 the College and the Church were unexpectedly surrounded, and the imprisonment and isolation continued until 16 July 1760, when the religious embarked for Lisbon. The carrack *Nossa Senhora da Natividade*, commanded by the Count of São Vicente, came to Funchal; he was charged with conveying to the capital the eighteen Jesuits who were in Madeira.
after: When the Marquis of Pombal ordered the expulsion of the Jesuits throughout the country, the members of the Society living on this island had to abandon their College, after being held there as prisoners, cut off from all contact, for more than a year. On 29 May 1759 the College and the Church were unexpectedly surrounded, and the imprisonment and isolation continued until 16 July 1760, when the religious embarked for Lisbon. The carrack the Nativity of Our Lady (*Nossa Senhora da Natividade*), commanded by the Count of São Vicente, came to Funchal; he was charged with conveying to the capital the eighteen Jesuits who were in Madeira.

before: During the imprisonment all their movable and immovable property was sequestrated. An inventory was drawn up of the rural and urban properties, the furniture, the objects of worship, the silver, the money, etc., and all the documents and papers found in the various residences were carefully collected. The Church and the College were placed in the keeping of the diocesan prelate. The properties were let and later sold at public auction. The Quinta Grande, which is today a parish (*freguesia*) and was the largest of the Jesuits’ properties, was sold for 140,000 *cruzados*; the *quinta* (country estate) of Pico do Cardo fetched 7 *contos*, and the residence of Pico dos Frias 9 *contos*.

before: A locality (*sítio*) in the parish (*freguesia*) of Santo António, Funchal. before: On the death of Bishop Dom Francisco he settled in Lisbon, and from there he was summoned to Madeira in 1844 by the prelate of this diocese, Dom José Xavier de Cerveira e Sousa. Protestant proselytism was then very active on the island, and the prelate was waging a fierce struggle against the propagandist Roberto Kalley and his followers. He needed at his side a man of prestige, prudence and learning to assist him in the arduous undertaking to which he was committed. Gonçalves de Andrade gave up the cultivation of letters, to which he was then actively devoting himself, and the close companionship he enjoyed with our leading men of letters, and came to live beside the prelate, to whom he rendered the most important and distinguished services. In 1846 he was appointed vicar general of this bishopric, and in 1853 dean of the Cathedral. When Empress Dona Amélia and her daughter, Princess Dona Maria Amélia, arrived in Madeira in 1852, Canon Andrade was appointed their chaplain and confessor, and he also served them as secretary. He was present at the last moments of the ill-fated princess, who held him in the highest regard and the deepest and most respectful esteem. Together with Dr António da Luz Pita, he was one of Empress Dona Amélia’s most devoted helpers in the definitive foundation of the Hospice, the hospice (*hospício*), and in the provisional installation of the hospital for tuberculosis patients, before the construction of the sumptuous building where it is housed today.

before: The *Carta Geo-Hydrographica da ilha da Madeira* by General A. Pedro de Azevedo marks this islet with the name of Ilhéu Vermelho or de Ametade; it is also known as the Ilhéu da Cevada or dos Embarcadouros, as other sources record. The Ilhéu de Agostinho, this Ilhéu dos Desembarcadouros and the Ilhéu de Fora are regarded as part of the Ponta de São Lourenço (see that entry) and lie in line with its extension. The smallest, and the closest to the point proper, from which it is separated by a narrow channel, is the Ilhéu de Agostinho (see that entry); next comes the Ilhéu dos Desembarcadouros and, to the east of it, the Ilhéu de Fora or do Farol. The Ilhéu dos Desembarcadouros thus lies between the Ilhéu de Agostinho and the Ilhéu de Fora. These two islets, dos Desembarcadouros and de Fora, are separated from each other by a channel called the Boqueirão Grande, which is 180 metres wide and about 8 metres deep. It is therefore navigable for the ‘barcos de carreira’ and coastal steamers, which frequently pass through it. The Ilhéu dos Desembarcadouros has a height of about 100 m, known as the Pico Vermelho, and a small beach that gives access to the upper part of the islet. Of these three islets, known as the Islets of the Ponta de São Lourenço, the Ilhéu dos Desembarcadouros has the largest area, and its terrain is quite rugged.

before: This is the moment to say that the administration of the donataries (*donatário*) of this captaincy, including the first, always left much to be desired. Let us hear Dr Álvaro de Azevedo in the following passages which, though somewhat long, give us a reliable idea of what that administration was: ‘The donatary captaincy (*donataria*) of Machico passed by succession from Tristão Vaz to his eldest son Tristão Vaz das Damas, so nicknamed “because (says Frutuoso) he was a great courtier, a fine talker, and composed many verses for the ladies”; his are the three songs collected in the *Cancioneiro Geral* of Resende, there attributed to “Tristão Teixeira, Captain of Machico”. He was succeeded by his son, also called Tristão Teixeira, and on his death the donatary captaincy was inherited by his son Diogo Teixeira, the fourth and last donatary descended from Tristão Vaz. The governments of these four captains were deplorable and in constant conflict with the royal power, which was severe with them. Tristão Vaz, for his despotism, especially towards Tristão Barradas, “whom he kept locked up with a shackle, grinding flour in a mill” (*Saudades*, p. 116), was summoned by the king to Lisbon and, by sentence, banished to the island of Príncipe, where he remained for some years, until, certainly in the reign of Afonso V and through the intercession of Prince Henry the Navigator, he was restored to the captaincy; he died around 1470. Tristão Teixeira das Damas, “because of charges brought against him”, was likewise summoned by the king to Lisbon, where he spent some years, with much toil and expense, seeking his acquittal and “finally clearing his honour”; but after him the king sent Dr Álvaro Fernandes and, later, Fernão de Perada as *corregedores* (royal district magistrate), with a special judicial commission (alçada) over the whole island of Madeira. Tristão Teixeira, succeeding Tristão das Damas, apparently did not take the title of captain-donatary (*capitão-donatário*) but simply that of governor, the capacity in which he had superintended the captaincy in his father’s absence; this reduced him, nominally at least, from holder of a right of his own to a mere royal delegate. Moreover, while he lived, the bachelor (*bacharel*, university graduate) Rui Pires was on the island as *juiz de fora* (crown-appointed judge from outside the district) and *ouvidor* (judicial officer of the donatary or the Crown) in the captaincy of Funchal, and after him Dr Diogo Taveira as *corregedor* in both captaincies; so watched, Tristão Teixeira behaved prudently. His son and successor Diogo Teixeira, however, “was a man of defective judgement… and almost feeble-minded;…. he governed so badly” that “King Manuel I and King John III… sought to take the captaincy from him, and over this he brought a lawsuit… until the year 1536”. During the suit Dr Francisco Diniz served as *corregedor* in the captaincy for nine years and, after him, the licentiate Antão Gonçalves for almost three years. Diogo Teixeira won the case, and so held the captaincy until 1538; but in the end John III took it and its revenues from him, ordering him to be placed in the custody of João Simão de Sousa, who “held him in his power until the year 1540”, in which year the captive died without a male heir or any other heir, so that “the house and inheritance passed to the Crown” (*Saudades*, pp. 117–119). Thus ended the line of Tristão Vaz. “Still in the year 1541 John III made a royal grant of this captaincy to António da Silveira, who had been captain of Diu, for services he had rendered him”; with royal licence he sold it to the Count of Vimioso, Dom Afonso de Portugal; on the latter’s death his son Dom Francisco succeeded to it, and on the death of the last it reverted to the Crown. None of these, however, governed it in person, but only through *ouvidores*, and there were always superintending *corregedores*, with whom these *ouvidores* had more or less serious conflicts.’

before: Prince Albert of Monaco, born in 1848 and died in June 1922, visited the seas around Madeira in 1879, 1888, 1901, 1904, 1911 and 1912, and in other years as well, aboard either the *Hirondelle* or the *Princesa Alice*. On every one of these occasions he made valuable collections for the study of the hydrobiology of this part of the Atlantic. In March 1888 he was on Deserta Grande, which he discusses in his book *La Carrière d'un navigateur*; the chapter on that island was translated by Mr Alberto Sarmento and published in the *Heraldo da Madeira*.

before: ‘The castle of São João do Pico’, says Dr Azevedo, ‘lies north-west of the city of Funchal, overlooking it and the harbour, on the height of the Pico dos Frias. This point and that of the Pena were already indicated in the regulations (*regimento*) of King Sebastian as the closing points of the walls for defence by land; but the Philippine building was perhaps designed for sea defence as well. Two of the manuscripts of the history of this archipelago in our possession state that the castle of the Pico was begun by the governor-general Dom Francisco Henriques: now he took office on 28 October 1622 and died on 23 July 1624; a stone tablet in the parade ground commemorates the governor-general Luís de Miranda Henriques Pinto as the builder of the rest of the work; and he, according to those manuscripts, took office on 6 June 1636 and left it on the same day in 1640; it is therefore clear that the castle of São João do Pico was built between 1622 and 1640’.

before: The first Arbour Day held in Funchal was organised by the Primary Education Inspectorate and took place on 29 March 1914, at 11 a.m. The procession set out from the Palácio de São Lourenço (St Lawrence Palace) for the Campo da Barca, or Campo de Miguel Bombarda, where some exotic tree species were ceremonially planted. Several speeches were made on the occasion, in which the speakers urged those present, and the children in particular, to regard trees as sacred objects because of the great benefits they bring us.

before: He was the son of Captain José Luís de Freitas Silva Nunes and Dona Ana Inácia Caetano Drumond, and was born in Câmara de Lobos in 1760. He graduated as a bachelor (*bacharel*, university graduate) in law from the University of Coimbra (*Universidade de Coimbra*). He was the first president of the Society of Friends of the Sciences and Arts (*Sociedade dos Amigos das Sciencias e Artes*) and held the offices of market inspector (*almotacé*), chief health officer of the port (*guarda-mor de saúde*), councillor (*vereador*) of the Council of Funchal, acting *juiz de fora* (crown-appointed judge from outside the district) and member of the board of the Lancasterian School (*Escola Lancasteriana*). At its session of 18 October 1803 the Municipal Council (*Câmara Municipal*) resolved to commission him to write a report on the state in which the city had been left by the flash flood (*aluvião*) of that year, to be kept in the Council’s archive. He published in the *Investigador Português* a memoir entitled *Noticias Mineralogicas da Ilha da Madeira*, and wrote the *Apontamentos Historicos e geographicos sobre a ilha da Madeira*, the autograph manuscript of which is in the municipal library, as well as several articles published in the *Patriota Funchalense*. He was an ardent constitutionalist, a distinguished lawyer and a man of considerable learning. He died without issue in March 1825. Among his contemporaries he was known by the nickname ‘Dr Piolho’ (‘Dr Louse’), because he was short in stature.

before: Between 1877 and 1882 some tobacco was planted in Madeira, chiefly in São Gonçalo and Santo António. In 1907 the plant was cultivated on the island once again, but it never became widespread, even though it grows well in our soils when they are properly fertilised. *Nicotina Tabacum* was the dominant species in the plantings made in 1907 and the years that followed, but in some localities *Nicotina rústica* could also be seen. The first of these species grows naturalised on Madeira and Porto Santo, and its cultivation is at present abandoned, or almost abandoned, throughout the archipelago.

The first of these species grows naturalised on Madeira and Porto Santo (‘holy harbour’), and its cultivation is at present abandoned, or almost abandoned, throughout the archipelago.

before: It is said in some quarters that at the top of the peak there is a small spring whose waters rise when the tide rises and fall when it falls. before: The epidemic of 1872 and 1873 claimed 1007 lives; after that of 1815, it was the one that did the most damage on this island. The disease was brought to Madeira by a passenger on the *Maria Pia*, who had come from Lisbon in October 1872 and was admitted to the Civil Hospital (*Hospital Civil*). It lasted until the end of 1873 or the beginning of 1874, and wrought great havoc, especially in the municipalities of Funchal, Santa Cruz, Calheta and Câmara de Lobos. Smallpox appeared in Madeira on several occasions after 1873, but thanks to the spread of vaccination and to certain sound measures adopted by the authorities, it never again reached the scale of the earlier epidemics. In 1907 many smallpox patients died in Funchal, but the epidemic was short-lived and never attained the intensity of those of 1815 and 1873. This was because, from a certain point onwards, patients who could not be isolated in their homes were admitted to the Lazaretto, where physicians and devoted nurses who knew their work gave them care and attention they would not have received at home.
after: The epidemic of 1872 and 1873 claimed 1007 lives; after that of 1815, it was the one that did the most damage on this island. before: To reach this height, one must take the roads that lead there from the parishes of Santana or Curral das Freiras, the route from the latter of the two being preferable. By the first, the summit of the peak is reached by way of the Cumeada Alta; the whole route offers the finest viewpoints and passes close to the curious column of lava known as Homem em Pé (see that entry). By the second, one climbs the road of the Lombo Grande and, at a certain height, comes upon a footpath that leads to the top of the lofty mountain. It can also be reached by setting out from Curral das Freiras and scaling the short cut known as the Lombo do Furão. However, besides being an extremely arduous ascent, this route is also full of dangers because of the ravines and precipices that flank it.

before: Pico do Areeiro with its reddish escarpments, the broad Pico das Torres, surrounded by several lesser summits, the highest of which is Pico do Gato, and the peaks of Canário, Cidrão, Grande and Santo António rise a short distance away, though separated from us by ravines of varying depth. Further off, to the west, one can make out the plateau of the Paul da Serra, entirely bare of vegetation, and to the east the long, winding Ponta de São Lourenço. The parish (*freguesia*) of Santana, the verdant uplands of São Jorge and Boaventura, part of the Caminho do Poiso, Porto Santo and the three Desertas can all be seen from the top of the peak. The sea around the island is also visible from there, except in the direction of Pico das Torres, which is only a little lower than Pico Ruivo.

before: As is well known, the island of Porto Santo formed one of the three captaincies into which this archipelago was divided (see vol. 1, p. 244). The letter of grant (carta de doação) to its first donatary, Bartolomeu Perestrelo, is dated 1 November 1446 and is transcribed on p. 457 of the *Saudades da Terra*. It states: ‘I give charge to Bartolomeu Perestrelo, *fidalgo* (nobleman of the lesser nobility) of my household, of my island of Porto Santo, so that the said Bartolomeu Perestrelo may maintain it for me in justice and right; and should he die, it pleases me that his first son, or another if such there be, shall hold this charge in the manner aforesaid, and so from descendant to descendant in the direct line; and should the said son be of such an age that he cannot govern, I or my heirs shall place there someone to govern until he is of age to govern. And it pleases me that he shall hold on this aforesaid island jurisdiction, for me and in my name, in civil and criminal matters, save for death or the cutting off of a limb, from which appeal shall come before me; yet notwithstanding the said jurisdiction, it pleases me that my orders and inspection (*correição*) be carried out there as a thing of my own.’ This letter mentions various rights, privileges and exemptions granted to the first donatary, including the collection of various contributions and taxes.

And it pleases me that he shall hold on this aforesaid island jurisdiction, for me and in my name, in civil and criminal matters, save for death or the cutting off of a limb, from which appeal shall come before me; yet notwithstanding the said jurisdiction, it pleases me that my orders and inspection (*correição*) be carried out there as a thing of my own.’ This letter mentions various rights, privileges and exemptions granted to the first donatary, including the collection of various contributions and taxes.

before: In the 17th century we find two distinguished musicians on the island of Madeira: the priests Father Manuel de Almeida and Father Miguel Pereira. before: The Administrative Committee (*Comissão Administrativa*) of the Levada de Santa Luzia tried on several occasions to obstruct the use of the waters of Tornos for the city’s supply, but the Municipal Council (*Câmara Municipal*) at last reached an agreement with it. A deed was signed on 3 July 1912 recognising the Municipality’s right to draw from those same springs, for that purpose, a continuous flow of 18 litres of water per second. This deed, under which the Council also made some concessions to the said levada (irrigation channel), was published in nos 11,291, 11,292 and 11,293 of the Funchal newspaper *Diário de Notícias*. Now that the Council had the means and resources needed to provide the city with drinking water and a good sewer network, it seemed impossible that any obstacle could arise to the completion of so important an improvement, above all once the works had been awarded. Neither the Council nor the public, however, had reckoned with the European war, which was to drive up the price of building materials extraordinarily and make it impossible to carry out the works on the terms of the award.

However, now that the European war is over and the main obstacles to continuing the works have gone, it is reasonable to hope that they will soon resume. before: At the council meeting of 13 November 1932 the Municipal Services (*Serviços Municipalizados*) were created, charged in particular with overseeing the sanitation works and the distribution of drinking water to homes. The tender for the award of the contract for the pipework in the middle and upper parts of the city twice attracted no bidders, so the Municipal Services took on these works themselves, estimated at 552,259.00 escudos, ‘a short section fed by a siphon to be built in the Ribeira de Santa Luzia still remaining to be completed’, and 3,700 metres of piping having already been laid.

before: We are not aware that any attempt to grow rice was ever made on this island at an earlier time. We do know, however, that in 1918 a grower of that cereal, a native of mainland Portugal, who was then living in the parish (*freguesia*) of São Vicente, carried out a trial of the crop there. It was crowned with the greatest success, yielding an excellent and abundant harvest. For this reason a petition signed by several landowners of that parish was addressed to the Madeira Agricultural Board (*Junta Agrícola da Madeira*), asking for special protection for the cultivation of this cereal. It seems to us, however, that no further trials were made to develop this industry.

before: From time to time enormous cetaceans pass off the islands of this archipelago. They are commonly called whales, but they may be either true whales or their close relatives, the sperm whales. Although the passage of these mammals is not very rare, especially in summer, there is no whaling industry in these islands, nor any hunting of any other cetacean. Now and then half-rotten carcasses are washed ashore; the last on record ran aground some years ago at Ponta Delgada, in the north-west of Porto Santo. These remains still included much of the spinal column, some ribs and part of the ventral and pectoral regions. The deep folds observed on the abdomen seemed to indicate a species of the rorqual group.

before: She was also called Dona Mariana de Vasconcelos e Câmara Alencastre, and was the daughter of Simão Gonçalves da Câmara, 3rd Count of Calheta and 7th captain-donatary (*capitão-donatário*) of Funchal. When her brother João Gonçalves da Câmara, 8th donatary, died without issue, Dona Mariana de Alencastre succeeded to the house of the countship of Calheta and was regarded as the 9th donatary of Funchal. before: This is a small church in the typical Manueline style, which makes it of particular interest to visitors, especially for certain details of its construction. It stands in the parish (*freguesia*) of Caniço, in the locality (*sítio*) to which it gave its name. It was built in the 16th century and is said to have been founded by a Salvago family, who held land there as a *sesmaria* (royal land grant to settlers on condition of cultivation). Services are still held in it, and it belongs (1921) to the heirs of João Maurício de Gouveia.

before: There is a chapel with the same dedication in the parish of Tabua, better known by the name of Mãe de Deus. We do not know the year it was built, but we know that around the middle of the 18th century it was completely destroyed by the violent current of the nearby stream. It was rebuilt around 1767 on the other bank of the stream, on a safer site, and was inspected on 9 December of the same year so that divine services could be celebrated there. A papal brief of 22 May 1781 grants a plenary indulgence to those who visit this chapel on the first Sunday of May.

before: We have found references to this procession, which left the church of the Sé, Funchal Cathedral (*Sé*), in documents from the beginning of the second quarter of the 19th century. It included three processional litters (*andores*): one with St Anthony as a canon, another with St Anthony as a friar, and a third with St Anthony as a choirboy. These litters were carried, respectively, by canons of the Sé, Franciscan friars and choirboys of the Cathedral. The minutes of the session of the Municipal Council (*Câmara Municipal*) of Funchal of 13 June 1815 show that the municipality accompanied the procession of St Anthony.

before: At Praia Formosa there are traces of old installations for crystallising salt, probably built by the first people to try salt-making here. Very close to this locality (*sítio*), at Ponta da Cruz, trials to produce salt were made about 15 years ago, but they came to nothing because the sea water had to be raised to a great height to get it into the reservoirs. It was José da Corte who tried to establish salt pans at Ponta da Cruz, but once the tuna-canning factory was set up, all attempts to extract salt at that locality ceased entirely.

before: Around 1865 António de Sousa had salt pans built at Paul do Mar, in the localities of Lagoas and Serra da Cruz. These passed, we believe around 1878, into the possession of Filipe António Gonçalves. Some 15 to 20 years ago other salt pans were established near the old ones, owned by José Maurício Gomes, João Martins da Silva, José da Corte and Alexandre da Silva (1921). A great deal of salt, not always of poor quality, was made in both the new and the old salt pans, but this did not prevent both from being abandoned because they yielded little profit, or perhaps losses, to their owners. Clay was even imported from Portugal to line the floors and walls of the reservoirs of these later salt pans.

before: On Porto Santo, too, there were some attempts to establish the industry of extracting salt from sea water. The earliest was that of Isidoro da Silva, who spent considerable capital building salt pans at the locality of Fontinha. In 1890 and the years immediately following, Augusto de Nóbrega Noronha succeeded in extracting a great deal of salt from salt pans he had built at Serra de Fora, in the north of the island. Around 1903 further salt pans were established at the same locality, owned by Dr António Luís Pimenta; these, however, did not give satisfactory results, owing, it was said, to defects in the construction of the reservoirs meant to receive the water.

before: Diogo de Ornelas de França Carvalhal Frazão Figueiroa, 1st Viscount and 1st Count of Calçada, came from old and noble families of this island and was born on 29 August 1812. before: The bridge over the Ribeiro Seco and the road that begins at it and leads to the parish (*freguesia*) of Câmara de Lobos are generally known as the Ponte Monumental and the Estrada Monumental (the Monumental Bridge and Monumental Road), because the original plan for their construction conceived of them as a monument raised to the memory of the King of Portugal Pedro IV. They were to bear his name and were intended to commemorate here his achievements as the liberator king. It was his comrade-in-arms and devoted friend, Luís da Silva Mousinho de Albuquerque, the first governor of Madeira in the constitutional period, who conceived this project in 1835; his short stay at the head of the administration of this district left it barely begun. Writing on this subject, Servulo Drumond de Meneses says: ‘Immediately on leaving the city towards the west, one comes upon a great landslide (*quebrada*) formed by the torrents, at the bottom of which runs the Ribeiro Seco. Mr Mousinho de Albuquerque intended to cross this landslide by means of a suspension bridge, and to that end he began by having two gigantic pillars built, besides the very strong abutments on each edge of the landslide. The plan included the idea of raising a monument to the memory of the Immortal Duke of Braganza, Magnanimous Liberator of the Portuguese, and accordingly the work was to be magnificent and grandiose. It happened, however, that when Mr Mousinho de Albuquerque left the island, the works already begun made no further progress. Thus the laudable and patriotic designs of the illustrious governor of Madeira were frustrated for a long time, although, tireless and persevering, he had not only already given a great impetus to the work but had also gathered many materials, which in the end were gradually lost.’

before: Only in 1767, when *juízes de fora* (crown-appointed judges) and *corregedores* (royal magistrates) began to be appointed on a permanent basis, did the administration of justice in this archipelago take on a regular form in keeping with the nature of the important services it performed. This situation lasted until 1838, when two judicial districts (*comarcas*) were created, both with their seat in the city of Funchal. They were named the western judicial district and the eastern judicial district. The first comprised the parishes (*freguesias*) of the municipalities (*concelhos*) of Funchal, Câmara de Lobos, Ponta do Sol, Calheta, Porto do Moniz and São Vicente, with the exception of the parish of the Sé (Funchal Cathedral); the second covered the parish of the Sé and the parishes of the municipalities of Santa Cruz, Machico, Sant’Ana and Porto Santo.

before: An inhabited locality (*sítio*) in the parish (*freguesia*) of Estreito da Calheta. It is usually divided into two localities, Igreja Acima and Igreja Abaixo, according to their position relative to the parish church. Here stands the chapel of Nossa Senhora da Conceição, founded by André de França e Andrade around 1672. It was the seat of one of the largest entailed estates in Madeira, whose last administrator was the 1st Count of Calçada (1812–1906).
after: An inhabited locality (*sítio*) in the parish (*freguesia*) of Estreito da Calheta (‘the narrows of Calheta’). It is usually divided into two localities, Igreja (‘church’) Acima and Igreja Abaixo, according to their position relative to the Igreja Paroquial (‘parish church’). Here stands the chapel of Our Lady of the Immaculate Conception (*Nossa Senhora da Conceição*), founded by André de França e Andrade around 1672. It was the seat of one of the largest entailed estates in Madeira, whose last administrator was the 1st Count of Calçada (1812–1906).

after: This famous privateer, in the service of the insurgents of the South of the Republic of the United States of America during the civil war that broke out in that country, called at the port of Funchal and then sheltered off the coast of the island of Porto Santo (‘holy harbour’) to repair damage, having fled the relentless pursuit of several ships loyal to the Northern government.

before: Attached to the Harbour Master’s Office (*Capitania do Porto*) of this city there is a Navigation School, created by decree of 14 November 1917, when the commander Arantes Pedroso was Minister of the Navy. The school owes its creation to the persistent and diligent efforts of the harbour master of Funchal, Commander Artur de Sales Henriques, who was entrusted with setting it up and has been its only teacher. Like other schools of this kind, its course lasts two years. The first year comprises arithmetic, elementary algebra, plane and solid geometry, plane trigonometry, general geography, compasses and dead reckoning; the second comprises spherical trigonometry, general astronomy, nautical calculations, astronomical navigation, handling under sail and steam, signals and meteorology.

before: The queen regent, Dona Luísa, beset by bitterness under the weight of government, faced with an incapable heir and a court that was like a backstage of tangled political intrigues, did not wish to take upon herself the responsibility of alienating Madeira, nor to incur the curse of God invoked in the letter of Manuel I when he made the island Crown land (*realenga*) (vol. 1 of the Archive of the Municipal Council (*Câmara Municipal*) of Funchal). She therefore had a grant from the late king to his daughter forged, and sent it to the councils (*Senados*) of Funchal and Machico so that the documents might be registered. This curious point of history is discussed by Dr Álvaro Rodrigues de Azevedo in the notes to *Saudades da Terra*, p. 384.

before: This distinguished engineer was born in Funchal towards the end of the first quarter of the 19th century, the natural son of Diogo Teles de Meneses, director of our customs house. After his preparatory studies he began his course in civil engineering in Lisbon, and later completed it with great distinction in Paris in 1848. He was engineer to the Municipal Council (*Câmara Municipal*) of Funchal from 1849 to 1850, and in 1852 was called to work on the Northern Railway, where he gave notable proof of his talent and love of work. He then held important posts: director of public works in Viana, Braga and Porto, member of the Public Works Council, director of the Eastern Railway and inspector of the northern lines. He travelled abroad several times on missions entrusted to him by our government. He was a man of great aptitude and remarkable energy, and died in Funchal, from overwork, on 14 November 1877.

before: On p. 404 of vol. II, in the article Popular riots, we have already referred to the cases of bubonic plague that broke out in Funchal in November 1905 and to the extraordinary events that followed them. These were caused by the people’s conviction not only that the disease did not exist on the island, but that the patients admitted to the lazaretto were being murdered by Dr Balbino do Rêgo and the nursing staff, with the consent of the local authorities. To what we said then, we need only add now that the bacteriological tests carried out in Lisbon fully confirmed Dr António Balbino do Rêgo’s statement that bubonic plague was present in Madeira. The only strange thing was the secrecy in which everything that went on inside the lazaretto was shrouded, which allowed the absurd and fanciful reports mentioned in that article to circulate in the city and beyond. Had full and precise information been given to everyone who sought news of the condition of the patients in the establishment, it may be supposed that the events of 7 January 1906 would not have taken place. Those events, however, did not bring about the harm to public health that many had predicted.

before: As we have said elsewhere, the first parish (*freguesia*) created in Funchal was that of Santa Maria Maior, although in the very earliest days of colonisation parish functions were carried out simultaneously in various chapels and hermitages (volume II, page 52). This parish, created around 1438 and established in the church of Nossa Senhora do Calhau (Our Lady of Calhau), moved its seat to the new church that later became the Cathedral (Sé Catedral), some years before the diocese was instituted. The royal decree (alvará régio) of 18 November 1557 divided it into two separate parishes, with their seats in the Cathedral and in the church of Nossa Senhora do Calhau. It was from the parish of the Sé that the parishes of São Pedro, Santo António, São Martinho, São Roque, Monte and, later, Santa Luzia were carved out.

before: The roads of Madeira were, beyond any possible dispute, the worst in the whole of our country. This was due to various causes, above all the almost unbelievably rugged terrain and other unavoidable conditions of the environment. Most of them did not deserve the name of roads, for in general they were narrow paths cut into ground that was arduous and extremely difficult underfoot, overhanging unfathomable chasms and skirting the flanks of high mountains, almost always subjecting travellers to the gravest discomforts and dangers. Until 1901, when administrative autonomy was granted to this district, there were only nine kilometres of good road, linking the city of Funchal with the town (*vila*) of Câmara de Lobos. Then began, and still continues, the construction of an extensive road network which, within a few years, will make it easy to travel the whole island by fast transport and to visit its principal localities quickly and comfortably.

before: In the early days of the colonisation of Madeira, Ponta do Sol was one of the most active centres of agriculture, above all in the growing of sugar cane and the associated products of the sugar industry. Many grantees of land (*sesmeiros*) from the mainland settled here, a great number of Moorish and Black slaves worked the land, and many mills were built for making sugar. All of this contributed to the growth and prosperity of this village (*lugar*, settlement rank below a town). Frutuoso states that João Esmeraldo (see that entry) had some eighty slaves on his property at the Lombada and that he came to produce twenty thousand *arrobas* of sugar a year, which seems to us an exaggeration.

before: As it grew in importance and population, and as it was the centre of other small settlements that gradually arose around it, it was natural that it should become a town (*vila*) and municipality with its own charter (foral), granting it the privileges and exemptions that the people of the time guarded so jealously. The government in Lisbon took this view, and in the relevant royal letter (*carta régia*) the monarch says: ‘we, of our own motion, without their requesting it, nor others in their names, see fit and do make the said *lugar* of Ponta do Sol a town...’ This document is dated 2 December 1501 and is recorded in volume 1 of the *Registo Geral da Camara do Funchal*, at fol. 67. According to the annotator of the *Saudades*, the copy held in the secretariat of the Ponta do Sol Municipal Council, which was taken from the register of the Funchal Council, contains various inaccuracies. The corresponding charter, which is shared with the municipalities of Funchal and Calheta, is dated 6 August 1515 and is transcribed on p. 494 ff. of the *Saudades da Terra*.

before: The new municipality was carved out of that of Funchal, and its area and jurisdiction extended from the Ribeira da Ponta do Sol to Ponta do Tristão. before: The town of Ponta do Sol is the seat of the judicial district (*comarca*) of the same name, which covers the municipalities of Ribeira Brava, Ponta do Sol and Calheta. It was installed on 28 April 1876, its first judge and first public prosecutor being Dr Martinho da Rocha Guimarães Camões and Dr António Augusto Ribeiro de Campos, who took up their posts on the day of, and at the ceremony marking, the installation of the judicial district.

before: There are twelve combined telegraph and post offices in Madeira: one of the first class, in Funchal; two of the second class, in Santa Cruz and Calheta; six of the third class, in Ribeira Brava, Ponta do Sol, Porto do Moniz, São Vicente, Sant'Ana and Machico; and three of the fourth class, in Câmara de Lobos, Ponta Delgada and Porto da Cruz. before: Garlic belongs to the family Liliaceae, and the best-known kinds in Madeira are common garlic (*Allium sativum*), leek-garlic (*A. ampeloprasum*) and wild or American garlic (*Nothoscordum inodorum*). In common garlic the bulb is made up of bulblets (cloves) enclosed in a common skin. This species is widely grown in Madeira and Porto Santo for culinary purposes, and it has diuretic, vermifuge and antiseptic properties. Wild garlic, native to subtropical America, is a plant that spreads with extreme ease both by its bulbs and by its seeds.

before: An inhabited locality (*sítio*) in the parish (*freguesia*) of Santo António, Funchal. On it stands a small hill known by the same name, which is today an obligatory attraction for every tourist visiting Madeira. The land stretching far from Ponta do Garajau to Cabo Girão forms a vast semicircle, and at the centre of its diameter rises the eminence of Pico dos Barcelos. From this point one of the most attractive and beautiful panoramas that could perhaps be offered to the eyes of any visitor can be enjoyed. The road leading there, built in 1917, makes the spot easy to reach, and it is frequented almost at all hours by countless visitors, Portuguese and foreign. It seems that this locality took its name from Diogo Barcelos, one of the early settlers, who owned several tracts of land in the area.

before: The annotator of the *Saudades da Terra* refers only very briefly to the legends that took shape over time among the peoples of this archipelago. He deals at length, and with great erudition, only with the well-known legend of Robert Machin and Ana d’Arfet, which we shall discuss in its proper place in this *Elucidário*. The legend of the Ilha Encoberta (the Hidden Island), which is not peculiar to this region and generally forms part of the beliefs of the Sebastianists, takes on a particular aspect here: the island is said to lie, if the expression may be allowed, near Madeira, and there are people who claim to have seen it distinctly on certain mornings of St John’s Day. Apart from these and some legends of a religious character, Dr Azevedo mentions no other legends that were current on this island. He says: ‘Religious legends abound on the island of Madeira, and we are forming a collection of them; besides the three already mentioned (that of the Senhor dos Milagres, in the Convent of São Francisco (St Francis of Assisi), that of Friar Pedro da Guarda, in Câmara de Lobos, and that of the foundation of the Convento das Mercês (Convent of Our Lady of Mercy)), we already have the following: that of Nossa Senhora do Monte, that of the Senhor dos Milagres of Machico, that of Santo António da Serra, that of the Senhor Jesus of Ponta Delgada, that of St Vincent of Saragossa of the islet (in the parish (*freguesia*) of São Vicente), that of São Martinho and that of Nossa Senhora of the *Recolhimento* (religious retreat house for women) das Órfãs. We reserve them for publication in a separate volume.’ This volume was never published.

before: Inside the fountain there is a brass plate bearing an inscription in English, which reads as follows: ‘Charles Murray, Consul General of His Britannic Majesty in the islands of Madeira and Porto Santo, founder and first owner of the *quinta* (country estate) of Belo Monte, in the year 1776 purchased the surplus water of this fountain from the holder of the entail (*morgado*) Henrique Felix de Freitas, for the sum of 5,000 *réis* a year, to be paid in perpetuity to the heirs of the said holder of the entail; and he ordered this structure to be built so that the waters might be better gathered, the fountain repaired and the aqueduct and fountain at the roadside constructed, all at his own expense, in the year of Our Lord 1778’.

before: At its session of 22 August 1895, the Municipal Council (*Câmara Municipal*) of Funchal gave the name of its president, Dr José Leite Monteiro, to the park at Monte. However, the municipal administrative commission (*comissão administrativa municipal*) appointed after the proclamation of the Republic annulled this decision at its session of 27 October 1910. On 13 February 1913, when Dr Manuel Gregório Pestana Júnior was president of the municipal administrative commission, the park’s original name was restored, a decision that was very well received by the people of Funchal.
after: At its session of 22 August 1895, the Funchal Municipal Council (*Câmara Municipal do Funchal*) gave the name of its president, Dr José Leite Monteiro, to the park at Monte (‘hill’). before: The Revd Father José Marques Jardim, the present parish priest of Monte, is engaged in the praiseworthy endeavour of raising a monument to the Most Holy Virgin near the Terreiro da Luta, that is, where local tradition holds that the miraculous apparition of Our Lady took place. To this end he travelled to North America to raise donations for the construction of the great statue that will form part of the monument (1921). See Monuments.

before: As a cliff overlooking the sea, several authors state that it is among the highest and sheerest to be found anywhere in the world. From some of the highest and most prominent points of that gigantic escarpment, one sees the ocean waves breaking at the foot of the sheer cliff some 600 metres below. That is why countless Portuguese and foreign works contain frequent references to the cliffs of Cabo Girão, which amply reward the scholar and the tourist with a subject for close and lengthy observation. Access to the highest points of the cliff is neither easy nor comfortable, for want of a good road leading there. A branch road 800 metres long is planned, to link these points with the national road that crosses the parishes of Quinta Grande and Campanário. (1921)

before: For the convenience of the people of the island, the parish of São Vicente became the seat of a vicariate forane (*vigairaria da vara*), that is, a deanery (*arciprestado*, group of parishes under an archpriest). It was created on 2 September 1812 by the diocesan prelate Dom Friar Joaquim de Meneses e Ataíde, and the first vicar forane or archpriest was Father Francisco Borges de Sousa e Melo, then parish priest of the parish, with jurisdiction ‘over all the parish priests, clergy and other persons of the said Town and its district’. By a warrant (*provisão*) of the vicar-general of 14 January 1814, this jurisdiction was extended to the parishes of Porto Moniz, Ribeira da Janela and Seixal, since he had learnt ‘that it is often better for them to go to the said Town than to that of Calheta’. We do not know what the powers of this vicar forane were, nor when the functions of the office ceased to be exercised, though it is certain that no such ecclesiastical authority has existed for some decades. Only very recently did the present diocesan prelate, within the powers conferred on him by the Code of Canon Law now in force, create the deaneries of Funchal, Calheta and São Jorge (1921).

before: ‘The parish of São Vicente,’ an educated person who has lived there for years tells us, ‘wedged at the foot of towering mountains, cut almost sheer, which surround it for dozens of kilometres like gigantic ramparts and leave it open only on the seaward side, is one of the loveliest places in Madeira, for its rugged look of grandly wild beauty. To the east it borders on Ponta Delgada; to the west its limits run as far as the Ribeira do Inferno, which nature thus sets between it and Seixal; to the north lies the sea; to the south stretches the plateau of the Paul da Serra, which divides it from Serra Alva, and, where the high backbone of the mountains dips, the gorge of the Encumeada. Its lands are thick and dense, and in them abound the richest woods of leafy laurels, til (*Ocotea foetens*, Madeiran laurel), *vinhático* and heather, which at present are held, beyond dispute, to be the finest in Madeira.’

before: At the far western edge of the parishes (*freguesias*) of Câmara de Lobos and Estreito de Câmara de Lobos, in the locality (*sítio*) of Garachico, stands the chapel of Nossa Senhora do Bom Sucesso, which is considered to belong to the latter of these parishes. The chapel had the peculiarity that its altar stood within the boundaries of one of these parishes while its door opened onto land of the other, neighbouring parish. It seems that in times more remote from ours doubts arose as to which parish the chapel should belong to, and there were even conflicts of jurisdiction between the respective parish priests. It was built in the early 17th century by Manuel João Ferreira, especially so that his son, Father Francisco Luís Ferreira, could say Mass in it. Some years ago it was enlarged by the inhabitants of the village (*lugar*, settlement rank below a town).
after: At the far western edge of the parishes (*freguesias*) of Câmara de Lobos (‘seals’ den’) and Estreito de Câmara de Lobos (‘the narrows of Câmara de Lobos’), in the locality (*sítio*) of Garachico, stands the chapel of Our Lady of Good Success (*Nossa Senhora do Bom Sucesso*), which is considered to belong to the latter of these parishes. The chapel had the peculiarity that its altar stood within the boundaries of one of these parishes while its door opened onto land of the other, neighbouring parish. It seems that in times more remote from ours doubts arose as to which parish the chapel should belong to, and there were even conflicts of jurisdiction between the respective parish priests. before: There is also a chapel dedicated to Nossa Senhora do Bom Sucesso in the locality of Lombo da Estrela, in the parish of Calheta, founded in 1683 by Lourenço da Costa. In the parish of Santa Maria Maior, beside the road known as Caminho do Meio, stands another chapel of the same dedication, which belongs to the Municipal Council (*Câmara Municipal*) of Funchal, as does the adjoining house, where a state school is housed. We do not know the name of the founder of this last chapel, nor the year in which it was acquired by the Funchal Council.

before: The church whose patron saint was Nossa Senhora da Conceição (Our Lady of the Conception), commonly known as Nossa Senhora do Calhau (Our Lady of Calhau), and which was destroyed by the flash flood (*aluvião*) of 1803, was already built by 1508 on the left bank of the Ribeira de João Gomes, near the spot where the so-called Poço do Calhau stands today. To the east of this church lay Rua dos Balcões and Rua de Santa Maria. The latter was probably shorter than it is now, but it had many large, well-built houses in which a number of noblemen and wealthy men lived.

before: The Largo do Pelourinho, Rua Direita and Rua dos Mercadores existed in 1508, though certainly with a very different appearance from the one they present now. The Largo do Pelourinho was planted with trees, probably native species, and on the site where Rua da Cadeia Velha now runs stood an enormous til (*Ocotea foetens*, Madeiran laurel) which, in the words of Manuel Tomaz, ‘embraced two streams with its outstretched branches’: the Ribeira de João Gomes and the Ribeira de Santa Luzia.
after: The Largo do Pelourinho (‘pillory’), Rua Direita (‘straight street’) and Rua dos Mercadores existed in 1508, though certainly with a very different appearance from the one they present now. before: The Chapel of Varadouros, demolished in 1911, already existed in 1508. Of the present customs house building, however, if anything existed at all, it can only have been the foundations, for it was in that year that the order came from mainland Portugal for it to be built.

before: The first parish church was that of Nossa Senhora do Calhau, but in 1508 the parish was transferred to the so-called great church, whose patron saint is Nossa Senhora da Assunção (Our Lady of the Assumption). Its construction had begun in 1493, funded by the revenues of the wine levy (imposição do vinho), and after the bishopric of Funchal was created in 1514 it became, as it still is, the Cathedral. Only in 1558 was the city divided into two parishes, that of the Sé (Funchal Cathedral) and that of Santa Maria Maior, and from then on the church of Nossa Senhora do Calhau became a parish church once again.

before: Beyond Rua dos Mercadores, at the point where the entrance to the city now stands, there were a few houses, but the place looked very different from how it does at present. The Fort of São Lourenço (St Lawrence) had not yet been built, and on the ground now occupied by Praça da Constituição there were plantations of sugar cane. These probably extended to somewhere near Rua da Carreira, since the building of the Hospital de Santa Isabel (St Elizabeth of Portugal) was begun only after 1686.

before: The Council’s house, then known as the Curral do Concelho, stood in the locality (*sítio*) where Avenida António José de Almeida now meets Rua da Alfândega, and in Largo de São Sebastião stood the chapel dedicated to this saint, which was one of the first churches built on the island. before: The *recolhimento* (religious retreat house for women) of Bom Jesus (Retreat of the Good Jesus) did not yet exist in 1508, nor did the street in which it stands, nor Rua das Hortas. The church of Carmo (Carmelite church) had not yet been built either, but the street that took its name from that church must have existed at the time. It connected with Rua Direita by the street later called Rua da Cadeia Velha and by Rua da Margem da Ribeira. It is likely that a wooden bridge at the end of Rua Direita linked the two banks of the Ribeira de Santa Luzia.

before: Rua da Carreira, the widest street in the settlement, though very different in appearance from today, probably did not extend beyond Rua dos Aranhas, which was built later. before: Outside the city stood the convent of Santa Clara (St Clare of Assisi), built in 1492 near the residence of the donatary, which was probably on the *quinta* (country estate) now called Quinta das Cruzes. There were also the chapels of São Paulo and of Santa Catarina (St Catherine of Alexandria), the latter with an attached hospice (*hospício*) where poor women lived. It is possible that the Hospital de São Lázaro (St Lazarus) had already been built by 1508.

before: At that time, although they looked different from today, the little streets of João Tavira, Santa Catarina, Cidrão and Hospital Velho already existed, as did the squares of Corpo Santo and São Paulo, besides other squares and streets whose names have not survived in local tradition.

before: From what has been said, then, it is clear that although the Funchal of 1508 was much smaller than the present city, it nonetheless covered an area large enough to form a city. To the west it extended a little beyond the convent of São Francisco, without, however, reaching the Ribeira de São João. To the east it reached as far as the chapel of Corpo Santo (Holy Body), which even in Frutuoso’s time adjoined the first houses of the city. Finally, to the north its limits were the Rua do Hospital Velho, the Rua do Carmo – which probably did not go beyond the point where the church stands – the Rua da Carreira, the Rua das Pretas and the Mouraria.

before: He was an engineer sergeant-major (*sargento-mor engenheiro*, a field-officer rank equivalent to major), a professed knight of the Order of Christ and a professor at the Royal Academy. He drew up the general map of Madeira in 1769, and in the same year he went to Porto Santo to study the needs of that island, on which he wrote a dissertation. Arrested in 1770 as a freemason on the orders of the governor João António de Sá Pereira, he was released shortly afterwards and restored to his post under instructions sent by the Marquis of Pombal to his representative on this island.

before: Near the parish church of the parish of São Jorge there is a chapel dedicated to St Peter. It had fallen into ruin and was restored in 1901 by the prelate Dom Manuel Agostinho Barreto, who himself blessed it and returned it to worship on 7 August of the same year.

before: In the parish of Porto Moniz, at the place known as Terra de São Pedro, there was once a small chapel dedicated to St Peter, of which not even traces remain.

before: In the locality (*sítio*) of Lamaceiros, in the same parish, there is a chapel consecrated to St Peter, to which the image of the saint from the other chapel of the same dedication was moved. It is not of recent construction, for as early as 1726 it was already in an advanced state of ruin. Some years later it was properly repaired through the efforts of Manuel Rodrigues Amarelo. The earthquake of 1748 caused it various kinds of damage, and it was promptly repaired. Only a few years ago important works were carried out on it. The chapel holds a greatly venerated image of Nossa Senhora do Monte.

before: For those less versed in Madeiran history, it should be recalled that Gonçalo Aires Ferreira was one of Zarco’s companions. He is credited with the authorship of a writing entitled *Descobrimento da Ilha da Madeira*, whose original passed down by inheritance, from father to son, among the captains-donatary of Funchal. Then, in the time of the sixth captain and second Count of Calheta, João Gonçalves da Câmara, Jerónimo Dias Leite, a canon of Funchal Cathedral (*Sé*), made use of this manuscript to write the notes he sent to Dr Gaspar Frutuoso, who drew on them for his important work *As Saudades da Terra*.

before: There is evidently a clear mistake on the part of the historian of the islands in seeking to fix the day of Madeira’s discovery with such precision. Subject to better-informed opinion, we are inclined to believe that the caravel *São Lourenço* rounded the point that later took this name and approached the bay of Machico on the afternoon of 1 July 1419, and that the landing took place on Sunday 2 July of the same year, the day of the Visitation of St Elizabeth.

before: For fuller and more reliable information on this subject, and to understand the legendary and historical phases through which it has passed, one must consult the most remarkable study by Dr Alvaro Rodrigues de Azevedo in notes III–IV (pp. 329–432) of the *Saudades da Terra*, as well as the articles ‘Machico’, ‘Machim’ and ‘Madeira’ in the *Diccionario Universal Portuguez Illustrado*, written by the same author. Some of his conclusions must nevertheless be disputed in the light of the important work of historical research and criticism carried out in recent years. Besides those learned notes and the works cited in them, it is absolutely essential to consult the following writings, which we list here simply as aids for the reader who wishes to gain a fuller knowledge of this subject: *Memoria sobre a descoberta das ilhas de Porto Santo e Madeira* by E. A. de Bettencourt, Lisbon, 1875; *Desenvolvimentos, guerras e conquistas dos portugueses em terras do ultramar nos seculos XV e XVI* by the same author, Lisbon, 1882; *As relações do descobrimento da Guiné e das ilhas dos Açores, Madeira e Cabo Verde* by Diogo Gomes, written in Latin at the beginning of the 16th century, translated into Portuguese by Gabriel de Almeida in 1899 and published in the *Boletim da Sociedade de Geografia de Lisboa* (17th series, 1898–1899, no. 5); *Quando foi descoberta a Madeira* by Jordão de Freitas, Lisbon, 1911; *A Lenda Infantista* by João da Rocha, 1916; *O Reconhecimento do Arquipelago da Madeira* by Pestana Júnior, Funchal, 1920; *Apontamentos de Historia Insular* by João Cabral do Nascimento, Funchal, 1927; *O Arquipelago da Madeira nos mapas e portulanos do século XIV* by António Ferreira de Serpa, in *Arquivo Histórico da Madeira* I-125 ff.; *D. Francisco Manuel de Melo e o descobrimento da Madeira* by Antonio Gonçalves Rodrigues, Lisbon, 1935; *A Relação de Francisco Alcoforado* by João Franco Machado, Lisbon, 1936; *Origens e evolução da cartografia náutica portuguesa, na época dos descobrimentos* by Antonio Barbosa, published in the review *Ocidente* (no. 8, 1938); *Zarco ou os efeitos da publicidade* by João Cabral do Nascimento, in *Arquivo Histórico da Madeira* V-81; *O Problema do descobrimento da Madeira* by Antonio Alvaro Doria, published in the review *Ocidente* (no. 19, 1939 and no. 27, 1940); *Quem descobriu o arquipelago da Madeira* by Duarte Leite, articles published in the *Primeiro de Janeiro* of Porto on 28 March and 4 April 1939 and reprinted in the Funchal daily newspapers; *O Descobrimento do Arquipelago da Madeira* by M. Higino Vieira, Lisbon, 1939. On the basis of what is known to date about this much-debated subject, which is of such interest to the history of Madeira, we may perhaps reach the following conclusions: 1. This archipelago was already known to Portuguese navigators before 1418; 2. The year of the original discovery and the names of the first discoverers are unknown; 3. The ‘reconnaissance’ carried out by João Gonçalves Zarco and Tristão Vaz Teixeira may be placed in the last years of the first quarter of the 16th century, that is, around 1418 to 1425; 4. The work of settlement undertaken by those two first donataries must have begun in the first years of the second quarter of the 15th century, that is, in 1425 or shortly afterwards.
after: For fuller and more reliable information on this subject, and to understand the legendary and historical phases through which it has passed, one must consult the most remarkable study by Dr Alvaro Rodrigues de Azevedo in notes III–IV (pp. 329–432) of the ‘Longing for the Homeland’, as well as the articles ‘Machico’, ‘Machim’ and ‘Madeira’ in the *Diccionario Universal Portuguez Illustrado*, written by the same author. Some of his conclusions must nevertheless be disputed in the light of the important work of historical research and criticism carried out in recent years. Besides those learned notes and the works cited in them, it is absolutely essential to consult the following writings, which we list here simply as aids for the reader who wishes to gain a fuller knowledge of this subject: *Memoria sobre a descoberta das ilhas de Porto Santo e Madeira* by E. A. de Bettencourt, Lisbon, 1875; *Desenvolvimentos, guerras e conquistas dos portugueses em terras do ultramar nos seculos XV e XVI* by the same author, Lisbon, 1882; *As relações do descobrimento da Guiné e das ilhas dos Açores, Madeira e Cabo Verde* by Diogo Gomes, written in Latin at the beginning of the 16th century, translated into Portuguese by Gabriel de Almeida in 1899 and published in the *Boletim da Sociedade de Geografia de Lisboa* (17th series, 1898–1899, no. 5); *Quando foi descoberta a Madeira* by Jordão de Freitas, Lisbon, 1911; *A Lenda Infantista* by João da Rocha, 1916; *O Reconhecimento do Arquipelago da Madeira* by Pestana Júnior, Funchal, 1920; *Apontamentos de Historia Insular* by João Cabral do Nascimento, Funchal, 1927; *O Arquipelago da Madeira nos mapas e portulanos do século XIV* by António Ferreira de Serpa, in *Arquivo Histórico da Madeira* I-125 ff.; *D. Higino Vieira, Lisbon, 1939. On the basis of what is known to date about this much-debated subject, which is of such interest to the history of Madeira, we may perhaps reach the following conclusions: 1. This archipelago was already known to Portuguese navigators before 1418; 2. The year of the original discovery and the names of the first discoverers are unknown; 3. The work of settlement undertaken by those two first donataries must have begun in the first years of the second quarter of the 15th century, that is, in 1425 or shortly afterwards.

before: This legitimate wish of the northern communities was fulfilled only in 1744, with the creation of the town of São Vicente. Dr Álvaro Rodrigues de Azevedo makes not the slightest reference to this event and was certainly unaware of the instrument that raised the parish (*freguesia*) of São Vicente to the rank of town. The royal decree (alvará régio) concerned, a lengthy and exceptionally interesting document, is dated 25 August 1744 and was first published in no. 14 and following issues of the newspaper *A Revista Madeirense* in 1902. With the establishment of constitutional government, the archipelago was divided into municipalities (*concelhos*), and the existing division into towns or municipalities was profoundly altered. The municipality of São Vicente was set up in 1835 and consisted, as it still does today, of the parishes of Boaventura, Ponta Delgada and São Vicente. The decree of 10 December 1867 abolished the municipality of Porto Moniz and incorporated the parishes of Seixal, Ribeira da Janela and Porto Moniz into that of São Vicente; shortly afterwards, however, the abolished municipality of Porto Moniz was restored. It was abolished again by the decree of 18 November 1895 and restored once more by the decree of 13 January 1898. During this short period the parishes of Seixal, Ribeira da Janela and Porto Moniz were once again part of the municipality of São Vicente.

before: Birds, being capable of flight and finding it no hard task to cross the roughly 350 miles that separate us from the Moroccan coast, are well represented in the fauna of the archipelago. Altogether, very nearly 200 species have been observed, more than in the Canary Islands and far more than in the Azores, despite the greater extent of those two archipelagos. According to Father Ernesto Schmitz, the number of species confirmed as breeding here is 36, with 12 peculiar forms. Of these, 3 – the *bisbis* (*Regulus madeirensis*), the chaffinch (*Fringilla Madeirensis*) and the long-toed black trocaz pigeon (*Columba Trocaz*) – are regarded by some as good species, while the remaining 9 are mere local varieties. Among the birds, some are regular passage migrants, others occasional visitors and still others vagrants. Notable for its commercial value is the *cagarra*, a native but not resident bird, which arrives in these seas in spring and leaves in autumn after each pair has laid a single egg in the crevices of the sea cliffs, chiefly on the Desertas and in the Savage Islands (*Selvagens*) group.

after: In the locality (*sítio*) of Fonte (‘spring’), in the parish (*freguesia*) of Monte (‘hill’), lies the so-called Largo da Fonte, a spot with a roofed public fountain containing a small image of Our Lady of the Mount (*Nossa Senhora do Monte*). before: He was born in the parish (*freguesia*) of Santa Maria Maior in this city in the last years of the 17th century, the son of José da Silva Pimenta and Josefa Maria Teixeira, and died in Lisbon on 17 August 1754.
