before: On these levadas, the illustrious commentator of the *Saudades da Terra* gives us some very interesting information, which we shall transcribe: ‘In that period (the beginning of the 16th century), the principal general or common levadas of the island of Madeira, the arteries through which, from then until now, although the institution has since become distorted, the lifeblood of its agriculture flows abundantly, the precious filter of its prosperity and constant renewal. As early as 1515 the levada of Sancta Luzia existed, in the suburbs north of Funchal; by a royal decree of that year (Arch. da Cam. do Funchal, vol. I, fol. 116 v.) King Manuel I ordered that it should not be altered in future. By another, of 26 September 1562 (ib. idem, old register, fol. 135), Queen Catharina, regent in the name of King Sebastian, decreed that the levadas of the Ribeira dos Soccorridos, the Piornaes and the Castellejo, west of Funchal, should be cleared and cleaned in due season at the expense of the *heréus* and landlords, the cost being advanced by the treasury of the customs house (*alfândega*) up to the sum of 120,000 réis; and by another, of 19 October of the same year (book II of the register of the Crown Revenue Office (*Provedoria*), fol. 185), she extended a similar provision to all the other levadas, “bisto se perderem muytas canas daçuquar e deixarem de se prantar outras por se nom tirarem e limparem as levadas em tempo” (since many sugar canes were being lost and others were not being planted because the levadas were not cleared and cleaned in time), and entrusted the donataries with their superintendence, both for that purpose and to “tirar novas levadas ou muda-las, destribuir” (open new levadas or alter them, distribute) the waters at a set price, “de preferência as pessoas que tevessem canaviaes ou engenhos” (preferably to persons who had cane fields or mills), and to take “conhecimento das demamdas sobre esso, decidimdoas, e dando apellaçom e agravo” (cognisance of suits concerning this, deciding them and granting appeal and redress). And, finally, Cardinal Henrique, regent in the name of the same King Sebastian, had three royal decrees issued in 1563: one, so that, under the superintendence of the senior councillor (*vereador*) of the Council of Funchal, the residents along the streams should regularly clean and reinforce them; another, so that the earlier provisions for the annual cleaning of the levadas should be carried out; and another, so that in the distribution of the waters the cane fields should take precedence, their price being fixed in each captaincy by the respective captain-donatary together with “hua pesoa honrrada, conforme a quantidade e o proveito que fezesem” (an honourable person, according to the quantity and the benefit they yielded).

before: Tristão Vaz is the well-known and intrepid companion of João Gonçalves Zarco in the discovery of this archipelago. We share the opinion of the distinguished annotator of the *Saudades* when he states that the surname Teixeira attached to the name of Tristão Vaz was an addition made by the chroniclers. This was certainly because the navigator’s descendants used that surname, which came from Branca Teixeira, Tristão Vaz’s wife. The letter of grant (*carta de doação*) of the captaincy of Machico, dated 1440, says only Tristão, and that is also what he is called by Gomes Eanes de Zurara, the earliest chronicler to deal with our archipelago, who wrote his chronicle around 1453. João de Barros, in the mid-16th century, and Damião de Góis, at roughly the same period – that is, a century after the death of the illustrious discoverer – name him, the former Tristão Vaz and the latter Tristão Vaz Teixeira; this is the first occasion on which the surname Teixeira appears.

before: It is worth transcribing one of the notes to Frutuoso’s work on this subject: ‘Besides António Cordeiro and José Soares da Silva, Damião de Góis and António Galvão also gave the first captain-donatary of Machico the name Tristão Vaz Teixeira. We consider this a manifest error, arising from the same causes pointed out with reference to those first two writers. All four came after the adoption of the maternal surname Teixeira by the descendants of Tristão Vaz, which is spoken of in the *Saudades*, and they confused him with those descendants. For that Tristão Vaz did not take the surname Teixeira, nor was he known by it, is proved by: 1. the letter of grant of the captaincy of Machico, which does not mention that surname; 2. the *Chronica de Guiné* by Gomes Eanes de Zurara, the only writer contemporary with Tristão Vaz, who calls him there only Tristão and Tristão da Ilha; 3. his will, cited by Frutuoso, in which the surname Teixeira likewise does not appear; and 4., finally, the customs of lineage, which would run counter to a husband adopting the surname of his wife’s family.

before: ‘But suppose all these reasons were ineffective; suppose the word of Góis, Galvão, Cordeiro and Soares da Silva prevailed over that of Frutuoso, over the testimony of Zurara, over the authentic proof furnished by the letter of grant, and over the ideas and customs of the age; suppose the first donatary of Machico were called Tristão Vaz Teixeira: for that very reason the heading in the *Cancioneiro de Resende*, “Tristão Teixeira, captain of Machico”, would not refer to him. before: We must nevertheless recall here, as we have noted elsewhere, that in the old chronicles and the old Madeiran genealogies the name of João Gonçalves Zargo is always surrounded by an aura of greater prestige and higher regard than that of Tristão Vaz. This leads us to believe that the first discoverer, through his personal qualities, his social position or perhaps distinguished services rendered earlier, had won the rights of precedence and superiority that placed him above his companion in the discovery. Dr Gaspar Frutuoso writes: ‘The deed held by the heirs of João Gonçalves says that he was the principal in this feat (the discovery), naming Tristão Vaz as Tristão da Ilha, as the King and the Prince named him in their warrants and grants, as a less principal person, and not of such age or quality as João Gonçalves.’ And elsewhere the historian of the Islands says further, referring to the first colonisation: ‘he sent two captains with João Gonçalves, namely Bartolomeu Perestrelo, who was to remain on Porto Santo, and Tristão, knight of the Prince’s household, both of whom came under the banner of the said João Gonçalves Zargo (although there is no lack of many who say otherwise)...’

before: Porto Moniz, like all the localities in the north of the island, belonged to the town and Municipality of Machico. When the Municipality and town of São Vicente was created in 1743, it became an integral part of the new municipality. In 1817 the engineer and inspector of public works Paulo Dias de Almeida impressed upon the government in Lisbon the need to create the Municipality of Porto Moniz. In a dispatch to the higher authorities dated 10 April 1825, the governor and captain-general Dom Manuel de Portugal e Castro gave a favourable report on the petition the people had made to that end, which merely answered long-standing aspirations already voiced on other occasions. According to the request then made, the new municipality would comprise the parishes of Seixal, Ribeira da Janela, Porto Moniz and Ponta do Pargo. Its boundaries would be the stream of João Delgado, from the sea up to the heights of the Paul da Serra, in the parish of Seixal, and the stream of Marinheiros up to the uplands of Fonte do Bispo, in the parish of Ponta do Pargo.

before: The decrees of 7 November 1849 and 10 December 1867, which abolished the municipality of Porto do Moniz, incorporated the parishes of Porto do Moniz, Seixal and Ribeira da Janela into the municipality of São Vicente, and that of Ponta do Pargo into the municipality of Calheta. On this last point we believe that the physician exaggerates, for the amount of dew deposited on objects overnight is truly noticeable only in the island’s upper region, and especially in the inland valleys. As for the other phenomena, without claiming to deny them, we attribute them to lack of ventilation or sunlight in the rooms or dwellings where they were noted. before: The mean temperature at Poiso (1,400 m) was 13.4° in the months of July to November 1904, and at Areeiro (1,700 m) 12.2° in the months of June to October 1895. Mr Guilherme Teles de Meneses, to whom these meteorological observations are owed, saw the thermometer at Areeiro register 2 degrees below zero in November 1895, and we read in *Excursões na Madeira*, by the late Father Pontes, that when the temperature in Funchal is 14 degrees centigrade, the thermometer on the Paul da Serra sometimes stands at zero or below.

before: This is the longest and fullest watercourse in Madeira. It rises on the Paul da Serra and, crossing the parish (*freguesia*) that bears the same name, flows into the ocean there. The well-known Rabaçal levadas (irrigation channels) draw much of their water from the springs of this stream, captured at its sources.

before: *Eucalyptus globulus*, a native of Australia, is the only species of the genus *Eucalyptus* commonly found in Madeira, where it grows at Monte, at Choupana and in various other places on the island. It reaches great size and grows very rapidly. It should not, however, be planted near springs, because its roots draw up a great quantity of water.

before: Two species are known by this name in Madeira: *Visnea mocanera*, of the family Ternstroemiaceae, and *Pittosporum coriaceum*, of the family Pittosporaceae. The first is a shrub or small tree, with leaves that are hairy while young, chiefly on the margins and the midrib of the underside; the second is always a tree, with leaves devoid of hairs at every age. The latter species is almost extinct in the mountains of Madeira, but it is cultivated on the *quintas* of Monte and Camacha; the former can be found on the rocks between Ribeira da Janela and Ribeira do Inferno, though it is quite rare. The wood of *Visnea mocanera* is dull in colour, sometimes tending slightly towards red, and very heavy and hard; that of *Pittosporum coriaceum* is light and yellowish or greyish.

The wood of *Visnea mocanera* is dull in colour, sometimes tending slightly towards red, and very heavy and hard; that of *Pittosporum coriaceum* is light and yellowish or greyish.

before: His works are the following: *O Livro d'um Democrata* (Coimbra, 1848); *Esboço critico-literario* (Funchal, 1866); *Curso Elementar de Recitação* (Funchal, 1869); and *Romanceiro do Archipelago da Madeira* (Funchal, 1880). He also published the part of Gaspar Frutuoso’s manuscript entitled *Saudades da Terra* that concerns the Madeira archipelago, enriching it with many notes intended to shed light on certain points of our history. These notes, the fruit of most patient study and research, are in our view Dr Azevedo’s most valuable work.

These notes, the fruit of most patient study and research, are in our view Dr Azevedo’s most valuable work.

before: Dr Álvaro de Azevedo’s name is inseparably linked with the history of Madeira through the notable and never sufficiently praised service he rendered this archipelago by publishing *Saudades da Terra*, and especially through the learned and most valuable annotations with which he enriched Gaspar Frutuoso’s text (see Saudades da Terra). The *Romanceiro do Archipelago da Madeira* (see that entry), the articles already mentioned, which fill some 100 pages of the great *Diccionario Universal Português Ilustrado*, the comedy of Madeiran manners *A familia do Demerarista* and the *Almanach para a Ilha da Madeira* for the years 1867 and 1868 are further powerful reasons that fully justify this land’s gratitude to the memory of the distinguished lawyer and teacher. Apart from his important and valuable works on Madeira, there is nothing here to recall his cherished memory to future generations. It would be only just for his worthy name to be perpetuated at least on a street corner, since it is not easy, and perhaps not possible, to pay him a more fitting and deserved tribute and homage.

before: Around 1460 João de Braga, a rich nobleman, came from the Kingdom (*reino*, i.e. mainland Portugal) to this island of Madeira, and was given lands as a *sesmaria* (royal land grant to settlers on condition of cultivation) in the parish of Santo António, at the locality (*sítio*) called Laranjal. He was the father of the celebrated Marcos de Braga, whom the old Madeiran chronicles praise highly for his deeds of bravery and courage. João de Braga married a daughter of Nuno Gonçalves, and from this union was born Domingos de Braga, who founded the entail (*morgado*) of Laranjal on the lands his grandfather had obtained as a *sesmaria*.

before: This is a cave (*furna*) close to Pico Ruivo, where people visiting the mountain usually spend the night. It takes about 20 minutes to walk from the cave to the summit of the peak.

before: A locality (*sítio*) incorporated into the inhabited locality of Florenças, in the parish (*freguesia*) of Arco da Calheta. It is also stated that João Portes Homem built a chapel dedicated to Santa Maria Madalena (St Mary Magdalene) in this locality in 1684.

before: In the parish (*freguesia*) of São Roque, at the locality (*sítio*) known as Alegria, lies the *quinta* (country estate) of the same name, with a house and a chapel dedicated to Nossa Senhora da Alegria (Our Lady of Joy), both belonging to the family of the Counts of Torre Bela. The chapel was founded in 1609 by Francisco de Abreu. A feast is held there every year and draws large numbers of people from the surrounding area.

before: There is a chapel of this name in the parish (*freguesia*) of Arco da Calheta, which was the seat of an entailed estate (*morgadio*) founded by the two sisters Antónia de Cristo and Leonarda do Horto in favour of their nephew Francisco Friz de Barros Maciel. It was he who built the chapel, around the third or last quarter of the 17th century. In 1694 he had the mortal remains of his uncle, Father Inácio Barbosa da Silva, moved there; he was the brother of the founders of the entail and had been one of the owners of the property on which the chapel stood. Having fallen into great ruin, the chapel was rebuilt in 1830 by António João Barbosa de Matos e Câmara, a descendant of the founders.

before: There is a chapel of the same name in the parish of Câmara de Lobos, founded in 1757 by Maria do Rosário Henriques, widow of Pedro Bernardes Cardeiro. Concerning her, or another owner of this chapel, Dr Álvaro de Azevedo gives the following curious information: ‘It is a tradition among the fishermen of Câmara de Lobos that at the beginning of this century the lady of the entail (*morgada*) of Nazaré, armed with a small sword, would take up her position on the height where the chapel stands; she would hail the fishing boats as they came into the landing place; and, by privilege or abuse, she would take from them whatever fish she wanted and pay for it as she saw fit.’

Shortly afterwards he sailed for Brazil, where his uncle Dom Manuel Joaquim Gonçalves de Andrade was a bishop and where his brother, Councillor (conselheiro, honorary title of the royal council) Francisco Justino Gonçalves de Andrade, was a distinguished professor at the University of São Paulo. He settled in Vassouras and was carrying out his ministry there when, on the advice of Dr Francisco Justino, he enrolled in the Faculty of Law of the University of São Paulo and took his doctorate there. Shortly afterwards he sat a competitive examination for one of its chairs and was appointed professor, a post he held until 1891, when he retired.

before: A locality (*sítio*) in the interior of the island, 15 kilometres from Funchal, much visited by Portuguese and foreigners alike for the enchanting landscapes it offers. It was once far more wooded than it is today, but the land nearby still has some woods, made up chiefly of laurels and heather. *Ranunculus grandifolius*, *Geranium anemonefolium*, *Carex peregrina*, *Carex elata* and *Orchis foliosa* are found at Ribeiro Frio, and salep can be extracted from the tubers of the last of these plants.

before: Following the Levada do Juncal, one soon reaches a belvedere (*mirante*) with astonishing views over the Ribeira da Metade. Further on there are some tunnels, though they are difficult to reach, because the levada wall (*mainel*) of the levada (irrigation channel) is narrow and at times unstable. The extremely rare *Goodyera macrophylla* and *Musschia Wollastoni* are found near the tunnel that follows the Quebrada da Azeda.

before: The locality of Ribeiro Frio is crossed by the Levada da Serra, and on the edge of the footpath that runs beside it, at the place called Balcão or Balcões, there is an astonishing panorama over the Ribeira da Metade and other parts of the interior, with the basalt column of Homem-Em-Pé (see that entry) visible in the distance. There is a mountain shelter there for travellers, which is also used by the levada’s staff. Since April 1932 the locality has had a small establishment called the Casa de Chá, offering a good service of tea, food and drink. The locality of Ribeiro Frio lies about 4 kilometres from the Casa do Poiso and 15 from the city of Funchal. The brook that crosses this locality, and from which the locality took its name, provides the source that feeds the Levada do Furado.

before: João de Sant’Ana e Vasconcelos was appointed civil governor of this district and took up office in mid-January 1862. On the very day he took office, the 1st Viscount of Nogueiras, the new governor’s brother-in-law, gave a splendid ball in his honour, attended by the most distinguished people of Funchal. When the party was at its liveliest and merriest, word was brought to the Viscount of Nogueiras that a warship had just anchored in our harbour carrying a new governor for Madeira, and that Governor Sant’Ana e Vasconcelos was therefore dismissed. Care was prudently and discreetly taken to hide the news of the new governor’s arrival from the guests – the new governor was Januário Correia de Almeida – and the party continued to the end with the same enthusiasm and gaiety. The political opponents of Governor Sant’Ana, who was then municipal administrator (administrador do concelho, the government’s representative) of the municipality (*concelho*) of Porto Santo, made mocking comments on the affair, one newspaper saying that he had been so absorbed in the administration of the district that he had not even had time to sleep while it lasted, since he was governor for only a few hours.

before: The annotator of *Saudades da Terra* mentions this priest as one of the most distinguished preachers of this diocese in the 19th century. He was born in Funchal in 1823 and died in Lisbon on 31 July 1859. Illness and an early death prevented him from revealing the full power of his talent and his remarkable gift for preaching. Even so, in his day he was regarded as a brilliant ornament of the pulpit, not only in Madeira but throughout the country. He held the honours of a canon and was curate of the Cathedral of this city, Funchal Cathedral (*Sé*). He died in Lisbon, where he had gone in search of better health, a victim of pulmonary tuberculosis.

before: An inhabited locality (*sítio*) in the parish (*freguesia*) of Arco da Calheta, home to the old chapel of Nossa Senhora do Loreto (Our Lady of Loreto). It is the focus of a well-attended pilgrimage, drawing many people from several distant parishes and above all from the surrounding parishes. Although small, the chapel has a certain architectural distinction, and it is a pity that an ill-suited porch should spoil the harmony of the whole. It dates from the first years of the 16th century and was founded by Pedro Gonçalves da Câmara, grandson of João Gonçalves Zarco, the first captain-donatary (*capitão-donatário*) of Funchal. A large manor house once adjoined it, for the founder made this the seat of the important entailed estate (*morgadio*) that he established. Others attribute the founding of the chapel and the entailed estate to Dona Joana de Eça, widow of the said Pedro Gonçalves da Câmara, chief lady of the bedchamber to Queen Catherine and patron of the Convento da Esperança (Convent of Our Lady of Hope), Lisbon, where she was buried. The nuns of this convent owned a great deal of land in the parish of Arco da Calheta, bequeathed to them by Dona Joana de Eça. In the first quarter of the 20th century the tomb of the patron, Dona Joana de Eça, was found in the ruins of the church of the Convento da Esperança.

before: The Council of Trent, held in the city from which it took its name, ordered that every diocese should create an establishment for religious instruction and education, intended for the ecclesiastical training of those who wished to become priests, and especially of those who would devote themselves to parish life. In fulfilment of that decree, King Sebastian created the Seminary of Funchal by royal letter (*carta régia*) of 20 September 1566. The foundation took effect only later, in a year we cannot state precisely, but which fell within the period from 1573 to 1586. The establishment of this house of education is owed to the efforts of Bishop Dom Jerónimo Barreto, and he is rightly regarded as the founder of the Seminary of Funchal.
after: The Council of Trent, held in the city from which it took its name, ordered that every diocese should create an establishment for religious instruction and education, intended for the ecclesiastical training of those who wished to become priests, and especially of those who would devote themselves to parish life. The foundation took effect only later, in a year we cannot state precisely, but which fell within the period from 1573 to 1586. The establishment of this house of education is owed to the efforts of Bishop Dom Jerónimo Barreto, and he is rightly regarded as the founder of the Funchal Seminary.

before: It was first housed in a building on Rua Direita, next to the dwelling of the prelate, who then had his residence there. At the end of the 16th century Bishop Dom Luís de Figueiredo e Lemos built the old bishop's palace, a considerable part of which still survives, together with the adjoining chapel, now deconsecrated. The Seminary moved to a building next to this palace and to its outbuildings at the end of that century or the beginning of the next.
after: It was first housed in a building on Rua Direita (‘straight street’), next to the dwelling of the prelate, who then had his residence there. At the end of the 16th century Bishop Dom Luís de Figueiredo e Lemos built the old bishop's palace (*Paço Episcopal*), a considerable part of which still survives, together with the adjoining chapel, now deconsecrated. The Seminary moved to a building next to this palace and to its outbuildings at the end of that century or the beginning of the next.

before: The construction of the new residence of the prelates, the one that can still be seen today in the former Rua do Bispo, led to the Seminary's move to the house on Rua do Mosteiro Novo. This had been intended for a convent of nuns (volume III, page 398), but was never put to the use for which it had been built. The earthquake of 1748 left this building so badly damaged that it had to be abandoned, and the establishment moved into another house or houses, whose location we do not know, remaining there until the year 1788.
after: The construction of the new residence of the prelates, the one that can still be seen today in the former Rua do Bispo, led to the Seminary's move to the house on Rua do Mosteiro Novo (the New Convent, *Mosteiro Novo*). The earthquake of 1748 left this building so badly damaged that it had to be abandoned, and the establishment moved into another house or houses, whose location we do not know, remaining there until the year 1788.

before: As to the places the *leste* strikes on reaching Madeira and the direction it takes afterwards, there are many obscure points that it would be in the interest of science to clarify. This can only be achieved, however, when meteorological stations are set up in the mountains and at the eastern tip of the island, and placed under the direction of capable men who are diligent in carrying out their duties. At the foot of the Pico de Teide, on Tenerife, there has been a meteorological observatory since 1908 which has rendered science many services, whereas here not a single step is taken to make proper use of a station built in 1895 near the Pico do Areeiro, which was never provided with the staff and instruments needed for observations!

before: During the *leste* that struck Funchal from 21 to 27 August 1919, the wind was at first not felt beyond Ponta da Oliveira. When a violent fire broke out in the pine woods of Monte and São Roque, we observed that the smoke, judging by the direction it took, seemed to be driven by a NE wind. That *leste* was especially noteworthy for its duration and for the enormous damage it did to crops. It should also be noted that it was while it lasted that the highest shade temperature ever observed in Funchal since meteorological observations began here was recorded. Relative humidity fell to 28 per cent at 3 p.m. on 23 August, while at the same moment the thermometer in the sun read 57°. This temperature cannot be regarded as the maximum, since, as we said when discussing the climate, the sun’s greatest strength occurs not at that hour but much earlier. See Climate (1-273).

before: The foreigners contributed considerably, though to their own profit, to the prosperity this island attained from the end of the 15th century to the middle of the following one. They engaged in various branches of trade, set up many sugar mills, and a good part of the export of that product to foreign countries passed through their hands. Gaspar Frutuoso asserts, though perhaps with some exaggeration, that João Esmeraldo produced twenty thousand *arrobas* of sugar a year on his properties at the Lombada. Many of them were at once farmers, manufacturers and merchants. By the middle of the 15th century there were already many foreigners on this island, living on good terms with the natives, most of them engaged in the sugar trade. At first the remarkable fertility of the soil and the rewarding price of the cane fields fully satisfied the tenant farmer (*colono*, under the *colonia* contract), the landlord and the merchant. Later, however, came the fall in prices, brought about by various causes, which roused the distrust and hostility of the producers of the raw material for sugar against the merchants, especially the foreign ones. The Funchal Council even took repressive measures against them, going so far as to order their expulsion from this island.

before: We have no knowledge of benefactions by foreigners on this island in times more remote from our own. In the first half of the 19th century, we know of the notable services rendered by the foreigners John March and Roberto Page, to whom we refer specifically elsewhere in this work. Everyone knows that in recent times some foreigners have amassed large fortunes in Madeira, running into millions. before: It became very well known, and has been much visited, since the time when Emperor Charles I lived there for some months and ended his days there on 1 April 1922. A few years ago its present owner, Luís da Rocha Machado, built in the house a beautiful chapel dedicated to the Sacred Heart of Jesus and consecrated to the memory of the ill-fated and much-missed emperor. He had arrived in Madeira with his wife, Empress Zita, aboard the British cruiser *Cardiff* on 10 November 1921, and took up residence at the ‘Vila Vitória’, an annexe of Reid’s Hotels. When the princes, the imperial couple’s children, arrived in Funchal on 2 February 1922, the whole imperial family moved to the Quinta do Monte on the 18th of the same month. There, as already stated, the unfortunate emperor died on 1 April of that year. On the 5th he was buried in a side chapel of the Parish Church of Monte, where his remains still lie. The emperor’s death and funeral stirred the deepest feelings of grief throughout the population of Funchal, which took on the character of true national mourning. Empress Zita left Madeira with her children on 19 May 1922.

before: He was the son of Diogo Afonso de Aguiar and of Dona Isabel Gonçalves da Câmara, third daughter of Zarco. before: An inhabited locality (*sítio*) in the parish (*freguesia*) of Santo António, Funchal. It has an old manor house with an adjoining chapel, which were the seat of the entailed estate (*morgadio*) of the Leme family, founded by Pedro de Leme before 1550. Its last direct representative was Francisco Aurélio da Câmara, who died without issue, so the administration of this entailed house (*casa vinculada*) passed to his nephew João de Carvalhal Esmeraldo, 1st Count of Carvalhal. The chapel, dedicated to the martyr St Philip, was built in 1536 by António de Leme and rebuilt in 1654 by Inácio da Câmara Leme. It was reconstructed once more in 1752, together with the adjoining manor house, because of the state of great ruin in which the earthquake of 1748 had left it. Having been deconsecrated for some years, it was restored to worship in 1942.

before: At the eastern end of Funchal lies the parish (*freguesia*) of São Gonçalo, one of the five suburban parishes of this municipality (*concelho*). It borders the parish of Santa Maria Maior to the west and that of Caniço to the east. Squeezed between these two parishes, it stretches from the edge of the ocean to the summits of the hills that enclose part of Funchal. The land that makes up this parish originally belonged to the parish of Santa Maria Maior. When that parish moved its seat to the church that later served as the Cathedral, the same land was incorporated into it as well, and it became part of the parish of Santa Maria Maior once again when Funchal was divided into two parishes, around 1558.

before: We have already given a brief account of the chapel of Nossa Senhora das Neves, where the seat of the parish was established, on page 462 of volume II. It had its own chaplain, who performed some parochial duties, and it was later raised to the status of a curacy (*curato*) by a royal decree (*alvará*) of 7 March 1566, the curate receiving an annual salary of 12,000 *réis* (old Portuguese money of account; 1$000 = 1,000 réis, 1:000$000 = one conto = 1,000,000 réis) in cash and one *moio* (dry measure of grain, 60 *alqueires*) of wheat. The General Index of the Register of the former Crown Revenue Office (*Provedoria*), which we have cited so often, mentions the following documents: a royal letter (*carta régia*) of 16 September 1574, awarding the curate 20,000 *réis* a year because the curacy had more than 100 households (*fogos*, literally ‘hearths’); a royal decree of 9 June 1581, setting this salary at 25,000 *réis*; a royal decree of 3 February 1589, adding thirty *alqueires* of wheat and a quarter of wine to the same salary; and a royal decree of 14 December 1592, fixing the corresponding stipend (*côngrua*) at 16,000 *réis* in cash, one *moio* of wheat and one *pipa* (wine cask and measure, c. 400–500 litres) of wine. None of these documents speaks of a parish or a vicarage; they refer instead to a beneficed curate (*beneficiado curado*), albeit one with the duties of a parish priest. The *Saudades da Terra* state that the parish was created by the royal decree of 12 March 1574, yet the decree cited above, of 16 September 1574, which is later than that one, still refers expressly to a beneficed curate. From our examination and comparison of many documents concerning the creation of various ecclesiastical posts, we can state that the decrees cited in the General Index of the Crown Revenue Office are more reliable in their dates than those cited by the illustrious annotator of Gaspar Frutuoso. What seems most probable to us is that the beneficed curate created by the decree of 7 March 1566 corresponds to the creation of the parish, and that at that time the duties belonging to certain posts were confused with one another.

before: The first settlement of this parish and the first farming in its area must, like those of the other parishes of this municipality (*concelho*), date from the colonisation and clearing of land that João Gonçalves Zargo began in Funchal immediately after the discovery and the fire that swept through the dense woods which no doubt covered the whole length of the valley. Of one early settler, the most distinguished of Zargo’s companions in the work of discovery, we know that he held extensive *sesmaria* (royal land grant to settlers on condition of cultivation) lands in this parish. They stretched from the right bank of the stream to which he gave his name as far as the Ribeira de João Gomes, and were bounded to the north by the ridges of the uplands. This was Gonçalo Aires, whom we have already discussed at some length on page 21 of volume II of this work. Within the bounds of this parish lie the magnificent *quinta* (country estate) of Palheiro (volume III, page 43) and the lazaretto of Gonçalo Aires, at the mouth of the stream of the same name (volume II, page 223 ff.). The principal localities are: Forca, Louros, Murteiras, São João de Latrão, Salões, Fonte, Boa Nova, Lombo da Quinta, Ribeira da Quinta, Palheiro do Ferreiro, Algarvio, Bica de Pau, Igreja, Ribeiro Seco, Neves and Cancela. It has 2,987 inhabitants (1921).

before: Below we give a brief account of the heights above sea level at which various points in this archipelago lie. As this work proceeds, we hope to give other altitudes not mentioned here, as the needs of each subject require. Of the altitudes ranging from close to the ocean up to the highest summit in Madeira, Pico Ruivo, we give a note of the principal high points in ascending order. This shows how rugged the ground that makes up the soil of this island is, over an area of less than 800 square kilometres, and the capricious relief that the orographic conditions present across the whole length and breadth of the island.

before: Many years ago, at Ribeiro do Meio, on a slope of the São Jorge valley, at the same spot where lignite occurs, various layers of tuff and clay were found, one of which contained numerous leaves of dicotyledons and ferns. Dr Heer, who studied these leaves, recognised that they belonged to 25 species, among them the til (*Ocotea foetens*, Madeiran laurel), the folhado (*Clethra arborea*, a native tree), the tree heath (*urze molar*), the Madeira blueberry (*uveira*, *Vaccinium padifolium*), the *tintureira* and the myrtle.
after: Many years ago, at Ribeiro do Meio (‘middle brook’), on a slope of the São Jorge valley, at the same spot where lignite occurs, various layers of tuff and clay were found, one of which contained numerous leaves of dicotyledons and ferns. Dr Oswald Heer, who studied these leaves, recognised that they belonged to 25 species, among them the til (*Ocotea foetens*, Madeiran laurel), the folhado (*Clethra arborea*, a native tree), the tree heath (*urze molar*), the Madeira blueberry (*uveira*, *Vaccinium padifolium*), the *tintureira* and the myrtle.

before: A locality (*sítio*) in the town (*vila*) of Porto Santo, where there is a public fountain whose waters were analysed in 1893 at the École Nationale des Mines de Paris. The residue found in one litre of these waters weighed 1.728 g, of which silica accounted for 0.048 g, sodium carbonate, including the alkaline-earth carbonates, for 0.891 g, sodium sulphate for 0.290 g and sodium chloride for 0.490 g. According to the analyst of that school, the mineral water of Porto Santo may be classed among the bicarbonated and sodium-sulphated waters. The analysis revealed very little lime and magnesia, and also showed that almost all the carbonic acid of the bicarbonates is combined with the alkalis.

before: In the article ‘Associado 4 de Setembro de 1862’ (I-97) we gave a brief account of the earliest efforts to establish the principles of mutualism here in Madeira. These principles have borne their valued fruit only very slowly, with the exception of the association just mentioned, which stands as an admirable commemorative pillar (*padrão*) testifying to their beneficial effect. A detailed article on this subject, published in the issue of *Trabalho e União* of 1 September 1917, is well worth reading. See also the pamphlet ‘Mutualismo’ by Dr Álvaro Reis Gomes.

before: At the end of November 1905 a case of suspected disease appeared in the household of Leopoldo Cabral, who lived in Rua dos Ferreiros in this city, affecting a member of his family. The patient and the rest of the family were promptly removed to the lazaretto of ‘Gonçalo Aires’, which had been turned into an isolation hospital. Other people were also taken there. To stop the disease from spreading, complete isolation was certainly necessary, but it seems to have been applied with excessive rigour, if indeed there can be excess in adopting measures of this kind. From the outset the most improbable and incredible rumours began to spread among the population, arising largely from the strict isolation maintained at the lazaretto and the lack of news of the people held there. Popular imagination, aided by factional politics and an unscrupulous press, gave free rein to the most deplorable frenzy, conjuring up every sort of crime within the lazaretto, from the cruellest ill-treatment to outright murder! These rumours spread so widely, and these fanciful inventions grew so large in the public mind, that before long the great majority of the people of this island firmly believed that the isolation hospital had become a veritable public butcher’s shop (*açougue*) for human beings, far outdoing the bands of brigands that infested the passes of the Sierra Morena, Calabria and the Black Forest, of which certain more than doubtful narratives tell us with such horror.

before: On 7 January 1906, at about 11 in the morning, an enormous mass of townspeople, followed by some men of the 27th Infantry Regiment (*regimento de infantaria n.° 27*), set off for the lazaretto in a plainly hostile mood, ready to commit the worst excesses. Through inexcusable lack of foresight the entrances to the lazaretto had been left without any defence, so the rioting mob easily broke into the enclosure and committed the greatest and most deplorable acts of vandalism. Everything there was completely destroyed: furniture, kitchen equipment, pharmacy, surgical instruments, linen, machines, provisions etc. Nothing escaped the insane fury of the attackers. The buildings themselves suffered serious damage: every windowpane was broken, the doors were destroyed and even the floors bear clear traces of the rioters’ rage.

before: The clinical director of the ‘Gonçalo Aires’ isolation hospital was Dr António Balbino do Rego, who held the post of director of the Bacteriology and Hygiene Post in this city. It was against him that the wrath of the populace was chiefly roused, for they regarded him as the author of, or the person chiefly responsible for, the alleged crimes committed at the lazaretto. The hatred aroused here against Dr Balbino do Rego (see that entry) is truly incredible, given that it had no serious basis, and even today his name is cursed as though he had been some great scourge that had ravaged this island.

before: In the article on Canon Jerónimo Dias Leite we have already referred to the account of the discovery of this archipelago attributed to Gonçalo Aires. On this subject the *Saudades da Terra* says: ‘He (the sixth captain-donatary (*capitão-donatário*) of Funchal) kept in his study the Discovery of the Island of Madeira, the most truthful yet found, which they say was written by Gonçalo Aires Ferreira, who went to discover that same island with the first Captain, João Gonçalves Zargo; and since this Discovery belonged to the Captains of the same island, they kept it in their studies as a thing inherited from descendant to descendant. And when information about this island of Madeira was requested, on my behalf, from the Reverend Canon of the Cathedral of Funchal, Jerónimo Dias Leite, he, having seen it in the possession of the said Captain João Gonçalves da Câmara, sent to ask him for it in Lisbon, where he then was; and the Captain had it copied by his chamberlain Lucas de Sá, and sent it to him written on three sheets of paper in the said chamberlain’s hand; and by his letter (because the discovery makes no mention of this) he sent word that Gonçalo Aires Ferreira, who had been one of the servants whom Zargo, the first Captain, took there with him, wrote down all that he saw with his own eyes, and, as he was neither a learned nor a lettered man, set it down in a rough style, with nothing else added’.

before: The poetic and moving legend of Machim, with its tragic twists, has been celebrated in prose and verse by Portuguese and foreign writers alike, stirring the morbid sensibility of those who believe such tales of love or are easily swayed by them. After the exhaustive work of Dr Álvaro Rodrigues de Azevedo, who subjected the case of Machim to all the rigour of historical criticism, no one may legitimately accept that this charming but fantastic invention could be true. From 1563, when António Galvão first set this legend in circulation in his *Tratado dos Descobrimentos*, down to some writers of our own day, it has been told with many variations. It takes its most interesting and attractive form, however, in the third *Epanaphora* of Francisco Manuel de Melo, above all for the beauty of its language and the vividness of its narrative. The best-known version, nevertheless, is that of Gaspar Frutuoso, which does not differ in essentials from that of Francisco de Melo. We shall transcribe the ingenuous account of the historian of the islands, so as not to commit the fault of omitting from these pages the story of the famous legend of Roberto Machim and Ana de Arfet.

before: When day broke and those who had stayed ashore could no longer see the ship, they were plunged into deep sorrow, at once giving themselves up for lost and despairing of ever being able to leave that place. Machim’s lady, seeing herself left there, was struck dumb and never spoke again, and three days later she died. Machim, for the great love he bore her, was bursting with grief; and, seeing himself banished from his homeland and his love dead, she who had been the whole comfort of his banishment, he no longer felt any longing for his country; he felt only an unbearable longing for his Anna de Harfet, whom he had so swiftly seen turned to earth before his eyes. With this grief that remained to him, and with ardent sighs and tears, he mourned her there; and in the place where they had taken shelter he had her buried, and set a wooden cross at the head of her grave, and a board (*mesa*) or slab of stone with his crucifix upon it, and at the foot of the crucifix he placed an inscription in Latin, in which he told the whole of his most sorrowful fate and all that had befallen him on that most unfortunate voyage, asking that, if Christians should ever live there, they build a church in that place with the dedication of Christ. This done, he asked his companions to take the clothing they had and such birds as they might catch, and to go wherever fortune might guide them, since he had not had the fortune to keep his beloved alive; and he said that he wished to stay there and die where he had killed Anna de Harfet, keeping company with her dead body with his longing alone, since she had kept him company while she lived. His companions, moved to pity, all told him that they would not leave him, and that they would die and remain there with him. Machim, who thanked them warmly for that love, and would have thanked them more for the cruelty of leaving him alone, lasted no more than five days, out of grief and sorrow for his beloved. His companions, who felt no small sorrow at the loss of his company, buried him beside his Anna de Harfet and placed another cross at his head; and, leaving the crucifix just as Machim had placed it, and leaving these two graves in that deserted land as a most sorrowful spectacle of longing and love, they boarded the ship’s boat in which they had come from the ship (although others would have it that they made it from the trunk of the tree, which was thick and could hold many people) and, reaching the coast of Barbary, were taken captive there by the Moors and carried off to Morocco, where the other companions from the ship were also already held captive, so joyless and unfortunate. Such are the brief, fleeting and costly pleasures of the world’s great and long-cherished hopes, whose custom, condition and nature always was and always will be to pay out very little or nothing to those who ask much.’ Dr Rodrigues de Azevedo, in some of his annotations to *Saudades da Terra* and in a lengthy article in the *Diccionario Universal Portuguez Illustrado*, deals with this subject at the greatest length, not only to show the utter falsity of the claims of those who believed they saw historical truth in the legend, but also to vindicate for the Portuguese the priority in the discovery of this archipelago. The assertions of the British writer Richard Henry Major in his monumental work on Henry the Navigator also led the annotator of the *Saudades* to undertake this study, since the recognised authority of the English scholar could lead readers of his notable book on our first maritime discoveries into serious errors. Anyone wishing to gain a deeper knowledge of this subject should turn above all to Dr Azevedo’s interesting and erudite dissertation included in note V of the *Saudades* (pp. 340–429) and in the *Diccionario Universal Illustrado Portuguez* (volume for the letter M, p. 190), and may also consult the *Historia de Portugal* (vol. II, pp. 230 ff.) by Pinheiro Chagas, which contains laudatory references to the annotator of the *Saudades*, ‘a Madeiran scholar and one of the most erudite writers that Portugal possesses’.

Machim, who thanked them warmly for that love, and would have thanked them more for the cruelty of leaving him alone, lasted no more than five days, out of grief and sorrow for his beloved. His companions, who felt no small sorrow at the loss of his company, buried him beside his Anna de Harfet and placed another cross at his head; and, leaving the crucifix just as Machim had placed it, and leaving these two graves in that deserted land as a most sorrowful spectacle of longing and love, they boarded the ship’s boat in which they had come from the ship (although others would have it that they made it from the trunk of the tree, which was thick and could hold many people) and, reaching the coast of Barbary, were taken captive there by the Moors and carried off to Morocco, where the other companions from the ship were also already held captive, so joyless and unfortunate. Such are the brief, fleeting and costly pleasures of the world’s great and long-cherished hopes, whose custom, condition and nature always was and always will be to pay out very little or nothing to those who ask much.’ Dr Rodrigues de Azevedo, in some of his annotations to ‘Longing for the Homeland’ (*Saudades da Terra*) and in a lengthy article in the *Diccionario Universal Portuguez Illustrado*, deals with this subject at the greatest length, not only to show the utter falsity of the claims of those who believed they saw historical truth in the legend, but also to vindicate for the Portuguese the priority in the discovery of this archipelago. The assertions of the British writer Richard Henry Major in his monumental work on Henry the Navigator also led the annotator of ‘Longing for the Homeland’ to undertake this study, since the recognised authority of the English scholar could lead readers of his notable book on our first maritime discoveries into serious errors. Anyone wishing to gain a deeper knowledge of this subject should turn above all to Dr Azevedo’s interesting and erudite dissertation included in note V of ‘Longing for the Homeland’ (pp. 340–429) and in the *Diccionario Universal Illustrado Portuguez* (volume for the letter M, p. 190), and may also consult the *Historia de Portugal* (vol. II, pp. 230 ff.) by Pinheiro Chagas, which contains laudatory references to the annotator of ‘Longing for the Homeland’, ‘a Madeiran scholar and one of the most erudite writers that Portugal possesses’.

before: Four months after Luís Mousinho’s arrival on this island, that is, around the middle of December 1834, the new charitable establishment began to operate. It was provisionally housed in some of the outbuildings of the Palácio de São Lourenço (St Lawrence Palace), under the direct supervision and the solicitous and loving direction of its founders themselves. It came to shelter 120 children and remained in a state of relative prosperity for as long as its founders stayed on this island. It was still thanks to that initial impetus that, by a ministerial order (*portaria*) of 13 January 1836, a house in the Campo da Barca belonging to the National Treasury (*Fazenda Nacional*) was obtained for the asylum to move into. It operated there for some years and ceased to exist at a date we cannot establish with complete accuracy. before: Planned asylum at the Angústias. In 1837 the Municipal Council (*Câmara Municipal*) of Funchal once again resolved to found an asylum to take in the old and infirm who begged in the streets of the city. It informed the central government of this resolution, which the government praised in a ministerial order (*portaria*) of 7 June 1838. To carry out this lofty and humane idea, the councillors lost no time in arranging the construction of a suitable building. The site chosen was the land where the Asilo da Mendicidade e Orfãos now stands, which the first Count of Carvalhal had given for that purpose shortly before his death. Construction work, carried out to the plan and design drawn up by the director of public works, the engineer Vicente de Paula Teixeira, began on 8 August 1837, and the municipality spent approximately thirteen *contos* de réis (*conto*: one million réis) on the building. The building was almost completed, but it was never put to the use for which it had originally been intended. It never opened its doors to inmates, because the councillors who had taken that initiative, or those who succeeded them on the Council, abandoned the idea of creating the asylum, for reasons entirely unknown to us.

before: In his pamphlet *As Selvagens*, Mr Alberto Artur Sarmento gives Selvagem Grande a length of 2.5 kilometres, a width of 2.2 kilometres and an area of some 5 square kilometres, adding that its coasts are steep and hard to approach because of the great number of rocks surrounding it. According to Mr Adolfo César de Noronha, the island’s sea cliffs can reach 100 metres in height, although the interior is more or less flat. The exceptions are the east, where Pico dos Tornozelos rises, and the west, where Pico da Atalaia stands above the sea, its altitude estimated at about 150 metres. To the south there is also a small knoll, that of Inferno, about 115 metres above sea level.

before: Selvagem Grande lies 250 kilometres from Ponta da Agulha on Bugio, one of the three Desertas, 280 from the port of Funchal, and 165 kilometres from Ponta do Hidalgo on Tenerife, so it is closer to the Canary Islands archipelago than to that of Madeira. Like the other two islets of the group, it is uninhabited, and its best anchorages are the cove of Pardelas, to the east, and another to the south, sheltered by the knoll of Inferno. At the locality (*sítio*) called Estancia, to the south-west, is the best landing place, which is why boats head there when they have people to put ashore. At that spot there is a shed and a cave with a wall and a door, where visitors can take shelter, and further inland there is a small hut roofed with zinc sheets, which can also shelter those who wish to spend the night in the central part of the island. Two cisterns have been built on Selvagem Grande, holding water all year round, and there are also three small springs – das Ovelhas, below Pico da Atalaia, the Salgada and das Galinhas – which yield some water for only part of the year. There are traces of some works having been carried out at the Galinhas spring, on the upper part of the island.

before: Shearwaters (*cagarras*) are the chief wealth of the Selvagens. Although some 20 to 22 thousand are caught every year, as the late Father Ernesto Schmitz stated in 1901 in an article published in *Cosmos*, their numbers do not fall, which proves how dense the population is. They must therefore exceed a total of 60,000, because each shearwater lays only one egg, and there must be at least 40,000 for an annual breeding of 20 thousand. The Selvagens, or rather Selvagem Grande, are visited every year, usually in September, by parties of hunters, who bring back many rabbits, shearwaters and salted fish, for which they always find buyers in Funchal. The shearwater lives on all three islands of the group, but the rabbit, which is a small breed like that of Porto Santo, is found only on Selvagem Grande, where it has destroyed many plant species that once grew there. Selvagem Grande also supplies large quantities of limpets, salted or pickled in vinegar (1921).

before: The Selvagens group is surrounded by an extensive barrier of reefs that makes its coasts hard to approach. Landing on Selvagem Pequena, and above all on the Ilhéu de Fora, is much more difficult than on Selvagem Grande. Selvagem Pequena has beaches of rounded pebbles, as in Madeira, and platforms of marine erosion, and between it and the Ilhéu de Fora there are some rocks at the surface of the water and others under the sea. The Palheiros are two rocks near Selvagem Grande, and to the north of the Ilhéu de Fora there are several reefs, two of which are known as the shoal of Sarmento (*baixa do Sarmento*) and the shoal of Noronha (*baixa do Noronha*).

before: The Hospital de Santa Isabel (St Elizabeth of Portugal), which belongs to the Holy House of Mercy (*Santa Casa da Misericórdia*) of Funchal, operated for 244 years in the building now occupied by the offices of the District General Council (*Junta Geral*) of this autonomous district. It began to be known as the Hospital dos Marmeleiros in 1931, when the various hospital services moved to the large new building in the locality (*sítio*) of Marmeleiros, in the parish (*freguesia*) of Nossa Senhora do Monte (Our Lady of the Mount).
after: St Elizabeth’s Hospital (*Hospital de Santa Isabel*), which belongs to the Holy House of Mercy (*Santa Casa da Misericórdia*) of Funchal, operated for 244 years in the building now occupied by the offices of the District General Council (*Junta Geral*) of this autonomous district. It began to be known as Marmeleiros Hospital (*Hospital dos Marmeleiros*) in 1931, when the various hospital services moved to the large new building in the locality (*sítio*) of Marmeleiros (‘quince trees’), in the parish (*freguesia*) of Nossa Senhora do Monte (Our Lady of the Mount).

before: The Marmeleiros building, whose construction had never been entirely completed, stood there utterly abandoned and exposed to every kind of weather until the central government, in a most praiseworthy and beneficial act of public administration, ceded it to the Misericórdia (Holy House of Mercy, a lay charitable brotherhood) of Funchal for the installation of its hospital, by the decrees of 9 and 29 March 1928. The first patients were transferred there in November 1930 and the rest the following year. The building was then fully completed and suitably adapted for that purpose, and it is one of the foremost hospitals of its kind in the country, not only as an appropriate facility but also for the way in which all its clinical and nursing services are provided. To this end, the Managing Board (*Mesa Gerente*) of the Holy House (*Santa Casa*, the Misericórdia) was authorised by the decree of 17 January 1930 to raise a loan of five hundred *contos* (one million réis) *de réis* from the Caixa Geral dos Depósitos, giving as security the proceeds of the 4% surcharge on the duties collected at the Funchal customs house, which had been created by the decree of 28 November 1927.

before: On the spot now occupied by the locality (*sítio*) of Casais there once stood a small chapel dedicated to Nossa Senhora da Piedade (Our Lady of Pity). The year of its foundation is unknown, but we presume that it must date from the third or last quarter of the 16th century. It had its own chaplain, who performed the religious services there under the authority of the vicar of São Jorge. It was this chapel that served as the seat of the new parish, created by the diocesan prelate Dom António Teles da Silva under the authority granted by the royal decree (alvará régio) of Peter II of 28 December 1676.

before: The principal localities (*sítios*) of this parish are Igreja, Casais, Lagoa, Poços, Arco Pequeno and Quebrada. The last owes its name to the great landslide (*quebrada*) that came down there more than two centuries ago, when a great deal of land broke away, chiefly from Arco Pequeno, and gave rise to that locality. Such events are common in Madeira: the parish of Jardim do Mar, part of the parish of Paul, the locality of Lugar de Baixo and others besides were formed in the same way. At the Quebrada of Arco de São Jorge, however, a most singular circumstance occurred which deserves special mention. We have found several references to it, for instance in the *Noticias Mineralogicas da Ilha da Madeira* by Dr Pereira Drumond, published in 1818 in the *Investigador Portuguez*, and in other Portuguese and foreign authors, and these references tally perfectly with local tradition, which still preserves the account of the event intact. Interesting details of this extraordinary occurrence are found in a letter discovered in 1848 in the Public Library of Lisbon (*Biblioteca Pública de Lisboa*) by General António Pedro de Azevedo, of which some years ago a Funchal newspaper published the curious extract that we reproduce below (see *Verdade*, no. 944): ‘I send Your Honour this news because it is a marvellous event. Behind the island, at Arco de São Jorge, the greater part of which is an estate of my entail (*morgado*), the ground had for many years been split open by a great fissure. The land being very steep, with the heavy winter rains of this year, at midnight on Easter Day the earth slid in great quantity into the sea for about half a *légua*, pushing the boulders and shoals before it so gently that the houses, trees and vine trellises remained standing. In one house two casks of wine on their supports (*canteiro*, natural ageing of the wine in casks on wooden supports, without artificial heating) did not overturn, a beehive on a stone slab did not fall, and a hen sitting on her eggs, tied to the foot of a fig tree – all were found there with no change and no disturbance of the ground. It formed an island in the sea of some twenty *moios* of sowing land, which is joining up with this one. It made a beach with two fine harbours, which that part needed, for being a shoal nothing could be shipped there. Where the land slid away there remained a hollow, with a sheer cliff above and below a *fajã* (strip of flat land at the foot of a cliff) of excellent new land reaching down to join the part in the sea, where before there had been a very high cliff dropping to the sea. And it slid without a crash and without being felt, except by one man who, seeing it moving in the night, was struck by a seizure; it went like a boat being launched into the sea running over its slipway timbers. And the marvel is that for some days before, along the whole width of the land that slid, the tide neither rose nor fell for three days, and the sea lay as if dead, while on either side it ebbed and flowed with the usual waves of the northern sea.’

before: A populous locality (*sítio*) of the parish (*freguesia*) of Machico, occupying a considerable part of the town (*vila*) of the same name and lying on the left bank of the stream, near its mouth. Most of the people of the place who make their living from fishing live here, and it is one of the most important fishing centres in the archipelago. In this locality stands the historic chapel of Senhor dos Milagres (Lord of Miracles), whose foundation is bound up with the discovery and first colonisation of this island. It is the centre of the best-attended pilgrimage in Madeira, held on 9 October each year, when several thousand people flock there. From this locality a fine road runs, partly skirting the picturesque cove, and leads directly to the landing quay. It has 243 households (*fogos*, literally ‘hearths’) and 1,090 inhabitants.

before: He was born in Funchal around 1864, the son of the distinguished Madeiran Francisco Joaquim de Sá Camelo Lampreia (see that entry). He attended the former Commercial Institute of Lisbon (*Instituto Comercial de Lisboa*) and pursued a diplomatic career, being appointed attaché to the legations in Stockholm and Copenhagen in 1883. In 1890 he left for Rome as secretary of embassy and remained there for some years, serving several times as chargé d’affaires. After serving at the legation in Madrid, he moved to Rio de Janeiro in 1896 as first secretary. By decree of 8 September 1900 he was appointed envoy extraordinary and minister plenipotentiary in Brazil, a post he held for some years. There he rendered notable services to his country, while at the same time winning the warmest regard not only of the important Portuguese community but also of the most eminent figures of the Brazilian Republic. With the establishment of the new political regime, he abandoned his diplomatic career and settled in the city of Rio de Janeiro, devoting himself to the labours of an active commercial life. He died in the city of Rio de Janeiro on 11 July 1943.

before: He was born in this city on 4 February 1828 and died in Caniço on 13 December 1904, the son of Lieutenant-Colonel Luís Agostinho Figueiroa de Albuquerque and Dona Maria Vicência de Freitas Bettencourt. He was a man of uncommon learning, acquired chiefly during his long residence abroad, and especially in the French capital. He devoted himself above all to economic studies, publishing a volume on the subject and many articles scattered through the newspapers. He held the posts of president of the Municipal Council (*Câmara Municipal*) of Funchal, secretary-general of this district and of that of Ponta Delgada, president of the Administrative Committee (*Comissão Administrativa*) of the Misericórdia of this city and member of the former District Council (*Conselho de Distrito*), and he also served for a time as acting civil governor of this archipelago. He contributed to the former newspaper *O Povo* and to other periodicals, and published separately the two volumes *Tratado Elementar de Economia Politica*, 171 pp., and *Compêndio Elementar do Novo Systema Geral de Pesos e Medidas*, 166 pp.

before: We have already devoted a short article to João Afonso, companion of Zarco, who became the founder of a noble and distinguished family on this island. He also bore the surname Correia, which he passed on to his descendants, and they were the first to use it on this island. João Afonso had a son named António Correia, who was born in Madeira in 1457 and who, several genealogists state, died in 1572, at the age of about 115. This António Correia was a valiant knight who fought bravely in Africa, chiefly at Arzila and Safi, where he maintained a large number of men and horses at his own expense. The old Madeiran chronicles speak of him in terms of high praise.

before: Shortly after the discovery, André Gonçalves, known as ‘Polonês’, came to this island; he settled in Estreito da Calheta and held land there as a *sesmaria* (royal land grant to settlers on condition of cultivation). His son João de França, who introduced this surname to the island, owned a great deal of land and a fine house in Estreito. He founded the original church of this parish (*freguesia*), where he established the seat of the entailed estate (*morgadio*) he created. He died in 1511 and was buried in the church of which he was founder and patron. The last holder of this entailed estate, one of the largest on the island, was the Count of Calçada, who died in 1906.

before: He was the brother of the well-known William Heberden and practised medicine in Funchal, where he rendered excellent service during the measles epidemic of 1751. When Banks and Dr Solander visited Madeira in 1768, he supplied them with many natural history specimens, as well as a copy of his observations on the island’s flora. The two naturalists named the genus *Heberdenia* after him; Aiton later merged it into the genus *Ardisia*. The meteorological observations made by Dr Herberden in Funchal from 1747 to 1751 were the first carried out on this island, and they were published in vol. X of the *Philosophical Transactions*.

before: Several entails (*vínculos* or *morgadios*) had come together in the Carvalhal house. The most important was that of Santo Espírito at Lombada da Ponta do Sol, founded in 1511 by the Flemish *fidalgo* (nobleman of the lesser nobility) João Esmeraldo on the vast property he had bought from Luís Gonçalves da Câmara, 2nd son of João Gonçalves Zarco, the discoverer of Madeira. The 2nd Count of Carvalhal was the 13th and last administrator of this entail (*morgado*). He had also inherited the entailed estate founded in the parish (*freguesia*) of Ponta Delgada by Manuel Afonso Sanha and his wife Dona Mécia de Carvalhal at the beginning of the 15th century, as well as the entails of Água de Mel, Paul do Mar, the Lemes, etc., not counting others situated in various parts of the island and also in the Azores and on the mainland of the Kingdom (*reino*, i.e. mainland Portugal). He owned vast properties in every parish of Madeira, and the Carvalhal house came to be the second or third in the country in landed wealth.

before: ‘We hold it beyond doubt,’ says the illustrious annotator of *Saudades da Terra*, ‘that tax farming was the first system of fiscal collection adopted in these islands, and consequently overseas. before: The royal letter (*carta régia*) of 15 March 1477 that created the Funchal customs house directed that a suitable house be rented for the purpose. It is not known precisely, however, where this fiscal house was first established. It has been claimed, and the illustrious annotator of *Saudades da Terra* echoed the claim, that the Funchal customs house was first installed in Rua do Esmeraldo, in the building known as the granary of the pool, or in its immediate vicinity. It is also stated elsewhere, as information drawn from local tradition, that the customs house was set up somewhere in the area of Santa Maria Maior. This is not at all surprising, and it is even very likely that this was so. The first nucleus of population settled mainly to the east of the stream later called Ribeira de João Gomes, and it was there that the young settlement of Funchal grew most. This was despite the fact that the discoverer and first donatary had made his residence on the heights of Santa Catarina, which certainly would not yet have borne that name.

before: Zarco or Zargo? [TN: The two spellings differ only in one consonant; the discussion concerns which form of the surname is correct.] This question is answered by the learned commentator of Frutuoso, who was also a distinguished philologist. He says that the first form is the more genuine way of writing this surname and has the best authors on its side, but that it became antiquated and usage adopted the second. We have consulted the oldest chroniclers and writers who dealt, if only briefly, with the discoverer of our archipelago, such as Gomes Eanes de Zurara, João de Barros and Damião de Góis, and found that all of them wrote Zarco. The accounts of the voyages made by Diogo Gomes, a contemporary of Prince Henry, and by Alvise Cadamosto (1450) adopt the same spelling. In a royal letter (*carta régia*) of Afonso V of the year 1449 we find the very antiquated form Zarquo, which corresponds to Zarco, the form adopted by our early chroniclers. The celebrated historian of the islands, who composed his work in the last quarter of the 16th century, uses the already modernised form Zargo. The spelling Zarco, found in two or three places in the *Saudades*, must be considered a copyist’s slip or a printing error, since Gaspar Frutuoso certainly writes Zargo many dozens and perhaps hundreds of times. This was also the spelling always adopted by the annotator of that work. Every reason suggests that the spelling to follow today should be the one used by the illustrious author of *Saudades da Terra* (‘Longing for the Homeland’) and by his learned commentator.

Captain João Gonçalves Zarco... sheltering the ships by the islets that lie off the cape (*cabo*) of this *lugar* (settlement ranking between a town and a parish), because there was a fine cove there, resolved to build his wooden dwelling on land, which he at once built right beside the sea on a high spot, where the captain’s wife (*capitoa*, wife of the captain-donatary) Constança Rodrigues later founded a church of Santa Catarina.’ This was Zarco’s first settlement, and the chapel that the navigator’s wife had built was also the first place of worship erected on Madeira. The small, primitive chapel underwent several rebuildings and repairs over the centuries; the present chapel is a building of the middle or end of the 17th century. It is nonetheless the only building in Funchal that truly recalls the discovery. As such, it ought to be religiously preserved. In its smallness, its modesty and its poverty, it commemorates the beginning of our brilliant maritime discoveries, and for Madeirans it stands, besides the discovery, for the start of the settlement and colonisation of this archipelago. The chapel still bears on the threshold of its portal the date 1425, which marks the year of the original construction. It was beside this small church that João Gonçalves Zarco had his first residence for some years, built perhaps of the rich, fragrant cedars that grew everywhere in dense forests. It was no doubt a more than modest and uncomfortable dwelling, of a single storey and stripped of all architectural display, as were all the earliest houses built here. We read somewhere that only later did a man named João Manuel build in the Campo do Duque the first two-storey house, made of dressed cedar wood, which caused no small wonder at the time.

before: From the solitary retreat of Santa Catarina – for the first and densest core of population, with its houses, took shape on the left bank of the easternmost stream (*ribeira*) of Funchal – Zarco directed the first work of colonisation and laid the foundations of the future town (*vila*), which progressed rapidly and grew extraordinarily even in his lifetime. There he would dream of the progress of the captaincy of which he was donatary (*donatário*), and of the rise of the house he had founded, glimpsing in the near future the honours and privileges that would be heaped upon his descendants and successors. Perhaps he had guessed that the monarch would reward him with the marks of nobility and the use of a coat of arms, already seeing his grandsons’ patents of nobility adorned with the coronet of count and of grandees of the Kingdom (*reino*, i.e. mainland Portugal), in homage to the services rendered by their grandfather. . .

before: A few years later Zargo moved his residence to the left bank of the stream, at the foot of the hill later known as Pico dos Frias, close to the chapel he had built there with the dedication to São Paulo (St Paul the Apostle). before: João Gonçalves Zargo does not seem to have stayed very long in his first two residences. He settled for good, and spent the greater part of his life, in the immediate vicinity of the spot where he built the church of Conceição de Cima. An old manuscript says: ‘he resolved also to build a dwelling for himself, as he did, on a height above the valley of Funchal: and directly opposite, a church of Nossa Senhora da Conceição as a family vault for himself and his kin, which they began to call Nossa Senhora de Cima, because it was founded on a stump of cliff at the foot of a peak’. It is in this church, which later took the name of the church of Santa Clara (St Clare of Assisi), that the mortal remains of the illustrious navigator lie, and it was surely in the dwelling houses he built nearby that he ended his earthly career. We read in the manuscript already cited: ‘the great Gonçalves Zargo reached such old age that he had himself carried in men’s arms to be set in the sun, which greatly invigorated him. From there he disposed the affairs of his jurisdiction, governing and administering justice with his understanding whole, never suffering the feebleness of a decrepit man’.

before: On the strength of various documents that we have examined closely, we have been able to establish, for the first time, that Gonçalves Zargo’s old residence corresponds to the former manor house of the Lomelino entailed estate holders (*morgados*), which today still bears the name of Quinta das Cruzes. before: It seems that this old and noble residence remained in the possession of his descendants. It is certain that a century after his death it belonged to his grandson Pedro Gonçalves da Câmara, who was married to Dona Joana de Eça, chief lady of the bedchamber to Queen Catherine. In 1575 it was in the usufruct and possession of a grandson of this couple, also named Pedro Gonçalves da Câmara, who by public deed of 16 September of that year sold it to his close kinsman Francisco Gonçalves da Câmara, grandson of João Gonçalves Zargo. It was this Francisco Gonçalves da Câmara who was governing the captaincy of Funchal, in the absence of his nephew João Gonçalves da Câmara, the sixth donatary (*donatário*), when in 1566 this city was attacked by French corsairs, who carried out a terrible sack here and massacred some three hundred people. Gaspar Frutuoso stated in 1590 that Gonçalves da Câmara lived near the convent of Santa Cruz ‘in a great and sumptuous palace’.

before: This house passed into the possession of a daughter of Francisco Gonçalves da Câmara, named Dona Joana de Noronha, and then to her son António de Carvalhal Esmeraldo, who owned it in 1624. At the end of the 17th century it belonged to Francisco Esmeraldo Henriques, who founded there the chapel of Nossa Senhora da Piedade (Our Lady of Pity). The date 1692 is still visible at the top of its doorway, but the deed of grant dates from 1695, and it was in that year that religious worship began there. In this chapel there is a marble burial vault said to hold the mortal remains of Urbano Lomelino, founder of the convent that once stood in the town (*vila*) of Santa Cruz and one of the founders of the Lomelino family on this island. The house at Cruzes was incorporated into the entailed foundation (*instituição vincular*, a morgado or capela) of this important entailed estate (*morgadio*), probably through marriage, in a year we cannot determine. It remained in this family until our own day, and a few years ago became the property of the barons of Jardim do Mar.

before: ‘In the year 1516,’ says Gaspar Frutuoso, ‘because he (the first Bishop of Funchal, Dom Diogo Pinheiro) was occupied in the King’s service as judge of the Desembargo do Paço (the royal supreme court; *desembargador do paço*) and detained by the affairs of the King and the Kingdom, he sent to the city of Funchal a bishop named Dom Duarte. Since he himself could not come, this bishop confirmed, conferred holy orders and gave regulations (*regimento*) in the Cathedral, and performed other ministries proper to his office and charge. He consecrated the Cathedral of the city of Funchal with great solemnity on St Luke’s day, 18 October, blessed one of the bells that were placed in its tower, and did other very necessary things.’ Dom Duarte came to Madeira two years after the creation of this diocese; earlier, in 1508, the Order of Christ had sent Bishop Dom João Lobo to this island.

before: Infante Dom Luís, later King of Portugal, first visited Madeira in 1858. He was the first member of the Portuguese royal family to visit the island. Commanding the corvette *Bartolomeu Dias*, he reached our harbour on 8 October of that year, accompanied by his chamberlain, the Count of Linhares. The gunboat *Sagres* sailed in company. He landed at the Cais da Pontinha the following day, and the reception was of the greatest splendour and grandeur. During the twenty days that Dom Luís spent in Madeira, besides the other festivities and public demonstrations of esteem and affection held in his honour, splendid private festivities took place, whose memory lived on in local tradition for many years because of their brilliance and extraordinary pomp. Outstanding among them were the festivity at Palheiro Ferreiro and the dinner and ball at the Palácio de São Pedro (St Peter Palace), given by the Count of Carvalhal, which greatly impressed the prince; the ball at the Club Funchalense, given by the Municipal Council (*Câmara Municipal*); and the reception at the house of the holder of the entail (*morgado*) of Cruzes, Nuno de Freitas Lomelino. Dom Luís made lengthy visits to the Asylum for the Destitute (*Asilo de Mendicidade*), the Hospício da Princesa Dona Maria Amélia, the Hospital de Santa Isabel (St Elizabeth of Portugal), the military hospital, the lyceum (state secondary school) and several public offices.

before: In the early days of colonisation many noblemen, both Portuguese and foreign, came to this island, together with an even larger number of merchants and adventurers. They came to seek their fortune, drawn by the fame of the remarkable fertility of the soil, by the spirit of adventure and also by the lack of resources in the lands they came from. These men were given large tracts of land in *sesmaria* (royal land grant to settlers on condition of cultivation), which they had cleared by Black and Moorish slaves imported from Africa and by free tenant farmers (*colono*, under the *colonia* contract) from mainland Portugal. Many of these *sesmeiros* (holder of a land grant, or *sesmaria*) built up fine houses with the large income that the exuberant fertility of the soil gave them, above all from the production of sugar, which was exported on a large scale. Then ‘the rich *sesmeiro*, in the words of the annotator of the *Saudades da Terra*, grew weary of country life, took pride in his original nobility and craved a residence of greater display and bustle; he therefore scorned the land and entailed it, with the aim of securing its revenues; he contracted its cultivation to the free tenant farmers for a half-share (*demidia*) or, in some parts, a third of the produce, and, to maintain himself in idle enjoyment, abandoned his estates and came to set up a luxurious and wasteful residence in the towns, chiefly in Funchal, Machico, Santa Cruz, Calheta, Ponta do Sol and Ribeira Brava.’
