before: It seems that some entailed estates (*morgadio*) were already being founded in Madeira in the second quarter of the 15th century. Gaspar Frutuoso implies as much, although he does not say so clearly and conclusively. Of entails created in the last quarter of the same century there is reliable record, such as that of Água de Mel, in Santo António, which was incorporated into the house of Carvalhal; that of Consolação, in Caniço, whose last representative was Councillor (conselheiro, honorary title of the royal council) Aires de Ornelas; that of João Afonso in Câmara de Lobos, which passed to the house of Torre Bela; that of Vasco Moniz, in Machico, whose last administrator was José de Betencourt e Freitas; those founded by João Gomes, beside the stream that took his name; that of Rodrigo Aires Furtado, in Ponta do Sol; and many others besides.

before: Even so, many entailed houses survived here in Madeira, and they struggled with great economic difficulties. Some even went so far as to request the commutation of the pious obligations to which they were bound, on the grounds that the income from their lands was insufficient to meet those obligations; we have found this in documents from the early 19th century, and we do not know whether it happened even earlier. On 17 February 1849 the Madeiran peer of the realm Dr Daniel de Ornelas e Vasconcelos, 1st Baron of São Pedro, presented to the upper chamber a bill abolishing all the entails existing in this archipelago, considering them not only useless but actually harmful, above all because they were a great obstacle to agricultural progress. The bill caused a great stir in Madeira and gave rise to extensive debate in the press. Thirty-odd representatives of old entailed houses addressed a petition to parliament, refuting the principles of the bill and asking for its rejection. It is an exceptionally interesting document that still deserves to be read today. Besides this petition and the debate in the local press, the following pamphlets were published on the subject: *Breves reflexões sobre a abolição dos morgados na Madeira*, by António Correia Heredia; *As contradições vinculadas*, by the author of *Breves reflexões sobre a abolição dos morgados na Madeira*; and *Resposta ao folheto «Breves reflexões sobre a abolição dos morgados na Madeira, pelo Sr. A. C. Heredia»*, whose author we do not know.

before: Gaspar Frutuoso states in the *Saudades da Terra*, a work written in 1590, that in 1587, when the donatary Tristão Vaz da Veiga was governor and superintendent of military affairs, the Portuguese succeeded in recovering two ships, one laden with wine and the other with wheat, which a corsair had seized in the bay of Funchal. He adds that in the following year an English carrack that had been plundering the ships entering or leaving our landing place was sunk. The same author also records that in 1582, when the French of Dom António’s fleet were expected to land on Madeira, António de Carvalhal brought 300 men to Funchal and maintained them at his own expense for five months, in the service of the Catholic king, Philip.

before: The law was not respected, and criminals, thanks to the protection they enjoyed, were seldom punished. When Dom Francisco Henriques was murdered, the culprit found refuge in the Colégio church (Igreja do Colégio, the Jesuit college church), where two clerics opposed his arrest. And when the *ouvidor* (judicial officer of the donatary or the Crown) captured a brother-in-law of the murderer and handed him over to the *alcaide* (town officer with police and jail duties), the man was snatched from the hands of the authorities by a second lieutenant and several soldiers of the Castilian garrison!

before: In 1617 the island of Porto Santo was attacked and sacked by the Moors, who carried off many captives. A record (*auto*) drawn up at the session of the Municipal Council (*Câmara Municipal*) of Funchal on 16 June 1632 shows that the fact that these pirates did not come to Madeira at the same time was attributed to the protection of the patron saint, St James the Less. The Fort of São Tiago (St James the Greater), the castle of São João do Pico, part of the encircling walls and the fort of Pico do Castelo on the island of Porto Santo are military works carried out in the time of the Castilians. From the same period dates an unfinished tunnel in the locality (*sítio*) of Rabaçal, which was apparently intended to carry the waters that lay unused at that point of the island. In the time of Philip II the office of governor-general was created, and from then on our archipelago was never again free of the superintendence of a higher authority appointed by the Crown. The donataries were not abolished, but the donataries, although they saw their privileges confirmed by the usurping kings, had to acknowledge the supremacy of the delegate of the central power in the lands their ancestors had governed as almost absolute lords.

before: At the locality (*sítio*) of Álamos in the parish (*freguesia*) of Santo António stands the chapel of Nossa Senhora do Amparo (Our Lady of Protection), which is in a fair state of repair; the Holy Sacrifice of the Mass is celebrated there from time to time. before: His name was Carlos Acciaioly Ferraz de Noronha. He was born in the parish of Santana on 15 July 1845 and died in Funchal on 1 February 1924. He served as a parish priest in several parishes of this island and for many years taught at the Diocesan Seminary, distinguishing himself as a notable preacher. He cultivated prose and poetry with brilliance, especially in the humorous and satirical genre, and his writings were read with the greatest appreciation. He became very well known here and is well remembered by his contemporaries, particularly for his witticisms, in which he achieved real celebrity; even today the stories and anecdotes featuring his phrases, full of the most spontaneous and sparkling wit, are frequently retold.

before: Marceliano Ribeiro made his name above all as a teacher, and as such he acquired a great reputation throughout the country. Besides his engaging manners and extremely affable disposition, which quickly won his pupils’ affection, he had the rare gift of knowing how to teach. His exposition was easy and clear, and it drew great brilliance and force from the tone of conviction in which he spoke and the enthusiasm he conveyed in his words. He was a speaker beyond compare with a profound knowledge of the subjects he lectured on, and his students never tired of hearing him, enraptured by the beauty of his expression and the loftiness of his ideas. He taught at the classes of the old Pátio, and when the Liceu do Funchal was founded in 1836 he joined the teaching staff of the new establishment, teaching the Portuguese and Latin languages and later holding the chair of philosophy.

before: Appointed rector of the lyceum (state secondary school) and schools commissioner (*comissário dos estudos*), he distinguished himself remarkably in these posts, above all through the impetus he gave to the spread of primary education, the new teaching methods he introduced and the scrupulous care with which he selected teachers. His reports in this field are truly exemplary, and some were published in the scientific review *O Instituto*. To encourage primary teachers in the exercise of their calling, he founded an ‘Associação de Conferencias’ (Lecture Association), in which the subjects most closely concerning popular education were discussed. Given the great zeal and dedication he showed in extending primary education, it may without doubt be said that he was the first person in this archipelago to take a genuine interest in popular education, and this fact alone is enough to make his memory blessed among us.

before: The Fojo, a deep chasm hollowed out of friable tuff behind the coastline and a little to the east of Ponta da Cruz, appears to be the result of the erosion and collapse of a volcanic channel that ran there in remote ages and opened into the sea. Its ruins, now piled up in confusion as blocks of blackened lava, show smoothed surfaces with the long, parallel striations that characterise the walls of lava tunnels. The sea water, having passed through a nearby cave formed by marine erosion and having eaten away the rocks beneath the channel, is thought to have caused this collapse, helped by the rainwater that flows into the pit, wearing away the tuff and widening its extent.

before: This distinguished German priest was born in Rheydt on 18 May 1845, the son of Frederico Schmitz and Elizabeth Schmitz, and entered the Congregation of the Mission of St Vincent de Paul on 25 September 1864. In 1874 he served for a time as chaplain of the Hospício da Princesa Dona Maria Amélia, but it was only in 1878 that he took up residence in Madeira. There he at first held that post again, and then, from 27 September 1881, that of vice-rector of the Funchal Seminary (*Seminário do Funchal*). In this latter office he rendered outstanding services to science and education, founding in 1882 a natural history museum that still exists today (see Seminary Museum), in which he succeeded in assembling the most varied specimens of the Madeiran fauna. In 1898 he withdrew to Theux, in Belgium, but at the end of 1902 he returned to the post he had left at the Funchal Seminary. He gave it up only on 7 July 1908 when, at the request of the Imperial German Government, he went to take charge of the hospice (*hospício*) of São Paulo in Jerusalem. In 1914 he moved to the German Hospice at Tabgha, on the shores of the Sea of Galilee (Lake Tiberias), and in the summer of 1920 he took over the direction of the Hospice of São Carlos in Haifa, where he died on 3 December 1922.

before: An inhabited locality on the island of Porto Santo. At the spot in this locality called Graça there stood an old chapel dedicated to Nossa Senhora da Graça (Our Lady of Grace), which gave the place its name. As it was badly ruined, its rebuilding on a larger scale was undertaken at the beginning of the 19th century, but the construction was never completed, and today only some ruins remain. It had a certain architectural pretension and an octagonal interior, and it is said somewhere that it is a miniature reproduction of a famous sanctuary in Italy. It has 16 households (*fogos*, literally 'hearths') and 70 inhabitants.

before: The cholera epidemic which, in the third and last quarter of 1856, killed some six thousand people on this island according to official figures – though information from other sources raised the toll to ten thousand – gave rise, once the panic of that great public calamity had passed, to the idea of founding a society that would not only practise mutual aid among its members but also assist the widows and orphaned children of deceased members. According to issue 13 of the newspaper *A Madeira*, published in this city from April 1857 to January 1858, the society was inaugurated on 17 December 1856 under the name Sociedade de Beneficência do Funchal. We do not know on what basis its statutes were framed; we know only that it did not last long. A new attempt, though once again without appreciable results, was made to found a mutual-aid society. It was inaugurated on 29 December 1858 under the name Associação dos Artistas Madeirenses, in the presence of some four hundred workers and many persons of standing in Funchal society, and on that occasion the distinguished teacher and illustrious Madeiran Marceliano Ribeiro de Mendonça delivered a most remarkable speech.

before: On the coast of the parish (*freguesia*) of Caniço there is a projection, or point, called Oliveira. When the discoverers João Gonçalves Zarco and Tristão Vaz Teixeira marked out the limits of their captaincies, the territory was divided by a roughly straight line running from Ponta da Oliveira to Ponta do Tristão, these points being regarded as the extremities of their donataries. At the south-eastern end an olive stake was planted as a boundary marker; it is said to have been sent from the mainland expressly for that purpose by Prince Henry the Navigator. This is why that projection of land bears the name Ponta da Oliveira.

before: An annual or biennial plant of the family Umbelliferae, frequent in Madeira and on Porto Santo. Its basal leaves are pinnatisect or 3-sect, with broad segments, and the stem leaves 3-sect or entire; its umbels are sessile or short-stalked, without involucre or involucel, and its fruits are subglobose. The root and fruits of celery are diuretic and stimulant, and the leaves and stalks can be eaten in soup or salad. Garden celery is not found in the archipelago.

before: As we have said elsewhere in this work, the English colony began to be of importance here at the end of the 16th century. From that time until the introduction of representative government, we have no record that members of that colony, or of any other Protestant nationality, tried to promote their religion among us by making converts within the Madeiran population. They had churches reserved for their own worship, attended only by their adherents, to the complete exclusion of the natives. And in fairness it must be said that, in general, the foreign subjects living in Madeira as merchants or invalids, and also the visitors who seek out our mild climate or the beauties of our privileged natural surroundings, do not devote themselves to propagating their religious ideals, nor do they try to turn Catholics away from the practice of the religion they profess. Several Protestant foreigners have even supported some Catholic works and helped to build and repair churches and chapels, as John Howard March did when he rebuilt the parish church of Santo da Serra.

before: A member of the Cupuliferae, cultivated in Madeira since the island began to be settled. Some years ago a chestnut tree could be seen at Achada do Campanário whose trunk measured 10.50 m in circumference, and at the locality of Fontes, in Ribeira Brava, we believe another still exists whose trunk measures 11.30 m, also in circumference. The chestnut, much less common today than formerly, produces besides its nuts, which are eaten locally, a good timber with many uses. Although it is characteristic of the 2nd botanical zone of Madeira, which runs from 150 to 200 metres, it can also grow near the coast: for many years a specimen stood in the Fort of São Lourenço (St Lawrence) that never failed to bear fruit in due season. Annual chestnut production in Madeira is around 4,000 hectolitres.

before: In 1750 the inhabitants of the localities of Lombo das Adegas and Terças, in the parish (*freguesia*) of Ponta do Sol, asked permission to build a chapel. They cited the distance at which they lived from the parish church and their wish to build a small sanctuary to house and venerate the revered image of Nossa Senhora do Monte, which stood in a small thatched oratory lacking the decorum due to the image. The chapel had a deed of endowment executed on 7 July 1750, and permission for its blessing was granted on 15 September 1751. Twenty-four years later it was enlarged, and it was blessed anew on 10 June 1775.
after: In 1750 the inhabitants of the localities of Lombo das Adegas (‘ridge of the wine cellars’) and Terças (‘thirds’), in the parish (*freguesia*) of Ponta do Sol (‘point of the sun’), asked permission to build a chapel. before: The chapel of Nossa Senhora da Graça was one of the oldest on Porto Santo. At the beginning of the 19th century, under the auspices of Manuel Inácio de Avelar Brotero, governor of that island, its reconstruction was begun because of its ruinous state, but it was never completed. The walls still stand, partly demolished by the action of time and the vandalism of men.

before: It is also called the Forte Novo (New Fort). It stood on the curtain wall (*cortina*, the defensive wall of the city) of Nossa Senhora do Calhau (Our Lady of Calhau), by the Corpo Santo (Holy Body). It had a Renaissance-style gorge doorway, topped by an inscription and surmounted by an ornate, finely worked crown in white marble, which showed that the fortification works ordered on the island by the captain-general (capitão-general, military governor of Madeira) Duarte Sodré Pereira were completed in 1707. The fort had a furnace for heated shot: the balls were taken out with iron tongs and inserted through the muzzle of the already loaded gun, with a wad of dampened tow. The heat set off the gun, and the red-hot ball reached the decks of wooden ships, where it holed them and set them on fire. The fort was demolished in 1897.

before: The brothers João Fernandes de Andrade and Diogo Fernandes de Andrade, noblemen of Galicia, were the first to come to this island bearing this surname. They obtained many lands as a *sesmaria* (royal land grant to settlers on condition of cultivation) at Arco da Calheta and settled there. John II, by royal decree (*alvará*) of 20 February 1485, granted the first of the two the use of the following arms: ‘on a field of gold a sagittarius, half man and half horse, the man naked in his natural colour, the horse between bay and dark chestnut, with a bow drawn in its hands, of red, and the string of silver, the arrow fletched with green; a closed helm of silver, mantling of gold and green, and for crest the demi-sagittarius with its bow’.

before: João Fernandes de Andrade, later known as João Fernandes do Arco because he lived in this parish (*freguesia*) and owned much land there, founded an entailed estate whose seat was the chapel of Nossa Senhora da Consolação (Our Lady of Consolation). He died on 9 April 1527 and was buried there; his tomb bore the following epitaph: ‘Here lie João Fernandes and Beatriz de Abreu, his wife, who were the first founders of this Arco’. To his nephew, Fernão Dias de Andrade, son of his brother Diogo, John III confirmed by royal decree of 17 April 1528 the coat of arms granted to his uncle. It is transcribed in full in the *Nobiliario* of Henriques de Noronha, of which a copy exists in the Funchal library.

before: This infantry officer was born in Funchal on 2 February 1856 and died in Lisbon on 17 November 1903, then holding the rank of major. He was technical inspector of the Monte Railway Company (*Companhia do Caminho de Ferro do Monte*). Although some errors in building the line between Pombal and Atalhinho have been attributed to him, the fact is that his energy and acknowledged zeal did much to drive those works forward. He was also the concessionaire for the construction and operation of the Madeiran levadas (irrigation channels), as was seen on page 248 of this volume, and later director of the Limoeiro prison (*Cadeia do Limoeiro*). He carried on a lengthy controversy in the press with the engineer Adriano Augusto Trigo, and sought to install a lift between Largo de São Pedro and Caminho da Achada. (See II-248.)

before: The former Campo de D. Carlos, today Campo do Almirante Reis, was begun in 1898 and completed in 1901. before: Friar Pedro da Guarda was a poor and humble Franciscan. He was born in 1435 in the city from which he took his surname, and he died in the convent of São Bernardino (St Bernardino of Siena), in the parish (*freguesia*) of Câmara de Lobos, in the year 1505. The austerity of his life, the harsh penances to which he gave himself and his most exemplary practice of all the Christian virtues won him a reputation for sanctity even during his earthly pilgrimage. After his death many miraculous events were attributed to his intercession, and several beatification processes were set in motion so that he might canonically receive the veneration of the altars. The last was some 32 years ago, and various extracts from the principal documents of the process were published in a folio volume of 163 pages. The Holy See never pronounced on the canonisation, but the prelates of this diocese allowed a certain public cult, which for centuries never waned but instead grew more fervent with time. The Holy Servant of God, the name by which he was known and still is today, had countless fervent devotees, who flocked from all over the island to his burial place to implore his protection and help for the ills from which they suffered.

before: In the city of Guarda lived João Luís, a weaver, and his wife Águeda Gonçalves, and of their marriage Pedro was born in the year 1435. At the age of twenty he entered the Franciscan order, where he took his vows as a lay brother. For thirty years he lived in convents on the mainland, where the austerity of his life became well known and some prodigious events were attributed to him. Wishing to escape the admiration that his virtues aroused, he asked to withdraw to a convent of his order in Madeira, which he did around 1485. Seeking an obscure refuge in the convent of São Bernardino, in the parish of Câmara de Lobos, he lived there for about twenty years, and died on 27 July 1505. The penitent life he led in this retreat, and above all the miraculous events attributed to his intercession, drew the attention of his contemporaries, as we have already noted. A true halo of sanctity formed around his name, and it grew and swelled still further after his death.

before: No sooner had the governor of this bishopric, António Alfredo Santa Catarina Braga, arrived on the island in 1835 than he set about erasing the traces of the influence exercised by the religious orders, which had been expelled the year before. Bound up with that influence was the cult paid to the Santo Servo de Deus, and he moved without delay to prohibit every manifestation of a religious character in honour of the humble Franciscan. On 2 June 1835 António Alfredo went to the convent of São Bernardino, accompanied by several clergymen and some persons of social standing, and conducted a summary inquiry into the miraculous deeds attributed to Friar Pedro da Guarda. He then ordered that the statue of this religious, which was venerated there, be publicly burnt in his presence, together with other objects used in the ceremonies of worship offered to that humble lay brother of the Franciscan order. He had a record (*auto*) of the whole proceedings drawn up on the spot, a document full of rancour, even though it displays the greatest zeal for the integrity of Catholic doctrine and the prestige of religion. The following day he had a warrant (*provisão*) published in which the cult of the Santo Servo de Deus was utterly condemned and prohibited, imposing severe penalties on any clergy who failed to obey the orders contained in that warrant.

before: It is rather surprising that Robert Page, who gave so many notable proofs of the nobility of his character and of his sympathy for the Portuguese, should have lent himself – moved, perhaps, by a misguided patriotism – to posing as the discoverer of the famous ‘relics of Machim’s cross’ to which Dr Azevedo refers on p. 417 of the *Saudades da Terra*. These ‘relics’, deposited in the mother church (*igreja matriz*) of Machico and which nobody has so far taken seriously, are kept in a wooden frame glazed on the front. The label accompanying them states that they were found in 1814 in the chapel of Senhor dos Milagres (the Lord of Miracles) in the same town (*vila*).

before: The doctrine they contained was extended and completed by the Regulations of 27 August 1562, promulgated by the queen regent, Queen Catherine, which may truly be called the ‘Forest Code of Madeira’. before: The report concludes by indicating the first works that should begin without delay, of which we give this brief summary: 1. to secure, by decree, the inclusion of all common lands (*baldios*) in the ‘Forest Regime’; 2. to obtain the creation of a ‘Forestry District’ provided with the necessary qualified staff; 3. to enter a substantial sum in the budget to begin the work; 4. to seek to have the central government take charge of these services and guarantee their continuity; 5. to have two houses built at the places indicated in the ‘Bases’; 6. to continue the afforestation of the upland woodland (*montado*) of Barreiros and of the Paul da Serra; 7. to establish a nursery near Funchal; and 8. to promote the enactment of a decree on the grazing regime.

before: Since 1897 these services have been the responsibility of a department headed by a forestry officer (*regente florestal*). To this day it has confined itself to planting some exotic trees on Porto Santo and to promoting the sowing of maritime pine in the mountainous region of Madeira. Nothing has yet been done to conserve and propagate the native trees, and many of them may soon disappear owing to the constant devastation wrought on them by woodcutters, charcoal-burners and livestock.

before: In Madeira, Porto Santo and the Desertas 373 species of algae have been found to date, 211 of which belong to the diatom group (Diatomaceae). Of the remaining 162 species, 127 are marine and 35 live in streams, tanks, damp places and levadas (irrigation channels); for many of them only the names of their genera are known. *Enteromorpha compressa* is extremely common on the stones uncovered at low tide, and *Ulva Lactuca*, *Padina Pavonia*, *Cystoseira ericoides*, etc., are also rare at certain points of the coast that are covered or washed by the sea.

before: In the Ribeira de João Gomes, under the bridge at Curral dos Romeiros, lives the very rare *Lemanea fluviatilis*, a filamentous, leathery alga, and in the nearby pools the following Desmidiaceae have been found: *Staurastrum muticum*, *Cosmarium Botrytis*, *C. margaritiferum* and *Closterium acerosum*. before: He was the son of António Lopes Rocha and Dona Vitória Maria Rocha, and was born in the parish (*freguesia*) of the Sé in this city on 18 July 1747. He graduated in canon law at the University of Coimbra (*Universidade de Coimbra*) in 1770 and was ordained priest in the same year. By a royal letter (*carta régia*) of 30 July 1775 he was presented as parish priest of the parish of Santa Maria Maior, and some years later he was appointed canon of our Cathedral (*Sé Catedral*), in whose chapter he later held the offices of archdeacon and dean. More than once he served as governor of the diocese (governador do bispado, administering the see in the bishop's absence). Thanks to his learning and great influence, he enjoyed the highest prestige here in Madeira and was held in great esteem by all social classes of this land. He came into conflict with the diocesan prelate Dom José da Costa Torres, above all at the time of the persecution directed against the secret societies of which Lopes Rocha had been a member (see Freemasonry). He then wrote a long letter to the Minister of State José Seabra da Silva, complaining of the persecutions of which he was the victim. Regardless of whatever justice may have been on his side, the letter is a document that reveals in its author a great independence of character, uncommon learning and a remarkable beauty and correctness of style. Written in 1793, this letter was published in London in the July 1820 issue of the *Campeão Portuguez*, some time after its author’s death, and filled about forty pages of that review.

before: Two species are known by this name in Madeira: *Genista maderensis* and *G. virgata*. The first is a shrub or small tree of 1.50 to 5 metres, with trifoliate leaves and small, satiny-pubescent leaflets, only rarely almost hairless on the upper surface. The second is a shrub that can reach 2.50 m in height, with very small, leafless-looking, satiny-pubescent and whitish leaves. These two Leguminosae, both belonging to the subfamily Papilionoideae, have yellow flowers arranged in racemes. *G. maderensis* occurs in some ravines of the interior and between São Vicente and São Jorge; *G. virgata* is common in the outskirts of Funchal, in the Ribeira de Santa Luzia, at Jardim da Serra, etc. The wood of the latter species, used exclusively for inlaid work (*embutidos*), is heavy, hard and compact, at first a yellowish white and later a reddish brown; that of the former, entirely unknown to cabinetmakers, is white or yellowish white. *Genista maderensis*, sometimes used as fodder for domestic animals, is, contrary to what Masferrer y Arquimbau supposed, a species quite distinct from the ‘gacia’ of the Canary Islands (*Cytisus stenopetalus*).

before: More commonly known as São João da Ribeira (St John the Baptist), this chapel stands on the right bank of the westernmost stream of Funchal. Over time the stream has been called the Santa Catarina, São Paulo, São Lázaro, Santo António and São João stream, the last being the name it bears today. Some attribute the foundation of this chapel to João Gonçalves Zarco. It is undoubtedly one of the oldest in the diocese and one of the few from the 15th century still standing, although nothing of the original building survives. The Franciscan friars who accompanied the discoverer to this island built a small monastery beside the chapel and remained there until the Convent of São Francisco (St Francis of Assisi) was built in what was then the town (*vila*) of Funchal. Frutuoso says that, ‘the place being deserted, and a friar there… having hanged himself, these religious set up a house further down…’.

before: This account differs from that of the annotator of the *Historia Insulana*, who states that the Franciscans ‘lived as hermits… and eleven years after the discovery, their number having increased… they gathered in community in the hospice (*hospício*) and chapel of São João, which they began to build in 1432 with some alms and the labour of their own hands, without Zargo having founded the chapel…; in 1459 the friars left the hospice of São João and set sail for Portugal…; fifteen years later Friar Rodrigo da Arruda arrived on the island…, and he re-established the community in the same hospice of São João… Around 1476 the friars settled in São Francisco’. before: In 1762 the diocesan bishop, Dom Gaspar Afonso da Costa Brandão, founded in this chapel a confraternity of St John the Baptist to maintain religious services there, but we believe it did not last long. Around the middle of the 19th century António Ferreira Nogueira and Manuel Fernandes Jardim carried out important repairs there at their own expense, restoring the chapel to worship. In former times it was the centre of a popular pilgrimage, with pilgrims coming from all over the island. Today the novenas and feast of the patron saint are celebrated with remarkable splendour and large crowds from the city and its surroundings. The *Serões* published an interesting and detailed article by the Madeiran writer João dos Reis Gomes describing the place, the chapel, the *arraial* (open-air popular festival at a church feast) and the festivities of the Espírito Santo that were once held there.

before: The first sugar mill (engenho) for crushing sugar cane in Madeira was built in 1452. By 1590, when Frutuoso wrote the *Saudades da Terra*, there were more than 30 mills scattered across the island, even though the sugar industry here was already showing signs of decline at that time. In 1730, according to Soares da Silva in the *Memorias para a historia del-rei D. before: When Bowdich visited Madeira in 1823, only an insignificant quantity of sugar was being made here, and in 1826 there was a single mill on the whole island. Severiano Ferraz (see that entry) set about building another the following year, and it was completed in 1828. In 1851 there were four factories in Madeira (Harcourt, *Sketch of Madeira*), and in 1856 there were ten in Funchal and 18 on the whole island, all for distilling spirit (*aguardente*, distilled from sugar cane or wine) (White, *Madeira its climate and scenery*). In 1861 there were twenty-nine factories on the whole island, five of which processed sugar. In 1872 Dr Azevedo stated in his notes to the *Saudades da Terra* that there were known here ‘seven steam factories, five of them in operation and one about to begin; nine water-driven mills; and some driven by oxen’. The first of these produced sugar and spirit, the latter almost all consumed within the country.

before: These religious acquired the open square where the Colégio church and the barracks of the 27th Infantry Regiment (*infantaria n.º 27*) stand today (1921), and settled there in modest lodgings with a small church attached. We conjecture that they moved there in the last years of the 16th century. Construction of the great college and the magnificent church must have begun towards the end of the first quarter of the 17th century, as appears to follow from a manuscript of the mid-18th century. This agrees, moreover, with the following words of the learned annotator of Dr Gaspar Frutuoso: ‘We have searched in vain in the building and church of the Jesuit college in Funchal for an inscription recording when they were built: we found only, above the outer door of the classroom courtyard, which belongs to the same college... the date 1619... The vault of the chancel has traces of an architectural design that is still Manueline. The crossing, the nave and the carved woodwork of the chapels are in the bastard taste of the Renaissance. The building work was carried out, it seems, slowly and would only have been regarded as finished around the middle of the 17th century, apart from certain details of ornamentation that would have been definitively completed later still, such as the placing of the statues on the church façade, the decoration of some chapels, etc.

before: The bay of Funchal is the widest in the archipelago, bounded by Ponta do Garajau to the east and Ponta da Cruz to the west. It forms a fairly regular curve and inlet between those two headlands and is sheltered from winds from every quarter except the wind that blows from SSE to SSW by way of S. Its breadth makes it a vast anchorage, but communication with the land can be established with relative ease only at the most accessible points of the shore. These stretch from the Ilhéu da Pontinha in the west to the vicinity of the Fort of São Tiago (St James the Greater) in the east, some two thousand metres apart. All the traffic and movement of the landing place takes place within these limits. It is bounded by a beach of rounded boulders, with deep water and free of reefs or shoals that might hinder access. High water, or the establishment of the port (time of high water at full and new moon), according to the geographical map of Madeira by General A. P. de Azevedo, is at 12 h 48 min, with a tidal rise of 2.28 m; the engineer Mariano F. Faria e Maia, however, states that the tidal range reaches 2.80 m. With regard to the harbour of Funchal and the tides of the Madeiran coast, the illustrious engineer Adolfo Loureiro says that little is known about the lunar influences on spring and neap tides, about their propagation, velocity and direction, about the height and force of the waves according to the direction of the wind, their thrust, duration, etc. The temperature of the waters and its distribution at the surface, and their periodic movements and conditions, which follow a law that seemed constant, ought to have become the subject of very interesting oceanographic studies, which unfortunately were never carried out.

before: Manuel Gonçalves, born in the parish (*freguesia*) of Arco de São Jorge in eighteen sixty-something and better known by the nickname of Feiticeiro do Norte (‘the Sorcerer of the North’), is an illiterate peasant without any degree of education. At about the age of forty he began to show an extraordinary aptitude for composing and improvising popular verses and songs, which soon won great renown among the country people of this island. To the sound of a *rajão* (Madeiran five-string guitar), in a monotonous chant, the Feiticeiro sang his verses. For their originality and picturesqueness, and above all for the interest their subjects aroused, they were eagerly listened to and were one of the great attractions at the various festivals (*arraiais*) of Madeira. From short verses and light recitatives he moved on to more elaborate compositions, many of which were printed as separate pamphlets. Among these we may mention: *Santo Antonio*, *Chegada de Suas Magestades*, *As Raparigas dos bordados*, *O Lavrador*, *A Cidade do Funchal*, *As Inundações*, *O meu galo preto*, *A antiguidade de meu pae*, *A vida do Feiticeiro do Norte escrita por ele mesmo*, *A Madeira*, etc. etc. Encouraged by the success of his compositions, Manuel Gonçalves went to Brazil, where he stayed for some time, and among the pamphlets he printed there is one entitled *Pedro Alvares Cabral*.

before: In this parish there is a locality (*sítio*) that has kept the name Fajã da Ovelha since the earliest days of colonisation; the name later spread to the surrounding land and eventually to the whole parish (*freguesia*). It is common for a simple episode, a chance circumstance or a minor event to have given rise to the name of a particular locality or village (*lugar*, settlement rank below a town), which later grows into a populous centre or an important settlement. before: The learned annotator of the *Saudades da Terra* states that this parish only began to be called Fajã da Ovelha when, at the beginning of the 18th century, permission was given to build a new church, which was put up a few years later at the locality that then bore, and still bears today, that name. We disagree with this opinion, authoritative though it is, for the reasons we shall briefly set out. It is true that for almost two centuries this parish had its seat in the chapel of São Lourenço (St Lawrence), at the locality of that name, and that around the middle of the 18th century it moved to the new church built at the locality of Fajã da Ovelha. Yet it was never known as the parish of São Lourenço, as it naturally would have been had it not had another name, which in fact it did. The oldest document relating to this parish, cited in the *Índex Geral* of the register of the former Royal Treasury Office (*Provedoria da Real Fazenda*) and in the *Memorias sobre a creaçâo e augmento do estado eclesiástico na ilha da Madeira*, dates from 1553, and it already refers to the church of the parish of Fajã da Ovelha, the name by which it was then known. If it was called neither São Lourenço nor Fajã da Ovelha, what name could it have had before the 18th century? None is known. From this we logically infer that this parish always bore the name Fajã da Ovelha, from the earliest days of colonisation or, more precisely still, from the time when the seat of a new parish was established there.

before: The chaplaincy with cure of souls (capelania-curada), not yet an autonomous parish, and the parish had their seat, as already stated, in the chapel of São Lourenço, and remained there until the second quarter of the 18th century. The royal decree of the Infanta Dona Catarina, regent of the Kingdom (*reino*, i.e. mainland Portugal), dated 27 June 1705, authorised the building of a new church and its transfer to whatever site was judged most suitable for the purpose and in keeping with the wishes expressed by the people, after the most repeated entreaties of the parish priest of the time. Despite this, the new church was not built until some years later, the locality (*sítio*) of Fajã da Ovelha being chosen as the place that best met the conditions required for its construction. The order of the Council of the Treasury (*Conselho da Fazenda*) of 24 January 1747 (and not 1737, as the *Saudades* say) awarded the work by public auction (*arrematação*) to the carpenter Francisco Gomes for the sum of 6,350,000 *réis*. We do not know when the work was completed or when the new church was blessed.

before: A chapel with this dedication stands in the parish (*freguesia*) of Caniçal, on top of a steep cliff overlooking the sea. Anyone rounding the Ponta de São Lourenço at once sees the little chapel gleaming white on the summit of the craggy hill. In former times it had an adjoining house to shelter the devout who came there on pilgrimage. We have read somewhere that, according to tradition, the chapel was built in fulfilment of a vow by sailors who, seeing their ship about to be dashed to pieces on the rocks of the coast, promised to raise a small chapel dedicated to the Most Holy Virgin on the crest of the hill. It is also said to have been founded by Garcia Moniz, the first administrator (administrador do concelho, government-appointed head of the municipality) of the entailed estate (*morgadio*) of Caniçal, or by one of his successors. Many years ago it belonged to the entailed house (*casa vinculada*) of São Gil, whose manor house stood at Calçada, in the parish of Santa Cruz.

before: Another chapel dedicated to Nossa Senhora da Piedade once stood in the locality called Vargem de Baixo, in the parish of Calheta. Within the lands of the entailed estate of Vale da Bica, on the Lombada dos Esmeraldos (see that entry), in the parish of Ponta do Sol, at the place called Jangão, a small chapel with the same dedication was built in a year we cannot establish. In 1777 the administrator of that entailed estate (*vínculo*), Francisco de Ornelas e Vasconcelos, enlarged and improved the chapel, and on 3 August of that year permission was granted for it to be blessed anew. On 12 October 1879 the Archbishop of Goa, Dom Aires de Ornelas e Vasconcelos, blessed the chapel again and celebrated Mass in it, after the repairs carried out at the orders of his brother, the peer of the realm Agostinho de Ornelas e Vasconcelos, 15th administrator of the said entailed estate of Vale da Bica.

before: A chapel with the same dedication existed in the parish of Porto da Cruz. It was one of the oldest in the captaincy of Machico and was already badly ruined in the first quarter of the 16th century. One of the later administrators of this chapel, Manuel de Carvalho Valdavesso, had it rebuilt in 1734, and permission to bless it was granted on 8 September of the same year. In 1814, when Tristão Teixeira de Vasconcelos Saavedra was its administrator, it was closed because of its ruinous state, and its church furnishings were taken to the parish church, where the old altarpiece that stood on the chapel’s altar can still be seen.

before: Having been present at the taking of Malacca, says Pinheiro Chagas, he was entrusted by the great Portuguese general with reconnoitring and exploring the Moluccas, islands whose great riches were the subject of marvellous tales. António de Abreu set out with three ships: the commander of the small squadron himself captained one of them, Francisco Serrão another, and Diogo Afonso the third. Well armed, and carrying 120 men on board, António de Abreu’s three ships left Malacca in November 1515. António de Abreu and his companions followed the coast of the island of Sumatra and then passed on to Java, continuing by way of Madeira, Bali, Sumbawa, Solor and even New Guinea. Finally António de Abreu reached Amboina, while Francisco Serrão lost his ship at Ternate but was saved together with his crew, and was very well received by the natives. António de Abreu thus visited the principal Moluccas, and returned with an extremely rich cargo.

before: Major, however, in the remarkable work on the Portuguese voyages that he published under the title *Vida do Infante D. Henrique*, goes further and supposes that António de Abreu reached the coasts of Australia. There is indeed a map of around 1530 that marks a large territory named Great Java, lying opposite Sumatra, which incorporates many of the islands we know António de Abreu visited, such as Sumbawa, and this territory extends to latitudes and longitudes that already belong to Australia. Major says that before 1530 no one could have given information about the distant lands of Oceania except António de Abreu, who visited them. He supposes, with considerable plausibility, that many of the islands scattered across the Indian Ocean and the South Sea, together with the Australian continent, which Abreu seems to have sighted, were taken to form a single, unbroken territory.

before: This, then, is a summary of what various writers have set out about the warrior and navigator António de Abreu, corroborated by the statements of some old Madeiran books of nobility, which regard him as born on this island and as belonging to the noble families of the ‘Andrades’ and ‘Abreus’. In volumes I and IV of the important publication *Arquivo Histórico da Madeira*, the certainty of this birthplace is contested with weighty arguments that raise doubts in the reader’s mind. We record it here simply as a pointer for those who may wish to investigate the truth of this claim more fully.

before: A distinguished son of this parish was Commander Manuel de Pontes Câmara, who made an enormous fortune in Brazil and performed acts of the most notable benevolence there. At the same time he earned a lofty and never-contradicted reputation for unsurpassed probity and a character of the most proven austerity. Born in 1815, he sailed at a tender age for the Brazilian empire and within a few years was able to acquire a small fortune. This grew steadily and became considerable as, with intelligent initiative and persevering work, he devoted himself to large commercial transactions, constantly widening the sphere of his activity and so acquiring the substantial wealth he left at his death. Although his commercial activity absorbed his time, he did not neglect the cultivation of his mind: he spoke foreign languages, possessed uncommon learning and was widely read in the best-known authors, which lent particular distinction and charm to his extremely unaffected, welcoming and affable manner. He visited his homeland only once, in 1881, but on his return to his home in Rio de Janeiro aboard the steamer *Douro* he died in a shipwreck off Cape Finisterre on 2 April 1882. before: His name is today entirely unknown here, but in his own time he won considerable renown as a poet and writer. Those who make deeper studies of our literary history know the pages devoted to him by Diogo Barbosa Machado in the *Bibliotheca Lusitana* and by Costa e Silva in the *Ensaio Critico dos Poetas Portugueses*. He was born in Funchal in 1654, when his father Bartolomeu de Vasconcelos held the office of governor and captain-general (*capitão-general*, military governor of Madeira) of this archipelago. He devoted himself to the thorough study of the humanities, displaying his vast learning above all in languages, especially Greek and Latin. He also applied himself to the study of various theological questions, which he chose to treat in his poetry, particularly in the work entitled *O Espelho do Invisivel*. In it he shows great poetic qualities, but its subject, unsuited to treatment in verse, made the poem difficult to understand and stripped it of the graces that should adorn compositions of this kind. This is so despite, as Inocêncio Francisco da Silva says, the purity of its style and its being little tainted by the faults of the Gongorist school that then dominated our literature.

before: This was the name of a private annual feast – private because it was not authorised by any liturgical provision – that was celebrated, sometimes with some pomp, inside nuns’ convents without the direct involvement of their chaplains. It nevertheless took an edifying form of devotion and piety that deserves particular esteem. In the Convent of Santa Clara (St Clare of Assisi) in this city it was established around the middle of the 17th century by the pious nun Clara da Chaga; the account of this feast and its details published in *O Jornal* of 6 January 1934 is of interest. The book *Ripas da Madeira* contains interesting details of the feasts of the ‘Menino de Jesus Perdido’, although these are drawn with some touches of pure fiction.

before: And when did the translation of the remains take place? When the showy mausoleum was removed? When the church was rebuilt in the second half of the 17th century? When the body of Gaspar Mendes de Vasconcelos was laid in the grave? Or on some other occasion still? Nothing is known for certain on this matter, and there has been no lack of people who have asserted that the translation never took place, and that the discoverer’s ashes still lie beside the high altar, in the original place where they were laid. Nevertheless, it is not easy to overturn with a simple denial the unbroken tradition that holds the discoverer of Madeira to be buried in the tomb of his son-in-law Martim Mendes de Vasconcelos (see Gravestones).

before: In March 1919, while a floor was being laid in the chancel of this church, the gravestones covering the bones of the 2nd, 3rd and 5th donataries (*donatário*) of Funchal were discovered. In the centre, beside the steps of the high altar, lies a dark-coloured sepulchral slab bearing this epitaph: ‘Tomb of João Gonçalves da Câmara, second captain of this island.’ In the same chancel, on the Epistle side, another stone of the same colour was found, with the following inscription: ‘Tomb of Simão Gonçalves da Câmara....3rd captain of this island. Here lies Simão Gonçalves da Câmara, Count of Calheta and fifth captain of this island.’ We should note that on the stone bearing these last epitaphs two lines have been struck through, a circumstance for which we cannot offer any plausible explanation. No gravestone was found on the Gospel side. These tombs contain no reference whatever to the burial of the discoverer, which would be strange if his mortal remains had in fact stayed there. The third donatary, Simão Gonçalves da Câmara, died in Matosinhos, but his remains were carried to Funchal and buried in Santa Clara, as the epitaph transcribed above shows. João Gonçalves da Câmara, the 4th captain-donatary (*capitão-donatário*), died in Funchal and was buried in Santa Clara, although no reference to his burial is to be found there.

before: ‘The island of Porto Santo,’ says Rebelo da Silva, ‘followed Madeira’s example as soon as it learned of the revolution of 1 December 1640. When the despatches from Funchal arrived on 5 February, the inhabitants, whom a squadron of twelve Ottoman sails had almost blockaded, greeted the news with repeated salvoes of artillery and musketry. The Turks, startled by the noise and ignorant of its cause, thought it prudent to withdraw, and disappeared.’ The separation of the Madeira archipelago from the Castilian dominions did not cost a single drop of blood, and it was accomplished with the evident assent of every social class. The horrors of a 60-year captivity had rekindled the love of liberty in Madeiran hearts, so that as soon as news of the revolution of 1 December became known, everyone united at once to celebrate it with enthusiasm, without fear of the Castilian troops then on the island.

before: – On 1 November 1923 the foundation stone was laid of the grand monument erected at the Terreiro da Luta, in the parish (*freguesia*) of Monte, in honour of the Most Holy Virgin under the dedication of Nossa Senhora da Paz. It consists of an exquisite marble statue set on a plinth flanked by artistic bronze bas-reliefs, which allude to the traditional belief that the Most Holy Virgin appeared on that very spot. Beside the monument stands a small and elegant chapel, where the holy sacrifice of the Mass and other acts of worship are frequently celebrated. The erection of this monument is due to the ardent zeal and untiring efforts of Father José Marques Jardim, who spared no sacrifice to give it the imposing and grand appearance that distinguishes it, even travelling abroad to collect donations to bring the work to completion. The formal inauguration, held with the greatest pomp and attended by thousands of people from every part of the island, took place under the presidency of the diocesan prelate on 14 August 1927.

before: Bivalves are rare in the first of these zones. Nevertheless, *Cardita caliculata*, *Lasaea rubra* and a few other small species are found there, living in recesses of the rock or covered by algae. In this same region live, among the univalves, two or three species of *Littorina* and four species of *Patella*, the latter all edible (see Limpets); *Haliotis tuberculata*, beautifully lined with mother-of-pearl; several species of *Trochus*, one of which, the *caramujo* (*Trochus colubrinus*), is edible and sought as bait for fish; *Mitra cornicula*, *M. zebrina*, *Columbella cribaria* and *C. rustica*. In the rock pools, the small *Fossarus ambiguus* and the tiny *Rissoa picta* are sometimes abundant at certain spots, such as Baixa Larga and Pôça do Governador, east of Ponta da Cruz.

Jacobaeus*, *P. corallinoides* and *P. pes felis*; the lovely shells of the genus *Venus*, among them *V. casina*, *V. verrucosa* and *V. chione*; the velvety *Pectunculus glycimeris*; the snow-white *Lima squamosa*; *Cardium tuberculatum*, *C. norvegicum*, *C. aculeatum* and many others, which are not hard to obtain where the bottom is flat and suitable for working a dredge. before: Further out, in the coral zone, an inedible species of oyster is abundant: *Ostra cochlear*, with its variously coloured shell. There, together with *Chama gryphoides*, lives *Avicula hirundo*, with its graceful outline and pearly interior, a close relative of the pearl oyster, which hangs like a strange fruit from the branches of the so-called sea trees (*Gorgonia verrucosa*). At depths of about 90 *braças* the curious *Venus effossa* is found, at such various places as the Ponta de São Lourenço and Ponta do Garajau and the waters around the Ilhéu de Cima, off Porto Santo. Among the univalves of this deeper zone, mention should be made of the rare *Mitra exilima*, dredged west of Garajau, *Trophon Lowei*, *Murex babelis* and the pelagic species of the genera *Atlanta*, *Limacina*, *Cavolina* and *Clio*, whose skeletons settle in myriads on the ocean floor, besides many others that it would take too long to list.

before: In the town (*vila*) of Porto Santo there is a small chapel with a little house attached, known as the church of the Misericórdia (Igreja da Misericórdia). It was the seat of an old confraternity of that name, the date of whose foundation we do not know. Although a royal decree (alvará régio) of 9 April 1767 approved its statutes (*compromisso*), it is nonetheless certain that it was created at a more remote date. It never had a hospital. We do not know what services it provided, and at present it gives no assistance of any kind to the poor.

before: He was born in Lisbon, the son of Inácio Mira and Dona Garcia Ferreira de Afonseca, both of illustrious lineage and lords of the entailed estate (*morgadio*) of Torre da Giesteira, on the outskirts of Montemor-o-Novo. He took his doctorate in the faculty of canon law at the University of Coimbra in 1711. before: Here in Madeira his name remains linked to one notable work: the building of the Bishop's Palace (*Paço Episcopal*). Although it was a heavy structure, stripped of any architectural refinement, it was nonetheless, for this small city and for the period in which it was built, a building of some importance, and one that did no discredit to the high rank of its occupants. It was built between 1748 and 1751, at a cost of twenty *contos* de réis (*conto*: one million réis), a large sum for the time (see Bishop's Palace).

before: He was the son of João Gonçalves da Câmara, 6th captain-donatary (*capitão-donatário*) of Funchal, and of Dona Maria de Alencastre. He was born in Lisbon and never came to this island. His father died in Almeirim at the beginning of June 1580, when he was only six months old. He may be regarded as the 7th captain-donatary of Funchal, although he never took up the government of the donatary captaincy (*donataria*), which from 1582 was administered by governors-general under Philippine rule. Nevertheless, he retained the title of captain-donatary of Funchal, as did many of his successors, as the warrant (*provisão*) of 10 October 1585 shows, and he enjoyed a considerable share of the substantial revenues that the donataries held in this archipelago. Simão Gonçalves da Câmara, who was the 3rd Count of Calheta, married Dona Maria de Vasconcelos, daughter and heiress of the 1st Count of Castelo Melhor. For this reason the countship of Calheta was incorporated into the house of Castelo Melhor, which was later raised to a marquisate.

before: The Hinton family, English by nationality, settled in Madeira more than 90 years ago. In 1838 William Hinton, then a student at the University of Oxford, came to this island for the sake of his health. At that time the British subject Robert Wallas was living in Funchal; he owned a steam-powered flour mill, set up on the same site where the Torreão Factory (*Fábrica do Torreão*) stands today. In 1839 William Hinton married Mary Wallas, daughter of Roberto Wallas and Mary Wallas. He sold the properties he owned in England and settled permanently in Madeira in 1841. Some years later he founded the Torreão sugar factory. William Hinton, who was the representative of an entailed house (*casa vinculada*) (esquire) at Greenhill House, in the county of Wiltshire, England, was born in Naples in 1817 and died in Funchal on 15 June 1904. He was the father of Harry Hinton, the present owner of the Torreão Factory.

before: A shrub from 1 metre to 2.50 m tall, with thick leaves, mucronate or spinulose at the tip and generally spinulose-serrate at the margins; peduncles 1-flowered, rarely 2–3-flowered. It is a rare species, found only at Ribeiro Frio and in the Serras de São Vicente, Seixal and Boa Ventura. The wood of this member of the Aquifoliaceae is white, light and takes a good polish; it is used for inlaid work (*embutidos*) and other small pieces of cabinetwork, after being boiled in two or three changes of water to remove all the sap. It can take on a bluish colour if steeped in urine or any ammoniacal solution.

before: It is the largest and most important of the islands of the archipelago. It lies between 32° 52′ 8″ and 32° 37′ 25″ north latitude, and between 16° 39′ 30″ and 17° 16′ 38″ west longitude (Greenwich). It is twenty-one and a half miles from Porto Santo (from Ponta de São Lourenço to the Ilhéu de Baixo, or Ilhéu da Cal) and eleven miles from the Desertas (from Ponta de São Lourenço to Ilhéu Chão (Flat Islet)). From the harbour of Funchal to the anchorage of the town (*vila*) of Porto Santo the distance is forty and a half miles. The island stretches from east to west and has a ‘shape tending towards a pentagon’, roughly defined by the points of São Lourenço to the east, Santa Cruz to the south, Pargo and Tristão to the west, and São Jorge to the north. Its greatest length, east to west, between the extreme limits of Ponta de São Lourenço and Ponta do Tristão, is 67 kilometres, and its greatest width, north to south, between the extreme limits of Ponta de São Jorge and Ponta da Cruz, is 28 kilometres. The perimeter of the coast is conjectured to be approximately 157 kilometres, and its area 500 square kilometres.

before: A high mountain range running from east to west divides Madeira into two coasts, the southern and the northern. In this range, whose heights rise from 1000 to 1861 metres, the island’s great streams have their source. In winter they carry large volumes of water, which have quite often caused damage in Funchal and at other points along the coast. The slopes of the central mountains are generally steeper on the north side than on the south. On the north side there are only two passable landing places, Porto do Moniz and Porto da Cruz, whereas on the southern coast there are several coves and bays where ships and boats can find shelter from the prevailing winds. The main spurs of these mountains are the Penha de Águia and the Cortado de Santana on the north coast, and Ponta do Pargo, Cabo Girão and Cabo Garajau on the south coast.

before: The highest summits of central Madeira are Pico Ruivo, Pico das Torres, Pico do Canário, Pico do Areeiro, Pico de Santo António, Pico Grande and Pico das Torrinhas. They surround the Curral das Freiras, a vast *profundidade* (deep, roughly circular mountain basin) regarded by some geologists as a crater and by others as a valley of erosion. The most notable streams of the island are those of Machico, Santa Cruz, São Pedro, Porto Novo, João Gomes, Santa Luzia, São João, the Socorridos, Câmara de Lobos, the Ribeira Brava, Ponta do Sol, Madalena, São Bartolomeu, Janela, Seixal, São Vicente, the Moinhos, São Jorge and Faial.

before: Funchal is linked to the Terreiro da Luta, above the church of Monte, by a lift or rack railway (1921), and Machico and Ribeira Brava can today be reached in reasonable comfort, since the roads now take motor traffic. The Cumeada de São Vicente, a point in the interior with astonishing views over both the north and the south of the island, has been accessible by car since 1916, and work has already begun on other roads intended to make it easier for tourists to discover the natural beauties of our land. In recent years the roads have been greatly developed, as will be seen in the article ‘Viação’.

before: Around 1486 there were many foreigners in Madeira who had become sugar growers and manufacturers, and for this reason they were twice ordered to leave the island and afterwards readmitted. When Frutuoso wrote the *Saudades da Terra* in 1590, there were many English and Flemish families in Funchal, who carried on their business in the Rua dos Mercadores. The Flemish colony, still important at the beginning of the 17th century, later disappeared or merged with the Madeiran population, whereas the English colony survived and even grew from 1640 onwards, coming in the 19th century to hold a real preponderance in the island’s trade.

before: There was one running between the former Praça da Constituição and Pombal, set up under a licence granted by the Municipal Council to José Ribeiro de Almeida and João Aluísio Virissimo to operate this means of transport in the city. before: On 21 February 1878 the Municipal Council (*Câmara Municipal*) of Funchal appointed a committee of councillors (*vereadores*) charged with promoting, under the supervision of the civil governor, the laying out of gardens on the convent grounds of the former Convent of São Francisco (St Francis of Assisi) and on the land between those grounds and the Praça da Constituição. before: From the very first moments of its formation the Governing Junta of Madeira displayed an astonishing energy, which seems to have surpassed the labours of its counterparts organised in many parts of Portugal. It appointed Manuel Joaquim da Costa Andrade, a teacher at the lyceum (state secondary school), as civil governor. He resigned shortly after taking up the post and was replaced by Lieutenant-Colonel Manuel José Júlio Guerra, who had also been appointed military commander of Madeira. Dr António Ribeiro Pacheco Nunes, Dr Luís da Costa Pereira and Dr Juvenal Honório de Ornelas were appointed deputy crown prosecutor, president of the Council and health officer (*delegado de saúde*) respectively. Many public officials were dismissed and replaced by individuals who had joined the revolutionary movement or embraced the principles proclaimed by the Junta of Porto. Some officers of the garrison were advanced in rank, and several sergeants were promoted to second lieutenant. The governing action of the Madeira Junta was at times felt in a truly arbitrary manner in many branches of public administration, provoking vigorous protests from the people, despite the discretionary powers with which the Junta had invested itself. According to a document of the period, it left the public coffers of the district completely exhausted.

before: It belongs to the municipality (*concelho*) of Porto Moniz and to the judicial district (*comarca*) of Ponta do Sol. It lies approximately 8 kilometres from the seat of the former and about 40 kilometres from that of the latter, by the road through Ponta do Pargo, Fajã da Ovelha, etc. It is divided into the following inhabited localities (*sítios*): Pinheiro, Achada da Arruda, Igreja, Cova, Lombo do Simão, Achada de Castro and Terça. Other localities of lesser importance are Quebrada Nova, Quebrada do Negro, Fajã das Malvas, Fajã Nova, Pomar Velho, Risco, Pico da Azeveda etc. It has a post box installed in the locality of Igreja. There are no state schools, but the parish priest runs two primary education courses, one by day and one in the evening, for boys and adult men. The parish is irrigated by the levadas (irrigation channels) of the Ribeira dos Moinhos, of Lagos and of Pico da Arruda. It has no harbour, only a small pebble beach (*calhau*) that is difficult to reach.

before: We do not know whether the name goes back to the earliest days of colonisation. We do know, however, that in the third or last quarter of the 16th century a small chapel was built there with the dedication of Vera Cruz (True Cross). It is possible that the common people’s tendency to simplify language shortened the longer expression Vera Cruz to the single syllable Cruz, and that in this way the chapel of the Cruz gave its name to the village (*lugar*, settlement rank below a town) or *achada* (small plateau) near which it was built. That is, unless we accept that the present name of the parish existed before the small chapel was built, which would not be easy to establish today. It was certainly in this chapel of Vera Cruz that, in the third quarter of the 16th century, a curacy (*curato*) dependent on the collegiate church of Calheta was established. It was short-lived, however, and was abolished in 1577 by Bishop Dom Jerónimo Barreto. Its abolition was due to the slow growth of the population, which at that time must have been very small and which, over the years, has still developed little. The abolition of this curacy and of three or four others in similar circumstances led to the creation and funding of a new canonry in Funchal Cathedral (*Sé*).

before: In 1611 the prelate requested the restoration of the old curacy, in view of the difficulty the 84 residents of the Achada had in getting to Porto Moniz, and the people made the same request in 1638, on the grounds that there were already some 18 households (*fogos*, literally ‘hearths’) there. These efforts always proved fruitless. Only a century after the abolition of the original curacy was Bishop Dom António Teles da Silva authorised, by a royal decree (*alvará*) of 28 December 1676, ‘to create the curacy of Nossa Senhora da Conceição of Porto Moniz, with the obligation of residence at Achadas da Cruz and to receive its salary from the tithe portion of the same parish’. The royal decree of 5 March 1680 set the curate’s annual salary at twelve thousand *réis* (old Portuguese money of account; 1$000 = 1,000 réis, 1:000$000 = one conto = 1,000,000 réis) in cash, one *moio* (dry measure of grain, 60 *alqueires*) of wheat and one *pipa* (wine cask and measure, c. 400–500 litres) of wine. The first curate appointed was Father Manuel Ferreira da Silva, on 20 July 1677.

before: The old chapel of Vera Cruz, which stood near the locality (*sítio*) of Calvário, did not give the name of its dedication to the patron saint of the parish. The patron became Nossa Senhora do Livramento (Our Lady of Deliverance) in the new chapel that was later built, in a year we cannot determine. before: We have found somewhere that João Gonçalves Zarco granted his son Garcia Rodrigues da Câmara extensive lands at the western end of his captaincy, part of which later came to form the parish of the Achadas. This grant included various lands at Ponta do Pargo and extended to the limit of the donatary captaincy (*donataria*), which lay at the stream or at Ponta do Tristão. There is no basis for the claim that Garcia da Câmara settled on the lands of the Achadas and, with his family and servants, formed the original nucleus of whatever population there was there. Old genealogies state that Garcia da Câmara died without issue, but it is conjectured that the entailed estate (*morgadio*) that existed at Achadas da Cruz was founded by one of his heirs; its last representative died there a few years ago and was called Luís Isidoro Carvalho Drumond.

before: He was born in the parish (*freguesia*) of Porto Moniz on 4 March 1851. He was a bachelor (*bacharel*, university graduate) in theology from the University of Coimbra (*Universidade de Coimbra*), completing his degree in 1879, and in that same year he was ordained priest. He was teaching at the Archiepiscopal Seminary of Évora (*Seminário Arquiepiscopal de Évora*) when, in 1888, he was presented to a canonry of Funchal Cathedral (*Sé*), and he was later raised to the office of dean of the same Cathedral. Here in Madeira he was professor and vice-rector of the Seminary, vicar-general and on several occasions governor of the diocese (governador do bispado, administering the see in the bishop's absence). He also carried out other duties, such as president of the Administrative Committee (*Comissão Administrativa*) of the Holy House (*Santa Casa*, the Misericórdia), etc.

before: A distinguished Madeiran craftsman and industrialist, he died in Funchal on 24 August 1856, aged 64. In 1822 he built a new steam still, very simple and with excellent practical results. In March 1828 he set up a sugar factory in Funchal, the first in Madeira since the collapse of the Madeiran sugar industry in the mid-18th century. The factory was greatly improved in 1856, shortly before its owner’s death. He was a corresponding member of the Funchal Society of Friends of the Sciences and Arts (*Sociedade Funchalense dos Amigos das Sciencias e Artes*) and a member of the Municipal Council (*Câmara Municipal*), and he wrote an article on precious stones in no. 50 of the *Patriota Funchalense*. He suffered persecution under the government of Miguel I because of his liberal ideas.

before: Following the example of other countries, Portugal also wished to glorify the Unknown Soldiers who had given their lives for their homeland in the fight against the Germans. To this end, a programme of honours to be paid to these heroes was drawn up and published in the *Diário do Governo*, 2nd series, of 26 March 1921. As was to be expected of the well-proven patriotism of the Portuguese people, the programme was carried out with the greatest splendour and solemnity in all the country’s major centres. In accordance with the instructions of this programme, made public in Funchal by a public notice (*edital*) of the civil governor, the competent authorities had the national flags raised at midday on 7 April 1921 – the day chosen for the lying-in-state of the coffins of the Unknown Soldiers of France and of Africa in the Palace of National Sovereignty – on the fortresses, barracks and public buildings, where they remained until sunset on the 10th. At the same hour the infantry band played the national anthem and the salute march, and the church bells rang for 15 minutes.

before: In 1705 the book *Il Primo Scuoprimento dell'isola di Madera fatto da Roberto Macico inglese...* was published at Tortona, Italy, translated from the Portuguese and greatly expanded by Father Teodoro de Pavia. It is a volume of 190 pages, divided into two chapters. The first, which gave the book its title, is a literal translation of the celebrated third *Epanafora* of Dom Francisco Manuel de Melo, first published in 1660 and later reissued in other editions. As is well known, it was through this narrative by Dom Francisco de Melo that the legendary adventure of Roberto Machim became widely known, and even came to acquire a certain standing as historical truth among some of the more credulous writers.

before: A tree native to the Mediterranean region, widely cultivated in Madeira and Porto Santo. The most prized Madeiran figs are the *doces*, the *martinhos*, the *brancos*, the *cotios* and the *beberas*, the last being distinguished from the rest by their black colour and elongated shape. Figs that pass the winter in a rudimentary state and develop early the following year are called *lampos*.

before: A marine web-footed bird, not very common in these islands. It frequents the open sea by day, returning to land late at night. As a day bird it is called *boieiro* by seafarers; as a night bird it is known throughout Madeira as *estrapagado*, *papagarro* or *patagarro*, onomatopoeic names that imitate its characteristic call fairly well. It breeds on the Desertas and on the less accessible cliffs of Madeira, such as Curral das Freiras, Areeiro and Penha de Águia. The clutch is a single pure white egg, laid in a hole in the rocks. Many people regard it as a bird of ill omen. According to popular belief, a death will soon occur among the occupants of a house whenever a *patagarro* alights on it during its nocturnal flight from the mountains to the sea, or vice versa. It migrates, leaving the archipelago during the winter and returning at the end of February or the beginning of March.

before: The *embate* generally comes from the south-west, owing to the strength of the north-east breeze, and that is why sailing vessels passing between the Ponta de São Lourenço and the Desertas take that course to enter the harbour of Funchal. before: The chapel of Santo António (St Anthony) in the parish (*freguesia*) of Santana dates from the second quarter of the 16th century. It was not built in 1730, as Dr Álvaro Rodrigues de Azevedo states, but rebuilt around that time. In 1729 the people asked the ecclesiastical authority for permission to reconstruct it, stating that it had been built by the parishioners roughly two centuries earlier. Its reconstruction was completed on 13 April 1730, the day it was inspected so that it could be blessed and then opened for worship.

before: Father Manuel Fernandes de Sant'Ana was born on 14 May 1864 in the parish (*freguesia*) of São Gonçalo, the son of Francisco Fernandes and Dona Ana Pereira Fernandes de Sant'Ana. In 1881 he abandoned the preparatory course at the seminary of this diocese to enter the Society of Jesus, in which he took his vows and remained until his death. Giving his schooling a new direction, he began his studies in Portugal, continued them in Spain, Germany and England, and completed them in the Netherlands. At Oña, in Spain, on a philosophy course for aspirants to the Society, he was judged the most talented of ninety select students, with the sharpest and most penetrating intellect. His academic triumphs were as many as the subjects and disciplines he studied. He distinguished himself in oriental languages – Greek, it is said, was as familiar to him as his own mother tongue – and in mathematics, biology and the social sciences; in theology he had a profound knowledge of everything connected with the vast field of Holy Scripture studies.

before: We do not know the date of the decree that established this parish, but we know that its creation goes back to the first years of the 16th century, the annotator of the *Saudades* assigning it to the year 1509. We believe that it had previously been the seat of a curacy (*curato*) in the chapel of Nossa Senhora da Graça (Our Lady of Grace), which stood there and was later turned into the parish church. before: We do not know when the chapel of Nossa Senhora da Graça was built. It gave its name to the new parish (*freguesia*), and the parish seat was established in it. The small church underwent major repairs at roughly the time the parish was created, and important works were also carried out there in the last quarter of the 17th century. We know of the following instruments, which we found noted in the General Index of the register of the former Royal Treasury Office (*Provedoria da Real Fazenda*): an order of the Council of the Treasury (*Conselho da Fazenda*), dated 23 September 1692, for the work on the new church, bought at auction by Francisco Rodrigues for 811,000 *réis* (old Portuguese money of account; 1$000 = 1,000 réis, 1:000$000 = one conto = 1,000,000 réis); an order of the same Council, dated 5 March 1748, for the building of the church, and for 194,000 *réis* to pay for one *alqueire* (dry measure for grain; as a land measure c. 900 m²) and half a *quarta* of the land needed for the said work, and for 551,662 *réis* for the vicar’s house, which was to be pulled down for the same purpose; and an order of 15 February 1764 for the work on the high altar to be awarded at auction to the master woodcarver Julião Francisco, for 2,000 *réis*. Beyond what the documents cited say, we were able to establish from a reliable source that around the middle of the 18th century the old church was demolished, leaving the chancel standing, which went on serving as the parish church for some years. On 3 February 1753 the foundation stone of the new church was laid and blessed. On 18 January 1756 the chancel was blessed and the Blessed Sacrament was carried into it, after which the rest of the building work continued. This church was consecrated in 1814 by the diocesan prelate Dom Joaquim de Meneses e Ataíde.

before: At the beginning of the 19th century the territorial militia formed a third-line corps, with the following *capitanias-mores* in Madeira: Funchal, Câmara de Lobos, Campanário, Ribeira Brava, Ponta do Sol, Madalena, Calheta, Porto do Moniz, São Vicente, Ponta Delgada, Porto da Cruz, Machico, Santa Cruz and Caniço. ‘After the Castilian rule,’ says Dr Álvaro de Azevedo, ‘the Portuguese militia underwent four reforms or renewals up to 1809: 1st, that of John IV, decreed by resolution of the Cortes (Portuguese parliament) around 1641, with two kinds of troops, paid and auxiliary, all other men remaining in the territorial militia, which served as a kind of nursery of recruits; 2nd, that of John V, instituted by the royal decree of 15 November 1707, which was given the name of the new *ordenanças*; 3rd, that of Joseph I, set out in the regulations (1763–1766) known as those of the Count of Lippe, because the reform was inspired by that illustrious general, then commander of the Portuguese troops; and 4th, finally, that of 1806–1809.’

before: Empress Elisabeth, wife of Franz Joseph, Emperor of Austria, who on 10 September 1898 fell dead under the treacherous dagger blow of the anarchist Lucheni, first visited Madeira in 1860 and stayed on the island for about five months. Her doctors had advised her to seek a temperate climate in which to spend the winter, where she could also escape for a while the burdens of the demanding etiquette of the court and so make a complete recovery of her shaken health. Funchal was the resort chosen for this purpose, and the house preferred for her residence was the Quinta Vigia. With its enviable situation, beautiful gardens, commanding position above the sea and fine view over the whole amphitheatre of the city, it was considered one of the most splendid residences in Madeira.
