before: Apart from the bays of Funchal, Porto Santo and Abra, the cove of Machico is the widest and most picturesque in the archipelago. It is fringed by a fine stretch of beach and overlooked by two roads, and it opens directly onto a most beautiful valley that extends for several kilometres along the green banks of the stream. The centre of the town (*vila*) is linked to the landing quay by a handsome tree-lined road, which makes the most pleasant of walks on calm summer evenings. Many years ago a landing place was built near the southern end of the cove, beside the chapel of São Roque (St Roch), but it was later entirely abandoned. On the other side of the bay a quay was planned, making use of a reef (restinga) there, together with a road connecting it to the interior of the town; these works were carried out between 1870 and 1873. As that landing place was considered inadequate, a new and larger quay was built in 1905, and it was altered and improved in 1907. At the end of 1931 three harbour lights were placed at the three points marking the entrance to this bay, and they are giving excellent service to the many fishing boats that make for this cove at night. The harbour is fairly large but shallow, so vessels of large tonnage cannot enter it. Above the site of the quay stood an old fort, known as the Desembarcadouro fort or the Fort of São João Baptista (St John the Baptist), now dismantled. On its esplanade a hospital was improvised in 1910, during the cholera epidemic that ravaged Madeira at that time.

before: The Fleming António de Leme held land by *sesmaria* (royal land grant to settlers on condition of cultivation) in the parish (*freguesia*) of Santo António, in the locality (*sítio*) still known today as Quinta do Leme, and there he built a house and chapel, which the annotator of the *Saudades* dates to 1536. From documents we have had occasion to examine, we see that this chapel of São Filipe was rebuilt in 1654 by Inácio da Câmara Leme, the founder’s successor in the administration of this entail. The earthquake of 1748 left it badly ruined, and it was rebuilt once more in 1752 by its administrator, Francisco Aurélio da Câmara Leme.

before: We have said elsewhere that not long ago the following inscription could still be read on a tombstone in this chapel: ‘Tomb of the innocents who were cruelly killed at the Achada of this city. 1621.’ We do not know the names of the persons to whom this inscription refers, nor the reasons for those deaths, but it may be supposed that they were members of the Limoges family, to whom the chapel belonged (1921).

before: Information gathered after that date allows us to state with certainty that the date inscribed on the tomb is 1666, and that the epitaph refers to the burial there of the bones of many children killed by the ‘foundling nurse’ (*ama dos expostos*) of that time. She took in the ‘foundlings’, killed them and buried them near her home in the well-known locality of Achada, in the parish of São Roque. This chapel, which was in an advanced state of ruin, was restored by its owner, the Countess of Torre Bela, and blessed by the diocesan prelate on 13 April 1925.

before: The idea of establishing a Natural History Museum is a fairly old one. Nearly a century ago the civil governor José Silvestre Ribeiro, a benefactor of the island, laid the foundations for such an institution: he made several rooms of the Palácio de São Lourenço (St Lawrence Palace) available for it and gave it devoted support, both with his prestige and with the means at his disposal, towards its permanent installation. When Councillor (conselheiro, honorary title of the royal council) Silvestre Ribeiro left the island, the Museum, which, though inadequate and of modest proportions, already represented a hope, soon disappeared entirely.

before: Valuable light is shed on this subject by what we briefly outlined in a newspaper of this city in 1934, which we shall partly transcribe. ‘The Municipal Council (*Câmara Municipal*) of Funchal, meeting a long-standing and acknowledged need, saw fit to create in this capital of the district a museum of natural-history specimens of a strictly regional character. In doing so it followed in the wake of the original initiative of the Civil Governor José Silvestre Ribeiro, which unfortunately did not last long, and it complemented the fine undertaking of Father Ernesto Schmitz in setting up the Seminary Museum, which has been the object of the greatest admiration and esteem on the part of distinguished naturalists, who have often referred to it in works of the highest scientific standing.

In doing so it followed in the wake of the original initiative of the Civil Governor José Silvestre Ribeiro, which unfortunately did not last long, and it complemented the fine undertaking of Father Ernst Schmitz in setting up the Seminary Museum (*Museu do Seminário*), which has been the object of the greatest admiration and esteem on the part of distinguished naturalists, who have often referred to it in works of the highest scientific standing.

before: Then came the decree of 7 March 1932, which deals only with museums of art, archaeology, etc., and makes not even a remote reference to establishments of the kind found in Funchal. But was the Council of this city obliged to adapt the conditions of its museum to the provisions of the new decree? It could no doubt do so voluntarily, but nothing in that enactment compelled it to. And since there was then no law, nor is there any yet, preventing a municipal council from establishing a museum on the terms on which Funchal’s operates, we consider that the Council acts lawfully in keeping its Regional Museum in the state in which it was created and in which it is at present. And is there any legal rule that forbids maintaining a small art section attached to a Museum of Natural Sciences?

before: It is conjectured that its original name was Madalesia or Santa Maria Madalena, and that the words ‘do Mar’ (of the sea) were added later because it is washed by the ocean – and perhaps still more to distinguish it from the locality and chapel of Santa Maria Madalena in the parish of Porto do Moniz, when that place became the centre of a well-known and much-frequented pilgrimage. The hypothesis is not entirely without foundation, and there are other examples that support it. The name by which it is generally known today, even in official documents, is Madalena do Mar, although the people, with their tendency to simplify language, also call it simply Madalena.

before: The parish grew out of a settled estate (*fazenda povoada*) that existed there from the earliest days of colonisation, with a chantry (capela) whose patron saint was, as is stated somewhere, Santa Maria Madalena; it is also claimed that the original chapel was dedicated to St Catherine. On this origin, several old books of noble lineages contain what is summarised in the notes to the *Saudades*, in the following terms: ‘... Henry the German, a legendary figure of the earliest days of the colonisation of this island of Madeira. It was said of him that he was a Polish prince, and that after Władysław III lost the battle of Varna against Murad II in 1444 he vowed to wander the earth and was dubbed a knight of St Catherine of Mount Sinai. When he came to the island of Madeira, João Gonçalves Zarco granted him, at the spot later called Madalena do Mar, a large tract of land as a *sesmaria* (royal land grant to settlers on condition of cultivation), by a charter confirmed by Prince Henry the Navigator on 29 April 1457 and by Afonso V on 18 May of the same year. Henry the German did indeed found a large settled estate there, with a chapel dedicated to Santa Maria Madalena, from which the place took its name. He married Senhorinha Anes, and met a disastrous death, crushed by a landslide (*quebrada*) that fell from Cabo Girão onto the boat in which he was travelling from the city of Funchal to Madalena. His widow later married João Rodrigues de Freitas. Even now there is, above the town of Ponta do Sol, the Fajã do Alemão, which the people corruptly call “do limão”.’

before: Towards the end of 1858 a society of eighteen young men was formed in this city with the aim of staging some theatrical performances and building a small playhouse. This society, named Esperança, included among others Júlio Galhardo de Freitas and Pedro de Alcântara Góis, who had already shown their remarkable talent for the stage in several performances. The merchant João de Freitas Martins came to the aid of this worthy society by placing at its disposal an excellent warehouse he owned on Rua dos Aranhas. Conversion work began at once. The Council of Funchal contributed 200,000 *réis* (old Portuguese money of account; 1$000 = 1,000 réis, 1:000$000 = one conto = 1,000,000 réis), and the Count of Carvalhal gave a similar sum and donated the scenery, this nobleman being the most devoted patron of the Esperança Society.

before: A distinguished English botanist who died in London, aged 80, on 19 May 1820. He was in Madeira from 12 to 18 September 1768 as botanist to the first expedition commanded by Captain Cook, and took from this island a large number of flowering plants, as well as a variety of information on matters of natural history. Banks’s manuscripts show that he and his companion Dr Solander collected 255 species in Madeira, even though the season was not among the best suited to botanical exploration. The small herbarium of the two naturalists is deposited in the Museum.
after: A distinguished English botanist who died in London, aged 80, on 19 May 1820. He was in Madeira from 12 to 18 September 1768 as botanist to the first expedition commanded by Captain James Cook, and took from this island a large number of flowering plants, as well as a variety of information on matters of natural history. Joseph Banks’s manuscripts show that he and his companion Dr Daniel Solander collected 255 species in Madeira, even though the season was not among the best suited to botanical exploration. The small herbarium of the two naturalists is deposited in the Museum.

before: Old Madeiran books of genealogy say that Afonso Álvares Columbreiro, a native of a settlement on the outskirts of Seville, was one of the first and noble settlers of the village (*lugar*, settlement rank below a town) of Ribeira Brava. They add that he founded there the chantries (capela) of Santa Catarina (St Catherine of Alexandria) and São Bento (St Benedict of Nursia) within the entailed estate (*morgadio*) he had established, whose seat lay in that parish (*freguesia*). One of his granddaughters, named Brígida Gonçalves, and her husband João Mealheiro or Malheiro, who held the rank of noblemen, were the ancestors of Father Manuel Álvares. He therefore came of noble lineage, which in any case adds little to his undeniable merits and virtues. His parents were Sebastião Gonçalves and Beatriz Álvares, who retained the privileges of nobility inherited from their forebears.

before: His vocation for the Church had dawned early, for as early as 1538 he had received the so-called minor orders from Dom Ambrósio Brandão, titular bishop of Rocina, who had come to this island to perform the episcopal functions temporarily. Father António Franco relates that a carrack bound for India put in at Funchal and, because of illness, landed a member of the Society of Jesus, who took refuge in the hospital to be treated for the sickness that had struck him. Manuel Álvares went to visit him to obtain news and information about an old friend and fellow student of his. From his dealings with the religious grew the desire to embrace the order of St Ignatius, which since its foundation in 1540 had enjoyed extraordinary renown and attracted many vocations to the Church. He soon left his father’s house and entered the Jesuit congregation in 1546, as already mentioned.

before: We shall close this biographical note with the very words of the author of the *Bibliotheca Lusitana*: ‘He was an exemplary model of all the religious virtues, earning for them the praise of his holy patriarch. before: (Parish of). It is not easy to establish the true origin of the name of this parish (*freguesia*). A learned person who lived there for some years and carried out serious research informs us that the name comes from Antónia Delgada, widow of Captain António Gonçalves de Castro, who died on 8 October 1606. Against this assertion we must set the existence of several royal decrees of the 16th century, the oldest dating from 1552, entered in the registers of the former Crown Revenue Office (*Provedoria*), which refer directly to the parish of Ponta Delgada. Gaspar Frutuoso, too, gives it the name Ponta Delgada in 1590, saying that it is ‘so called because there is a very dangerous passage there, which is crossed on top of two poles laid from one cliff to the other, and the sea lies so far below that it is lost to sight’. Nor, certainly, is it a very satisfactory explanation that a narrow and dangerous passage overhanging the sea should be called Ponta Delgada.

before: In the earliest days of colonisation this village (*lugar*, settlement rank below a town) was called Senhor Jesus, after the chapel of that dedication which stood there, and it was still known by that name after the parish was created. There is no doubt, however, that from the middle of the 16th century the name Ponta Delgada came into general use, and it was by this name that the place later became known.
after: In the earliest days of colonisation this village (*lugar*, settlement rank below a town) was called the Lord Jesus (*Senhor Jesus*), after the chapel of that dedication which stood there, and it was still known by that name after the parish was created. There is no doubt, however, that from the middle of the 16th century the name Ponta Delgada came into general use, and it was by this name that the place later became known.

before: Manuel Afonso de Sanha was one of the earliest settlers of this island, and in 1469 he obtained extensive lands by *sesmaria* (royal land grant to settlers on condition of cultivation), stretching from Ponta Delgada to the Ribeira das Vacas. He founded the chapel of Senhor Bom Jesus (Lord Good Jesus), which became the centre of a settled estate (*fazenda povoada*); this estate formed the original nucleus of inhabitants who made up the future parish.

before: The area of this parish comprised the land that constitutes it at present and also the present parish of Boaventura. before: The chapel of Senhor Bom Jesus was the centre of an ancient pilgrimage, which is still today one of the best attended on the whole island. It is recorded as already taking place in 1577, which makes it the oldest pilgrimage festival held here in Madeira. The pilgrimages of Senhor Jesus of Ponta Delgada, of Nossa Senhora do Monte (Our Lady of the Mount) and of Senhor dos Milagres at Machico are the oldest, the best attended and the most characteristic of this diocese.

before: This parish has the Chapel of Reis Magos (Three Kings), which belonged to the house of Carvalhal. There was formerly a chapel of Santo António at the locality of Pico, and another at the locality of Ladrilhos; we shall deal with these elsewhere in this work.

before: António de Carvalhal was a former resident of this parish and died here on 15 July 1598. Of him Gaspar Frutuoso says: ‘a man as chivalrous as he was personally valiant, noble and magnificent by his station and great virtue, through which, by his magnificence, he has acquired such fame and won such renown in the hearts of men that they obey him for it; and should it be necessary to raise a cry, he will gather five hundred men from the northern side to his service, for any feat of war, as has already happened to him, or for any other purpose; and not without reason, for his house is a hospital and shelter for every poor person, a lodging for travellers and, in short, a refuge for the needy. Thus he spends all his estate (and he owns a great deal on this side) on these works, so that in his house thirty *moios* of wheat are consumed each year, besides many others that he lends, and with it he succours those in need, all of which he gathers from his own farming’. The historian of the islands then goes on to narrate in detail many feats and episodes of strength and valour performed by António de Carvalhal, as may be read on pp. 101 and 102 of the *Saudades da Terra*.

before: The parish of Ponta Delgada was once called the ‘court of the north’, because it contained many houses of old and noble families, who lived there or spent a considerable part of the year there. Several entailed estates had their seat in the parish. Manuel Afonso de Sanha founded the entails of Ribeiro do Pêso and Ribeira do Inferno.

before: The principal crops are the vine and sugar cane, and there are two mills for making spirit (aguardente, distilled from sugar cane or wine). before: He was born in Funchal in 1806. On 9 August 1834 he was appointed superintendent (provedor) of Porto Santo, later becoming municipal administrator (administrador do concelho, the government's representative) of the same island, a post he held for many years. He was also interim Civil Governor of the district of Funchal from 8 to 18 January 1862. He wrote the *Anais do Município do Porto Santo*, the original of which is held in the archive of that municipality, and he was one of the men who rendered the greatest services to that island. He died in Funchal on 22 June 1874.

before: In the letters granting the three captaincies to the first donataries, the prince mentions a ‘Foral’, a charter (*foral*), and we do not know whether this was a document distinct from the instructions we have referred to. It certainly existed, however, because the ‘Foral’ granted in 1515 by King Manuel I to the municipalities of Funchal, Ponta do Sol and Calheta contains an express reference to the charter granted by Prince Henry, as can be seen on page 494 of the notes to the *Saudades da Terra*. Elsewhere we refer at greater length to the documents cited here and to the prince’s role in the great enterprise of the early colonisation of this archipelago, and to those pages we direct the patient reader’s attention.

before: This is one of the most important watercourses on the island. It forms the boundary between the parishes (*freguesias*) of São Martinho and Santo António, on its left bank, and those of Câmara de Lobos and Estreito de Câmara de Lobos, on its right bank. São Martinho and Câmara de Lobos flank the mouth of the stream. It rises in the interior of the island, in the locality (*sítio*) of Torrinhas, and crosses the parish of Curral das Freiras.

before: A locality (*sítio*) in the parish (*freguesia*) of Estreito da Calheta, where there is a chapel dedicated to Nossa Senhora da Conceição (Our Lady of the Immaculate Conception), built in 1673 by André de França e Andrade. It was the seat of one of the largest entailed estates in Madeira, and the last representative of this entailed house (*casa vinculada*) was Diogo de Ornelas de França Carvalhal Frasão Figueiroa, 11th Viscount and Count of Calçada (see that entry).

before: We have scant information about capital executions carried out in this archipelago by public sentence. It has been suggested that the locality (*sítio*) known as Forca, in the parish (*freguesia*) of Santa Maria Maior, was the place where a death sentence was once carried out, with the gallows as the instrument of punishment applied to the criminal. We do not know, and we are even inclined to believe that the explanation given for the name of that locality has no serious foundation.

before: At the dawn of the 17th century a man named Francisco Rodrigues Jardim, of plebeian origin, was hanged in effigy in the Largo do Pelourinho of this city for abducting a lady named Dona Maria de Ornelas, who belonged to old and noble Madeiran families. Had he not escaped the reach of justice by flight, he would have paid for the audacity of his crime on the gallows.

before: This prelate of the diocese of São Paulo (Brazil) was born in the parish (*freguesia*) of Campanário on 14 March 1767, the son of Nicolau Gonçalves de Andrade and Maria de Andrade. before: It seems that the existence in Funchal of the Teatro Grande (see that entry), a large and showy playhouse, did not justify the construction of a new theatre, which was given the name Teatro de Bom Gosto and was built a few metres away from it. We do not know exactly when it was built, but we conjecture that it was between 1818 and 1820; it certainly already existed in 1821. It stood between Rua de São Francisco and the Misericórdia building (*Edifício da Misericórdia*) (1921), with access both to that street and to the side of the old public promenade (*passeio público*). We do not know what led to the building of this new theatre, although some years ago we heard it said that it was chiefly owed to a whim of the 1st Count of Carvalhal.

before: We do not know whether that nobleman had it built, but we do know that it belonged to him and that, on returning from exile at the end of 1834, he had major repairs carried out there. before: At the locality (*sítio*) of Piedade, on the Ponta de São Lourenço, there are numerous calcareous bodies that look like petrified tree trunks and branches. Many of them show concentric layers similar to those seen in certain woody plants. Some of these bodies extend at their lower end into a kind of root, with the shape and direction of the roots of dicotyledonous plants.
after: At the locality (*sítio*) of Piedade (‘pity’), on the Ponta (‘point’) de São Lourenço, there are numerous calcareous bodies that look like petrified tree trunks and branches. before: The naturalists who have visited Piedade do not agree on how to explain the origin of these bodies. The botanist Lowe regarded them as sandy-calcareous concretions; Macaulay as a coral formation of the family Alcyonidae; the geologist Smith as mere casts formed in spaces once occupied by plants; and Mousinho de Albuquerque and Bowdich as the petrified remains of an ancient forest.
after: The naturalists who have visited Piedade do not agree on how to explain the origin of these bodies. before: An inhabited locality (*sítio*) in the parish (*freguesia*) of Porto da Cruz, with 105 *foros* and 651 inhabitants. There was once a chapel there dedicated to Nossa Senhora da Fé (Our Lady of Faith), founded in 1826 by the holder of the entail (*morgado*) Diogo Dias de Orneias e Vasconcelos. There was also a chapel there dedicated to Santo António (St Anthony of Padua), belonging to the Nunes Caldeira family and founded around 1760. This locality belonged to the entailed estate (*morgadio*) founded by the Genoese João Baptista of the Italian Usodimare family, who married a child of the first donatary (*donatário*) of Machico, Tristão Vaz Teixeira; its last representative was João Bettencourt Baptista.

before: Dr Álvaro R. de Azevedo gave the name *profundidades* (‘depths’) to certain places of considerable altitude, fair extent and roughly circular shape, because the generic term ‘valleys’ did not suit them. He mentions the *profundidades* of Curral das Freiras, in the parish (*freguesia*) of that name, the most remarkable of them all; that of Fanal, in the mountains of the parish of Ribeira da Janela; that of Rabaçal, in the valley of the said stream; and that of Fõjo, near Praia Formosa, in the parish of São Martinho.

before: As is well known, the ship that João Gonçalves Zarco commanded at the discovery of Madeira was called the São Lourenço, and when he first approached that tongue of land he gave it the name of the caravel that carried him. The tip of this point, or rather a small isolated rock lying opposite it, was always considered the most suitable site for a lighthouse, since its light would reach a considerable part of the north and south of the island, as well as the crossing that separates Madeira from Porto Santo. This rock is an islet next to the point, from which it is separated by a narrow channel navigable only by small vessels.

before: In the angle formed halfway along the street that runs from the convent of Santa Clara (St Clare of Assisi) to the site where the convent of Nossa Senhora das Mercês (Our Lady of Ransom) once stood, a small and unusual chapel opens into the living rock. It is known as the Capela or Capelinha das Almas. That mass of basalt probably offered a hollow, or there may even have been a small grotto or cave there, which gave rise to the idea of building the chapel. Local tradition, however, tells a legend which, it seems to us, has also been used to explain similar buildings in other places and localities. It is said that a man sought a safe hiding place in a dense cane field that grew there, intending to murder a bitter enemy who was in the habit of passing that way at late hours. Night after night, and on successive days, he failed to carry out his wicked plan, because the intended victim always passed by in the company of other people. In the end the would-be killer resolved to abandon the idea that had obsessed him for so many days. When the man thus spared from his enemy’s savage fury later learned of the planned murder, he saw in it a clear miracle, since he had always passed that spot alone and entirely unaccompanied. He attributed his escape from becoming the innocent victim of that attack to the intervention of the souls in purgatory, to whom he had the most fervent devotion. From this arose the idea of building the chapel on the very spot where he believed the miracle had taken place. Major A. A. Sarmento used the subject of this legend for one of the chapters of his book *Migalhas*, introducing variants and episodes better suited to a romanticised treatment of the scene.

before: The landing place serving this parish and other neighbouring parishes (*freguesias*) handles a relatively large amount of traffic. It is much to be regretted that no small quay has yet been built there, given the difficulty of access to the narrow cove bordering the locality (*sítio*) of Vila, the only point where passengers and goods may be landed and embarked. Adjoining the town (*vila*) is a beach of large rounded boulders, which bounds the same landing place. All this traffic takes place chiefly at two points: the main one is the so-called Rampa, and the other is in the locality of Serra de Água, near the mouth of the stream of that name. The steamers of the coastal shipping service call there regularly. The landing place lies 2.3 miles from Fajã do Mar and 2.1 from Jardim do Mar respectively, these being the nearest landing places to it.

before: This surname descends from João Salviati, a native of Florence who, with several members of his family and other compatriots, joined in defending his homeland against the oppression and tyranny of the Medici around the middle of the 15th century. When they failed, some of them were hanged, while others had to seek safe refuge in exile and flight from the persecution of the Medici’s supporters. An archbishop, João Salviati’s uncle, was hanged from one of the battlements of his palace, while João Salviati found asylum in Madeira from the persecution directed against him. Here he was received with distinction, in recognition of the noble cause he had defended and of his aristocratic descent, and he retained the privileges of nobility he had enjoyed in his homeland. He held lands as a *sesmaria* (royal land grant to settlers on condition of cultivation) on the bank of the Ribeira dos Socorridos, in the parish (*freguesia*) of Câmara de Lobos, where he settled, and also in the parish of Arco da Calheta, in the locality (*sítio*) that still bears the name Florenças today. There one of his descendants, named João Homem de El-Rei, founded an entailed estate (*morgadio*).

before: Wheat is grown in every parish of the archipelago, but its cultivation appears most important in the parishes of Santa Cruz, Calheta, Arco da Calheta, Ponta do Pargo, São Vicente, Porto do Moniz and Porto da Cruz. It is almost always sown by hand, and it is harvested either by pulling it up or by cutting it with a sickle, the latter method being more common than the former. Threshing is done in one of three ways. It may take place on threshing floors, where the ears are trodden by oxen harnessed to a board with stones and pieces of iron fixed to its underside; or with hand-driven machines; or, finally, with flails, this last method being used only when the quantities of wheat harvested from a given plot are small.

before: A native web-footed bird of the family Procellariidae. It is a seabird that migrates between October and November, returning at the end of February or the beginning of March, and breeds in June. It then lays a single, entirely white egg on the steep coastal cliffs, which is ready to hatch after a month. It is hunted on all the islands, but it is chiefly on the Desertas and the Selvagens that its capture becomes profitable. At present the number of young birds taken each year on the Selvagens by men from São Gonçalo and Caniço, who go there for that particular purpose, averages 18,000. Once salted, the *cagarra* is brought to Madeira, where it is sold mainly to the poorer classes, who value it highly despite the marked fishy aftertaste and oily character of its flesh. The hunters of the Selvagens also call it *pardela*, as do the Spaniards of the Canary Islands.

before: Our region has 102 endemic species and 54 that are shared between the Madeira archipelago and other groups of islands in the Atlantic. before: Almost beside the road that leads from the Ponte Monumental (Monumental Bridge) to the town (*vila*) of Câmara de Lobos stands the chapel of Nossa Senhora da Ajuda (Our Lady of Help). It was built by Fernão Favila on the estate he owned in São Martinho, and he made it the seat of an entailed estate (*morgadio*). This Fernão Favila was a nobleman of the Royal Household (*fidalgo da Casa Real*) and fought valiantly in Africa, afterwards settling on this island, where he married Beatriz Pires. Other genealogists, however, state that it was António Favila, son of Fernão Favila, who founded the entail (*morgado*) of the Piornais, with its seat in the chapel of Ajuda, where he lies buried, having died in October 1545. Councillor (conselheiro, honorary title of the royal council) Manuel José Vieira, as owner of this chapel, carried out major restorations there in 1876, and it was blessed on 16 August of that year.

before: Faria e Castro was in Madeira in 1898 and 1903, and in both years he also visited several European cities. before: The importance and commercial traffic of the settlement of Santa Cruz earned it a customs house long before it was raised to the rank of town (*vila*). Thus we find that the royal letter (*carta régia*) of 15 March 1477 – that is, 38 years before the municipality was created – ordered a revenue house to be established there for collecting taxes and royal dues. We do not know whether it began to operate immediately; the oldest document concerning it that we know of dates from 1549.

before: The building of the Santa Cruz customs house must have been demolished towards the end of the second quarter of the 19th century. Some people still alive today remember it. It stood in the centre of the town, at the beginning of the street that now bears the name of Dr Barros e Sousa and leads to the public promenade. It had a certain air of grandeur and was built in the Manueline style of the period, with pointed-arch windows and doors, in every respect similar to those of the building of the Municipal Council (*Câmara Municipal*). It was a pity that it was not preserved with the respect owed to the venerable relics of the past. It was a monument bearing witness to the prosperity of the old town of Santa Cruz, which lost its former importance as Funchal grew and prospered.

before: The *Saudades da Terra* devotes eight long pages to one Gaspar Borges who, after the sack by the French pirates, unspiked the artillery pieces. These had been judged completely useless, and to everyone’s great amazement he managed to restore them to their original use. Judging by the detail into which Frutuoso goes and the praise with which he extols Gaspar Borges’s work, he must indeed have been a most skilful mechanic of uncommon competence, whatever hyperbole there may be in the chronicler’s account. To us it seems very strange that Gaspar Frutuoso should have taken the detailing of the affair so far and become so enthusiastic a eulogist of the unspiking of those guns! (Anyone wishing to learn in detail of the strange skill of the notorious Borges should read the *Saudades* from page 283 onwards. Marceliano Ribeiro de Mendonça published an interesting historical novel entitled *Gaspar Borges*, whose main protagonist is the skilful craftsman to whom the *Saudades* refers at such length.

before: Among the outsiders of noble birth whom the hazards of fortune brought to this island in the days of colonisation, one stands out: the Flemish *fidalgo* (nobleman of the lesser nobility) João de Esmenaut, whose name was Portuguesised as João de Esmeraldo and who seems to have landed in Funchal around 1480. He proved his noble descent, and by a royal letter (*carta régia*) of 13 August 1511 Manuel I ordered that the privileges of a *fidalgo* be upheld for him, since he was one in Picardy, the land of his birth. Later, by a royal decree (*alvará*) of 16 May 1520, which is transcribed in the nobiliary of H. Henriques de Noronha, he was granted a coat of arms and made a nobleman of the Royal Household (*fidalgo da Casa Real*), an honour that Charles V of Spain had already conferred on him earlier. This coat of arms comprises, besides the arms proper to the Esmenauts, the arms of Piennes, Hallwin and Nedenchel, families allied to the former and among the most illustrious in the north of France.

before: João Esmeraldo held a great deal of land on this island by *sesmaria* (royal land grant to settlers on condition of cultivation), and by a deed of 28 January 1498 he bought, or took on quit-rent, from Rui Gonçalves da Câmara, son of João Gonçalves Zarco, the great property called Lombada da Ponta do Sol. It later took the name of Lombada dos Esmeraldos, and we shall deal with it in a separate article. There he founded the entail (*morgado*) of Santo Espírito. By a deed of 12 June 1522, with the consent of his second wife, Agueda de Abreu, of his son by his first marriage, João Esmeraldo, and of his son by his second marriage, Cristovão Esmeraldo, he divided it into two entailed estates (*morgadio*), called Santo Espírito and Vale da Bica. By lot, the first fell to Cristovão and the second to João Esmeraldo, and all this was confirmed by John III by royal decree (alvará régio) of 13 November of that year.

before: Despite its size and the 80 slaves it held, we find a production of twenty thousand *arrobas* on a single property excessive, especially at a time when a considerable part of the land was still uncultivated and its difficult clearing proceeded very slowly, owing chiefly to the relief and ruggedness of the terrain. It should also be noted that João Esmeraldo was Flemish or French, and not Genoese as Frutuoso asserts. Although we consider the chronicler’s words somewhat hyperbolic, we cannot help believing in the wealth and prosperity of the Lombada, if we bear in mind the importance it still has today, the large dwelling house and handsome church that Esmeraldo built there, and the many references we have found to this property, which was regarded as the most important entailed estate of the opulent house of Carvalhal.

before: ‘On 25 January 1641 the people went in a crowd to the Council and threw out the judge Luís Fernandes de Oliveira, because he was a Castilian. They appointed a new judge, a municipal procurator (*procurador do concelho*), a councillor (*vereador*) and a market inspector (*almotacel*). From there they went to the house of Paio Rodrigues Pais da Cunha, clerk of the Council (*escrivão da Câmara*), who had been suspended for misconduct, reinstated him in his office and threw out the deputy holder, Manuel Teixeira Pereira. A certain Manuel da Ceia and a nephew of his, who had indiscreetly spoken about the new tax, would hardly have escaped death and the fury of the people but for the efforts of the governor, the bishop and the cathedral chapter, whom the people respected. From here the rioting people went on to the customs house, threw out the superintendent (*provedor*) Manuel Vicente Cardoso and put in his place João Rodrigues de Teive. He lived at Nossa Senhora do Calhau (Our Lady of Calhau), and they went there to fetch him; when he tried to slip away as they passed the church, the crowd, on the pretext of saying a prayer, would not let him. Thus brought to the customs house, he was acclaimed superintendent by the people, with the threat that if he refused he would be killed by them on the spot. The doorkeeper, because he had kept the doors shut, was in danger of his life. In this popular commotion great help came from the good name of Dom António Fernandes, the bishop’s nephew and an officer of the Council, and the regard in which the people held him, and above all from the prelate, who knew how to calm the people with prudence and save the lives of those pointed out as their persecutors. As soon as they had taken an inventory of the superintendent’s property, the people grew quiet, and of this whole event the necessary records and entries were made, as is recorded in Book 4, fol. 202.’ John IV ordered an official inquiry into these events and the punishment of those who had shown disrespect to the superintendent Vicente Cardoso, though it is not known whether any penalty was actually imposed on them.

before: On 18 September 1668 the governor, Dom Francisco de Mascarenhas, accompanied by the *juiz de fora* (crown-appointed judge from outside the district), was on his way to the country house that the Jesuits owned in the locality (*sítio*) of Pico do Cardo, in the parish (*freguesia*) of Santo António, which is still known today as Quinta dos Padres. On reaching the locality of Água de Mel, where the manor house of the holders of the Bettencourt and Sá Machado entail (*morgado*) stood, he was confronted by a group of armed men, among them several members of that family. They violently assaulted the governor and wounded the *juiz de fora* with a sword cut.

before: It is an old public thoroughfare, short and of secondary importance compared with other streets of this city. Among the streets of old Funchal, however, it was one of the most important and also one of the longest, beginning at the Pelourinho and running along the left bank of the Ribeira de Santa Luzia to the vicinity of the Torreão. Gaspar Frutuoso, writing of it in 1590, says that it was ‘a great, wide street and the largest in the city’, adding that Bishop Dom Jerónimo Barreto (1574–1585) had there ‘his very rich lodgings, with their cool gardens’. In this old street stood the church of São Bartolomeu (St Bartholomew) and its hospice (*albergaria*), and some of the most distinguished people of Funchal had their residences there.

before: The oldest and most glorious traditions concerning the discovery of this island and its first settlement are inseparably bound up with the name of the place that later became the parish (*freguesia*), the town (*vila*) and the seat of the captaincy of Machico. The history of Madeira begins at the very moment when the caravels commanded by João Gonçalves Zarco and Tristão Vaz Teixeira dropped anchor in the picturesque and enchanting bay of this locality. At this moment the history of Machico also begins. As they rounded the promontory of São Lourenço, which had been given that name shortly before, there opened before the enraptured eyes of the navigators a small but lovely cove, bounded by a beach of rounded pebbles, which met a smiling valley hemmed in between steep and towering mountains. Everything invited them to make their first landing. It seems that the discoverers put in here on a warm, calm July afternoon, when the sun was already sinking fast towards the horizon. Despite the eagerness that overwhelmed those spirits, hungry for adventure and the unknown, the captains did not allow anyone to set foot that day on the virgin soil of this remote and unknown island. before: If we were to believe the romantic legend of Robert Machin and Ana de Arfet, we would have to accept that the discoverers, on landing on the beaches of Machico, found the graves of the two ill-fated lovers, and on them the epitaph that told of their unhappy adventure and asked that a chapel dedicated to Christ be built there. What does seem established, however, is that on the very day the captains of the small fleet made their first landing, they had a makeshift altar set up, and there one of the Franciscan friars whom Gonçalves Zarco had brought with him celebrated the sacrifice of the Mass. It was an ardent expression of faith, offering Providence without delay the humblest thanks for the fortunate and momentous discovery they had just made. It is said that the discoverers vowed to build a church on that spot, and this is the true origin of the foundation of the chapel of Cristo, or of Senhor dos Milagres (Lord of Miracles) (see Capela de Cristo, p. 332 of vol. I).

before: Dr Álvaro de Azevedo gives 1430 as the year in which the parishes (*freguesias*) of Câmara de Lobos and Calheta were created, and 1440 for those of Caniço and Ribeira Brava, while fixing 1450 for Machico. This is rather surprising, considering that Machico was one of the first places settled and one of those that grew and prospered most quickly; it was, moreover, the seat of a captaincy and a very important centre of the early colonisation. We are inclined to believe that the parish of Machico was created around the middle of the 15th century, whereas the others were at first merely constituted as chaplaincies with cure of souls or autonomous curacies (*curatos*) in the years indicated. Machico must have had a more or less regular religious service from the building of the chapel that Tristão Vaz erected there at the very start of settlement and land clearance. It was in 1450 that Dom Friar Pedro Vaz, prior (title of the parish priest) of the Order of Christ, sent Friar João Garcia to Madeira as the first vicar of the recently created parish of Machico. A similar case occurred in Funchal with Friar Nuno Cão, also sent by the Order of Christ to serve as parish priest at the seat of the captaincy and to superintend religious services throughout the island. In the article Parishes we expressed the opinion that the first parish created in Madeira had its seat in Funchal; we now add that the foundation of the parish of Machico was probably almost contemporary with it, just as the two towns were created at the same time.

before: The parish, as has been said, was created around 1450 and its parochial jurisdiction extended over the whole area of the captaincy. Chaplaincies with cure of souls, dependent on the mother church (*igreja matriz*), were later established in Santa Cruz, Porto Moniz, São Vicente, Ponta Delgada, São Jorge, Santana, Faial and Porto da Cruz. That of Santa Cruz was soon made an independent parish, and the other chaplaincies gradually became autonomous parishes. The rapid growth of the population at the seat of the captaincy led to the creation of new ecclesiastical posts: a collegiate church with six beneficed clerics was established before 1572, and a curacy by royal decree (*alvará*) of 15 November 1576.

before: Within this parish chapels were built to the Senhor dos Milagres (Lord of Miracles), which we have already discussed (vol. 1, p. 332), São Roque, Nossa Senhora do Rosário, Nossa Senhora da Graça, Nossa Senhora das Preces, São Cristóvão, Nossa Senhora do Amparo, São José, Santo António and Santana, to which we shall refer at greater length elsewhere in this work. Among the events of interest to the history of this parish, special mention should be made of the floods of 1724 and 1803 (see Floods, vol. 1, p. 54 ff.), the attack by the Miguelist squadron and troops on this town (see Occupation of Madeira by the Miguelist troops) and the killings that took place in the mother church (*igreja matriz*) of this parish in May 1870 (see Popular Riots).

before: The royal decree (alvará régio) of Cardinal Henry, dated 3 March 1579, empowered the diocesan prelate Dom Jerónimo Barreto to create the parish of São Roque, and set the parish priest’s annual stipend (*côngrua*) at 14,000 *réis* (old Portuguese money of account; 1$000 = 1,000 réis, 1:000$000 = one conto = 1,000,000 réis) in cash, half a *moio* (dry measure of grain, 60 *alqueires*) of wheat and a quarter of wine. before: The parish (*freguesia*) took its name from the small chapel of São Roque (St Roch) that stood there, where the seat of the new parish was established. The chapel had been built by the inhabitants of the locality (*sítio*) in a year before the parish was created. Dr Álvaro Rodrigues de Azevedo, basing himself on the order of the Council of the Treasury (*Conselho da Fazenda*) of 19 May 1704, which directed that the building of the new church and sacristy be put out to award by public auction (*arrematação*) for the sum of 795,000 *réis* (old Portuguese money of account; 1$000 = 1,000 réis, 1:000$000 = one conto = 1,000,000 réis), appears to conclude that the present church was built in that year. This construction, or rather enlargement, was carried out on the chapel that stood in the locality still known today as Igreja Paroquial, which we believe to be the site of the original chapel of São Roque. The work seems to have been none too sound, for around 1790 the church collapsed and could no longer be used for worship. Religious services were then held in a small chapel whose dedication we do not know.

before: The Quinta Vigia, the Quinta do Deão, the Municipal Garden and the garden of the Hospício da Princesa Dona Maria Amélia are the grounds within Funchal most notable for the luxuriance and variety of their trees. Here one sees fine specimens of the flora of many latitudes of the globe, alongside native types with tough, evergreen foliage. *Liriodendron tulipiferum*, *Bombax ceiba*, *Astrapaea Wallichii*, *Mammea americana*, *Euphoria Lit-chi*, *Pachira aquatica*, *Spondias lutea*, *Podocarpus neriifolius* and *Taxodium distichum* are trees growing in the Quinta Vigia. In the nearby gardens of the Hospício da Princesa Dona Maria Amélia, meanwhile, the woody species include, among others, *Pittosporum Tobira*, *P. eigenioides*, *Brachychiton populneum*, *Erythrina senegalensis*, *E. poianthes*, *E. Caffra*, *Schotia brachyata*, *Acacia Julibrissin*, *Aleurites triloba* and *Gingko biloba*. *Crescentia cucurbitina* is one of the chief ornaments of the Quinta do Deão, while in the Municipal Garden the principal adornment consists of the palms, prominent among them *Phoenix canariensis*, together with *Pandanus odoratissimus* and *Dammara australis*.

before: The group of small islands called the Desertas (Ilhéu Chão, Deserta Grande and Bugio) lies on a north-north-west to south-south-east line with Ponta de São Lourenço, Ilhéu Chão being the one nearest to that point. ‘Ilhéu Chão,’ says Dr A. Rodrigues de Azevedo, ‘so called because it is flat, is the smallest of the three islands; it is one mile or 1852 metres long by a third of a mile or 617 metres at its greatest width; its coasts are of steep rock, but it is level and of good soil; it is separated from Ponta de São Lourenço by a channel of 11 miles or a little over 20 kilometres, through which ships of every size pass. Its greatest height is 98 metres. To the south of Ilhéu Chão lies Deserta Grande, from which it is separated by a passage or channel navigable only by small boats. To the north of Ilhéu Chão lies the small Ilhéu do Navio, also called Prego do Mar.

before: According to Frutuoso, it is the surname of a *fidalgo* (nobleman of the lesser nobility) and noble family. In 1566 two members lived in Funchal: Manuel Vieira, syndic (síndico, lay agent managing a religious house's property) of the nuns of Santa Clara, and a certain Favila Vieira, whom Frutuoso describes as a *fidalgo*. At about the same time a *fidalgo* named António Vieira held the office of bailiff (meirinho) of the jurisdiction of Machico; he married a daughter of the donatary (*donatário*) Diogo Teixeira. There are other branches of the Vieira family, two of which came from the Azores. One of them appeared in Madeira in the second quarter of the 19th century; the other began with Manuel Vieira de Afonseca, a native of the island of Terceira, who was clerk of the Council (*escrivão da Câmara*) of Funchal.

before: The palace on Rua do Comércio, formerly Rua dos Ferreiros, which houses the Municipal Council (*Câmara Municipal*), the Municipal Administration (*Administração do Concelho*, the government's local civil office), the police, the land registry (*Conservatória*), etc. (1921), belonged to the entailed house (*casa vinculada*) of the Count of Carvalhal and is one of the largest buildings on the island. It was built in 1758, and it contained improvements (*benfeitorias*, buildings and walls made by the tenant, which remained his property) that formed part of the unentailed property of the holder of the entail (*morgado*) João Agostinho Figueiroa de França e Albuquerque. The part of the palace that belonged to the Count of Carvalhal was ceded by him to the trading firm Freitas & Macedo in payment of debts. The remaining parts, owned by Afonso de Albuquerque, the Count of Calçada, Francisco Roque de Albuquerque, Dr Luís Vicente de Afonseca and others, were acquired by the same firm through purchases made at different times.

before: Before it acquired the magnificent building facing the Largo do Município, or Largo do Colégio, the Council met in various parts of Funchal. The first building it owned, though not the first in which it held its meetings, was built under an order of Duke Manuel dated 1486, which directed that a ‘stronghold, council chamber, notaries’ house & pillory’ be built on the square called the Campo do Duque, the ground on which the Cathedral (the Sé) and its adjoining squares and streets now stand. As early as 1470 a letter from Infante Ferdinand to the donatary João Gonçalves da Câmara had asked him to undertake ‘to build the council house & the council pound’ out of the money from the fines of the judge-auditor & of João Gonçalves himself’. The same Infante ordered land to be given beside the great church for this building, which was estimated at 213,096 *réis* (old Portuguese money of account; 1$000 = 1,000 réis, 1:000$000 = one conto = 1,000,000 réis).

before: Until 1784 the town hall remained in the building erected on the Campo do Duque, but in that year the Council began to hold its meetings in the Casa da Saúde, at the Entrada da Cidade, because that building was in a very poor state of repair. The Campo do Duque building stood on the site occupied today (1921) by house no. 61 in the street named after Lieutenant-Commander Carvalho de Araújo, formerly the Rua do Aljube. Its ruins, valued at 432,000 *réis*, were sold by award by public auction (*arrematação*) to Dr António José Monteiro for 432,250 *réis* on 30 March 1805.

before: As various works were carried out on the town hall in 1824 so that the gaol could be installed there, the Municipality spent some time in a rented house, returning to the building on the Largo da Sé on 29 April 1825, once those works had been completed. In 1837 the Council again left the building ‘because of the noxious smell of the prisons, where there were 180 prisoners’. It settled first in the Casa da Saúde and then in a building belonging to Dr Daniel de Ornelas, which it resolved to leave at its session of 16 May 1838, to occupy a house on the Largo do Pelourinho, on the site where today (1921) stands the flour mill that belonged to the commercial firm Viúva de Romano Gomes & Filhos.

before: Some 80 years ago the Municipal Council (*Câmara Municipal*) sought to put up, on the site then occupied by the convent of São Francisco and now by the Jardim Municipal, a building to house the law courts, the town hall and the administration and tax office of the municipality (*concelho*). In 1864 it opened a competition for the design and estimate of this building. The rules laid down that the design placed first would receive a prize of 240,000 island *réis* (old Portuguese money of account; 1$000 = 1,000 réis, 1:000$000 = one conto = 1,000,000 réis) (50 pounds) and the runner-up the sum of 72,000 island *réis* (15 pounds). The ranking was to be made by a committee made up of the district judges and public prosecutors of the two judicial districts (*comarcas*) then existing on the island, the two engineers directing the public and military works of the district, and the president of the Council.

before: He was born in Funchal on 18 January 1879, the son of Francisco Joaquim da Costa Ferreira and Dona Teodolinda Augusta de Freitas da Costa Ferreira. He holds a licentiate in philosophy and is a bachelor (*bacharel*, university graduate) in medicine of the University of Coimbra. He has been assistant in anatomy at the Lisbon Medical School (*Escola Médica de Lisboa*), supernumerary professor at one of the secondary schools (*liceus*) of the same city, director of the Casa Pia, and professor of general pedagogy and the history of education at the teacher-training college (*Escola Normal*). He is a member of the Anthropological Society of Paris, the Portuguese Society of Natural Sciences, the Lisbon Geographical Society, the Academy of Sciences of Portugal, the Institute of Coimbra, etc. He belongs to the Evolutionist Party and was minister of finance in the government headed by Duarte Leite. From a very early age he has devoted himself to anthropological studies, and he is today the Portuguese who best knows the branch of the natural sciences that deals with man and the human races. He has published various works in this field, among which we shall mention *Cranios Portugueses* (1898–1899), *La Capacité du Crâne et la Composition Ethnique probable du Peuple Portugais* (a paper presented to the Anthropological Society of Paris in 1895) and *O Povo Português sob o ponto de vista antropologico* (a lecture given at the Lisbon Geographical Society on 6 March 1909).

before: Dr Costa Ferreira was in Funchal in June 1922, travelling on from here to the Cape of Good Hope and then to Lourenço Marques, where he intended to organise the Anthropological Museum and carry out various studies in the province. He never began this work and these studies, however, for he took his own life in that Portuguese city in Africa on 15 July 1922, that is, only a very few days after arriving there. Parliament granted Costa Ferreira’s widow an annual pension of 3,600 escudos (written 3:600$00), and the Municipal Council of Funchal, at its meeting of 21 September 1922, gave the name of our ill-fated fellow countryman to the former Rua do Carmo.

before: The office was originally called Judge of Pious Bequests and Superintendent of Chantries, Hospices, Hostels, Leper Houses and Orphans of the Ilha da Madeira. In 1486 João do Porto was appointed to this post (*lugar*); he is the earliest holder of whom we have found any record. The office, whose powers later became less extensive, served chiefly to oversee the fulfilment of pious legacies and of the obligations attached to many chantries (*capelas*) and churches, and the registration of the properties burdened with those obligations, etc.

before: The *juiz de fora* was the *ex officio* president of the Municipal Council (*Câmara Municipal*) of Funchal and exercised his functions only within the *termo* (municipal jurisdictional district, a subdivision of the comarca), which was a subdivision of the judicial district (*comarca*). When he was unable to act, he was replaced by the eldest councillor (*vereador*), who was then called the judge by operation of law (*juiz por bem da lei*), and his lodging allowance was paid by the Council. Both he and the *corregedor* were required to hold a degree in law.

before: In the 16th century the springs of João Diniz gushed out onto the pebble beach (*calhau*). The Bânger pillar was built on a shoal, and in the 18th century people crossed by canoe between it and the city’s defensive wall. The chapel of the Misericórdia (Holy House of Mercy) of Machico stood at the mouth of the stream and is now about 200 metres from the sea. The Ribeira de São João is gradually silting up the cove of Pontinha. One need only see how the streams become choked in the winter floods, and look at the muddy fringe of the sea, to understand readily the work done by the waters.

before: For the time and place in which it was built, our Cathedral is undoubtedly a magnificent and imposing church, not only in its architectural style but also for certain works of art it contains, which have caught the attention of many distinguished visitors. before: The manuscript *Noticia das cousas da Ilha da Madeira desde o seu segundo descobrimento pelo Zargo* states that our Cathedral was built to the measurements of the church of Carmo (Carmelite church), Lisbon, which, as is well known, was commissioned by Nuno Álvares Pereira. That magnificent church, one of the finest examples of Gothic architecture in Portugal, was destroyed by the earthquake of 1755. However, an old engraving, which Oliveira Martins reproduced in his work on Nuno Álvares, shows that its façade was very different from the frontage of Funchal Cathedral, except for the pointed portal with its archivolts and the rose window with its ornaments embroidered in stone. As for the interior, we can say nothing about any resemblance there may have been between the two churches, since we do not know any of the old chronicles dealing with Nuno Álvares and the Carmelite convent, where a description of its church will surely be found.

before: The earliest date known to us relating to the construction of our Cathedral is 5 June 1485. On that day Prince Manuel, Duke of Viseu and Grand Master of the Order of Christ, by a letter signed at Santiago do Cacém, made a grant of land in the Campo do Duque (volume I, page 225) so that there might be built upon it ‘a church and square and churchyard and houses for the municipality (*concelho*)’. A letter from the same duke, dated 22 October 1488, granted half of the fines that ‘may be imposed on the island’ for ‘the making of the church which, God willing, I hope to have built in the said Funchal’.

before: Accounts of the year in which the work began are not entirely in agreement. Nevertheless, the most probable view to adopt is that of Dr Álvaro Rodrigues de Azevedo, who states that the ‘building of the church began shortly after 1493, for in that year the Duke of Viseu, later King Manuel, ordered, by a letter registered on fol. 174 of volume I of the Archive of the Municipal Council (*Câmara Municipal*) of Funchal, that the revenue of the wine levy (imposição do vinho) be applied to that work.’ The annotator of the *Saudades* further adds: ‘…and by 1502 it was already under way, the proceeds of that levy then being assigned to it not only in the municipality of Funchal but also in those of Ponta do Sol and Calheta, as can be seen from the royal letter (*carta régia*) of the same King Manuel of that year 1502’. This letter is transcribed on page 488, not 503 as note XX states, and the following passages bear on the subject of this article: ‘Firstly, you ask us that the levy of the towns of Ponta do Sol and Calheta should always go to the works of the church of that town and of the municipality. To this we reply that it pleases us that, for as long as the works on the said church last, the levy of the aforesaid places be collected for them alone and for nothing else. Item, that the inhabitants of Ponta do Sol and Calheta should pay towards the church of that town whatever they are assessed until it is finished. To this we reply that it pleases us that each should pay what he is assessed according to his means’.

This letter is transcribed on page 488, not 503 as note XX states, and the following passages bear on the subject of this article: ‘Firstly, you ask us that the levy of the towns of Ponta do Sol and Calheta should always go to the works of the church of that town and of the municipality. before: The main construction work on the Cathedral must have been finished by 1516, the year of its consecration, while the interior decoration and work on certain parts of the church continued slowly after that time. The distinguished annotator of the *Saudades da Terra* considers the church completed in 1508 and says it was consecrated in that year by Bishop Dom João Lobo, whereas Gaspar Frutuoso gives 16 October 1516 as the day of the consecration and states that the consecrating bishop was Dom Duarte. On this point we side with the author, not the annotator, of the *Saudades*. In various old manuscripts we have found the statement that our Cathedral was consecrated in 1516, and Dr Rodrigues de Azevedo is perhaps the only one to assert that it was in 1508. Moreover, all the old ecclesiastical chronicles we have been able to consult state that the consecration was performed by Bishop Dom Duarte, and there is not the slightest doubt that this prelate came to the island at the behest of the first bishop, Dom Diogo Pinheiro, appointed in 1514 when the bishopric was created.

before: After the consecration, as we have already said, work continued on the interior decoration, which was not yet finished, and over the course of time very important works were carried out there for the complete and final conclusion of the whole building. The order of the Council of the Treasury (*Conselho da Fazenda*) of 30 March 1560 directed that ‘the enclosure behind the chapel of the Santíssimo Sacramento be built’, and that of 28 February 1635 ordered the completion of the works on the chancel, whose paintings were only placed there in the second quarter of the 18th century. The construction of the great sacristy and of the chapter house also dates from the second quarter of that century; these were let by award by public auction (*arrematação*) for 3,050,000 *réis* (old Portuguese money of account; 1$000 = 1,000 réis, 1:000$000 = one conto = 1,000,000 réis) in 1733. The present chapel of the Santíssimo Sacramento (Most Holy Sacrament), which replaced the old one, began to be built around the middle of the 18th century. The altars in the side aisles were built at the beginning of the 19th century.
after: After the consecration, as we have already said, work continued on the interior decoration, which was not yet finished, and over the course of time very important works were carried out there for the complete and final conclusion of the whole building. The altars in the side aisles were built at the beginning of the 19th century.

before: As prelate of Funchal, he marked his time on the island by the persecution he waged against freemasonry, in agreement with the governor and captain-general (capitão-general, military governor of Madeira) and under orders issued by the central government. It is nevertheless claimed that he exceeded the orders he had received, so that the government in Lisbon itself had to intervene against the excesses committed by the prelate. Among those persecuted was the dean of Funchal Cathedral (Sé do Funchal), Dr João Francisco Lopes Rocha, who wrote a long letter on the matter to the minister José Seabra da Silva, complaining of the abuses of power committed by Dom José Torres. The letter is a document of interest on many counts and was published in 1822, in London, in the *Campeão Portuguez*. On 22 June 1796 he was transferred to the see of Elvas. When he was already preparing to leave Madeira, he had to bring forward his departure in haste and abandon the island, as a document of the time says, ‘on the night of 6 October 1796, without taking leave of anyone, nor of the Most Holy Sacrament: and to this day the reason for this contrived embarkation by night and by back ways is unknown’.

before: A locality (*sítio*) on the island of Porto Santo. An old chapel dedicated to Nossa Senhora da Graça (Our Lady of Grace) once stood here and gave the place its name. As it was badly ruined, its reconstruction on a larger scale than the original was begun in the early 19th century, on the initiative of the governor of that island, Manuel Inácio de Avelar Brotero. The rebuilding was never completed, however, and today the chapel is reduced to a heap of ruins. It was unusual in being octagonal, and it is said to have reproduced in miniature a famous church in Italy.

before: This is the old Caminho da Pontinha, built around 1874. It runs south of the Quinta Vigia and Quinta Lambert, and to open it some coastal rocks lying next to these *quintas* had to be destroyed.

before: He was born in the parish (*freguesia*) of Santa Cruz on 25 November 1859 and died in the town (*vila*) of Ponta do Sol on 16 March 1917. He was secretary of the municipal councils of São Vicente and Porto Moniz, and secretary of the Municipal Administration (*Administração do Concelho*, the government's local civil office) of the municipality (*concelho*) of Ponta do Sol. He distinguished himself greatly as a solicitor (*solicitador*) and licensed advocate (*advogado provisionista*, practising by licence without a law degree), leaving valuable legal works that many distinguished jurists would not have disdained to sign. He contributed extensively to many newspapers and was the founder and editor of the *Brado d'Oeste*, which was published for many years in the town of Ponta do Sol.

before: Common name of *Asparagus lowei*, a plant of the Liliaceae-Asparagoideae widely cultivated in the gardens and *quintas* of Madeira, which also grows wild at Porto do Moniz and between São Jorge and Santana. It has woody, sarmentose or twining stems, fasciculate, bristle-like cladodes and white flowers, with jointed peduncles shorter than the cladodes. The fine-leaved *esparto*, much grown in gardens, is *Asparagus plumosus*, and near Gorgulho *H. scoparius* has been found, a pretty plant now almost extinct on the island.

before: Henrique Veitch was so fond of Madeira that he spent a considerable part of his fortune here buying a great deal of property and putting up several buildings. Outstanding among them is the house in Rua 5 de Outubro, between the Bom Jesus and Nova bridges, whose architecture is highly original for Madeira and at once catches the eye of any curious observer passing by. The houses in Rua das Queimadas de Baixo, in the locality (*sítio*) of Calassa and in the town (*vila*) of Câmara de Lobos are also characteristic buildings. Special mention is due to the lovely residence at Jardim da Serra, for the originality of its construction, for the pleasantness of the spot and also for the strange mausoleum that stands a short distance from the house, out in the open mountains, where the mortal remains of the English consul Henrique Veitch rest.

before: As we have already mentioned, the protection Veitch gave to many Madeirans during the turbulent period of our civil wars was invaluable. His houses served as a safe and hospitable refuge for many victims of political persecution. In 1828, when the absolutist troops occupied Madeira, he arranged the escape of many inhabitants of this island on board the frigate *Alligator*. Among them were the governor Travassos Valdez, the Count of Carvalhal and two of his nephews, the dean Januário Camacho, Colonel Albuquerque, the *juiz de fora* (crown-appointed judge from outside the district), the *corregedor* (royal district magistrate) and many others.

before: Francisco d’Ornelas, the second brother of Manuel d’Ornelas, understood early on that the whole of their father’s fortune would go to the latter. He heard the fantastic tales of the riches of Brazil, to which settlers were sailing on every ship. While still very young he ran away from his father’s house, joined a party of emigrants and sailed with it to try his luck through work. The first job he obtained in Pernambuco was as a servant. That was too humiliating for the lineage of the Dornelas. He changed his name. Even so, he took the surname Fernandes from his great-grandfather António Fernandes, of Covas, in Faial, and the surname Vieira from his paternal great-great-grandfather Pedro Vieira, great holder of the entail (*morgado*) of the Ribeira de Machico, on the island of Madeira, and joined them to the forename João, also from his maternal great-grandfather João Mendes. And so he created the full name of João Fernandes Vieira, under which he made his way in Brazil and passed into history, a name more dignified by his deeds than the one his parents had given him at the baptismal font’.

before: The Spanish *fidalgo* (nobleman of the lesser nobility) Dom Antonio Herédia served in the army that entered Portugal under the command of the Duke of Alba in 1580. In 1602 he came to Madeira as captain of the Company of the Castilian Garrison (*Companhia do Presídio Castelhano*), later becoming commander of that garrison, and afterwards he governed the whole archipelago in the absence of the governor in office. He was the founder of the Herédia family in Madeira, whose last representatives were Francisco Correia Herédia, António Correia Herédia and Francisco Correia Herédia, Viscount of Ribeira Brava (see those entries). Dom Antonio Herédia and his descendants married into the most distinguished Madeiran families. The Heredia family absorbed the important entailed estate (*morgadio*) of the Britos, whose principal seat was in the parish (*freguesia*) of Ribeira Brava, at the chantry (capela) of Nossa Senhora da Apresentação (Our Lady of the Presentation), in the locality (*sítio*) that still bears this name today. Attached to it was a large manor house, one of the biggest residences outside Funchal. House and chapel were demolished long ago.

before: This is a very old family surname here in Madeira. Among the first settlers who came from mainland Portugal, says the annotator of the *Saudades*, Vasco Martins Moniz de Meneses established himself on this island and held a *sesmaria* (royal land grant to settlers on condition of cultivation) at Caniço. He was a nobleman of the Royal Household (*fidalgo da Casa Real*) and the second son of Henrique Moniz, *alcaide-mor* (royal governor of a castle and town) of Silves, and of his wife Dona Inês de Meneses, daughter of Gonçalo Nunes Barreto, *alcaide-mor* of Faro. Vasco Martins Moniz kept a great house in the town (*vila*) of Machico and, by a will approved in 1489, founded an entail (*morgado*) from the disposable third (*terça*) of the estate; he died in 1510 in the town of Torrão. Nicolau Florentino (António Maria de Freitas) writes at length about Vasco Martins Moniz in his pamphlet *A mulher de Colombo*, extolling his deeds and qualities. He says that in the town of Machico, where Moniz had settled, he stood out among all the Portuguese and foreigners living there for his generosity, the nobility of his manners and the princely splendour of his house. Its comforts and attractions did not make him soft; on the contrary, whenever the king and the country called for his services, he left his family to lend his arm and often his purse. Vasco Moniz’s daughter, Dona Isabel Moniz, was the wife of Bartolomeu Perestrelo, the first donatary (*donatário*) of Porto Santo, and from this marriage was born Dona Filipa Moniz, wife of the great navigator Christopher Columbus. The pamphlet by Nicolau Florentino cited above also deals at length with all these figures.

before: He was born in the parish (*freguesia*) of Ponta do Pargo on 17 December 1869. He studied at the Seminary of this Diocese and was ordained priest in 1893. before: The house in Rua da Boa Viagem, which belonged to the chantry (*capela*) founded by Bento da Veiga, had two windows, whose stones were sold to a British subject, who had them shipped to his own country. before: José Gonçalves de Aguiar was born of humble parents in the town (*vila*) of Câmara de Lobos on 8 October 1831, the legitimate son of Vitorino Gonçalves Rocha and Vitorina Rosa de Jesus. Like some of his brothers, he used the surname Aguiar, which was that of his maternal grandfather. He was a student at the Funchal Seminary (*Seminário do Funchal*) when, thanks to the patronage of the Russian Waxel family, who were then in Madeira, he went to study in the faculty of theology at the University, where he graduated in a year we cannot establish. Shortly afterwards he settled in Lisbon and remained there until his death. In the capital he held, among other posts, those of high court judge (*desembargador*) of the patriarchal curia and prosynodal examiner (diocesan examiner of clergy).

before: The only public library in Funchal is that of the Municipal Council (*Câmara Municipal*), created by a resolution of 12 January 1838. It began with 193 volumes of the *Enciclopédia Metódica*, bought from the heirs of the Count of Carvalhal, and numbered 2,000 volumes in 1850, 2,096 in 1851, 2,496 in 1863, 10,351 in 1889, 10,812 in 1902, 10,929 in 1904, 11,035 in 1908, 21,641 in 1915, 21,786 in 1916 and 21,874 in 1917. In 1913 the Library received a gift of 9,863 volumes from the British subjects Mr William and Mr Alfredo Reid. These volumes had formed the book collection of the late municipal librarian João Joaquim de Freitas, and the two gentlemen had acquired them for the express purpose of enriching that municipal institution.

before: The first of this surname on the island of Madeira, says the distinguished annotator of the *Saudades*, was Álvaro de Ornelas, only son of Lopo Esteves de Ornelas, head of this ancient and noble family, which is one of the principal families of this island. before: During the administration of Councillor (conselheiro, honorary title of the royal council) José Silvestre Ribeiro, large quantities of pine seed came to Madeira, which he had distributed among the Municipal Councils and rural landowners. It was from then on that the cultivation of the maritime pine began to expand greatly on the island. The cultivation of this species now covers an area which we suppose to be no less than 2,000 hectares, while that of the stone pine is today abandoned or almost abandoned (1921).

before: António Aluísio Jervis de Atouguia, 1st Viscount of Atouguia, belonged to a noble Madeiran family. He was born on 7 July 1797 in the locality (*sítio*) of São Francisco das Furnas (St Francis of Assisi), on the Estrada de Santo António, in the parish (*freguesia*) of São Pedro in this city, in the house of the entailed estate (*morgadio*) that his parents owned there. before: The liberal ideas he professed made him unsafe in Portugal. Fearing the persecution suffered by many of his fellow countrymen and friends, he resolved to seek the warm hospitality of the country he knew so well, where he had spent some years of his youth. He emigrated to England in June 1828, and in August of the same year sailed for this island with other Portuguese, to join the governor and captain-general José Lúcio Travassos Valdez, later Count of Bonfim, and to help him in the resistance he was preparing against the attack of the absolutist forces. It is well known that this resistance never took place, and that the troops commanded by General Lemos bombarded the town (*vila*) of Machico, took it without difficulty and set off for Funchal. Captain José Maria Monteiro, who had come aboard Dom Miguel’s fleet, was then installed in the government of the island.

before: He remained there until the end of 1831, when he left for Terceira to join the movement that had begun on that island to free Portugal from the clutches of absolutism. Shortly after his arrival, in March 1832, an expedition was organised against Madeira to free it from the Miguelite (supporter of the absolutist King Miguel) yoke. This expedition, commanded by Luiz Mousinho de Albuquerque and in which Jervis de Athouguia took part, proved fruitless: the liberal forces did not even attempt an attack on this archipelago, in view of the superiority of the enemy troops defending it. Only Mousinho de Albuquerque and the officers of his party stayed for some weeks on Porto Santo, before returning to the island of Terceira.

before: Among the Customs House books referred to above are those of the former Crown Revenue Office (*Provedoria*), which was attached to that revenue house and exercised superintendence over it until 1775, when it was abolished. The enactments issued by the central government concerning the collection of certain contributions and taxes, the creation of posts and the appointment of those who were to hold them, the construction and repair of buildings, the reorganisation of various public services, etc., etc., were addressed to the Royal Treasury Office (*Provedoria da Real Fazenda*). This office filed and registered these enactments and partly carried them out, so its register books are of great interest and value for the history of our island. The importance of these documents becomes clear on reading the ‘*Index da antiga Provedoria da Real Fazenda. . .*’, a bulky folio volume held in this city and partly published some years ago in the *Heraldo da Madeira*. It gives a brief, methodically arranged list of the enactments registered in twenty-four volumes, covering the long period from 1566 to 1775. This index ought to be reproduced again in some newspaper or review, since the first printing was riddled with typographical errors, and the opportunity should be taken to accompany the new publication with short explanatory notes on the text.

before: Câmara is a very old family surname here in Madeira. The first to bear it on the island was João Gonçalves da Câmara, eldest son of the discoverer and 21. captain-donatary of Funchal. Even so, it can be said that the name derives from João Gonçalves Zarco, although he himself may perhaps never have used it. This claim rests on the royal letter (*carta régia*) of 4 July 1460, which in more than one place calls the discoverer of Madeira João Gonçalves de Câmara de Lobos, when conferring on him his title of nobility and granting him the corresponding coat of arms. This document of Afonso V, an interesting one, was first published on p. 836 ff. of the *Saudades da Terra*.
