before: In the *Saudades da Terra*, Dr Álvaro Rodrigues de Azevedo transcribes a genealogical work by José Freire Monterroio Mascarenhas, which remains unpublished in the Public Library of Lisbon and contains the words we reproduce below: ‘There is no ground for saying that his descendants took the surname Câmara because of the chamber of sea wolves that João Gonçalves Zarco found on that island; for this was not a deed worthy of being perpetuated in memory and remaining as a surname…’. This statement by Mascarenhas flatly contradicts the origin that the books of nobility and the old chronicles of this archipelago assign to that surname. This statement by Mascarenhas flatly contradicts the origin that the books of nobility and the old chronicles of this archipelago assign to that surname. It is also in plain contradiction with the heraldic indications of the coat of arms itself, and with the words of the royal letter cited above. The way in which that letter calls the discoverer of Madeira João Gonçalves de Câmara de Lobos shows us that these words contain an evident reference to the episode of the sea wolves found at the place that later took the name Câmara de Lobos. It is true that the deeds of João Gonçalves Zarco as a warrior at Ceuta and a distinguished navigator, and above all the discovery of Madeira itself, would have given the kings of arms and the heraldry of the time precious material for a coat of arms of loftier significance and more ostentatious ancestral lineage for Zarco’s descendants. But it is equally beyond doubt that in matters of this kind whim and fancy sometimes won the day, leaving in a very secondary place memorable facts and heroic actions that deserved to be set in brilliant and marked relief.

before: He was born in Funchal on 23 December 1802, the son of João Nepomuceno Correia Drumond and Dona Maria Isidora de Meneses e Brito. For reasons unknown to us he did not pursue this path, and instead entered the office of his uncle, Inácio Correia Drumond, clerk of the corregedor's court (*escrivão da correição*; the corregedor was the royal district magistrate), as a trainee. In 1826 he secured appointment as a court clerk (*escrivão*), and later, after the proclamation of the Constitution, as a licensed advocate (*advogado provisionista*, practising by licence without a law degree). He was president of the Municipal Council (*Câmara Municipal*) of Funchal and, years later, one of its councillors (*vereadores*). before: According to the zoologist Carlos França, the Porto Santo rabbit has the characteristics and appearance of the common wild rabbit of southern Europe, differing from it only in the shape and dimensions of the skull. before: ‘When the governor and captain-general José Correia de Sá made known his intention of walking behind the canopy, together with the knights of the habit of Christ, in the Corpus Christi procession due to take place on 21 May 1762, the Council sent the municipal procurator (*procurador do concelho*) to ask him “that, for the service of His Majesty, he should not seek to disturb the good harmony that ought to exist between the Senate and the governors, nor alter the legitimate custom always practised, thereby violating the regulations of the Council and the royal warrants (*provisões*); for on this island it had never been the custom for the knights of the Order of Christ to attend the said procession, but should they wish to attend, they should walk in the body of the procession, in the place belonging to the said Order; behind the canopy, however, or holding its poles, they could not walk, both because this had never been the custom and because the place behind the canopy belonged to the Senate, and it was for the Senate alone to choose who should carry the poles of the canopy, not only because the direction of the procession belonged to the Council, but also because it had always been the unalterable custom that, by order of the Senate of the Council, the poles of the canopy were carried by those of the governing body (*governança*, the notables eligible for municipal office) – from the Cathedral to the College of São João Evangelista (St John the Evangelist) by the married men, and from the said College to the Sé by the unmarried men and those who had already served as councillors, bearing torches – and all this by order of the Senate”.’

before: Because of their great altitude and their distance from inhabited centres, the mountains of Madeira always pose a serious danger to travellers who must cross them when storms break over them, especially torrential rain accompanied by strong gales and hail. Few winters pass without the death of several people who succumb to the violence of the storms. To help these wayfarers, who are at times imprudent and unaware of the danger to which they so easily expose themselves, small houses have been built at the most exposed points of our mountains. Some of them are already quite old, and they have rendered notable service, saving from certain death many people who have sought shelter in them, even though they lack the most rudimentary means of warmth and comfort for those who arrive there driven by the storms. We give below a list of the mountain shelters existing in our mountains, some of which also serve the upkeep of the levadas (irrigation channels) and forestry inspection. It is much to be regretted that not all of them have the staff needed to fulfil their purpose effectively, and that their state of repair leaves so much to be desired. They are: Casa do Caramujo (see that entry), in the mountains of São Vicente; Casa do Lombo do Mouro (see that entry), in the mountains of the parish (*freguesia*) of Ribeira Brava; Casa do Monte Medonho (see that entry), in the mountains of the parish of São Vicente; the Casas do Rabaçal, at the well-known locality of the same name; Casa da Bica da Cana, on the plateau of the Paul da Serra; Casa da Fajã das Nogueiras (see that entry), in the mountains of Faial; Casa das Queimadas (see that entry), in the mountains of the parish of Santana; Casa do Ribeiro Frio (see that entry), in the parish of São Roque do Faial; Casa dos Alpires (see that entry), not very far from the locality of Choupana, in Funchal; and the one at Poiso, at the locality of that name, in the mountains of the parish of Camacha. This last is perhaps the only one that truly deserves the name of mountain shelter, for its size, its good state of repair and the relative comfort it offers to those who seek it. At other points in the mountains there were once some small shelters, long since destroyed by time and human neglect.

before: This was the name given to the walls that protected Funchal against any enemy attack, from both the landward and the seaward side. On the east, the walls ran from the pillory (*pelourinho*, stone column symbolising municipal jurisdiction) to the Pena, following the right bank of the Ribeira de João Gomes; on the west, from the mouth of the Ribeira de São João (formerly the Ribeira Grande) to the cliff of Pico dos Frias, following the left bank of the same stream; and on the south, from the mouth of the Ribeira de São João to the Fort of São Tiago (St James the Greater).

before: According to an inscription on the parade ground and arms of the Fort of São João do Pico (*Castelo de São João do Pico*), which Dr Azevedo transcribed on p. 625 of his notes to the *Saudades da Terra*, almost all of the curtain wall joining that fort was built by the governor Luís de Miranda Henriques, who was on this island from 1636 to 1640. This part of the wall had, however, already been designated in King Sebastian’s regulations as necessary for the landward defence of the city.

before: João da Costa e Brito, governor-general of the archipelago from 1680 to 1684, seems to have improved the city walls. before: There is a letter from Duke Dom Manuel, dated 21 June 1493, ordering an enclosure and walls to be built in the town (*vila*) of Funchal. On 9 January 1494, however, a royal letter (*carta régia*) appeared revoking that order and directing that only a few bastions be built and some gateways blocked up for the proper defence and protection of the island. After this, Vicente Sodré came to Madeira on the orders of the same duke to deal with the said enclosure and walls. But, as Dr Azevedo says, this mission achieved nothing, for the island only acquired fortifications once royal power had been consolidated there through the Manueline reforms.

before: The Fort of São Filipe, the redoubt of Santo António da Alfândega, the Fort of São Lourenço (St Lawrence) and the battery of Fontes lay within the old walled enclosure, although all these fortifications, except that of São Lourenço, were built after the walls. ‘The Alfândega redoubt,’ says Dr Azevedo, ‘was the first excrescence on Funchal’s belt of walls; it was the first blow to the system of circumvallation, and the first deliberate step towards a system of maritime defence based on the range and crossfire of cannon.’

before: Of the old city wall only a few remnants still stand, more or less hidden among the houses, and the gates and gateways that once pierced it have also disappeared. The redan at the entrance to the city and the walls near the present São Pedro Market and between the Fortress and the fort of Fontes disappeared in 1839; in 1888 the gun emplacement near the old British cemetery, by the Ribeiro Real, disappeared; on 20 September 1897 demolition began of the branch (*lanço*, *ramal*) of the city wall adjoining the Fort of São Pedro (St Peter), north of the old Praça Académica; and finally, in May 1911, the part of the wall beside the chapel of the Varadouros was removed. Following representations made to the Government in August 1895 and February 1896, the Council now owns the branch of the old walls that can be seen near the spot where the Avenida de João de Deus comes out. On 29 May 1914 the same body resolved to acquire the part of the city wall needed to extend the Largo da Sé down to the beach, since it had been authorised to do so by a note from the War Ministry. Demolition of this part of the city wall began in March 1920 to open the Avenida António José de Almeida. On 15 October 1896 the Council ordered a halt to the demolition of the part of the city wall bordering Rua Pimenta de Aguiar, because of a complaint from the head of the engineering section on this island. That wall still stands today, perfectly useless, although the said official attributed military importance to it, so we believe.

before: Of the old gates and gateways of the city wall only two exist today: that of the Customs House and the one near the fortress of São Tiago. before: Ninety-nine species of spider are known in the Madeira archipelago, the largest of which is *Lycosa (Trochosa) ingens*, which lives on the Desertas. The large black spider of Madeira is *Lycosa (Trochosa) Blackwallii*, and that of Porto Santo is *L. tarentuloides maderiana*. *Epeira aurelia* (the ‘tarântula’ of the Madeirans) lives on spurge bushes (*tabaibeiras*) and other plants, fixing the threads of its webs to them; the country people say that in these webs it writes the name by which it is known. There is no record of the bite of *Epeira* producing notable swelling or inflammation; the bite of the *Lycosa* species, spiders that prefer dark places and holes and crevices in the rocks, is perhaps more dangerous. *Cyrtophora citricola*, recently introduced into Madeira by an English lady, is now found on trees, telephone wires, etc., etc. The spiders of the Madeira archipelago were recorded or described in a work published by Mr Kulczynski, of Kraków, in 1899. See Kulczynski, Fauvel and Schmitz.

before: It is evident that Brito Rebêlo carried his conclusions much too far. There are acceptable probabilities in his conjectures, but the truth is that the document transcribed cannot demonstrate that the sailor Machico, to whom Ferdinand I granted some houses in Lisbon, took part in the expedition of João Gonçalves Zarco. It does prove that the name Machico existed in Portugal, which constitutes a new argument against the truth of the story of Roberto Machim, and further confirms the account given by Azurara and other early chroniclers of the discovery of this archipelago. The document found by General Brito Rebêlo in the Archive of the Torre do Tombo is nonetheless very valuable and interesting.

before: The well-known novelist Arnaldo Gama (1828–1869) wrote, among other books, the novel *A Caldeira de Pêro Botelho*, whose plot is largely set on this island; some of its characters are also natives of Madeira, notably the noblemen Diogo and Pêro Botelho. On the sources he used for weaving this historical novel, Arnaldo Gama says in a final note to his book: ‘In closing, I must say that the story of the love of Diogo Botelho and Dona Beatriz, as well as that of the Caldeira de Pêro Botelho, were taken from the *Relação de uma viagem a Espanha*, written by Tomé Pinheiro da Veiga, who is said to be the author of the famous *Arte de Furtar*; the manuscript of this account is owned by Mr António Rodrigues da Cruz Coutinho, proprietor and publisher of this book.’

before: The Funchal Commercial Association is one of the most important bodies in this city, and also the oldest of all those in existence here. The history of this worthy association is likewise the history of our economic life over the long span of eighty-four years, for the matters of closest concern to Madeiran commerce and industry have found in it their most strenuous champion. It has placed unconditionally at the service of this archipelago all the prestige, influence and credit that it deservedly enjoys in our community. There may have been some rare exception, which will serve only to confirm the general rule.

before: According to an official report, the landing places (*portos*) of Madeira were until recently graded as follows. Those of Funchal (see Funchal (bay) and Port of Funchal) and of the south of the island of Porto Santo (see that entry) were considered good. Those of Abra, Machico, Santa Cruz, Câmara de Lobos, Ribeira Brava, Ponta do Sol, Porto do Moniz and Porto da Cruz were deemed fair. Those of Caniçal, Porto Novo, Reis Magos, Oliveira, Campanário, Lugar de Baixo, Madalena do Mar, Anjos, Fajã do Mar, Calheta, Jardim do Mar, Paul do Mar, Pesqueiro, Seixal, Fajã da Areia, Ponta Delgada, Boaventura, São Jorge and Faial were considered poor. The landing places of the parishes of Porto do Moniz and Porto da Cruz are regarded as good when the winds blow from the southern quarter, for at such times no traffic at all is possible along the whole southern coast of Madeira, although this happens only a few times each year. Over the last thirty years, conditions at the landing places of these localities have improved considerably, thanks to the building of small quays and landing stages and to the extension and repair of those already in existence (see each of the entries named above).

before: It has been said that Madeira has no beaches, perhaps because they are not sandy and are of limited length. Indeed, the beaches of this island, with the exception of Prainha at Caniçal, are made up of small stones or rounded pebbles of dark basalt; all of them look sombre, and walking on them is difficult and uncomfortable. By way of compensation, the neighbouring island of Porto Santo has one of the finest and longest beaches in the whole country. The principal beaches of Madeira, some of them very short, are the following: Prainha, Caniçal, Machico, Seixo, Santa Cruz, Porto Novo, Reis Magos, Funchal, Formosa (see those entries), Câmara de Lobos, Ribeira Brava, Lugar de Baixo, Madalena do Mar, Calheta and Paul do Mar, on the south coast, and those of Porto do Moniz, São Vicente, Fajã da Areia, Ponta Delgada, São Jorge and Porto da Cruz on the north coast. (See those entries, under the heading ‘Ports’ or ‘Beaches’, and also the article Ports.)

The principal beaches of Madeira, some of them very short, are the following: Prainha, Caniçal, Machico, Seixo, Santa Cruz, Porto Novo, Reis Magos, Funchal, Formosa (see those entries), Câmara de Lobos, Ribeira Brava, Lugar de Baixo, Madalena do Mar, Calheta and Paul do Mar, on the south coast, and those of Porto Moniz, São Vicente, Fajã da Areia, Ponta Delgada, São Jorge and Porto da Cruz on the north coast. (See those entries, under the heading ‘Ports’ or ‘Beaches’, and also the article Ports.)

before: Of Medina e Vasconcelos’s compositions, it was the *Zargueida* that brought him the greatest renown, and it is still today the best known of them all. It is an epic poem in *ottava rima*, modelled on the classical forms of the ancient epic. It is divided into ten cantos and contains more than five thousand lines. It deals with the discovery of Madeira by João Gonçalves Zarco, taking the discoverer’s surname as the title of the poem. It contains a series of interesting episodes with some felicitous poetic digressions, among which the legend of Robert Machin stands out. The actual discovery of this island is described only in Canto X. The poem is preceded by a sonnet dedicated to Bocage, to which that distinguished poet replied with another sonnet, which is without doubt the finest composition in this volume.

before: There is little material to enable us to write a biography of the poet Medina in any detail. Some of the poems in his volume *Poesias Lyricas* show that he was twenty years old when he enrolled at the University of Coimbra, which must have happened in 1788; he adds that ‘in the space of only two winters he heard the learned lectures of the sages who explain the mysteries of the sciences.’ Dr Azevedo says that, Medina having been ‘from his youth a follower of the ideas of the philosophers of the 18th century, this led, around 1790, to his being imprisoned for a year and a half in Coimbra, and afterwards forced to leave the city and expelled from the University for ever.’ The severity of this punishment seems to indicate that very serious charges weighed on Medina, but he utterly rejects them when he declares that it was ‘a false crime, never even conceived by me’. The poet wrote two *Epistolas* in verse to the rector of the University, Dom Francisco Rafael de Castro, one shortly after his imprisonment and the other when ‘already, sir, twelve moons have passed since I began weeping among tyrannous irons’. These letters were meant to implore the prelate’s protection and to obtain his release. It is not known whether Medina’s heartfelt poetic inspiration moved the inflexible magistrate, who was perhaps little swayed by the plaintive pleas of a poor, helpless student. It is certain, however, that he was set free a few months later, returning to his native land around 1792.

before: Medina e Vasconcelos, who, in the words of Dr Álvaro de Azevedo already cited, showed himself from his youth a follower of the ideas of the 18th-century philosophers, was also a staunch supporter of the Constitution of 1821. For this reason he was caught in the net of the special judicial commission (alçada) that came to this island in 1823 (vol. I, p. 32) to conduct a rigorous and oppressive judicial inquiry (*devassa*) into the events that had taken place here at the proclamation of the first representative government in our country. The six magistrates who made up the commission arrived in Funchal on 26 August 1823 and delivered their sentence on 24 October of the same year. It states that Medina e Vasconcelos, ‘forgetful of the duties of honour and of a loyal subject, and of the ties that bound him most closely as a public official, had the reckless audacity to utter in public most grievous insults offensive to the decorum, veneration and respect due to the Throne and to the royal persons of Their Majesties, so grave that they are judged unworthy of being written in this judgment’. The same sentence asserts that he belonged to Freemasonry and took part in its work, having contributed notably to the proclamation and establishment of constitutional government in this archipelago. He was sentenced ‘to eight years of penal exile (degredo) in the State of Angola, with disqualification from offices of Justice or the Treasury, and to fifty thousand *réis* (old Portuguese money of account; 1$000 = 1,000 réis, 1:000$000 = one conto = 1,000,000 réis) to the Exchequer’.

before: A fish of the family Trichiuridae, almost peculiar to the deep seas of Madeira, where it lives in great numbers. Caught exclusively by the fishermen of Câmara de Lobos, it is a tasty fish that supplies the Funchal market on a large scale. It is fished at a depth of about 1000 *braças*, which makes this one of the deepest fisheries in the whole world. The scabbardfish, once very cheap, now sells for as much as 60, 70 and 80 centavos each in the Funchal market.

before: All this laborious study still awaits a powerful intellect and a conscientious researcher who, with a remarkable gift for generalisation, will carry out this longed-for work, drawing on the fragmentary and scattered material to be found in various places. The learned and valuable notes to the *Saudades da Terra* are indisputable proof that their talented and most erudite author had ample breadth and a sure sense of direction for so great an undertaking. However, his modest aim of acting simply as annotator of the work of Gaspar Frutuoso did not allow him to leave us the work that he could have produced without effort, and perhaps even with great pleasure to his mind. There are points of our history that Dr Álvaro Rodrigues de Azevedo treats with the necessary fullness and with all the rigour of historical criticism. Others he left only in outline, without the commentary the subject demanded, because they lay outside the plan he had drawn up and would have forced him to give the notes to the *Saudades da Terra* an excessive scope. In spite of everything, it is above all in this valuable and abundant storehouse of news and information, of appraisals and criticism, of observations and philosophical reflections, that the future author of the history of Madeira will find his richest treasure when he sets out to prepare and write his work.

before: The four periods into which Dr Álvaro Rodrigues de Azevedo divides his sketch of the history of the archipelago run as follows: the 1st from the discovery to the death of John I in 1433; the 2nd from that year to the liberation from the Spanish yoke in 1640; the 3rd extends to the establishment of constitutional government in 1834; and the 4th runs from that year to the present day. In the article Bibliography we said that in the article Sources for Madeiran History we would give a short survey of the works offering the richest store of news and information on the history of this archipelago. In that article we dealt at some length with the public archives and other manuscript sources, but through a mere oversight we did not include a brief list of printed works, which we shall now do in this place. As we have said more than once, and as everyone generally knows, the *Saudades da Terra*, and above all its valuable and abundant notes, are the richest, fullest and most reliable repository of material we possess for the history of our archipelago. We shall deal with that monumental work at the appropriate point in this *Elucidário*. Next in importance and value come the *Historia Insulana* and the *Archivo da Marinha e Ultramar*, to which we have already devoted separate articles in this *Elucidário*. Of more secondary importance, but still offering valuable information and news, we may mention the *Epocha Administrativa* (3 vols, 1849, 1850, 1852) and the other pamphlets by Sérvulo de Meneses on the model administration of Governor Silvestre Ribeiro; *Breve Noticia sobre a Ilha da Madeira*, by Paulo Perestrelo da Câmara (1841); *Catalogo dos Bispos da Igreja do Funchal*, by Dom António Caetano de Sousa (1721), in the *Colecção dos Documentos e Memórias da Academia Real de Historia Portugueza*, vol. 1; *As Dezertas* and *As Selvagens*, by A. Artur Sarmento (1903 and 1906); *Os Portos Marítimos de Portugal e Ilhas Adjacentes*, by Adolfo Loureiro (1910, vol. V); various pamphlets on the *colonia* contract (Madeiran sharecropping tenancy; produce divided, improvements owned by the tenant) (see the bibliography of the article *Colonia* contract); *Documentos para a Historia das cortes geraes da nação portugueza*, by the Baron of São Clemente (1888, vol. V); *Constituições Sinodais do Bispado do Funchal* (see the article Constitutions of the Bishopric); various works on the discovery of this archipelago, cited on pp. 330, 349, 350 and 906 of the *Saudades*, to which we must add *Memória sobre a descoberta das ilhas do Porto Santo e Madeira*, by E. A. Betencourt (1875), *Quando foi descoberta a Madeira?*, by Jordão de Freitas (1911), and *O Reconhecimento do Arquipelago da Madeira*, by Manuel Gregório Pestana Júnior (1920); some pamphlets on the entailed estates of Madeira and their abolition (see the article Entails); various leaflets on the proclamation of the Constitution of 1821 in this archipelago (see the article Constitution of 1821); three pamphlets on Madeiran chorography (see the article Chorography); *Statistica Historico-Geografica das ilhas da Madeira e Porto Santo*, by Joaquim Pedro Cardoso Casado Giraldes (Paris, 1815); *Ilha da Madeira*, by Acúrsio Garcia Ramos (2 vols, 1879 and 1880); some leaflets on the Protestant proselytism of Dr Robert Kalley (see the article Kalley); and the precious collection of Madeiran newspapers belonging to the company of the *Diário de Notícias* of Funchal, which is the subject of the pamphlet *Resenha Chronologica do Jornalismo Madeirense* (1908). before: It is the larva of *Nonagria sacchari*, an insect of the order Lepidoptera. As early as 1502 this larva was devastating Madeira’s sugar plantations: on 15 November of that year a royal letter (*carta régia*) was sent to the judges and councillors (*vereadores*) of the Municipal Council (*Câmara Municipal*) of Funchal, recommending the use of ash to destroy the cane borer. before: At Lombo dos Reis, in the parish (*freguesia*) of Estreito da Calheta, stands the old chapel of Reis Magos (Three Kings). It was founded around 1529 by Francisco Homem de Gouveia and his wife, Dona Isabel Afonso, who made it the seat of an entailed estate (*morgadio*). This chapel and the entailed foundation (*instituição vincular*, a morgado or capela) attached to it were discussed at length in an article published in the *Brado d'Oeste* of 2 September 1916. There is also a chapel dedicated to the Reis Magos in the parish of Ponta Delgada, which belonged to the house of Carvalhal. It is of very old construction, for a document of 1577 states that it was already in a poor state of repair at that time. It was rebuilt in 1778 by João de Carvalhal Esmeraldo e Câmara, administrator of the entail to which it belonged. A few years ago it was restored once more, and today it is the property of João Fidélio de Canha.

before: From a strictly religious point of view, every diocese has its own special patrons, and that of Funchal could not have departed from this praiseworthy custom, or rather obligatory precept, which is followed everywhere and always marked by fervent devotions on particular days of the year. It is well known that this diocese has as its first and chief patron the apostle St James the Less, and as lesser patrons St Sebastian and St Roch; and that, since 1803, the city of Funchal and its surroundings have been solemnly consecrated to the protection of Nossa Senhora do Monte. before: For centuries the first of May has been solemnly celebrated on this island, and especially in this city. Long before the workers had dedicated that day to commemorating the assertion of their rights, and before the Municipal Council (*Câmara Municipal*) of Funchal had resolved to adopt the first of May as the municipality’s annual public holiday, the feast of the apostle St James the Less, which the Church celebrates on the first of that month, was already solemnly observed here. The day was kept as a holy day; the feast of the patron saint was celebrated in the church that is the seat of the parish of Santa Maria Maior; and, above all, there was a splendid procession that set out from the Cathedral (Sé Catedral) and made its way to that church.

before: ‘Never again has the said evil (plague) been on this island. before: The flash flood (*aluvião*) of 9 October 1803 caused many deaths and enormous material damage in Madeira, which greatly alarmed our people. On 13 November of the same year, therefore, Bishop Dom Luís Rodrigues Vilares, the cathedral chapter and the rest of the clergy met in the choir of the Cathedral to implore divine protection for this island. It was resolved ‘by unanimous agreement’, as we read in a record drawn up on that occasion, ‘to celebrate a most solemn festival on the 9th day of the month of October each year in honour of the patronage of the Most Holy Virgin, Mother of God and of sinners, taking her as protector and special advocate before Our Lord Jesus Christ, her only-begotten Son, to obtain from Him in the first place a general pardon for all our sins, and in the second the suspension of the punishment with which He justly wished to chastise us, so that this city may not again find itself in so lamentable a crisis; on that same day the office of the patronage of the same Most Holy Virgin shall be recited with first-class rite, and a most solemn procession shall be held, attended by His Excellency the Bishop, the Chapter and the rest of the secular and regular clergy, as is customarily done at the feast and solemnity of our most amiable and most devout patron saint, St James the Less; for which the necessary licences of the Prince Regent, Our Lord, and Briefs of the Holy Apostolic See shall be sought; the procession shall go from this cathedral church to the chancel of the aforesaid church of Nossa Senhora do Calhau (Our Lady of Calhau), which was thrown to the ground, should it be preserved in memory of this fatal calamity, and, should it not survive, to the new church that is to be built, where solemn vespers shall be sung in the presence of the Chapter and Clergy, and Mass shall be celebrated on the said 9th, with a sermon, in which this dreadful night shall be commemorated, so that the peoples and future generations may always remember the fate with which we were punished, and the powerful intercession of the Most Holy Virgin, in whom we take refuge so as not to suffer a second punishment and to be preserved from similar calamities.’

before: In connection with the same procession, a meeting of the nobility and people was held on 11 November of that year, 1803, in the building of the Municipal Council (*Câmara Municipal*). Its purpose was to consider a letter from the diocesan prelate, addressed to the *juiz de fora* (crown-appointed judge from outside the district) on the 9th of the same month, ‘concerning the proposed vow that he wishes to be made of an annual procession and festival of the patronage of Our Lady on 9 October each year, so that all the people of this colony may merit the protection of the Mother of God and may not suffer a repetition of the punishment it endured with the flood and flash flood of the said 9th...’. It was decided unanimously that the nobility and people should conform to the prelate’s intention, although this resolution was to remain suspended until the Prince Regent had pronounced on it’. After the flash flood of 9 October 1803 (vol. I, p. 54), the diocesan bishop, chapter, clergy and faithful placed the island, and especially the city, under the protection of Nossa Senhora do Monte. This was confirmed by an Apostolic Rescript of Pius VII dated 21 July 1804, and the feast of the Patronage of Nossa Senhora do Monte was then instituted. It was celebrated on 9 October each year, with a solemn procession that went from the Cathedral to the parish church of Santa Maria Maior. The ninth of October was formerly a holy day of obligation, preceded by its own vigil with fasting.

before: He was a brother (*freire*) of the Order of Christ, to which the Madeira archipelago belonged in spiritual matters (see Order of Christ). He was one of the first priests whom the Order of Christ sent to this island at the request of Prince Henry the Navigator, and he held wider powers of canonical jurisdiction than the other clergy then in Madeira. He exercised parochial duties at Nossa Senhora do Calhau (Our Lady of Calhau) and was later parish priest of the parish (*freguesia*) of the Sé, being invested as dean of the Cathedral when this diocese was created in 1514. He was the representative of the Order of Christ and therefore carried out duties of inspection and superintendence over various branches of public administration. He left an honoured memory.

before: The flood waters divide on the south coast of Madeira, running west and east from the stretch between Ponta do Sol and Ponta do Jardim do Mar. From this point to Ponta do Pargo, the sea currents generally set from the north-west close to the coast. These currents run parallel to the coast or slightly inclined towards it, and are at times quite strong offshore (in the zone of approximately 500 m depth). Near the headlands they become stronger, sometimes producing a meeting of waters, as can be seen at Ponta do Pargo and above all at Ponta de São Lourenço, where their speeds reach about 2 miles at spring tides.
after: The flood waters divide on the south coast of Madeira, running west and east from the stretch between Ponta do Sol (‘point of the sun’) and Ponta do Jardim do Mar (‘point of the garden by the sea’). From this point to Ponta do Pargo (‘sea bream point’), the sea currents generally set from the north-west close to the coast. These currents run parallel to the coast or slightly inclined towards it, and are at times quite strong offshore (in the zone of approximately 500 m depth). Near the headlands they become stronger, sometimes producing a meeting of waters, as can be seen at Ponta do Pargo and above all at Ponta de São Lourenço, where their speeds reach about 2 miles at spring tides.

before: The flood currents are felt chiefly on the south coast, at Ponta do Pargo and Ponta de São Lourenço, and also on the north-west coast, at Ponta do Tristão and near Ilhéu Mole (Soft Islet) (Porto do Moniz).
after: The flood currents are felt chiefly on the south coast, at Ponta do Pargo and Ponta de São Lourenço, and also on the north-west coast, at Ponta do Tristão (‘Tristão’s point’) and near Ilhéu Mole (Porto Moniz).

before: The ebb waters produce strong currents towards the south-south-west at Ponta de São Lourenço, towards the west at Ponta de São Jorge and towards the south-west at Ilhéu Mole and Ponta do Tristão. before: The phylloxera invasion of Madeira, says F. de Almeida e Brito in a report published in 1883, was confirmed in 1872. By then many vineyards had already been lost and land laid completely waste in the municipalities of Funchal and Câmara de Lobos, which suggests that the disease had been present here since 1865 at least. According to the same agronomist, the pest was brought to Madeira in cuttings of the Isabella, or American vine, which had been admitted to cultivation because of its proven resistance to oidium or *mangra* (powdery mildew of the vine, oidium). This opinion was shared by many of the island’s winegrowers, who had closely followed the course and development of the new disease.

before: To make it possible to replant the devastated land with reliable American hybrids and stocks, two nurseries of cuttings and rooted vines were set up, one at Ribeirinho and the other at Torreão, and as early as 1883 some 60,000 young vines were distributed among the island’s landowners. Riparia, Jacquez, Herbemont, Rupestris, Solonis, Taylor, Clinton, Elsimbro and York Madeira were the first stocks grown in these nurseries; they were followed by Cunningham, Viala, Elvira, Othello, Cinerea, Black Pearl and Gaston Bazile. According to Inspector Almeida e Brito in his report, Taylor was the stock that could be used with greatest confidence in Madeira, since it had ‘already seven years of trial, growing admirably in phylloxera-infested soils’.

before: A contemporary English writer, who died in London in June 1901. He was a member of the Royal Geographical Society and keeper of the department of maps and charts at the British Museum. The work he published in 1868 under the title *The Life of Prince Henry of Portugal* became very well known in our country; it is a true commemorative pillar (padrão) raised to the memory of Prince Henry the Navigator, and also an unimpeachable tribute to the maritime odyssey accomplished by the Portuguese in the course of the 15th century. Henry Major regards the legend of Robert Machin as historical truth, but Dr Álvaro de Azevedo triumphantly refuted the English writer's assertions, devoting to this subject some of the most interesting pages of his learned notes to the *Saudades da Terra*. Dr Rodrigues de Azevedo's irrefutable argument reduced the Machin affair to the proportions of a charming and poetic legend without the slightest glimmer of historical foundation. Major published another work entitled *The Discoveries of Prince Henry the Navigator and their results* (London 1877), and his first work was translated into Portuguese by José António Ferreira Brandão.
after: A contemporary English writer, who died in London in June 1901. He was a member of the Royal Geographical Society and keeper of the department of maps and charts at the British Museum. Richard Henry Major regards the legend of Robert Machin as historical truth, but Dr Álvaro de Azevedo triumphantly refuted the English writer's assertions, devoting to this subject some of the most interesting pages of his learned notes to ‘Longing for the Homeland’ (*Saudades da Terra*). Dr Rodrigues de Azevedo's irrefutable argument reduced the Machin affair to the proportions of a charming and poetic legend without the slightest glimmer of historical foundation. Major published another work entitled *The Discoveries of Prince Henry the Navigator and their results* (London 1877), and his first work was translated into Portuguese by José António Ferreira Brandão.

before: Adolfo de Noronha was appointed director of the Funchal Municipal Library in 1928 and at once began to campaign for the creation of a ‘Natural Science Museum’. He was its most strenuous and persevering champion, both in the press and among those who could lend their prestige and influence to the project. He always linked this idea with that of acquiring a suitable building to house the Municipal Library and the attached science museum, with sections for art, archaeology, ethnology, etc. With the authorisation of the Municipal Council (*Câmara Municipal*), he spent some months in Lisbon arranging the issue of a postage stamp to pay for these planned premises. The scheme succeeded in full, and that public department is now housed in a fine, spacious building known as the Palácio de São Pedro (St Peter Palace), the former manor house of the Counts of Carvalhal. It is beyond dispute that the realisation of this important improvement is due chiefly to Adolfo de Noronha. When he retired from his public duties, the Council paid him a well-deserved tribute, in which various official bodies joined, by unveiling a stone inscription placed in one of the rooms of the Museum.

before: He waged bitter struggles with the governor and captain-general Dom José Manuel da Câmara. These lasted a long time and eventually erupted into violent conflict, so that the central government had to intervene in the regrettable dispute that had arisen between the two highest authorities of the archipelago. The disagreements went back a long way. The prelate had opposed the quartering of English troops in the Jesuit College (*Colégio dos Jesuítas*), which Maria I had granted for use as the diocesan seminary, but he had to yield before force. When the troops withdrew to England, Dom Luís Vilares pressed for the building to be handed over. The governor refused, on the grounds that it was indispensable for quartering the garrison forces. Other causes arose that aggravated the disagreement still further. Claiming that he had been slighted by the prelate in the Cathedral (Sé Catedral), Dom José Manuel da Câmara ordered him to leave the city immediately. This took place on 18 June 1803, when Dom Luís Vilares went to a property that the mitre owned in the parish (*freguesia*) of Santo da Serra, where he remained for about four months.

before: At the head of the procession went the processional banner of the Third Order of St Francis, with its coat of arms exquisitely embroidered in gold, followed immediately by the so-called tree of penance, which bore a crucifix adorned with hawthorn branches, a rosary and a set of scourges. Behind came the brotherhood of penance, with four brethren walking beside the cross: one carried a tray with two crossed bones and a skull, another a glass urn holding ashes from palm and olive branches blessed on Palm Sunday, another an hourglass with two wings, and the fourth a lamp-stand with an extinguished lamp. Next came the cross of the Order and the litter of the Senhor dos Passos, with its confraternity, and then the litters of St Francis carrying the cross on his back; of the Confirmation of the Rule, showing the same saint, Pope Innocent III and a cardinal; of St Anthony of Noto (black); of St Lucius and St Bona (the two siblings); of St Rose of Viterbo; of St Margaret of Cortona; of St Joan; of St Elizabeth, daughter of the Queen of Hungary; of St Elizabeth, Queen of Hungary; of St Roch; of St Elzéar and St Delphine (the happily married couple); of St Henry, King of Dacia; of St Louis, King of France; of St Ivo, doctor; and of St Elizabeth, Queen of Portugal, all these images being accompanied by their respective confraternities. The religious cortège was brought up by the board (*mesa*) of the Third Order, the litter of St Francis embracing Christ, the corporation of Chaplains, and the purple canopy, beneath which walked three clergymen in copes of the same colour, the one in the middle carrying a reliquary with the Holy Wood of the Cross; and finally the Bishop of the Diocese, in his cappa magna (the bishop's long ceremonial cape with train), the train of which was held by five seminarians.

before: A plant of the family Plantaginaceae, common on Madeira, Porto Santo and the Desertas. Its leaves are arranged in a rosette, elongated, hairy or almost glabrous, usually 1–2-pinnatipartite, and its spikes are narrow, with basal peduncles. before: Luís Alexandre Ribeiro Mendonça, Baron of Úzel, was born in this city in 1839 and died on 2 June 1903. He had a thorough knowledge of the French and English languages, and left some unpublished compositions in prose and verse in the former. before: He was born in the town (*vila*) of Ribeira Brava on 26 May 1857, the son of António de Sousa da Silva Pereira and Dona Luísa da Conceição Pereira. He attended the Funchal lyceum (state secondary school) and the former Polytechnic School and Army School, and was commissioned second lieutenant of artillery on 7 January 1885. He served at Vendas Novas, where he also taught at the Practical School of Artillery (*Escola Prática de Artilharia*), and from there he moved to Funchal. There he served as a subaltern and later, after promotion to captain, as commander of No. 3 Garrison Artillery Company. He was also commander of war material on the island of Madeira. In every military duty and commission he undertook, he proved a highly intelligent, spirited officer and a firm disciplinarian.

before: A family surname descending from the Englishman William Reid, who came to Madeira in 1844 or 1845 and set up a hotel here in the old Rua do Mercado de São João. His sons William and Alfred Reid, who carried on their father’s line of business, wrote a short work in 1881 entitled *Madeira, a guide book of useful and varying information*. Their chief service to the island, however, was their gift to the Funchal Municipal Library of nearly 10,000 volumes from the library of the late Madeiran João Joaquim de Freitas.

before: Several people bearing this surname are found, but one of the first settlers was Antão Alvares de Carvalho, who held a *sesmaria* (royal land grant to settlers on condition of cultivation) in Santa Cruz and later founded on it the entail (*morgado*) of São Gil. Luís Alvares da Costa founded the original convent of São Francisco (St Francis of Assisi) in Funchal in 1473. In 1523 Pedro Alvares was judge of the Council (*juiz da câmara*) of Funchal. In the last quarter of the 15th century João Alvares, an ancestor of the celebrated grammarian Father Manuel Álvares, was living in Ribeira Brava.

before: He was born in Funchal on 29 August 1877, the son of Dr Joaquim Gonçalves Marques and Dona Maria Gonçalves Marques. He qualified as a physician and surgeon at this city’s now defunct Medical-Surgical School (*Escola Médico-cirúrgica*), completing the course in 1897. For some time he was a physician in Seixal, and later moved to Porto do Moniz as the Council’s district medical officer. He remained there until 1904, when he was appointed secretary of the emigration police in Funchal, a post he held until after the establishment of the Republic in our country.

before: When the Republic was proclaimed and the old monarchist parties dissolved, Dr Vasco Marques joined the Democratic Party, led by Dr Afonso Costa, and under the new regime he continued to display his great intellectual gifts and his tough fighting temper. He edited the *Liberal* and the *Democrata*, and was municipal administrator (administrador do concelho, the government's representative) of Funchal in 1912 and 1913. After the death of the Viscount of Ribeira Brava he was elected president of the District Committee (Comissão Distrital) of that party. In 1920 he joined the Republican Party of National Reconstitution, in which he now holds a post identical to the one he last held on the district committee of the Portuguese Republican Party (1921).

before: As president both of the District General Council (*Junta Geral*) and of its executive committee, he has rendered many services to his homeland. To him is owed the great expansion of the district's roads in recent years, the acquisition of the Incarnação building, where the Episcopal Seminary was housed, and of the house that serves as the old people's home, the construction of a new pavilion at the Camara Pestana asylum, etc., etc. The plan of improvements that he and the executive committee of the General Council drew up and intended to carry out includes the construction of several new roads and the repairs that many existing ones need, the harnessing of water for irrigation, the reforestation of Madeira's mountains, the construction of a modern housing district, etc., etc.

before: Dr Vasco Marques rendered excellent services on Porto Santo during an epidemic that broke out on that island, and in Porto do Moniz, where, as we have said, he spent many years, he left a great deal of goodwill through the way he carried out the duties of his post. before: The author of the *Saudades da Terra* refers to him in the following laudatory terms: ‘he is a man most skilful in all his exercises of war, very temperate, of great virtue and little given to softness: he was brought up in hardship, away from the pleasures of his brethren, for which reason he endures toil well, and is a most valiant knight, as he showed when the French entered the city of Funchal, where, serving as Captain-General (as he then served and serves now) in the absence, and later upon the death, of his nephew, he most honourably wounded the French captain the Viscount of Pompador at the entrance to the Fortress, where he showed the spirit of a valiant captain; and for this the king gave him the habit with a certain pension (*tença*), and exempted him for eight years from paying the fifth and the tithe on his estate, a good part of which he holds in the *termo* (municipal jurisdictional district, a subdivision of the comarca) of Funchal, in sugars and wines. The learned annotator of the *Saudades* does not share Gaspar Frutuoso’s opinion, stating that Francisco Gonçalves da Câmara, ‘in whose charge was the government of the island of Madeira, far from attacking, did not even know how to defend it from the aggressors: there was only, at the entrance to the city of Funchal and at the gate of the fortress of São Lourenço, a clash of desperate defence and some illustrious feats of individual valour, which redeemed the good name of Madeira...’ The same annotator further adds that there were ‘rewards for the faint-hearted captain Francisco Gonçalves da Câmara, who, in the moment of danger, went to take refuge among the women...’ Francisco Gonçalves da Câmara owned the *quinta* (country estate) now called Quinta das Cruzes, and lived there ‘in great and sumptuous halls’, in the words of Frutuoso.

before: Since the city of Funchal once had its Moorish quarter (*mouraria*), and tradition holds that many Moors lived at Ponta do Sol, it is not surprising that these people, in whom Arab blood almost always predominated, left notable traces of their stay on the island in certain songs, just as they did in the old costume and in the anthropological characteristics of part of the Madeiran population. The Arabs, one author notes, never pass from one note to another, whatever the distance between them, whether rising or falling, without running through all the intermediate intervals. These glissades, not always pleasant to a European ear, can be heard in some of the music of our countryside, probably introduced to the island during the 15th century.

before: On 15 October 1846 a meeting of the principal authorities and officials of the district, called by the governor, was held in the offices of the Civil Government. It was resolved that the three key-holders (*claviculário*, one of the officials each holding a key to the strongbox) of the central treasury should advance up to 1 500$000 *réis* (old Portuguese money of account; 1$000 = 1,000 réis, 1:000$000 = one conto = 1,000,000 réis) for clearing debris from the watercourses. This made it possible to give work, and therefore a cash income, to a great many men struggling with destitution.

before: São Pedro is the most populous and the most important of the four urban parishes (*freguesia*) of Funchal. It was within its bounds that the first colonisation and settlement began, because the discoverer Gonçalves Zarco himself made his first settlement there, on the height later called Santa Catarina. On the day the caravels first made for the bay that was to take the name of Funchal, they sought shelter by the islets lying to the west of that bay, as the day was already well advanced, and the captain decided that the discoverers should spend that night there. When they returned to this island from the Kingdom (*reino*, i.e. mainland Portugal) a second time, to begin the work of colonisation in earnest, the ships again anchored in the shelter of the same islets. The first settlers took refuge aboard them for several days, when the fire raging fiercely through the woods forced them to leave the land scorched by the flames. These islets were later named the Ilhéus da Pontinha, and they lie within the parish of São Pedro.

before: ‘The parish of São Pedro, in the city of Funchal,’ says Dr Álvaro Rodrigues de Azevedo, ‘had its origin in the chapel of São Paulo (St Paul the Apostle) (see that entry), founded by João Gonçalves Zarco, which was served by Franciscan friars and later by the curates of the Funchal Cathedral (*Sé*), until it was separated from the latter and constituted a parish in its own right by the royal decree (*alvará*) of King Sebastian of 20 June 1566, with the Ribeira de Santa Luzia as its boundary to the east and the Ribeira dos Socorridos to the west. It was abolished by the royal decree of 3 March 1579 of the Cardinal-King Henry, its urban part being reincorporated into that of the Sé, while from its suburban part the same decree created the parishes of São Roque and São Martinho; but a few years later, by the royal decree of Philip II of 14 August 1587, it was re-established with the boundaries it still has today.’

before: In 1851 he was appointed a teacher at the Liceu do Funchal (Funchal secondary school), a post he held for only a few years. He then served as schools commissioner in the district of Braga, where he likewise did not stay long. A fickle and restless spirit, he failed to make use of the gifts with which nature had enriched his exceptional intellect. That is why Bulhão Pato said of him, with complete justice: ‘I never knew anyone who combined so many faculties, nor anyone who strove more doggedly to destroy them. It was not mere aptitude that he possessed; they were lofty faculties. A blessed constitution, powerful in everything, even in the strength with which it managed to hide in the shadows a light that should have shone among the most brilliant.’

before: Luiz da Costa Pereira settled in Lisbon and for many years devoted himself almost exclusively to the theatre, for which he had a decided vocation. before: In 1895 the central government had some houses built on the slopes of the Pico do Areeiro to accommodate a weather station and to serve as the residence of its staff. About five *contos* de réis (*conto* (one million réis)) were spent on them, and the upkeep of the buildings was entrusted to the district Public Works Department (*Direcção das Obras Públicas*). When the Agricultural Council (*Junta Agrícola*) was created in 1911, the Areeiro Meteorological Station passed to this administrative body. before: Once those buildings were finished, however, what many had already predicted came to pass: the station had not been supplied with the essential instruments, and the staff needed to run it properly had never been appointed. Exposed to every kind of weather and to the frequent gales that sweep the area in winter, the building soon began to suffer extensive damage and quickly fell into an advanced state of ruin. The vandalism of the woodcutter and the cattle-herder completed the destruction that the storms had begun, and the supervising authorities made no beneficial effort to put an end to such criminal neglect. Thus the former Public Works Directorate (*Direcção das Obras Públicas*), the Agricultural Council (*Junta Agrícola*) and the District General Council not only always showed the utmost indifference to the operation of the Meteorological Station created by the government of mainland Portugal, but also allowed the buildings erected for that purpose on one of the slopes of Pico do Areeiro to collapse and disappear.

before: He was born in the parish (*freguesia*) of Ponta Delgada on 16 July 1874 and has devoted himself to industrial studies and research, succeeding in making paper from sugar-cane straw and in extracting from Madeiran trachytes the silica needed to make glass. before: The town (*vila*) of Porto Santo is also known by the name of Baleira, and we have already given an account of it on p. 117 of the 1st volume of this work, to which we refer the reader. As the seat of a captaincy, its donataries held the almost discretionary powers conferred on them by the letters of grant (carta de doação). But as it was also the seat of a municipality, the municipality, through its charters (foral), granted the people certain rights and privileges that tempered the powers of the captain-donataries. The letter of grant given to Bartolomeu Perestrelo on 1 November 1446, as donatary of Porto Santo, makes express reference to the charter that was to be given to the future town, which was created a few years after that date. We have found no trace of this charter, however, although one generally accompanied the establishment of new municipalities. It must nevertheless be supposed that it was modelled on the same lines as those of the other towns and municipalities of this archipelago.

before: 1748. On 31 March of this year, between one and two o’clock in the morning, a strong earthquake was felt in Madeira, followed by two further shocks. An account of the event written at the time, and reproduced on page 697 of the *Saudades da Terra*, states that some trustworthy persons claimed to have seen ‘towards the east of the said island a great band of fire rise into the air, and that shortly afterwards they observed a great glow of the colour of that same fire, which lasted for the space of a quarter of an hour, and it was felt that the air was unusually warm’.

before: From 1 April to 26 May further earthquakes were felt in Madeira on various days, but none of them reached the violence of the shock of 31 March, which caused considerable damage in many parts of the island. The Cathedral was left with several cracks and its façade leaning outwards, and the church tower also suffered badly. The same earthquake also caused considerable damage to the churches of Santa Maria Maior do Calhau, Santo António, São Gonçalo, Camacha, Machico, Caniçal, Porto do Moniz, Prazeres, Paul, Arco da Calheta, Canhas, Serra de Água, Câmara de Lobos and Estreito de Nossa Senhora da Graça. The house in which the bishop lived was left uninhabitable, and the buildings of the Customs House (*Alfândega*) and the Contos, despite their very strong walls, were left with thirty-two cracks, besides other more or less notable damage.

before: An inhabited locality (*sítio*) in the parish (*freguesia*) of Santo António, Funchal. The name is a corruption of João Boto, an early settler. before: The Clube Funchalense, to which we referred above, lasted almost 60 years. It was established in a house at Carmo, from where it moved to the mansion in Rua dos Ferreiros, which it occupied until it was dissolved. Only people of a certain social standing belonged to it, whereas the Clube Unido, founded at almost the same time and dissolved early in 1879, was less demanding in the requirements it set for its members, who in any case had to be of good conduct and hold a respectable position in society. The great merchants were admitted to the Clube Funchalense, but shopkeepers and other traders with retail establishments could not join as members. When a certain British merchant, highly esteemed and respected in Funchal but the owner of a drapery shop, sought to join the club, some members who were his friends warned him that the vote of the general assembly would go against him unless he first sold or transferred the shop!

before: See Freemasonry. Cochineal (*Cocus cacti*). A homopterous insect of the family Coccidae, imported from the Canary Islands in the second quarter of the 19th century, the female of which yielded the scarlet used in dyeing. It was bred on the cactus called prickly pear (*tabaibeira*) (*Opunti tuna*), but the industry never managed to flourish, despite the persistent efforts of some Funchal merchants. Its failure was due in part to the opposition of the peasants, who preferred the prickly pear (*tabaibo*) to the insect that spoiled this much-prized fruit for them, even though it was a colouring matter of high value at that time.

before: Almost opposite the old Rua das Dificuldades there once stood a most curious wooden building, known as the Vapor, whose ends rested on the two banks of the Ribeira de Santa Luzia. before: According to Paulo Perestrelo da Câmara, Madeira exported its Malmsey and dry wines to the court of Francis I of France, who came to the throne in 1515 and died in 1547, at the time of the wars in which that sovereign had embroiled his realms; and Rebelo da Silva says in the *Historia de Portugal* that Belgium was already importing the island’s wines in 1567. before: In 1852 *Oidium Tuckeri* appeared on the island and destroyed most of its vineyards, bringing poverty to many homes and forcing many Madeirans to emigrate to Brazil and other countries. Yet the dreadful crisis that then ravaged our land regenerated it, as Dr Álvaro de Azevedo judiciously remarks in his notes to *Saudades da Terra*. ‘With the wine gone, the English merchant wound up his affairs as best he could and withdrew; of the old British houses there remained only those of Newton Gordon & Comp.ª, J. W. & T. Selby, Blandy, and Rutterford & Grant, the last two sustained chiefly by the valuable coal trade. Thus Madeira was freed from its capitalist masters. The peasant, spurred by necessity, devoted himself to the lands he farmed, working them not with a single crop, as the vine had been until then, but with several: sugar cane, which soon gave him more and quicker money than wine had in recent times; and cereals, pulses, sweet and ordinary potatoes, yams and vegetables, which soon brought back to his home the prosperity and joy that had so long eluded it.’

before: After clarification the wines are sent to the *estufas* (heated store for ageing Madeira wine), unless they are being matured by the canteiro system (natural ageing of the wine in casks on wooden supports, without artificial heating). It was once the custom to add alcohol to the wine before heating, but today the most common practice is to add none until afterwards. Alcohol distilled from sugar cane is now used in treating our wines. Around the middle of the 19th century, however, the alcohol used for this purpose was made from the wines of the north, and at the beginning of that century foreign brandies were often used to treat the island’s wines. The records of the Municipal Council (*Câmara Municipal*) of Funchal contain several petitions from the Senate (*senado*, the municipal council) asking for the import of these brandies into Madeira to be banned.

before: An example of the close union of two monogenetic volcanic elevations (that is, elevations due to a single volcanic cause, even if it manifests itself at long intervals of time) is provided, on a far larger scale than Pichincha in Ecuador, by the island of Madeira. The whole mass of its mountains, which over a length of nearly 60 kilometres and a width of 15 to 20 rises to an altitude of 1,800 metres, was simply the product of two eruptive centres. And both of them, as can be concluded with great certainty from the way in which they are joined, were active at the same time.
after: An example of the close union of two monogenetic volcanic elevations (that is, elevations due to a single volcanic cause, even if it manifests itself at long intervals of time) is provided, on a far larger scale than Pichincha on the Equator, by the island of Madeira. The whole mass of its mountains, which over a length of nearly 60 kilometres and a width of 15 to 20 rises to an altitude of 1,800 metres, was simply the product of two eruptive centres. And both of them, as can be concluded with great certainty from the way in which they are joined, were active at the same time.

before: ‘The larger and higher of these two monogenetic structures is a caldera-shaped elevation that occupies more than two-thirds of the island. The caldera proper, which lies almost at the centre of the whole mass, is nearly 4 1/2 kilometres in diameter and 1,200 metres deep. A long valley (the former crater), which becomes very narrow in its lowest part and turns into a ravine, and which falls 600 metres over a length of 11 kilometres, drains the waters of this caldera, called Curral das Freiras. Among the many peaks surrounding the caldera, the highest, and indeed the highest point on the island, is Pico Ruivo (1850) metres. From the rim of the caldera immense ridges stretch out in every direction, and although these differ greatly in length, structure and shape, the observer is left with the impression that this main part of the island is, in broad outline, a symmetrical structure produced by volcanic forces. ‘Very different is the second mass of the island, much smaller in extent, but only 300 metres lower than the first. It is a dome-shaped elevation, flattened at the top, where one would expect a crater; it forms a plateau more than 3 kilometres in diameter, called the Paul da Serra.

before: The two eruptive centres, with their piled-up masses, lie so close to each other that their rocks not only touch but, to a certain extent, interlock. The boundary between the two masses is still clearly visible, marked by two very deep valleys running in opposite directions: one to the north, that of São Vicente, and the other to the south, that of Ribeira Brava. The headwater regions of these valleys, which erosion has widened and transformed into calderas with several branches, are separated only by a relatively very thin but high wall, a kind of crest bristling with peaks, which connects the plateau of the Paul da Serra with the western wall of the Curral das Freiras caldera.

before: ‘In addition, the island, whose volcanic activity died out long ago, possesses a number of well-preserved crater formations, although they are small. Their position and their connection with the main mass of the island make it more than probable that the source of their scanty eruptive material must be placed within the mass of the island itself, and not in the immense depths beneath it from which the island itself took its origin. We may mention, for example, the shallow crater of the pond (*lagoa*) of the Serra de Santo António at the far eastern end of the island, as well as the small eruptive cones and lava flows that form the base of the plateau above Porto Moniz at the far north-western end of the island.

before: ‘We do not wish to go into detail here about the tectonic structure of the volcanic mountains and their ramifications, but we should like to point out that the gradients of the mountain slopes and of the *lombos* show angles of inclination almost identical to those of the volcanic mountains of Ecuador. As there, the spurs that radiate in all directions from the central mass remain fairly horizontal in their upper part, but descend in very steep slopes as they approach their bases.

before: ‘The valley of Machico, in which the town (*vila*) of the same name stands, is,’ says Dr Álvaro Rodrigues de Azevedo, ‘some five to six kilometres long and two to three wide. It runs from north to south between two mountain ridges. One, to the east, rises above the town to form the Pico do Facho, then extends towards Caniçal and, running out into the sea, forms the towering Ponta de São Lourenço, on whose furthest pinnacle there has stood for some years a good revolving lighthouse, visible from beyond the island of Porto Santo; the other ends in the high plateau called the Queimada, overlooking the sea. From these ridges spring and flow abundant and beautiful waters that fertilise its already exceedingly rich soil; draining through the rugged ground or feeding the lesser brooks, they form its full-flowing stream, which winds along the valley to the beach, where it empties into the Atlantic. In these conditions the valley of Machico is rich in the most varied vegetation, from grasses to fruit-bearing and non-fruit-bearing trees; picturesque and most delightful, it must have been astonishing when, still virgin forest, it was beheld by Zarco and Tristão Vaz. The vast landing place and wide cove, protected to the east by the Ponta de São Lourenço and sheltered to the west by the towering coast known as the South coast, and therefore safe in all winds except those from that quarter, complete the general panorama of the site of Machico. The town lies at the very bottom of the valley, by the sea, cut lengthwise by the stream into two parts or quarters. To the west is the old quarter, the town proper, with the houses of the nobility, the modestly Manueline mother church (*igreja matriz*), the town hall of the municipality (*concelho*) and, along the beach, the charming tree-lined promenade. To the east is the Banda de Além, a suburb of poor seafaring folk, with humble dwellings and narrow, twisting alleys, but with little white houses rising in an amphitheatre, for they are already climbing the slope of the neighbouring Pico do Facho; and, on the bank of the stream, towards the sea, stands the small church of Cristo (Christ), or, more exactly, of the Order of Christ, as the crosses of that military order adorning its original portal still proclaim – this little church being without doubt the first built on the island of Madeira. Between these two quarters rise the thick walls within which the stream flows, gentle and clear almost always, torrential and fearsome in the winter storms: such is the town which, set in that frame, enhances its beauty..... This whole varied scene, beheld from the heights of the Queimada or of the Pico do Facho, which command the valley and the slopes, the stream and the crops, the town and the hamlets, the landing place and the cove, the sea as far as it merges with the horizon, the Ponta de São Lourenço turning blue in the haze, and the south coast fading little by little into the twilight of sunset. . is majestically beautiful. . . ’

before: The municipality of Machico corresponded in area and extent to the old captaincy. It was sharply cut back when the town and municipality of Santa Cruz were created in 1515, and it suffered no lesser mutilation when the municipality and town of São Vicente were established in 1744.

before: With the introduction of constitutional government and its new administrative organisation, the municipality of Machico was once again reduced to narrower dimensions when the municipality of Santana was created in 1835. Despite the protests of the Senate (*senado*, the municipal council) of Machico, the new municipality was maintained. It was made up of the parishes (*freguesias*) that compose it at present, together with the parish of Porto da Cruz. By the decree of 19 October 1852 this parish was detached from the municipality of Santana and incorporated into that of Machico.

It was made up of the parishes (*freguesias*) that compose it at present, together with the parish of Porto da Cruz. By the decree of 19 October 1852 this parish was detached from the municipality of Santana and incorporated into that of Machico.

before: Under the same decree, certain localities in the parishes of Machico and Santo da Serra were annexed to the municipality of Santa Cruz. This provoked vigorous protests from the Municipal Council of Machico and from various official and private figures prominent in the municipality. After a series of incidents and vicissitudes that seemed endless, the secretary-general of the district, António Lopes Barbosa de Albuquerque, acting as civil governor, convened a meeting at the Casa dos Romeiros (pilgrims’ house) of Santo da Serra on 11 September 1862. Present were representatives of the municipal councils of Machico and Santa Cruz, the municipal administrators, various public officials and other persons of standing. There a new division of municipalities and parishes was definitively agreed, the one in force today, and so an end was put to the claims and protests raised on both sides.

before: The name ‘Norte da Ilha’ (‘North of the Island’) is generally given to the northern coast of Madeira, which stretches from Ponta do Tristão to Ponta de São Lourenço – that is, from the parish (*freguesia*) of Achadas da Cruz to the parish of Porto da Cruz. It takes in all the parishes of the municipalities (*concelhos*) of Porto do Moniz, São Vicente and Santana, together with the parish of Porto da Cruz in the municipality of Machico. after: The name ‘Norte da Ilha’ (‘North of the Island’) is generally given to the northern coast of Madeira, which stretches from Ponta do Tristão (‘Tristão’s point’) to Ponta de São Lourenço (‘St Lawrence Point’) – that is, from the parish (*freguesia*) of Achadas da Cruz (‘plateaus of the cross’) to the parish of Porto da Cruz (‘harbour of the cross’). See the north coast (*Costa do Norte*).

before: A glaucous annual crucifer, with the lower leaves stalked and oblong and the upper ones sessile and arrow-shaped; small yellow flowers gathered in a corymb; pendulous silicles, indistinctly winged. From the leaves of this plant a blue colouring principle is extracted, capable of replacing indigo, which was once much used by Madeiran dyers. Madeira formerly exported some woad to Portugal, as can be seen from some notes that João Gonçalves Zarco received from Prince Henry the Navigator, in which he said: ‘let it be a reminder to you to send the woad once it has been prepared, and tell João Affonso to send some if it is prepared.’ Preparing the woad probably meant simply drying it in the sun, or else crushing its leaves, letting the resulting mass lose its water and forming it into balls, after allowing it to undergo the beginnings of fermentation for 8 to 12 days. Woad is not only useful in dyeing; it is also a fodder valued by cattle and sheep. In Câmara de Lobos its juice is used to treat pimples and other skin complaints.

before: A bird of the finch family (Fringillidae), common on Madeira and Porto Santo, which feeds on seeds and insects. On the one hand it damages crops through the great quantity of grain it eats; on the other, it should be regarded as an ally of the farmer, because of the great numbers of harmful insects it destroys, especially when it has young to feed in the nest. There were once municipal bylaws (*posturas*) aimed at destroying this species. A particularly curious one was that of the Municipal Council (*Câmara Municipal*) of Porto Santo, which obliged every head of household to present 25 sparrow heads during the whole month of June each year.

before: In 1920, when the industry was very prosperous, there were as many as 60 commercial houses in the city of Funchal, most of them foreign, which dealt exclusively in the purchase, finishing and export of embroidery. At that time there were more than 35,000 embroiderers spread across all the parishes of this island and Porto Santo. By the end of 1923 the number of exporting houses had risen to 100, and the value of the goods exported, chiefly to North America, was then estimated at 70,000 *contos* (1 conto = 1,000,000 réis, from 1911 1,000 escudos). See what we have already said about this industry at some length on pp. 162 ff. of vol. I of this work, under the heading Embroidery.

before: In the *Saudades da Terra*, in various articles and chronicles and in many books of genealogy, there are countless references to Madeirans who distinguished themselves in the strongholds of Morocco in the assaults against the Moors. Particularly deserving of honourable mention is the prompt and valuable relief sent from this island when those same strongholds were threatened and in danger of being destroyed by the warlike followers of Muhammad. The donataries of Funchal organised several expeditions, some of them well equipped and supplied and at no cost to mainland Portugal, which rendered the most notable services to the Fatherland. Various items of information bearing on this subject can be found in scattered articles of this work, and especially in the pamphlet *A Madeira e as Praças de Africa* by Colonel Alberto Artur Sarmento.

before: Thanks to the plant-collecting of the young Madeiran botanist José Gonçalves da Costa, a 3rd-year theology student at the Episcopal Seminary of Funchal, the herbarium of that seminary is today (1921) one of the richest known in plants of the Madeira archipelago. before: We have so far referred to collections of Phanerogams and Vascular Cryptogams. before: Ordained priest in 1815, he then served as parish priest in the parishes of Serra de Água, Ribeira Brava and Santo António, in Funchal. It is said – on what grounds we do not know – that, having been passed over in the competition he had entered for the vicarage of Santo António, he complained to John VI of the injustice done to him. before: Calheta was an important settlement from the earliest days of colonisation, and it lent its name to other localities that grew up in its immediate vicinity. Such were Estreito and Arco da Calheta. The name Arco (‘arc’) comes from the distinctive semicircular shape of its hills. These orographic features, as also happens elsewhere on the island, fully explain the name the first settlers gave it. This parish (*freguesia*) was created in 1572. Its seat was established in the chapel of São Brás (St Blaise), although it should be noted that religious services had already been held there before that year by its own original chaplain, as in other places, for Arco was then a settlement of some importance with a sizeable number of inhabitants. Brás Ferreira, one of the oldest settlers of this parish, is named as the founder of the chapel of São Brás, as he himself states in his will made in 1493; but João Fernandes de Andrade is also regarded as the man who had it built, for his wills made in 1520 and 1523 refer clearly to this. João Pedro de Freitas Drumond and the annotator of the *Saudades da Terra* note this glaring discrepancy, the latter saying that Brás Ferreira had left a bequest for the building of the chapel, but that it was actually built only by João Fernandes de Andrade. He died on 9 April 1527 and was buried in the said chapel, and it is recorded somewhere that the following epitaph could be read on his tomb: ‘Here lie João Fernandes and Beatriz de Abreu his wife, who were the first founders of this Arco.’

before: It was the royal decree (alvará régio) of 18 June 1572 that authorised the creation of a curacy (*curato*) held by a beneficed cleric (*beneficiado*) with the powers of a vicar, with an annual salary set at 13,000 réis (the Portuguese money of account before 1911; 1,000 réis = 1 mil-réis, 1,000,000 réis = 1 conto). The royal decree of 10 July of the same year added 110,000 réis on the appointment of the first parish priest, Friar Pedro Delgado, and the royal decree of 20 April 1589 made a further addition of half a *moio* (dry measure of grain, 60 *alqueires*) of wheat and a quarter of wine. It seems that other royal instruments later increased the stipend (*côngrua*) of the parish priest still further. The diocesan prelate, Dom Friar António Teles da Silva, under the authority granted by the royal decree of 28 December 1676, created a curacy in this parish with an annual salary of 12,000 réis in cash, one *moio* of wheat and one *pipa* (wine cask and measure, c. 400–500 litres) of wine, paid for by the ‘third superfluous beneficed cleric of Câmara de Lobos’. An old book in the parish archive states that this curacy was one of the best in the whole bishopric.

before: Gonçalo Fernandes, a mysterious figure mentioned in the old Madeiran chronicles, of whom we shall speak in a separate article, had a residence and a *sesmaria* in this parish. The parish has the chapels of Nossa Senhora do Loreto (Our Lady of Loreto), Nossa Senhora da Nazaré (Our Lady of Nazaré), Sagrado Coração de Jesus, Nossa Senhora da Conceição and Nossa Senhora da Vida. Of the old chapels of Nossa Senhora do Desterro and Nossa Senhora da Boa Hora only a few heaps of rubble remain today. Other chapels once existed that have vanished completely: those of Nossa Senhora das Mercês, Nossa Senhora da Consolação, Nossa Senhora da Visitação, Nossa Senhora da Conceição, Santo António and Santa Maria Madalena.
