before: Almost all these chapels were entailed foundations (*instituição vincular*, a morgado or capela), and some of them were the head and seat of various entailed estates (*morgadio*), of which there were not a few in this parish. Among them we shall mention that of Píncaro, founded by Braz Ferreira, the original founder of the chapel of São Braz, which, says an old manuscript, ‘began at the estate surrounding the parish church and continued along this line straight from the sea to the uplands, as far as the Pinheiro. . .’; the entailed estate founded by Iria Pires, later enlarged by its administrator Pedro Barreto, ‘which lies along the line of the Ribeira do Ledo, which bounds it to the north, and so continues as far as the Cova do Arco’; the entail of Consolação, which today belongs to the house of Torre Bela and seems to have been joined to that of Píncaro; the important entailed estate founded by Gonçalo Fernandes, headed in the chapel of Conceição at Serra de Água; that of Loreto, created by Dona Joana de Eça; the entail (*morgado*) whose seat was the chapel of Nazaré, founded by Antónia de Cristo and her sister Leonarda do Horto; that of Florenças, founded by João Homem de El-Rei; and others besides.

before: The popular uprising that broke out in 1834 in the parish (*freguesia*) of Calheta, with such grievous consequences (see Calheta), also spread to the parish of Arco: the people rioted and joined those of that parish, though we cannot say whether any parishioner of Arco da Calheta was among the victims. In 1887 the sad and notorious events surrounding the parish councils (*juntas de paróquia*) (see that entry), which in many parts of the island drove the people to the most extreme violence, also found a loud echo in the parish of Arco. The people rose up, threatening to break out into deplorable excesses, and seized the opportunity to demand the right to pay the landlords a third of the harvest instead of the half-share (*dimídia*, half of the harvest owed to the landlord) that they then paid, and which, despite everything, they continued to pay. The intervention of armed forces was needed, and they seem to have committed reprehensible excesses there. This parish has three state schools: one for boys, in the locality (*sítio*) of Ledo; one for girls, in the locality of Ladeira e Lamaceiros; and one mixed school, in the locality of Lombada.

before: An inhabited locality (*sítio*) in the parish (*freguesia*) of Calheta. before: The office of dean (*deão*) of Funchal Cathedral (*Sé*) was created by the very papal bull that established the diocese, and the bull expressly named the priest who was to hold the post. Nuno Cão (see that entry), whom the Order of Christ sent to Madeira with special powers, was the first parish priest of the Cathedral when this parish (*freguesia*) was created, and also the first dean; in the early days both offices were held jointly by the same man. Nuno Cão was succeeded by Filipe Rebelo, and on the latter’s death the post of dean was separated from that of parish priest, two curacies being created at that time exclusively for parish duties. The last clergymen to hold the deanery (office of dean of the cathedral chapter) of Funchal Cathedral were António Joaquim Gonçalves de Andrade, Aires de Ornelas e Vasconcelos and João Joaquim Pinto (see those entries). Until the establishment of the Republic, a degree in law or theology was required for appointment to this post. On the deanery of Funchal Cathedral and the priests who held this high ecclesiastical office, see the series of articles published in *O Jornal* in December 1935 and January 1936.

before: He was born in this city on 26 May 1824, the son of Severiano Alberto de Freitas Ferraz and Dona Leonor Filomena Ferraz. He completed the course of a higher school of engineering in Paris. In the practice of his profession as an engineer he left his name attached to works of great scale, such as the artificial harbour of Ponta Delgada and the building of Lisbon Penitentiary (*Penitenciária de Lisboa*). From 1866 to 1870 he directed the works on that harbour, and he wrote a report on the way he had directed its construction. He went abroad to make special studies of the various penitentiary systems and of prisons for offenders sentenced to major penalties, in order to guide the construction of Lisbon Penitentiary. He designed, planned and directed that work until this great building was almost finished. The way he carried out these important works provoked some debate in the press. Among the posts he held in Lisbon was that of director of the Water Company (*Companhia das Águas*).

before: The chapel of Nossa Senhora da Penha de França stands in Rua da Penha de França, in this city. It was founded in 1622 by António Dantas and rebuilt in 1712. It became the centre of a well-attended pilgrimage, with pilgrims coming from various parts of the island. Attached to it was a house for those who came from the more distant parishes to fulfil their vows to Our Lady of the Crag. In 1755 major repairs were carried out on it, paid for by the donations of the faithful. Around 1818 it was incorporated into national property (*bens nacionais*) and given to the diocesan bishop, and the pilgrims’ house was then turned into a summer residence for the prelates of this diocese. At that time the locality (*sítio*) was still regarded as a suburb of the city. For some time, for reasons unknown to us, it ceased to belong to the mitre; in 1838 it passed back into the possession of the prelates. Some years later repairs were made there at the expense of the State, which gave rise to a question and a debate in parliament. The Penha chapel had its own chaplain, and for many years its worship was maintained by the house of Carvalhal.

before: Several of the prelates have lived there for a time, and Bishop Dom Manuel Agostinho Barreto made the little house his permanent home, drawn by the pleasantness of the spot, its position overlooking the sea and its distance from the centre and noise of the city. The prelate Dom José da Costa Torres was living there when, on 6 October 1796, he found the house surrounded by troops and was forced to embark at once, ‘without taking leave, says a manuscript of the time, of any person, nor of the Most Holy Sacrament; and to this day the reason for this contrived embarkation by night and by back doors is unknown’. From 27 November 1840 to 9 January 1841 our great poet Castilho (see that entry) lived in this house. He had come to the island to accompany his brother, Canon Augusto Frederico de Castilho, who died there on 30 December and lies buried in the Angústias cemetery. In his historical eulogy of his brother, delivered at the Royal Conservatory of Lisbon, Castilho referred to his stay in Madeira, and in particular to the house adjoining the chapel, in these terms: ‘... a dwelling in a lovely suburb of the city, the parochial residence of Nossa Senhora da Penha de França; a humble house, cheerful and solitary like that of our hermitage, and not only neighbour to its church but embraced by it, shaped as if on purpose for both kinds of health: for that of the body through the freshness of the air, the tranquillity of the spot and the nearness of the sea, which bathes the feet of its modest garden and almost mirrors its banana trees; for that of the spirit through all these same circumstances of the beauty and grandeur of creation and through the worship of the Virgin...’

before: In the parish (*freguesia*) of Monte, Luís Gonçalves Mercador built a chapel dedicated to Nossa Senhora da Penha de França in 1620, and in 1685 a chapel with the same dedication was built in the locality of Fazenda, in the parish of Faial. This latter chapel has the peculiarity of being hollowed out and built within a single solitary block of soft cut stone (cantaria mole). The walls, the ceiling, the floor, the altar and the portico were all carved from the enormous stone, forming a single piece. It was founded by António Teixeira, 5th-generation grandson of the discoverer Tristão Vaz Teixeira, and the deed of endowment is dated 13 August 1685.

before: An interesting article published in the *Correio da Madeira* of 22 September 1922, which we believe to be the work of Father Fernando de Meneses Vaz, contains some curious details about this chapel. The most striking of them is that it was originally intended to serve as a small mosque for a number of Moorish slaves. The author of the article gives the chapel as founded by Irvão Teixeira in the first quarter of the 16th century, whereas the date we have recorded above was taken from an official document kept in the archives of the Diocesan Chancery (*Câmara Eclesiástica*) of the diocese.

before: For the Holy Week ceremonies, the so-called *camarim* (tiered throne erected for Holy Week), or throne, is set up in the chapel of Senhor Jesus; taken as a whole, it is of rare beauty and elegance. It is very tall and fills the whole of the chapel, which is quite spacious, and it is made up of hundreds of pieces, many of them in fine gilt carved woodwork (*talha dourada*). It dates from the first quarter of the 19th century.

before: In the article Englishmen (p. 164) we made a brief reference to John Howard March, saying that he was of English nationality, whereas in fact he was born in the United States of North America and was a citizen of that country. He was a wealthy merchant in Funchal and on several occasions served as American consul. He became well known here in Madeira for his great acts of benevolence. He not only relieved the poor of this land and some of its charitable institutions with extraordinary generosity, but also contributed liberally to various public improvements, the upkeep of schools, etc. Although a Protestant, he rebuilt the church of Santo da Serra and the large churchyard surrounding it. In 1828 he lent the money needed to pay the Miguelite troops who had seized Funchal, while at the same time sheltering many Constitutionalists in his house to protect them from persecution by the Absolutists. During the famine that ravaged this island in 1846 and 1847 he rendered notable services and did much to ensure the success of the subscriptions opened in this archipelago and abroad for the poor of Madeira.

before: He was an early settler of this island, whose identity the old Madeiran genealogies shroud in mystery, although he appears to have been a son of King Afonso V and of the king’s niece Dona Joana, the ‘Excelente Senhora’. The annotator of the *Historia Insulana*, following several genealogists, says that ‘this man has glimmerings of the Man in the Iron Mask, in Paris, and came to Madeira expressly forbidden to leave this island. He lived in grand style, and every year the royal household sent him in abundance all that he needed, yet it was never known who his parents were. When he died on 13 July 1539, he was buried in his chapel, on which he had placed as arms the Portuguese *quinas* in saltire over the cross of the Order of Christ. His name is inscribed on the marble tombstone, which bears in half-relief the figure of a boy with his face resting on his left hand and his elbow on a skull, pointing with his right hand to this maxim from the Book of Wisdom: *Sic et nos nati continuo desivimus esse*. His arrival in Madeira after the peace concluded between Afonso V and Queen Isabel of Castile led to the conjecture that he was that king’s son and that reasons of state prevented his being acknowledged.’ The chapel referred to here is the one that stood near the sea, on the bank of the stream of Serra de Água, in the parish (*freguesia*) of Arco da Calheta; we shall deal with it in a separate article. It was the seat of an entailed estate (*morgadio*) founded by Gonçalo Fernandes, to which his son Pedro Gonçalves de Andrade succeeded. This entailed house (*casa vinculada*) later passed to the Freitas da Madalena family, whose last representative was the holder of the entail (*morgado*) Nuno de Freitas Lomelino.

before: The palm family is represented in Madeira by several species, none of them native. The most widespread at present are *Phoenix dactylifera*, native to northern Africa, and *Ph. Jubae*, native to the Canary Islands. The latter has dark green, closely set leaves; the former has greyish-green leaves, usually somewhat spaced apart. The dates of the Canary Island palm are smaller than those of the desert palm, and their stones are not elongated as they are in that species. *Ph. jubae* is cultivated in the municipal garden and in the *quintas* (country estates) to the east and west of Funchal; *Ph dactylifera* appears in many localities of the lower zone of Madeira, and also on Porto Santo. On this last island the fruits of the desert palm reach full ripeness only after they have fallen. Besides these two palms, Madeira also has *Trachycarpus excelsus*, *pritchardia filifera*, *Latania borbonica*, *Seaforthia elegans*, etc., etc.

before: On 26 January 1915 the Funchal Municipal Council (*Câmara Municipal*) resolved to authorise the removal of various objects belonging to it to the Convent of Santa Clara (St Clare of Assisi), in order to begin founding an archaeological museum that might later be greatly expanded. Following this decision, a number of valuable objects that had lain forgotten or neglected in the municipality’s storehouses and elsewhere were taken there. Among the objects moved to the convent were the marble coat of arms and crown of the Convent of São Francisco (St Francis of Assisi); the turn (*roda*, revolving hatch in the convent wall) of the Convento das Mercês (Convent of Our Lady of Mercy); an inscription from the Ponte de São João; several paintings from the Bishop’s Palace (*Paço Episcopal*); the vestments of the chapel of the same palace; the marble coat of arms of the old gaol; the marble coat of arms and crown of the Varadouros arch, together with the Latin inscription, in local basalt, from the same arch; various items from the defunct Hospital de São Lázaro (St Lazarus); the old measures of the weights and measures office; the portrait of Canon Viveiros, founder of the Convento da Encarnação (Convent of the Incarnation), etc., etc.

before: The spiteful campaign waged by the Administrative Committee (*Comissão Administrativa*) of the Holy House of Mercy (*Santa Casa da Misericórdia*), chaired by Francisco Gomes de Gouveia, against the establishment of the archaeological museum in the building of the former convent, together with the little energy the Council showed in asserting its rights to possession of certain parts of that building, caused the museum to stall almost from the outset, so that it failed to render the services that might reasonably have been expected of it. In January 1916 the Municipal Council (*Câmara Municipal*) did resolve to petition the Government, requesting the grant of all the articles belonging to the convent of Santa Clara that had any historical value, so that they might be kept in the archaeological museum. However, this show of interest in an institution which, once properly set up, could well have fed the spirit of inquiry of learned people, is the last of which we have any knowledge. Nothing more has since been said about properly housing the countless objects of value that may deteriorate or go astray, because they have been left in the most complete neglect (1921).

before: According to João Augusto de Ornelas’s own statement, made in the *Direito* of 24 August 1863, he was born in the parish (*freguesia*) of Estreito de Câmara de Lobos on 26 June 1833. He started out as an apprentice printer and later attended some classes at the lyceum (state secondary school) of this city. He made his literary debut with a few pieces in the *Estudo* and the *Baratíssimo*, and contributed to other newspapers. He took over the editorship of the *Direito*, where for more than twenty years he devoted himself actively to journalism. He cultivated the novel with great success, publishing several works of fiction that were much admired and received high praise from some of our most illustrious men of letters. We shall mention the following: *A Arrependida*, Funchal, 1871, 190 pp., with a letter by José Vieira de Castro and an introduction by Júlio César Machado; *Maria*, Lisbon, 1873, 200 pp., with a prologue by António Augusto Teixeira de Vasconcelos; *A Mão de Sangue*, Lisbon, 1874, 266 pp., with an introduction by Camilo Castelo Branco; *A Justiça de Deus*, Funchal, 1876, 199 pp., with a critical letter by Pinheiro Chagas; *a Victima dum Lazarista*, Porto, 1879, 266 pp.; and *O Engeitado*, Porto, 1886, with an introduction by Pinheiro Chagas.

before: The observations we make here in passing, without the slightest intention of any disparagement that might be misconstrued, do not seek to belittle the value of the recent edition of the *Saudades*, which we acknowledge to be great, and we take this opportunity to pay its illustrious author of the preface and annotator the sincere tribute of our heartfelt admiration (1925). As 1922 marked the fifth centenary of the birth of Doctor Gaspar Frutuoso, a committee was formed in the city of Ponta Delgada to commemorate the date fittingly, taking the opportunity to give due prominence to the eminent qualities as prose writer, historian and humanist that brought renown to that illustrious native of São Miguel. To the warmest applause of all, the committee organising the centenary decided that the greatest tribute that could be paid to the author of *Saudades da Terra* would be the publication of his vast work in full, thereby strengthening his memory and making it endure through the ages, while at the same time giving his contemporaries and future generations knowledge of the history of the eastern group of the Azores in the 15th and 16th centuries. For weighty reasons, the committee did not carry out its original plan, but it succeeded in publishing the third and fourth books of the *Saudades*, which contain the history of the islands of São Miguel and Santa Maria, which form the administrative district of Ponta Delgada.

before: Francisco Róscio was born on this island around 1740, the son of Manuel Gonçalves Róscio, a native of Tenerife, and of Maria da Graça Rodrigues Jardim, a native of the parish (*freguesia*) of Arco da Calheta. He studied at the Military Academy in Lisbon, and in 1762 was appointed infantry adjutant. He then served as a military engineer in the strongholds of Almeida and Elvas, showing remarkable competence, for which he was praised by the eminent engineer Jacques Funk, who had come from abroad expressly to direct the works on our fortifications. Róscio afterwards formed part of a commission of engineers sent to Brazil, where he again gave proof of his energy and knowledge. After 12 years away he returned to Portugal, then went back to Brazil to carry out the important mission of commissioner for the boundary demarcations in southern Brazil. He discharged it with the greatest zeal and competence, despite the enormous difficulties that arose at the time.

before: He was one of the most distinguished Madeirans of the 17th century. He belonged to an old and noble family of the parish (*freguesia*) of Calheta, and he was born there on 14 June 1616, the son of Manuel Dias de Lira and Dona Mécia Rosa de Couto. After completing his studies in the humanities on this island, he enrolled at the celebrated University of Salamanca, which at that time was attended by many Portuguese. He was about to complete, or had perhaps already completed, his doctorate in theology when the revolution broke out that threw off the Castilian yoke and placed the Duke of Braganza on the throne. A considerable number of Veloso de Lira’s compatriots, almost all of them students, were then in that Spanish city. He did more than anyone to ensure that they all returned home immediately to join the movement for liberation and independence that at once spread throughout the country. Camilo Castelo Branco refers to this event in the article ‘Estudantes Portugueses em Salamanca’, included in his book *Coisas leves e pesadas*. In his work *Espelho de lusitanos*, António Veloso de Lira makes a brief reference to this episode, stating that more than four hundred Portuguese were then in Salamanca.

before: He devoted himself to letters and in his day enjoyed a reputation as a man of wide learning. In 1643 he published a book entitled *Espelho de Lusitanos em o cristal do psalmo 43*, which went into a second edition in 1753. Like Father António Vieira and other superior minds, he could not escape the prevailing taste of the age, and his writings are riddled with that detestable Gongorism which then infested Portuguese and Spanish literature. Despite its faults, the work reveals a superior intelligence and uncommon learning, and as late as the middle of the 19th century Alexandre Herculano published lengthy extracts from it in the review *O Panorama*. We do not know whether he published any other works; Barbosa Machado says that he left the following unpublished: *Política Christiana*, *Zodiacus Ecclesiae*, *Stella Matutina in medio nebulae*, *Domus Sapientiae*, *Philosophia muta*, *Glosa sobre os Evangelhos* and *Antiguidades da ilha da Madeira*.

before: He was born in Funchal on 19 August 1819 and studied with distinction at our lyceum (state secondary school) and at the University of Coimbra, where he obtained high marks, graduating in law in 1852. He set up as a lawyer in Funchal and held several important offices here. He was deputy for Madeira in the legislative sessions of 1858–1859, 1860–1861, 1861–1864, 1865, 1865–1868 and 1882–1884. In the Cortes (Portuguese parliament) he proved a distinguished parliamentarian, serving as rapporteur on several bills. In 1862 he was appointed director-general of ecclesiastical affairs in the Ministry of Justice, a post he held until his death. This distinguished Madeiran died in Lisbon at the beginning of November 1884.

before: As for Porto Santo, the annotator of the *Saudades* states that in 1529 the island had more than 800 inhabitants, and Frutuoso asserts that in 1590 there were some 400 households (*fogos*, literally 'hearths') there, which would mean about 1600 inhabitants. On this statement of Frutuoso’s, Dr Álvaro de Azevedo says: ‘although this seems an exaggeration, since the *Annais da Ilha do Porto Santo* record that in 1850 the population was 1799 persons, that is, some 450 households, and the census of 1864 that there were 363 households with 1425 inhabitants, we believe Frutuoso’s statement to be accurate; the island of Porto Santo made progress only in the first hundred and fifty years after its discovery; afterwards the scarcity of its natural means of production, the frequent raids of corsairs, and the neglect in which it was left by the donataries, by its wealthiest inhabitants and even by governments, the Marquis of Pombal excepted, condemned it to the state of decline in which it has lain until now.’

before: He won extraordinary fame as a preacher, not only in Madeira but also on the mainland of the Kingdom (*reino*, i.e. mainland Portugal). This was due in good part to his rare and overwhelming eloquence, but above all to the freedom with which, from the height of the pulpit, he lashed out at the excesses of those in government and the abuses committed by the authorities, sparing not even the real or supposed excesses of his own superiors in the hierarchy. The sacred rostrum at times served him as a political stage, from which he struck at his adversaries or at those he believed to be his enemies and persecutors. It often happened that, alongside a remarkable beauty of language and passages of rapturous eloquence, his sermons revealed malicious insinuation, hostile aggression and even offence and insult aimed at persons of standing who were among the congregation. Once, in the church of Carmo (Carmelite church), he violently attacked the governor José Silvestre Ribeiro while the governor was present, seated beside the diocesan prelate. On another occasion, in the Cathedral, he was ordered by the ecclesiastical authority to come down from the pulpit and was suspended from preaching, before he had even finished his sermon. His contemporaries state that these excesses of language stirred up against Canon Nery the ill will, and at times the persecution, of those struck by these veritable diatribes. They add, however, that the boldness and courage with which he spoke, the tribune’s eloquence with which he thundered his attacks from the pulpit, and the beauty and pithy elegance of his diction softened the effects of the orator’s errors and follies. He had many ardent defenders, who forgave him the unseemly outbursts of his fiery and aggressive eloquence.

before: In 1750 one of the canes had not yet been replaced by a vine branch, since, as we have already said, the original arms appear on the Madeiran coins struck in that year. In 1798 the two sugar canes still featured in the arms of the municipality of Funchal, as can be seen on a silver inkstand in the old chamber where the council sessions were held. By 1837, however, one of the canes had been replaced by a vine branch, although no resolution authorising this change is recorded in the minute books. The presence of the Council’s arms, already modified, on the spines of many old books in the municipal archive means nothing, for everything suggests that these books were bound only in the 19th century. The record (*auto*) of a vow transcribed on p. 726 of the *Saudades da Terra* shows that in 1523 it was resolved that the image of St James the Less should be painted ‘na bamdeyra & sello da çidade’ (on the banner and seal of the city), but we have no proof whatever that this resolution was ever carried out.

before: He is the son of the late lyceum (state secondary school) teacher Daniel Simões Soares and was born on the island of Porto Santo on 23 May 1864. In 1875 he enrolled at the Military College (*Colégio Militar*), moving from there to the Funchal lyceum, where he completed his preparatory studies for the Army School (*Escola do Exército*). Posted overseas as a second lieutenant in 1885, he served in the province of Cape Verde, where, among other assignments, he held the Military Command (*Comando Militar*) on the island of Santo Antão. He was in Guinea in 1891, where he took part in the military operations against the Papel people. After retiring with the rank of general, he was president of the Municipal Council (*Câmara Municipal*) of the municipality (*concelho*) of Santa Catarina, on the island of Santiago, municipal administrator (administrador do concelho, the government's representative), etc. He has lived in Funchal for some years, where he held the post of civil governor three times, taking office on 28 September 1917, 21 June 1919 and 17 November 1923. He was also municipal administrator of Funchal, police commissioner, a member of the now defunct Agricultural Council (*Junta Agrícola*) and senator for Madeira, having been elected on 13 June 1915. He is a member of the present District General Council (*Junta Geral do Distrito*) of Funchal and has already been president of this administrative body (1921).

before: When the illustrious annotator of the *Saudades da Terra* discusses the origin of Madeira wine, he includes the following passage, which bears closely on the subject of this article: ‘Between Malmsey wine and the Acciaiuoli family, one of the most distinguished on this island, there is a remarkable historical coincidence. This family is of Florentine origin and derives its surname from steel (*acciaio*, in Italian), the object of the trade that had made it wealthy. From it descended Reniero Acciaiuoli, on whom the titular Empress of Constantinople, Maria de Bourbon, conferred in 1364 the lordships of Vestitza and Corinth, which he took possession of, as he did of the duchy of Athens, with Thebes, Argos, Megara and Sparta, forming the principality of Acciaiuoli. Increasingly harassed by the Turks, it was finally destroyed in 1456 by Mehmed II. The island of Minoa, where the Malvasia wines come from, if not part of that principality, bordered on it or lay close by. It is therefore not only possible but natural that the Acciaiuolis, coming, as they did, to settle on the island of Madeira (the first of whom we have record was Simão Acciaiuoli, 1515), should have brought the Malvasia vine here, out of their own curiosity or for some reason now unknown’.

before: The municipality (*concelho*) of the same name, with its seat in the *lugar* (settlement ranking between a town and a parish) of Câmara de Lobos, was created in 1832, but it was never actually installed. Only after the establishment of constitutional government, in 1835, was this municipality created, and it was finally installed on 16 October of the same year. From its creation it comprised the parishes (*freguesias*) of Câmara de Lobos, Estreito de Lobos, Curral das Freiras and Campanário. In 1848 the new parish of Quinta Grande was formed from several localities detached from the parishes of Câmara de Lobos and Campanário, and the municipality of Câmara de Lobos gained this further parish, although its total area did not change at all. When the recent municipality of Ribeira Brava was created in 1914, the parish of Campanário became part of the new municipality and was detached from that of Câmara de Lobos. The coat of arms of the Municipal Council (*Câmara Municipal*) of this municipality shows two seals, or monk seals, between which appears the shield of the arms of Portugal.

before: He was born on the island of Terceira in 1834. For some years he lived in Funchal, serving as a military physician. before: Overlooking the sea in the parish (*freguesia*) of Caniçal rises a height known as Monte Gordo or Piedade. On its summit stands out the chapel of Nossa Senhora da Piedade (Our Lady of Pity), which ships approaching the coast can see from a great distance. It is said to have been founded in the 16th century by Garcia Moniz, the first administrator (administrador do concelho, government-appointed head of the municipality) of the entail (*morgado*) of Caniçal. Ownership later passed to the entailed house (*casa vinculada*) of São Gil, whose manor house stood in the locality of Calçada, in the parish of Santa Cruz.

before: Gonçalo Anes, or Gonçalo Anes de Velosa, was one of the first settlers of this island. He was born in Celorico and had been a squire of the Infante Dom Fernando, son of King Duarte. He founded the church of São Bartolomeu, beside which he established a hospice (*hospício*) for poor clergy, which, it seems, never actually functioned. It served to lodge missionaries who called at Madeira on their way to India and Brazil. It was in this house and church that the Jesuits settled when they came to Madeira in 1570, and they remained there until the College of São João Evangelista (St John the Evangelist) (*Colégio de São João Evangelista*) was built. Gonçalo Anes founded an entail with the obligation of having a Mass celebrated in the said church every Friday for the soul of the Infante Dom Fernando. Gonçalo Anes died in 1497 and was buried in the church he had founded.

Gonçalo Anes founded an entail with the obligation of having a Mass celebrated in the said church every Friday for the soul of Infante Ferdinand. before: It was as professor of the chair of Civil Law that he truly made his name, and he was regarded as the foremost Brazilian civil lawyer of his time. As happened with those distinguished Madeirans Dr Patrício Moniz, Ferreira de Freitas and others besides, he left no work that matched his great merits or bore witness to his profound knowledge and vast erudition in the difficult and thorny speciality to which he devoted his whole life. Nevertheless, his lectures as a professor, the consultations sent to him from every part of Brazil, the high regard in which the most eminent Brazilian jurists held him, and the fact that he was appointed a member of the commission charged with reporting on the draft Civil Code drawn up by the illustrious jurist Dr Felicio dos Santos amply prove that Dr Justino de Andrade possessed the talent and learning needed to have left an enduring work, one that would have displayed more eloquently the remarkable gifts of his privileged mind and his immense erudition.

before: Countless verse compositions sing and extol the beauties of the Madeiran landscape, the marvellous ruggedness and capricious relief of its terrain, the incomparable mildness of its climate, and the variety, charm and fragrance of its flowers, etc. It would be quite impossible to gather them all, or even to make a selection of those that stand out most for the loftiness of their conception or the refinement of their form. We wish only to mention the poems devoted exclusively to this archipelago, which are the following: *Insulana*, by Manuel Tomás. . . , Antwerp, 1635; *Zargueida*. . ., by Francisco de Paulo Medina e Vasconcelos, Lisbon, 1806; *The Ocean Flower*..., by T. M. Hugues, London, 1845; and *Auto da Lenda*, by J. Brito Câmara, 1943. References to these three poems, one of which is written in English, and some biographical details about their authors are to be found elsewhere in this *Elucidário*.

before: On 9 and 22 May 1912 several Gypsy families landed in Funchal and settled in huts on the Campo da Barca. The men were coppersmiths, and the women practised fortune-telling (*ler a buena dicha*); some of them had quite regular features. They stayed in Madeira for about two months, and their dress and way of life aroused considerable interest among the Madeirans.

They stayed in Madeira for about two months, and their dress and way of life aroused considerable interest among the Madeirans.

before: After 14 years away in the leading cities of Europe, Monteiro Teixeira returned to his native land, where he devoted himself to literature and to his duties as consul of France on this island. He systematically refused every honour with which others sought to distinguish him, including a chair in parliament. Only to oblige some friends did he accept the post of councillor (*vereador*) of the Municipal Council (*Câmara Municipal*) of Funchal, at a time when only men of proven worth or high social standing were called to such positions.

Only to oblige some friends did he accept the post of councillor (*vereador*) of the Funchal Municipal Council (*Câmara Municipal do Funchal*), at a time when only men of proven worth or high social standing were called to such positions.

before: English painter and draughtsman who accompanied Captain Cook on his first voyage round the world. He drew 22 Madeiran plants during the few days he spent in Madeira. His drawings are in the British Museum; some of them were engraved, but they were never published.
after: English painter and draughtsman who accompanied Captain James Cook on his first voyage round the world. He drew 22 Madeiran plants during the few days he spent in Madeira. His drawings are in the British Museum; some of them were engraved, but they were never published.

before: Luís de Atouguia was one of the first settlers of this island and perhaps the first here to bear this surname. He was a native of Beja, the son of Luís Afonso de Atouguia and Dona Isabel Telo. In Madeira he served as treasurer to Dom Manuel, the future Manuel I, when he was Duke of Beja and Grand Master of the Order of Christ. This Luís de Atouguia, or one of his close descendants, held *sesmaria* (royal land grant to settlers on condition of cultivation) lands in the parish (*freguesia*) of Calheta, at the locality (*sítio*) still called the Lombo do Atouguia today, to which he gave his name. Arms: ‘On a field gules, quartered by a cross of gold voided of the field, and in each quarter a fleur-de-lis of gold; a bordure of the same; crest, a demi-lion rampant of gold.’
after: Luís de Atouguia was one of the first settlers of this island and perhaps the first here to bear this surname. He was a native of Beja, the son of Luís Afonso de Atouguia and Dona Isabel Telo. This Luís de Atouguia, or one of his close descendants, held *sesmaria* (royal land grant to settlers on condition of cultivation) lands in the parish (*freguesia*) of Calheta (‘small cove’), at the locality (*sítio*) still called the Lombo do Atouguia today, to which he gave his name. before: Dr Damião Peres, a distinguished professor at the University of Coimbra and former rector of the Funchal lyceum (state secondary school), whose name is linked to valuable works on the history of our country, published in 1924 and 1925 two interesting pamphlets entitled *O Desembargador João Leitão Governador Geral da Madeira* and *O Problema dos Governadores Gerais da Madeira*. In them he set out to show that there was no basis for the generic title of governors-general given by Dr Álvaro Rodrigues de Azevedo, the learned commentator on the *Saudades da Terra*, to the highest authorities of this archipelago during Castilian rule, and that they were entitled only to the name of captains-general, as can be read in some official documents of the period. The co-author of this *Elucidário*, C. A. de Meneses, in a series of articles published in the *Diário da Madeira* in September 1925, explains and justifies the title used by Dr A. R. de Azevedo, putting forward weighty arguments that invalidate Dr Damião Peres’s assertion. It is worth noting that this is a matter of secondary importance, of no great interest to the history of this island.

before: This is the name of the monument erected within the Angústias cemetery to the memory of those barbarously killed by the shells of a German submarine on 3 December 1916. before: There are, it seems, two branches of this surname. One descends from Rui de Sousa, a *fidalgo* (nobleman of the lesser nobility) of the household of John II, who married on this island Constança Cabral, daughter of Diogo Cabral and of Brites Gonçalves da Câmara, Zarco’s daughter. The other derives from Antão Álvares de Sousa, a noble knight, who settled in Santa Cruz around 1480.

before: Towards the end of the 18th century, a violent storm drove a Norwegian vessel onto the rocks of the coast, near the Pontinha. João de Carvalhal Esmeraldo, later Count of Carvalhal, arrived near the scene of the disaster. As he looked on at the sad plight of the poor castaways, his attention was caught by a child of about twelve, the cabin boy of the wrecked ship, whose engaging features, lively expression and intelligent, searching gaze aroused his keen interest and moved him to the tenderest compassion. The wealthy *fidalgo* (nobleman of the lesser nobility) took the child under his protection and, some years later, sent him to England to attend the University of Edinburgh. Having completed his medical studies, with the most brilliant results, he returned to Madeira, where he settled and raised a family, and he died in this city in 1845. He was Dr Luiz Henriques.
after: Towards the end of the 18th century, a violent storm drove a Norwegian vessel onto the rocks of the coast, near the Pontinha (‘little point’). The wealthy *fidalgo* (nobleman of the lesser nobility) took the child under his protection and, some years later, sent him to England to attend the University of Edinburgh. Having completed his medical studies, with the most brilliant results, he returned to Madeira, where he settled and raised a family, and he died in this city in 1845. He was Dr Luiz Henriques.

before: Dr Álvaro Rodrigues de Azevedo, the authoritative commentator on the *Saudades da Terra* and also a distinguished literary critic, disagrees with Teófilo Braga’s opinion and makes the following sensible observations: ‘We hold that the group of Madeiran poets of this period does not constitute a distinct cycle but merely a branch of the mainland cycle, because it has no character of its own; the nature and form of these poets’ productions are shared with those of the other court poets of the same school, collected in the *Cancioneiro Geral*. But that most notable group is nonetheless sufficient grounds for the island of Madeira to have an honourable share in the pre-classical history of the national literature, a share that T. Braga claimed for it.’
after: Dr Álvaro Rodrigues de Azevedo, the authoritative commentator on the ‘Longing for the Homeland’ (*Saudades da Terra*) and also a distinguished literary critic, disagrees with Teófilo Braga’s opinion and makes the following sensible observations: ‘We hold that the group of Madeiran poets of this period does not constitute a distinct cycle but merely a branch of the mainland cycle, because it has no character of its own; the nature and form of these poets’ productions are shared with those of the other court poets of the same school, collected in the ‘General Songbook’ (*Cancioneiro Geral*). But that most notable group is nonetheless sufficient grounds for the island of Madeira to have an honourable share in the pre-classical history of the national literature, a share that T. Braga claimed for it.’

before: João Gonçalves da Câmara, son of João Gonçalves Zarco and second captain-donatary of Funchal, appears in Garcia de Resende’s collection with three poetic compositions under the heading *Joham Gonçalves capytão da ilha*. From the information given by Frutuoso, he must have been born around 1414; he died in Funchal on 25 March 1501 and was buried in the church of the Convent of Santa Clara (St Clare of Assisi), beside the steps of the high altar, where the stone covering his grave was discovered a few years ago. He greatly advanced the work of colonisation begun by his father and contributed considerably to the progress and growth of the old town of Funchal. In our hard-fought struggles in Morocco against the Moors he stood out for his fearless courage, and also for the material aid with which he several times helped to relieve the imminent danger facing the Portuguese possessions in that region. He founded the convent of Santa Clara, to which he gave the large property of Curral das Freiras in 1492. He also appears as a notable character in the novel *A Filha de Tristão das Damas* mentioned above.

before: A locality (*sítio*) in the town (*vila*) of Machico, where the chapel of Senhor dos Milagres (Lord of Miracles) stands. It was destroyed by the great flash flood (*aluvião*) of 1803; it was then called the Chapel of Christ or of the Misericórdia (Holy House of Mercy, a lay charitable brotherhood), to which it belonged at the time, and it was rebuilt shortly afterwards. See Cristo (chapel), p. 332 of vol. 1.
after: A locality (*sítio*) in the town (*vila*) of Machico, where the chapel of the Lord of Miracles (*Senhor dos Milagres*) stands. before: The old church of São Bartolomeu was built in the Rua Direita of the early settlement of Funchal, a street that then ran along the left bank of the Ribeira de Santa Luzia as far as the vicinity of the present Ponte do Torreão. It was founded by Gonçalo Eanes de Velosa, and attached to it was a hospital or hospice (*albergaria*) intended to shelter poor and infirm clergy. In it he founded an entail with the obligation of having a Mass said there every Friday of the year for the soul of Prince Ferdinand. He was buried in this church, and according to what we have read in an old nobiliary, the following epitaph was carved on his tombstone: ‘Here lies Gonçalo Annes de Veloza, squire of Prince Ferdinand, whom God keeps, a native of Celorico, builder of this church of São Bartholomeu and hospital, who died in the era of 1497, on 1 August.’ The annotator of the *Historia Insulana* says that this hospice was never occupied by poor clergy, as its founder had stipulated, and that it often served as lodging for missionaries who stopped in Funchal on their way to India.
after: The old church of St Bartholomew (*São Bartolomeu*) was built in the Rua Direita (‘straight street’) of the early settlement of Funchal, a street that then ran along the left bank of the Ribeira de Santa Luzia (‘St Lucy’) as far as the vicinity of the present Ponte do Torreão (‘turret’). It was founded by Gonçalo Eanes de Velosa, and attached to it was a hospital or hospice (*albergaria*) intended to shelter poor and infirm clergy. In it he founded an entail with the obligation of having a Mass said there every Friday of the year for the soul of Infante Ferdinand. He was buried in this church, and according to what we have read in an old nobiliary, the following epitaph was carved on his tombstone: ‘Here lies Gonçalo Annes de Veloza, squire of Infante Ferdinand, whom God keeps, a native of Celorico, builder of this church of São Bartholomeu and hospital, who died in the era of 1497, on 1 August.’ The annotator of the ‘Island History’ (*Historia Insulana*) says that this hospice was never occupied by poor clergy, as its founder had stipulated, and that it often served as lodging for missionaries who stopped in Funchal on their way to India.

before: The church of São Bartolomeu, long since deconsecrated, was demolished in the second quarter of the 19th century.
after: The church of St Bartholomew, long since deconsecrated, was demolished in the second quarter of the 19th century.

before: At the entrance to the city a temporary wooden quay was built and colourfully decked out. before: In the afternoon a splendid banquet for 60 guests was given in the rooms of the former ‘Club Funchalense’, presided over by the Count of Carvalhal. Several speeches were made, which Roberto Ivens movingly acknowledged in his own name and in that of his companion.

before: The spacious and elegant rooms of the ‘Club Funchalense’ opened again on the following night for a splendid ball, a magnificent occasion that greatly impressed the illustrious explorers and touched them deeply.

before: The streets flanking the Jardim Municipal to the south and north were named after Hermenegildo Capelo and Roberto Ivens respectively.
after: The streets flanking the Jardim Municipal (‘municipal garden’) to the south and north were named after Hermenegildo Capelo and Roberto Ivens respectively.

before: On 13 November 1803, in the presence of Bishop Dom Luís Rodrigues Vilares, the cathedral chapter and the rest of the clergy in the choir of the Cathedral (Sé Catedral), it was unanimously resolved to hold a procession on 9 October each year in honour of the patronage of the Virgin, in order to obtain the protection of the Mother of God and prevent any repetition of the disasters and damage caused by the flash flood (*aluvião*) of 9 October of the same year. The Municipal Council (*Câmara Municipal*) had already taken the same decision on 11 November. In accordance with these resolutions, a procession was held for many years that set out from the Sé and made its way to the church of Santa Maria Maior (St Mary Major), accompanied by the ecclesiastical and civil authorities, the municipality and the clergy. This procession, which is often moved to the Sunday nearest to 9 October, is still held today, but it now goes only round the churchyard of the Sé, accompanied by the confraternity of the parish. (See Vow to the Most Holy Virgin.)
after: On 13 November 1803, in the presence of Bishop Dom Luís Rodrigues Vilares, the cathedral chapter and the rest of the clergy in the choir of the Cathedral (Sé Catedral), it was unanimously resolved to hold a procession on 9 October each year in honour of the patronage of the Virgin, in order to obtain the protection of the Mother of God and prevent any repetition of the disasters and damage caused by the flash flood (*aluvião*) of 9 October of the same year. The Municipal Council (*Câmara Municipal*) had already taken the same decision on 11 November. In accordance with these resolutions, a procession was held for many years that set out from the Sé and made its way to the church of Santa Maria Maior (St Mary Major), accompanied by the ecclesiastical and civil authorities, the municipality and the clergy. This procession, which is often moved to the Sunday nearest to 9 October, is still held today, but it now goes only round the churchyard of the Sé, accompanied by the confraternity of the parish. (See Vow to the Blessed Virgin.)

before: A locality (*sítio*) in the parish (*freguesia*) of Santo da Serra. It has a small house that can shelter those passing through, and it is also where the waters of the Levada da Serra, which irrigates the parishes of Caniço, São Gonçalo and Santa Maria Maior, are separated into their own channel. As far as Lombo da Raiz these waters run together with those of the Levada do Juncal, destined for the parishes of Santo da Serra, Água de Pena and Santa Cruz, and with those of the Levada Nova do Furado, which waters the lands of the parish of Santa Cruz.
after: A locality (*sítio*) in the parish (*freguesia*) of Santo da Serra (‘the saint of the uplands’). It has a small house that can shelter those passing through, and it is also where the waters of the Levada da Serra (‘upland channel’), which irrigates the parishes of Caniço, São Gonçalo and Santa Maria Maior, are separated into their own channel. As far as Lombo da Raiz (‘root ridge’) these waters run together with those of the Levada do Juncal (‘rush-bed channel’), destined for the parishes of Santo da Serra, Água de Pena and Santa Cruz, and with those of the Levada Nova do Furado (‘new channel of the tunnel’), which waters the lands of the parish of Santa Cruz (‘Holy Cross’).

before: The adjoining sea floor is very rugged in relief. Beyond the 100-*braça* sounding line – which around the main island lies sometimes only half a mile from the coast, as off Ponta do Garajau, and at most 3 or 4 miles away, as off Porto da Cruz and Ponta do Pargo – the floor falls rapidly towards the abysses of 2,000 *braças* and more that yawn between the Canary Islands and Madeira, or between Madeira and mainland Portugal.

before: The nets amount to a few seine nets – of the *xávega* type – which are worked from time to time on the great beach of the island of Porto Santo and in three or four open, sandy nooks on the south coast of Madeira, together with some set nets, generally without trammel. before: In 1937 the ‘Casas dos Pescadores’ (Fishermen’s Houses) were created, and they have rendered such notable services to the fishing community; the decree of 20 August of that year laid down the basis of their operation. The founding of one of these ‘Casas’ in Madeira was not long in coming, thanks to the efforts of the then harbour master of Funchal, Artur Barbosa Carmona. It began operating in 1939, with first-aid posts in the most important fishing centres. In Machico a house was acquired for this purpose, and it was formally inaugurated on 17 July 1943. The ‘Casas dos Pescadores’ provide medical assistance, allowances for invalids and their families, the upkeep of a school, shelter for the destitute, etc., as circumstances permit. In the parish (*freguesia*) of Paul do Mar, as already mentioned, the District General Council (*Junta Geral do Distrito*) had ten blocks built containing fifty dwellings for the poorest members of this community.

before: This Madeiran was born on 19 August 1868 and enlisted in the army on 22 January 1884, being commissioned second lieutenant of infantry on 15 March 1900. He was an officer risen from the ranks, but also a bachelor (*bacharel*, university graduate) in law from the University of Coimbra, having completed his secondary studies at the Funchal lyceum (state secondary school). He was senator for the constituency of Ponta Delgada (the Azores), and formed part of the column that left for southern Angola in 1915. He died, as a captain of the 17th Infantry, at the battle of the water-holes of Mangua (Cuanhama) on 19 August 1915, while going along the firing line encouraging the soldiers.

before: The so-called fajãs (Volume II, p. 7), both inland and on the coast, owe their origin to the fall of great *quebradas*. These now rarely occur, but in winter small *quebradas* are frequent and cause considerable damage. Many date from before the discovery, such as that of Jardim do Mar, while some are of more recent formation, such as that of Lugar de Baixo (Volume II, p. 285), and others.

before: The most distinguished son of this parish was António Gil Gomes, whom we shall discuss at greater length in the appropriate place. Also a native of the parish was António Januário Moderno, born on 25 February 1789, the son of Captain João Rodrigues Moderno and Dona Antónia da Incarnação Moderno. He was superintendent (*provedor*) of Machico, which then included the municipality (*concelho*) of Sant’Ana, and held other public offices. In his day he was famous throughout the island, not only for the gallant and hospitable way in which he received guests at his house in Arco, but above all for the herculean strength with which he was endowed; the many remarkable feats of strength and daring he performed made him feared and respected. In London, where he lived as a political exile, he also became known among his compatriots for his courage and the might of his arm. He died in Funchal on 11 October 1864. His son was Dr António Januário Moderno, who graduated in medicine from a foreign university and practised with great success and skill in the United States, where he made a large fortune. He too was a native of the parish of Arco de São Jorge. He spent almost his entire life away from Madeira, but died in this city some thirty years ago, shortly after returning to his native land. He had earned a reputation as a man of exceptional talent and an eminent physician. He died in Funchal, aged 67, on 11 February 1885.

before: The present city entrance was formerly called Porto da Saúde, and since 27 October 1910 it has been named Avenida João Gonçalves Zarco. A small, narrow street once stood there, closed at its southern end by a redan and one of the city gates. Beside the gate, or very close to it, stood the so-called Casa da Saúde (see that entry), which was rebuilt or considerably enlarged in the last quarter of the 18th century. This is the building that for many years housed the Commercial Association, the Health Station and the Harbour Master's Office (*Capitania do Porto*). It belonged to the Funchal Municipal Council (*Câmara Municipal*), which sold it at public auction in 1914.

before: Câmara de Lobos was one of the first places in Madeira to be put under cultivation immediately after the discovery. Many people from mainland Portugal, the Kingdom (*reino*, i.e. mainland Portugal), settled there, raised families and founded large lines of descendants. Several people of noble origin held extensive lands by *sesmaria* (royal land grant to settlers on condition of cultivation) and founded their entails and entailed estates there. Among them we may mention João Afonso (see that entry), a companion of Zarco, and João Caldeira the Elder, who gave his name to the locality still called Caldeira today. Later João Salviati (see that entry), the founder of the Florença family, also held *sesmaria* grants there, as did João Saraiva, who gave his name to the locality that still bears his surname; Brás Gil de Faria, who had lands on the right bank of the Ribeira da Caixa; Diogo Lopes da Estacada, who owned much land in the locality of Torre that passed to the Correia family; and also Álvaro Figueira, among others. When we deal specifically with the chapels of this diocese, we shall name the founders of the many that existed in this parish, almost all of which were entailed foundations (*instituição vincular*, a morgado or capela) and the seats of various entailed estates.

before: It was perhaps the parish in Madeira with the greatest number of chapels. Those of São Bernardino, Espírito Santo, Nossa Senhora da Boa Hora, Jesus-Maria-José, Nossa Senhora da Nazaré, Nossa Senhora das Preces, Nossa Senhora da Boa Morte, Nossa Senhora da Conceição, São Francisco, Nossa Senhora da Piedade, Nossa Senhora da Fátima and Nossa Senhora das Dores in the cemetery still exist today, while those of Nossa Senhora de Belém, São João and São Cândido, and others besides, have disappeared.

before: This parish was once home to the convent of Franciscan nuns of São Bernardino. It was then closed and incorporated into the Seminary of the Encarnação (*Seminário da Encarnação*; Incarnation).

before: In the parish (*freguesia*) of Caniço there stood a chapel dedicated to Nossa Senhora do Livramento, in the locality (*sítio*) that still bears this name today. Since the chapel was demolished, the pilgrimage has been made to the parish church, and it still takes place at present; not even traces of the chapel remain today. It seems to have been built around the middle of the 17th century, and its foundation is attributed to Sebastião de Oliveira, who owned land in that locality.

before: Major Francisco Xavier Pereira da Silva, later Count of Antas, who won great distinction in the campaigns for liberty, was in Madeira in 1828 to assist the governor and captain-general José Lúcio Travassos Valdez in the defence he was preparing against the attack of the Miguelite (supporter of the absolutist King Miguel) squadron. Pereira da Silva had arrived in Funchal from England on 20 August 1828 and was at once placed in charge of defending several strategic points on the heights of Caniço. The liberal forces, however, were compelled to yield to the invading troops, and this officer, together with Valdez and others, boarded the English corvette *Alligator* and sailed for England.

before: Observations of wind direction made at Ponta de São Lourenço from 1901 to 1909 show that the wind that prevails there most throughout the year is the NE, followed by the NNE, N, NW, SW and E. before: Funchal Bay is the widest bay in the archipelago. It is bounded by Ponta do Garajau to the east and Ponta da Cruz to the west. Between these two points it forms a fairly regular curve and inlet, and it is sheltered from winds from every quarter except those blowing from SSE to SSW by way of S. Its breadth makes it a vast anchorage, but communication with the shore can be established with relative ease only at the most accessible points of the coastline. These stretch from the Ilhéu da Pontinha in the west to the vicinity of the Fort of São Tiago (St James the Greater) in the east, some two thousand metres apart. All the traffic and activity of the port takes place within these limits. The port is bounded by a beach of rounded pebbles, with deep water and free of reefs or shoals that might hinder access. According to General A. P. de Azevedo’s map of Madeira, high water, or the establishment of the port (time of high water at full and new moon), is at 12 h 48 min, with a tidal rise of 2.28 m; the engineer Mariano F. Faria e Maia, however, states that the tidal range reaches 2.80 m. Regarding the port of Funchal and the tides of the Madeiran coast, the distinguished engineer Adolfo Loureiro says ‘that little is known about lunar influences on the phenomenon of spring and neap tides, or about their propagation, speed and direction, or the height and force of the waves according to the direction of the wind, their impetus, duration, etc. The temperature of the waters and its distribution at the surface, and their periodic movements and conditions, which follow a law that seemed constant, ought to become the subject of very interesting oceanographic studies, which unfortunately have never been carried out’.

before: It should be noted that the marked decline in shipping at the port of Funchal from 1914 onwards was due to the great European conflagration, which drove a considerable number of vessels away from Madeira. With the recent world war the decline became even greater, the number of ships entering being 389, 234, 190 and 187 in the years 1940 to 1943.

before: Manuel José Vieira, son of Manuel José Vieira and Dona Luísa Correia Vieira, both natives of the Azores, was born in Funchal on 7 August 1836. He attended secondary school in this city and in 1855 left for Coimbra, where, after sitting the so-called maturity examination, he enrolled at the University, completing his degree in law in 1860. That same year he entered the competition for the post of teacher of geography and history at the Funchal lyceum (state secondary school). After brilliant examinations he was appointed to the post, which he held for about 40 years with the greatest competence and with a zeal that might be equalled but not surpassed. From 1864 to 1868 he was president of the Municipal Council (*Câmara Municipal*) of Funchal, an office he held again from 1899 to 1908. In directing the affairs of the municipality he gave ample proof of his concern for the improvement of the city and of the conditions of those who live in it. Had he not left the presidency of the Council in 1908, the city might perhaps possess today a sewerage network and a good supply of drinking water, improvements in which, as is well known, he took a keen interest.

before: Dr Manuel José Vieira was deputy for Madeira in the legislatures of 1879, 1882–1884, 1884–1887, 1887–1889 and 1894–1895, and in 1889 he was elected peer of the realm for the district of Vila Real, although he never took his seat in that chamber. Among the benefits he obtained for Madeira as a deputy were the unification of the currency; the studies for the road around the island by the engineer Tellier, for which he secured a credit of 30 *contos* (1 conto = 1,000,000 réis, from 1911 1,000 escudos); the special legislation that gave the levadas (irrigation channels) of Madeira legal standing to safeguard their rights; the collection of the land on which the theatre and the municipal garden were built; the exemption from tonnage dues for steamers calling at the port of Funchal; the exemption from duties on the import of maize from 1882 to 1886; and the construction of the artificial harbour at the locality (*sítio*) of Pontinha, etc., etc.

before: Besides serving as deputy and as president of the Municipality, Dr Manuel José Vieira held many other offices. before: The creation of the towns and municipalities of Funchal, Machico and Porto Santo dates from the middle of the 15th century, these places being the capitals of the three captaincies into which the Madeiran archipelago was divided. The captaincy of Funchal, and particularly its seat, the town (*vila*) of the same name, grew remarkably from the earliest days of colonisation and quickly prospered. Important settlements formed within it and soon reached a high level of development, so that autonomous municipalities (*concelho*) became necessary, for the convenience of the inhabitants and the sound administration of public affairs. This is what happened with the establishment of the towns and municipalities of Ponta do Sol and Calheta.

before: As we have already seen in the article on Customs Houses, this town was the seat of a small customs office, or revenue guard post (*posto fiscal*), as it was then called, and the duty on sugar was originally collected there, later being collected at the Funchal customs house. before: The present municipality (*concelho*) of Calheta, created in 1835, and the former municipality or town do not differ very markedly in the extent of their areas. Since 1835, however, it has undergone some changes, some of which we can record here. In 1849 the municipality of Porto do Moniz, which had also been created in 1835, was suppressed, and the parishes (*freguesias*) of Achadas da Cruz and Ponta do Pargo became part of the municipality of Calheta. The decree of 26 June 1871 detached the parish of Ponta do Pargo from the municipality of Porto do Moniz and annexed it to that of Calheta. before: Construction of the convent began in 1492, but the first nuns did not enter it until 1497. By a deed of 11 September 1480 the founder, João Gonçalves da Câmara, bought from Rui Teixeira and Branca Ferreira, residents of Campanário, the Curral estate, later known as Curral das Freiras, for the sum ‘of 23,500 réis at five *ceitis* to the *real* (pl. *réis*; old Portuguese money unit, 1,000 réis = 1 milréis) and 50 gold *cruzados*... its area extended from the Passo da Cruz and the Ribeira dos Socorridos up to where the stream rises, from rocky crest to rocky crest, on either side’. This rural property, the largest and most important the convent ever owned, was what the founder gave to the monastery when his daughters were admitted to it as nuns. Even earlier, the Infante Dom Manuel, Duke of Beja and later king, had urged and stressed the need to found a convent of nuns on this island. He did so in the letter which, as Grand Master of the Order of Christ, to which this archipelago belonged, he had addressed to its inhabitants on 17 July 1488. In this curious document, which we first came across in the newspaper *O Reclame* of 26 November 1890, he says that the Supreme Pontiff had written to him asking for a monastery to be founded at the church of Conceição de Cima, and adds that ‘as soon as you see this, gather at once in council with the captain and discuss it all very well, and may it please you that it be so done... it will please me to give for this such alms as seem good to me, and henceforth for the maintenance of the nuns I shall always be glad to give all the alms I well can...’. We do not know whether it was the Grand Master’s request that led João Gonçalves da Câmara to found the convent four years later, and still less do we know whether Manuel I, who came to the throne in 1495, contributed to the building of the monastery.

before: The first abbess of the convent of Santa Clara was Dona Isabel de Noronha, daughter of the aforementioned João Gonçalves da Câmara. before: By the middle of the 18th century the convent of Santa Clara had an annual income of more than seven *contos* (*conto*: one million réis), and in 1821 its revenues rose to 14 *contos*. That year, however, it ran a deficit of two *contos de réis*, owing to the lack of careful and diligent administration. Under the disentailment (*desamortização*, the sale of Church property by the State) laws, all the property of this convent, which was considerable, was sold by the public treasury; the sum raised by the sale is not known. When the religious orders were abolished, the convent had little more than sixty nuns. The last survivor was Maria Amalia do Patrocinio, who died in November 1890.

before: This was the first convent founded on this island outside Funchal. It belonged to the Franciscan order and was dedicated to St Bernardine of Siena, one of the order's great saints. It stood in the parish (*freguesia*) of Câmara de Lobos, in a remote and solitary *lugar* (settlement ranking between a town and a parish), some distance from the mother church (*igreja matriz*). Its origins were humble and obscure, but it later became celebrated and renowned throughout the island, and it seems even in mainland Portugal, the Kingdom (*reino*, i.e. mainland Portugal), because a man of outstanding virtue named Friar Pedro da Guarda lived and died there, whom the people called, and still call, the Holy Servant of God. For this reason it became a magnet for many devotees and pilgrims, who came from the most distant places on the island to invoke the intercession of the saintly and humble Franciscan. With the extinction of the religious orders and the stance taken by the vicar capitular and governor of the diocese (governador do bispado, administering the see in the bishop's absence), António Alfredo de Santa Catarina Braga, these acts of devotion and piety cooled and dwindled. They did not die out entirely, however, for every year a considerable number of people still visit the grave in which the mortal remains of Friar Pedro da Guarda were laid. We say nothing more here about his life, his virtues and the veneration paid to him, since we shall devote a separate article to him.

after: The lands that now make up the parish of Ponta do Pargo originally belonged to the parish of Fajã da Ovelha (‘the ewe’s flat’), and were separated from it when Ponta do Pargo was constituted as an independent parish. The exact year of its creation is not known, but it must have been before 1560, since the royal decree (*alvará régio*) of 4 March of that year added one *moio* (dry measure of grain, 60 *alqueires*) of wheat and a quarter (*quarto*) of wine to the stipend (*côngrua*) of the parish priest, which was then 11,000 *réis* (old Portuguese money of account; 1$000 = 1,000 réis, 1:000$000 = one conto = 1,000,000 réis) a year. The royal decree of 1 March 1577 set the parish priest’s annual salary at 20,000 *réis*, and that of 9 June 1581 raised it to 25,000 *réis*, likewise a year.

before: It was the chapel of São Pedro (St Peter), about whose founder and year of construction we have no information, that served as the seat of the new parish. It underwent enlargements and rebuildings in years we cannot specify. Its reconstruction was ordered by a warrant of the Treasury Council (*Conselho da Fazenda*) of 20 July 1620, the works being estimated at 2,231,606 *réis*; it is not known whether the rebuilding was carried out immediately, which did not always happen. In 1851 major repairs were made to this church, at a cost of about 1,700,000 *réis*. We are informed that the parish church, through its successive constructions and reconstructions, has occupied three different places, though always within the same locality of Salão. It stood first at the spot called Pé do Pico, then at Achada da Igreja, and finally where it stands today.

before: This parish has the chapels of Nossa Senhora do Amparo (Our Lady of Protection) and Nossa Senhora da Boa Morte (Our Lady of the Good Death), which we have mentioned elsewhere.

before: Farming here is served by the levadas (irrigation channels) of Moinhos, Cabo, Lombada da Velha, Ribeira da Vaca, Serrado, Serra, Ribeiro Velho, Lombadinha, Amparo and Lombo, as well as the Levada do Rabaçal, which also waters part of this parish. The coasts of Ponta do Pargo and Achadas da Cruz were extremely dangerous waters for shipping. A lighthouse was therefore needed in the first of these parishes, since it forms the most prominent point of that coastline and lies at a height from which the lantern’s light could easily be cast several miles out to sea. Some years ago the building to house the lighthouse was constructed on the initiative of the District General Council (*Junta Geral do Distrito*), which paid all the construction costs, and the lighthouse came into operation on 5 June 1922. The parish also has a post and telegraph office and a semaphore station.

before: This parish belonged to the municipality (*concelho*) of Porto Moniz from the time that municipality was set up, in 1835, until 1849, when it was abolished; the parish then became part of the municipality of Calheta. When the municipality of Porto Moniz was restored in 1855, the parish of Ponta do Pargo was again incorporated into it. The law of 26 June 1871 detached it from the municipality of Porto Moniz and returned it to the municipality of Calheta, to which it belongs today. Principal localities: Cabo, Lombada Velha, Ribeira das Vacas, Serrado, Salão, Corujeira de Dentro, Corujeira de Fora, Lombadinha, Amparo and Lombo. According to the 1911 census, the population of the parish is 2,546 inhabitants.

before: An inhabited locality (*sítio*) in the parish (*freguesia*) of Monte. It takes its name from the chapel dedicated to Nossa Senhora do Livramento (Our Lady of Deliverance) that stands there. It was built at the behest of Inácio Ferreira Pinto in 1684 and rebuilt a century later by João José Bettencourt de Freitas, and it is an entailed foundation (*instituição vincular*, a morgado or capela). In the same locality there is a chapel consecrated to the Sagrado Coração de Jesus (Sacred Heart of Jesus), built a few years ago by Father Jorge de Faria e Castro.

before: On Rua da Saúde, in the parish (*freguesia*) of São Pedro, near Largo do Marquês, the chapel of this dedication still stands, although it is not open for worship. It was founded by Dr Pedro Cardoso Valdavesso and his wife Dona Maria Gondim in 1659, the deed of endowment being dated 4 January of that year.

before: In Madeira this name is given to *Brama raii*, a pelagic fish of the mackerel family (scombrids), and to *Ostrellata mollis*, a web-footed seabird of the petrel family (procellariids) native to the archipelago. *Brama raii* is eaten, but its flesh is of poor quality. *Ostrellata mollis* is a rare species, known to nest in the mountains near Curral das Freiras and on the sea cliffs of the Desertas, where it has been observed in the summer and autumn months.

before: The common tern (*garajau*) leaves these islands in October and November and returns in the first months of spring. See Capes.

before: An evergreen tree with narrow, oblong, acuminate, serrate, glabrous leaves and white flowers borne in long axillary racemes. It has only recently been found, in the Ribeira da Janela. It yields a yellowish-pink or reddish-brown wood that is very durable.

before: A village (*lugar*, settlement rank below a town) and mountain height roughly equidistant from Lombo do Mouro and Monte Medonho, on the boundary between the parishes (*freguesia*) of Ribeira Brava and São Vicente.
after: A village (*lugar*, settlement rank below a town) and mountain height roughly equidistant from Lombo do Mouro (‘the Moor’s ridge’) and Monte Medonho (‘fearsome hill’), on the boundary between the parishes (*freguesia*) of Ribeira Brava (‘wild river’) and São Vicente.

before: Seals are generally called *lobos marinhos* (‘sea wolves’), and the article on the parish (*freguesia*) of Câmara de Lobos (p. 210, vol. 1) explains the reason for the name given to that parish. These amphibious mammals, which once abounded in the seas of our archipelago, have almost entirely disappeared from these waters, and only a few of them have been caught at long intervals. As recently as a few decades ago it was not rare to see them on the neighbouring Desertas, where fishermen hunted them. On this subject it is worth reading p. 79 onwards of A. Artur Sarmento’s book *Mamíferos do Arquipelago da Madeira*.

The diocesan prelate Dom António Teles da Silva dies in this city and is buried in the Cathedral. 1690 – Two corsair ships sack the island of Porto Santo and burn the church and other buildings. 1691 – Death of the distinguished Madeiran Canon António Veloso de Lira. 1699 – Great fire in the fortress of São Lourenço, destroying the residences of the governors and captains-general of the archipelago. 1704 – The governor and captain-general of the archipelago, João da Costa de Ataíde e Azevedo, dies in Funchal. 1708 – The island of Porto Santo is sacked by French pirates. 1724 – A great flash flood (*aluvião*) causes considerable damage. 1729 – Death of the distinguished Madeiran poet Troilo de Vasconcelos da Cunha. 1730 – Death of the Madeiran writer and distinguished genealogist Henrique Henriques de Noronha. 1733 – The curacies (*curatos*) of Boaventura, Ribeira da Janela and Prazeres are created. 1734 – The curacy of Jardim do Mar is created. 1743 – The town of São Vicente is created. 1748 – A violent earthquake causes considerable damage and some casualties. 1753 – The diocesan bishop Dom João do Nascimento dies in Funchal. 1755 – Dr Julião Fernandes da Silva writes the curious and interesting book entitled *Carta critica sobre o methodo curativo dos medicos funchalenses*. 1756 – The construction of a harbour of refuge in Funchal is decreed. 1760 – The Jesuits are expelled from Madeira. 1765 – A great flash flood causes enormous damage. 1767 – Judicial reform that definitively establishes in Madeira a *corregedor* (royal district magistrate) and a *juiz de fora* (crown-appointed judge from outside the district). 1770 – Celebrated royal decree (*alvará*) adopting important measures concerning the island of Porto Santo, which became known as the Law of Fifths and Eighths (*lei dos Quintos e Oitavos*). 1772 – Several primary schools, three Latin classes, one philosophy class and one rhetoric class are created in Madeira. 1775 – The Treasury Board (*Junta da Fazenda*) of this archipelago is created. 1777 – The illustrious governor of Madeira João António de Sá Pereira leaves this island, summoned by the government in Lisbon to Dom Diogo Pereira Forjaz Coutinho, dies in Funchal. 1801 – Madeira is occupied by British troops. 1803 – A great flash flood causes the greatest damage and kills several hundred people. 1806 – The Madeiran poet Francisco Álvares de Nóbrega, known by the sobriquet of ‘Camões Pequeno’ (the Little Camões), dies in Lisbon. 1807 – Brigadier Reinaldo Oudinot, who directed the channelling of the captain-general of Madeira, Luís Beltrão de Gouveia e Almeida, dies in Funchal. 1815 – Napoleon passes by Madeira. 1815 – A great flash flood causes great damage. 1821 – The Constitution is proclaimed some people are killed by the bullets of the armed forces, which found themselves compelled to use violence. 1872 – A great smallpox epidemic kills about a thousand people. 1873 – The Companhia Fabril de Açúcar Madeirense is organised; 4th captain-donatary, João Gonçalves da Câmara, dies in Funchal. 1540 – The captain-donatary of Machico, Diogo Teixeira, dies, and the captaincy reverts to the crown. 1550 – Creation of the parish of Faial. 1551 – The archbishopric of Funchal is abolished and the archipelago of Arguin is added to the jurisdiction of this diocese. 1552 – Creation of the parish of Santana. 1553 – Creation of the parish of Seixal (‘pebble shore’). 1557 – Creation of the parishes of the Sé and Santa Maria Maior (‘St Mary Major’). 1558 – Creation of the parish of Gaula. 1560 – Creation of the parish of Água de Pena. 1561 – Creation of the parish of Caniçal (‘reed bed’). 1565 – Creation of the parishes of Monte and São Gonçalo. 1566 – Terrible sack of the city of Funchal by French corsairs. 1566 – Foundation of the Funchal Seminary. 1566 – Creation of the parish of São Pedro. 1568 – Creation of the parish of Tabua (‘bulrush’). 1569 – The distinguished Madeiran and illustrious prelate Dom Manuel de Noronha, son of the 3rd captain-donatary of Funchal, Simão Gonçalves da Câmara, the Magnificent, dies at Lamego. 1570 – The Jesuits establish themselves in Madeira. 1571 – Creation of the parish of Fajã da Ovelha (‘the ewe’s flat’). 1572 – Creation of the parish of Arco da Calheta (‘arc of Calheta’). 1575 – Death of the illustrious Madeiran Father Luís Gonçalves da Câmara, celebrated tutor of Martinho. 1580 – Deaths of the 5th and 6th captains-donatary of Funchal, Simão Gonçalves da Câmara and João Gonçalves da Câmara. 1581 – Madeira begins to be ruled by governors-general, the first being
