grammarian and distinguished Madeiran Father Manuel Álvares dies at Évora. 1588 – The distinguished Madeiran Dom Sebastião de Morais, the first bishop of Japan, dies in Mozambique on his way to his bishopric. 1590 – Dr Gaspar Frutuoso writes his celebrated work ‘Longing for the Homeland’ (*Saudades da Terra*); he died the following year on the island of São Miguel. 1593 – The phenomenon of atmospheric incandescence known as the ‘fire from heaven’ occurs on this island; it burnt all the vegetation and even set some houses alight. 1595 – Death of the illustrious Madeiran and eminent jurist Dr António da Gama Pereira. 1608 – The diocesan bishop Luís de Figueiredo e Lemos dies in Funchal and is buried in the Cathedral. 1624 – Death of the governor and captain-general of Madeira Dom Francisco Henriques, who was buried in the church of the Colégio. 1626 – Death of the governor and captain-general of this archipelago, Fernão de Saldanha. 1641 – The restoration of Portugal is proclaimed in Madeira with the acclamation (*aclamação*, formal public proclamation of a new king) of John IV. 1650 – Foundation of the convent of the Incarnação by Canon Henrique Calaça de Viveiros. São Lourenço, destroying the residences of the governors and captains-general of the archipelago. 1704 – The governor and captain-general of the archipelago, João da Costa de Ataíde e Azevedo, dies in before: A chapel of the same name exists at the Quinta dos Reis, in the parish (*freguesia*) of Monte; it was built by order of Duarte Mendes de Vasconcelos in 1554. See Reis Magos (chapels).
after: A chapel of the same name exists at the Quinta dos Reis (‘the kings’ estate’), in the parish (*freguesia*) of Monte (‘hill’); it was built by order of Duarte Mendes de Vasconcelos in 1554. See Reis Magos (chapels).

before: On the coast road that leads from Funchal to Câmara de Lobos, on the left bank of the Ribeira dos Socorridos, stands the chantry (capela) of Nossa Senhora da Vitória (Our Lady of Victory), at the far edge of the parish (*freguesia*) of São Martinho. The annotator of the *Saudades* gives 1594 as the year of its construction and says that it was founded by Francisco de Bettencourt on the lands of the entailed estate (*morgadio*) he established there. It was rebuilt in a year we cannot determine, and roughly forty years ago it was enlarged and underwent considerable repairs.
after: On the coast road that leads from Funchal to Câmara de Lobos (‘seals’ den’), on the left bank of the Ribeira dos Socorridos, stands the chantry (capela) of Nossa Senhora da Vitória (Our Lady of Victory), at the far edge of the parish (*freguesia*) of São Martinho (‘St Martin’). The annotator of the *Saudades* gives 1594 as the year of its construction and says that it was founded by Jean de Béthencourt on the lands of the entailed estate (*morgadio*) he established there. It was rebuilt in a year we cannot determine, and roughly forty years ago it was enlarged and underwent considerable repairs.

before: The office of dean was, and still is today, the highest dignity of the cathedral chapter. Under a law of our country that remained in force until the proclamation of the Republic, it could be filled only by a cleric holding a degree in law or theology. Nuno Cão was the first to hold this office here, followed by Filipe Rebelo and then by Dr António da Costa. The last priests to occupy the deanery (office of dean of the cathedral chapter) at Funchal Cathedral (*Sé*) were, in order, António Joaquim Gonçalves de Andrade, Aires de Ornelas e Vasconcelos and João Joaquim Pinto (see those entries). before: Many mountain heights, ridges and crags, valleys and ravines, streams, landing places and headlands along the coast were named at that time, and their names have remained for ever inscribed in the toponymy of Madeira. Thus words such as Seixo, Oliveira, Garajau, Cruz, Formosa, Socorridos, Espírito Santo, Girão, Vera-Cruz, etc., etc., became proper names and came to designate things and places that have survived unchanged through five centuries to the present day.

before: The greatest obstacle to immediate and effective settlement was the dense, gigantic forest that covered the whole surface of the land judged suitable for the first agricultural ventures. A violent fire, perhaps recklessly started but also necessarily imposed by the pressing force of circumstances, opened up vast clearings suitable for bringing these wide tracts of hitherto unproductive land under the plough. How far this fire’s destruction reached, and what its immediate consequences were, is not easy to say today; of particular interest on this point is what may be read in the *Saudades da Terra* and its annotations, and also in the pages of the *Elucidário Madeirense*. See Fires.

before: To determine with true precision the year in which the settlement of this island began, one would need to be able to fix the date of its discovery, which has still not been established with complete certainty. In the letter of grant (carta de doação) from Prince Henry to the Order of Christ, dated 18 September 1460, to which the publication entitled *Alguns documentos do Archivo Nacional da Torre do Tombo acerca das navegações e conquistas dos portuguezes* refers, we read: ‘I began to settle my island of Madeira some thirty-five years ago now, and likewise that of Porto Santo...’ From these words it follows that colonisation began around 1425, that is, a few years after the discovery, which agrees with the indications of various chroniclers.

before: On the so-called ‘settled farmsteads’ (*fazendas povoadas*), established at various points on the island, many chapels were built, each with its own private chaplain. Most of them became ‘curacies’ (*curato*) and ‘chaplaincies’ (capelania) with the standing of a parish, and they were the seats of the future, legally constituted parishes (*freguesia*). For this reason, given the evidence the old chronicles provide, it is not easy to determine with complete precision the date on which some of the parishes organised in the 15th and 16th centuries were created, if we take the meaning of these groupings of inhabitants in the sense given to them today. ‘Chaplaincy’, ‘curacy’ and ‘parish’ are terms used, at times interchangeably, to designate what today we very properly call a parish. Thus these chronicles state, and the annotations to the *Saudades da Terra* repeat, that the parishes of Câmara de Lobos and Calheta were created in 1430, and that the parish of Machico – capital of the captaincy and a village (*lugar*, settlement rank below a town) intensively settled from the beginning of colonisation – was created in 1450. It is known that this locality came to rival Funchal in its expansion and development, although only in the early days of that colonisation.

before: It was around 1430 that the first parish was established in Funchal, covering a vast area. Its centre was one of the chapels mentioned above, although some reasons argue in favour of the small chapel of São Sebastião. In 1438 its seat was fixed in the church of Santa Maria, or of the ‘Conceição de Baixo’, which Prince Henry the Navigator had ordered to be built on the left bank of the Ribeira de João Gomes, a short distance from the beach, and which took the name of Nossa Senhora do Calhau (Our Lady of Calhau).

before: By the end of this period (1425-1450), the work of settlement had already reached a remarkable stage of development: one or two years later, that is, in 1451 or 1452, the settlement of Funchal was raised to the rank of town (*vila*), with the privileges and prerogatives belonging to municipalities, as happened at about the same time with the seats of the captaincies of Machico and Porto Santo.

before: On 23 December 1920 the Municipal Council (*Câmara Municipal*) of Funchal resolved to contribute 200 escudos (Portuguese currency from 1911, = 1,000 réis) towards setting up an oceanographic museum, and 50 escudos a month towards its running costs. Some building work was even begun in the premises of the Holy House of Mercy (*Santa Casa da Misericórdia*) to house the planned museum. It had to be abandoned, however, once it was recognised that with the meagre sum voted by the Municipal Council nothing of scientific interest could be achieved, especially where oceanography was concerned. (1921). (See that entry).

before: The three captaincies into which the Madeira archipelago was divided had as their highest authority in the administration of public affairs the captains-donatary, who wielded almost absolute power and judged all criminal cases, ‘saluo em semtemcia de morte ou talhamento de membro’ (save in sentences of death or loss of limb). The curtailment of their jurisdiction and of the wide privileges they enjoyed (see Donataries) began with the creation of the municipalities. The first to be created were those of the seats of the three captaincies, Funchal, Machico and Porto Santo, around 1451. Within the captaincy and municipality of Funchal, the town (*vila*) and municipality of Ponta do Sol was created in 1501, and at almost the same time the municipality and town of Calheta. Within the captaincy and municipality of Machico, the town and municipality of Santa Cruz was created in 1515. At the beginning of the 16th century, therefore, this archipelago had the municipalities (*concelhos*) of Funchal, Machico, Porto Santo, Ponta do Sol, Calheta and Santa Cruz, which were at the same time towns, except for the first, which had been raised to the status of city in 1508. More than a century later, in 1743, a new municipality was created: São Vicente. In 1832 the municipalities of Santana, Câmara de Lobos and Porto Moniz were created, but they were only definitively established after constitutional government was introduced. Finally, in 1914, the municipality of Ribeira Brava was created. There are thus eleven municipalities in this district:

before: This is a noble and ancient family surname on this island. before: An inhabited locality (*sítio*) in the parish (*freguesia*) of Calheta. It was named after Dr Pedro Berenguer de Lemilhana, who founded an entailed estate (*morgadio*) here. He was a native of Spain and a *moço fidalgo* (junior nobleman of the Royal Household) of the Royal Household. The chapel of Jesus-Maria-José once stood in this locality, founded in 1708 by João de Andrade Berenguer Neto, a descendant of Dr Pedro Berenguer. There was also a chapel of Santa Catarina here, built by Rodrigo Enes in 1505. The well-known village (*lugar*, settlement rank below a town) of Vale da Bica lies in this locality.

before: Several species of Diptera are known by this name. The commonest is *Musca domestica*, a troublesome insect that lives mainly in and around dwellings, but whose larvae are found in dunghills and wherever there is manure. The blowfly (*Calliphora erythrocephala*) is also common, and the greenbottles (*Lucilia Caesar* and *L. sericata*) appear on trees, on human and animal excrement, etc. It is a fly of the genus *Hypoderma* that, by laying its eggs under the skin of cattle, causes through its larvae the tumours seen fairly often in these animals; the larvae are known in Madeira and Porto Santo as *berros*.

before: The original chapel was founded by Cristóvão Pires, who had it built around 1551. He lived in the parish of Faial. It has undergone various repairs, and in 1889 it was considerably enlarged, when Father Casimiro Augusto de Freitas e Abreu was vice-vicar.

before: This chapel was cramped and its parts were out of proportion, which gave the whole a most unattractive appearance. It also stood in a dangerous position and was in an advanced state of ruin, so that a new church became absolutely necessary. The parish priest Daniel Nicolau de Sousa boldly took on this risky undertaking in a parish of limited population and scant resources. Through persistent and diligent efforts, he succeeded in building a new, larger church on a safer and more accessible site, thus endowing his parish with a remarkable and much-appreciated improvement. The site chosen lies in the locality (*sítio*) of Chão do Cedro Gordo, and the new church was solemnly blessed by the diocesan prelate in December 1927.

before: An urban building on Rua da Conceição, at the corner of Rua da Figueira Preta, was long known as the Casa dos Cônsules. It seems to have been an old manor house. before: Anyone moderately versed in the history of Portuguese literature knows the celebrated romance of chivalry *Amadis de Gaula*, attributed to Vasco de Lobeira. Its origin, the language in which it was written, the period of its composition, etc., have been the subject of various works of literary criticism and historical research, especially the books of Teófilo Braga: *Introdução e Theoria da Historia da Literatura Portugueza*, *Poetas Palacianos* and *Amadis de Gaula*. Is there any connection between the name given to this parish and that of the famous romance? Dr Álvaro de Azevedo neither denies nor affirms it, making a vague and ambiguous reference to the parish (*freguesia*) of Gaula when he deals with the narrative romance and its devotees in this archipelago. He seems to have deliberately avoided giving an opinion that might perhaps have been called risky or rash. Meanwhile, let us transcribe the words of the annotator of the *Saudades*: ‘Tristan of Léonois, Lancelot of the Lake and Yseult are among these characters; Gaula is the homeland of the protagonist of one of them; *Amadis de Gaula* is the title of the celebrated romance attributed to our Vasco de Lobeira, a contemporary of John I. And in these islands, at the beginning of this period, Tristãos abounded, from Tristão Vaz Teixeira, or simply Tristão, Tristão da Ilha, first captain-donatary of Machico, so called, not because of any inferiority with respect to Zargo, but on the contrary, through a kind of poetic celebrity of the name, in honour of his singular chivalry and nobility,” as Frutuoso writes, copied by António Cordeiro in the *Historia Insulana*, book III, ch. IX, § 54: there was also in these islands more than one *fidalgo* (nobleman of the lesser nobility) named Lançarote, a manifest corruption of Lancelot; Bartolomeu Perestrelo, first donatary of the island of Porto Santo, gave his second daughter the name Yseu, or Hiseua, also a clear corruption of Yseult; and, finally, Gaula was the name then given to the vast lands west of the town of Santa Cruz which, since 1558, have formed the parish of Gaula.’

before: Dr Teófilo Braga refers to the subject in almost the same terms as Dr Álvaro de Azevedo in his book *Amadis de Gaula*, from which we transcribe the following passages: ‘It is worth noting that the only place where Portuguese tradition preserves the romance of Lancelot is where there are the most traces of a knowledge of the *Amadis* in aristocratic society: the name of Grimanesa, lover of Apolidão, lord of the Firm Island, was also that of the wife of Tristão Teixeira, third captain of Machico. “The fourth and last son of Captain Tristão was called Lançarote Teixeira: he was one of the best horsemen of the island; for besides being by inclination a very good rider, he had a great hand at taming horses and was much given to it, so much so that in his time sixty well-appointed knights with golden spurs gathered in the town of Machico, mounted through the efforts of this Lançarote Teixeira; and when a feast of St John or of Corpus Christi came round, there were so many knights for the cane games (*jogos de canas*, equestrian tournament with thrown canes) and skirmishes that it looked more like an army at war than a festive pastime; and though all were very skilled in this art, he nevertheless stood out so much among them that it may rightly be said he was the light and ornament of Machico.” Of this Lançarote Teixeira were born, besides other children, a son called Lançarote Teixeira de Gaula and a daughter who married Fernão Nunes de Gaula. Gaspar Frutuoso describes this village (*lugar*, settlement rank below a town) at some distance from Machico: “Going on from this stream (the Boaventura) almost a *légua*, there is a settlement of thirty households of the same *termo* (municipal jurisdictional district, a subdivision of the comarca) of Santa Cruz, called Gaula, and it has many vineyards of Malmsey and many vineyards of other varieties.” The influence of the romance of *Amadis de Gaula* in this very place is easily proved, knowing that this Lançarote Teixeira de Gaula was the grandson of Tristão Teixeira das Damas, a love poet of the Songbook of Resende (*Cancioneiro de Resende*): “He was called ‘das Damas’ [of the Ladies] because he was a great courtier, a fine speaker, composed many verses for the ladies and was very eloquent in speech. This poet, married to Dona Guiomar de Lordelo, lady-in-waiting to the Excellent Lady, was a contemporary of Zurara, and his character and taste would necessarily have made him acquainted with the adventures of *Amadis de Gaula*.”’

before: Among the localities, special mention is due to that of Achada, known as the Achada de Gaula, where there is a large cluster of dwellings. Many of them are surrounded by tall box hedges, which shelter them from the winds and give the place a rather interesting and picturesque appearance. The spot bears a strong resemblance to the charming parish of Sant'Ana, even in the make-up of the soil itself. From the Pico dos Eirós, which overlooks the parishes of Camacha, Santo da Serra and Caniço, a vast and astonishing panorama opens out, stretching eastwards as far as the Ponta de São Lourenço. The locality of Lombadinha deserves particular mention because it was once almost entirely held by quit-rent (*foreiro*) from the Captives’ Fund (*Cofre de Cativos*). The Fund had its seat in Lisbon and was intended for ransoming Portuguese taken prisoner by the Moors in Morocco, where they suffered the greatest outrages and the harshest cruelties.

before: At the end of 1760 a School of Geometry and Trigonometry, intended especially for those following a military career, was established in Funchal. It was housed in the Jesuit College (*Colégio dos Jesuítas*), today the barracks of the 19th Infantry Battalion, and its first teachers were the sergeant-major (*sargento-mor*, a field officer ranking as major) Francisco de Alincourt and the engineer Francisco Salustiano da Costa. Nine years later, that is, in 1769, the governor and captain-general João António de Sá Pereira reported to the government in mainland Portugal the good results obtained from the school. We do not know when it ceased to exist, nor any other circumstances concerning it.

before: Wollaston, the author of *Insecta Maderensia*, found 629 Coleoptera on Madeira, 163 on Porto Santo and 89 on the Desertas, and noted that many of these species have no wings or only very imperfectly developed ones. In Darwin’s view, this is a consequence of natural selection, probably combined with the disuse of those organs. Insects that do not feed on the ground but, like certain Coleoptera and Lepidoptera, feed on flowers, and must therefore use their wings to find food, have, as Wollaston observed, well-developed wings rather than rudimentary ones, the same naturalist adds.

before: The first steam vessel used in the coastal service of this island was the so-called *Vapor Valente*, which arrived in Funchal from England on 1 September 1872 and ran aground on 11 November 1876. It was imprudently left anchored close to the shore by the Ilhéu just as a violent storm from the south was beginning to blow; it was driven against the coast below the Quinta Lambert, where it was completely destroyed.

before: Issue no. 152 of the *Correio da Madeira*, in September 1922, published an interesting document taken from a copy of Book I of Baptisms and Marriages of the parish of Faial, which reads as follows: ‘On the twenty-ninth day of the month of June of . . . I [baptised] in this Church Fran[cisco], son of Francisco dor Nellas and of Ant[óni]a Mendes, and the godparents were Braz P[erei]ra and … of Beatriz oriz, and thus the godparents with the baptised are parishioners of this Church of N[ossa] S[enhora]... I made this *termo* (municipal jurisdictional district, a subdivision of the comarca) this day, month, year as above—Sebastião Gonsalves=and Braz P[erei]ra’. Since this record lies between two others from the year 1596, it seems evident that it was made in that year. There are also strong reasons to believe that the individual to whom the record refers is the celebrated João Fernandes Vieira, whose real name was Francisco de Ornelas Moniz and whose parents were Francisco de Ornelas Moniz and Antónia Mendes. If Fernandes Vieira was born on 29 June 1596, he died short of his 85th birthday, and not at 68, as was stated in the 1st edition of this work.

before: When Luís de Figueiredo e Lemos, the seventh prelate of Funchal and the third to come in person to administer his bishopric, arrived in Madeira in 1586, he took up residence in Rua das Pretas, in some private houses that later belonged to the chief standard-bearer (*alferes-mor*) of this island, Tristão Gomes de Castro, and where his predecessors are said to have had their usual residence already. It was this prelate, one of the most illustrious of this diocese, which he governed from 1586 to 1608, who built the old bishops’ palace and also the original seminary building, which adjoined it. Of these there remain some apartments, the episcopal chapel and a kind of cloister, a structure typical of old conventual residences, which today form outbuildings of the present palace in Rua do Bispo. The chapel, which ceased to be used for worship after the new bishop’s palace was built, was dedicated to São Luís de Tolosa (St Louis of Toulouse), and its founder, who died in this city on 26 November 1608, was buried there. In view of the state of complete neglect into which this old chapel had fallen, the prelate of this diocese, Dom Manuel Agostinho Barreto, had the mortal remains of Luís de Figueiredo e Lemos transferred from there in 1903 to Funchal Cathedral (*Sé*). They lie just inside the entrance of the church, covered by the same white marble tombstone that could be seen on the original grave.

before: Bishop Dom Friar António Teles da Silva (1675–1682) enlarged the original palace, and the prelate Dom José de Sousa de Castelo Branco (1698–1721) incorporated into it the adjoining seminary, when the latter moved to Rua do Mosteiro Novo. The earthquake felt in Madeira on the night of 31 March to 1 April 1748 caused considerable damage throughout the island to many public and private buildings, and the old bishops’ palace and the adjoining seminary were also badly ruined. The bishop of Funchal at the time was Dom João do Nascimento, who governed this diocese from 1741 to 1753. He proved an eminent prelate who marked his time on this island with various notable works, both in the performance of his episcopal duties and in serving for some years as acting governor and captain-general of this archipelago.

before: It is to him that we owe the building of the bishop’s palace, where the lyceum (state secondary school) is housed today (1921). Obliged to abandon the old residence of the bishops, which the earthquake had left in ruins, he promptly set about building a new palace, which he planned to raise near the Cathedral (the Sé). The insurmountable difficulties that arose in acquiring a new site forced him to make use of that of the ruined palace, which was entirely demolished, except for the part that still stands today. There he had the new bishop’s palace built from its foundations. Although it is a heavy building devoid of any architectural refinement, it is nonetheless, for this small city and for the period in which it was built, a building of some importance, and one that in no way dishonoured the rank of its occupants.

before: When the present prelate of this diocese came to take charge of the bishopric in 1915, he found a house ready to serve as the episcopal residence, which the Catholics had rented and furnished and then handed over to the head of the Funchal church. This house stands in Rua dos Netos, on the corner with Rua dos Ferreiros, on the right-hand side as one goes up the latter street. The diocesan prelate’s residence did not remain there long, for, through the acquisition by grant and inheritance of an excellent dwelling house in the Largo do Ribeiro Real, this house was definitively made the Bishop’s Palace. The prelate lives there at present, and the ecclesiastical offices are housed in the outbuildings of the property.

before: This distinguished lady was born in Madras, in British India, on 3 October 1840. She settled in Madeira in 1880, and two years later she founded a school in the Palácio de São Pedro (St Peter Palace), which she named St. Georges High School and which was widely attended by girls from the best Funchal society. Having closed the school around 1892, she rebuilt the old hospital of the town (*vila*) of Santa Cruz with money raised from alms. There she took in a number of patients and set up a pharmacy, rendering outstanding services to the sick and the poor of that municipality (*concelho*). She was the founder of a diocesan religious community which, through its hospital work and its teaching in many schools scattered across various parishes, earned the highest praise and the gratitude of the people of this island.

before: The churches of this diocese contain no tombs whose showy architecture, rich marbles or fine ornamentation would catch the visitor’s eye. Only on the side walls of the chancel of the church of Carmo (Carmelite church) are there two mausoleums which, without being grand or of remarkable artistic refinement, are nevertheless regarded as a work of value that deserves to be visited and duly appreciated. These tombs belong to the family of the church’s founder, and on two slabs of black marble the following epitaphs can be read: ‘Tomb of Pedro Gonçalves Brandão, and of his brother Manuel Martins Brandão and their heirs’ and ‘Tomb of António de Carvalhal Esmeraldo, *fidalgo* (nobleman of the lesser nobility) of His Majesty’s household, and of his wife Dona Maria Brandão’. In the church of Santa Clara (St Clare of Assisi) is the tomb of Gaspar Mendes de Vasconcelos, in which the discoverer Gonçalves Zargo is said to be buried (volume II, page 31).

before: Among the privileges granted to the donataries of this archipelago was the exclusive right to build mills or water mills; when they saw fit, they could license others to do so in return for a special levy. This privilege was one of the richest sources of the captain-donataries’ revenues, which were very large indeed. At the locality still called Moinhos today, along the right bank of the Ribeira de Santa Luzia, they owned a considerable number of water mills that have survived to our own day, many of which the Marquises of Castelo Melhor, at a time not very distant from ours, leased to various people. The square known as Largo dos Moinhos or Largo do Marquês keeps these names because there were several water mills there belonging to the house of Castelo Melhor, into which the entailed foundation (*instituição vincular*, a morgado or capela) of the donataries of Funchal was incorporated.

before: A letter or set of instructions sent by Prince Henry the Navigator to João Gonçalves Zarco states: ‘... to order João Afonso to fit another millstone and to build a water mill like the one at Tomar’. before: English naturalist and traveller who was in Madeira in 1823, staying from 14 to 26 October. The results of Bowdich’s studies of the fauna, flora, geology and meteorology of Madeira and Porto Santo are set out in a work published only after his death, entitled *Excursions in Madeira and Porto Santo, during the autumn of 1823* (London, 1825). This work, curious for many reasons but containing many inaccuracies, was translated into French and published in Paris in 1826. Bowdich died on 10 January 1824.

before: An inhabited locality (*sítio*) in the parish (*freguesia*) of Calheta. Here stands the chapel of Nossa Senhora do Bom Sucesso (Our Lady of Good Success), built by Lourenço da Costa in 1683. before: Name given to two fish of the weever family (Trachinidae), *Trachinus vipera* and *T. draco*. They do not live in deep water but are found close to the shore, preferring sandy places. They have the habit of burying themselves in the sand, leaving only the head uncovered. A sting from the opercular spines, and above all from the rays of the first dorsal fin, is highly venomous and can cause, besides terrible pain, violent inflammation, sometimes accompanied by fever. Fishermen and bathers have suffered serious accidents of this kind on the great beach of Porto Santo, where the two species are not rare.

before: A shrub, rarely a small tree, 1 to 5 metres tall, usually with a twisted trunk; the leaves are scale-like, imbricate and almost always appressed; the galbuli are subglobose and dark brown when ripe. This member of the Pinaceae has been found at Rocha do Navio, in Santana, on the Caminho de Larano (Porto da Cruz), etc. On Porto Santo, where it was once very common, only a single specimen survived in 1903, on the slopes of Pico Branco. It yields white or yellowish-white wood, much less aromatic than that of the cedar.

before: This body was created by the royal letter (*carta régia*) of 20 July 1810. Dr Rodrigues de Azevedo states that its creation was inspired by the Instructions on agriculture which the *corregedor* (royal district magistrate) Dr Veloso de Oliveira (see that entry) left recorded at the Council of Calheta. Its purpose was not only to protect and develop farming in general but also, in particular, to promote the cultivation of the common lands (*baldios*) by dividing them into leaseholds, thereby extending the area of arable land and making productive the many plots that lay waste and barren. This measure, which was reinforced by the royal decree (alvará régio) of 18 September 1811, was also intended to remedy some of the damage that the terrible flash flood (*aluvião*) of 1803 had caused to Madeiran agriculture.

before: It was these ties of friendship, and no doubt the favours he had received, that led Dr Oliveira to stage the abduction of Dona Eugénia de Meneses, lady-in-waiting to Princess Carlota Joaquina, so as to shield the sovereign from his wife’s suspicions and from a scandal at court. He embarked secretly at Caxias bound for Cádiz and, after leaving Dona Eugénia de Meneses there in a safe refuge, went on to the United States, where he remained for some years. The scandalous affair, whose truth only the Prince Regent knew, took on the proportions of a great crime, and the higher courts promptly took it up. João Francisco de Oliveira was sentenced to death, and Dona Eugénia de Meneses, who belonged to the highest nobility of the Kingdom (*reino*, i.e. mainland Portugal), was stripped of all the honours and favours attached to her rank, expelled from court and barred from any share in the property or privileges of her family. Anyone wishing to learn more about this episode, in which João Francisco de Oliveira took part to save the sovereign’s honour and which can be explained only by the customs of the time, should consult the lengthy account of it, with the relevant documents, given by the writer Alberto Pimentel in his most interesting work *A ultima Côrte do Absolutismo em Portugal*.

before: In April 1803 the Prince Regent granted Dr Oliveira extensive lands in São Jorge and the Quinta de Sant’Ana in the parish (*freguesia*) of Monte, which had belonged to Pantalião Fernandes and had been incorporated into the Royal Property (*Reais Próprios*) or the National Treasury (*Fazenda Nacional*), as it is called today. These and other properties were inherited by his son, Dr Alexandre de Oliveira, who in the middle of the 19th century built the house on the *quinta* (country estate) at São Jorge. He bequeathed the properties in that parish and the family residence in Funchal to his sister, Dona Maria Leopoldina de Oliveira, who had been born in the United States while Councillor Oliveira was living there. The universal heir of Dona Maria de Oliveira was the lamented and eminent Bishop of Funchal, Dom Manuel Agostinho Barreto, who applied the entire proceeds from the sale of this inheritance exclusively to building the great edifice of the Seminary of the Incarnação (*Seminário da Incarnação*; Incarnation). It was never entirely completed, and the offices of the District General Council (*Junta Geral do Distrito*) are housed (1921) there. Dona Maria Leopoldina de Oliveira died in Funchal on 3 February 1902.

before: An inhabited locality (*sítio*) in the parish (*freguesia*) of Quinta Grande. The Quinta do Pomar lies in this locality, and on it stands a chapel dedicated to St Anthony, founded by Father António Silvino Gonçalves de Andrade in 1883; there is also a state primary school here. At the spot in this locality known as Ponta da Quinta there was once a small chapel dedicated to the Virgin, Our Lady, of which not even a trace now remains.
after: An inhabited locality (*sítio*) in the parish (*freguesia*) of Quinta Grande (‘large estate’). before: Of this António Espínola, the *Historia Insulana* says that he was a native of Genoa and descended from the most ancient families of that city, and that he counted several Doges of that republic among his forebears. ‘King Manuel I granted him a coat of arms and the noble rank (*foro de fidalgo*) of his household. He held lands granted as *sesmaria* (royal land grant to settlers on condition of cultivation) in Santiago and other places; and by a deed of 30 April 1524 he donated a small plot of land at the edge of the city, on which were built the chapel of Santiago, patron saint of the whole island, the sacristy and churchyard, on condition that members of his family should be buried there, and that the chaplain should ask for an Our Father and a Hail Mary for his soul. The deed was drawn up on parchment and is in the archive of the Chapter of Funchal.’

before: The church of São Tiago, known today as the church of Socorro, where the seat of the parish (*freguesia*) of Santa Maria Maior was installed in 1803, is not the original building. Nothing of that first structure remains at present, and it was much smaller than the present church. Some years later it underwent major repairs, and it was blessed by the diocesan bishop, Dom Jerónimo Fernando, on 25 July 1632. A century later, as the chapel had fallen into considerable disrepair, the Funchal Council decided to build a larger church. The old chapel was demolished in 1752, and the works were declared complete in 1768.

before: When the great flash flood (*aluvião*) of 1803 swept the church of Nossa Senhora do Calhau (Our Lady of Calhau) (see that entry) into the sea, the Council gave the church of São Tiago to serve as the seat of the parish, on condition that the image of the patron saint and protector of the city should always be kept there. A stone tablet was then placed on the church’s façade, where it still remains, bearing the following inscription: *Hic lapis indicat liberalitatem senatus et populi hanc ecclesiam Fidelissimo Principi Regenti offerentium in locum parochiae per inundationem aquarum destructae Anno Domini MDCCCIII* (This stone records the generosity of the council and people, who offered this church to the Most Faithful Prince Regent in place of the parish church destroyed by the flood waters, in the year of Our Lord 1803). See Patron saints.

before: An inhabited locality (*sítio*) in the parish (*freguesia*) of Santa Cruz. before: The parish of Serra de Água, which lies in the interior of the island, must have been, as can still be seen today, a centre of vast and rich woodland. Since it is crossed by a fast-flowing stream, it would have been relatively easy to set up a water-powered sawmill there, and the nearby landing place of Ribeira Brava invited the shipment of the timber. There was a locality of that name, which spread to the surrounding area and later to the parish. When the parish was created, that village (*lugar*, settlement rank below a town) was already known by the name of Serra de Água.

before: This harbour enjoys the reputation of being one of the best in the archipelago, and it is unquestionably the safest and most sheltered on the whole north coast of Madeira. It has even been claimed that embarking and landing are always possible there, whatever quarter the wind blows from. The truth is that, although communication with the shore is often easy, it is equally certain that at times it is genuinely impossible to make for the inner harbour, and entering it is very risky and dangerous. The coastline stretching from Ponta do Tristão to beyond the islet of Porto Moniz is battered by frequent storms, especially in winter, and the sea there is not infrequently very rough and turbulent.

before: Yet another weighty reason counsels and urges this: its venerable antiquity. before: About this chapel, an old book in the parish archive of the parish (*freguesia*) of Arco da Calheta contains the following passage: ‘this chapel is magnificent in its architecture and workmanship; it was built in the early days of this parish... its first founder was an illustrious man of the most notable family of the Câmaras, as the escutcheon of his arms above the main door shows. . . in this chapel lies the seat of an entail (*morgado*) which the priors of the Esperança of Lisbon administered for many years... and it comprises all the properties that the Ribeiro do Ledo divides on the eastern side. . . .’. Henrique Henriques de Noronha gives the following further details: ‘Pedro Gonçalves da Câmara, 3rd son of the second donatary João Gonçalves da Câmara, married Dona Joana de Eça, who was a lady-in-waiting to Queen Catherine, wife of John III. . . he rebuilt the monastery of the Esperança, in Portugal, and built the chapel of Nossa Senhora do Loreto, in Arco da Calheta, where he had noble houses, of which nothing but ruins can be seen today: his portrait can be seen in that chapel’. Dona Joana de Sá left this chapel and the lands attached to it to the nuns of the Convento da Esperança (Convent of Our Lady of Hope), Lisbon, who in turn sold them to Francisco Luís de Vasconcelos Bettencourt, and he established there the seat of an entailed estate (*morgadio*). before: While the vicar capitular (administrator of the vacant diocese elected by the chapter) and governor of the diocese (governador do bispado, administering the see in the bishop's absence) António Alfredo de Santa Catarina Braga was staying at Santo da Serra, he issued from there a warrant (*provisão*), dated 13 June 1836, abolishing the parish (*freguesia*) of Água de Pena and creating that of Santo – or rather, annexing the former to the curacy (*curato*) of Santo da Serra and making the latter the seat of the new parish, under the name of the parish of Santo da Serra e Água de Pena. Santo da Serra was a subsidiary curacy of the parish of Machico, created in 1813, but its curate did not normally reside there. With the annexation of the parish of Água de Pena to the curacy of Santo da Serra, the latter became the seat of the parish, and the parish priest took up permanent residence there. The measure taken so arbitrarily by the vicar capitular António Alfredo did not last long. By the law (*carta de lei*) of 24 July 1848 this parish was restored once more. It lost the locality (*sítio*) of Achada do Barro from its former area, which remained part of Santo da Serra, but it gained the localities of Torre and Ventrecha, which had belonged to the parish of Santa Cruz.

before: The locality of Bemposta (see that entry) was the seat of an entailed estate (*morgadio*) dating from the first quarter of the 16th century. João Afonso Escudeiro, a man of noble descent, came from mainland Portugal to Madeira around 1450 and held *sesmaria* (royal land grant to settlers on condition of cultivation) lands in Água de Pena. There, by his will made on 21 June 1512, the year of his death, he founded the entail (*morgado*) of Bemposta, as well as that of São Lázaro in Santa Cruz. His daughter and heiress Catarina Anes Escudeiro, the first administrator of this entailed estate (*vínculo*), married Lopo Franco de Monção. From this marriage was born João Franco, who succeeded to the entailed estate and died without issue, so that the administration of the Bemposta entail passed to a nephew of his named Diogo Lopes Tavares. Squeezed between the parishes of Santa Cruz and Machico, the parish is bounded to the north by the latter and by that of Santo da Serra, to the south by that of Santa Cruz, to the east by the Atlantic Ocean and to the west by the parishes of Santa Cruz and Santo da Serra. It forms part of the municipalities of Santa Cruz and Machico: the inhabited localities of Torre and Ventrecha belong to the former, and those of Bemposta, Lombo, Logarinho, Igreja and Queimada to the latter. Its patron saint is the Roman virgin and martyr St Beatrice, and its parish church stands in the locality called Igreja. Besides this church, it has the chapel of the Sagrado Coração de Jesus (Sacred Heart of Jesus) in the locality of Cardiais, founded in 1907 by Canon Henrique Modesto de Betencourt, and that of Nossa Senhora do Perpétuo Socorro (Our Lady of Perpetual Help), built by Francisco de Freitas Correia in 1924 in the locality of Queimada. The post box and the telephone booth are in the locality of Igreja, where the parish cemetery is also found. The towns of Santa Cruz and Machico lie about eight kilometres apart, and the most central part of the parish of Água de Pena is roughly equidistant from those two towns and some 20 kilometres from the city of Funchal. It belongs to the judicial district (*comarca*) of Santa Cruz and, as stated above, to the municipality of that name and to that of Machico. Since a fair stretch of it is washed by the sea, it is served by a small landing place with a beach of rounded pebbles known as the Calhau do Seixo, at the mouth of the stream of the same name. The land of this parish is watered by the Levada do Juncal and the Levada Nova do Furado, which rise in the north of the island, and also by the Levada do Moinho da Serra, which rises in the parish of Santa Cruz, the Levada Nova, which draws from the Machico stream, and the Levada do Logarinho, whose flow starts in the locality of the same name within this parish. Some have asserted that the illustrious Madeiran João Fernandes Vieira, who distinguished himself so notably in Brazil in the war against the Dutch, was born in this parish. However, according to investigations made there some years ago, his baptismal record is not to be found in the parish archive. Today it seems established that he was born in the parish of Faial, as will be explained more fully later. A native of the parish of Água de Pena is Canon Francisco Fulgêncio de Andrade, a doctor of the Pontifical University of Rome and currently a professor at the seminary of this city.

From this marriage was born João Franco, who succeeded to the entailed estate and died without issue, so that the administration of the Bemposta entail passed to a nephew of his named Diogo Lopes Tavares. Squeezed between the parishes of Santa Cruz and Machico, the parish is bounded to the north by the latter and by that of Santo da Serra, to the south by that of Santa Cruz, to the east by the Atlantic Ocean and to the west by the parishes of Santa Cruz and Santo da Serra. It forms part of the municipalities of Santa Cruz and Machico: the inhabited localities of Torre and Ventrecha belong to the former, and those of Bemposta, Lombo, Logarinho, Igreja and Queimada to the latter. Its patron saint is the Roman virgin and martyr St Beatrice, and its parish church stands in the locality called Igreja. Besides this church, it has the chapel of the Sacred Heart of Jesus (*Sagrado Coração de Jesus*) in the locality of Cardiais (‘thistle patches’), founded in 1907 by Canon Henrique Modesto de Betencourt, and that of Nossa Senhora do Perpétuo Socorro (Our Lady of Perpetual Help), built by Francisco de Freitas Correia in 1924 in the locality of Queimada. The post box and the telephone booth are in the locality of Igreja, where the parish cemetery is also found. The towns of Santa Cruz and Machico lie about eight kilometres apart, and the most central part of the parish of Água de Pena is roughly equidistant from those two towns and some 20 kilometres from the city of Funchal. It belongs to the judicial district (*comarca*) of Santa Cruz and, as stated above, to the municipality of that name and to that of Machico. Since a fair stretch of it is washed by the sea, it is served by a small landing place with a beach of rounded pebbles known as the Calhau do Seixo (‘pebble shore of the flint’), at the mouth of the stream of the same name. The land of this parish is watered by the Levada do Juncal and the Levada Nova do Furado (‘new channel of the tunnel’), which rise in the north of the island, and also by the Levada do Moinho da Serra, which rises in the parish of Santa Cruz, the Levada Nova (‘new channel’), which draws from the Machico stream, and the Levada do Logarinho, whose flow starts in the locality of the same name within this parish. Some have asserted that the illustrious Madeiran João Fernandes Vieira, who distinguished himself so notably in Brazil in the war against the Dutch, was born in this parish. However, according to investigations made there some years ago, his baptismal record is not to be found in the parish archive. Today it seems established that he was born in the parish of Faial, as will be explained more fully later. A native of the parish of Água de Pena is Canon Francisco Fulgêncio de Andrade, a doctor of the Pontifical University of Rome and currently a professor at the seminary of this city.

before: About 70 species of sponges have been collected in the seas of Madeira, many of them siliceous or calcareous. Among the latter is *Melia Normani*, discovered by Mr Adolfo César de Noronha in the waters off Porto Santo and described by Mr Randolph Kirkpatrick, a naturalist at the British Museum. The largest species found so far in the seas of the archipelago measures about 60 centimetres, is somewhat bowl-shaped and consists of tightly interwoven glassy threads. When fishermen’s lines reach great depths, they sometimes bring up sponges of the same kind as the one just described, caught on the hooks. At Ponta de São Lourenço we have seen small fibrous sponges floating near the coast, which certainly came from the nearby depths.

before: This name is given to a small beach and stretch of coastline lying between the Ilhéu da Pontinha and the mouth of the Ribeiro Seco.

before: The parish takes its name from the *faia* (*Myrica Faya*). There was once a locality (*sítio*) there where this member of the Myricaceae grew in abundance; it took the name *faial*, which later spread to the surrounding land and eventually to the whole parish. Referring to the origin of the name, Frutuoso says that this parish (*freguesia*) bears it because a great many *faias* grow there. One might perhaps say of this parish, allowing for the difference in scale, what António Cordeiro says in the *Insulana* of the island of Faial: ‘it was called Faial because the said island was entirely full of many large *faias*’.

before: The lands that made up this parish and those of Porto da Cruz were the first on the north side to be worked and settled in the days of the earliest colonisation. One of the oldest settlers was Lançarote Teixeira, fourth son of Tristão Vaz Teixeira, the first donatary of Machico, whom the *Saudades* praise as follows: ‘he was one of the finest horsemen of the island; for besides being by inclination a very good rider, he had a great hand at breaking horses and was much given to it, so much so that in his time sixty knights with gilded spurs gathered in the town of Machico, very well turned out and mounted through the efforts of this Lançarote Teixeira, so that when St John’s Day or Corpus Christi came round, there were so many horsemen for the cane games (*jogos de canas*, equestrian tournament with thrown canes) and skirmishes that it looked more like an army at war than a festive pastime; and though all were very skilled in this art, he nonetheless stood out among them, so that it may rightly be said that he was the light and ornament of Machico’. This Lançarote Teixeira held much land in Faial by *sesmaria* (royal land grant to settlers on condition of cultivation), including the lands stretching from Ribeiro Frio to Ribeira da Metade and taking in the Penha de Águia, and there he founded a numerous line of descendants.

before: Even at present this church is the object of a well-attended pilgrimage on 7 and 8 September each year. After the great pilgrimages of Nossa Senhora do Monte (Our Lady of the Mount), of the Milagres at Machico and of the Senhor Jesus at Ponta Delgada, it is one of those that draw the greatest crowds of pilgrims from every part of the island, and it offers the observer one of the most interesting and picturesque sights. Frutuoso’s testimony shows that it is quite ancient and has always been remarkably well attended, and so it has remained through several centuries.

before: For centuries the soil of Madeira was abundantly watered by the sweat of slaves. In the early days of colonisation, the hard and gruelling work of clearing the land of this island was done by Black slaves, captive Moors and Canary Islanders. Slavery, which had begun at Rio de Oro (Rio do Ouro) around the middle of the 15th century, grew steadily with the exploitation and cultivation of the land of the recently discovered islands, that is, the archipelagos of Madeira, the Azores and Cape Verde.

before: At the end of the 15th century and the beginning of the next, the Fleming João Esmeraldo had eighty slaves – Moors, Black Africans and mulattoes – on his estate of Lombada da Ponta do Sol alone. Frutuoso says that in 1552 the confession rolls recorded 2,700 slaves in Funchal, and that in the same year their number rose to 3000, because four ships brought another 300 to this island. If we bear in mind that the total population of the archipelago at that time was around twenty thousand inhabitants, we must conclude that the number of slaves here was considerable, and it is worth noting that three hundred were imported within a single year! Half a century later, when French corsairs sacked the city of Funchal in 1566, they carried off only three hundred Black captives, because the capacity of their ships allowed no more.

before: Slavery seems to have grown further as time went on, but we lack reliable evidence on which to judge, even approximately, the number of slaves and the periods when they were brought to this island. To them is owed in large part the rapid and remarkable growth of the sugar industry, which was the most important source of the wealth and prosperity of this archipelago in the 15th and 16th centuries. The settler who came from the mainland became a *sesmeiro* (holder of a land grant, or *sesmaria*), then made himself lord of the land and in many cases turned it into an entail (*morgado*). He left the cultivation and tilling of his rural properties to the slaves and went off to the city or the court to enjoy the income from his fields and estates. The slaves gradually freed themselves from their master’s tutelage. By cultivating the *sesmaria* lands on their own account and loading them with houses, walls and other improvements (*benfeitorias*, buildings and walls made by the tenant, which remained his property), they considerably increased their value. In this way they contributed to the creation of the *colonia* contract (Madeiran sharecropping tenancy; produce divided, improvements owned by the tenant) and very nearly became co-owners of those same lands and properties. It seems that slaves in this archipelago were treated with somewhat more humanity, and that their material situation was less to be lamented than in other Portuguese colonies. This may perhaps have been due to the natural fertility of the soil, the various military expeditions to Morocco, the considerable number of foreigners who landed on this island, with gentler customs and more civilising tendencies, and still other causes unknown to us. Writing of Machico, Frutuoso records ‘that in this town (*vila*) there are many mulatto women, very well treated and with rich voices, which is a sign of the ancient nobility of its inhabitants, for in all great and wealthy houses there is this multiplication of those who serve them’. It is certain, however, that in 1505 the donataries obtained the royal decree (alvará régio), recorded in volume 1 of the archive of the Council of Funchal, at fol. 111, under which they could have the ears cut off slaves who deserved it by law. And at about this time, when some slaves of João Rodrigues Castelhano murdered a factor (*feitor*) of the same Castelhano, five of them were hanged in the town of Calheta.

before: The names of Rua da Mouraria and Rua das Pretas still bear witness to the presence of Moors and Black people in Funchal. The eighty slaves of João Esmeraldo on the Lombada da Ponta do Sol, and the many others there on various “settled farmsteads” (*fazendas povoadas*), show us that a large number of people of African descent lived in that parish (*freguesia*). Curral das Freiras (see that entry), as we have already said, was in the earliest days of colonisation a refuge for criminals and runaway slaves, who in this remote and almost inaccessible *lugar* (settlement ranking between a town and a parish) found their true letter of manumission. They formed a centre of population, which later merged with the settlers who established themselves there.

before: In the early days of colonisation, and long afterwards, a good many chapels were built in various localities of this island. They generally gave their names to these places, which were often important centres of population and became the origin of future parishes. This is why every parish (*freguesia*) in Madeira that keeps a name of a religious character takes it from a chapel that already existed and was later turned into a parish church. The same is true of the parish of Prazeres, whose name comes from a small chapel dedicated to Nossa Senhora dos Prazeres (Our Lady of Delights), built there long before the parish was created. It is to be presumed that the original chapel was known as the chapel of Prazeres, and that this name, thus simplified, became that of the new parish.

before: The land that makes up the greater part of the parish of Prazeres originally belonged to the parish of Estreito da Calheta. It was detached from that parish to form, together with a few hamlets of Fajã da Ovelha, an independent parish, created by the royal decree (alvará régio) of 28 December 1676. It was only around 1684 that the new parish was established, with its seat in the chapel of Nossa Senhora dos Prazeres. Its parish priests were Father Manuel Dias Pinheiro (1684–1692), Francisco Correia da Silva (1692–1693) and José Cordeiro de Andrade (1693–1700). In that year, 1700, the parish of Prazeres was abolished, or at least part of the parish services held there was suspended and transferred to the church of Estreito da Calheta, to whose parish the hamlets of Prazeres were annexed. We have not discovered the reasons behind this measure, which seems strange to us but did in fact take place. The locality did, however, have a chaplain of its own, who celebrated some acts of worship there.

before: Thirty-three years later, by the royal decree of 12 November 1733, the curacy (*curato*) of Nossa Senhora dos Prazeres was created, and it was then made dependent on the parish of Paul do Mar. The only parish in this diocese that we know to have been abolished and soon afterwards restored as a parish was that of São Pedro, in this city. But of an autonomous parish that was suppressed and afterwards reduced to the subordinate rank of a curacy, we know only of Prazeres.

before: As happened with Jardim do Mar, Achadas da Cruz and others, the curacy of Prazeres gradually freed itself from its dependence on its mother church (*igreja matriz*) and went on to become an autonomous parish, in a year we cannot determine. This is the place to say that the last parishes in this diocese to bear the name of curacies, such as those of Curral das Freiras, Achadas da Cruz, Prazeres, etc., were in recent times genuinely autonomous parishes, independent of the parishes from which they had been separated, although they kept the traditional name of curacies. Shortly before 1880 the priests who performed parochial duties in Prazeres began to sign the relevant official documents as parish priests, and the first collated vicar, in 1881, was Father João António Marcial. The old, original chapel stood in the locality of Estacada, beside the road. No trace of it remains, as it was demolished when the present parish church was built. In 1745 the works on the new church were put out for award by public auction (*arrematação*) for 4,100,000 *réis* (old Portuguese money of account; 1$000 = 1,000 réis, 1:000$000 = one conto = 1,000,000 réis), but construction began only some years later: the foundation stone was laid and blessed on 9 September 1751, and the licence decree stated that the old church was ‘small and unfit to serve’. In 1922 the building was substantially altered: the main body was enlarged and a tower and two sacristies were added, giving it more ample proportions. It was in this church, in December 1827, that a sacrilege was committed with the theft of the sacred vessel containing the Holy Eucharist. It caused a great sensation throughout the island, and for that reason many acts of reparation were held in all the churches of the diocese.

before: Lighting the other end of Madeira’s south coast is also a recognised need, with the São Lourenço lighthouse (*Farol de São Lourenço*) to the east and the projected Ponta do Pargo lighthouse to the west. The building and other premises intended to house the lighthouse and its staff were built some years ago, and all the work has been completed. All that remains is the purchase of the lantern and the other apparatus needed to fit out the lighthouse, which the European conflict prevented from being in operation already. The continuation of the building is owed to the District General Council (*Junta Geral*) of this district, which will shortly acquire the light and install it. (1921).

before: The Ponta do Pargo lighthouse was inaugurated on 5 June 1922. It stands on the Ponta da Vigia, some 375 metres above sea level, at the locality (*sítio*) where there was once a telegraph station and which was known as Casa do Rei. We have read somewhere that this lighthouse ‘emits three successive beams of white light with a power of 5,500 carcels, each lasting 0.5 of a second, at intervals of 3.5 seconds’.

before: It was from 1902, when collection of the revenues granted to the General Council began, that this administrative body started to carry out a great number of public improvements, especially the construction of the road network. The General Council’s administrative action also extended to many other public services, some already existing and others newly created, and the inestimable benefits that the grant of ‘administrative autonomy’ had brought to this district became ever more evident. Later decrees sanctioned certain services of the General Council and gave them legal standing, but they did not essentially alter its economic and administrative life. Besides its own departments of secretariat, treasury and public works, the General Council was given particular charge of the services for the maintenance and upkeep of the Asylum, the Foundlings and Destitute Children, the Land Disinfection Station, the Bacteriology and Hygiene Laboratory, the police for the suppression of clandestine emigration, the agricultural and livestock services, and others besides.

before: Communications in Madeira were, beyond any possible dispute, the worst in the whole of our country. This was due to various causes, above all the almost unbelievably rugged terrain, and also to other unfavourable local conditions. Most of them did not deserve the name of roads, for in general they were narrow paths trodden into the ground, hard and extremely difficult underfoot, overhanging bottomless chasms and skirting the flanks of high mountains, and they almost always exposed travellers to the gravest discomforts and dangers. Until 1901, when administrative autonomy was granted to this district, there were only nine kilometres of good road, linking the city of Funchal with the town (*vila*) of Câmara de Lobos. The construction of an extensive network of roads then began and is still continuing; within a few years it will make it easy to travel the whole island by fast transport and to visit its main localities quickly and comfortably.

before: The offices of the General Council were housed in various buildings. By the decree of 12 August 1919 the building of the former Seminary of the Incarnação (*Seminário da Incarnação*; Incarnation) was ceded to this administrative body for the sum of 7,500.00 escudos (escudo: Portuguese currency from 1911, = 1,000 réis), and most of the Council’s departments were installed there. When the decree of 25 April 1927 restored possession of the said Seminary building to the Commission for Worship of the Diocese of Funchal, the General Council moved its offices to the old premises of the Hospital de Santa Isabel (St Elizabeth of Portugal), where they have been amply accommodated since October 1933.

before: The prince travelled through many parishes of Madeira and also visited Porto Santo, proving an enthusiastic admirer of the natural beauty of our archipelago. before: This Belgian subject took up residence in this archipelago long ago. For many years he lived at the Quinta dos Cedros in Santo António, and more recently on the island of Porto Santo. He is regarded in his own country as a distinguished writer, with a notable body of literary work already to his name. Among his works that may interest Madeirans is the study entitled *Au Nord Ouest de l'Afrique/Madère, les iles Canaries, le Maroc*, published in Brussels in 1882. In the Belgian review *La Jeune Wallonie* he published the interesting narrative *Voyage aux iles Salvages*, which fills 50 pages of that review and is accompanied by excellent engravings. Some claim that in this author’s comedies *Les Titularisés* and *Le Mariagicide* several of the characters embody certain well-known figures of Funchal society.

before: At Porto Moniz, on the north coast of Madeira, and at Gorgulho, near Funchal, there are lava flows of very curious appearance. The Porto Moniz flows, a drawing of which appears in Charles Lyell’s *Elements of Geology*, look particularly recent. One of them forms a mass bristling with jagged points that extends beyond the coastline. The Gorgulho lavas lie on the shore, close to the spot where a small fort once stood, and contain various hollows in which seawater collects.

before: He was one of the *fidalgos* sent by the king to this island to marry the daughters of João Gonçalves Zarco, and he married Zarco’s third daughter, Catarina Gonçalves da Câmara. before: The Franciscan friars who accompanied João Gonçalves Zarco when he began the settlement and colonisation of Funchal were the first priests to perform ecclesiastical and parochial duties on this island, in the chapels of Santa Catarina (St Catherine of Alexandria), São Paulo (St Paul the Apostle), Nossa Senhora do Calhau (Our Lady of Calhau), Conceição de Cima, São Sebastião (St Sebastian), São João, etc. The first parish (*freguesia*) to be created was undoubtedly in Funchal, but it is difficult today to determine precisely where its first seat was. It is probable that the seat was not always the same, and even that parish duties were performed in more than one chapel at the same time. The annotator of the *Saudades* says that the first parish was perhaps established in the chapel of São Sebastião, but this is no more than a simple conjecture. Dr Álvaro de Azevedo asserts that the first church built in Funchal was that of São Sebastião, which seems to us not to be true, as we shall see elsewhere, and from this he deduces that the first parish was probably created in that chapel. The discoverer João Gonçalves Zarco first set up his residence on the height of Santa Catarina and later at São Paulo. It is certain, however, that the first and most important nucleus of population grew up not far from the beach, along the left bank of the stream that later came to be called Ribeira de João Gomes. It is therefore more likely that the seat of the first parish was established there, at least once the parish took on a more permanent character and a more definite organisation.

before: The original chapel of Nossa Senhora do Calhau dates from the second quarter of the 15th century, having been built around 1438. The creation of the parish that had its first seat there must date from this time or shortly afterwards.

before: The Order of Christ, ever jealous of its privileges and prerogatives, feared that the Franciscan friars would claim for themselves the rights that belonged to the Order by the grant of spiritual jurisdiction over this archipelago that had been made to it. It therefore sent to this island a qualified member of the Order, Friar Nuno Cão (see that entry), to oversee all religious services and to uphold the rights and exemptions that King Duarte had granted to the Order by the royal letter (*carta régia*) of 26 September 1433. Friar Nuno Cão took charge of the parish of Nossa Senhora do Calhau. When the parish moved its seat in 1508 to the church that later became the cathedral, he remained parish priest until 1514, when he was appointed dean on the creation of the diocese.

before: The first parish, both while its seat was at Nossa Senhora do Calhau and after it was transferred to the Igreja Grande, covered a very large area, and new parishes were gradually carved out of it, as happened in many other parts of the island. Around 1558 Funchal was divided into two parishes, with their seats in the churches of the Cathedral (the Sé) and of Nossa Senhora do Calhau. By then the chapels of São Martinho, Santo António, São Roque, Nossa Senhora do Monte and Nossa Senhora das Neves each formed a centre of population and constituted “settled farmsteads” (*fazendas povoadas*) of some importance. They were soon turned into autonomous parishes or curacies and became the seats of new parishes. The parish of São Pedro had been created in 1566, but it was short-lived: it was abolished in 1579 and restored again in 1589.

before: Outside Funchal, Câmara de Lobos seems to have been the first parish created, in the year 1430, followed perhaps at the same time or shortly afterwards by that of Calheta. Both are considered older than Machico, even though Machico was the seat of a captaincy. Around 1440 the parishes of Ribeira Brava and Caniço were created, and after them those of Ponta do Sol and Santa Cruz. New parishes were carved out of all of these as the population spread out and climbed the mountains and ridges of the interior.

before: Common name of *Chrysanthemum pinnatifidum* and *C. dissectum*, shrubby Compositae of the Tubuliflorae, growing wild in Madeira. The first species is common in the north and the interior of the island; the second occurs only at Ponta do Pargo and Cabo Girão.

before: In the locality (*sítio*) of Quinta das Freiras, in the parish (*freguesia*) of Santo António, on the right bank of the stream of the same name, stands the chapel known as Nossa Senhora das Brotas. In trying to trace the origin of this name, which strikes us as so strange, we have been able, despite our best efforts, to arrive only at mere presumptions and conjectures, which may perhaps be very far from the truth. We first supposed that the name came not from the dedication or patron saint of the chapel but from the place where it had been built. Since there is a medicinal herb of that name, it is possible that the plant grew there and gave its name to the spot and later to the chapel. We then conjectured that, since the province of the Alentejo has a parish called Brotas, with a notable shrine dedicated to Nossa Senhora das Brotas, the chapel might perhaps have been given that name for reasons now unknown. Both hypotheses hold true in various parts of this island. It was common for the first colonists, who came from Portugal, to give the names of their home districts or favourite spots to many of the places where they settled here or held land by *sesmaria* (royal land grant to settlers on condition of cultivation).

before: In support of the first hypothesis, we must mention that in former times, and still at present, Our Lady of Brotas has been venerated under the dedication of Nossa Senhora da Luz. This leads us to presume that the name refers to the place and not to the patron saint of the chapel.

This leads us to presume that the name refers to the place and not to the patron saint of the chapel.

before: A locality (*sítio*) in the parish (*freguesia*) of Ponta do Sol, lying between the town (*vila*) and the parish of Tábua. It is one of the many *fajãs* formed along the coast by the collapse of the land that towered above them. ‘Since 1804 the *Logar de Baixo*,’ says the annotator of the *Saudades*, ‘has been much larger than before, because in that year a great part of the land of the *lombada* (long ridge between valleys) that overlooks it, split open by the storms of the preceding years, fell towards the sea and there formed a broad and productive plain. The shock of the fall was such that the sea rose above its level along the whole adjacent coast, and the tremor was felt both on land and at sea at a distance of more than ten kilometres: the sea came far inland into the town of Ponta do Sol.’ Lugar de Baixo formed part of the great estate of Lombada dos Esmeraldos (see that entry). However, when, on the death of João Esmeraldo, the property was divided anew between his two sons and his widow, Águeda de Abreu, she reserved the Lugar de Baixo property for herself as an integral part of her dowry. It is possible that on her death it reverted to the entailed estate (*morgadio*) of Santo Espírito; it is certain, at any rate, that it was incorporated into it at a date unknown to us. It was sold at public auction at about the same time as the Lombada, being bought by the English merchants A. Criorgi & C.ª. There stands the chapel of Santo António (St Anthony of Padua), with a fine house attached, which we shall discuss elsewhere in this work.

before: He was born in Funchal on 10 October 1844, the son of Manuel José Vieira and Dona Josefa Carolina do Nascimento Vieira. He attended the lyceum (state secondary school) of Funchal and the Medical-Surgical School (*Escola Médico-cirúrgica*), but did not complete the 1st-year course at the latter institution. He was a copying clerk and later secretary of the Municipal Administration (*Administração do Concelho*, the government’s local civil office) of Funchal. From a very early age he devoted himself to journalism: while still a student he contributed to the *Recreio* and the *Crepusculo*, and later to the *Fusão*, *Imprensa Livre*, *Povo*, *Diário Popular*, etc. He is a good poet, but his poems are either scattered through the old Funchal periodicals or were never printed, and are known only to a few friends. He was one of the authors of the *Guyaneida*, a mock-heroic poem to which we referred on page 670 of the 1st volume of this *Elucidário*.

before: When churchmen had their own separate jurisdiction, they also had their own prisons or special gaol, known as the ecclesiastical prison (*Aljube*). The old Aljube of Funchal stood in the area bounded by the Travessa da Sacristia, Rua de João Gago and Rua do Aljube. The post of gaoler (*aljubeiro*) of the Aljube of this city was created by King Sebastian by a royal decree (*alvará*) of 6 July 1562. The founding of the Aljube must date from this period or a little before it, and it was still in existence in 1834. During the political struggles between Miguelists and Constitutionalists, and at the time of the special tribunals that then came to this island, many priests were held in the Aljube because of their party sympathies, some of them being sent on to the Limoeiro and to the penal settlements of Africa.

before: There was a chapel of the same name in the parish of Ribeira Brava, founded by Francisco Fernandes and Brásia Fernandes in a year unknown to us. In the parish of Calheta, in the locality of Atouguia, there was also a chapel dedicated to Nossa Senhora da Boa Morte, which we have found mentioned somewhere under the name of Nossa Senhora da Piedade. Of this last chapel, built in 1661 and founded by Francisco Homem de Couto, not even traces remain today, but the locality where it stood is still called Boa Morte.

before: ‘It consists, says the *Dicionário Universal Portuguez Ilustrado*, already cited, of a lofty range of mountains from twelve hundred to nineteen hundred metres high, from whose back a number of peaks rise. It runs from east to west from Ponta de São Lourenço until it finally forks, extending north-westwards over Porto do Moniz to form Ponta do Tristão, and sending out a smaller branch to the south-west, whose tip is Ponta do Pargo. This longitudinal range, descending with its foothills and some secondary spurs to the north, west and south along its whole length down to the sea, divides the island into three great regions, namely: the northern, from Ponta de São Lourenço to Ponta do Tristão; the western, from Ponta do Tristão to Ponta do Pargo, which covers the territory within the said fork; and the southern, which runs from Ponta do Pargo to Ponta de São Lourenço. However, as the western region slopes towards the north-west and is already largely under the influence of the northern quarter, seafarers, and with them Madeirans in general, distinguish only two regions: one, which they call the South Coast, being the one marked out above on this side, and the other the North Coast, which comprises the northern and western regions mentioned’ (on these coasts, see what is said on p. 324 of vol. I).
after: ‘It consists, says the *Dicionário Universal Portuguez Ilustrado*, already cited, of a lofty range of mountains from twelve hundred to nineteen hundred metres high, from whose back a number of peaks rise. This longitudinal range, descending with its foothills and some secondary spurs to the north, west and south along its whole length down to the sea, divides the island into three great regions, namely: the northern, from Ponta de São Lourenço to Ponta do Tristão; the western, from Ponta do Tristão to Ponta do Pargo, which covers the territory within the said fork; and the southern, which runs from Ponta do Pargo to Ponta de São Lourenço. before: As already stated, the mountain range that crosses Madeira lengthwise from east to west, with high summits and without a break, clearly separates the northern and southern coasts. Along its back rise many peaks of considerable height, among which stand out Pico Ruivo, the highest of all, Pico do Cidrão, Torrinhas, Canário and Arieiro. Besides those already named, we shall mention the best known: Pico do Castanho, Pico da Maia, Pico do Arco de São Jorge, Pico das Torres, Pico da Neve, Pico do Poiso, Pico da Lagoa, Pico de Santo António, Pico do Arrebentão, Pico do Infante, Pico Grande, Pico dos Bodes, Pico da Urze, Pico do Gato, Pico da Amendoeira, Pico Queimado, Pico da Suna, etc. As offshoots of the mountains and peaks of the central range, many other heights also stand out, sometimes extending as far as the coastal areas. Among these we shall mention Pico dos Barcelos, Pico da Cruz, Pico do Cardo, Pico dos Eirós, Pico do Facho, Pico das Favas, Pico da Cruz, Pico da Relva, etc. (see each of these entries).

before: The mountainous and extremely rugged terrain of this island gives rise to many valleys, some of remarkable depth, though in general they are of fairly limited length. The principal ones are the valley of Funchal, especially at the locality called Val Formoso; that of Machico, which stretches from the beach of the town (*vila*) of the same name between the banks of its stream; that of Jardim da Serra, at the northern end of the parish of Estreito de Câmara de Lobos; that of São Vicente, lying in the drainage basin of the stream of the same name and including the town and its surroundings; that of Penha de Águia, which curves round the cliff of that name (see Penha de Águia); that of Metade, near Ribeiro Frio; and that of Ribeira da Janela, between the banks of the stream of that name (see Valleys). The articles Fajãs and Quebradas are related to this subject.

before: large or medium-sized, sometimes reddish, cobwebby on the lower surface or covered here and there with floccose hairs, less tomentose or glabrous on the upper surface; all the lobes, or only the upper ones, clearly visible and pointed; middle lobe almost always larger than the lateral ones; teeth unequal, triangular or triangular-lanceolate, acute; petiolar sinus more or less open; upper lateral sinuses open or closed; bunches generally not exceeding 20 centimetres, cylindrical or cylindrical-conical, more or less dense, winged or not; berries slightly unequal, 12–18 millimetres, firm, sweet when ripe, globose, with pale or violet pulp and a fairly tough skin; pedicels regular. The stock is vigorous, with light-brown canes, sometimes striped; internodes elongated. before: The formal inauguration of the Sociedade Agrícola Madeirense took place on 21 November 1849, attended by Prince Maximilian, Duke of Leuchtenberg, and by all the authorities and most prominent figures of our community. before: Diocesan constitutions are the laws and instructions peculiar to each diocese, intended to implement and regulate the general laws of the Church. The bishopric of Funchal also has its Constitutions, very old and entirely obsolete, which today have merely historical value. Copies are rare nowadays, but they are highly prized for the study of the religious customs of the time when these Constitutions were drawn up. The first edition is entitled *Constituiçôes Synodaes do Bispado do Funchal. Feitas e ordenadas por D. Jeronimo Barreto, Bispo do dito Bispado*, Lisboa, por Antonio Ribeiro, 1585, folio, XVI-188 pp. They were drawn up at the diocesan council held in our Cathedral (Sé Catedral) on 13 October 1578, under the presidency of Bishop Dom Jerónimo Barreto, and were approved and ordered to be put into effect by a decree (*alvará*) of the same prelate, dated 4 May 1579.

before: In the locality of Atalaia, in the parish (*freguesia*) of Caniço, and roughly equidistant from Ponta da Oliveira and Ponta do Guindaste, lies the projection of coast or headland called Ponta da Atalaia. It overlooks a small landing place, Porto da Atalaia, of the same name.
