before: If we accept the opinion of T. V. Wollaston, the most recent of the authors to have dealt with the subject at length, there are 176 species, of which 131, counting only the land species, are peculiar to these islands.
after: If we accept the opinion of Thomas Vernon Wollaston, the most recent of the authors to have dealt with the subject at length, there are 176 species, of which 131, counting only the land species, are peculiar to these islands.

before: Many of the Madeiran pulmonates have been observed in the sub-fossil state in prodigious quantities, their dense aggregation sometimes giving them the appearance of conglomerates. The deposits of these fossils consist either of calcareous sand, sometimes compacted as if it were sandstone, or of clay mixed with angular stones; in the latter case they are clastic rocks or transported ground, almost always formed on the flanks of certain hills. Such deposits exist on Madeira, east of Caniçal; on the summit of Bugio, one of the Desertas; and on Porto Santo at various places, such as Ilhéu de Baixo, Ilhote, Vigia da Ponta, Campo de Baixo, Ribeiro da Vigia, Penedo, Mornos and Zimbral da Areia.

before: Of the 176 species of pulmonates – a figure established according to Wollaston’s criteria, as already stated – 82 have been found in the fossil state, and of these only 12 have not been observed living, so they may be considered extinct. *Helix Lowei*, peculiar to Porto Santo and the largest of all the snails of the archipelago, measuring 5 centimetres or more in diameter, was long considered extinct. However, the botanist J. M. Moniz succeeded in discovering a living specimen on the rocks of Ilhéu de Cima, and the English naturalist Dr Alfred Merle Norman obtained from a shell dealer in Frankfurt a recent, well-preserved specimen which had evidently left these islands by unknown means and ended up in the German dealer’s shop.

before: In Curral das Freiras and other valleys of the interior of Madeira there are a great number of dykes, and at Cabo Girão there are both vertical and horizontal dykes.

before: Dykes sometimes taper to a point at the top. There are also some, such as the one at the hillock of Piedade on the Ponta de São Lourenço, that are cut off or intercepted at the base by horizontal strata.

before: The basalt dyke that forms a knoll (*cabeço*) or nipple at the top of Garajau can be made out on either side of this cape, and is double on its eastern side. There are also double dykes at Ribeiro Frio, on the seaward side of Penha de Águia and elsewhere, which probably result from a fresh penetration of lava into the same fissures.
after: The basalt dyke that forms a knoll (*cabeço*) or nipple at the top of Garajau (‘tern’) can be made out on either side of this cape, and is double on its eastern side. before: Some dykes stand isolated because the surrounding ground has been destroyed by denudation. The peaks of Empinos, near Curral, are formed of isolated dykes, and at Ribeiro do Juncal, at the head of the Ribeira da Metade, there is a dyke in the same condition, about 45 metres high and 18 wide.

before: It is supposed that in most of Madeira’s dykes the molten material was forced upwards from below. In the Piedade dyke already mentioned, however, and in another at Ribeiro dos Piornais, between Caniço and Funchal, the opposite seems to have occurred, since both are interrupted or cut off at the base.

before: Varadouros was the name given, on the beach of Funchal, to the principal point for the embarkation and landing of passengers and goods, and to the spot set aside for hauling small boats ashore. This stretch of beach must have corresponded roughly to the space occupied by the present capstans, from the waterline up to the street that today lies above them. Nearby stood the small chapel of Nossa Senhora (Our Lady), which we believe had the Assumption of the Virgin as its patron saint (*orago*), and which took the name Varadouros from its position. After the chapels of Santa Catarina (St Catherine of Alexandria), São Sebastião (St Sebastian) and São Paulo (St Paul the Apostle), it was among the oldest in Funchal.
after: Varadouros (‘slipways’) was the name given, on the beach of Funchal, to the principal point for the embarkation and landing of passengers and goods, and to the spot set aside for hauling small boats ashore. before: While his father was still alive, and when he was in the Kingdom (*reino*, i.e. mainland Portugal), John II asked him to relieve the stronghold of Arzila. He responded promptly with a force of three hundred men, armed, equipped and maintained at his own expense during the six months they remained in Africa. Another important relief was the one he gave to Diogo de Azambuja, governor of Safi, who, after taking that stronghold, found himself in imminent danger of losing it. When Azambuja turned to Simão Gonçalves, the latter sent him three hundred armed men within three days, and shortly afterwards went in person at the head of another nine hundred, whom he maintained and provisioned during the three months they stayed there. The help he gave in the capture of Azemmour was also considerable. For this great expedition, commanded by Jaime, Duke of Braganza, Simão Gonçalves sent his son João Gonçalves da Câmara with 600 foot soldiers and 200 horsemen. Among them was a large number of Madeiran noblemen, who were among those who most distinguished themselves in the celebrated capture of Azemmour.

before: We would go too far if we tried to describe in detail the various battles in which Simão Gonçalves da Câmara fought on the fields of Morocco, and the great deeds of bravery and heroism he performed there. Frutuoso and several other chroniclers recount some of these glorious actions minutely. We shall say only that at Safi, Azemmour, Arzila, Castelo Real, Cabo de Gué, Mazagan, Ceuta and Tangier he always boldly showed the strength of his arm and the unbreakable courage of his spirit.

We shall say only that at Safi, Azemmour, Asilah, Castelo Real, Cape Ghir, Mazagan, Ceuta and Tangier he always boldly showed the strength of his arm and the unbreakable courage of his spirit.

before: Among the displays of pomp and grandeur that adorned the ostentatious life of Simão Gonçalves, one stands out, not so much for its intrinsic value as for its singular originality: the gift he made to Pope Leo X. This illustrious pontiff, who gave his name to his century, had as his private secretary Bishop Dom Manuel de Noronha, son of Simão Gonçalves da Câmara, who enjoyed great prestige and influence in Rome. The offering could be regarded as an embassy, and it was presented to the pontiff by Dom Manuel de Noronha. The ambassador, or bearer of the gift, was a Madeiran *fidalgo* (nobleman of the lesser nobility) named João de Leiria. He was accompanied by Vicente Martins, a canon of Funchal Cathedral (*Sé*), who, being deeply versed in Latin, delivered a brilliant oration in that language in the presence of the great pontiff. Other persons, and many servants dressed in the Portuguese fashion in black velvet, made up this remarkable retinue.

before: When the king sent the *corregedor* (royal district magistrate) Diogo Taveira to Madeira to investigate certain irregularities committed in the government of the captaincy, Simão Gonçalves da Câmara considered himself gravely injured in the privileges and exemptions he enjoyed as donatary of Funchal. He resolved to leave the country and settle in Spain. Forced by the hazards of the voyage to put in at the Algarve, he learned there of the perilous straits in which our African stronghold of Arzila found itself, and at once went to its relief, compelling the besiegers to raise the siege. This episode, set out in great detail, provided the subject of one of the chapters of the interesting book by Inácio de Vilhena Barbosa entitled

before: Feeling old and weary, Simão Gonçalves gave up the government of his captaincy, which passed to his son and successor João Gonçalves da Câmara, and retired to the *lugar* (settlement ranking between a town and a parish) of Matosinhos, near Porto. There he died at the beginning of 1530, having directed in his will that his mortal remains be taken to this island and laid in Santa Clara, in the family vault of his parents and grandparents. ‘Not many years passed, says an old book of Madeiran historical matters, before this clause of his will was fulfilled, and when the coffin with his bones was landed in Funchal, a most solemn funeral procession was made for him from the beach to the said Convent, accompanied by the cathedral chapter of canons, the clergy and the religious who were in the land, and his obsequies were held with the greatest solemnity, the whole people accompanying and attending with many tears, for he was much loved by all.

before: After the São Lourenço lighthouse (*Farol de São Lourenço*), the building of a lighthouse on the island of Porto Santo was always recognised as the first and most urgent need. The lack of lighting on those coasts caused several disasters, with loss of lives and vessels, which are recorded in the Annals of that island. Some studies were carried out and projects and estimates drawn up, but it was only forty years after the São Lourenço lighthouse began operating that the lighthouse on the neighbouring island of Porto Santo began to light those waters, over a radius of eleven miles. The site chosen was a small islet known as Ilhéu de Cima, separated from the island of Porto Santo by a narrow and short channel. The lantern stands 118 metres above sea level. It was a fixed white light, visible at a distance of 11 miles. It began operating in 1901. It has rendered valuable service to shipping, and especially to vessels making for the port of Funchal.

before: Gago Coutinho and Sacadura Cabral were given an imposing reception in Funchal on their return to Europe aboard the steamer *Porto*, after their daring flight to Brazil. They landed at the Pontinha quay at 10.30 a.m. on 21 October 1922, amid the liveliest and most spontaneous displays of enthusiasm. They then went to the Palace of São Lourenço, accompanied by various dignitaries, where the head of the district once again offered them his greetings of welcome. Afterwards they went to the town hall, where they received the diplomas conferring on them the freedom of Funchal, and then left for the Cathedral, where they attended a solemn Te Deum presided over by the diocesan prelate, who delivered an excellent patriotic address.

before: Work on the fortifications began only in the reign of Manuel I, with the bastion and tower being started. The new contributions levied in the reign of John III, especially the meat levy (*imposição das carnes*), gave it fresh impetus. The defence plan was later modified in 1572. It ordered that a fortress with three bastions be built, that the houses standing in its way be demolished, and that the balconies on the frontage facing the pebble beach (calhau) be cut back. There the city walls were to be built with five gates: two to the south, facing the sea, one to the east and two to the west. The walls were to run between the Ribeira de João Gomes and the Ribeira de São Francisco (today the Ribeira de São João), abutting on the hills of Pena and Pico dos Frias.

before: The corsair attack on the city in 1566, made by way of Praia Formosa, turned attention to the defence of the coast. Entrenchments were built at points commanding the sea, on the rocks overlooking the settlements; these were called *fortes roqueiros* (rock forts) and were placed under the watch and supervision of the captain-corporals, ‘& os portos se empossebillytaram asy & da maneyra que se fez de camara dellobos atee a cidade’ (and the landing places were made impassable in this way and manner, as was done from Câmara de Lobos to the city).

before: Under Philippine rule (Spanish Habsburg rule over Portugal, 1580–1640) the rules of defence were changed to follow the polygonal layout. The forts of São Tiago (St James the Greater), São Felipe, Loures and Penha de França were completed, and work began on the Pico fortress (*Fortaleza do Pico*) in Funchal, on São Roque in Machico and on the Castelo do Pico on the island of Porto Santo.

before: ‘Because of old and widespread customs, the adoption of the new legal system of weights and measures met with stubborn resistance everywhere. In this archipelago, too, there were several riots in violent opposition to the system, which profoundly altered what had been practised for centuries in all kinds of commercial transactions. In the municipality (*concelho*) of São Vicente the rioters forced the authorities and the most prominent people to throw the weights and measures of the new system into the sea, and the same happened in the parish of Ribeira Brava; in Ponta do Sol the people set fire to the town hall. before: A tree of the family Rhamnaceae with ovate or ovate-oblong serrated leaves, usually bearing 2 to 4 small glands or projections on the lower part of the upper surface. before: Leaves medium-sized, cottony on the underside, sub-glabrous or pubescent on the upper side, with the 3 upper lobes clearly visible, sometimes acuminate, the lower ones usually poorly defined; teeth unequal, generally sub-obtuse, less often acute; petiolar sinus closed or slightly open; upper lateral sinuses often barely visible because the lobes overlap; bunches large, strongly winged, dense; berries almost always elliptical, 15–22 millimetres, firm, greenish-yellow, turning golden when ripe, very sweet. before: When an extraordinary event stirs the soul of the people and drives it to give noisy expression to the feelings that possess it, the spontaneous, rough poetic inspiration of the common people at once makes itself felt. Artless lyres then appear, singing in laboured laments or lashing out in fiery songs of indignation at the events that provoked this passion and at the circumstances that gave it weight and prominence in the heated minds of the crowds. This has been observed here more than once, but it showed itself in a truly remarkable way at the time of the so-called Plague of the Lazaretto, to which we have already alluded on p. 224 of volume II and on p. 77 of this volume. Popular poetry – simple, artless and incorrect, but spontaneous, vehement and passionate – poured out in a profusion of compositions which, printed as small pamphlets and loose sheets, were bought and eagerly read by people of every social class. The fever of poetic inspiration set many imaginations alight, and the fertility of these verse productions was truly astonishing: the presses could not keep up with the multitude of poems written at that time.

The 1st Viscount of Torre Bela was Fernando José Correia Brandão Bettencourt de Noronha Henriques, son of the holder of the entail (*morgado*) António João Correia Brandão Bettencourt Noronha Henriques and of Dona Ana Rosa de Vilhena. He was born on this island on 21 February 1768 and died in the city of Naples on 31 October 1821. He followed a diplomatic career and served as our country’s envoy extraordinary and minister plenipotentiary in Hamburg, Stockholm, Berlin, Vienna and Naples. He was colonel of the Calheta regiment, Councillor (conselheiro, honorary title of the royal council) to John VI and commander of the Order of the Tower and Sword. He came of noble ancestry and represented the ancient house founded by João Afonso, a companion of Zargo, who held extensive lands on this island as a *sesmaria* (royal land grant to settlers on condition of cultivation) and served here as *almoxarife* (royal revenue officer and storekeeper) to Prince Henry the Navigator. Sanches de Baena states that the Viscount of Torre Bela was the 5th-generation grandson of António Correia Bettencourt and his wife Dona Joana Henriques, who were lords of Alcáçovas and descended from King Henry II of Castile.

before: This is the name by which we know the islet that lies at the western end of the harbour of Funchal and that today (1921) forms one of the limits of the Pontinha mole (breakwater), or harbour of refuge. before: Referring to the first exploration along the coast, made by the discoverers, Gaspar Frutuoso says: ‘at the end of which (the valley of Funchal) there are two islets, where they went to shelter because it was already late’. Anyone who knows the place is aware that the two small islets lay a short distance from each other.

before: Hail is almost unknown on Porto Santo. Nevertheless, on 4 February 1860 it fell on that island in such abundance that the hills and valleys were covered with it. ‘In the town (*vila*) there was so much of it’, say the *Anais do Porto Santo*, ‘that many people filled plates and tubs, and even made sorbet; a thing unheard of among these people’. In our climate hail appears only from the end of autumn to the beginning of spring, and it contributes notably to increasing the volume of water in the springs and streams. It is said that nearly 60 years ago a hailstorm caused great damage to the crops of the parish (*freguesia*) of Caniçal, and it is also recorded that some years ago hail destroyed a good part of the foliage of the fruit trees and other plants in the parish of Canhas. Fortunately, however, such cases are so rare that the Madeiran farmer, when cultivating his land, does not even think of this enemy, so much to be feared in more northerly latitudes.

before: Guilherme Teles de Meneses, who made some meteorological observations at the station on the Pico do Arieiro (1700 metres), saw the thermometer there register 2 degrees below zero in November. It is therefore reasonable to suppose that still lower temperatures occur at the same spot in January and February, which in Madeira are the coldest months of the year. In the opinion of the late English naturalist James Yate Johnson, the limit of perpetual snow at the latitude of Madeira must lie at 3,450 metres, an altitude that our Pico Ruivo does not even approach…

before: Under this heading we give a brief account of the quays, coves, landing places, beaches, shoals, islets and streams of this island. On the southern coast of Porto Santo, running almost the whole length of the island, lies the bay of the same name. It is bounded by the Ilhéu de Cima, or Lighthouse Islet, to the east, and the Ilhéu de Baixo, or Lime Islet, to the west, and measures about four nautical miles between these two points. It forms a fairly spacious harbour and offers easy anchorage to ships of every tonnage. For most of its length the bay is edged by a most beautiful beach of fine yellow sand, free of any reefs or rocks, quite wide and approximately nine kilometres long, which is without doubt one of the finest beaches in the whole of our country. Gently sloping, washed by a sea that is always calm and crystal-clear, and free of marshes or stagnant water, this beach meets every requirement of an excellent seaside resort. The harbour of the town of Porto Santo is today served by a pier, which has proved very useful for the passengers who land there.

before: Lying next to the island of Porto Santo and very close to its coast are the ‘Ilhéu de Baixo’, or Ilhéu da Cal, and the ‘Ilhéu de Cima’, or Ilhéu do Farol. These are the largest and most important islets in the whole archipelago, and they have already been described on pp. 116 and 272 of volume I and in the article Faróis. Mention should also be made of the small islets of ‘Fora’, or ‘Rocha Nordeste’, of ‘Fonte da Areia’ and of ‘Ferro’. Compared with the long, abundant streams of Madeira, the small watercourses that cross the neighbouring island of Porto Santo do not deserve that name. The most important of them is the so-called Ribeira da Vila, which stays dry for most of the year and carries a small flow in the winter season, running into the ocean at the locality (*sítio*) of Vila. Other small brooks worth mentioning are those of Pedregal de Fora, Pedregal de Dentro and Perregil, to the north; those of Serra de Fora and Serra de Dentro, to the east; those of Santo António, Fontinha, Cochino and Salgado, to the south; and the Ribeiro Fundo, to the west.
after: Lying next to the island of Porto Santo and very close to its coast are the ‘Ilhéu de Baixo’, or Ilhéu da Cal, and the ‘Ilhéu de Cima’, or Ilhéu do Farol. These are the largest and most important islets in the whole archipelago, and they have already been described on pp. 116 and 272 of volume I and in the article Faróis (‘lighthouses’). before: Minister of the Colonies of the French Republic. He arrived in Madeira aboard the cruiser *Gueydon* on 17 October 1921 and landed at about 2 p.m., having been greeted on board by the civil governor, the harbour master and the military commander. The due military honours were paid to him at the quay, after which he went on to the Palácio de São Lourenço (St Lawrence Palace), where he was received by the civil governor and the secretary-general (*secretário geral*). Accompanied by the civil and military authorities, he visited the Angústias cemetery and laid a wreath with a dedication on the tomb-monument of the sailors of the *Surprise*, who died when that ship was torpedoed inside the bay of Funchal. before: The oldest document concerning this parish, cited in the *Indice Geral do Registo da Provedoria*, is the royal decree (alvará régio) of 5 December 1580, which fixed the vicar’s annual salary at 24,756 *réis* (old Portuguese money of account; 1$000 = 1,000 réis, 1:000$000 = one conto = 1,000,000 réis). The royal decree of 9 July 1590 raised this to 15,000 *réis* in cash, 4 *moios* of wheat and 2 *pipas* (wine cask and measure, c. 400–500 litres) of wine. A further 3,000 *réis* a year was added in 1600. The earliest parish priest known from the parish archive is Friar Hercules da Cunha, a native of Calheta, who was already serving there in 1538. He was succeeded by João Drumond; around 1597 by the licentiate Belchior Rebelo (1604); then Francisco Duarte Morais (1622), António da Rocha (1637), Henrique Madureira de Figueiredo (1650), Tristão de Mendonça Vasconcelos (1674), Manuel Ferreira Teixeira (1687), the licentiate António Ferreira de Andrade (1693) and Estêvão Lomelino de Vasconcelos (1709).

before: The parish had its seat in a small chapel built there in the very first days of the colonisation, whose dedication was probably São Salvador, the present patron saint of the parish church. An old nobiliary tells us that this church was built in 1533 under the direction of João de Freitas (volume II, page 54), a nobleman of the Royal Household (*fidalgo da Casa Real*). By a warrant (*provisão*) of 29 September of that year the king made him a royal grant of the chancel as a family vault for himself and his family, in recognition of the expense and labour the building had cost him. The church has undergone various repairs and restorations, and some have suggested that the side aisles are not part of the original building, which seems to us hardly admissible. It is the largest church outside Funchal and has three aisles, although one reads elsewhere that they are not three clearly defined aisles. It is in a fair state of repair and, says the annotator of the *Saudades*, contains ‘besides the altars, three further chapels, namely: the chancel, which the king granted to João de Freitas for his services, and especially for having given the land for the church and overseen its building; the chapel of São Tiago, now of the Santíssimo Sacramento, founded by João de Morais; and that of the Almas, belonging to the Pereiras, who came from Porto Santo’.

before: Several members of the family of João de Freitas distinguished themselves heroically in our campaigns in Africa and Asia. The following passages, which we found in an old document, bear on the subject of this article: ‘Jordão de Freitas, whose deeds the historians of Asia describe at length, was born in the town (*vila*) of Santa Cruz and was captain of Moluco, lord of the islands of Amboina and Siam by grant of Dom Manuel, King of Ternate, in the year 1537, confirmed by King John III in the year 1543. Gonçalo de Freitas da Silva, his son and a native of the same town, served valiantly in India, where he held the same lordship, confirmed by King Sebastian in the year 1574. Jordão de Freitas da Silva, son of the latter, was sent as ambassador to France concerning the recovery of the artillery and other property of the fleet that was lost there in the year 1626; he died while pursuing this claim, and for this service his son Gonçalo de Freitas received the commandery of Santa Maria de Lisboa in the Order of Christ.’

before: He was the 3rd Bishop of Funchal and one of the most illustrious prelates of his time. The contemporary Madeiran chronicles tell us nothing worth mentioning about this head of the Funchal church, because he never came to his bishopric, owing to the high offices he held in mainland Portugal, such as professor at the University of Coimbra, president of the Board of Conscience and Orders (*Mesa da Consciência e Ordens*), theologian of John III at the famous Council of Trent, etc. He was one of the most learned Portuguese of his age and left many printed works, almost all written in Latin.

before: Sugar cane was introduced to Madeira, it seems, in 1425. The first cuttings of the plant, which are said to have come from Sicily on the orders of Prince Henry the Navigator, were planted in the Campo do Duque, the ground in the city of Funchal now occupied by the Cathedral (the Sé), its churchyard and open square, the Largo da Sé, the Rua do Aljube and the Largo do Comércio, formerly Largo de São Sebastião. From the Campo do Duque the cane passed to Machico, where its cultivation prospered so greatly that it yielded thirteen *arrobas* of sugar, which was the first sugar sold on the island.
after: Sugar cane was introduced to Madeira, it seems, in 1425. before: Cane cultivation prospered and expanded in Madeira until the middle of the 16th century, when the island came to produce 300,000 *arrobas* of sugar. By 1590, however, when Gaspar Frutuoso wrote the *Saudades da Terra*, the once flourishing sugar industry was already tending to decline, owing to the influx of sugar from Brazil and the Spanish colonies into European markets, although valuable plantations of the grass still existed here.

before: The illustrious annotator of the *Saudades da Terra* gives the year 1748 as marking the end of the sugar period on this island. before: Bowdich, who was in Madeira in 1823, says that an insignificant quantity of sugar was made here, and the author of *Rambles in Madeira*, who visited us in 1826, says much the same about this product, adding that there was then only one mill for crushing sugar cane on the whole island. before: Then came the sugar factories: that of Ferraz Irmãos, begun some years earlier, and that of William Hinton & Son, both in Funchal, and that of Ferreira Nogueira in São Martinho, all in 1856; in 1858, that of Ornelas Frazão in Santa Cruz; in 1859, that of Joaquim da Silva in Funchal; between then and 1866, that of Diogo Frazão in Arco da Calheta and that of Wilbraham in Ponta do Sol; and lastly the great São João factory, some of the last seven also making spirit.’

before: The price of cane has varied considerably in Madeira. In 1872 the Companhia Fabril de Assucar Madeirense paid 55 centavos for every 30 kilograms of cane of 9 to 10 degrees Baumé, 60 for cane of 10 to 11 degrees and 65 for cane of over 11 degrees. These prices did not last long, however: as soon as the enemies of the São João factory succeeded in destroying it, the price of the product fell quite markedly. In 1881 the Torreão factory paid 45 centavos for cane, but this price, which was still profitable, did not hold either, and shortly afterwards the canefields disappeared because of the disease we have already mentioned. Around 1862 the factories paid 30 centavos for cane; later they sometimes paid 32 and 35 centavos. Finally came the decree of 30 December 1895, which set prices of 40 to 45 centavos per 30 kilograms for the product, and the decree of 24 September 1903, by which Madeira obtained a further 5 centavos on the minimum cane prices, an increase that the decree of 18 March 1911 left unchanged.

before: ‘The oldest document relating to the sugar industry in the archive of the Funchal Council dates from 1562, as can be seen from the notes to the *Saudades da Terra*, and it shows that the first advances of this industry in Madeira date from that time: it authorises the building of the first water-driven mill for making sugar that existed here, and its wording makes clear that before it there was no other here, powered by any means whatsoever. Until that time, therefore, sugar production could only have been scanty and a purely domestic activity.’

before: In the offprint of the *Comunicações da Comissão de Trabalhos Geológicos*, vol. II, fasc. II, a study was published with the following title: *Noticia de alguns fosseis terciarios do archipelago da Madeira* by J. C. Berkeley Cotter, accompanied by another note on some fossil land molluscs of the same archipelago by Alberto A. Girard. The preface to this work reads as follows: ‘The materials submitted for our examination are not sufficient to determine precisely the subdivision of the stratigraphic system to which the deposits containing them belong; but they serve, we believe, to confirm in general the conclusions reached by the learned Zurich professor (Karl Mayer) that the fossiliferous strata of the island of Porto Santo and neighbouring islands, which Bowdich had already identified as Tertiary in 1823, belong to the Helvetian stage, though the possibility should not be excluded that part of these deposits belongs to the Tortonian, or higher stage of the Miocene system.’ The materials mentioned in the passage of the preface quoted above were supplied by the Revd Father Ernesto Schmitz, then a professor at the Funchal Seminary (*Seminário do Funchal*). Berkeley died in December 1919.

before: As described in earlier entries, there were four friaries of the Seraphic or Franciscan order in Madeira: São Francisco (St Francis of Assisi) of Funchal, São Francisco of Calheta, Nossa Senhora da Piedade (Our Lady of Pity) of Santa Cruz, and Nossa Senhora da Porciúncula (Our Lady of the Angels of the Portiuncula) of Ribeira Brava. before: The parish (*freguesia*) of Santo António da Serra, or Santo da Serra as it is more commonly known, lies largely on a plateau overlooking the parishes of Santa Cruz and Machico, at an average altitude of 700 metres above sea level. It is considered one of the most beautiful and enchanting resorts on this island. Although its winter season brings frequent rain and wind and marked drops in temperature, it is much sought after in the hot season for the freshness and mildness of its climate, together with the striking beauty of its admirable landscape. There are some excellent country houses there, where several families, especially from Santa Cruz and Machico, usually spend the hottest months of the year. In former times it was much visited by the English, who built several *quintas* here that still exist.

before: ‘Gil de Carvalho,’ says Father Fernando Augusto de Pontes, ‘originally built two chapels there. The first he never finished, at Alcoforado, the locality where he lived, which still bears the name Ermida. The second occupies the parish seat of this village.’ The same priest states, in his book *Excursões*, that Gil de Carvalho died in Santa Cruz in 1541, which would place the building of the chapels at an earlier date, for we are of the opinion that this construction would not have predated the last quarter of the 16th century. The one that was turned into the parish church already existed in 1612, since a royal decree (alvará régio) of 3 September of that year ordered the sum of 70,000 *réis* (old Portuguese money of account; 1$000 = 1,000 réis, 1:000$000 = one conto = 1,000,000 réis) to be applied to the purchase of an altarpiece for that chapel. It may be supposed that by this time a population centre of some importance already existed there. This chapel had its own chaplain, and in 1790 he was permitted to administer the last sacraments in sudden cases.

before: The illustrious annotator of the *Saudades* writes: ‘The parish (*freguesia*) of Santo da Serra was originally an old chapel subordinate to the vicar of Machico. Because he and the vicars of Santa Cruz and Água de Pena fiercely disputed possession of this chapel, Bishop Dom Friar Lourenço de Távora took it under his protection in 1612 and probably made it a curacy (*curato*). As time went on these disputes over jurisdiction continued, and later the same struggles broke out again over the boundaries of the municipalities of Santa Cruz and Machico. It was certainly from that period, that is, in the first quarter of the 17th century, that the chapel of Santo António da Serra came under the direct jurisdiction of the bishop, and that this prelate took under emphyteutic lease (*aforamento*, perpetual lease for an annual quit-rent) the lands surrounding the chapel, which were always regarded as belonging to the mitre of Funchal. By special concession of the diocesan bishops, these lands were later made available to the parish priests as part of their glebe (*passal*). The curacy, however, was only created in 1813. It was made up of the localities (*sítios*) of Preces, Ermida, Margaça and Madeira da Igreja, belonging to the parish of Machico; the localities of Mouro, Ameixieiras, João Ferino, Curral Velho, Ribeiro de João Gonçalves and Madre de Água, in the parish of Santa Cruz; and the locality of Achada do Barro, in the parish of Água de Pena.’

before: This was one of the parishes in which the Protestant proselytism begun and carried on by Dr Robert Kalley (volume II, page 208) put down the deepest roots and brought the greatest disturbance into the midst of Madeira’s peaceful population. Public order was disturbed here in 1844. Many arrests were made, inquiries and investigations were held in the seats of the municipalities of Santa Cruz and Machico, and various proceedings were brought against the rioters and some apostles of the new doctrines. The propagandists have not forgotten the original Calvinist evangelisation and have kept up their proselytising to the present day, though without appreciable results. It was Dr Kalley himself who, in this parish, at the *quinta* (country estate) of Serrado das Ameixieiras, led a large number of people to follow Calvinist ideas through his rare and overwhelming eloquence. We have already referred above to the striking landscape of this parish and the captivating panoramas to be enjoyed there, above all at the localities of Lamaceiros, Portela and Macelas. Father Fernando de Pontes, already cited, says: ‘At Portela, the parish of Porto da Cruz lies at the spectator’s feet. At Lamaceiros there is not only the view of Porto da Cruz and Penha de Águia, but also part of Faial and Santana, wrapped in the luxuriance of an opulent vegetation. At Macelas, there are the green-clad heights of the hills to the north, an immense expanse of verdure and countless cottages beneath one’s eyes; in the centre a stream winding and slipping away like ribbons of silver; down below, the gleaming white of many houses beside a church; further on, the wave breaking against the cliff; beyond, the sombre majesty of the cliffs of São Lourenço gazing at themselves in the sleeping waters, and the vastness of the ocean at the end...’.

before: Prostitution already existed in Madeira in the 15th century, as is clearly shown by various old decrees and by a petition addressed to the Municipal Council (*Câmara Municipal*) of Funchal on 8 October 1495. This asked that the brothel quarter ‘be removed from beside the sea, because the men from outside went ashore with the harlots, caused disturbances and took refuge in the boats, and the law did not arrest them’. The *mancebia* was the place set aside for prostitutes to live.

before: We do not know when syphilis appeared in Madeira, but it is reasonable to suppose that this dreadful disease was already known here at the end of the 15th century or the beginning of the 16th. If the sailors of the ships that called at our port ‘went ashore with the harlots’ and withdrew to their boats without the police being able to arrest them, nothing could be more natural than to accept the contagion and spread of an illness that, even in those times, was known and feared in Europe. Dr Sloane, who visited this island in October 1687, found syphilitic symptoms in some of the people who consulted him.

before: In the article devoted to the Angústias cemetery, we stated that in 1662 Daniel da Costa Quintal founded, on land belonging to his entailed estate (*morgadio*), the chapel of Nossa Senhora das Angústias (Our Lady of Sorrows), which gave its name to the street running nearby and also to the localities around it. As we have also already noted, we cannot now say for certain whether the chapel of Nossa Senhora das Angústias that stands on the *quinta* (country estate) of the same name (Lambert) is a reconstruction of the old chapel of the same dedication, or whether Daniel da Costa Quintal’s property might have been located there. We are inclined to think so. When the Quinta das Angústias passed into the possession of Nicolau Hemiterio de la Tuelière, and later into that of the Count of Lambert, the house, the chapel and the adjoining grounds were greatly improved, and it became one of the most pleasant and comfortable residences in Funchal. Queen Adelaide of England (see that entry) lived on this *quinta* from 3 November 1847 to 11 April 1848, and the Duke of Leuchtenberg (see that entry) also lived there from 27 August 1849 to 23 April 1850. The widowed Empress of Brazil, Empress Amélie (see that entry), accompanied by her daughter Princess Maria Amélia (see that entry), took up residence there on 28 August 1852. The ill-fated princess died in this house on 4 February 1853. Three months later, on 6 May, the coffin containing the princess’s mortal remains left the chapel of the *quinta*, followed by the empress, and was taken on board at the Cais da Pontinha.

before: The municipalities of Funchal and Câmara de Lobos have the largest wine production, followed by those of São Vicente, Porto do Moniz, Porto Santo and Calheta. It is on the southern coast of Madeira that the vines are found which supply the raw material for the fortified wines of worldwide reputation, and the parish (*freguesia*) of Câmara de Lobos deserves special mention as the place where the finest musts of the archipelago are produced. The principal and most celebrated varieties grown were Sercial (white grape variety), Malmsey, Boal and Verdelho, from which specialised types of wine were made; the first two, once aged, were the most precious kinds of fortified wine in the whole world. With the phylloxera invasion, new resistant rootstocks were introduced onto which the old varieties were grafted, but the specialised selection for making the different kinds has been maintained only on a very limited scale.

before: Bugio is one of the three Desertas and one of the five islands that make up the Madeira archipelago. According to the *Dic. Univ. Port.* II, its name derives from its resemblance to the monkey known by that name. It is five miles, or a little over nine kilometres, long and half a mile, or 926 metres, across at its widest point. To the south it ends at Ponta da Agulha, one of the extreme points of the archipelago. The island is made up of high rocks and is almost inaccessible, but it has good pasture. The highest peak on Bugio stands 411 metres above sea level.

before: The secretary to the government of this archipelago, Joaquim Pedro Cardoso Casado Giraldes (see that entry), published in Paris, in the first quarter of the 19th century, in Portuguese and French, an *Estatística Historico-Geographica das Ilhas da Madeira e Porto Santo*. It contains the list of the donataries of Funchal and governors of Madeira, with the designation of the decrees of their appointment, their taking of office and the duration of their governments. The list runs from the discoverer João Gonçalves Zarco to the governor and captain-general Florencio José de Melo, who began to administer this archipelago in April 1815. The French and Portuguese editions of this *Estatística*, which differ from each other in the nature of their information, are, despite their shortcomings, an extremely valuable and almost unique document for drawing up the list of the governors of Madeira. They served as the main basis for the list that Dr Álvaro Rodrigues de Azevedo published in the notes to the *Saudades da Terra* in 1873. The meritorious civil governor of this district, José Silvestre Ribeiro, continued Casado Geraldes’s list up to the time of his own government. It covers 1815 to 1847 and is published in the second volume of the *Epocha Administrativa*, on page 141 and following.

before: The southern coast of Madeira, commonly called the Costa do Sul, stretches from the sharp projection of the shoreline known as Ponta do Pargo to the tip of Ponta de São Lourenço. The southern region is very mild and picturesque, with more inlets and landing places. This, together with the shelter that the general mass of the island provides against the prevailing winds, means that ships and boats find on this coast the safety that the northern coast denies them, as in the bay of Funchal. This southern coast contains the parishes (*freguesias*) of the municipalities of Calheta, Ponta do Sol, Ribeira Brava, Câmara de Lobos, Funchal, Santa Cruz and Machico, with the exception of the parish of Porto da Cruz and the northern shore of Caniçal, which belong to the last of those municipalities.
after: The southern coast of Madeira, commonly called the Costa do Sul (‘south coast’), stretches from the sharp projection of the shoreline known as Ponta do Pargo (‘sea bream point’) to the tip of Ponta de São Lourenço (‘St Lawrence Point’). The southern region is very mild and picturesque, with more inlets and landing places. This, together with the shelter that the general mass of the island provides against the prevailing winds, means that ships and boats find on this coast the safety that the northern coast denies them, as in the bay of Funchal. This southern coast contains the parishes (*freguesias*) of the municipalities of Calheta, Ponta do Sol, Ribeira Brava, Câmara de Lobos, Funchal, Santa Cruz and Machico, with the exception of the parish of Porto da Cruz (‘harbour of the cross’) and the northern shore of Caniçal (‘reed bed’), which belong to the last of those municipalities.

before: Mousinho de Albuquerque, already cited, says of the seaboard of the south coast: ‘Starting from Ponta do Pargo, the southern coast of the island runs SE as far as Ponta do Jardim, presenting along this stretch some small shoals and rocks very close to the coast, particularly off Paul do Mar and Jardim itself. The coast then follows an ESE direction as far as Ponta do Sol, and from there to Ponta da Cruz, the southernmost point of the island, it runs in general, disregarding the lesser bends and points, in the direction ESE ¼ E. From Ponta da Cruz to Cabo Garajau, where the bay of Funchal lies, the direction of the coast is approximately E ¼ N; past this cape and as far as Ponta dos Picos da Atalaia it becomes roughly ENE, and from there to Caniçal, at the root of Ponta de São Lourenço, the general direction of the coast is NNE ¼ E. Along almost the whole length of this coast the sea is deep and free of shoals, with the exception of the Ilhéu do Gorgulho, the Baixa do Carneiro, the fortified islet and the tip of Ponta de São Lourenço, which is surrounded by a number of isolated rocks and small rocky heads that the waters cover.’
after: Mousinho de Albuquerque, already cited, says of the seaboard of the south coast (*Costa Sul*): ‘Starting from Ponta do Pargo, the southern coast of the island runs SE as far as Ponta do Jardim (‘garden point’), presenting along this stretch some small shoals and rocks very close to the coast, particularly off Paul do Mar and Jardim itself. The coast then follows an ESE direction as far as Ponta do Sol, and from there to Ponta da Cruz (‘point of the cross’), the southernmost point of the island, it runs in general, disregarding the lesser bends and points, in the direction ESE ¼ E. From Ponta da Cruz to Cabo Garajau (‘tern cape’), where the bay of Funchal lies, the direction of the coast is approximately E ¼ N; past this cape and as far as Ponta dos Picos da Atalaia (‘point of the watchtower peaks’) it becomes roughly ENE, and from there to Caniçal, at the root of Ponta de São Lourenço, the general direction of the coast is NNE ¼ E. Along almost the whole length of this coast the sea is deep and free of shoals, with the exception of the Ilhéu do Gorgulho (‘weevil islet’), the Baixa do Carneiro (‘ram shoal’), the fortified islet and the tip of Ponta de São Lourenço, which is surrounded by a number of isolated rocks and small rocky heads that the waters cover.’

before: The locusts vanished as quickly as they had come, but for several days large numbers of them could be seen floating in the waters of the bay of Funchal and off Porto Santo. ‘The Municipal Council (*Câmara Municipal*) of Porto Santo,’ say the *Anais* of that island, ‘passed a resolution (acordam) ordering each inhabitant to deliver one *alqueire* (dry measure for grain; as a land measure c. 900 m²) of those insects to the secretary of the said Council, João António Pedroso, and in this way within a few days 360 *alqueires* of that monstrous plague were buried.’

before: This was the name formerly given to the small house at the Entrada da Cidade where the Port Captaincy and the Commercial Association were housed for many years. before: In former times it was the custom for the chief health guards to wait at the Casa da Saúde for the papers of ships arriving in our port to be presented to them. The chief health guards were appointed by the Council and, unlike today, were not required to have medical training. Besides the chief health guards, the Casa da Saúde had an interpreter, also appointed by the Council, who received a salary of 17 réis a year.

before: The Casa da Saúde served as the town hall from 1784 until the end of the 18th century or the beginning of the 19th. before: After the discovery, and to begin the work of colonisation, João Gonçalves Zarco and Tristão Vaz Teixeira divided the lands of Madeira into two captaincies (see Captaincies), setting their limits and marking out the areas of their jurisdiction. A dividing line running from Ponta de Oliveira to Ponta do Tristão separated the domains of the two captains-donatary. Caniço’s name is therefore linked to this drawing of boundaries, and later the parish (*freguesia*) had the peculiarity of belonging to the jurisdiction of both captaincies.

before: Some of these settlers were of noble origin. They kept their privileges of nobility and founded several entailed houses here. Particularly notable are that of Consolação, instituted by Álvaro de Ornelas, one of the oldest in Madeira, dating from the end of the 15th century; the entailed estate (*morgadio*) founded by Vasco Martins Moniz; that of Matos Coutinho; and that of João Afonso.

before: Within a few years the growing number of new settlers and their immediate descendants formed a very substantial nucleus of population, which soon made the creation of a parish advisable. The densest settlement stretched along both banks of the stream, which was the boundary between the two captaincies. On either side of this watercourse two parish churches were built: the one on the right bank had the Espírito Santo (Holy Spirit) as its patron saint, and the one on the left bank Santo Antão (St Anthony the Great). The lands around the first were called Caniço towards the city, and those around the second Caniço towards Machico. These names clearly indicated the captaincies to which they belonged.

before: Dr Álvaro Rodrigues de Azevedo gives 1440 as the year in which this parish was created, and it is certainly one of the oldest on the island. The learned annotator of *Saudades da Terra* places the church of Espírito Santo in the captaincy of Machico and that of Santo Antão in the captaincy of Funchal, which is not correct, as we were able to establish from documents in the archive of this parish. before: The ministerial order (*portaria*) of 8 November 1848 required the Municipal Councils to keep a book entitled *Anais do Município* (‘Annals of the Municipality’) and to have entered in it, in the month of March each year, a summary of all the events, notes and information that might be of interest to the history of the municipality concerned. The illustrious civil governor of this archipelago, José Silvestre Ribeiro, who never neglected any matter that might contribute to the material and intellectual progress of the people under his administration, called for compliance with that order in his circulars to the councils and to the municipal administrators (*administradores do concelho*) of the district, dated 3 January 1848 and 22 January 1850. In them he set out, with the most persuasive arguments, the advantages and the necessity of carrying out that government measure. Few municipal councils, starting with that of the district capital, complied with so useful and necessary a directive.

before: On Porto Santo it was the municipal administrator (administrador do concelho, the government's representative), João de Sant'Ana e Vasconcelos, who in 1848 gathered the necessary notes and gave the annals of that municipality (*concelho*) their final form. It is a valuable work and may be regarded as an interesting monograph on the island of Porto Santo, both from the historical point of view and for its description of the island and its statistics of produce, population, customs, etc. Despite its shortcomings, it is a work that does great honour to its author's memory. It was published in full in the *Heraldo da Madeira* in January, February and March 1906, and some passages had already appeared long before in the *Diário de Notícias* of this city.

before: We saw the first yellow leaves on 16 September. Once yellow, the leaves remain on the trees and fall only very late, when the new leafing is already well advanced. In the parish (*freguesia*) of Monte, which lies at an altitude of 600 metres, the oaks did not begin to leaf until 15 January, that is, 43 days later than in Funchal.

before: The work by the Revd Father Ernesto Schmitz entitled *Die Vögel Madeira's* records thirty-eight birds that nest in the archipelago and one hundred and fifty-seven that are migrants.
after: The work by the Revd Father Ernst Schmitz entitled *Die Vögel Madeira's* records thirty-eight birds that nest in the archipelago and one hundred and fifty-seven that are migrants.

before: The birds that nest in the archipelago are mostly European species, whereas the migrants generally come from the African coast. Of the latter, those that appear most often are, according to J. Y. Johnson, the following: *Accipter nisus*, *Fringilla chloris*, *Upupa epops*, *Ardea cinerea*, *A. nycticorax*, *Limosa melanura*, *Numenius arquata*, *Gallinago major*, *Gallinula chloropus*, *Fulica atra*, *Mareca penelope*, *Larus tridactylus* and *Sula alba*. *Cegialitis vociferus*, an American species, has been recorded several times in Madeira, and *Phyloscosus superciliosus*, from Asia, was collected some years ago on Porto Santo. Of the native species, the canary, the *corre-caminho*, the *andorinha da serra*, the *pombo trocaz* and the *anjinho* are common to Madeira and the Canaries and have not been found elsewhere. The *tintilhão* occurs only in Madeira, the Canaries and the Azores, and the *bisbis* is a species peculiar to our island. The *toutinegra de capelo* is a curious variety which we suppose has not been found outside Madeira.

before: Exports of embroidery grew steadily, we believe, until 1878, when they were estimated at 55,252,000 *réis*. By 1880, however, they had fallen to 12,937,000 *réis*, because luxury embroidery had gone somewhat out of fashion in England. Large sums nevertheless remained on the island from sales of embroidery to the many foreigners who visited us. It was this that sustained and encouraged an industry which, although it brought no great profit to the women who practised it, did in some measure help to improve the situation of many families. Madame Counis’s shop in Rua de João Tavira made more sales than any other in the city at that time. It offered work of the most varied kinds, from white embroidery of simple design to silk embroidery and tapestry work in single or double stitch. It was a little over 50 years ago, around 1890, that the first German embroidery export houses established themselves in Funchal. This was of clear benefit to an industry that had long stood still for lack of consumer markets. Our embroidery, until then well known only in England, began to spread not only to Germany but also to the United States and other countries. The result was a considerable increase in production, greatly benefiting not only the rural economy but the economy of the whole district. The sum required to pay for labour across the whole archipelago, which was 200 *contos* in 1893, rose to 461 *contos* in 1906. This was due to greater exports and to a considerable increase in sales within Funchal, thanks to the arrival in our harbour of a larger number of steamers carrying passengers in transit.

Madame Counis’s shop in Rua de João Tavira made more sales than any other in the city at that time. It offered work of the most varied kinds, from white embroidery of simple design to silk embroidery and tapestry work in single or double stitch. It was a little over 50 years ago, around 1890, that the first German embroidery export houses established themselves in Funchal. This was of clear benefit to an industry that had long stood still for lack of consumer markets. Our embroidery, until then well known only in England, began to spread not only to Germany but also to the United States of America and other countries. The result was a considerable increase in production, greatly benefiting not only the rural economy but the economy of the whole district. The sum required to pay for labour across the whole archipelago, which was 200 *contos* in 1893, rose to 461 *contos* in 1906. This was due to greater exports and to a considerable increase in sales within Funchal, thanks to the arrival in our harbour of a larger number of steamers carrying passengers in transit.

before: At its session of 30 June 1803 the municipal senate (*Senado da Câmara*, historic title of the Council) took possession of the house on the Largo da Sé, where it had been holding its meetings for some time. before: In an official letter addressed to the Municipal Council (*Câmara Municipal*) of Funchal on 31 March 1847, Councillor (conselheiro, honorary title of the royal council) José Silvestre Ribeiro, that benevolent civil governor, proposed that the gaol be set up in the former convent of São Francisco, that the town hall move into the house then serving as the gaol, and that the *recolhimento* (religious retreat house for women) for beggars be transferred to the house of the Angústias. These suggestions were not taken up. Much later, following a petition made on 17 May 1888, the Council obtained the use of the Pico fortress (*Fortaleza do Pico*) for 10 years for the provisional installation of the prisons. It never took advantage of this favour from the Government, however, because it lacked the means needed to build a structure fit to serve as the gaol of the judicial district (*comarca*).

before: Only after the closure of the Hospital de São Lázaro (St Lazarus) on 5 June 1912 could the old project of giving Funchal a gaol in good condition finally be carried out. The Municipal Council resolved that the new establishment should be built on the land occupied by that hospital, and it pressed ahead with this decision so vigorously – towards the end work even went on at night to hasten completion – that on 29 November 1913 the prisoners were transferred to the new building intended for them. On that same day demolition began of the old building on the Largo da Sé, where the gaol of the judicial district had been housed for nearly a century.

before: It was Dr Fernando Tolentino da Costa, a member and later president of the Municipal Council of Funchal, who took the greatest interest in the building of the São Lázaro gaol and the demolition of the Largo da Sé building. It was thanks to his efforts and acknowledged zeal that these two improvements were carried out so quickly. The public celebrated the fall of the first stones of the old gaol with a few sprays of rockets, and everyone rejoiced at the disappearance of a building which not only failed to serve the purposes for which it had been intended but also considerably disfigured one of the most central spots in the city.

before: This chapel, which was completely demolished some twenty years ago (1921) and had long before fallen into total ruin, stood in the locality (*sítio*) to which it gave its own name. It was built at the behest of Nuno Fernandes Cardoso and his wife Leonor Dias, who, by a will made in 1511, founded the entailed estate (*morgadio*) of São João de Latrão, which took its name from the chapel that served as its seat. Referring to this will, the annotator of the *Saudades* says: ‘This will, of which we have a copy, is a model of its kind, for the sound probity, simplicity of faith and virtuous pride that dictated it. The moral and historical justification of entails finds in that venerable document a most honourable commemorative pillar (padrão) in its favour. The pure type of entails (*instituições vinculares*) is there. Our age cannot accept them, that is evident. But the just and enlightened historian judges by a subtler and loftier standard than the mere comparison of the past with the present.’

before: The author just cited says that Bertrand de Montluc, caring little for the leisure he enjoyed in France and weary of the intrigues of the court, had resolved to risk his life in African waters by attempting to found a fortress in East Africa, intended to protect French trade with those regions and with the countries of the East. He adds that when they reached Funchal and landed some men to take on water, they were met by the Portuguese with cannon fire, and that then ‘Montluc, carried away by his fervent enthusiasm and his great desire to make a name for himself, seized the opportunity to strike a real surprise blow and so affront the pride of Spain and Portugal, regarded at the time as the true masters of the seas’. The Madeiran chronicles and the Portuguese historians make not the slightest reference to any hostile reception of Charles IX’s subjects. Relations between France and our country were then quite friendly, and it is hard to believe that the Madeirans would have acted in that way, unless Montluc’s squadron appeared at Funchal in warlike array and with every appearance of true corsairs, as indeed they were. To understand the intentions of the pirate Montluc, it is enough to recall that on the eve of the day he assaulted Madeira he made a landing on Porto Santo, unleashing all his fury on the defenceless inhabitants of that island. Moreover, the ferocious rage with which he attacked the city, the unheard-of cruelties he committed and, above all, the terrible sack to which he subjected Funchal, stripping it of its riches and loading them into eleven vessels, are eloquent and undisputed proof that this was an act of plain and simple piracy, and never a reprisal to avenge an injury received.

before: The pirates landed at Praia Formosa at about nine o’clock in the morning on 3 October and at once marched on the city, entering it at two different points. At the Portão de São Paulo (St Paul’s Gate) they met stubborn resistance, and several dozen men fell dead there on both sides. Having forced this entrance, they made for the Fort of São Lourenço (St Lawrence), where the governor, with the forces at his disposal, resisted them bravely but had to yield to the seasoned strength and numbers of the attackers. Some pockets of resistance also formed in other parts of the city, but they proved entirely useless in the face of the fury and numbers of the pirates. Forces were organised in various parts of the island, ready to march on the city. However, persuaded by reports sent from Funchal that their presence would only further inflame the corsairs’ rage, they decided to turn back, leaving the corsairs complete masters of the situation.

before: On the origin of the name of this parish (*freguesia*), the lineage and services of its inhabitants and the fertility of its lands, let us hear the celebrated historian of the islands, albeit with his customary hyperbole: ‘…and they spent many days on the way until, three *léguas* further on, they reached a furious stream, on whose beach the captain was waiting. He had gone ashore and had laid out a settlement there, which he named Ribeira Brava after the stream that ran through this place. The settlement later founded here became so pleasant and noble, one of the best on the island, that besides having many fruits and provisions in abundance, it is and always was so generous with the inhabitants who live in it that, when it suited the captains of Funchal to go later to the relief of the strongholds of Africa with men, from this one place alone they drew such noble knights and distinguished people, who went at their own expense to serve the King, and who won such renown, as will be seen later in the course of this history; besides other noble people, retainers of the captains, who always had very knightly men of noble birth from here. This place is not a town, not because it lacks many inhabitants and a good site, nor because it is the least on the island – on the contrary, it is the best situated and most magnificent of all – but because it lies within the *termo* (municipal jurisdictional district, a subdivision of the comarca) of the City of Funchal, and is a pleasant *quinta* (country estate), from which the inhabitants of the city obtain, and where they are supplied with, the best wheat, fruit, game and meat, and in greater abundance than in the whole island; and it may rightly be called the granary of Funchal, as the Island of Sicily is called the granary of Italy.’ Elsewhere the author of the *Saudades* also says: ‘A *légua* west of Campanário lies Ribeira Brava, which bears this name to the full: it is a village of about three hundred households (*fogos*, literally ‘hearths’), with a church of St Benedict and a good landing place of fine shingle. Its houses stand up along the floor of the stream, and it has much sugar cane, two sugar mills and very rich orchards with many apples and pears, walnuts and plenty of chestnuts, so that it is the pleasantest village on the island. For this reason, and because it deserves it, having a good landing place and being very lush, the inhabitants have many times tried to have it made a town. It also has many vineyards, although the wine is not as good as that of Funchal. The stream is so furious when it floods that it sometimes carries away many houses and does great damage, because it comes down from great mountains and high ranges; and because it is like this, they came to call it *brava* [wild].’

before: This locality owes much to the Viscount of Ribeira Brava. It was he who secured its elevation to the seat of the municipality (*concelho*) and of a school district, and who endowed it with important material improvements, transforming the locality (*sítio*) of Lugar into a pleasant settlement well worth a visit. The opening and widening of streets and roads, the building of a small theatre, the rebuilding of the small fort of São Bento and other works carried out there place the people of Ribeira Brava under a duty to be grateful to his memory and to perpetuate it in a worthy manner through the times to come.

before: Camacha belonged to the parish (*freguesia*) of Caniço until the year of its own creation. It was the high, mountainous part of that parish and came to form its northern boundary. The name Camacha seems to be quite old, and it is without any doubt much older than the time when the area was separated from Caniço. Dr Álvaro de Azevedo conjectures that the name may come from some *sesmeiro* (holder of a land grant, or *sesmaria*) or settler with the surname Camacho, who perhaps owned land or had his residence there. We do not consider plausible the idea of attributing the origin of the name to an early colonist who, in memory of his distant homeland, gave this place the same name as some *lugar* (settlement ranking between a town and a parish) or village on the mainland. As far as we have been able to ascertain, the name is not found in Portuguese territory, except for a small locality (*sítio*) on the island of Porto Santo.
after: Camacha belonged to the parish (*freguesia*) of Caniço (‘reed’) until the year of its own creation. It was the high, mountainous part of that parish and came to form its northern boundary. The name Camacha seems to be quite old, and it is without any doubt much older than the time when the area was separated from Caniço. Dr Álvaro de Azevedo conjectures that the name may come from some *sesmeiro* (holder of a land grant, or *sesmaria*) or settler with the surname Camacho, who perhaps owned land or had his residence there. We do not consider plausible the idea of attributing the origin of the name to an early colonist who, in memory of his distant homeland, gave this place the same name as some *lugar* (settlement ranking between a town and a parish) or village on the mainland. As far as we have been able to ascertain, the name is not found in Portuguese territory, except for a small locality (*sítio*) on the island of Porto Santo (‘holy harbour’).

before: There is a vague tradition that a small chapel once stood in the locality of Salgados, and we do not know whether it was perhaps in this chapel that the parish was installed at the time of its creation. The foundation stone of the present church was laid on 30 September 1783. Around 1886 the side walls, which were in imminent danger of collapse, were rebuilt. In recent years the church and its churchyard have undergone major repairs and have been considerably improved in their embellishment and decoration, thanks to the zeal of several parish priests.

before: Outside Funchal, this is the parish with the finest and most numerous *quintas*. Among them the Quinta do Vale Paraíso stands out; it belongs to the viscounts of the same title and is a charming residence, well worth a visit. The former summer residence of the Ornelas family is also a fine and pleasant country house; its owner today is Councillor (conselheiro, honorary title of the royal council) Aires de Ornelas e Vasconcelos, who was born there in March 1866. before: One of the attractions for visitors to this parish is the well-known Achada, a square of some size and perfectly flat, which causes Madeirans a certain wonder and surprise, since they live in a very mountainous region where the relief and ruggedness of the land show themselves everywhere, except on the plateau of the Paul da Serra. On entering this square, the visitor’s attention is at once caught by the tower rising at one end of it, within the bounds of the *quinta* that belonged to Dr Miguel Grabham. It was this English physician who, some 40 years ago, had the tower built and placed in it an excellent, finely made clock, which is certainly one of the best on this island. Inside the tower is a marble tablet bearing the following inscription: The Clock And Bell Here Placed, Were Brought From the Parish Church of Wolton Near Liverpool By Michel C. Grabham, M. D. F. L. S. E. R. C. P.-Who built this Tower For their Reception, And the Clock Was Set Going By Mary Anne Grabham (Wife of the above) On Easter Monday 6.th April 1896. The building of this tower and clock was an excellent service that Dr Miguel C. Grabham rendered to the inhabitants of this parish.

before: Camacha is crossed along most of its length by the rich and abundant stream of water called the Levada da Serra, to which we shall refer in the appropriate place. When this levada (irrigation channel) was planned and dug, many landowners gave the land for its construction and for the footpath alongside it free of charge, convinced that it would benefit this parish through irrigation. When the works were finished and the water was shared out, however, they saw with deep sorrow that Camacha had been entirely forgotten and had no share in the benefits granted to other parishes. A walk along the levada path (*esplanada*) of this levada is truly delightful for the varied and surprising views it offers. The footpath beside this aqueduct, level and easy underfoot, is passable from Choupana to Santo da Serra, a distance of more than 40 kilometres.

before: A great political event on the Portuguese mainland, which had repercussions in all the island and overseas dominions, was the immediate cause of the publication of Madeira’s oldest newspaper, which took the name *Patriota Funchalense*. The advance of the so-called liberal ideas, which brought about the Porto Revolution and the resulting Constitution of 1822, was soon felt on this island. However, it was only some months after the events in the capital of the north that the political principles which were to establish the representative system in Portugal were solemnly proclaimed in Funchal. The official consecration of these principles took place on 28 January 1831. The event was commemorated on its anniversary the following year by the laying of the foundation stone of a monument to the Constitution, in front of the churchyard of the Cathedral (Sé Catedral), Funchal Cathedral (*Sé*), and this commemoration was marked by extraordinary and remarkable pomp.

before: A ‘press’, as it was then called – in fact a modest printing workshop – was bought in Lisbon and brought to Madeira. With it came the typesetter and printer Alexandre Gervásio Ferreira, who for about two years directed the composition and printing of the *Patriota Funchalense*; from no. 179 onwards he was replaced by the typesetter Inácio S. de Abreu. The workshop, management and editorial office were installed in a house in the Rua dos Ferreiros, which bore the street number 7 and must have stood not far from the former editorial office of *O Jornal* (1921).

before: On 2 July 1821, regarded as the anniversary of the discovery of Madeira, the first issue of the *Patriota Funchalense* appeared. It was a twice-weekly publication, coming out regularly on Wednesdays and Saturdays. It had four pages of text, but many issues were accompanied by ‘supplements’ of two and sometimes four pages. It was of small format, the printed area not exceeding 23 by 16 centimetres. In all, 214 issues were published, the last on 16 August 1823.

before: He was born in the parish (*freguesia*) of Madalena do Mar on 26 January 1836 and died in the town (*vila*) of Ponta do Sol on 26 May 1875. He was a surgeon trained at the Funchal School and secretary of the Municipal Administration (*Administração do Concelho*, the government's local civil office) of Ponta do Sol. According to the testimony of his contemporaries, Policarpo dos Passos Sousa possessed a prodigious talent, which misfortune did not allow to show itself with the vigour and brilliance that might have been so much wished for. He contributed to several newspapers and was regarded in his day as an inspired poet, his verse compositions enjoying great popularity. One of his compositions appears in the 1st vol. of the *Flores da Madeira*.

before: Its first name was Teatro D. Maria Pia, which the Municipal Council changed in November 1910 to Teatro Dr. Manuel de Arriaga. However, this former deputy for Madeira flatly refused, in an official letter of 31 December, to allow his name to be given to the theatre. The Municipal Council therefore resolved, at its session of 12 January 1912, to name it Teatro Funchalense. On the death of Dr Manuel de Arriaga, whose name is bound up with the history of Madeira because of the way he championed the interests of this archipelago in parliament, the Council decided to perpetuate his name here in Madeira by calling our foremost theatre the Teatro Dr. Manuel de Arriaga (1921).

before: During the European war a wireless telegraphy station was operated on behalf of the British government at Quinta Santana, and the news it received from abroad was passed daily to the Funchal public through the newspapers. By order of the Ministry of Finance, the installation of a radiotelegraph station at Quinta Santana was authorised on 12 December 1921, but it was never carried out.

before: It is certain, however, that as early as the century of the discovery there appeared several poets of notable merit who feature in the *Cancioneiro* (songbook) of Garcia de Resende. In his book *Poetas Palacianos*, Teófilo Braga went so far as to regard them as a group apart, characteristic and distinct, which he called the *Cyclo Poético da Ilha da Madeira* (Poetic Cycle of the Island of Madeira), a classification with which the annotator of the *Saudades da Terra* disagrees. Nevertheless, Dr Álvaro de Azevedo states that ‘that very notable group is none the less sufficient title for the island of Madeira to have an honourable share in the pre-classical history of national literature, a share which Senhor Teófilo Braga claimed for it.’ The chief of these poets who feature in the songbook are Tristão Teixeira, 2nd donatary of Machico, known as Tristão das Damas; João Gomes, the Troubadour; João Gonçalves da Câmara, 2nd donatary of Funchal; Rui de Sousa; João de Abreu; Manuel de Noronha, son of the 2nd captain-donatary João Gonçalves; and Rui Gomes. We know of no Madeiran prose writer who lived in the 15th century (see Cancioneiro de Resende, 1-233).

This point, of minor importance to us, does not seem to have been fully cleared up, despite what Agostinho de Ornelas and Dr Álvaro Rodrigues de Azevedo wrote about it. We are inclined, however, in view of the text of the Madeiran genealogies and the words of Frutuoso, to believe that it was the Fleming who had the house built, and that it passed to his descendants as their manor house. The genealogies, without referring specifically to this dwelling, state that Esmeraldo built large houses in the street that took its name from him, and the author of *Saudades da Terra* says that Rua do Esmeraldo was so called because the Fleming ‘had his old dwelling there, with a house of two storeys, marble pillars in the windows and terraces on top’.

before: Nevertheless, we shall say this. In 1928 and 1929 two curious books by Patrocínio Ribeiro and Pestana Júnior appeared, entitled *A Nacionalidade Portuguesa de Christovam Colombo* and *Cristóbal Colom ou Simão Palha*, in which their distinguished authors seek to prove that the illustrious discoverer of America was Portuguese. They were followed by two no less curious volumes under the titles *Salvador Gonçalves Zarco (Cristóbal Colon)* and *Cristobal Colon Salvador Gonçalves Zarco Infante de Portugal*, written respectively by G. L. dos Santos Ferreira and António Ferreira de Serpa, and by Artur Lobo de Ávila and Saul dos Santos Ferreira. These attempt to demonstrate, with skilful reasoning but unconvincing arguments, that the great navigator was the illegitimate son of Infante Ferdinand and of a granddaughter of João Gonçalves Zarco. It is well known that Ferdinand, heir and successor of Henry the Navigator in the grand mastership of the Order of Christ, took a very direct part in the government of our archipelago, which ‘in spiritual matters’ belonged to that order. Needless to say, the Gonçalves Zarco to whom those authors refer is the first captain-donatary (*capitão-donatário*) of Funchal and the most illustrious pioneer of the early colonisation of Madeira.

before: An inhabited locality (*sítio*) in the parish (*freguesia*) of Calheta, named after the early settler Luís de Atouguia, who held *sesmaria* (royal land grant to settlers on condition of cultivation) lands here and founded an entailed estate (*morgadio*) on them. There was once a chapel here dedicated to Nossa Senhora da Boa Morte, founded by Francisco Homem de Couto in 1661. The chapel of São Pedro de Alcântara (St Peter of Alcántara), formerly also known as São João Baptista, still stands here; João Baptista Teixeira had it built in 1783. before: As the final resting place for himself and for his successors in the government of the donatary captaincy (*donataria*), João Gonçalves Zarco had the chapel of Nossa Senhora da Conceição (Our Lady of the Conception) built. It became known as Conceição de Cima and, when the adjoining convent was founded, took the dedication to Santa Clara, which it still keeps today. Enlarged and later entirely rebuilt in the second half of the 17th century, nothing of the original building is likely to remain there, but within its walls it holds the venerable ashes of its founder, the first captain-donatary of Funchal. It must be regarded as our most precious and revered ‘memorable landmark’, inspiring in all the most respectful and heartfelt veneration.

before: *O Patriota Funchalense* was still appearing with complete regularity when, on 17 February 1823, the second newspaper ever to exist here came out. It bore the grandiloquent title *O Prégador Imparcial da Verdade, da Justiça e da Lei*, which would amply have sufficed to christen four different periodicals. Its editor and owner was Father Dr João Crisóstomo Espínola de Macedo, a distinguished lawyer and parish priest in the town (*vila*) of Santa Cruz. Although he possessed a lively intelligence and an uncommon culture, he wrote in language so violent and unbridled that it brought him the greatest troubles and the most outrageous humiliations. He was a worthy rival of Father José Agostinho de Macedo, even though he professed political principles diametrically opposed to those of the author of *Burros*, *Besta Esfolada* and *Tripa Virada*. *O Pregador Imparcial…* was a weekly, and 61 issues of it appeared, the last on 2 July 1824.

before: In that year a literary and scientific association called the Sociedade Funchalense dos Amigos das Ciências e Artes was founded here. It had 27 full members, 45 corresponding members and 24 honorary members, and included the most distinguished Madeirans of the time. Among the full members were such eminent names as Pimenta de Aguiar, Canon Gonçalves de Andrade, Nicolau Betencourt Pita, Lourenço José Moniz, Dr Caetano Alberto Soares, Dr João Pedro de Freitas Drumond and José Marciano da Fonseca, among others, to whom the *Elucidário Madeirense* devotes detailed notices. This society was the first to publish a small work in print: its constitution, entitled *Estatutos e Regulamentos da Sociedade Funchalense dos Amigos das Ciencias e Artes*. It is a small pamphlet of twenty-three pages, printed in 1822 at the press of the *Patriota Funchalense* and now extremely rare, and it enjoys the well-deserved distinction of being the first work of typography printed on this island.
