before: In 1842 a modest charitable establishment, then given the name of Asilo dos Inválidos (Asylum for Invalids), was set up in some of the ground-floor rooms of the Misericórdia (Holy House of Mercy, a lay charitable brotherhood) building in this city. It was an adjunct of the Holy House of Mercy (*Santa Casa da Misericórdia*) and was run by its governing bodies, but the asylum had been founded by the Municipal Council (*Câmara Municipal*) of Funchal. The Council was the official body that paid for the upkeep of the inmates, under a contract concluded between it and the administration of the Holy House (*Santa Casa*, the Misericórdia). We do not know when it ceased to operate, but its existence was short-lived. Project for a beggars’ asylum. By a royal decree (*alvará*) of 22 March 1844, the civil governor of the district, Dr Domingos Olavo Correia de Azevedo, appointed a commission, chaired by Dr António da Luz Pita and with Maurício Castelo Branco as secretary, to propose the most suitable means of creating an asylum to house beggars. We do not know what work this commission may have presented, but we do know that the asylum project never became more than a happy and generous idea, and nothing more.

before: Extraordinary events, generally of a political nature, that were regarded as attacks on the laws or institutions in force led to the creation of special tribunals. Armed with powers that were at times discretionary, these tribunals conducted rigorous inquiries and passed their sentences in the very places where the abuses or the offences had occurred. These improvised but fearsome tribunals came to Madeira several times; on some occasions only magistrates came, with wider powers than ordinary ones, to investigate and judge crimes or events that the central government considered deserving of more effective and exemplary punishment. The *Saudades da Terra* mentions some of these *alçadas* and several magistrates who came here invested with extraordinary powers to try certain cases, and we have already referred to this in the article Judicial Administration.

before: In 1486, while still Duke of Viseu, Manuel I ordered the building of ‘praça, camara, paço dos taballiães & picota no seu campo’ (a square, a council house, a notaries’ hall and a pillory (*picota*) in his field). This field, then called the Duke’s Field (Campo do Duque), was the ground now occupied by the square and the church of the Sé, Funchal Cathedral (*Sé*), the former Praça da Constituição, the former Rua do Aljube and the Largo do Comércio, or Largo do Chafariz. We do not know whether the pillory was ever actually set up in that field, as the council house was. before: The Campo da Barca lies on the left bank of the Ribeira de João Gomes. Its southern boundary was the Larguinho de São João, where the Rua do Oudinot, the Rua da Infância and the Rua do Ornelas come out. The street that continues the Avenida de João de Deus and crosses this square has divided it into two quite distinct parts. The southern part has been turned into a square named after Tenerife, the Praça de Tenerife. before: He was born around 1585, the son of Francisco de Andrade and Dona Constança de Atouguia. He was the great-grandson and great-great-grandson respectively of Fernão Dias de Andrade and Diogo Fernandes de Andrade, to whom we refer in the article Andrade. He distinguished himself greatly as a soldier and took part in the recapture of Bahia, in which he commanded a galleon. He fought in other battles, in which he gave proof of his courage. He was a commander of the Order of Christ and held the post of *mestre de campo* (colonel commanding a *terço*) in Brazil. He died in 1638 in the Cape Verde Islands, while serving as *mestre de campo* of a fleet bound for the recapture of Pernambuco.

before: Valentim Fernandes, also known as Valentim Fernandes Alemão, was a German printer and publisher who settled in Lisbon towards the end of the 15th century. He earned a place in the history of our maritime discoveries by collecting a number of unpublished writings of interest to the history of those same discoveries. In 1845 Dr Schmeller published a curious memoir on these unpublished texts, of which Henrique Major gives a detailed account in his work on Prince Henry the Navigator. These narratives of certain maritime discoveries made by the Portuguese in the 15th century bear on the history of the discovery of this archipelago, and for that reason Dr Rodrigues de Azevedo deals with them at length on pp. 366–372 and 905 of the *Saudades da Terra*. Part of these narratives, concerning the Azores, was published in volume 1 of the *Archivo Açoreano*. It seems to us that the remaining manuscripts of Valentim Fernandes’s collection are still unpublished.
after: Valentim Fernandes, also known as Valentim Fernandes Alemão, was a German printer and publisher who settled in Lisbon towards the end of the 15th century. In 1845 Dr Johann Andreas Schmeller published a curious memoir on these unpublished texts, of which Richard Henry Major gives a detailed account in his work on Prince Henry the Navigator. These narratives of certain maritime discoveries made by the Portuguese in the 15th century bear on the history of the discovery of this archipelago, and for that reason Dr Rodrigues de Azevedo deals with them at length on pp. 366–372 and 905 of ‘Longing for the Homeland’ (*Saudades da Terra*). before: In the year 1533 there lived on Porto Santo a certain Fernando or Fernão Nunes, nicknamed o Bravo (‘the Fierce’), who had a seventeen-year-old niece named Felipa Nunes, paralysed for some years. This Fernão Nunes sought to pass himself off as a prophet. One night he came down from the hills where he lived and entered the town (*vila*) ‘to see his niece, ringing a little bell, says Frutuoso, and on reaching the place where she was, he told her that the Holy Spirit had sent him to her, so that both might preach to the people of that island and tell them their sins..... And that Philipa Nunes answered him that the Holy Spirit had revealed to her that he was coming in that manner’.

before: A great many people gathered to find out what was happening, and, as Frutuoso relates, Fernão Nunes pointed out to each of them the sins they had committed. For this reason the pair were readily believed, not only by the ignorant common people but also by the judges, councillors (*vereadores*) and leading men of the island. Some days later, at the orders of the prophets Fernando and Felipa, the people went in procession, with the vicar and clergy, to Nossa Senhora da Graça (Our Lady of Grace). There Fernão Nunes said such things ‘that all went about confused, and astonished, and disconsolate, without eating; the women threw into the sea all their face paints, without regard for their precious garments, but rather took off the poor ones they wore, and remained in their shifts, as if doing penance, eating but little, and standing on their feet.’

before: From the book *Diocese do Funchal*, recently published, we extract the following passages: The *Saudades da Terra* dwell at length on the strange case that occurred in 1533 on the neighbouring island of Porto Santo, in which Fernão Bravo and Filipa Nunes, uncle and niece, common folk without any education, set themselves up as ‘prophets’. They revealed the hidden acts and deepest secrets of many people with such power of suggestion that even the island’s own clergy came to believe them and to attend the ‘sermons’ that these ‘seers’ preached to a crowd gripped by fear and the greatest wonder. The extraordinary event caused a considerable sensation and even had wide repercussions in mainland Portugal. It was the Franciscan friar and celebrated preacher Friar Gaspar Gato who, going to that island and making contact with the ‘prophets’, exposed the whole cunning fraud of these deranged people, who were brought as prisoners to Madeira and tried and sentenced. The clergy of Porto Santo suffered the consequences of their extreme credulity, being likewise arrested and severely punished by the competent ecclesiastical authority, the governor of the diocese (governador do bispado, administering the see in the bishop’s absence), the diocese being then vacant through the death of the prelate Dom Diogo Pinheiro.

before: Little is known of the personal circumstances of this Madeiran, although in his day he enjoyed great renown as a poet and as the author of several plays (*autos*), which the common people read avidly and which went through many editions. Diogo Barbosa Machado says in his *Bibliotheca Lusitana* ‘that he was one of the celebrated poets who flourished in the reign of King Sebastian, chiefly in the composition of *autos*, with the circumstance of being blind from birth’. We disagree with this claim (see Santa Catarina, chapel of), and are even of the opinion that it was not the first to be built in that parish (*freguesia*). before: In the short article entitled ‘Legislation’ in the first edition of this work, we stated that we would give in the ‘Supplement’ a brief account of the legislative enactments promulgated concerning this archipelago, as a valuable aid to the study of the measures adopted by the governments of mainland Portugal in the public administration of Madeira over the long period of five centuries. The ‘Supplement’, which was to have formed the third volume of the *Elucidário Madeirense*, was never published, and in this new edition the gap cannot be filled, because a summary of that legislation would take up far too much space. The deficiency has been partly remedied by the publication of the book *O Arquipélago da Madeira na Legislação Portuguesa*, by Father Fernando Augusto da Silva. It contains a summary of these legislative enactments for the period from 1934 to 1939, accompanied by a detailed, annotated index, and occupies more than a hundred pages of the book. Should a second edition of that work be produced, it ought to add a summary of the legislation promulgated before the constitutional period. For this the learned notes to the *Saudades da Terra* offer us an abundant repertory, as do several old collections of Portuguese legislation, and in particular the works of José Anastacio de Figueiredo and José Justino de Andrade e Silva.

before: Once the troops had landed, the British general lost no time in demanding that the governor and captain-general of Madeira, Pedro Fagundes Bacelar de Antas e Meneses, immediately surrender the archipelago. Since any resistance was impossible, the governor promptly agreed, and the capitulation was drawn up without delay. Its first article contained the clause that ‘the island of Madeira and its dependencies shall be handed over to the commanders of the forces of His Britannic Majesty, to be held and governed by His said Majesty with the same rights, privileges and jurisdictions as the Crown of Portugal has enjoyed them until now.’ This deed of capitulation, consisting of 7 articles, was signed on 26 December by Pedro Fagundes and Beresford. On the 30th of the same month Beresford issued a proclamation to the inhabitants of the island, which is transcribed in the *Saudades da Terra* and is in many respects a most interesting document.

before: He commanded the military expedition that came to Madeira in 1828 to bring the island under the Miguelite (supporter of the absolutist King Miguel) government. before: The illustrious annotator of the *Saudades da Terra* is of the opinion that Machico was raised to the status of town (*vila*) at the same time as Funchal, that is, around 1452, although the royal diplomas granting these privileges and prerogatives to the two settlements are not to be found in the archives of their respective captaincies. Santa Cruz, set within the captaincy of Machico, grew in importance soon after the discovery of Madeira. The increase in its population, together with its commercial and agricultural development, allowed it to rival its neighbour, so much so that its inhabitants asked for it to be granted the privileges of a town. Manuel I granted this by royal letter (*carta régia*) of 20 June 1515.

before: The municipality (*concelho*) of Santa Cruz is at present made up of the parishes (*freguesia*) of Santa Cruz, Água de Pena (part), Santo da Serra (part), Gaula, Camacha and Caniço. The decree of 19 October 1852, which detached the parish of Porto da Cruz from the municipality of Santana and incorporated it into that of Machico, also separated some localities from the latter municipality and joined them to the municipality of Santa Cruz. This provoked vigorous protests from the Municipal Council (*Câmara Municipal*) of Machico and from various official bodies and private individuals of the same municipality. After a series of incidents that seemed endless, the secretary-general of the district, António Lopes Barbosa de Albuquerque, acting as civil governor, convened a meeting at the Casa dos Romeiros in the parish of Santo da Serra on 11 September 1862. It brought together representatives of the Municipal Councils of Machico and Santa Cruz, the administrators of the municipalities, various public officials and other persons of standing. There a new municipal and parish division – the present one – was definitively agreed, and so the complaints and protests raised on both sides came to an end.

before: Anyone moderately familiar with the work of Camões knows that the well-known episode of the ‘Island of Love’ has given rise to many questions of a critical and literary nature, and that a sizeable Portuguese literature deals with them at length. Leaving aside the older authors, it is enough to name contemporaries such as Teófilo Braga, the Count of Ficalho, Epifânio Dias, José Maria Rodrigues, Ludovice de Meneses and others still to gauge the interest this subject has aroused among many commentators on *The Lusiads* (*Os Lusíadas*). One of the points most widely discussed is the ‘location’ or ‘geographical situation’ of the fantastic island. It is this point that is of particular interest to us here, because of the close or remote connection that may exist between it and the island of Madeira.

One of the points most widely discussed is the ‘location’ or ‘geographical situation’ of the fantastic island. It is this point that is of particular interest to us here, because of the close or remote connection that may exist between it and the island of Madeira.

before: Both hypotheses have been put forward, and both have found their fervent champions. ‘The poet,’ says a notable commentator on *The Lusiads*, ‘by a graceful effort of the imagination, took a mythological island with all its features and transported it from the regions of the Mediterranean – the homeland of ancient poetry – to the seas of the East... Its true geographical situation lies in the poet’s imagination, and it is not badly placed there.’ Some interpreters, however, no less illustrious and respected, allow that the islands of Angediva, Ceylon, Zanzibar, Ascension Island, Terceira and Madeira may each have been a stage on which the glorious poet ‘rested’ his incandescent imagination and received the first motifs of inspiration for the design of his sublime and still unsurpassed creation.

before: Set amid the bare cliffs that make up part of the coastline of the parishes (*freguesias*) of Calheta and Paul lies the tiny parish of Jardim do Mar. before: Gaspar Frutuoso says: ‘Half a *légua* from here is a parish called Jardim, of forty households (*fogos*, literally ‘hearths’), with a church dedicated to Nossa Senhora da Graça (Our Lady of Grace). before: Jardim do Mar began as a curacy (*curato*) dependent on Prazeres or on Paul – which of the two we have not been able to establish. It seems that it was first a daughter curacy of Prazeres and later of Paul do Mar, and that it was created in the second quarter of the 18th century. In the *Índice Geral do Registo da Provedoria da Real Fazenda* (general index of the register of the Royal Treasury Office (*Provedoria da Real Fazenda*)) we read on p. 132: ‘Royal decree (*alvará*) of the Lord King John V, of 15 November 1734, creating the curate of Jardim do Mar, with a salary of one and a half *moios* (dry measure of grain, 60 *alqueires*) of wheat and one and a half *pipas* (wine cask and measure, c. 400–500 litres) of wine, in view of the grave inconvenience suffered by the inhabitants of this *lugar* (settlement ranking between a town and a parish) in going to hear Mass in the parish (*freguesia*) of Prazeres or Paul, as a result of which they not only missed Mass but also died without the sacraments.’ And in the *Memorias sobre a criação e augmento do Estado Eclesiástico na Ilha da Madeira* we find the following further instrument cited: ‘Royal decree of the said Lord, of 12 March 1736, granting the respective salary of one and a half *moios* of wheat and one and a half *pipas* of wine to the said curate of Jardim do Mar, Father Manuel do Nascimento, with the certificate of the vicar of Prazeres that he fulfils his obligations.’

before: This priest was born in the parish (*freguesia*) of Madalena do Mar on 1 June 1774 and died in the city of Rio de Janeiro on 12 April 1858. He left for Brazil in 1808, already ordained a priest, and settled in the then newly founded settlement of Cantagalo, which within a few years grew considerably and became the city of the same name. Father Lessa devoted himself to politics and contributed a great deal to the independence of Brazil. He was a deputy in two legislatures and enjoyed the highest prestige among the politicians of his day. Several Brazilian writers refer to his persistent role in the events that preceded independence and also in the political struggles that followed. He left a printed book entitled *Cartas de Cantagalo*. In 1929 his nephew Clado Ribeiro de Lessa wrote and published a 160-page volume entitled *Esboço Biográfico do Padre António João de Lessa*, which describes the eventful life of this Madeiran priest.

before: He was the son of Manuel Ferreira Pestana, captain-major (*capitão-mor*, commander of the local militia) of Ribeira Brava, and of his wife Dona Ana Teresa Sousa Pestana, and was born there on 26 March 1795. After completing his preparatory studies in Funchal and enlisting in the artillery battalion of that city, he left for Coimbra in 1815 to enrol in the faculties of philosophy and mathematics of the University. Ferreira Pestana’s academic life was an unbroken series of triumphs, which earned him a proposal from the university congregation concerned to receive the degrees of licentiate and doctor free of charge; he received the doctoral hood (*capelo*) in the faculty of mathematics on 3 July 1820. Returning to his native island, where he spent some time teaching a chair of mathematics, he later settled in Coimbra to serve as assistant at the astronomical observatory and to prepare for the competitive examination for a university teaching post. The civil conflicts forced him to leave Coimbra, and it was only in 1834, by decree of 14 July of that year, that he was appointed professor in the faculty of mathematics.

before: They were judges appointed by the donataries and in many cases acted as their deputies. In the donataries’ absence they received the oath of the councillors (*vereadores*), and they exercised judicial and police functions, with power to arrest persons accused of any crime. To curb the excesses of jurisdiction of the donataries and their *ouvidores*, there were already *corregedores* in Madeira in the 15th century, charged with conducting judicial inquiries and punishing judges who abused their office. before: It stands in the parish (*freguesia*) of Santo António. The chapel is dedicated to Nossa Senhora do Pópulo, but nobody knows it by this name; it is commonly called the chapel of Pico do Cardo or of the Quinta dos Padres. This name comes from its standing in that locality (*sítio*) and at the residence that the Jesuits owned there. We do not know the year of its foundation, but we presume that it is no earlier than the first quarter of the 18th century. The Jesuits acquired this property between 1635 and 1714 and built the house and chapel there, which in 1770, together with the adjoining land, were sold at public auction for seven *contos de réis* (*conto*: one million réis; *réis*: old Portuguese money of account). This small chapel is hexagonal in shape and stands almost adjoining the residence. It is in a good state of repair, and divine services are celebrated in it.

before: He was born in Funchal on 17 July 1845 and died in the same city on 31 October 1911. before: ‘... What must be recorded and made known’, Cayola Zagalo tells us, ‘is that the revelation of the Artistic Heritage of Madeira forms one of the noble parts of the National Heritage.... An equal abundance is found in no less beautiful pieces of goldsmiths’ work, sculpture, ceramics, tapestry and furniture... The preponderance of the schools of Bruges and Antwerp and of the Portuguese school is such that I can point to only one exception: the small painting of St Jerome, presumably of Dutch provenance, belonging to the bishop’s palace in Funchal. Gérard David, Jean Provost, Jean Gossart and other masters yet to be identified, but of equal merit, are the authors of the island’s beautiful Flemish altarpieces; some of the panels whose artistic affiliation is as yet unknown are executed in the style of great painters such as Van der Weyden, Hans Memling, Quentin Metsys, etc. The explanation for so large a percentage of paintings from Flanders and Brabant, together with many other items of similar origin, most of them now lost, among them sculptures, furniture, tapestries and most of the tombstones faced with bronze plates, rests almost exclusively on sugar cultivation...’

An equal abundance is found in no less beautiful pieces of goldsmiths’ work, sculpture, ceramics, tapestry and furniture... The preponderance of the schools of Bruges and Antwerp and of the Portuguese school is such that I can point to only one exception: the small painting of St Jerome, presumably of Dutch provenance, belonging to the bishop's palace of Funchal (*Paço Episcopal do Funchal*). Gérard David, Jean Provost, Jean Gossart and other masters yet to be identified, but of equal merit, are the authors of the island’s beautiful Flemish altarpieces; some of the panels whose artistic affiliation is as yet unknown are executed in the style of great painters such as Van der Weyden, Hans Memling, Quentin Metsys, etc. The explanation for so large a percentage of paintings from Flanders and Brabant, together with many other items of similar origin, most of them now lost, among them sculptures, furniture, tapestries and most of the tombstones faced with bronze plates, rests almost exclusively on sugar cultivation...’

before: Princess Maria Amélia was the only child of the marriage of Pedro IV and the Empress Dona Amélia. She was born in Paris on 1 December 1831 and died in Funchal on 4 February 1853. The warrant (*provisão*) of 10 March 1805 ordered that these ruins be carefully preserved in the same state in which the flash flood (*aluvião*) had left them, as a reminder to future generations of the event that had been the most calamitous for the inhabitants of this island. before: In February 1848 the *Correio da Madeira* published the following report on the capstan on the city beach: ‘The establishment responsible for landing export and import goods on this island, known as the administration of the Funchal Capstan, was founded more than two centuries ago and carried out its functions as a privileged royal concession (patronado), by royal order, until 1807. At that time General Beresford, then governor and captain-general (capitão-general, military governor of Madeira) of this island, heeding the representations made to him by the Portuguese and foreign merchants of this stronghold, abolished the said Patronado, ordering that the ownership and management of that establishment should pass into the possession and administration of merchants, who bought all the Proprietor’s boats and equipment. By a royal notice dated Rio de Janeiro, 25 July 1808, His Royal Highness the Prince Regent ordered that the establishment for the business of the pebble beach (calhau), as General Beresford had shaped it, should be provisionally maintained until His Royal Highness decided what he judged most suitable to his royal service and to the public. The capstan establishment of the Calhau has thus continued from 1808 until now, with no other contrary provision by the government of which the petitioners are aware.’

before: This chapel, at the Lombada dos Esmeraldos (see that entry) in the parish (*freguesia*) of Ponta do Sol, was the seat of one of the two entailed estates (*morgadio*) founded there by the Fleming João Esmeraldo (see that entry); the other was known as the entailed estate of Vale da Bica. The chapel of Santo Espírito, now called Nossa Senhora da Conceição, was built at the beginning of the 16th century by this same João Esmeraldo. It was blessed, or rather consecrated, in 1508 by Bishop Dom João Lobo, who, before the diocese was created, had come to this island to exercise episcopal functions by order of the Grand Master of the Order of Christ, to which the archipelago belonged in spiritual matters. The following inscription can still be read today on one of the inner walls of the church: ‘This church was consecrated by Dom João Lobo, Bishop of Taiere, on 27 August 1508.’ There is no doubt that the present church is not the original building. It was rebuilt around the middle of the 17th century on a larger scale than the first design. A few years ago it underwent further repairs and was blessed in 1904, as recorded by the following words found there: ‘This chapel, having been repaired, was blessed again on 10 June 1904, with the customary solemnities, by the diocesan prelate His Most Reverend Excellency Dom Manuel Agostinho Barreto.’ It is the largest, most elegant and richest chapel in the whole diocese. The *azulejos* (painted glazed tiles) covering the lower walls of the nave and chancel are worthy of admiration; they depict the gifts and fruits of the Holy Spirit in symbolic figures. This chapel, which has five altars, contains some artistically and masterfully carved statues that at once catch the visitor’s attention. Near this church there still stands, though badly damaged, the large and imposing house of the administrators of this entailed estate, of which the 2nd Count of Carvalhal was the last holder.

before: Who wrote this interesting book? Neither Inocêncio Francisco da Silva in the *Diccionario Bibliographico* nor Dr Álvaro Rodrigues de Azevedo in his valuable annotations to the work of Dr Gaspar Frutuoso gives us the slightest indication on this point. It was pure chance that allowed the distinguished Madeiran Councillor (*conselheiro*, honorary title of the royal council) Manuel José Vieira to discover the name, hidden perhaps for more than a century, of the talented and learned author of the *Carta critica*. Among the papers left by the late physician César A. Mourão Pita (see that entry), Councillor Vieira found a printed copy of the work and a manuscript copy, both of which we presume belonged to the illustrious Madeiran and eminent physician Dr António da Luz Pita (see that entry). A quick and simple comparison of the two volumes at once revealed that they were one and the same work. The manuscript, which appears to be the author’s own autograph, contains something the printed copies lack: an excessively laudatory letter dated 28 August 1755 from the Convent of São Francisco (St Francis of Assisi) in this city, written by Friar João de São José and addressed to the author of the book. For reasons unknown to us, this letter did not accompany the printed edition of the work. The manuscript names Dr Julião Fernandes da Silva as its author, and his name matches the initials found at the end of the printed volume perfectly. This interesting manuscript was discovered in July 1907 and promptly acquired by the Funchal Municipal Library, where it is at present. Dr Julião Fernandes da Silva was the son of Manuel da Silva and was born in Funchal between 1723 and 1726. He graduated in medicine from the University of Coimbra (*Universidade de Coimbra*), completing the course on 17 November 1748. Besides the *Carta Critica*, he wrote a work entitled *Exame de Sangradores*, which is mentioned in the *Diccionario Bibliographico Portuguez*.

before: This distinguished chronicler of ours from the 15th century dealt with the discovery of the Madeira archipelago in his *Chronica do Descobrimento e Conquista da Guiné*. He was almost contemporary with the events he narrated, spoke with people who had lived through them, and had at his disposal the documents that could enable him to write history with complete truthfulness and with direct knowledge of the facts. His testimony in narrating the events recorded in his *Chronica* therefore has great value and unquestionable authority. The circumstances of the discovery of Madeira that he describes, albeit briefly, offer the conscientious researcher the surest material for reconstructing the historical truth on this very interesting and crucial point of the discovery of our archipelago. On this subject, see note III to the *Saudades da Terra*. The *Chronica da Guiné* remained unpublished for about four hundred years, until it was published in Paris in 1841 by the Viscount of Santarém.

before: This is a very old surname among us. One of the first to bear it was Gonçalo de Freitas, who settled in the village (*lugar*, settlement rank below a town) of Santa Cruz and had his residence there, on the *quinta* (country estate) called da Torre. He was a nobleman of the Royal Household (*fidalgo da Casa Real*) and Master of the Royal Hunt to Infante Ferdinand. His daughter Catarina de Freitas founded an entailed estate (*morgadio*) on the land she inherited from her father, in the locality (*sítio*) that later took the name of Santa Catarina. Gonçalo de Freitas’s son was João de Freitas, who enjoyed the privileges of nobility inherited from his father. An old nobiliary (book of noble genealogies) says that he built the church of Salvador (the Saviour) in Santa Cruz by order of the king, and for this received the royal grant of the chantry (capela) of that church as his family vault, in recognition of his services and of the expenses he had incurred on the church. One of his sons, named Jordão de Freitas, distinguished himself valiantly in India, where he was lord of an island and captain of the Moluccas. A member of this family was João de Freitas da Silva, who in 1631 raised on this island a company of 100 men at his own expense and went with it to serve in Pernambuco, where the Dutch killed him.

before: Some years later, around 1697, the Diocesan Seminary was installed there; until then it had operated beside the Bishop's Palace (*Paço Episcopal*). The earthquake of 1748 left the house of the Mosteiro Novo badly damaged, and it had to be abandoned. After suitable repairs, it served once more as the seminary from around 1760. In 1788 the Diocesan Seminary was transferred to the Jesuit College (*Colégio dos Jesuítas*), and from there it returned to the Mosteiro Novo in 1801, when Madeira was occupied by British troops. It remained there until 1909, when it was installed in the spacious building erected in the convent grounds of the convent of the Incarnation. The seminary of this diocese was suppressed by the decree of 20 April 1911, but it has continued to operate since that year, without official status, in the old house in Rua do Mosteiro Novo. (1921).

before: In the first years after the discovery of the archipelago, and in the early days of colonisation, communications with mainland Portugal were infrequent. A manuscript article states ‘that the King and the Infante (Dom Henrique) had news of the island from year to year in the summer, because in those early days no one sailed in winter.’ Improvements in the art of navigation and the rapid commercial and agricultural development of Madeira made these communications less rare, not only with the mainland of the Kingdom (*reino*, i.e. mainland Portugal) but, very particularly, with certain ports of Europe. A considerable number of outsiders, Portuguese and foreign, were drawn here by the fame of the soil’s great fertility; they settled in Funchal and amassed substantial fortunes. This helped to widen and multiply these communications, which were no longer very rare by the middle of the 15th century and could be called frequent by the beginning of the following century. The sugar trade, and later the export of our wines, which soon acquired a worldwide reputation, made Madeira an important commercial emporium and, consequently, made Funchal a port frequently sought by many vessels to carry those products. The same was not true of maritime relations between this archipelago and the mainland. Although less rare than in the early days of colonisation, they never became very frequent. The prelates of this diocese and the governors and captains-general almost always travelled to Madeira in state ships, not so much because of the rank of their office as because of the scarcity of vessels to carry them.

before: According to the geologist James Smith, of Jordan Hill, three kinds are known in Madeira: compact basalt (*pedra viva* (‘live stone’: compact basalt used for building) or *alvenaria* (local name for compact basalt used as building stone)), vesicular basalt (*cantaria rija* (hard dressed stone of vesicular basalt)) and scoriaceous basalt. Tuffs often alternate with the basalts, and compact basalts are frequently seen resting on layers of scoriaceous basalt. When it occurs in thick layers, compact basalt often splits vertically into columns of polygonal section, as is often seen in quarries and can also be observed near Gorgulho, at Tem-te não Caias (Porto da Cruz) and at Faial.

before: Around the supposed or real existence of this island many hypotheses have been constructed and varied conjectures invented, which are of particular interest only to those who wish to study the subject in greater depth. Another legend, mentioned by some authors, is that of the islands of St Brendan, an Irish monk who is supposed to have travelled to various islands of the Atlantic, one of which would have been Madeira. Others further assert that the Phoenicians, the Arabs, the Carthaginians and the Normans, at different periods, sailed along the western coasts of Africa and visited many of the islands scattered across the Atlantic, leaving traces of their passage on some of them. Many writers have dealt in particular with the Carthaginian Hanno and his *Periplus*, or description of his sea route, and some authors of good repute and sound critical judgement regard this voyage as genuine. This would allow for the possibility that the Madeira archipelago was a point of passage on one or more of these doubtful and problematic voyages. It is generally believed, and on the firmest grounds, that such voyages were made only along the coasts. This was owing to the backward state of the art of navigation, the small size of the vessels, the terror inspired by the vastness of the ocean, the belief in sea creatures of enormous bulk capable of swallowing ships or sinking them, and yet other legends and superstitions. The chief beacons and points of reference were the most prominent capes, promontories and headlands of the land, and navigators did not then venture on voyages on the high seas or on long, distant runs that would take them too far out of sight of the mainland. It is for these weighty reasons that, although the possibility of these remote voyages is admitted, all the probabilities favour the generally accepted and acknowledged fact that the Madeira archipelago was not visited before João Gonçalves Zarco and Tristão Vaz Teixeira made for these unknown waters. The distinguished geographer and historian M. d’Avezac, in the second part of his notable work *Iles de l’Afrique*, pp. 2 to 41, deals at length with the legends and traditions to which we make only a brief reference here; they are also dealt with by the illustrious annotator of the *Saudades da Terra*, in one of his learned notes to the work of Gaspar Frutuoso. We do not refer here to the well-known legend of Machim, because we shall deal with it in a separate article.

before: In the article on the grant (*doação*) of the island of Madeira to the Infanta Dona Catarina we have already referred to the attempts said to have been made by the English government to obtain possession of this archipelago at the time of the marriage of the Portuguese infanta Queen Catherine to Charles II, King of England. The question was treated at length by Dr Álvaro Rodrigues de Azevedo in one of the notes to the *Saudades da Terra*. Although he does not prove conclusively there that negotiations were opened between the two governments for the cession of Madeira, there can be no doubt that on this and other occasions British diplomacy sought to seize the opportunity to voice these aspirations, which are believed to go back a long way. After that period there are positive and eloquent facts that clearly demonstrate the wishes of our old ally. The two occupations of Madeira by English troops, carried out in the name of protection and defence against supposed attacks by Napoleonic forces, amounted to a genuine conquest. This is proved not only by many diplomatic documents of the time but also by the way the British administered the public affairs of this archipelago: the Portuguese authorities kept only a semblance of power, which in reality lay solely with the commander-in-chief of the British forces (see Occupation of Madeira by English troops). The Madeirans suffered every kind of humiliation during the eight years that these occupations lasted. Despite the resolutions adopted at the Congress of Vienna, under which England was to evacuate this island without delay, it is certain that in many European chancelleries, and even in the highest circles of the Portuguese government, the occupation of Madeira was thought to amount to absolute and permanent possession. It is to the distinguished diplomat then representing Portugal in London, Dom Domingos António de Sousa Coutinho, that the evacuation of this archipelago and its return to the Portuguese nation are owed. Through his eminent qualities as a statesman and his numerous writings published abroad, he rendered many signal services to his country. Our government honoured him with the title of Count, and later Marquis, of Funchal, a title still borne today by the representatives of his family. If we are still Portuguese, it is chiefly to him that we owe it; and yet there is nothing in this city to commemorate this fact or to pay even a small tribute to the memory of the illustrious diplomat.

before: From 1640 the British colony took hold of almost all trade, above all the wine trade, which came to be entirely in the hands of English merchants. As a result of this veritable monopoly, as the annotator of Gaspar Frutuoso says, these merchants built up large fortunes for themselves, while the landowners and vine-growing farmers grew poorer. Some Portuguese wine-exporting houses later emerged, but they could not compete with the English giants. They lacked capital, they could not easily find outlets for their products abroad, and besides there were the privileges and exemptions those foreign merchants enjoyed. The administrators of entailed lands (*terras vinculadas*), who generally led idle lives, and many rural landowners too, not excluding the tenant farmers themselves, would draw large sums from the English houses in the course of the year, to be repaid at harvest time. Those houses thus became the creditors of the poor vine-growers, who were left at the mercy of the whims and greed of the wine merchants. On one of these occasions, when the exporting houses set an unprofitable price for the must, João de Carvalhal, later Count of Carvalhal, rescued the farmers from their distress by buying the wine at remunerative prices and forcing the English merchants to follow his salutary example. But João de Carvalhal enjoyed the greatest prestige and influence here in Madeira. He was an extremely rich landowner in every parish of the island and, what is more, held some three million *cruzados* in banks in England. before: This is the place to say that the study of certain branches of the natural history of this archipelago is owed to a relatively large number of English subjects. There are very valuable works, the fruit of deep and lengthy scientific research, which cannot and must not be forgotten by Madeirans. In this Elucidário we have tried to bring out the names of the authors of these works, giving, however briefly, an account of the nature of their studies and of the services they rendered to the natural sciences. The distinguished men of science Richard Thomas Lowe, T. V. Wollaston, James Yate Johnson, Dr Alfred Merle Norman, etc., etc., will always be remembered by all who devote themselves to the study of Madeiran matters, and their names are inseparably linked with the history of our archipelago. If, as someone has already suggested, a gallery of marble or bronze busts were opened in our public garden, representing some of the most distinguished sons of Madeira or those who had rendered notable services to this land, two or three of the most illustrious English naturalists who studied the flora and fauna of the islands of the archipelago would certainly, and with complete justice, have their place there.

before: The square that the people commonly call ‘do Chafariz’ (of the Fountain) used to bear the name of São Sebastião, and a few years ago received from the Municipal Council (*Câmara Municipal*) its new name of Largo do Comércio. Before the square was laid out with the area it keeps today, a narrow street ran there. It was the continuation of Rua do Aljube and was also called Rua de São Sebastião. Between Rua de São Francisco and the building of the Misericórdia (Holy House of Mercy, a lay charitable brotherhood) (see Jardim Pequeno) stood a public fountain commonly known as ‘the Fonte’. Its basins were requisitioned by the Council in 1838 for use in the present public fountain of Largo do Comércio, which was built in 1827.

before: Simão Gonçalves spent most of his time at court, where he was held in great esteem, and in 1574 he accompanied King Sebastian on his first expedition to Africa. By a royal decree (*alvará*) of 20 August 1576 he was granted the title of Count of Calheta, not only in recognition of his own services but chiefly of those rendered by his forebears, and also because he was the head of so great and important a house. He styled himself: Count Simão Gonçalves da Câmara, of the Council of the King Our Lord, Captain and Governor of Justice in the island of Madeira and in the jurisdiction of Funchal, Overseer of His Majesty’s revenues throughout that island and in Porto Santo, Lord of the Desertas Islands, etc. The *Saudades da Terra* states that, besides various rights and exemptions, he had an income of four *contos* (1 conto = 1,000,000 réis, from 1911 1,000 escudos), which, four centuries later, would today correspond to a very considerable sum.

before: His definitive home, where he spent most of his life, was in the immediate vicinity of the site where he had the church of Conceição de Cima built. An old manuscript says: ‘he also resolved to build a dwelling for himself, as he did, on a height above the valley of Funchal, right opposite a church of Nossa Senhora da Conceição, as a family vault for himself and his kin’. This is the present church of Santa Clara (St Clare of Assisi), and his residence is the old manor house of the Lomelino entailed estates, known today as the Quinta das Cruzes, as can be seen at greater length in the article Moradias de Zargo, on page 395 of volume II of this work, to which we refer the reader.

before: The first person on this island who appears to have used this surname was Brites or Beatriz de Abreu, daughter of Rui de Abreu, *alcaide-mor* (royal governor of a castle and town) of Elvas. She married João Fernandes do Arco, so called because he held extensive *sesmaria* (royal land grant to settlers on condition of cultivation) lands in Arco da Calheta, and of whom we shall speak in a separate article. Their sons took their mother’s surname, and some of them distinguished themselves in Africa and India. Among the daughters were the celebrated Isabel de Abreu (see that entry) and Águeda de Abreu, wife of João Esmeraldo, the owner of the Lombada da Ponta do Sol. To this family belonged António de Abreu, the discoverer of the Moluccas (see that entry).

before: It is said that the first Indian fig tree in Madeira came on a ship bound for Europe that was wrecked in the harbour of Funchal at the end of the 18th century. A sailor from that ship managed to bring the fig tree ashore, and it was planted in the grounds of Quinta Vigia, where it lived for many years and became the parent stock of all the specimens of the same species that later appeared on the island.

before: A web-footed seabird of the family Procellariidae which comes to breed in the Savage Islands (*Selvagens*) during the spring. This elegant little bird appears there at the end of winter and stays until July or August, when it heads back south. The egg is laid at the end of a winding underground burrow; there is a single white egg with small purplish spots, which sometimes cover the whole surface and at other times cluster around the broader end. On Selvagem Grande its enemy is a mouse that abounds there, which not only attacks the bird but also devours its egg. The breeding of this bird has been found at only two almost diametrically opposite points of the earth: the Selvagens and the west coast of Australia.

before: The Hospice remained open for only a few months, closing its doors around the middle of July 1862. The Sisters of Charity had been ordered by the Portuguese government to leave our country, and on 9 June of that year they sailed for France aboard the French naval frigate *Arenoque*, which had come to the Tagus expressly to collect them. An exception had been made for Madeira, but M. Etienne, superior general of the congregation, ordered the Sisters of Charity to give up the running of the Hospício da Princesa D. Maria Amelia and return to their own country without delay; they left Funchal on 2 August 1862. The Empress then ordered that the house she had founded be closed provisionally, pending a further decision.

before: ‘The hospital of São Lázaro,’ says Dr Barral, ‘situated in the locality (*sítio*) of Santa Catarina, to the west of the city, is a small, old house intended to take in patients afflicted with elephantiasis, and maintained by the municipality. It holds more or less twenty-six patients, of both sexes and of different ages, and has at times sheltered more than thirty-four. There they find a home, a bed, food, a physician’s care and medicines. before: Over the last 30 years the hospital of São Lázaro rarely housed more than ten lepers, most of them natives of the municipalities of Ponta do Sol and Calheta. Elephantiasis of the Greeks is the most common form on the island. Those who suffer from it show tubercles or ulcerations on the face, hands, legs, etc., have difficulty breathing and seldom reach the age of 50; the disease almost always appears between the ages of 15 and 25. Of the patients we knew in the hospital, almost all died suddenly, from suffocation caused by oedema of the respiratory organs.

before: Dom Jerónimo Fernando was the ninth prelate of this diocese, which he governed for the long period of thirty years. Ungracious in manner and by nature harsh and brusque, he was nicknamed ‘Bravo’ (the Fierce) as a result. He was nevertheless able to soften the meaning of that word through the impeccable correctness of his conduct and the irreproachable way in which he discharged the high duties of his office. A serious accusation was, however, made against him, though a political one: that he had supported Spanish rule and had not joined in the demonstrations held here at the time of the Restoration. It was Dr Álvaro Rodrigues de Azevedo who echoed this accusation in one of his notes to the *Saudades*. Yet a manuscript from the middle of the 18th century certainly states that ‘when Luís de Miranda Henriques was governor of this island, and this news (that of the Restoration) arrived on the tenth of January, the said lord was at once acclaimed king throughout the island, the bishop playing a great part in calming the tumult of the people, to whom the governor had become suspect because of the homage he had paid to King Philip II’. This statement contradicts the assertion of the annotator of the *Saudades da Terra*, and today it is not very easy to establish on which side the historical truth lies.

before: Leaves medium-sized, rounded, wavy, glabrous or bearing a few hairs on the upper surface, downy on the lower, but with the indumentum sparse and irregularly distributed, sometimes almost absent over the whole blade or part of it; lobes very shallow or barely outlined, with obtuse or acute teeth; petiolar sinus usually very closed; bunches small or medium-sized (15–22 cm), generally winged and dense, cylindrical or cylindrical-conical; berries 15–20 millimetres, very sweet, firm or fairly firm, elliptical or oblong, greenish-yellow, generally golden when ripe. The stock is tall and very vigorous; canes greyish-brown or reddish greyish-brown, with short internodes. – It occurs in Funchal, in Câmara de Lobos and in Estreito de Nossa Senhora da Graça; it was once very common in both the north and the south of Madeira. It is also grown on Porto Santo. The rather strong grapes are very good for eating and produce a dry wine of pleasant flavour that is considered one of the finest in Madeira. The Madeiran Verdelho appears to be identical in its botanical characters to the *gouveio* of the Alto Douro.

before: Several species of the genus *Jasminum* occur in Madeira, two of which – *J. odoratissimum* and *J. azoricum* – are native. The first of these Oleaceae, which generally has trifoliate leaves and yellow flowers, is found at São Gonçalo, at Caniço, etc. The second, which also has trifoliate leaves but with larger leaflets, and white flowers, has been found only in the vicinity of Serra de Água. *J. grandiflorum*, from Malabar, and *J. revolutum*, from India, are grown in gardens, the former with white flowers and the latter with yellow.

before: 1755. Bory came to Madeira in this year aboard the *Comète*, and made some observations here on the variation of the compass needle. 1764. On 13 July of this year the ships *Dolphin* and *Tamar* arrived in the harbour of Funchal, carrying the expedition led by Commodore John Byron, which set out to discover new lands between the Cape of Good Hope and the Strait of Magellan. The expedition merely took on some fresh provisions. 1766. On 7 September the *Dolphin*, the *Swallow* and the *Prince Frederick* anchored in the harbour of Funchal, carrying the expedition commanded by Captain Samuel Wallis, which included among its officers Philip Carteret, a companion of Byron. The expedition merely replaced here the provisions it had already used up. 1768. It was on 13 September of this year that the scientific expedition commanded by the celebrated English navigator James Cook reached Madeira, on its way to observe the transit of Venus across the disc of the Sun on the island of Tahiti. The expedition included the naturalists Joseph Banks and Dr Solander and the astronomer Charles Green, and the first two carried out various scientific studies on this island. The *Endeavour*, which carried the expedition, left the harbour of Funchal on 19 September. 1772. On the second voyage that Captain Cook made in the southern seas, he called at Madeira on 19 July of this year aboard the *Resolution*. The naturalists Johann Reinhold Forster and his son Georg, who were members of the expedition, made some botanical observations here. 1785. The scientific expedition commanded by Jean-François Galaup de La Pérouse arrived in Funchal aboard the *Boussole* and the *Astrolabe* on 13 August of this year, leaving three days later for the Canary Islands. The expedition included the engineer Monneron, the geographer Bernizet, the surgeon Rollin, the astronomer Lepaute-Dagelet, the physicist Lamanon, the botanist Collignon and the illustrious Monge. The last of these escaped the unhappy fate of his fellow travellers, having gone ashore on Tenerife on 29 August 1785. 1792. The illustrious orientalist Sir John Barrow visited Madeira in this year on his voyage to Cochinchina. 1816. The English scientific expedition under the command of Captain James Kingston Tuckey came within sight of Madeira on 31 March of this year, and encountered a great number of turtles (*Testudo caretta*) sleeping on the surface of the water. 1838. On 16 September of this year a small American squadron arrived in Funchal, made up of the *Porpoise*, the sloops *Vincennes* and *Peacock* and the schooners *Sea-Gull* and *Flying-Fish*, under the command of Lieutenant Charles Wilkes. The scientists aboard these ships measured the height of Pico Ruivo and made some geological observations here, leaving Madeira on 25 September. 1839. The English ships *Erebus* and *Terror*, under the command of James Clark Ross and Francis Rawdon Crozier, visited Madeira in October of this year. Their officers measured the height of Pico Ruivo and made magnetic observations at Cape Verde, St Helena and the Cape of Good Hope before heading for the Antarctic regions and the other countries they explored. 1857. In June of this year the Austrian frigate *Novara*, commanded by Commodore Bernhard von Wüllerstorf-Urbair, was at Madeira on a voyage round the world. The expedition’s scientists measured the height of Pico Ruivo and received a great deal of information from the physician Dr António da Luz Pita, the military engineer Major António Pedro de Azevedo, the botanist João Maria Moniz and the Austrian consul Carlos Bianchi. 1883. In this year a French scientific expedition led by Alphonse Milne-Edwards, charged with carrying out oceanographic studies in the Atlantic, was in Madeiran waters aboard the *Talisman*. According to Milne-Edwards, there is in this sea an immense volcanic chain parallel to the coast of Africa, of which the islands of Cape Verde, the Canaries, Madeira and the Azores may be the only points not now covered by the waters. (See Atlantis.) 1897. On 12 September of this year the barque *Belgica* arrived in the harbour of Funchal from Ostend, carrying the Belgian scientific expedition that, under the command of Lieutenant Commander Adrien Gerlache, was bound for the Antarctic regions. The members of the expedition visited Curral das Freiras; among them were Lieutenant Danco, in charge of magnetic observations, Dr Artoski, in charge of meteorology and oceanography, and Dr Emil Racoviță, responsible for botany and zoology.

before: On 6 September of the same year the Norwegian ship *Fram* anchored in the harbour of Funchal to take on various goods brought by the German steamer *Hans Hoermann*. The *Fram*, bound for the Antarctic regions under the direction of Captain Amundsen, left our harbour on the 10th of that month. 1911. During the scientific campaign carried out this year by Prince Albert of Monaco aboard the *Hirondelle II*, Dr Luís Gain made some collections of marine algae along the coasts of the archipelago. Prince Albert also visited the waters of the archipelago in 1901, 1904, 1912 and in other years, aboard either the *Hirondelle* or the *Princesa Alice*, and on one of his voyages he visited Deserta Grande, which he described in his book entitled *La Carrière d'un navigateur*.

before: The process for the Funchal quay made no progress, and only in 1886, when the construction of the Pontinha mole (breakwater) had already been approved, was the carrying out of the work taken up. before: It is probable that before the parish was created, as happened in almost all the parishes of this island, there was some chapel with its own chaplain who performed the ecclesiastical duties there. before: The seat of the parish remained in the chapel of Piedade for only a few years. In 1580 Dona Guiomar Lomelino, who lived in this parish (*freguesia*), donated to the parish priest Nicolau de Abreu the land needed to build the new church, presbytery and adjoining glebe (*passal*). We do not know when the building of the church was finished or when services began to be held in it. It underwent various alterations over time, and around 1637 and 1688 major repairs were carried out. The royal decree (*alvará*) of 30 October 1748 authorised the payment of 2,450,000 *réis* (old Portuguese money of account; 1$000 = 1,000 réis, 1:000$000 = one conto = 1,000,000 réis) for the works on a new church, which turned out to be too small for the population of the parish. The chapel of the Santíssimo Sacramento (Most Holy Sacrament) was built in 1763 on the orders of Manuel Caldeira da Silva, as administrator of the entailed estate (*vínculo*) founded by Marcelino de Moura and in fulfilment of a vow the latter had made; this chapel belonged to the same entailed estate. Around 1820 the building of a new parish church was planned, estimated at twenty-six *contos* (one million réis) de réis, but the attempt never went beyond a mere project.

before: In some interesting articles on this parish published in the *Correio da Madeira*, we find the following lines on the creation of the curacy (*curato*): ‘As parish activity kept growing after 1700, at the request of Father Caetano Alberto de Araújo and by royal decree of Maria I dated 31 July 1797, the curacy of this parish was created, with the obligation of residence near the chapel of São João Nepomuceno (St John of Nepomuk), at Lombo dos Leais, the curate receiving an annual stipend (*côngrua*) of one and a half *moios* of wheat and one and a half *pipas* of wine. before: Several entails (*instituições vinculares*) had their seat in this locality, and we give a brief account of some of them. The entailed house (*casa vinculada*) of the Baptistas was founded at the end of the 15th century by the Genoese Micer Baptista; its last representative was João Bettencourt Baptista, who died a few years ago (1921). The entailed estate (*morgadio*) of Referta was established by Manuel Telo Moniz de Meneses, who died in 1713; its last administrator was Manuel Raimundo Telo Moniz Torresão, and its representative today is his granddaughter Dona Cristina de Campos Soares (1921). There was also the entail founded by Father Cristóvão Moniz de Meneses, whose last representative was the holder of the entail (*morgado*) António Caetano de Aragão; and the entailed estates founded by Captain Brás Moniz Telo de Meneses and by Captain Inácio de Carvalho Favila.

before: The private levadas, or levadas of *heréus* (co-owners of the water rights of a levada), were originally administered by those who had built them and held rights of ownership over them. Later the owners, or more precisely the usufructuaries of the waters, began to appoint an administrator to manage the affairs of these levadas, whom they called the levada judge (Juiz da Levada, the administrator of a levada). It is true that the State always regarded itself as the sole owner of the springs that fed the various aqueducts, and at times official documents even asserted that the levadas themselves belonged to the State. In practice, however, what was observed, and what amounted to customary law throughout the archipelago, was that the *heréus* considered themselves the owners and masters of the levadas and the proprietors, or at least the perpetual usufructuaries, of the flows that fed them. As a result, the levadas were administered by the *heréus* through judges they elected, although this choice had to be approved or ratified by the donataries, the governors-general, the governors and captains-general or the civil governors. In many cases, though not always, the governors appointed the judges and countersigned the warrants of appointment. These acts of interference in the administration of the levadas, however, were generally a mere formality, since the choice had in fact already been made by the *heréus* concerned. With the promulgation of the Civil Code in 1868 this form of approval disappeared, and the owners of waters and levadas began to administer them through management committees elected annually by the general assembly of the *heréus*. The law of 26 July 1888 gave legal capacity to the assembly of the *heréus*, which thereby became a true association with all the privileges the law guarantees to such bodies, making the administration of the levadas still more independent.

before: He arrived in Madeira on 8 July 1844 and governed this bishopric until the beginning of 1848, when he was transferred to the diocese of Beja by decree of 18 April of the same year. He left behind him here the most honourable memories of his diocesan administration, despite the struggles he had to sustain and the great difficulties that beset his episcopate. It was in his time that Protestant proselytism rose at its most tenacious and threatening. Its bold leader, a propagandist of talent and learning, was Dr Roberto Kalley, a most distinguished physician and a born orator who drew the crowds after him. Much was written in the press, in pamphlets and in books about the Calvinist propaganda in Madeira, whose chief promoter was Dr Kalley, but the history of that agitated and tumultuous period of Madeiran history has yet to be written. To escape the people’s fury, the celebrated Scottish physician had to embark in secret, carried to the beach in a hammock (*rede*, slung from a pole and carried by two bearers) and dressed in women’s clothes. When his flight was discovered, his furniture and his choice library were set on fire at his residence at Vale Formoso, for which our government had to pay compensation of several *contos* (one million réis) de réis.

before: In the Fort of São Lourenço (St Lawrence) there was a chapel dedicated to the martyr St Lawrence. It is quite old and already existed in 1566, the year in which French corsairs sacked the city. It had its own chaplain, and the oldest royal decree (*alvará*) we have found appointing that chaplain is dated 15 November 1641. We have seen somewhere that on 3 October 1846 Councillor (conselheiro, honorary title of the royal council) José Silvestre Ribeiro ordered an inventory of the silver objects belonging to this chapel, which weighed 36 pounds, and had them deposited in the Central Treasury. A new inventory was made on 3 December 1856, with further pieces added, the whole weighing 65 pounds of silver. In 1856 the chapel’s vestments were given to the church of Achadas da Cruz (see Palácio de São Lourenço).

before: The chapel of São Lourenço in the locality (*sítio*) of the same name in the parish (*freguesia*) of Fajã da Ovelha is quite old, for in the first years of the 16th century it was already the seat of a chaplaincy (capelania), which later became a parish. It served as the parish church until the middle of the 18th century, when the new church was built. An old tradition records that this chapel belonged to the Afonsos Jardins, who were among the earliest settlers there and owners of the *lombada* (long ridge between valleys) on which the chapel stands.

before: A tree of the laurel family (Lauraceae), found mainly in the north of Madeira, where it grows down almost to the sea. It can reach more than twenty metres in height and has leathery, hairless leaves, sometimes almost opposite, and small flowers arranged in panicles shorter than the leaves. The protuberances often seen on the upper surface of the leaves of this tree are a gall of the *Erineum* type. Barbuzano wood is very little used by cabinet-makers because it is extremely hard. On the island of Porto Santo the name barbuzano is given to *Sideroxylon Marmulano*, a species known in Madeira as *marmulano* (Sideroxylon marmulano, a shrub).

before: The street runs from the Praça dos Lavradores until it meets the southern end of Rua da Rochinha and the Travessa do Arcipreste. It is one of the oldest streets in Funchal and was once called Diogo Afonso. Its name comes from the fact that the Hospital de Santa Isabel (St Elizabeth of Portugal) stood in it for many years, before it moved to the building it occupies at present. Later it was also called Rua de Santo António, a name many people still use today, because a chapel with that dedication was built there; its ruins lie on the south side of the street. Next to the hospital stood the old parish church of the parish (*freguesia*) of Santa Maria Maior.

before: Walls have long existed along the banks of some streams, to prevent the water from eroding the land or flooding the settlements. On 28 June 1613 the Municipal Council (*Câmara Municipal*) of Funchal protested against various acts of the Governor, Dom Manuel Pereira Coutinho, and in particular against the way in which he opposed it in the direction of the works on the streams ‘in manifest violation of the royal provisions’. The charters of 4 January 1660, 9 August 1747 and 18 July 1748 ordered, respectively, the building of protective walls on the streams of Ribeira Brava, Santa Cruz and Machico.

before: On 30 May 1772 the captain of engineers Domingos Rodrigues Martins was summoned to the Municipal Council (*Câmara Municipal*) of Funchal to draw up the estimate for rebuilding the walls of the streams, without which the Council could not petition the Monarch to carry out this improvement. The *Relação dos Estragos causados pela Tempestade que houve na noite do dia 9 de Outubro de 1803 na ilha da Madeira* (‘Account of the damage caused by the storm on the night of 9 October 1803 on the island of Madeira’), published on p. 723 of the *Saudades da Terra*, refers to the destruction by the waters of ‘high and strong walls, built of stone and lime along the eastern and western banks of the three streams, for the safety of the city’. This shows that something was done in that year of 1772, or shortly afterwards, to protect Funchal against the danger of floods. The present walls of the city’s streams were begun, or greatly improved, in 1804 under the direction of Brigadier Reinaldo Oudinot, who also proposed various urgent works on the streams of Santa Cruz, Machico, Porto da Cruz, Calheta, Madalena, Ponta do Sol, Ribeira Brava and Tábua, some of which were carried out. On 9 December 1804 the brigadier reported to the Viscount of Anadia ‘that the rains had produced great floods in the streams, which had demonstrated the effectiveness and solidity of the works already built both in Funchal and in Machico, Santa Cruz, Ponta do Sol and in the parishes of Tábua and Madalena.’

before: A small reptile, very common in Madeira, which does great damage to grapes, tomatoes, etc. It already existed on the island before the discovery, for Gaspar Frutuoso refers to it in the following terms: ‘on this fresh island no other kind of creature was found but some little lizards the size of a finger, which do no notable harm and are not venomous’. Frutuoso also recorded lizards on the island of Porto Santo (see *Saudades*, p. 50), and the naturalist Richard Thomas Lowe found among the calcareous formations of Piedade the jaws of a small vertebrate which Professor Owen identified as a reptile. For lack of material for comparison, however, Owen could not state whether it was identical to the Madeiran lizard.

before: By a charter of 22 September 1460, Henry the Navigator made a grant to the University of Coimbra (*Universidade de Coimbra*) of ‘twelve marks of silver’, to be paid out of the tithes that the Order of Christ collected in the Madeira archipelago and intended specifically for the professor holding the ‘prime’ chair of the faculty of theology. before: He was born in the parish (*freguesia*) of Camacha in 1826 and died in Funchal on 8 July 1887. He worked as a primary schoolteacher in Machico, and at his death was a copying clerk in the Municipal Administration (*Administração do Concelho*, the government's local civil office) of Funchal. For many years he edited the *Voz do Povo*, in which invective and diatribe were at times the main arguments of his polemics and press campaigns. He handled the scurrilous verse of the *gazetilha* (satirical verse column in a newspaper) with great ease, using it to wound and deride his opponents and adversaries. He did not spare even his own son-in-law, the journalist João Augusto de Ornelas, whom Silveira sought to wound and humiliate in *Filho do Ferreiro*, a pamphlet that has gone through several editions, intended especially for the Madeiran colonies in Demerara, Trinidad, etc. His journalistic output is vast, but his writings are generally modelled on the *Tripa Virada* and the *Besta Esfolada* of José Agostinho de Macedo. Some of his poems appear in the *Flores da Madeira*.

before: Outside Funchal, the epidemic first appeared in the parish of Ponta do Pargo on 11 July and in Machico on the 14th, and then successively in the remaining parishes, in some of which the mortality rate was very low. The heaviest influx of patients was at the Misericórdia hospital, where on some days it was impossible to admit cholera patients, so great was the number of sufferers filling the wards and every room with space to lay a straw mattress. before: ‘If the epidemic’, says an official report, ‘had proved terrifying in the municipality (*concelho*) of Funchal through the havoc it wrought, in the rural municipalities its horrors were redoubled, for besides the large number of victims, the population was also struggling with hunger and had neither physicians nor medicines to help the sick. The state of despondency, distress and misery these municipalities reached was truly indescribable. Many patients died for complete want of medical aid; others perished from lack of food. Most of the makeshift hospitals were in dreadful condition, and all lacked the most basic supplies. The sick lay on the floor on wretched straw mattresses, and men and women, and the living and the dead, were often found there together.’ In view of this, the authorities decided that the medical sub-delegates Branco and Brand should travel round the island, taking medicines and other aid to the cholera sufferers. No more could have been done than was done. According to the official figures, cholera killed 7,041 people, but it has always been claimed that the number who succumbed to the epidemic was about ten thousand. In the municipality of Funchal 2,014 people died: 311 in the parish of the Sé (Funchal Cathedral (*Sé*)), 519 in São Pedro, 376 in Santa Maria Maior, 69 in São Roque, 129 in São Martinho, 315 in Santa Luzia, 214 in Santo António, 83 in Monte and 88 in São Gonçalo.

before: The first cases to attract the attention of doctors were those of two sisters who lived near the Paiol. One fell ill on 20 October 1910 and the other on the 23rd of the same month, and the latter died on 4 November following. The proper precautions were taken at once: the house was isolated, disinfection was carried out, contacts were medically examined, etc. Two more cases then appeared in the Rua da Imperatriz Dona Amélia, and others were soon recorded in various parts of the city. Before long the disease appeared in Câmara de Lobos, Machico and other places. The population began to grow alarmed. The chief authority of the district, deeply concerned at the spread of the disease, convened the Consultative Board of Hygiene (*Junta Consultiva de Higiene*) on 17 November, and more vigorous and effective measures were then taken. At the same time he pressed the central government to adopt extraordinary measures and to send indispensable resources that could not be found in Madeira.

before: It is also known as the Ilhéu do Farol (Lighthouse Islet). Next to the Ponta de São Lourenço, and separated from it only by a narrow channel, lies the small islet called Agostinho. Very close to it is the Ilhéu dos Desembarcadouros, and a short distance away the Ilhéu de Fora, or do Farol. The last two are separated from each other by a channel known as the Boqueirão Grande, which is about 180 metres wide and 8 deep and gives easy passage to the coastal steamers that frequently pass that way. This islet is the easternmost point of Madeira, and since September 1870 it has had a working lighthouse, which has rendered valuable service to shipping. Its lantern stands about 100 m above sea level and is situated at 32° 41' north latitude and 16° 39' west longitude (Greenwich). It is a white light with intermittent flashes, visible from 25 miles away. There is also a telegraph station there, linked to the central station in Funchal. To the south-west of the Ilhéu de Fora lies the dangerous shoal of Badajeira (see that entry). The altitude of this islet is 107 m.

before: Under the letters of grant of Prince Henry the Navigator, only the donataries could sell salt on this island and on Porto Santo. This privilege did not disappear when the donataries' captaincies of Madeira were turned into chief alcaideships, but it seems to have been little respected in later times. On 6 February 1769 an order was issued that the representative (*procurador*) of the Marquis of Castelo Melhor should not be obliged to supply the population with salt, and that anyone might unload and sell this commodity, as had been the practice before.

before: The regulations (*regimento*) of the Hospital de Santa Isabel (St Elizabeth of Portugal) in this city, approved by the Managing Board (*Mesa Gerente*) of the Holy House of Mercy (*Santa Casa da Misericórdia*) on 10 August 1816 and confirmed by royal warrant (*provisão régia*) of 19 October 1819, created, in the nineteen articles that make up Title V, a medical-surgical public class (*aula*) attached to the hospital. Its purpose was ‘to prevent the ruin of humanity in this Colony through the ignorance of the Barbers, who without the proper knowledge go about the countryside treating people, bringing to the grave those who would still be alive if they were treated by skilled practitioners, or by men less ignorant than such quacks’.

Its purpose was ‘to prevent the ruin of humanity in this Colony through the ignorance of the Barbers, who without the proper knowledge go about the countryside treating people, bringing to the grave those who would still be alive if they were treated by skilled practitioners, or by men less ignorant than such quacks’.

before: We do not know when this class began to operate or how long it lasted, but we know that it had a short existence, for in 1824 the governor and captain-general informed the government in mainland Portugal of the urgent need to create a Class of Operative Surgery. He pointed out that on Porto Santo and in the Madeiran countryside there was not a single operating surgeon, and that ‘one found only the odd wretched bloodletter, of whose competence many of those who called him in for the treatment and cure of their diseases have been victims’. The same governor took up this weighty matter again the following year, without his efforts and endeavours producing the slightest practical result.

before: The decree of 29 December 1836 created a medical-surgical school in each of the capitals of the overseas districts. Each school was to have two chairs: the first would teach anatomy, physiology, surgical operations and the art of obstetrics, and the second pathology, materia medica and therapeutics. They were to be held respectively by the principal physician and the principal surgeon of the hospital to which the school was attached. The first chair would have an assistant demonstrator, who would prepare the anatomical work, and the hospital's pharmacist would give lessons in pharmacy in the hospital dispensary. The ministerial order (*portaria*) of 16 January 1837, addressed to the administrator-general (*administrador geral*) of this district, ordered the provisions of that decree to be carried out in full in Madeira. The Medical-Surgical School of Funchal had been created.

before: The Administrative Committee (*Comissão Administrativa*) of the Holy House of Mercy (*Santa Casa da Misericórdia*), then chaired by João Agostinho Jervis de Atouguia, set about carrying out the orders issued by the central government. Without delay it adapted the former ward for British subjects and two adjoining rooms to house the new School, which thus became the highest-ranking educational establishment here in Madeira. The surgeon, physician and apothecary of the Santa Isabel Hospital at the time were, respectively, Dr Luís Henriques, Dr Lourenço José Moniz and the pharmacist Nicandio Joaquim de Azevedo. In accordance with the express wording of the decree, they were entrusted with teaching the chairs that made up the new School's course. Because the illustrious Madeiran Dr Lourenço Moniz was a deputy for this island and had given up his post as professor at the School, he was replaced in this office by Dr António da Luz Pita. The Funchal medical school had the good fortune to begin its work under the direction of two eminent physicians, who brought great honour to this new establishment of higher education. From the outset it began to earn the good reputation it always enjoyed, not only in our country but also in some foreign lands.

before: At dawn on 22 August the squadron set course for the bay of Machico, and at 11 in the morning the brig *Infante D. Sebastião* opened fire on the Forte do Ancoradouro (Anchorage Fort) and then on the Amparo battery. Both put up only a weak and short-lived resistance, their garrisons fleeing in disorder almost at the first shots fired by the enemy squadron. The Miguelite (supporter of the absolutist King Miguel) troops then landed ‘without the slightest resistance and in complete comfort’, according to the unimpeachable testimony of a contemporary of the events.

before: This name was formerly given in the archipelago to *Sempervivum glutinosum*, a member of the Crassulaceae now known as *saião* or *ensaião*. ‘Less than half a *légua* (league, about 5 km) beyond the Ilhéu da Fonte da Areia,’ says Frutuoso, ‘towards the east on the northern side, there is a settlement of up to fifteen inhabitants, which is called Farrobo because there grows there this herb so called, with which the fishermen dye their lines.’

before: *Sempervivum glutinosum* has disappeared from Porto Santo, but it is quite common on the rocks of Madeira, where it is still used to dye fishing lines and make them tougher and stronger. The lines are rubbed with the crushed bark of the plant and then soaked in urine, a process that gives them a black colour, making them barely visible to the fish.

before: The Lancasterian School, founded in 1819, was first housed in a building at Ribeirinho. From there it moved to Travessa do Surdo and then to the building on Rua da Princesa, today Rua 31 de Janeiro, which now houses the boys’ school of the parish (*freguesia*) of Santa Luzia. This building was commissioned by the Associação Funchalense, which existed to promote mutual instruction; the association had acquired the land at the end of 1822.
