before: After Fitzgerald, others introduced cattle from England and elsewhere to Madeira. Crossed with the island’s animals, these gave rise to a breed of medium build, but larger than the local breed. The crossbreds predominate today among Madeiran cattle and are generally known as ‘English cattle’, whereas on Porto Santo the local breed predominates, having become smaller there than on Madeira.

before: Within the local breed two sub-breeds may be distinguished: the red and the *alvaçã* (whitish). The first, the more common, is found in every parish of Madeira and is recognised by its red or dark yellow coat. The second is confined to the municipalities of Porto do Moniz and Calheta and is characterised mainly by its white or whitish coat. Cattle of the red sub-breed are also known as *profetas* or ‘Porto Santo cattle’, while those of the *alvaçã* sub-breed are often called *gado maneiro* or ‘Ponta do Pargo cattle’.
after: Within the local breed two sub-breeds may be distinguished: the red and the *alvaçã* (whitish). before: Crossbreeding increased the milk yield of the native breed, but weakened its spirit for work and its ability to haul heavy loads over the rugged terrain of our island. Crossbred cows are said to give between 900 and 1500 litres of milk a year, but the agronomist Eduardo Grande allows that the yield may reach 1770 litres in the parishes from Ribeira da Janela to Canhas, owing to the atmospheric humidity, the quality of the grazing and other conditions found there. Daily yield at the peak of lactation does not generally exceed 6 to 8 litres, although cases of 14 and 15 litres are cited.

before: Formerly numerous cattle of the archipelago’s breed were raised in the uplands, but at present almost all these animals are kept in stalls or under a mixed regime of grazing and stall-feeding. On the Paul da Serra, at Achadas da Cruz and in a few other places, some free-ranging cattle are still found, generally destined for slaughter.

before: Around 1891 a stallion of good breed was brought to Madeira to improve the quality of the local animals. No benefit came of this introduction, however, perhaps because of the great difference in size between the breeding stallion and the island’s mares. After spending some time in Fajã da Ovelha, the horse came to Funchal, where it was kept for a while by the Municipal Council (*Câmara Municipal*), and it finally went on to Lisbon, to return to the stud or establishment that had lent it.

before: Horse breeding, which is of no importance on the island at present, is confined to the Paul da Serra and Santo da Serra. The animals are generally raised in the open, but when they are two or three years old the breeder brings them in to sell them if they have reached a certain size; those of inferior quality are sent back to the uplands if they can be put to no use. Very small colts are usually castrated to prevent them from breeding.

before: According to Eduardo Grande, in 1802 the regent sent a dispatch to the captain-general (capitão-general, military governor of Madeira) Dom José Manuel da Câmara, congratulating him ‘on the good result of the introduction of long-woolled sheep’. This stock degenerated on the island, however, as did other well-bred animals introduced later. Eduardo Grande found documents in the archive of the civil government showing that in that same year of 1802 the Irishman Fitzgerald offered the Government a pair of wool-bearing sheep of the finest breed in England.

before: The Desertas goat, descended from animals released on those islands from time to time, is smaller than the Madeiran goat, and differs from it also in its sturdier limbs and straighter horns. The billy goats’ horns are stout and twisted at the tip. Among the goats brought into Funchal every day to supply milk, many belong to the breed of the neighbouring archipelago of the Canary Islands; they differ from the local goats in their thicker muzzle, much longer hair, large drooping ears and some other features.

before: The first bombardment was preceded by the torpedoing of the gunboat *La Surprise*, of the French navy, the *Kanguroo*, a steamer of the same nationality, and the *Dacia*, a British merchant steamer in the service of the French government. These vessels, which lay at anchor in our harbour, were torpedoed a short distance from the shore, the pirate having managed to approach them without being seen by their crews. The American yacht *Eleanor A. Percy*, which was also in the waters of our bay, was spared by the submarine, because Germany was not yet at war with the United States at that time.

The American yacht *Eleanor A. Percy*, which was also in the waters of our bay, was spared by the submarine, because Germany was not yet at war with the United States of America at that time.

before: The bombardment lasted from 9 to 11 in the morning; *La Surprise* had been torpedoed at about half past eight. The Vigia battery fired 34 rounds and the Fort of São Tiago (St James the Greater) 18, none of which hit the submarine. The submarine fired some 50 shells at the city. Some burst in the air, and the rest fell at the following points: 2 in Rua Júlio da Silva Carvalho, 1 in Rua das Queimadas de Cima, 1 in Rua do Bispo, 2 in Calçada de Santa Clara, 1 in Rua Direita, 1 on the Pelourinho factory, 1 on the Quinta Vigia, 1 in the Municipal Garden and 1 in the Angústias cemetery.
after: The bombardment lasted from 9 to 11 in the morning; *La Surprise* had been torpedoed at about half past eight. Some burst in the air, and the rest fell at the following points: 2 in Rua Júlio da Silva Carvalho, 1 in Rua das Queimadas de Cima, 1 in Rua do Bispo, 2 in Calçada de Santa Clara, 1 in Rua Direita, 1 on the Pelourinho factory, 1 on the Quinta Vigia, 1 in the Jardim Municipal and 1 in the Angústias cemetery.

before: No one died in the city, and the material damage caused by the shells was not great. Only at sea were there dead and wounded. The wounded were taken to the civil hospital by the staff of the Red Cross delegation in Funchal, who gave excellent service.

before: The steamers suffered no damage, but in the city there was considerable destruction: 5 people were killed and some 30-odd wounded, some slightly, others seriously. Shells fell at the following points: in front of the fortress of São Tiago; 1 in Rua de São Filipe; 1 on the Lombo da Boa Vista; 1 at the Quinta Mãe dos Homens (Mother of Mankind); 1 on the Levada do Bom Sucesso; 2 on the Lombo do Terço; 1 in Rua do Dr. Juvenal; 1 at Choupana; 1 in the Municipal Garden; 1 in Travessa de Santa Catarina; 1 in Rua dos Aranhas; 1 at the Fort of São Lourenço (St Lawrence); 1 at the church of Santa Clara (St Clare of Assisi); 3 on the beach, 1 of them in front of the customs house and 2 beside the Funchal Harbour Master’s Office (*Capitania do Porto do Funchal*); 1 in Rua da Bela Vista; 1 near the Torreão factory (this one did not explode); 1 near the Pico de São João; 1 in Rua 5 de Junho; 1 near the Jewish Cemetery; 1 near the Hotel Jones; 1 near the Castelo do Pico (Peak Fort); 1 in the sea, opposite the point where the submarine cable comes ashore; and 1 near Travessa do Pasto. Other shells burst over the city, but caused no damage.

before: The shell that burst in the church of Santa Clara wounded Father Manuel da Silva Branco, who was celebrating Mass there, the sacristan and two women, one of whom died shortly afterwards at the Red Cross branch in Rua dos Netos.

before: ‘Diogo Lopes, da Estacada, says the annotator of the *Saudades*, was one of the first settlers of the island of Madeira: he lived in Câmara de Lobos, at the locality (*sítio*) of Torre, and his *sesmaria* (royal land grant to settlers on condition of cultivation) comprised a good part of the land lying from the Pico towards Funchal as far as the Covão.’

before: A very picturesque locality (*sítio*) in the parish (*freguesia*) of Santo da Serra, offering lovely views over the parishes of Porto da Cruz, Faial and Santana. It lies three kilometres from the parish church of Santo da Serra. As far as this locality the waters of the levadas (irrigation channels) of Furado, Juncal, Nova do Furado (or the Shareholders’ Levada) and Serra do Faial flow in a shared aqueduct. There the first passes into its own channel and the second goes on to the parish of Porto da Cruz. The waters of the other two levadas continue together as far as the locality of Lombo da Raiz (see that entry).
after: A very picturesque locality (*sítio*) in the parish (*freguesia*) of Santo da Serra (‘the saint of the uplands’), offering lovely views over the parishes of Porto da Cruz, Faial and Santana. before: The land that now forms the Jardim Municipal, Rua Hermenegildo Capelo and the site of the Teatro Manuel de Arriaga once made up the grounds of the Convent of São Francisco (St Francis of Assisi). Despite the opposition of the Franciscan friars, the street was opened there in 1814 and was given the name Rua dos Frades. In 1823 the market built by order of the city Council (*Câmara Municipal*) opened to the public on the site later set aside for the theatre, and the adjoining street became known as Rua do Mercado de São João. In 1885, when the explorers Hermenegildo Capelo and Roberto Ivens called at this island (see those entries), the Municipal Council resolved to give their names to the streets bordering the Jardim Municipal on the south and north.

before: One branch of the family of this surname descends from Gonçalo Alves de Araújo, who came to this island at the end of the 15th century and held land by *sesmaria* (royal land grant to settlers on condition of cultivation) in the village (*lugar*, settlement rank below a town) of Jardim do Mar, for which reason he was known as Gonçalo Alves do Jardim. Another branch comes from Afonso Enes de Araújo.

before: Calcium carbonate; orthorhombic system. It occurs on the basalts of Madeira and Porto Santo. On Madeira it is found in several forms: in geodes; in transparent twinned crystals resembling hexagonal prisms, but with re-entrant angles between the prism faces; in groups of needle-shaped crystals (acicular form), etc.

before: The highest eminence on Selvagem Grande, rising one hundred and fifty metres above the sea and falling sheer to the island’s western coast. It is a volcanic cone cut open on the west side. According to recent observations, its geological make-up includes various rocks. At the base, decomposed phonolites, overlain by compact basalts, stand out on one side, and on the other perfect phonolites, supporting horizontal strata of volcanic tuffs. On top of this assemblage lie masses of more or less scoriaceous, reddish limburgite, which form the summit of the Peak. The appearance of this cone, much of it already collapsed, seems to lead to the conclusion that in very remote ages it was one of the craters from which the materials that now form Selvagem Grande were ejected.

before: An inhabited locality (*sítio*) in the parish (*freguesia*) of São Martinho, where there is a chantry (capela) with the dedication of Nossa Senhora da Vitória (Our Lady of Victory). before: This is an old family surname in the archipelago, particularly on the island of Porto Santo, although it is almost extinct today. Belchior Baião, of noble lineage, was the first of this name to settle in Madeira. The family held an entailed estate (*morgadio*) on Porto Santo and was patron of a chapel in the parish church that is still known at present as the Capela da Morgada. Until a few years ago this chapel kept the characteristic stamp of Manueline buildings, and it was certainly the only part of the parish church that remained from the original construction.

before: It is likely that the striped skirts and embroidered bodices derived from old Moorish costumes, all the more so as it is known that there were once many Moors, chiefly in Funchal and Ponta do Sol. As for the *carapuça*, however, it is hard to guess its origin, although White tells us that in some of Rubens’s paintings an object very similar to this old Madeiran cap can be seen on ladies’ heads. The *carapuça* protected the head so poorly that it is surprising the people of this island wore it at all.

before: Sloane, Ovington, Captain Cook, Forster and Barrow make no mention of the *carapuça* in the accounts of their voyages, which leads us to believe that this cap only began to be worn in Madeira in the first quarter of the 19th century. Paulo Dias de Almeida, in his *Descrição da ilha da Madeira*, written in 1817 and published in the *Archivo da Marinha e Ultramar*, includes two plates showing *carapuças*, but without the long points that gave these caps the shape of inverted funnels.

before: In the parish (*freguesia*) of Caniço the men wear hats made of palm leaf which, although very durable, have nothing to recommend them in elegance or suppleness. We do not know when these hats first came into use.

before: Around the middle of the 19th century the councillors (*vereadores*) of the Municipal Council (*Câmara Municipal*) of Funchal wore capes, breeches and stockings at official ceremonies. It was still in this dress, together with the obsolete plumed hats, that the members of the municipality appeared at the funeral rites of Luís I and at the acclamation (*aclamação*, formal public proclamation of a new king) of Carlos I, both held in 1889, even though the municipal uniform had by then been reduced to the said capes, which were of black silk lined with white.

before: It runs from Rua de São Pedro to the Ponte Nova (New Bridge) over the Ribeira de Santa Luzia. Formerly, however, it ended at Rua dos Ferreiros, today Rua do Comércio, and the stretch bounded on the east by the said Ribeira de Santa Luzia was included in Rua da Ponte Nova.

before: Madeira has *Morus nigra* (black mulberry), whose sorosis fruits are edible and are used to prepare the mulberry rob employed as a gargle for quinsy, and *M. multicaulis* (white mulberry), whose leaves serve as food for silkworms. In May 1877 the Municipal Council (*Câmara Municipal*) of Funchal granted the Praça da Rainha (today Praça do Marquês de Pombal) for a nursery of white mulberries, and the late Count of Canavial went so far as to establish the nursery there, but it was short-lived. The cultivation of these mulberries is at present utterly abandoned. The black mulberry is widely grown on Porto Santo.

before: Vine-growing received a certain impetus in the 16th century, when the sugar industry began to decline in Madeira (see Wines), but it was after 1640 that we see it expand more strongly. At that time the English, settling here in greater numbers than before to engage in the wine trade, became the chief promoters of the crop. Frutuoso refers in several places in the *Saudades da Terra* to vine-growing in Madeira, but as regards grape varieties he mentions only Malmsey, which seems to have been the variety producing the island’s finest and most celebrated wines in the 16th century.

before: At the end of the 18th century many vines were planted in Madeira. Some time before, vine-growing had been introduced on Porto Santo, on the land of Areias and on other coastal ground: men maintained by the State were sent there to carry out the planting, which was done with cuttings supplied by the government.

before: The vineyards extend from the land near the coast up to 400 or 500 metres, and may even reach 600 and 700 metres in places less affected by mists. Vines are grown in the vicinity of Jardim da Serra, but the grapes ripen there much later than in Funchal.

before: In the archive of this city’s Council we found a reference to a request made by the Funchal Senate (*senado*, the municipal council) in 1493 for the construction of a *Tronco*, the name then given to the house intended for the detention of the insane. We believe that this request was not granted by the government in mainland Portugal or by the grand mastership of the Order of Christ. We do not know where the unfortunates afflicted by mental illness, particularly the poor and destitute, might have been confined, if indeed a house specially devoted to that humane purpose ever existed.

before: The regulations (*regimento*) of this city’s Civil Hospital, drawn up in 1816, were an excellent piece of work for their time and extremely thorough, at times descending into unnecessary detail. Yet they make no reference at all to the hospitalisation or detention of the insane, which leads us to suppose that such people were not then admitted there. The same is true of the regulations of 1834. It is only in the Regulation of 1844 that we first find an express provision for ‘some secure rooms for the insane, which must be separate from the other wards...’. Until the Manicómio Câmara Pestana was built, the poor insane were kept in some outbuildings of the hospital, and the inhumanity with which the hospital’s nurses and servants treated them became proverbial here.
after: The regulations (*regimento*) of this city’s Civil Hospital (*Hospital Civil*), drawn up in 1816, were an excellent piece of work for their time and extremely thorough, at times descending into unnecessary detail. before: Councillor (*conselheiro*, honorary title of the royal council) José Silvestre Ribeiro, who as head of the administration of this district sought to meet every public need, wrote to the Administrative Committee (*Comissão Administrativa*) of the Holy House of Mercy (*Santa Casa da Misericórdia*). He set out the reasons in favour of building a suitable edifice for the hospitalisation of the insane and promised his full support for this important improvement. The founding of an asylum went the same way as the removal of the old gaol and the construction of the quay, the Pontinha mole, the theatre and the fruit and vegetable market: they were stock subjects of the local press, especially at election time or when a shortage of news led the journalist to brew Tolentino’s tea once again.

before: What had long been regarded as an important improvement to be made, however, became the answer to a pressing and urgent need. The proportion of people afflicted by mental illness grew alarming, above all for the reasons we briefly set out in the article Junta Agrícola, where we spoke of the need to curb alcoholism by the strictest restriction of the production of spirit (*aguardente*, distilled from sugar cane or wine). The press intensified its campaign in view of the well-founded refusal to admit the insane to our hospital, the repugnant crowding of these wretches in the foul cells of the police station, and the large number of them wandering the streets and roads. The public then felt a deep compassion for this human misery and, at the same time, a general indignation at the criminal neglect to which the authorities abandoned the insane who were poor and lacked the means to be placed in suitable nursing homes. Madeira contributed to the official hospitalisation of the insane, but the Rilhafoles asylum refused to admit patients sent from this island, no doubt for lack of the necessary accommodation. A distinguished alienist who passed through this city vigorously condemned the distressing situation of the poor insane, and so brought into sharper relief the need to found a hospital to house those deprived of the light of reason.

before: These gentlemen formed themselves into a committee, with the first as chairman and the last as secretary, and the Viscount of Cacongo proposed founding an establishment for the hospitalisation of the insane. This would also serve as the monument to Dr Câmara Pestana and would bear the name of our illustrious fellow countryman. Another committee was joined to this one: it had been organised in this city to collect donations for the flood victims of the Azores and was made up of Dr António Jardim de Oliveira, the Count of Ribeiro Real, Dr João Augusto Teixeira and Canon Manuel Correia de Figueiredo. That committee held about two *contos*, and this sum became the nucleus or fund of the Manicómio Câmara Pestana committee.

before: The committee worked with great zeal and ardour, but the Madeirans failed to respond to its diligent efforts. A public subscription raised only about eight *contos* de réis (*conto*: one million réis), a sum far from sufficient for the undertaking, not only for constructing the building and installing the hospital but above all for running the establishment properly, even though only a small number of patients were to be admitted. Various proposals were put forward for the site of the hospital building, with particular preference for the convent grounds of the former Convento da Encarnação (Convent of the Incarnation). Despite the efforts made, however, the central government could not be persuaded to cede a plot of land for the construction. Housing it in part of the Hospital dos Lázaros (lepers' hospital) was also suggested, and one of the outbuildings of the Misericórdia building was likewise considered, but it was later recognised that these premises were unsuitable for properly accommodating an asylum, even if the indispensable and costly adaptation works were carried out. In the end, after hearing the opinions of the health authorities, the committee resolved to acquire the Quinta do Rochedo, in the parish (*freguesia*) of São Gonçalo. The purchase was completed on 28 March 1904 for the sum of five *contos*.

before: The first places in this archipelago to be raised to the rank of towns (*vila*), on account of their growth and because they served as the seats of the three captaincies, were Funchal (II-59), Machico (II-298) and Baleira (I-117). Despite his research, the learned commentator of the *Saudades da Terra* was unable to discover the charters creating them, or even the precise dates on which this took place. He conjectures, however, with the strongest probability, that it happened around 1451, as has already been stated in the articles on those towns. Funchal, which thanks to its situation, climate, fertile soil, spacious harbour and other notable circumstances soon reached an unusual growth in population, was raised to the rank of city by the royal decree (alvará régio) of 21 August 1508, which is transcribed on page 61 of volume II of this work.

before: The royal decree (*alvará*) of 2 December 1501 created the town and municipality of Ponta do Sol, whose area stretched from the parish (*freguesia*) of Tabua to that of Achadas da Cruz (see III-99). It was soon reduced to much more limited proportions when the parish of Calheta was raised to the rank of town and municipality by the royal decree of 1 July 1502 (see I-191). The parish of Santa Cruz, which soon rivalled that of Machico, became a municipality with the status of a town by the royal decree of 26 June 1515, despite the opposition raised by the judicial district (*comarca*) of Machico and by the head of that captaincy (see III-246).

before: The old Madeiran chronicles devote attention to Dona Isabel de Abreu because she was the chief protagonist of a drama that must have caused the most extraordinary sensation in its day, for her contemporaries and later generations alike to have written about it at such length. The facts are these. Dona Isabel de Abreu, widow of João Rodrigues de Noronha, son of the third captain-donatary (*capitão-donatário*) of Funchal, Simão Gonçalves da Câmara, was living in her house at Arco da Calheta, the owner of a considerable fortune. António Gonçalves da Câmara, a nephew of the same captain-donatary, who lived nearby, then forced his way into Dona Isabel’s house at an unseemly hour, intending to make her marry him. Dona Isabel managed to convince António Gonçalves da Câmara that a proposal of marriage made in such circumstances was improper, and invited him to return the following day, when the formalities of the marriage could be arranged, to which she would gladly consent. António da Câmara set out with a retinue of some fifty horsemen from Ponta do Sol and Ribeira Brava and made for Dona Isabel’s house. In the words of one chronicler, however, she ‘made herself strong in her houses with her people, of whom she had many, and António Gonçalves, finding himself mocked, insulted and affronted, returned to his estate, embarking a few days later for Lisbon’.

before: Some years later António Gonçalves da Câmara returned to his house in Madeira, still bent on his old aim of marrying Dona Isabel de Abreu. One day, as she was riding to the town (*vila*) of Calheta with some relatives and passed in front of António Gonçalves’s residence, he seized the reins of her horse and, helped by armed men, forced her into his house. News of this extraordinary affair was brought to the *ouvidor* (judicial officer of the donatary or the Crown) of Funchal, since the captain-donatary was absent. The *ouvidor* arrived with a large armed force, which was to face the resistance António Gonçalves meant to offer, for he was preparing to defy the *ouvidor*’s orders and keep Dona Isabel de Abreu captive in his house. A fierce fight was imminent, with supporters, relatives and friends on both sides, when António Gonçalves da Câmara and Isabel de Abreu appeared on a balcony of the residence. They declared that they had reached an amicable agreement and that the *ouvidor* and the force with him could withdraw.

before: As these men were preparing to leave, Dona Isabel de Abreu let her intended husband know that, ‘since many of his relatives and friends had come with the Ouvidor, it was not right that they should go back so long a way without eating and, now that all was at peace, he should invite them’. Heeding Dona Isabel de Abreu’s wishes, António Gonçalves ordered ‘the ouvidor with his men, the alcaides, bailiffs and judges of all the towns and places of that captaincy to enter the hall; and Dona Isabel rushed forward and clung to him, saying and complaining that António Gonçalves was holding her by force in that house and that he should aid her with justice’. In the company of the *ouvidor* and the one hundred and fifty men who made up the armed force, Dona Isabel de Abreu set out for Funchal. before: Águeda de Abreu, sister of Isabel de Abreu, would not accept either the marriage or the violence that had preceded it, and she laid her complaints before the monarch. He sent the high court judge (*desembargador*) Gaspar Vaz to Madeira to investigate this strange affair, as a result of which some were sentenced to death and others to banishment. António Gonçalves da Câmara went into hiding and later fled to the Canary Islands, while his wife withdrew to the Convent of Santa Clara (St Clare of Assisi). From the Canaries he went on to Africa, where he rendered valuable service and distinguished himself by his bravery and courage. This, and still more, no doubt, the intercession with the monarch of his mother, Dona Joana de Eça, who was chief lady of the bedchamber to the queen, won him a pardon, and he was able to return to his homeland, where he lived for some years more with his wife, Dona Isabel de Abreu.

before: This is one of the busiest streets in Funchal, running from Rua 5 de Outubro to the Ponte do Torreão. In former times the name Ferreiros applied only to the part of the street running from its beginning to the so-called Largo do Chafariz, or Largo de São Sebastião. In relatively recent times, the section between the Largo do Chafariz and the Largo do Colégio was still called Rua do Peru; the section between the Colégio (College) and Rua dos Netos was called Rua do Estudo; and the section from Rua dos Netos to the Torreão was called Rua do Pinheiro. The name Ferreiros (‘Blacksmiths’) must certainly have come from the presence there of a number of blacksmiths’ workshops. ‘Christovão Martim de Agrinhão,’ says an old nobiliary, ‘was a *fidalgo* of the Household of the Duke of Bragança and came to this island from Peru, in the Spanish Indies, and was therefore called o Peru, a name he gave to the street where he lived.’ For many years the Jesuits held their classes in Rua dos Ferreiros, and after their expulsion the so-called Aulas do Pátio continued there; the lyceum (state secondary school) was also installed there in 1837. This amply explains the name Estudo (‘Study’) given to part of the street. Frutuoso, speaking of Rua Direita, says that ‘it is the largest in the city, and leads to the Pinheiro, which is a tree standing at its end, the largest and most beautiful in the city’. It should be noted that, although the Pinheiro (‘Pine Tree’) stood on the left bank of the stream, the place known by that name extended to the right bank. It should also be borne in mind that a considerable part of the present Rua dos Ferreiros ran alongside the stream, rather than at a distance from it as it does today.

before: ‘Now, this was the period when the islands of Porto Santo and Madeira were discovered, in the first quarter of the 15th century. From then until past the middle of the 16th century, many settlers flocked here – nobles, merchants and commoners, Portuguese in the greater number, but not a few foreigners too: Spaniards, Italians, Flemings, Englishmen, Frenchmen and Germans – who, together with the still medieval ideas and customs of each country, brought their ancient poetry to these islands. Many Moors, captured on the opposite Moroccan coast and brought here, spread their tales and rigmaroles here. Finally, Philippine rule, besides the garrison of some four hundred Castilian soldiers it placed in this Archipelago, gave occasion for new peninsular inhabitants to emigrate here, and both groups inevitably brought with them some of those old ballads that so abound in their homeland. – This was the period of Madeiran progress and prosperity. The island of Madeira then became extremely rich through the sugar industry and its building timber; these two branches of trade and its geographical position raised it to an emporium of national and foreign shipping. And because it was the first and chief of the Portuguese colonies, it was made the diocesan metropolis of all our newly discovered overseas territories, from Brazil to Asia. All this contributed powerfully to attracting new settlers to this island and, with them, new examples of the narrative poetry of the Middle Ages. – From all these elements, the nucleus of the Madeiran population, one may deduce the provenance, variety and richness of the traditional narrative poetry of this archipelago.

before: ‘Once medieval narrative poetry had taken root in this way, causes no less particular kept it alive until now in the oral tradition of these islands. The island of Porto Santo, from the time it was discovered and settled, remained almost forgotten in its smallness and its poorer productive conditions; and its poetic tradition, scant but genuine, has lain there for almost four centuries, like its neglected population, geographically and socially isolated in the vastness of the Atlantic. The island of Madeira, supplanted in the sugar and timber industries by America and Africa, declined suddenly from the end of the 16th century. As a result of this, and of other causes, it lost its pre-eminence as a nautical emporium and its metropolitan crozier, and for almost two centuries it remained as if abandoned to misfortune in the solitude of the waters, until its precious wines restored it to wealth and to European society. Each of its larger or smaller centres of population, separated from one another by the deep basalt clefts of the land, converged on the parish community, within sight of each bell tower; there, in turn, each family of settlers or farmers, bound by the need for daily labour on the lord’s land that it made fruitful, toils and vegetates around the hearth, which is both its refuge and its prison. And the population, thus doubly isolated from outside contact by the sea and by adversity, and ever more inwardly concentrated by the ruggedness of the country and the servile condition of the farmer, has for that very reason preserved the medieval narrative poetry entrusted to its tradition: prosperity brought it, decline preserved it. In this lies the history of the Madeiran poetic tradition up to the middle of the 18th century. ‘And it was time to collect this tradition and preserve it in a book; for modern institutions and reforms, the new schools and better means of internal and external communication will produce their natural effects; and after another half-century, the new life to which civilisation calls these peoples will have diluted, if not entirely extinguished, the old traditional poetry in their memory.’ In a letter from Dr Álvaro Rodrigues de Azevedo to the illustrious writer Teófilo Braga, in March 1880 (*Quarenta anos de vida literária*, page 118), the learned annotator of the *Saudades* says: ‘Besides the *Romanceiro*, I have collected the *Cancioneiro Popular* of this archipelago in two volumes, still in draft. I consider it of no less value than the former. And, being unable to meet my friend’s request with any example of the ballad genre, which I do not have, because I included all of them in the *Romanceiro*, I offer you the whole *Cancioneiro*, for which purpose I shall set about putting it in order in good time.’ In a note to this letter, Dr Teófilo Braga reports that, unfortunately, this promise was never fulfilled. It is greatly to be regretted that the songbook collected by Dr Álvaro de Azevedo should have gone astray, if indeed it was ever sent to Dr Teófilo Braga. Or might it still be in the possession of his heirs? If so, it would be desirable to obtain a faithful copy of it and to entrust a competent person with overseeing its publication. We do not know what kinds of poetic composition make up the *Cancioneiro* referred to above. Notwithstanding the recognised authority of Dr Álvaro de Azevedo shown in his books of literary criticism, we wish to draw the attention of those who may be interested to an interesting article on the *Romanceiro* of Madeira written by that consummate master of these subjects, the notable philologist Dr Leite de Vasconcelos, published on pages 184–192 of volume XXXIII of the *Revista Lusitana*, which deserves to be read and considered. He disagrees with some of Dr Azevedo’s assertions, setting out the arguments he judged most compelling to prove his case, while paying the illustrious commentator of the *Saudades* the tribute of his highest esteem. The length of that article does not allow us to reproduce it in these pages.

before: He was a half-prebendary canon (*cónego de meia prebenda*) of Funchal Cathedral (*Sé*), a position he took up in 1572, and in 1590 he was appointed a canon with a full prebend. We do not know where he was born, nor any other personal details concerning him. His name is well known to those engaged in research into Madeiran history, because he was perhaps the first person here in Madeira to devote himself to studies of this kind. Taking as the basis of his work a short account of the discovery of Madeira left by Gonçalo Aires (see that entry), a companion of Zarco, and ‘drawing, says Frutuoso, on the registers of the councils of the whole island (all of which were handed over to him)’, he wrote the *História e Informação dos ilustres capitães da ilha da Madeira*.

before: Was the work of Canon Jerónimo Dias Leite lost? Referring to the authors who deal with the Machin affair, Dr Álvaro de Azevedo states that he owns an anonymous manuscript entitled *Historia do descobrimento da ilha da Madeira e da descendência nobilissima dos seus valerosos Capitães*. He presumes it to be the original written by Dias Leite shortly before 1590, and adds elsewhere that it is ‘written on 22 small quarto leaves and a few lines more, that is, eleven sheets of paper’. This seems to indicate that it is the very original manuscript of which Gaspar Frutuoso speaks.
after: Was the work of Canon Jerónimo Dias Leite lost? Referring to the authors who deal with the Robert Machin affair, Dr Álvaro de Azevedo states that he owns an anonymous manuscript entitled *Historia do descobrimento da ilha da Madeira e da descendência nobilissima dos seus valerosos Capitães*. He presumes it to be the original written by Dias Leite shortly before 1590, and adds elsewhere that it is ‘written on 22 small quarto leaves and a few lines more, that is, eleven sheets of paper’. This seems to indicate that it is the very original manuscript of which Gaspar Frutuoso speaks.

before: He was the son of João Pestana Santos and Dona Carlota Amália Drumond da Veiga Pestana, and was born in Funchal on 25 December 1895. Having completed his preparatory studies at the lyceum (state secondary school) of this city in 1913, he enrolled in the Faculty of Sciences of the University of Coimbra to study civil engineering. However, when he was called up for the army in 1916, after Portugal entered the Great War, he was at once summoned to the school for militia officers on account of his scientific qualifications. He was posted as an officer cadet to the 30th Infantry Regiment (*infantaria 30*) on 1 May 1917 and commissioned second lieutenant on 5 September of the same year. Mobilised to serve with the Portuguese Expeditionary Corps (*C. E. P.*) in France, he left for that country on 11 September of the same year. There he met a glorious death at the Battle of the Lys on 9 April 1918, after spending seven months in the trenches and giving countless proofs of his military spirit and valour there. The Portuguese press wrote at length about the ill-fated officer João Paulo da Veiga Pestana, and the *Ilustração Portuguesa* published his portrait together with some biographical details.

before: He was born in Funchal on 28 September 1870, the son of the distinguished Madeiran writer Francisco Clementino de Sousa. Having enlisted in the army on 3 November 1888, he was commissioned second lieutenant of engineers on 25 October 1894, after studying with great distinction at the former Polytechnic and Army Schools. He was a professor in the 3rd section (natural sciences) of the Faculty of Sciences of the University of Lisbon and a member of the Mineralogical Society of France and other scientific bodies. He devoted himself especially to geological, mineralogical and seismological studies, and in the last of these he was the foremost authority in our country. His research on the effects of the earthquake of 1755 is truly remarkable, not only from the scientific but also from the historical point of view. Works: *Subsidios para o estudo dos calcareos do distrito de Lisboa* (1897); *Elementos de geographia physica da Europa* (1901); *Estudo Geologico do polygono de Tancos* (1902); *Idêa geral dos calcareos empregados nas construções de Lisboa* (1904); *Os calcareos do distrito de Leiria* (1905); *Os calcareos mais empregados em Portugal* (1908); *Effeitos do terremoto de 1755 nas construções de Lisboa* (1909); *Alguns trechos do relatorio do engenheiro Rego Lima sobre a sua missão ás minas de Cassinga em 1898* (1911); *Le Raz de marée du grand tremblement de terre em 1755, en Portugal* (Paris, 1911); *Ideia geral dos effeitos do megasismo de 1755 em Portugal* (1914); *O Megasismo do 1.° de Novembro de 1755 em Portugal–distrito de Faro* (1915); *O Terremoto do 1.° de Novembro de 1755 em Portugal e um estudo demografico–dos distritos de Faro, Beja e Evora* (1919). He died in Lisbon on 25 September 1931.

before: Three lichens known by the name of orchil (a dye lichen) exist in the Madeira archipelago: *Nemaria fuciformis*, *N. rocella* and *N. fucoides*. These species, which contain a red colouring principle, were once exported in large quantities, but with the industrial processes for extracting aniline dyes their use in dyeing is today nil. *Nemaria rocella* and *N. fuciformis* were gathered mainly on the Desertas, but both abound on the rocks of the north and south of Madeira.

before: According to the *Livro de Exéquias e Aclamações*, held in the archive of the Municipal Council (*Câmara Municipal*) of Funchal, Joseph I was acclaimed king in the city of Funchal on 4 January 1751; Maria I on 29 June 1777; John VI on 7 April 1818; Pedro V on 7 September 1855; Luís I on 20 January 1862; Carlos I on 28 December 1889; and Manuel II on 6 May 1908. The said book does not record the day on which Maria II was proclaimed queen in the city of Funchal, but it is known that this ceremony, together with the recognition of the Constitution, took place at the town hall on 6 June 1834. before: With the peace, Portuguese arms were also glorified. Who could set a barrier against this free will of the people to glorify their heroes and leave a commemorative pillar (padrão) to the vitality of their race, which, if at times it knew fear, never knew cowardice! Nossa Senhora do Monte is their Patron. The soul of our people is made of a clod of the Homeland and a breath of Faith. To destroy the latter is to dissolve the former. That is why the festivals of Religion here among us are the apotheosis of our Homeland and the glory of our warriors.

before: He was born in the parish (*freguesia*) of Ponta do Sol on 10 November 1854 and died in this city on 12 December 1903. before: He was born in Funchal on 22 March 1897, the son of João Crawford do Nascimento and Dona Palmira Cabral do Nascimento. He attended the lyceum (state secondary school) of this city and in 1922 completed his law degree at the University of Coimbra. From an early age he showed a decided inclination for letters, making his name above all as a poet. He published the verse pamphlets *As tres Princesas mortas num Palácio em ruína*, 1916, *Além-Mar*, 1917, and *Hora de Noa*, 1917. He has contributed to various newspapers and reviews and was an editor of the *Restauração* of Coimbra (1921). When the District Archive was created in 1931, Dr Cabral do Nascimento was appointed its first director. He promptly launched the review *Arquivo Histórico da Madeira*, of which he has been the principal contributor and of which six volumes have already appeared.

before: On 29 September 1833 the people’s judge (*juiz do povo*, elected representative of the craft guilds) petitioned the Municipal Council (*Câmara Municipal*) of Funchal to collect and publicly burn, ‘as unworthy and shameful acts of a loyal people’, all documents and orders issued by the Constitutional Government. The Council granted the petition, and the burning took place on 4 October of that year, at about 4 in the afternoon, in the Largo da Sé, before a large crowd and the military corps of the 1st and 2nd line. According to the *Pregador Imparcial*, the documents burnt were ‘the minutes of the elections and all the other autographs and powers of attorney of the substitute deputies’. After the ceremony the *juiz de fora* (crown-appointed judge from outside the district) raised several cheers for John VI, absolute king, which the people warmly echoed.

before: Higher education was represented here by the creation of the Funchal Medical-Surgical School (*Escola Médico-cirúrgica do Funchal*) in 1837, which came to an end in 1910 (see Medical-Surgical School). In some localities of Madeira a shortage of doctors is already being felt (1921), and it will soon be severe. Before very long, no doubt, it may again be said, as the governor and captain-general of this archipelago told the government of mainland Portugal in 1824, that on Porto Santo and in the Madeiran countryside there was no operating surgeon at all and that ‘one found only some wretched bloodletter, of whose competence many of those who called him to treat and cure their diseases have been the victims’. Our Medical School ought to have been reorganised in its original structure and in the range of its classes, making the teaching of the subjects taught there more effective; but the needs of the island districts did not warrant its abolition, which was due mainly, it is said, to the insistence of the director of public health, Dr Ricardo Jorge. Special education was provided here through the teaching of theology at the Diocesan Seminary, from its foundation in the last quarter of the 16th century (see Seminary). There were also special courses in theology at the Convent of São Francisco (St Francis of Assisi) and at the Jesuit College, for the exclusive use of their respective religious. The following may be regarded as special courses: the public class (*aula*) in drawing and painting, created in 1810; the drawing class that ran in this city for some years, maintained by the Funchal Municipal Council (*Câmara Municipal*); and the Industrial School, established in 1889. We have already given a detailed account of all of these in the article Escola Industrial António Augusto de Aguiar. In the first quarter of the 19th century there was a course of military studies in this city, whose organisation, workings and period of existence are entirely unknown to us. Among the courses of special education we must also mention the teacher-training college (*Escola Normal*) (see that entry), which lasted from 1900 to 1910, the Higher Primary School (*Escola Primária Superior*) (see that entry), created in 1919, and the Piloting School (*Escola de Pilotagem*) (see that entry), which opened in 1914.

before: The first public secondary classes held here in Madeira were those the Jesuits taught at their College of São João Evangelista (St John the Evangelist) (*Colégio de São João Evangelista*), covering Latin, philosophy, rhetoric and literature. We do not know when they began, but they already existed in 1590, for the author of the *Saudades* refers to them, and they ended with the expulsion of the Jesuits in 1759. This secondary course was known as the *Aulas do Pátio* ('Courtyard Classes', the public secondary classes held in the former Jesuit college), because it was held in an inner courtyard that formed part of the college. The college stood in Rua do Estudo, and after the expulsion of the Jesuits some secondary classes continued to be taught in the same building under the same name of *Aulas do Pátio*. It was also in this building that the lyceum (state secondary school) of this city was established in 1837 (see Lyceum), and it remained there for about 50 years. We cannot say exactly how much time passed between the expulsion of the Jesuits and the resumption of the *Aulas do Pátio*, nor can we tell whether these courses ran without interruption until our lyceum was established. In 1772 public classes in philosophy, Latin, mathematics and rhetoric were created, and around 1825 classes in French and English (see Secondary classes). Everything suggests that these were created to make up for the loss of the classes taught by the Jesuits, and it must then be accepted that there was a break in these courses in the period from 1759 to 1772.

As he left the ring, a troop of cavalry fell upon him: Sant'Ana, still clutching a pitchfork, threw himself at the cavalry! The commander drew a pistol from its holster and told him he would fire. Sant'Ana replied: “That will not go off!” And it did not! More troops came, more cavalry. Sant'Ana was finally arrested and ordered to leave, in the third canto of his Odyssey! The first had taken place in Coimbra, the second in Paris, the third in the land of Santa Cruz! The fourth was to take place in Lisbon. ‘This man, who could clear a fairground, was an elegant gentleman of exquisite breeding, talent and lively wit! ‘…. In June 1851 Sant'Ana e Vasconcelos was appointed secretary-general of Horta, and the following year transferred to Aveiro. ‘Before he left, one night – it was summer, and Sant'Ana was going through a period of heroic calm – we went to the Martinho for ices. We gathered round a table: Mendes Leal, A. Pedro Lopes de Mendonça, José Maria d'Andrade Ferreira, Luís de Vasconcelos, author of a drama entitled *a Cruz* which was a success at the Dona Maria II theatre, António Correia Heredia and I. The last two are still standing; the others have all fallen. ‘Shortly afterwards a ship’s captain came in at the door, a man well known at that time in the Baixa set, accompanied by a tall, broad-shouldered, strong man. He was a German. The seaman had suffered a setback at Sant'Ana’s hands in Rio de Janeiro and still had the bone stuck in his throat, but he came up very amiably and introduced the German, who spoke French fluently. Sant'Ana received him with his characteristic courtesy. I, however, noticed something constrained about him. With his lynx’s eye he saw that the seafarer, a crooked sort, had brought the other along as a mastiff. After a few words Jacinto took his leave and was about to go out when the German suddenly grabbed the collar of his frock coat and tore it! Sant'Ana e Vasconcelos took a step back and punched him: the man went down flat! He got up, his face badly swollen, and charged wildly. Another punch, and the colossus was on the ground. He got up yet again and returned to the attack… Then Sant'Ana, in a surge of fury, seized him and hurled him over the table that stood beneath the large mirror! This time the aggressor lost consciousness. When he came to, he left, staggering, on the seaman’s arm. ‘Sant'Ana sat down panting, his nose pinched, his moustache bristling and his eyes flashing. António Heredia, who had known his fellow countryman, friend and kinsman since childhood, was nonetheless astonished at this act of bull-like strength! ‘After entering politics, Sant'Ana fought two duels: one with a Frenchman named Clavel, with swords, and the other with A. before: In the volume *Livres das Feras* by Augusto Forjaz we read the following: ‘Another episode in which he took part occurred in December 1859. The royal commissioner of the São Carlos theatre, Dom Pedro Brito do Rio, had engaged the two rival singers Marcellina Lotti della Santa and Fortunata Tedesco de Franco. One night, when the opera *Lucrécia Bórgia* was announced, the two ladies deliberately declared themselves ill. Factions formed, and Tedesco won over most of the theatre’s regular audience and almost the entire Lisbon press. Sant’Anna e Vasconcellos took up Lotti’s defence in the *Revolução de Setembro*. On the night of the 19th Tedesco reappeared; the great majority gave her an ovation, intending to receive the rival lady with hostility. Dom Pedro do Rio and his wife, Dona Maria Krus, were in a box with Sant’Anna e Vasconcellos, who calmly went down to the stalls. Approaching the group of demonstrators, he asked them to abandon the planned hostile demonstration. Only four refused, pleading the freedom of their heels. Sant’Anna e Vasconcellos then warned them with the utmost courtesy: “You gentlemen say you are within your rights to stamp your feet in protest. That may be so. But you gentlemen express yourselves with your feet, and I am accustomed to express myself with my arms. So use your freedom, and in the first interval we shall settle accounts between feet and hands.” ‘Marcelina Lotti della Santa was not booed. ‘At that time there was also published in Lisbon a satirical newspaper called *O Asmodeu*, which spared no unpleasant remarks about Dom Pedro do Rio, an honourable man and therefore incapable of bowing to the whims of the artists and of a certain public. Some spectators in the stalls declared themselves for or against the artists according to how generously they rewarded their applause. This demand of a particular public was called the *molhadura* [TN: literally ‘wetting’, i.e. a tip or bribe], and the royal commissioner could not prevent it. The editor of *O Asmodeu*, Marciano de Azevedo, took the side of those making demands, boasting that there was no watchdog that could frighten him. Sant’Anna e Vasconcellos took the phrase as aimed at himself, linking it to the failed demonstration against Marcellina Lotti. Seeking out Marciano de Azevedo in the stalls, he demanded an explanation. In the midst of the uproar the editor of *O Asmodeu* slipped away to the stage and shut himself in the dressing room of the dancer Emilia Bellina, who was extremely ugly and was said to be his mistress. Sant’Anna broke down the door with a punch, but when that fearsome-looking woman appeared before him he burst out laughing, adding that Marciano de Azevedo was already well punished by his relations with such a scarecrow....’ ‘His consular and diplomatic career was remarkable, and the country owed him no small interest and many benefits, above all in every matter relating to commercial expansion. I believe there exist in the archives of the ministries of foreign affairs and of finance some unpublished reports which well deserved to be published, since they served as the basis for several treaties and conventions... But since it is true, as it is, that those who do most are least appreciated, the patriotic work of Sant’Anna e Vasconcellos went unrecognised, to which his withdrawal from our political world also greatly contributed. ‘So long an absence had brought oblivion. His fine athletic figure had faded from memory through his lengthy stay abroad. When one day he returned for a visit, none of the younger generation recognised the brilliant poet, the incisive journalist, the distinguished orator who from 1851 to 1872 had attracted attention by his talent, his elegance, his humour and the episodes of his bravery. Jacintho Augusto Sant’Ana e Vasconcellos, Commander of the Order of Christ and of the Order of Charles III of Spain, nobleman of the Royal Household (*fidalgo da Casa Real*) and 2nd Viscount of Nogueiras since 2 July 1875, found his old companions and best friends in the peace of the grave. His hair was turning white; his body was beginning to stoop. The circles of his former society had disappeared, giving him the impression of being a stranger, sorely tried by the reverses of Fortune. One night in January, leaving the Dona Maria II theatre, he found himself alone. For him, who had known so many friends and enemies, devoted to the former and intimidating the latter, that isolation sent shivers down his spine. He went into the Rossio café, then in the former Mattos Moreira shop, in the building on the corner of Largo de Camões. He sat down and ordered tea and toast. At the table opposite, two rakes of the day, strapping, quarrelsome young men, burst out laughing. To them, knocking back glasses of cognac, that old man drinking tea and eating toast was a figure of fun. Sant’Ana e Vasconcellos smiled. Then he clapped his hands and ordered the waiter: “Bring two more teas and two more rounds of toast.” The young men’s mirth grew. What a magnificent bumpkin they had found in that bourgeois! When the waiter carried out the order and returned with the tray, Sant’Anna e Vasconcellos told him, in a loud voice, to place it on the table of the impertinent would-be dandies. In the packed room silence fell, for an imminent clash was foreseen, all the more so since the two young athletes, mocking the harmless waiter, had pushed the tray away with contempt. Sant’Ana e Vasconcellos rose and approached. His voice rang out like a bugle of war: “You gentlemen laughed because I take tea, being an old man. Now I am going to laugh at you gentlemen, who have not yet taken it, being a pair of overgrown children. My name is Sant’Anna e Vasconcellos. So, whether you like it or not, you must swallow that tea.” And under his menacing gaze the two obeyed, resigned.’

before: Those who bear this family surname descend from various lines: some from Mem Rodrigues de Vasconcelos, who married a daughter of Bartolomeu Perestrelo; others from Garcia Rodrigues da Câmara, father of Aldonça Delgado, wife of the 3rd donatary (*donatário*) of Porto Santo, who murdered her; others from João Rodrigues, who lived in the 16th century and held a settled estate (*fazenda povoada*) near Calheta; and others, finally, from João Rodrigues Neto, who died in 1531, held a *sesmaria* (royal land grant to settlers on condition of cultivation) in São Martinho and died in the street called Rua dos Netos, in the parish (*freguesia*) of São Pedro.

after: Despite these instructions, and although on 8 July 1816 the Council had petitioned John VI for a loan of the sum needed to build the lazaretto, the work was never carried out. A short time afterwards the Governor ordered that ships arriving from suspect ports should anchor off Praia Formosa (‘beautiful beach’), and that their passengers should undergo quarantine in the house known as the Engenhoca (‘small mill’), which probably stood in that locality (*sítio*) or close by.

before: In 1848, when José Silvestre Ribeiro was civil governor of Madeira, a lazaretto was established at the Quinta do Gorgulho, a *quinta* (country estate) belonging to the British subject Henrique Veitch. The newspaper *O Madeirense* published the regulations of the establishment on 11 November of the same year.
after: In 1848, when José Silvestre Ribeiro was civil governor of Madeira, a lazaretto was established at the Quinta do Gorgulho (‘weevil estate’), a *quinta* (country estate) belonging to the British subject Henrique Veitch. The newspaper *O Madeirense* (‘The Madeiran’) published the regulations of the establishment on 11 November of the same year.

before: From the Quinta do Gorgulho, the lazaretto moved in 1851 to some houses that Councillor (conselheiro, honorary title of the royal council) José Silvestre Ribeiro had ordered to be built on land belonging to the National Treasury (*Fazenda Nacional*), at the mouth of the Ribeira de Gonçalo Aires. It was on this same land that the buildings of the present lazaretto were later erected; work on them began on 22 April 1866 and ended in 1874. In 1857 one of the outbuildings of the lazaretto built on the orders of José Silvestre Ribeiro was destroyed by fire.

before: In 1919, 280 political prisoners implicated in the monarchist revolution that broke out in Portugal that same year were held in the Lazaretto.
after: In 1919, 280 political prisoners implicated in the monarchist revolution that broke out in Portugal that same year were held in the Lazareto (‘quarantine hospital’).

before: The Gonçalo Aires Lazaretto had a director and a physician appointed in 1889, and an inspector appointed in 1890. These employees, whom the Government had engaged under article 59 of the decree with force of law of 3 December 1868, ceased to serve at the lazaretto after the publication of the Health Regulations (*Regulamento de Saúde*) of 24 December 1901, which turned the establishment into an observation post.

before: The Municipal Council (*Câmara Municipal*) of Funchal once had a salaried preacher, who was required to deliver the sermons at official festivities. In 1831 Father Friar José de Jesus was appointed preacher to the Council; before him the post had been held by Friar João José da Purificação, appointed in 1829 with a salary of 24,000 *réis* (old Portuguese money of account; 1$000 = 1,000 réis, 1:000$000 = one conto = 1,000,000 réis) a year.

before: Referring to the exploration that João Gonçalves Zarco and Tristão Vaz Teixeira made in order to fix the boundary between the two captaincies into which Madeira was divided, Frutuoso says the following: ‘Arriving at Câmara de Lobos. . going further on to some very high lands, there he laid out another church of the Vera Cruz, and all these heights he took for his heirs...’. This chapel and the lands taken by Zarco lay within the boundaries of the parish of Campanário, and today they belong to the parish of Quinta Grande, which was separated from it in 1848. Elsewhere the same Frutuoso also says: ‘half a *légua* to the west there is a *lugar* (settlement ranking between a town and a parish) of a hundred scattered households (*fogos*, literally ‘hearths’) (he is referring to the end of the 16th century), which they call Campanário... these are lands of livestock and of wheat and rye growing, the people being highland folk, more given to raising cattle than to cultivating vines or other fruit trees; but for all this it must be understood that in these and in all the places of the island there have always been, and are today, honourable and noble people of lofty thoughts’.

before: This parish has the chapels of Nossa Senhora do Bom Despacho and Nossa Senhora da Glória. The chapels of Nossa Senhora do Carmo, Nossa Senhora do Rosário, São João Baptista and Nossa Senhora dos Remédios no longer exist. We shall deal with all of them in the appropriate place.
after: This parish has the chapels of Nossa Senhora do Bom Despacho and Nossa Senhora da Glória. The chapels of Our Lady of Mount Carmel (*Nossa Senhora do Carmo*), Nossa Senhora do Rosário, São João Baptista and Nossa Senhora dos Remédios no longer exist. We shall deal with all of them in the appropriate place.

before: Among its early grantees of land (*sesmeiros*) and settlers were Manuel de Noronha, son of the second captain-donatary (*capitão-donatário*) of Funchal, who held vast tracts of land that today belong to Quinta Grande; Vasco Delgado, who established himself on the banks of the Ribeira dos Melões, where he founded an entail (*morgado*); Pedro Enes; and others. The largest properties that the Jesuits owned on this island lay within the bounds of Campanário, and they made up chiefly the so-called Quinta Grande, which later gave its name to this parish. This rural estate yielded, 160 years ago, more than two *contos* (one million réis) *de réis*, which today would correspond to a very considerable income.

before: It is in this parish that the locality of Fajã dos Padres lies, so called because it belonged to the fathers of the Society of Jesus. It is a *fajã* (strip of flat land at the foot of a cliff) beside the sea, beneath towering rocks. It is carefully cultivated and produces the finest and most celebrated Malmsey in Madeira. This locality was sacked more than once by pirates, who in January 1625 destroyed the chapel that the Jesuits had there.

before: With the creation of the municipality (*concelho*) of Ribeira Brava in 1914, the parish of Campanário ceased to belong to the municipality of Câmara de Lobos and was included in the area of the new municipality. Born here were the bishop of São Paulo, Dom Manuel Joaquim Gonçalves de Andrade (1767–1847), the distinguished jurist Francisco Justino Gonçalves de Andrade (1821–1902) and Canon João Jacinto Gonçalves de Andrade (1825–1894), both eminent professors at the law faculty of that Brazilian city (see those entries).

before: In former times there were many chestnut groves in this parish. Partly eaten away by time, it had at its base a door-shaped opening that gave access to a hollow able to hold several people.

before: The discoverer and 1st captain-donatary (*capitão-donatário*) died around 1467 and was succeeded in the captaincy of Funchal by his son João Gonçalves da Câmara. He must have been born in 1414, for Frutuoso states that he died in 1501 at the age of 87. While his father was still alive he fought valiantly in Africa, and was present at the siege of Arzila when this Moroccan stronghold was taken by Afonso V. On other occasions he went there to aid our fortresses when they were threatened by attacks from the Moors, rendering notable services and always giving proof of strenuous valour. He distinguished himself remarkably, together with his brother Luís Gonçalves da Câmara, in the defence of Ceuta, when the town was under siege and in danger of falling into the hands of the besiegers. When an expedition was organised to relieve the stronghold of Larache, to be led by John II, João Gonçalves da Câmara fitted out a fleet on this island at his own expense, which went to the Algarve to join the main body of the army. There the second captain-donatary of Funchal was received by the monarch with marks of such particular esteem and regard that, says an old chronicler, he even wished ‘that he should pour water over his hands at table, which at that time was one of the highest marks of consideration bestowed on a vassal’.

before: Shortly after he took over the government of his captaincy, while our country was at war with Spain, Madeira was attacked by a Spanish fleet of a good many ships carrying large numbers of armed men. Despite the scant means of defence at his disposal, João Gonçalves displayed such energy and gave such examples of extraordinary valour that he succeeded in putting the Castilians to flight. They then went on to attack the island of Porto Santo, which they seized without the slightest resistance from its inhabitants. The captain-donatary went to Porto Santo to dislodge the Spaniards, who suffered considerable losses, hastily withdrew to their ships and sought, in headlong flight, to escape pursuit by the forces that had come from Madeira.

before: The surname Câmara, used by the second donatary, derives from the well-known fact that the discoverer of Madeira found, on the coast of what later became the settlement and parish (*freguesia*) of Câmara de Lobos, a cave of sea wolves [monk seals], which gave their name to the *lugar* (settlement ranking between a town and a parish) and which strikingly marked Zarco’s first voyage of exploration along the island’s south coast. In 1460 Afonso V granted João Gonçalves da Câmara the following coat of arms: on a green field a silver tower with two merlons and a spire topped by a gold cross, and two wolves in their natural colour standing upright and rearing against the tower, with one of the wolves as the crest. The second captain-donatary (*capitão-donatário*) was thereafter called João Gonçalves de Câmara de Lobos, a surname his successors were also to use, but ‘this addition of the Lobos to the surname, as we read in an old manuscript, was gradually dropped over time, and only that of Câmara remained’.

before: This second donatary of Funchal was the founder of the Convent of Santa Clara (St Clare of Assisi), begun in 1492. It was attached to the church of Conceição de Cima, later called Santa Clara, which the discoverer João Gonçalves Zarco had ordered to be built as a family vault for himself and his descendants. Diogo Cabral had the chapel of Nossa Senhora da Estrela (Our Lady of the Star) built at Calheta; it had been designed by Zarco, who had earnestly urged its construction on his children. He died on 15 December 1486 and lies buried in the chapel he built. He was the grandfather of Tristão Vaz da Veiga. He was the first on this island to bear the surname Cabral.

before: In Madeira, at least in the early days of colonisation, all civil and criminal jurisdiction lay with the donataries (*donatários*). Their powers in the administration of all public affairs, and even in the trial of criminal cases, were very broad, except for serious offences punishable by death or the cutting off of a limb, in which case the imposition of the corresponding penalty belonged to the king or to the higher courts of the royal court. These wide powers were gradually curtailed as time went on. The kings’ assumption of the privileges that the Order of Christ held in this archipelago, the creation of the municipalities, the institution of *sesmarias* (royal land grant to settlers on condition of cultivation) and entailed estates, the various agrarian laws, above all those concerning water, timber, livestock and sugar, and still other measures of the central power contributed powerfully to the gradual curtailment of the civil, military and judicial powers that the captains-donatary (*capitão-donatário*) had widely enjoyed in this archipelago. Abuses of jurisdiction by the donataries, which sometimes went as far as encroaching on royal power, were not rare. On many occasions this led to the dispatch to this island of *ouvidores* and *corregedores* (royal district magistrate), invested with almost discretionary powers, whose special mission was to investigate and judge these excesses of jurisdiction. It was these magistrates, sent at first in extraordinary cases and later in more normal circumstances, who mitigated and corrected those encroachments of power. Conflicts sometimes arose between them and the captains-donatary, and the central government always put an end to them in the appeals lodged before the Crown.

before: A fishing rig consisting of two slender quince rods, joined at their thicker ends and carrying at their thinner ends one or two lines one *braça* (fathom, about 2.2 m) long, to which the hooks are attached. At the point where the two rods meet there is a loop or eye, to which the line holding the rig is tied; the rig is sunk by a weight fastened to the rods just below the loop. This weight may be a piece of lead, in which case it is called a lead sinker (*chumbada*); or it may be a simple rounded stone, and then it is called a stone sinker (*pandulho*). On Porto Santo the quince rods are sometimes replaced by tamarisk stems. This rig is generally used for the fine fish that live on rocky bottoms, such as groupers, pargos, *requemes*, alfonsinos, etc.

before: This square (*largo*) lies on the left bank of the Ribeira de João Gomes, as a continuation of Rua da Infância and Rua Oudinot, both of which open into it. It also gives access to Rua do Hospital Velho. Every Saturday a fair used to be held in this square for the sale of pine poles and chestnut stakes, used for the vine trellises known in Madeira as ‘corredores’. The square is also the site of the main entrance to the city’s large market, known as the Mercado dos Lavradores, which was opened in 1939.

before: On this island, says the *Diccionario Universal Ilustrado Portuguez*, ‘there are valleys of indescribable scenery, in every variety of rustic beauty: everything there that is art, cultivation, the work of man, becomes incidental, paltry, almost nothing to the beholder, and nature alone displays her grandeur in the profusion of her spontaneous splendours. There the brush will fall from the hand, the string of the lyre will snap trembling, and the pen of the prose writer who attempts a description will exhaust itself in grandiloquent commonplaces, for only the power that produced these pictures with its creative *fiat*, taking volcanoes and the sea as its instruments, could render their lines and hues. Of these valleys we shall mention five. To the east, that of Machico. To the south, that of Funchal, including within it the Vale Formoso, the whole forming a vast amphitheatre-like panorama, the delight of every traveller who enters the bay and the most ample harbour that adorn its shores. Twelve and a half kilometres from here, in the high reaches of the parish (*freguesia*) of Estreito de Câmara de Lobos, the valley of Jardim da Serra, rich in varied native vegetation, in the rugged recess of the wild mountains, dark green with untamed native woodland, which shelter it in an almost complete circle, leaving it open only to the south; in that direction, threaded by two streams that at last unite in a showy waterfall, it stretches with them down to the sea. To the north, the valley of São Vicente, where the little town stands, seat of the municipality (*concelho*) and judicial district (*comarca*) of that name: a broad valley, most pleasant in itself and striking for the contrast of the inaccessible, uncultivated mountains that, touching the clouds, surround it on all sides except the north, by the sea. And finally, towards the east, the encircled valley of Penha de Águia, a graceful name which in its sublime concision declares that there stands a very lofty promontory, dark green, towering over the surrounding land, majestic, a worthy throne for the queen of the air. This valley is formed by the parish of Faial and that of Porto da Cruz, and its setting, together with the crag that gave it its name, is so astonishingly beautiful that it has no rival to humble it among the Edens of Europe, perhaps of the world....’

before: The first is an 18th-century manuscript by an anonymous author, found among the papers of the late bishop of this diocese, Dom Patrício Xavier de Moura. It contains interesting information on the discovery, the early colonisation, the first donataries, etc., and ends with a detailed account of the descendants of João Gonçalves Zarco. The second, which dates from the beginning of the 19th century, was kept in the former secretariat of the seminary of this diocese. It deals chiefly with the creation of the diocese and of the various parishes, naming the enactments that established them, the stipends of the parish priests, ecclesiastical salaries, etc. It was one of the most valuable sources used by Dr Álvaro Rodrigues de Azevedo in writing note XIX of the *Saudades da Terra*. The third, which we have already mentioned, was the work that supplied the most data for the preparation of the previous one, and the annotator of Gaspar Frutuoso seems not to have known of it. The fourth deals briefly with the bishops of this diocese and at considerable length with the episcopal administration of the prelate Dom João do Nascimento, who died in 1753; the information in this manuscript ends in that year. The fifth came from the pen of the learned priest Father António Gomes Neto and was written around the middle of the 19th century. It holds interesting information of an ecclesiastical nature, and also contains much information on the customs house, the creation of various public offices, etc., with valuable comments, though not always acceptable ones, shaped by the political ideas the author professed. It seems to us to be a different work from those cited in the notes to the *Saudades*. All these manuscripts were published in large part in the former *Heraldo da Madeira*, thanks to the efforts of one of the authors of this *Elucidário*, who was then an editor of that newspaper. However, not only did the proofreading leave much to be desired, with many errors and slips, above all in dates and personal names, that need correcting, but there are also great gaps and shortcomings in the transcriptions made there, in the division of the material, etc. All this calls for a new and more careful publication, to which some explanatory notes on the text should be added.

before: The sixth and last manuscript is the work of Henrique Henriques de Noronha, of which the *Diccionario Bibliographico* says the following: ‘Manuscript in folio of 225 leaves, with an additional Appendix of 34 leaves. This autograph manuscript, said to be a complete work of Madeiran History, was bought some years ago in Lisbon, by weight, by a person who keeps it in his possession.’ Dr Álvaro Rodrigues de Azevedo refers several times to Henriques de Noronha’s study. At first he supposed it to be the same as the work we have listed above as number 2, but later he stated that the two manuscripts were entirely different; and finally, in the article in the *Diccionario Universal Português Illustrado*, he again maintained that the *Memorias sobre a criação e augmento do Estado Eclesiastico* and Noronha’s *Memórias...* are one and the same work. Some years ago the distinguished researcher and our fellow Madeiran Dr Jordão de Freitas told us that he had had occasion to examine Henrique Henriques’s manuscript in Lisbon. We have just been informed that Dr Manuel Monteiro Velho Arruda, who lives in Vila Franca do Campo on the island of São Miguel, owns this much-vaunted historical work and will shortly publish it; that will be the moment for all the doubts raised about it to be entirely dispelled. Among the old writings that have been lost altogether, special mention is due to the one cited in no. 2 of the newspaper *Flor do Oceano*, of the year 1834: ‘The second most important work of which we have knowledge is the one entitled *Memorias authenticas e curiosas da ilha da Madeira*, a manuscript in seven large folio volumes, composed by Father Manuel Carlos de Vasconcellos, beneficed cleric (*beneficiado*) of the parish of Nossa Senhora do Calhau. This interesting collection passed, so we are told, together with Canon Leite’s pamphlet, into the hands of Father J. L. de N., and contains interesting documents relating to the island, from its discovery up to the period when the British troops under the command of Marshal Beresford took possession of it.’ It seems to us that the initials J. L. N. are meant to designate the canon and archdeacon of Funchal Cathedral (*Sé*), José Luís de Nóbrega, who died around the middle of the 19th century. Another writing that has likewise gone astray is the one mentioned in the already cited article ‘Madeira’ in the *Diccionario Universal Português*, in the following terms: ‘The same happened with the manuscript of a historical and statistical work on the island of Madeira by the ill-fated and talented Madeiran writer Januário Justiniano de Nóbrega, for which he was paid from the funds of the Council of Funchal, to which it therefore belongs: the writer of these lines possesses fragments of the draft of the work and the authentic document of the payment order for its price.’

before: It is worth mentioning here that the Arquivo Histórico da Madeira (Historical Archive of Madeira) was created in July 1931. The following year it was provisionally housed in one of the rooms of the palace of the District General Council (*Junta Geral do Distrito*), where the various departments of the Diocesan Seminary operate today (1940). In 1933 the Historical Archive was transferred to the Palácio de São Pedro (St Peter Palace), where it is now permanently established, answering technically and administratively to the Directorate-General of Archives and Libraries (*Direcção Geral dos Arquivos e Bibliotecas*). Several thousand codices and documents scattered among various archives and public offices have been incorporated into it, making it the richest and most valuable repository of material for the history of this archipelago. It directs the important publication *Arquivo Histórico da Madeira*, of which six volumes have already appeared; it contains valuable material and most interesting information, and has today become indispensable to researchers of Madeiran history. It is regrettable that publication has not begun of the index of the documents in the municipal archive compiled by António José de Lamedo, to which we refer above. This publication has long been desired, and as early as 1873 the illustrious commentator of the *Saudades da Terra* considered it absolutely essential that it be carried out without delay.

before: Prominent among this valuable documentation are the precious holdings of the Funchal municipal archive, referred to above, of which a brief but interesting catalogue or inventory, well worth consulting by scholars, can be found in the six published volumes of the *Arquivo Histórico da Madeira*. It hardly needs saying that the National Archive of the Torre do Tombo, the richest, most abundant and most select collection of manuscripts in our country, also holds a vast and valuable body of documents concerning every subject that may be of interest to the Madeira archipelago. This precious seam remains almost entirely unexplored, and there is not yet even a brief inventory of the documents relating to this island that might guide any scholar wishing to undertake particular historical research. Meanwhile, we note here an article published in the *Diário da Madeira* of 21 December 1933, which gives a detailed account of many collections of documents of great use to researchers. No less useful is a reading of the articles in the aforementioned volumes of the *Arquivo Histórico da Madeira* on the manuscripts in the Torre do Tombo relating to the affairs of the Madeiran archipelago.
