before: Austrian botanist, well known for his studies of the flora of Portugal and Angola. He was in Madeira in 1853, staying only a very short time. The year before, he had proposed to the government the creation of two acclimatisation gardens, one in São Paulo de Luanda and the other in Funchal, so that the latter would receive tropical plants destined to be taken to colder climates, and plants from those climates that it would be advantageous to grow in hot regions. Once such plants had adapted to our climate, it would then be easy to make them grow in countries colder or hotter than ours. The few plants collected by Welwitsch in Madeira in 1853 are in the herbarium of the Faculty of Sciences of the University of Lisbon. Works: *Aforismos acerca da fundação dos jardins de aclimação na Ilha da Madeira e em Angola, na Africa Ocidental* (1921).

before: A nearly flat locality (*sítio*) a short distance from the Poiso mountain shelter, crossed by the road that leads from the shelter to Ribeiro Frio. Bracken (*Pteridium aquilinum*) is very abundant there.
after: A nearly flat locality (*sítio*) a short distance from the Poiso (‘resting place’) mountain shelter, crossed by the road that leads from the shelter to Ribeiro Frio (‘cold brook’). Bracken (*Pteridium aquilinum*) is very abundant there.

before: Madeirans have been liable to taxes since early times, as the charter (foral) of the city of Funchal and of the towns of Ponta do Sol and Calheta shows, together with various documents recorded in the municipal archives. When King Duarte granted his brother, Prince Henry the Navigator, the lordship of the islands of the archipelago, he gave him ‘all the rights and revenues thereof’. From the grants of the three captaincies of Funchal, Machico and Porto Santo, we know that the prince authorised their respective donataries to receive ‘one in ten of everything he should have in revenue, according to the charter, in the said captaincies. The charter of 1515, transcribed on p. 494 ff. of the *Saudades da Terra*, contains a reference to Prince Henry’s charter, which shows that the tax burdens he imposed on the people of this archipelago were heavy indeed.

before: The fifth was paid by the chantries (capela) and by the donataries’ *redízima* (a tenth of the Crown’s revenues due to the donatary). In 1836 the administrator-general (*administrador geral*) ruled that the Marquis of Castelo Melhor should be assessed for the said *redízima* from 1831 until the abolition of the chief castellanship (*alcaidaria-mor*) of Funchal. In former times the fifth was assessed on donataries who held Crown property and chantries before the *corregedores* (royal magistrates), but the law of 24 April 1835 required the Municipal Councils to appoint, for each parish (*freguesia*), a board of six citizens charged with apportioning this levy. On folio 31 verso of volume XVIII of the General Register of the Municipal Council of Funchal there is a list of the chantry properties in the municipality (*concelho*) of Funchal that were subject to the fifth.

before: Around the middle of the 19th century a boy of tender age, a native of the parish (*freguesia*) of Campanário, left Madeira and settled in the Argentine Republic. There, after some years, he acquired a great fortune, and he later became one of the richest men in that prosperous South American nation. What deserves special mention here, however, is the astonishing energy and enterprising spirit of this Madeiran. As a merchant, coloniser of vast uncultivated territories, director of banking houses and negotiator of high-finance operations, he attained the greatest prestige and influence. He extended the network of his dealings to the whole of Argentina, Brazil and Paraguay, and it was not unusual for the governments of those countries to turn to his experience and knowledge to solve many problems closely bearing on the highest interests of the state. He died in the city of Buenos Aires, at an advanced age and possessed of great wealth, on 28 December 1930, known as ‘Gonçalves the millionaire’.

before: The asylum remained in the Convent of São Francisco for only a few months. Everything pointed to installing it permanently in the house that the Municipal Council (*Câmara Municipal*) had had built expressly for that purpose in 1837. The move took place in December 1847, to the great material benefit of the inmates and of the orderly running of all the services of this charitable institution. This is the moment to give a brief account of the history of the building. As we said above, it was built in 1837, but was never put to the use for which it had originally been erected. At a council meeting on 2 July 1841 it was resolved that the Casa das Angústias should serve as the public gaol, house of correction and law courts, if the central government approved; the government, however, took no decision on the matter. The flash flood (*aluvião*) of 24 October 1842 caused serious damage to the building in the Largo do Pelourinho that housed the town hall, the municipal library and the Municipal Administration (*Administração do Concelho*, the government's local civil office). The Council therefore decided to move these offices to the Casa das Angústias once the necessary alterations had been made, and the move took place around the middle of 1843. Barely two years later the Municipal Council took a new decision: to move its offices to the house in the Largo da Sé, where the gaol then was, and to transfer the gaol to the Casa das Angústias. Very substantial works were carried out on the building for this new arrangement, and large sums were spent on them.

before: On 27 March, a few days after the asylum was founded, the civil governor, accompanied by various authorities and other official figures in a splendid procession, personally conducted about 400 inmates to the new premises prepared in the convent of São Francisco. In the former Praça da Constituição an abundant dinner was served to all the poor, at which José Silvestre gave a heartfelt and eloquent speech that deeply moved the large audience listening to him. The Administrative Committee (*Comissão Administrativa*) of the new asylum was then appointed, made up of the diocesan bishop Dom José Xavier de Cerveira e Sousa, Fidelio de Freitas Branco, Severiano Alberto Ferraz, Vicente de Brito Correia, António Machado Cota, Dom Jorge da Câmara Leme and Carlos Blandy.

before: The cholera epidemic of 1856, which killed some ten thousand people in Madeira, left many hundreds of children orphaned and destitute, and suitable shelter and care had to be found for them. Governor Gromicho Couceiro, who rendered such distinguished services to Madeira in that calamitous period, had some outbuildings of the former convent of São Francisco repaired and adapted to house an asylum intended solely for children. Its management was entrusted to the administrative committee of the Beggars’ Asylum. The two asylums were later joined, and this is the origin of the name given to the establishment at Angústias: the Asilo da Mendicidade e Órfãos do Funchal (Funchal Asylum for Beggars and Orphans).

before: An inhabited locality (*sítio*) in the parish (*freguesia*) of Santo António, Funchal. before: The auxiliary artillery corps of Madeira, established in 1805, had a staff and fifteen companies under the regulations given to it by Luís da Silva Mousinho de Albuquerque on 12 November 1834. before: He was born in the parish (*freguesia*) of Ponta do Pargo on 18 October 1883 and attended the diocesan seminary, the Funchal lyceum (state secondary school), the industrial institute and the Army School. before: The royal letter (*carta régia*) of 14 May 1804, calling for observance of that of 17 June 1800, ordered the sowing and planting on the mountain tops, on both Madeira and Porto Santo, of whatever tree species the ground proved suited to. Unfortunately, of the seeds the government sent us on that occasion, very few belonged to species easily adapted to our soil and climate. *Abies canadensis* and *Robinia Pseudacacia* – the former grown on some *quintas*, the latter naturalised in many places around Funchal – were introduced into Madeira on 29 October 1800, the seeds having been sent by the government of John VI.

before: Around 1476 the Franciscan Friar Rodrigo de Arruda arrived in Funchal with some companions. They occupied the hospice of São João and organised a small religious community there, under a brief granted by Pope Sixtus IV in 1476. Taking advantage of the goodwill of the inhabitants of the town (*vila*), Friar Rodrigo set about building a convent in the centre of the settlement, on land belonging to Clara Esteves, who in her will had entailed it in favour of her kinsman João do Porto. In exchange, the friars gave up their hospice of São João and also undertook to celebrate an annual sung Mass on All Saints’ Day. All this was authorised by the Infanta Dona Beatriz, as guardian of her son Diogo, Duke of Viseu, Grand Master of the Order of Christ, to which this island belonged. The *Saudades da Terra* states that the reason for the move was ‘because the place was deserted and in it a friar, at the prompting of the Devil, who always weaves such webs, hanged himself, these friars established a house below, in the town of Funchal, on grounds and lands opposite Santa Catarina, beyond the stream, where now (1590) stands one of the finest houses of this order that the Province has in Portugal; which convent is of the Observance, as sumptuous as it is cool, in which there are always nearly fifty friars, very learned, religious men of virtue and example, as much as can be found in the world’.

All this was authorised by the Infanta Dona Beatriz, as guardian of her son Diogo, Duke of Viseu, Grand Master of the Order of Christ (*Ordem de Cristo*), to which this island belonged. ‘Longing for the Homeland’ (*Saudades da Terra*) states that the reason for the move was ‘because the place was deserted and in it a friar, at the prompting of the Devil, who always weaves such webs, hanged himself, these friars established a house below, in the town of Funchal, on grounds and lands opposite Santa Catarina, beyond the stream, where now (1590) stands one of the finest houses of this order that the Province has in Portugal; which convent is of the Observance, as sumptuous as it is cool, in which there are always nearly fifty friars, very learned, religious men of virtue and example, as much as can be found in the world’.

before: Crowned with a reputation for the most sublime Christian virtues, Mother Virgínia da Paixão died on 17 January 1929 in the locality of Lombo dos Aguiares, in the parish (*freguesia*) of Santo António. before: 1804. On 8 and 11 January of this year there were violent storms, and two English full-rigged ships were wrecked. 1828. On 22 January the American brig *Calixto* was driven ashore opposite the Customs House and was completely destroyed by the sea within a few hours; on 1 March the English full-rigged ship *Britannia* was wrecked at Praia Formosa, with the loss of one crew member. 1834. This year saw the wreck of the English full-rigged ship *Greenwelle*, in which five crew members died. 1836. The great storms of 18 October drove the Portuguese barque *Maria Adelaide* and the yacht *Conceição e Almas* ashore near Santa Catarina, and one member of the latter vessel’s crew died. At the same time a boat laden with wine, coming from the north, was also wrecked there. 1842. On 26 October of this year the sea hurled five ships onto the beach, and another vanished and was never seen again. 1846. From 8 to 11 January there were great gales in the harbour of Funchal, which wrecked the works on the quay, and on the 10th of the same month the Tuscan *patacho* (small two-masted merchant vessel) *Duque de Sussex* was driven ashore at São Lázaro. 1848. On 10 December the yacht *Senhor dos Passos* and the schooner *Eugenia* were lost, and on the 31st the yachts *Fevereiro I.°* and *Boa Fé*, both Portuguese, and the patachos *Delfim* and *Levant*, the latter American and the former Portuguese. During this last storm the English warship, the corvette *Daphne*, very nearly ran aground. 1858. On 5 March of this year the English brig *Reliance* was wrecked in the harbour of Funchal as a result of a strong gale, and on the 15th of the same month the Brazilian patacho *Liberato Terceiro*, whose master was Thomás Whister, met the same fate. 1858. On 14 November the Portuguese full-rigged ship *Defensor* entered the harbour of Funchal on the point of sinking. She was on a voyage from Rio de Janeiro to one of the ports of Portugal, carrying her crew and some passengers, 23 persons in all. The vessel had come from an infected port and the sea was very rough, so that only with great difficulty could 16 people be landed; they were isolated in the old fort of Pontinha. The others stayed on board, refusing to land on that occasion, but during the night they lowered a boat and tried to reach the shore; six of them died and only one could be saved, beyond the fort of São Tiago. The ship ran aground at the mouth of the stream of Gonçalo Aires on 16 November. 1872. A violent storm on 22 December drove the English patacho *Champion* ashore near the Lazaretto, and the captain and four other crew members died. 1875. On 2 February 1875 the English steamer *Soudan* ran aground on the beach opposite the former Praça da Rainha, today Praça do Marquês de Pombal. The sea was calm, and the disaster was attributed to the incompetence or carelessness of those in charge of the anchoring manoeuvre. 1876. This year there were two great storms in Funchal bay, the first on 13 May and the second on 11 November. The first drove ashore the English schooner *Orphey*, the Portuguese patacho *Barbosa 2.°*, the Portuguese sloop *Moura 7.°* and the American patachos *Maurice* and *Nellieclifford*; the second brought the same end to the German boat *Fear-Not*, the Portuguese yacht *Fontes Pereira de Melo* and the English schooner *Theodosia*. During the November storms the *Valente*, a small Madeiran steamer, was flung onto the rocks below the Quinta Lambert, more than 15 metres above ordinary sea level; and as early as 3 January a storm less violent than the two we have mentioned had wrecked the English barque *Patagonia* near Santa Catarina. 1881. On 6 January of this year the Portuguese yacht *Aliança* was driven onto the beach by the south wind. 1884. On 26 November the sea hurled the schooner *Eulalia* and the Italian brig *Torquato* onto the beach. 1892. The storms of 28 February damaged the mole (breakwater) of Pontinha. 1896. During the night of 26 to 27 October of this year the French brig *René Adrienne* and the Portuguese brig *Comercio* came ashore, the latter at the Ribeira de São Lázaro and the former against the sea wall of Pontinha. Although Funchal bay is bounded by Cabo Garajau and Ponta da Cruz, which are a little more than 8 kilometres apart, it is to the east of the Ilhéu, opposite the city, that ships usually drop anchor, the bottom there consisting of basaltic sand and some mud. The quantity of stones, sand and mud that the waters of the streams carry down every year is considerable, and as a result the sea in the bay has become shallower and the beaches have gradually grown. Banger’s pillar, whose base was washed by the sea when it was built (1798), now stands at a distance from it, and the Rua da Praia, the fish and fruit markets and the Praça do Marquês de Pombal are built on places the waters reached in former times (1921). We shall now give a brief account of other shipwrecks that occurred at various points of this archipelago. In March 1720 a boat carrying eight people was making its way from Machico to Porto Santo when it was caught by a violent storm and driven onto the coasts of the Canary Islands, where they were able to land. They returned to Porto Santo two months later, when everyone there believed them to have perished in the storm. Around 1730 a Swedish ship coming from India with a valuable cargo was wrecked on that island, at the locality of Pedregal, at the place called the cliff of Guilherme, and some of the crew perished. Some months later a ship of the same nationality came to the site of the disaster and managed to salvage a considerable part of the cargo, including several objects of great value and, it seems, also some chests of money. At the beginning of 1768 the French warship, the carrack *Balance*, commanded by the Baron of Arras, sank near the island of Porto Santo; her crew, numbering 239, were taken aboard by a French ship, which carried them to the harbour of Funchal. In 1790 a coastal packet boat laden with wine, bound from the north of Madeira to Funchal, sank in the channel of the Ilhéu de Baixo, on Porto Santo, having been driven to that spot by a great storm. The whole crew died except for one man who, clinging to a wooden plank, managed to reach the Ilhéu de Ferro.

before: To the article on the creation of this diocese (1-363) it should be added that it is the Portuguese ecclesiastical circumscription with the smallest area, covering only the territory of the Madeiran archipelago; the small island of Arguin once also belonged to its jurisdiction. It comprises 50 parishes, which correspond exactly to the 50 civil parishes into which the district is divided. For the purposes of ecclesiastical administration these parishes are grouped into four archpriest districts (see that entry). Its seat is the city of Funchal, with its Cathedral – Funchal Cathedral (*Sé*) – and cathedral chapter, the bishop's palace, the seminary, ecclesiastical offices and various religious services, all under the direct supervision of the diocesan prelate, who actually resides in the same city.

before: The first to exercise ecclesiastical functions here were the Franciscan friars and, after them, the priests sent by the Order of Christ, to which the archipelago belonged in spiritual matters. The rapid growth of the population led to the creation of a diocese, in which its prelate could freely perform all the acts of worship proper to his episcopal rank. The bull (papal bull) *Pro excellenti praeeminentia* of 12 June 1514 established the Diocese of Funchal, and on the same date Diogo Pinheiro, one of the highest-ranking members of the Order of Christ, was appointed its first prelate, though he never came to his diocese.

before: The Cathedral (Sé Catedral) is a fine and spacious church, classified as a National Monument (*monumento nacional*), and it well deserves an unhurried visit. The pure Gothic of its architectural lines, the slender columns of its naves, the ceiling made of native cedar in the Moorish style and inlaid with ivory, the magnificent chapel of the Santíssimo Sacramento (Most Holy Sacrament), the sumptuous processional cross of silver gilt presented by Manuel I, a number of excellent paintings and other exquisite works of art are objects of admiration and esteem for all who visit this church. Its construction began in the last years of the 15th century and it was consecrated in 1516, although the ornamental work and interior decoration of the church as a whole had not yet been entirely completed.

before: ‘Certainly, from Barbosa Machado down to the present day, the wish must often have arisen for a fuller knowledge of the *Insulae Materiae historia*. . . It was the only printed work dealing exclusively with this archipelago, since no other published works existed apart from the few pages to be found in some chroniclers, such as Zurara, Barros, Galvão and Damião de Góis. It seems that Constantino’s work became very rare from the outset, perhaps because it had been printed in Rome and perhaps also owing to other unknown circumstances. We know of only two references that show an accurate knowledge of the book: that of the annotator of the *Historia Insulana* in 1866, and that of Dr Jordão de Freitas, in 1911.

before: It was our esteemed friend Dr Jordão de Freitas, a distinguished scholar of the historical sciences, who gave us this news in a most interesting letter received at the time. We did not publish it in full, as we had intended, because it has regrettably been lost. What had happened was this: the learned director of the Ajuda Library, in connection with the printing of the *Insulae Materiae Historia*, had told our illustrious friend Mr Henrique Hinton of the existence of this work predating Constantino’s, of which he knew only the title, the author’s name and the year of publication. Mr Hinton had a search made in London, through an authorised intermediary, in the famous library of the British Museum, and there discovered the extremely rare book, perhaps the only surviving copy. He at once had a complete photographic copy made of it, which he presented to the Municipal Library of Funchal.

before: He was born in Funchal on 16 June 1861, the son of Councillor (conselheiro, honorary title of the royal council) Silvano de Freitas Branco and Dona Maria Cândida de Sant'Ana Branco. He graduated in law at the University of Coimbra in 1884 and then practised as a lawyer in Lisbon for some time, but gave up this career to devote himself to agriculture and the management of his estate. He represented Madeira in parliament in the legislatures of 1887–1889, 1890–1892, 1894–1895 and 1895–1897. He was also deputy for a constituency on the mainland, and among the public-service posts he held was that of civil governor of one of the mainland districts. He died in Sintra on 29 October 1918.
after: He was born in Funchal on 16 June 1861, the son of Councillor (conselheiro, honorary title of the royal council) Silvano de Freitas Branco and Dona Maria Cândida de Sant'Ana Branco. before: It extends from the Ribeiro do Pisão to the Terreiro das Águas, and it contains land for pines and wild trees and land for pasture. There are some woods of laurel and tree heath. The Montado do Barreiro is extremely rich in water: the Levada do Barreiro rises here, as do some of the springs that help feed the levadas (irrigation channels) of Santa Luzia das Hortas, of Dona Isabel, etc. The Tornos springs, overlooking the Ribeira de Santa Luzia, lie within this upland woodland (*montado*). According to the experts who measured them a few years ago, the total flow of the waters of the Montado do Barreiro is 4,140 litres per minute: 512 litres belong to the Levada do Barreiro, 2,728 litres to the Ribeira de Santa Luzia and the levadas that rise in it, and 900 litres to the Tornos springs, these last waters being assigned by the Council to the city’s water supply. The works channelling the Tornos waters to a reservoir at the locality (*sítio*) of Saltos were completed on 22 October 1910, while the remaining works, which consist of bringing the same waters to the city, have only just begun. The owners of the Montado do Barreiro claimed that the Council should pay them compensation of 387,517.00 escudos (the Portuguese currency from 1911: 1 escudo = 100 centavos = 1,000 réis) for the expropriation of the land of the montado and its waters, excepting those of the Levada do Barreiro. By court judgment, however, this sum was reduced to 42,163.07 escudos, which, as far as we know, has not yet been paid in full. Of particular interest on this subject are the pamphlets *A Expropriação do Montado do Barreiro . . .* by Pedro de Góis Pita and *Acção de expropriação do Montado do Barreiro requerida pela Câmara do Funchal* by Juvenal Henriques de Araújo.

before: The crisis that Madeira went through in 1847 was also felt on the neighbouring island of Porto Santo. Relief in kind and in money had to be sent there on several occasions, but even so, ‘the people could certainly not have withstood so great a scourge’, say the *Annais do Porto Santo*, ‘had it not been for the very great abundance of fish, chiefly mackerel, which came to be sold at 50 for half a *tostão* (coin of 100 *réis*)’. There was also famine on Porto Santo in 1802, in 1806, in 1815, in 1816 and in 1829, when relief in kind had to be sent there, and after 1847 the scourge struck the island several more times, for example in 1850, in 1854, in 1855 and in 1883.

before: We suppose that at the end of the 17th century or the beginning of the 18th important works of rebuilding or enlargement were carried out on the old church, for in the General Index of the register of the former Royal Treasury Office (*Provedoria da Real Fazenda*) on this island we find a reference to the royal decree (alvará régio) of 9 September 1711, which ordered the continuation of the works on the church of Santo António, estimated at 2,233,920 *réis* (old Portuguese money of account; 1$000 = 1,000 réis, 1:000$000 = one conto = 1,000,000 réis). We have no evidence to state that the works were completed in accordance with that estimate, but it is certain that major repairs were made to the old parish church at various times. With the building of the present church, demolition of the old one began in 1785, leaving standing the chapel of the Santíssimo Sacramento, which served as the parish seat until 1789. Next to the parish priest’s residence there still survives a stretch of wall which tradition says belonged to the old church.

before: On the façade, above the main door, is a stone tablet bearing the following inscription: *Antonio Lusitanorum Protectori Templum Dedicat Aug. Reg. Maria Prima Illius Liberalitatem Efundentibus Suis In Hac Insula Ab Aerario Ad Ministris. Anno MDCCLXXXIII.* (To Anthony, protector of the Portuguese, the august Queen Maria I dedicates this church, her liberality being dispensed by her ministers of the treasury in this island. Year 1783.) Although religious services began to be held in the new church in 1789, its final interior completion took many more years. Work on the chapel of Nossa Senhora de Guadalupe was not declared finished until 1798; the chancel was still not entirely complete in 1801, and the chapel of the Santíssimo Sacramento was only finished at the beginning of the 19th century.

before: The chapel of São João e Santana stands on the Quinta do Trapiche, which has an excellent country house attached and was the property of Dona Maria Paula Rego, heiress of the old Gouveia Rego entailed estate (*morgadio*) to which this *quinta* (country estate) belonged. It served as the summer residence of the last prelates of this diocese, and a few years ago the diocesan seminary was temporarily housed there. Plans are under way to adapt this rural and urban property for a mental asylum, and some Brothers of St John of God have already begun the work (1921).

before: The building took six years and was declared finished in 1789, although work on the interior ornamentation of the church, and especially of the altars, continued for some years. The guarantor and inspector of the works was Second Lieutenant António Francisco da Cruz Camacho, who died in the locality (*sítio*) of Ladeira in this parish (*freguesia*) on 21 August 1815. He was buried beneath the arch of the chancel, and his tombstone bears this epitaph: ‘tomb of Second Lieutenant António Francisco da Cruz Camacho and of his wife and children and heirs, who was the guarantor and inspector of this church, which was begun in the year 1783 and completed in 1789’. He always showed the greatest dedication and selflessness in advancing the works, which at times proceeded very slowly, though for reasons beyond his control, and his memory deserves great gratitude for the unsurpassed zeal he displayed in bringing the new church to completion.

before: ‘Folklore studies of the dress peculiar to different regions have established conclusively that clothing, in its cut, arrangement and colouring, always corresponds to the way of life of the inhabitants and, above all, to the nature of the surroundings, through their climate, relief and the tones of the landscape. Where the landscape is richly flowered, splashed with many intense colours, dress – especially women’s dress – is equally colourful, so that the figure harmonises with and becomes part of the scene in which it lives and works. A Madeiran who visits the Minho at once finds there a landscape that recalls that of Madeira. And in the dress of the Minho woman he will recognise, in the bright, many-coloured stripes of the skirt, a close likeness to the dress of our own countrywomen. Porto Santo, luminous but colourless, has not given women’s dress – not even by imitation – the liveliness and hues that, in the eyes of Portuguese and foreigners alike, have made the charm of the peasant costume of this “Flower of the Atlantic”.

before: Born into a humble family, Dr António da Luz Pita came into the world in the town (*vila*) of Ponta do Sol on 2 September 1802. Having completed his secondary studies in this city, he went to Montpellier, where he took the degree of bachelor (*bacharel*, university graduate) of letters in 1826, that of bachelor of physical sciences in 1827 and a doctorate in medicine in 1830. The following year he received the degree of doctor of surgery from the Paris faculty.

before: The author of the *Saudades*, summarising the first exploration carried out by the discoverers along the south coast of this island, says that João Gonçalves Zarco, setting out in the boats at Ribeira Brava, ‘came to a point which lies a league below, and juts far out into the sea; and, because on the cliff above the point one can make out from afar, and see clearly, a round vein in the rock itself with rays that look like the sun, the captain named it Ponta do Sol…’ Another passage of the same work reads: ‘…Ponta do Sol is so called because it has a point to the west of the town which has the appearance… where the Sun also strikes first, before it reaches the town, when it rises’. Such is the explanation the chronicler offers for the origin of the name of this place. It does indeed seem plausible, since there are no weighty reasons that entirely contradict it. We do not know whether other places with the same name, such as a locality on the island of Santo Antão, Cape Verde, derived their names from circumstances similar to those recorded by Dr Gaspar Frutuoso.

before: João Agostinho de Freitas, an intelligent and patient researcher into the affairs of his native corner of the island, does not depart significantly from Frutuoso’s opinion. He says that the name ‘derived from an arm or reef (*restinga*) of living rock which, because it advances out into the sea, is called a point, and from a projection with concentric veins or cracks, in the form of a halo, as the Sun is customarily depicted, which existed on the face of the rock of the Passo that stands directly above the Fojo, beside the said point’. And he adds: ‘this rock lies to the south-east of the town and not to the west, as is stated, perhaps through a copyist’s error, in Dr Frutuoso’s manuscript, which is in the library of the Council of Funchal’.

before: The colonisation of Ponta do Sol began around 1440. One of its earliest settlers was Rodrigues Enes, the Lame, who obtained extensive lands there and established a large settled estate (*fazenda povoada*), which was the origin and original nucleus of the future parish (*freguesia*). It is said somewhere that the lands Rodrigo Enes began to clear, which had been granted to him as a *sesmaria* (royal land grant to settlers on condition of cultivation), lay to the west of the stream and stretched from the edge of the ocean up to Arrebentão, near the Paul da Serra.

before: This church venerates the image of Nossa Senhora da Luz, its patron saint, whose particular cult was at one time very widespread in this and many other parishes. Friar Agostinho de Santa Maria, in volume X of his well-known work *Santuario Mariano*, devotes a chapter to the veneration then paid to that revered image. Father Miguel Francisco Velosa, vicar of this parish church, petitioned for and obtained from the Holy See a brief dated 30 July 1805, granting a plenary indulgence, on the occasion of the patronal feast, its novenas and the octave – that is, from 30 August to 15 September each year – to all persons who, duly prepared, visit the parish church of this parish.

before: Thanks to its rapid and extensive development, the parish (*freguesia*) of Ponta do Sol attracted a considerable number of people from mainland Portugal – the Kingdom (*reino*, i.e. mainland Portugal) – and even from abroad. They obtained a great deal of land there as *sesmarias* (royal land grant to settlers on condition of cultivation), and some of them founded important entailed houses that had their seat in this locality and have survived to our own day... Among these people we shall mention Rodrigo Enes Furtado, of whom we have already spoken above, a man of noble lineage who left numerous descendants in this parish; Luís Gonçalves da Câmara, whom we have already discussed (vol. The fleet left Madeira on 30 June, and on 15 July following, off the Canary Islands and within sight of the island of La Palma, it was attacked by Huguenot corsairs, who plundered the Portuguese ships and slaughtered the forty religious, throwing their bodies into the sea. before: He was a native of Portugal, but lived for many years on this island while carrying out various public-service commissions. He came here appointed *corregedor* (royal district magistrate), taking up office on 4 October 1790. He later held the posts of inspector of tobacco and soap works and of judge conservator (*conservador*, special judge for British subjects) of the British Conservatorial Court (*conservatória britânica*, special court for British subjects). He also served as inspector of agriculture, and in that capacity he left on record at the Council of Calheta a set of instructions on agricultural matters, which for the time were a valuable piece of work and can still be read with interest today. Laudatory references to these instructions are found in various works and documents.

before: ‘In Madeira I am going to meet an old friend, the great poet António Nobre... I then remembered that in the spring of that year, 1897, we had met in Lisbon and that he had asked me many questions about the advantages of Madeira’s climate for consumptives. And I remembered that, so as not to discourage him, I had told him of cases of cure and of the prolonged lives of consumptives who had settled in Madeira. António Nobre came to talk to me with an attempt at cheerfulness and said: “My dear Leal, I had the feeling I would never see you again. I followed your advice and here I am on your island. I have liked everyone in this land and all this lovely scenery immensely, but it seems to me that I have come to Madeira too late. You were right, if I were in the condition of those you told me about...” I felt a kind of inner tear that must not show in the eyes. . . and we went to talk at the “Casa Havanesa”..., while I sensed that I would never see him again...’

before: Finally António Nobre returned to Lisbon, because ‘it is in Madeira that he has no faith at all’. Poor poet! What remained of his life was a mixture of suffering and hopelessness. before: The woody flora of Madeira still contains today some species that yield timber of great value in cabinet-making. From the wood of the Madeira mahogany (vinhático, *Persea indica*) and the *til* (*Ocotea foetens*, Madeiran laurel), the latter black and the former reddish, fine furniture is made, the former closely resembling mahogany. From cedar, which is pale, light and aromatic, excellent boxes are made that, as a rule, are not attacked by moths. From *maçaroco*, *fustete*, *seixo*, *piorno*, *pau branco*, holly, *tintureira*, etc., inlaid work (*embutidos*) of various colours is made for tables, boxes, cases and other small pieces. The woods of the *faia*, *barbuzano*, laurel, *aderno*, *folhado* (*Clethra arborea*, a native tree), heath, wild cherry, *sanguinho*, *mocano*, etc., also have or could have uses in various kinds of work, but their use in cabinet-making is generally very limited, because nearly all of them are now very rare. Valuable information on this subject is given in the articles of this *Elucidário* entitled Afforestation, Fires, Forest Regime and Forest Services.

before: It is one of the oldest parishes on the island and one of the first to be worked by the earliest colonists. There were also others who founded chantries (capela) there with entails (*instituições vinculares*) attached. Other early settlers of this parish were the Neapolitan knight Afonso de Aragão, to whom we have already referred in the article Aragão, and João Assuna Teixeira and João Salviato, who held a great deal of *sesmaria* land there. before: Two features deserve special mention: the ceiling of the chancel of the parish church, built like that of our Cathedral (Sé Catedral), and above all the tabernacle, a work of rare artistic value made of ebony with exquisite silver inlays, which was a gift of King Manuel I. It is a pity that this precious piece of 16th-century religious art has been somewhat neglected in its state of preservation. Its antiquity, its historical value and the remarkable artistic refinements it contains demanded the most careful and attentive effort to prevent and avert, as far as possible, the corrosive and destructive action of time.

before: Of the species that yield rubber, only *Ficus elastica*, of the family Urticaceae, and *Manihot Glaziovii*, of the family Euphorbiaceae, exist in Madeira. The first is found in several *quintas* of Funchal; the second exists, as far as we know, only in the grounds attached to the Disinfection Station, at Campo da Barca, where it thrives. In many places on the island there grows a composite, called *visco*, whose latex solidifies into a whitish, elastic mass, but which has no industrial applications.

before: He was born in the parish (*freguesia*) of Santa Cruz on 27 December 1837. He studied at the Funchal lyceum (state secondary school) and became a primary-school teacher, later holding the post of revenue clerk (*escrivão de fazenda*) in several municipalities of this district. He contributed extensively, in prose and verse, to various Madeiran newspapers and was principal editor of *A Pátria*. According to Inocêncio Francisco da Silva, he wrote the novellas *Um Sacrilegio* and *Romance em seis capítulos*, which he had ready for printing but which were never published in book form; only a few extracts appeared in various newspapers. He lived for many years in Demerara, where he was editor of the newspaper *O Portuguez*. He became a merchant but had little success in his business dealings, and he died in New York, on a hospital cot, on 3 August 1915, destitute and in the most complete obscurity.

before: The taste for academies, so fashionable in mainland Portugal in the 18th century, also made itself felt in Madeira, although some of them were of very minor importance and even of manifest uselessness. In this city there was one called the Assembleia dos Únicos do Funchal, which existed in 1746, as can be seen from the autograph manuscript owned by Dr Álvaro de Azevedo entitled *Oração Académica*, which Francisco João de Vasconcelos Bettencourt recited on 15 May 1746, the day on which he took up the place of Academician in the Assembleia dos Únicos do Funchal to which he had been appointed. The end of this speech is published on page 787 of the *Saudades da Terra*. There was another academy, devoted to the cultivation of poetry, called the Arcadia Funchalense, to which we have found only two references. One is in the epicedium, on page 80 of the second volume of the *Colecção Poética* of Francisco Manuel de Oliveira, dedicated to the death of Valisio Alceo, a member of the Arcadia Funchalense. The other is in the sonnet published on p. 31 of the *Obras* of Dom Aires de Ornelas e Vasconcelos, dedicated to Francisco Xavier de Ornelas, a founding member of the same Arcadia. We cannot establish exactly when the Arcadia Funchalense existed. We know only that Oliveira’s *Collecção* was published in 1794 and that Francisco Xavier de Ornelas was born in 1748. Its foundation must be later than 1770, given the sonnet’s reference to the ‘profound learning’ of Francisco de Ornelas, who ‘was surpassing the Tullies’. The Sociedade Funchalense dos Amigos das Ciências e Artes, established in this city in 1821, was also a kind of academy; it was short-lived because of the political events of 1823. It held many meetings, at which a number of speeches were given and various papers on literary and historical subjects were read. The *Patriota Funchalense* of 7 September 1822 gives an interesting, if brief, account of it. See also *Saudades da Terra*, p. 794.

before: The importance of this archipelago is set out concisely but strikingly in the following words from the authoritative pen of Dr Álvaro Rodrigues de Azevedo, the learned annotator of the *Saudades da Terra*: ‘This archipelago has been the subject of study by learned naturalists, both foreign and Portuguese. It is famous, especially the island of Madeira, for the fertility of its soil, its excellent wines, the breathtaking beauty of its landscape and the healthiness of its climate. It is historically notable as the first of the Portuguese discoveries in the 15th century and, afterwards, until the close of the 16th century, as the secular and ecclesiastical metropolis of our overseas dominions and the emporium of our colonial navigation and commerce. For this reason the Madeiran archives, especially those of the Municipal Council (*Câmara Municipal*) of Funchal, that of Machico, that of the former and now extinct Treasury Board (*Junta da Fazenda*) and that of the Civil Government of Funchal, hold precious documents and records, perhaps not to be found elsewhere, for the history of the institutions and government of our possessions beyond the sea.’

before: The Madeira archipelago consists of the islands of Madeira (see Madeira (island)), Porto Santo (see that entry) and the Desertas group (1-357), which comprises Deserta Grande (1-356), Ilhéu Chão (Flat Islet) (1-269) and Bugio (1 - 176). Because this archipelago lies relatively close to the European continent, and also because it is regarded as a group of ‘Adjacent Islands’ (Ilhas Adjacentes) of a country on that continent, there has been no shortage of geographers who have considered Madeira part of Europe. This opinion, however, is not followed or adopted today by any authoritative writer.

before: The relative positions of the islands of Madeira and Porto Santo and the Desertas group form a scalene triangle. Its shortest side is the channel between the Ilhéu de Fora, at the eastern tip of Madeira (Ponta de São Lourenço), and the Prego do Mar or Ilhéu do Navio, near the Ilhéu Chão (Desertas). The next longest side is formed by the channel (the Travessa) running from the same Ilhéu de Fora (Ponta de São Lourenço) to the Ilhéu de Baixo or da Cal (Porto Santo). The longest side is the channel stretching from the Ilhéu de Baixo or da Cal (Porto Santo), already mentioned, to the Prego do Mar or Ilhéu Chão (Desertas). The three channels measure 11, 27 and 32 miles respectively, these being the distances that separate Madeira, Porto Santo and the Desertas group from one another.

The longest side is the channel stretching from the Ilhéu de Baixo or da Cal (Porto Santo), already mentioned, to the Prego do Mar or Ilhéu Chão (Desertas). The three channels measure 11, 27 and 32 miles respectively, these being the distances that separate Madeira, Porto Santo and the Desertas group from one another.

before: At the northern end of the parish (*freguesia*) of Estreito de Câmara de Lobos lies the charming and delightful spot known as Jardim da Serra. The pleasantness and beauty of the place justify the name. It consists largely of a picturesque valley set deep among rugged mountains and surrounded by dense, luxuriant vegetation. It is unquestionably one of the most enchanting spots in Madeira, and from its heights some of the broadest and most astonishing panoramas of the whole island can be seen. On the Pico dos Bodes and the Boca dos Namorados, which overlook it, we are above all enraptured by the sight of the abyss of the Curral das Freiras and the mountains that surround it. As we have already noted, this is one of the places in Madeira where nature appears at its most grandiose and striking, because of the great height and fanciful shapes of the mountains, the steepness and sheer drop of the slopes, the ravines scattered everywhere and the rugged, wild character of the landscape. All this gives the whole such grandeur and majesty, and such extraordinary and enchanting beauty, that even the least prepared and least sensitive traveller is astonished and spellbound on beholding this scene of so many incomparable wonders. And it is from the heights of Jardim da Serra that these astonishing panoramic views can best be observed, drawing a considerable number of Portuguese and foreign visitors to the spot.

before: It was in this locality that the cultivation of tea was first attempted here in Madeira, in the early 19th century, under the direction of H. Veitch, who, it is said somewhere, managed ‘to offer a genuine Madeira tea, which was much appreciated by all his guests’. We believe that not a single specimen of *Thea sinensis* now survives there. We know that recently (1921) the learned farmer Augusto César de Gouveia tried planting tea on his properties at Fajã da Ovelha with the greatest success, obtaining an excellent product that rivals the best tea imported here from England. It seems to us that, besides the attempts at Jardim da Serra and Fajã da Ovelha, others were made on this island to grow the plant.

before: The Madeiran archipelago had the distinction of being the first of these captaincies or overseas provinces: one had its seat on the island of Porto Santo, and the other two in Machico and Funchal. It is impossible today to determine precisely when they were created, but it must be taken as certain that they date from the time when the colonisation and settlement of this archipelago began. When the first captains-donatary of these islands came to settle here permanently, they lost no time in dividing and demarcating the lands that were to belong to their respective jurisdictions. It is to be believed that they were already invested with the privileges and prerogatives that the donation charters would later confer on them in a more legal and authentic manner, with the confirmation of the authority of Prince Henry the Navigator and also of the monarchs.

before: The royal power did not abdicate its prerogatives; Prince Henry the Navigator called this island ‘my island of Madeira’, not only because he had initiated its discovery but also because of the donations the monarchs had made to him; and the powerful Order of Christ held all spiritual jurisdiction over these islands, as well as various privileges in the administration of certain public matters. Even so, the government of the donataries was almost sovereign, at least in the early days. This was not only for the reasons we have briefly outlined, and in particular the distance separating them from the mainland, but chiefly because the monarchs, Prince Henry the Navigator and later the grand masters of the Order of Christ largely confined themselves, in the earliest period of colonisation, to collecting the rents and taxes and the various war levies with which the people were at first heavily burdened.

before: We have already referred briefly elsewhere to the life of pomp and grandeur led by the donataries of Funchal. It seems that some of them sought to rival the monarchs in luxury and magnificence, appearing at court solemnities and at the lavish wedding ceremonies of princes with such extraordinary brilliance and unusual pomp that they dazzled the richest and noblest gentlemen who frequented the royal palaces. They organised great expeditions to conquer and relieve our strongholds in Morocco, in which fleets of dozens of ships and many hundreds of men and horses at times remained in Africa for several consecutive months, all at their own expense and at no cost whatever to the government of mainland Portugal. Among the displays of pomp and grandeur that adorned the ostentatious life of the third donatary, Simão Gonçalves da Câmara (see that entry), known as the Magnificent, one stands out: the lavish gift to Pope Leo X of the Sacred College made in *alfenim* (white sugar paste for modelling figures), presented by an embassy, as described elsewhere. In 1576 the 5th captain-donatary (*capitão-donatário*), Simão Gonçalves, was given the title of Count of Calheta, in recognition of the services of his forebears and the splendour and wealth of his great house.

before: The owner of the Selvagens was astounded when the explorer, in that dry, direct language so characteristic of the English, asked his permission to search the islets for the treasure, which would be divided between the two of them. before: ‘Around the “Terreiro da Luta”, very high mountains rise to the north, east and west, the site itself being a mountain plateau covered with dense, fragrant pine woods; to the south, however, the bay of Funchal opens out, vast and smiling, spreading in a gentle curve from the projection of the Balancal in the east to the abrupt cliff of the highest promontory in the world: the famous Cabo Girão. ‘The eye, gradually leaving behind the wilder aspects of this singular landscape – unexpected, deep abysses and astonishing rises of slope and height, all covered with intertwining vegetation – descends by imperceptible degrees along the valley that opens at our feet, the Curral Velho, and, passing over the tall bell towers of the white church, links us to civilisation: it passes over the orderly houses of the city, stretches out over the harbour, where warships and towering transatlantic liners lose their unsettling size, and reaches beyond to the vastness of the horizon, blending on the dazzled retina the indigo of the waters with the luminous blue of the sky.

before: The now defunct Agricultural Council (*Junta Agrícola*) began to build a road intended to link Terreiro da Luta with Santo António da Serra. If this road is ever completed, it will allow Portuguese and foreigners alike to travel quickly to one of the most beautiful spots the island possesses. Had that body applied part of its substantial revenues to finishing the road, instead of acquiring upland commons (montados) and making other expenditure that was practically useless, we could today travel in about three hours to a place which, for its lovely landscapes and the freshness and greenness of its fields, fully deserves our admiration. before: Someone had the happy idea of raising in this paradisiacal spot a grand monument in honour of Nossa Senhora da Paz (Our Lady of Peace). It consists of an exquisite marble statue set on a plinth flanked by artistic bronze bas-reliefs alluding to the traditional belief that the Most Holy Virgin appeared on that very spot. Attached to the monument stands a small, elegant chapel, where the holy sacrifice of the Mass and other acts of worship are frequently celebrated. The monument owes its erection to the ardent zeal and unremitting efforts of Father José Marques Jardim, who spared himself no sacrifice to give it the imposing and grand appearance that distinguishes it, even travelling abroad to raise donations so that the work could be carried out. before: Organised play seems to date back to 1888, when the game was first played competitively by teams. The club rented the grounds of the field at the Achada, in the parish (*freguesia*) of Camacha, from their owners, and played its inaugural match there on 20 March of the same year, between sides of bachelors and married men. before: A subshrub 2 to 8 decimetres tall, with highly variable leaves (toothed, more or less cut, or linear and entire) and mediocre flower heads with yellow flowers. It belongs to the family Compositae, subfamily Liguliflorae. The milky sap that flows from the roots of the *visco*, once solid, has the elasticity and appearance of rubber, and can replace that substance for rubbing out pencil marks on paper. This is the only use of the Madeiran *visco*, nor can any other be found for it, since the quantity of sap produced by each plant is very small. The *visco* is a very common species in Madeira, and it has also been found on the Pico de Ana Ferreira, on Porto Santo.

before: When the cholera epidemic raged in Madeira at the end of 1910 and the beginning of 1911, the idea arose of founding an Asilo de Artes e Ofícios (Arts and Crafts Asylum), intended especially to house the children whom the epidemic had left orphaned and destitute. It was Dr José Alfredo Mendes de Magalhães, then serving here as High Commissioner (*alto comissário*) of the Republic, who conceived this generous initiative and went so far as to lay the first foundations for it. A public subscription and other donations provided the funds raised for the project. These reached the sum of 16,995,120 réis (the Portuguese money of account before 1911; 1,000 réis = 1 mil-réis, 1,000,000 réis = 1 conto) and, with accumulated interest, amounted to 22,000,000 réis by June 1917. At that time the very grave crisis caused by the European war led the Administrative Committee (*Comissão Administrativa*) of these funds to give their income to the Asilo da Mendicidade e Órfãos do Funchal, to relieve the distressing situation of that most worthy and useful institution. The Asilo de Artes e Ofícios was never founded. The Administrative Committee of its funds, made up of the civil governor, General Norberto Teles and Major J. Reis Gomes, considered handing them over to the Asilo da Mendicidade e Órfãos to build a pavilion for workshops, with the remainder going to increase that asylum’s funds, and received the favourable opinion of Dr Alfredo de Magalhães for this.

before: It seems to have begun as a *recolhimento* (religious retreat house for women) under the name of Santa Teresa de Jesus, whose inmates followed the Third Order of Carmel and entered it in the year 1652. Only in 1660 was it turned into a convent, under the Franciscan rule of St Clare. Its first abbess was a nun from the Convent of Santa Clara (St Clare of Assisi), chosen by the ecclesiastical authority. It was in that same year of 1660, that is, two years before his death, that Canon Calaça de Viveiros gave all his property to the convent he had founded. The convent and church underwent major repairs around the middle of the 18th century, when a new and spacious choir was built to replace the old one, which was cramped. The Royal Treasury (*Fazenda Real*) contributed one *conto* (one million réis) de réis to these works, as granted by the royal decree (*alvará*) of 10 February 1750. The following year the Royal Treasury also contributed 750,000 *réis* (old Portuguese money of account; 1$000 = 1,000 réis, 1:000$000 = one conto = 1,000,000 réis) towards building the great wall that flanks the road leading to the church of Santa Luzia (St Lucy).

before: The nuns of the Incarnação had to abandon their convent when the British occupied this island for the second time, in the period from December 1807 to October 1814. The British troops were quartered mainly in the Jesuit College (*Colégio dos Jesuítas*), which was then serving as a seminary, and in the convent of the Incarnação; the nuns left for the convent of Santa Clara on 7 January 1808. Various works were carried out there to lodge and quarter the British forces suitably, and they did the building considerable damage; the church was turned into an Anglican place of worship. Henrique Calaça’s patriotic and genuinely Catholic foundation was occupied by foreign troops and given over to a heretical cult! For the purpose of enforcing the laws of disentailment (*desamortização*, the sale of Church property by the State), this convent was valued by order of the government in August 1862, the valuation putting the worth of the building, church, convent grounds, chaplain’s house, etc., at 10,320,000 *réis* (old Portuguese money of account; 1$000 = 1,000 réis, 1:000$000 = one conto = 1,000,000 réis).

before: There are twenty-six quays (*cais*) in Madeira, spread along the north and south coasts, almost all of them built or improved by order of the District General Council (*Junta Geral*) between 1905 and 1916. Thanks to these quays, it is now fairly easy to embark and land at many points on the island. It is much to be wished that others will be built, not only in Madeira but also on Porto Santo, so as to end the inconvenience suffered by those who visit certain parts of the coast of the two islands. These works, although sometimes costly, amply repay the sacrifices they require, because they bring great benefits to the people by easing communications between the various parishes of the archipelago.

before: In the parish (*freguesia*) of Câmara de Lobos there was a chapel, now extinct, of Nossa Senhora de Belém (Our Lady of Bethlehem), which stood in the locality (*sítio*) of that name. It was founded in 1649 by Gaspar Vasconcelos Henriques and his wife Dona Bernardina de Carvalho, and the deed by which they made the endowment of this chapel is dated 9 February of the same year. When it fell into ruin, it was rebuilt in 1758 by Dom Francisco Inácio Telo de Meneses, a descendant of the founders. The new chapel was built a short distance from the old one, next to the residence, with which it communicated internally. In the locality of Referta, at Porto da Cruz, there was a chapel with the dedication of Nossa Senhora de Belém, which was later renamed Nossa Senhora do Socorro. See Nossa Senhora do Socorro (chapels).

before: The formation of the islands that make up the Madeira archipelago goes back to the Tertiary era, in the Miocene. Submarine uplifts formed columns of emergence, in which volcanic activity continued into the earliest Quaternary. In successive periods of upheaval these altered the islands’ outline, Madeira and Porto Santo branching apart at a depth of 2,000 m and surfacing in the Atlantic 21 miles apart.

before: On Madeira the main eruptive focus lay in the central part of the island, at Curral das Freiras. It was immense and violent, producing partial reliefs in stages that rose from 300 m to 600 m and from there to 1,200 m in a great deluge of lava. This marked and defined the backbone of the central chain, piling up scoria engulfed in fresh torrents and rising progressively to altitudes greater than those the island shows today.

before: Trachydolerites alternate with trachytes and extend chiefly to the west and north. It is worth noting that lavas of this kind in the Boaventura valley are younger than those of the upper formation of the Curral.

before: The Paul da Serra, considered until recently to be a crater choked by internal collapse (the opinion of Stuebel), is seen in the most recent studies as a lava bank, with tuffs and scoria identical to those of the Lombo Gordo formation in the Curral (the opinion of Gagel).

before: Had all the volcanic activity been concentrated in the central caldera, Madeira’s highest point would rise, at Pico Ruivo or another peak, to an altitude of 2,500 metres.
after: Had all the volcanic activity been concentrated in the central caldera, Madeira’s highest point would rise, at Pico Ruivo (‘russet peak’) or another peak, to an altitude of 2,500 metres.

before: The last volcanic surge appears outside the central zone: at the ends of the island (Porto do Moniz and Caniçal), after the Desertas had already separated, and in the southern region, at Câmara de Lobos, Funchal and Caniço, where the most recent cones are found.

before: Basalts show contraction cracks caused by cooling, and they break into large prismatic blocks of polygonal section, mostly irregular hexagons, as can be seen in quarry workings. before: Where the flow is thinner and gently sloping, lamellar basalt is found, contracted into parallel faces that come apart under the violent blow of the pick. Columnar basalt is called *pedra viva* (‘live stone’: compact basalt used for building). Its density varies, so it needs different charges of explosive to be split into blocks, which are then partly dressed for use as building material. Lamellar basalt yields the slabs used for kerbs, levadas (irrigation channels), washing places, paving, etc. The flagstones of the churchyard at Monte were taken from a quarry, now worked out, which, from the nature of its rock, gave its name to the locality (*sítio*) of Lajinhas. These basalts cannot be carved.

Columnar basalt is called *pedra viva* (‘live stone’: compact basalt used for building). Lamellar basalt yields the slabs used for kerbs, levadas (irrigation channels), washing places, paving, etc. The flagstones of the churchyard at Monte were taken from a quarry, now worked out, which, from the nature of its rock, gave its name to the locality (*sítio*) of Lajinhas (‘little flagstones’). These basalts cannot be carved.

before: In 1816 he enrolled in the faculty of canon law at the University of Coimbra. After a brilliant course of study, in which he won first prize in every year, he received the doctoral hood (*capelo*) in 1822 and was then admitted to the teaching staff of that institution of higher education. During his studies he showed such extraordinary talent that his fellow students sought him out as their tutor and coach, and the professors admitted him into their intimate circle. This was remarkable at a time when the rigidity of university discipline did not allow such closeness between teachers and students. It seems that, while still a student at the University, he took holy orders and had even celebrated Mass, but he later abandoned his ecclesiastical career, to the great scandal of his contemporaries. On taking his doctorate he defended a thesis attacking a very important precept of Church discipline, which he published under the title *Memória sobre o celibato eclesiastico...* The volume was seized and ordered to be destroyed, and few copies circulated. In 1866, after his death, a second edition of this work appeared in a volume of two hundred and some pages.

before: Although Dom Felipe was proclaimed king of Portugal in September 1580, the first governor-general of the Madeira archipelago appointed by the usurping government did not reach Funchal until long after that proclamation. The man chosen for the post was the high court judge (*desembargador*) João Leitão, who enjoyed the full confidence of the Governor of the Kingdom. He was also charged with conducting a judicial inquiry (*devassa*) into the political events that had taken place on this island at the time of the proclamation of Philip II. His powers covered the administration of the royal treasury and the trial of criminal cases, as well as general oversight of civil and military affairs. A writ of lodging (*provisão de aposentadoria*) recorded in volume 2 of the General Register of the Municipal Council (*Câmara Municipal*) of Funchal shows that he was sent to Madeira on 5 January 1582.

before: On this subject, the following words were printed in the ‘Addenda and Corrigenda’ of the second volume of the 1st edition of this work, and they are worth recording here: ‘In the present year of 1924 Dr Damião Peres, former rector of our lyceum (state secondary school) and now a professor at the University of Porto, published a short pamphlet entitled *O desembargador João Leitão, primeiro governador geral da Madeira*. Its sole purpose is to show that the high court judge (*desembargador*) Leitão was governor-general of this archipelago not by law but only in fact, and that he came to Madeira in 1582 and not in 1581, as we read in the *Saudades da Terra* and in vol. 1 of this *Elucidário*. As for the correction of that date, it should be noted here that it was made more than a year ago, on p. 44 of this volume. As for the fact that the document appointing that magistrate to the post of governor-general is not known, this does not prove that he did not hold that office on an interim basis and in fact, as Dr Damião Peres seems to acknowledge. When Spanish rule was established in Portugal, would the government in Madrid have left an important colony such as Madeira for a long time without an official representative of its own to oversee the various affairs of public administration? That representative was João Leitão. Indeed, the proven fact that he “was invested with a multiplicity of powers and privileges”, to which must be added that he was charged with conducting a judicial inquiry (*devassa*) of a political nature, sufficiently explains why his appointment to that post was not made definitive.’ (1921)

before: A locality (*sítio*) in the parish (*freguesia*) of Água de Pena. It was the seat of the entailed estate (*morgadio*) founded by João Afonso Escudeiro in 1512. He was a native of mainland Portugal, the Kingdom (*reino*, i.e. mainland Portugal), and came to this island around 1450. He was of noble descent, and his rank as a *fidalgo* (nobleman of the lesser nobility) was recognised here. He died in 1512 at an advanced age, and by a will made on 21 June of that year he founded the entail of Bemposta, in the parish of Água de Pena, and that of São Lázaro, in the parish of Santa Cruz. The first administrator of the entailed estate of Bemposta was Dona Catarina Anes Escudeiro, daughter of José Afonso, who married Lopo Franco de Monção, so called because he was a native of the town (*vila*) of that name. He came to Madeira around 1480, and in 1515 he was the first judge of the Council (*juiz da câmara*) of Santa Cruz. He was succeeded in the administration of the entailed estate of Bemposta by his son João Franco, and in the *quinta* (country estate) and chantry (capela) of São Lázaro by a daughter named Maria Franco. The third administrator of the entailed estate of Bemposta was Diogo Lopes Tavares, who also inherited the entail of São Lázaro, because Dona Maria Franco had died without issue. This family had a family vault in the old convent of Santa Cruz, where until not many years ago its tombstone could still be seen, bearing a shield with the arms of the Tavares and Borralho families.

before: It was in the peaceful retreat of the presbytery of the parish (*freguesia*) of Ribeira Grande, on the island of São Miguel, where he was parish priest, that Dr Gaspar Frutuoso (volume II, page 57) wrote the *Saudades da Terra* (‘Longing for the Homeland’). It is a very extensive work, divided into six books, covering the history of the archipelagos of the Canary Islands, Cape Verde, Madeira and the Azores. In the second book, which deals with our archipelago, Dr Frutuoso refers in more than one place to Jerónimo Dias Leite (volume I, page 361), a canon of Funchal Cathedral (*Sé*), who supplied him with much material for writing that book. In his own words: ‘And of Gonçalo Aires Ferreira, the root of these, they all say that he wrote the Discovery of the Island of Madeira, set down in truth, as I have said, on three sheets of paper; and the reverend Canon Jerónimo Dias Leite, no less learned than inquisitive, Chaplain to His Majesty, afterwards compiled it, enlarged it and polished it with his grave and refined style, written on eleven sheets of paper, and sent it to me when it was requested on my behalf, through the intercession of the noble Belchior Fernandes de Crasto, resident in the City of Ponta Delgada, on this island where we are, and because the most magnificent Marcos Lopes, a wholesale merchant of great and honourable dealings who lived on this island of São Miguel, much esteemed and loved here for his good qualities and magnificent disposition, and now residing in Lisbon with a great house and a greater name, had it requested of him at my entreaty. From this writing, and from many other accounts that I sought from various persons of the island of Madeira and of other parts, all worthy of trust, and from other things that I saw and read, I gathered and composed this whole account of the discovery of the said Island, ordering, arranging, reducing, adding, and putting everything into chapters, in the manner in which I am telling it.’

before: In his *Bibliotheca Açoreana*, the illustrious native of São Miguel Dr Ernesto do Canto states that the copy used by Dr Álvaro de Azevedo ‘lacked the necessary accuracy’, which is much to be regretted. Dr Canto made a long and conscientious comparison between a printed copy of the work published by Dr Azevedo and Dr Gaspar Frutuoso’s own autograph. In that printed copy, which is today in the public library of Ponta Delgada, he entered ‘many important corrections and additions... resulting from the collation’, as we read in the introduction to Book 3 of the *Saudades da Terra*, published in 1922. In Dr Álvaro Rodrigues de Azevedo’s edition Dr Frutuoso’s text fills 310 pages, but Dr Ernesto do Canto’s collation covers only the first 239.

In Dr Álvaro Rodrigues de Azevedo’s edition Dr Frutuoso’s text fills 310 pages, but Dr Ernesto do Canto’s collation covers only the first 239.

before: The people of São Miguel wished to pay fitting tribute to their most illustrious fellow islander by marking the fourth centenary of his birth, which fell last year, 1922, with the publication of his celebrated work *Saudades da Terra*. The first volume, containing the history of the island of Santa Maria, has already been printed, and three more volumes on the island of São Miguel are to follow. This first volume is preceded by several chapters, running to two hundred long pages, on Dr Gaspar Frutuoso and his vast and valuable work. They are thorough and complete studies, which set the figure of the historian of the islands in brilliant relief and assign him the true place he deserves in the history of Portuguese literature. They are remarkable works of research and criticism, which greatly honour and distinguish their authors and at the same time bring well-deserved fame and renown to the Azores. The introduction to this work contains various references to Madeira and to Book 2 of the *Saudades*, which deals with this archipelago, and every moderately educated Madeiran ought to own a copy of this book (1921).

before: As is well known, the commentator of the *Saudades* did not confine himself to writing a few brief explanatory notes on the text, expanding or completing it. To cite only giants of unquestioned authority on the subject, we would recall that Camilo Castelo Branco, Pinheiro Chagas and Teófilo Braga referred to these works with the most fervent praise, and it is known that the first and the last were not in the habit of squandering their literary judgements on easy and commonplace compliments...

before: A luxurious edition of the 2nd book of the *Saudades da Terra* has just been produced in Porto (1925). It contains only the text of Gaspar Frutuoso, omitting the extensive and learned commentary of Dr Álvaro Rodrigues de Azevedo. The edition was ably directed by Dr Damião Peres, former rector of our lyceum (state secondary school) and now a distinguished professor at the University of Porto, who added some valuable, though not very numerous, annotations. It undoubtedly represents a good service to letters, but it will benefit above all scholars and those who devote themselves particularly to the study of our literature and its history in the period to which that work belongs.

before: Under the original system of colonisation, our overseas dominions were divided, for the purposes of public administration, into provinces of greater or lesser extent, which were then called captaincies. Each was headed by a captain-donatary (*capitão-donatário*), its supreme local authority, who generally enjoyed wide powers in the conduct of the various public affairs. The first captaincies of our discoveries and conquests were those of the Madeira archipelago: one had its seat on the island of Porto Santo, and the other two in Machico and in Funchal.

before: The island of Madeira was divided into two captaincies, with their seats in Funchal and Machico. After the discovery, in order to begin the colonisation and settlement of its lands, the two discoverers lost no time in dividing and demarcating them, fixing a dividing line that ran from Ponta da Oliveira to Ponta do Tristão. Frutuoso says: ‘... Ponta de Oliveira, where a boundary mark was planted for the division of the two captaincies, which are divided by this stream, that of Machico lying to the east and that of Funchal to the west, and along it, they say, runs the demarcation from the seashore in the south to the other side in the north’, adding elsewhere: ‘...it comes out at the other point on the southern side, where a branch or stake of olive wood, which had come from the Kingdom (*reino*, i.e. mainland Portugal), was driven in as a boundary mark of this jurisdiction, whence the point took the name Ponta da Oliveira ... ’

before: The letter of grant (carta de doação) of the captaincy of Machico to Tristão Vaz by Prince Henry the Navigator is dated 8 May 1440. In it the grantor states: ‘dou carreguo a Tristão caballeyro de minha casa na minha ylha da madeyra de a terra dees de além da ribeyra do Caniço dez passos como se bay pella ribeyra acima & de hi atrabeçar a serra ate a ponta de Tristam... ’ (I give charge to Tristão, knight of my household, in my island of Madeira, of the land from ten paces beyond the Ribeira do Caniço, going up the stream, and from there across the uplands as far as the point of Tristão...). This document is couched in terms identical to the letter of concession issued in favour of Bartolomeu Perestrelo, and is six years older than the latter. The observation we have already made about the grant of Porto Santo applies here too: it must be supposed that in 1440 only the confirmation in law took place, but that the grant had existed in fact long before. Tristão Vaz’s son, grandson and great-grandson succeeded to the captaincy. The last of them, named Diogo Teixeira, was removed from it for lack of the ability to govern it, and died much later in Funchal, in the year 1540. In 1541 the monarch gave the captaincy to António da Silveira, who greatly distinguished himself in India. Some years later he sold it to the Count of Vimioso, and it then passed to his son Francisco de Portugal, who died in a naval battle in the seas of the Azores, after which this donatary captaincy (*donataria*) reverted to the Crown. Under Castilian rule Tristão Vaz da Veiga (see that entry) was invested in the office of captain-donatary (*capitão-donatário*) of Machico.

before: It is in the royal letter (*carta régia*) of 16 August 1461, in which Afonso V confirms the grant of the Madeira archipelago to his uncle Prince Henry, published on p. 451 ff. of the *Saudades da Terra*, that the document granting the captaincy of Funchal to João Gonçalves Zarco, dated 1 November 1450, is inserted. The grants of the captaincies of Porto Santo, Machico and Funchal date respectively from 1446, 1440 and 1450. It is rather strange that the most recent should be that of Funchal, later even than that of Porto Santo, when there are many reasons to suppose that the concession made to Gonçalves Zarco was the oldest of all. We cannot explain this fact, about which the learned annotator of the *Saudades* keeps the most complete silence.

before: When he was prefect (*prefeito*) of Madeira, the illustrious Mouzinho de Albuquerque conceived the plan of building a suspension bridge over the Ribeiro Seco. To this end he began the construction of two gigantic piers, besides two very strong abutments, one on each bank of the brook. ‘The plan of the work, says Sérvulo de Meneses in the *Colecção de documentos relativos á construção da ponte do Ribeiro Seco*, included the idea of raising a monument to the memory of the immortal Duke of Braganza, the magnanimous liberator of the Portuguese, and accordingly the work was to be magnificent and grand.’

before: The decree of 31 October 1912 ceded the former convent of Santa Clara to the Holy House of Mercy, except for the church, the land needed to widen the streets bordering the convent, and the land already ceded to the Auxílio Maternal association. The decree of 22 September 1913 confirmed the cession made to the Misericórdia by the decree of 31 October 1912 for the building of the hospital, and introduced some changes to the way the land and buildings were to be divided among the Municipal Council (*Câmara Municipal*), the Auxílio Maternal and the Holy House of Mercy. before: The Confraternity of the Misericórdia of Funchal was established by royal letter (*carta régia*) of 1514, according to a record we found in the archive of this institution. By another royal letter, of 18 September of the same year, the hospital was annexed and handed over to the said Confraternity, under whose supervision and administration all the hospital services were placed, ‘provided that the poor and sick who come to the said hospital are always provided for’. The Confraternity was installed in the parish church of Santa Maria Maior, which adjoined the hospital. The annotator of the *Saudades* states that John III revoked this concession made by Manuel I, and adds the following: ‘we presume that from then on it functioned in the chapel of the Santos Reis, near the hospital, which had been donated to it in the year 1514’.

before: The political events that had taken place in the country and the absence from the island of many members of the confraternity prevented the election of its managing board (*mesa*) in July 1834. The prefect (*prefeito*) of this province, Luís da Silva Mousinho de Albuquerque, by decree of 16 August that year, appointed a committee to examine the accounts of the Holy House, study the causes of its decline during the period of our civil wars and propose means of remedying it. Following the committee’s recommendations, he then ordered by decree of 8 November 1834 that, on a provisional basis and until the central government reached a final decision on the matter, the Municipal Council (*Câmara Municipal*) of Funchal should appoint an Administrative Committee of five members to manage the affairs of the Holy House from 1 January 1835, and that the appointment of three members should be renewed at the start of each year. He also ordered that the Council should propose six suitable persons, from whom the prefect would choose three to form a committee charged with settling the Holy House’s overdue accounts and collecting all debts owed to the establishment.
