before: Until 1834 the Madeira archipelago was an overseas province and colony whose administration came chiefly under the Navy Ministry. In that year, with the creation of the island districts, it became part of the Adjacent Islands (Ilhas Adjacentes), with an administration entirely identical to that of the mainland districts. The official correspondence sent from Madeira at that time was addressed mainly to the Minister of the Navy and to the Overseas Council (*Conselho Ultramarino*), which handled a large part of the business concerning the administration of our overseas provinces. The valuable and extremely numerous documents on our colonial administration held at the Ministry of the Navy and Overseas were moved a few years ago to the National Library in Lisbon (*Biblioteca Nacional de Lisboa*), where they were duly arranged and catalogued. The worth of this priceless treasure then became better known, as did the outstanding service these papers could render to any studies that might be undertaken on the whole of our colonial and maritime life. When the National Library created the *Archivo da Marinha e Ultramar* section, which comprises some thousands of codices and a countless number of loose documents, Dr Eduardo de Castro e Almeida was entrusted with inventorying and cataloguing them. He began his arduous and most useful task by arranging the loose manuscripts relating to Madeira and Porto Santo, which cover the period from 1613 to 1833. Under the title *Biblioteca Nacional de Lisboa. Archivo da Marinha e Ultramar. inventario . . . Madeira e Porto Santo, I, 1613-1819*, he published in 1907 a volume of 402 pages in folio, and in 1909 volume II, of 487 pages in the same format. Together they form a rich and most valuable repository of news and information, absolutely indispensable to anyone wishing to study the history of this archipelago in the period to which those documents refer.

before: The surname Alemão, now extinct, ‘derives’, says the annotator of the *Saudades da Terra*, following the genealogies, ‘from Henrique Alemão, a legendary figure from the earliest days of the colonisation of this island of Madeira. It was said of him that he was a Polish prince and that, after the battle of Varna was lost in 1444 by Władysław IV against Murad II, he vowed to go on pilgrimage to the Holy Land and was dubbed a knight of St Catherine of Mount Sinai. When he came to the island of Madeira, João Gonçalves Zarco granted him, at the locality (*sítio*) later called Madalena do Mar, a large tract of land as a *sesmaria* (royal land grant to settlers on condition of cultivation), by a charter confirmed by Prince Henry the Navigator on 29 April 1457 and by Afonso V on 18 May of the same year. Henrique Alemão did indeed found a large settled estate (*fazenda povoada*) there, with a chapel dedicated to St Mary Magdalene, from which the place took its name. He married Senhorina Anes and died a dreadful death, crushed by a landslide (*quebrada*) that fell from Cabo Girão onto the boat in which he was travelling from the city of Funchal to Madalena. His widow later married João Rodrigues de Freitas. Even now there is, above the town of Ponta do Sol, the Fajã do Alemão, which the common people corruptly call “do Limão”.’

before: A member of the Rubiaceae from the Andes, Peru and Ecuador, introduced to Madeira in 1867 by the late botanist João Maria Moniz. Of the 20 specimens that came to the island at that time, only one survived in 1909, on a *quinta* (country estate) a little above the church of Santa Luzia (St Lucy), where it flowered every year without, however, producing fertile seeds. Some cinchona trees planted in the parish (*freguesia*) of Monte did not last long there. According to the late Richard Thomas Lowe, the places in Madeira where the cultivation of the red cinchona might perhaps be tried with success are the Ribeira da Metade and the Ribeira da Boaventura, the Lombada das Vacas in São Vicente, the Montado dos Pessegueiros on the Ribeira do Inferno, the Ribeira Funda near Seixal, etc., etc. *Cinchona calisaya*, mentioned in a work on the climate of Madeira as growing in the garden of the hospice (*hospício*) of Princess Dona Maria Amélia, was never cultivated on our island.

before: The municipality of Ponta do Sol was established in 1501 and that of Calheta in 1502. To this end the municipality of Funchal was divided up; in the 15th century it had stretched from Ponta do Tristão to the Ribeira do Caniço, and was bounded inland by the mountain range running from this stream to the same point. before: The municipalities of Câmara de Lobos, Santana and Porto do Moniz date from 1835. In his royal decree (*alvará*) of 10 August of that year, the prefect (*prefeito*) of the province ordered that the proceedings for the municipal elections, which were to be held throughout the archipelago on 4 October, should be presided over in the first of these municipalities by a councillor of the Funchal Council, in the second by a councillor of the Machico Council, and in the third by a councillor of the São Vicente Council. On that occasion the electors of the municipality of Funchal elected 7 councillors (*vereadores*); those of Porto Santo, 3; and those of the remaining municipalities, 5. The municipalities of Câmara de Lobos, Santa Cruz and Santana were abolished by the decree of 10 December 1867 and restored shortly afterwards. The municipality of Porto do Moniz was abolished by this same decree, which remained in force for only a very short time, and also by the decrees of 7 November 1849 and 18 November 1895; it had already been restored by 1855 and by the beginning of 1898 respectively. The municipality of Ribeira Brava, the most recent in the archipelago, was created by the decree of 16 August 1914.

before: The full title of this work is *Historia Insulana das Ilhas a Portugal sugeitas no Oceano Occidental*. Its author was Father António Cordeiro (see that entry), and it appeared in two editions, in 1717 and 1866. Until 1873 it was a very well-known work, highly regarded by everyone interested in the history of the Madeiran archipelago. With the publication that year of the *Saudades da Terra* and the extremely valuable notes that accompany them, however, Father Cordeiro’s work came to be of very secondary value, chiefly because it is a summary, not always free of defects, of Dr Gaspar Frutuoso’s extensive manuscript. Apart from the few pages that some chroniclers had devoted to the history of Madeira, nothing else in print was known on the subject, and for that reason the appearance of Father António Cordeiro’s book aroused genuine interest. As Dr Álvaro Rodrigues de Azevedo points out in the preface to the *Saudades da Terra*, the *Historia Insulana* neither replaces Frutuoso’s work nor surpasses it in any respect, because Cordeiro’s work is a summary of the *Saudades* and goes no further than 1590, the year in which they were written, even though the *Historia Insulana* was published in 1717. While Book II of the *Saudades* fills 300 printed pages, Book III of the *Historia Insulana*, which deals with Madeira, runs to no more than 44 pages of text in the second edition of this work.

before: The *Historia Insulana* consists of nine books. The first deals with the various peoples who occupied ancient Lusitania, the second with the Canary Islands and Cape Verde, the third with Porto Santo and Madeira, and the remaining six with the islands of the Azores, to which Cordeiro devotes the greater part of his work. The *Historia Insulana* had long been out of print and was already quite rare when a second edition appeared in 1866. It was identical to the first in every respect except for an addendum entitled *Algumas notas e adições á História Insulana do padre Antonio Cordeiro na parte relativa á ilha da Madeira*, by A. J. G. A. In a brief introduction the annotator, referring to the vast work of Gaspar Frutuoso, says, if somewhat exaggeratedly: ‘this work contained materials gathered without critical judgement, heaps of genealogies, in which its author was strong, set down without order, which called for a man of another calibre, capable of writing a continuous history, free of the many defects that Gaspar Frutuoso himself would perhaps have avoided had he been granted more years of life. Such a man Father Cordeiro was not! He did not undertake this task, nor did he seek to verify the facts related by his predecessor; rather, content to compile them, as Justin had done with the history of Trogus Pompeius, he fell into the same faults as his original, and the *Insulana* is still far from perfect’.

A. before: We cannot list, even in summary, the services by which José Silvestre Ribeiro marked his time among us. Yet it is impossible not to mention, however briefly, the founding of the Asylum; the swift and salutary measures taken to overcome the terrible famine crisis of 1847; the creation of the Agricultural Society; the building of the Ponte Monumental (Monumental Bridge); the introduction of public lighting; the exhibition of Madeiran industries; the organisation of a natural history museum; and the creation of many primary schools. Nor can we pass over his very important measures for the replanting and preservation of woodland; the major repairs to the roads and to almost all the buildings of the State, including most of the churches; and the effective and strict measures he adopted concerning the management of charitable institutions, municipal taxes, cemeteries, foundlings, council revenues, etc. We must also mention the way he defended the interests of Madeira in parliament, the great expansion of public works, the remarkable impetus given to the cutting of levadas (irrigation channel), especially that of Rabaçal, and the building of shelters in the mountains and on the ridges. There was no public need he did not seek to meet, nor any area of administration that his effective initiative and tireless energy did not reach. We would go far, very far, if we wished to descend into details and particulars, which do not fit within the narrow limits of this article, which cannot be long.

before: The name of José Silvestre Ribeiro is still well remembered here and is regarded, beyond any possible dispute, as that of the most illustrious and beneficent governor the Madeira archipelago has ever had. In Funchal, the blessed memory of José Silvestre Ribeiro has been perpetuated only by giving his name to one of the city’s thoroughfares, better known by the shortened form Rua do Conselheiro; even the general public does not know that it represents a tribute to this governor. One thing could still be done, and the press has already suggested it: to give the Asilo da Mendicidade (poorhouse) the name of its founder. Anyone wishing to gain a fuller knowledge of his administration in this district should read *Uma Época Administrativa na Madeira e Porto Santo*, 3 thick volumes; *Colecção de Documentos relativos à crise da fome por que passaram as ilhas da Madeira e Porto Santo no ano de 1847*; *Colecção de Documentos relativos ao Asilo da Mendicidade do Funchal*; *Colecção de Documentos relativos á construção da Ponte do Ribeiro Seco*; and *Brevíssima resenha de alguns serviços que no distrito do Funchal tem prestado o conselheiro José Silvestre Ribeiro*.

before: This high ridge lies between the parishes (*freguesias*) of Serra de Água and São Vicente, at an altitude of over a thousand metres, on the crest of the mountain range that runs lengthwise through the interior of Madeira. The road from Ribeira Brava to São Vicente passes here, and from this point both the northern and southern coasts of the island can be seen – or, as the local people say, ‘you can see the north sea and the south sea’, which is indeed the case on days with clear horizons. In 1939 the Madeira Tourism Delegation had a comfortable rest house and shelter built in the parish of Serra de Água; it is much to be regretted that this building was not put up closer to that height.

before: He first arrived in Funchal on 8 February 1869 and returned in 1870 and 1871. According to some notes published in the former magazine *Serões*, which we consider reliable, Júlio Dinis lived, if only briefly, in a house at the Ilhéus (islets), where the distinguished lawyer Nuno Ferreira Jardim once resided, and for longer in a building on Rua da Carreira belonging to the family of the late merchant António Pinto Correia. A pharmacy is now installed on its ground floor, and it stands almost opposite Rua de São Francisco. The Funchal Council would perform an act that all its citizens would regard with grateful praise if it had a simple metal plaque placed on that house, if nothing more could be done, commemorating the stay in our land of one of the greatest figures of our contemporary literature.

before: It was in this city that Júlio Dinis wrote his remarkable novel *Os Fidalgos da Casa Mourisca*, which some consider superior to, and many place on the same level as, *As Pupilas do Senhor Reitor* and *A Morgadinha dos Cannaviaes*. For thirty-odd years a long letter he wrote from Madeira remained unpublished. In it he describes the island’s incomparable beauties in broad strokes, sharing with a friend the personal impressions he received on arriving at the lovely island that rises from the foam of the sea like the mythological Cytherea... to borrow a phrase of the great writer. It is a passage of fine, evocative prose, first published in the aforementioned review *Serões* and reproduced in the book of Júlio Dinis’s unpublished writings entitled *Ineditos e Esparsos*. This work published 17 letters by Júlio Dinis written in Funchal, the last dated 20 February 1870. The 1919 edition of this work includes 31 letters written in Funchal, omitting 7 from the earlier edition, making a total of 38. The *Diário da Madeira* of 24 August 1919 published two further unpublished letters by the great novelist, also dated from Madeira.

before: 9. João Paulo da Veiga Pestana, militia second lieutenant of infantry. He was 20 years old and studying engineering in Portugal when he was called up to attend the school for militia officers. Shortly afterwards he left for France, where he met a glorious death in the battle of 9 April 1918. At a session of the Municipal Council (*Câmara Municipal*) of Funchal on 10 April 1919, councillor (*vereador*) Francisco Gomes de Gouveia proposed that Rua das Hortas be renamed Alferes Veiga Pestana, and the proposal was approved unanimously.

before: On 30 March 1921, shortly after 8 o’clock in the evening, the mortal remains of an unknown soldier were landed at the Cais da Pontinha. He had fallen, giving his life for his country, on the distant shores of East Africa in the struggle against the Germans. The urn containing the remains, which had come on the steamer *Briton* of the Union Castle Mail, spent the night at the Maritime Disinfection Post. At around 1 p.m. the following day it was taken to the town hall, where it remained until 3 April, when it was embarked on the cruiser *Republica*, charged with carrying it to Lisbon. Both when the urn was brought to the town hall, where it lay in state, and when it was taken back to the quay for embarkation, splendid and imposing processions were formed. On 1 April these were joined by the civil and military authorities, the consular corps, some British officers, representatives of the various schools and associations, contingents of the military forces of the Funchal garrison, etc. etc. In the article Unknown Soldier we shall endeavour to describe the spectacular demonstrations held in this city from 1 to 3 April 1921 to glorify the humble soldier, whose remains now rest in the majestic Batalha Monastery, built by order of King John I after the heroic battle of Aljubarrota.

before: A composite plant widely grown at Camacha and elsewhere in Madeira. before: Because of its small area and small population, the island of Porto Santo has always formed a single parish (*freguesia*). It has borne, and still bears today, the name of Nossa Senhora da Piedade (Our Lady of Pity), the patron saint of its parish church. Although Frutuoso stated in 1590 that the patron saint and name of the parish was the Salvador (the Saviour), the truth is that documents earlier than that date already give the patron saint as Nossa Senhora da Piedade, and we believe it was never any other.

before: We believe that the seat of the parish was established in the chapel of Nossa Senhora da Piedade (Our Lady of Pity), which already stood there before the parish was created. It underwent various repairs and extensions, and was completely rebuilt around 1667. Nothing remains of the original building except the so-called chapel of the Morgada, which belonged to an old Baião family. It still keeps its pointed arch, which, since some of the stones forming it were somewhat damaged, was rendered with a cement coating a few years ago! No church in the diocese ever suffered so many profanations and outrages as this one, owing to the raids that corsairs made on that island from time to time. As there were no defences of any kind there, the inhabitants thought only of taking refuge on the Pico do Castelo and in other safe places whenever they sensed the pirates approaching, leaving them a free hand to carry out their work of destruction and plunder. In 1617 Porto Santo was invaded by Algerian corsairs, and the mother church (*igreja matriz*) was sacked and set on fire; the same happened again in 1667, after which the church was rebuilt. In 1556, 1690 and 1708 it was not Moors but French ships fitted out as privateers that attacked the island and thoroughly plundered it, the parish church again being a target of the attackers’ fury. It should be remembered that in those times French ships were protected by high-ranking personages – some even claim by the kings of France themselves. These ships often roamed the seas as pirates, committing the gravest crimes with impunity, slaughtering and robbing defenceless settlements. Such was the case with the French invasion of Madeira in 1556, as we shall see in its proper place.

before: This illustrious Madeiran was born on 2 March 1822 and died in Lisbon on 23 June 1899. He was the son of Francisco Correia Herédia (see that entry) and Dona Ana Margarida de Bettencourt Acciaioly e Sá Escórcio Drumond, and descended from old and noble families of this island. We do not know whether he held any formal academic qualifications, but his lack of higher or university education did not prevent him from being a skilful and talented journalist. He might perhaps have become a distinguished writer, had his many occupations not wholly absorbed the great energy of his mind. The writings he left prove it. He held many public offices: he was president of the Municipal Council (*Câmara Municipal*), representative (*procurador*) on the District General Council (*Junta Geral*), secretary-general (*secretário geral*), civil governor, director of the customs houses of Funchal, Porto and Lisbon, director-general of customs, deputy, peer of the realm, and president of many commissions for the reform of various public services, etc. In the course of some of these offices he wrote several reports, regulations and bills that amply prove his learning, his competence and his great capacity for work. Besides his journalism, which is extensive, he published: *Breves reflexões sobre a abolição dos morgados na Madeira*, Lisbon, 1849; *As contradições imaculadas*, Funchal, 1850; *A Boa Fé do «Archivista»*, Funchal, 1852; *Observações sobre a situação económica da ilha da Madeira e sobre a reforma das Alfândegas*, Lisbon, 1888, 96 pp.; *Relatório do Projecto do Regulamento Geral das Alfândegas*, Lisbon, 1876, 129 pp.; *Exposição e Documentos enviados à Câmara dos Dignos Pares*, Lisbon, 1886; *António Correia Herédia — Ao Público*, Lisbon, 1885, 235 pp.

before: Luís de Ornelas Pinto Coelho was born in the parish (*freguesia*) of São Pedro in this city on 21 February 1843, the son of Joaquim Pinto Coelho and Dona Maria Carlota de Ornelas Pinto Coelho. We believe he held no academic qualification at all, not even a primary-school certificate, but he made up for that deficiency through a persevering love of reading and study, and came to hold a true pre-eminence among us in the literary and journalistic field. He contributed extensively to many Madeiran newspapers, notably the *Diario de Noticias*. It may be said that in this paper, as its editor over a period of several decades, he published many hundreds of articles, which would fill a dozen thick volumes. He rarely sent the paper anything other than the leading article or a polemical piece, and his prose had an elegant and correct form that gave particular pleasure. He fought hard battles in the press, in which, as always happened here at that time, excesses of language were not rare on either side.

before: The well-known writer and poet Bulhão Pato was a close friend of the 2nd Count of Carvalhal, and in his company spent several seasons on this island. He refers to this in some of his books with the most vivid and fond recollection. In the book *Sob os Ciprestes* and in the three volumes of his *Memórias* he writes about a number of Madeiran people and things. They contain extensive references to the Count of Carvalhal, Jacinto de Sant'Ana e Vasconcelos, the Viscountess of Nogueiras, Jaime Moniz, Luís da Costa Pereira and others. In cantos VI and VII of his poem *Paquita*, Bulhão Pato gives a fine poetic description of Madeira. Bulhão Pato stayed on this island from 7 August 1850 to 6 March 1851.

before: In 1611, on land in the parish (*freguesia*) of Monte that later came to belong to the parish of Santa Luzia, Tristão Gomes de Castro founded a chapel dedicated to Nossa Senhora dos Prazeres. There was a chapel of the same dedication in the parish of Santa Maria Maior; it was entailed, and in 1610 its administrator was João Gomes de Castro. We do not know the year of its foundation.
after: In 1611, on land in the parish (*freguesia*) of Monte (‘hill’) that later came to belong to the parish of Santa Luzia (‘St Lucy’), Tristão Gomes de Castro founded a chapel dedicated to Our Lady of the Joys (*Nossa Senhora dos Prazeres*). There was a chapel of the same dedication in the parish of Santa Maria Maior (‘St Mary Major’); it was entailed, and in 1610 its administrator was João Gomes de Castro. before: As the annotator of the *Saudades da Terra* judiciously observes, the island of Porto Santo had a station or revenue guard post (*posto fiscal*) rather than a customs house in the proper sense. We do not know the date of its creation, but it already existed in 1556, because the royal decree (alvará régio) of 8 April of that year appointed Gaspar Calaça to the post of *almoxarife* (royal revenue officer and storekeeper), the most important office of that customs house, with an annual salary of two thousand *réis* (old Portuguese money of account; 1$000 = 1,000 réis, 1:000$000 = one conto = 1,000,000 réis) in cash, two *moios* of wheat and two *pipas* of wine. The last appointment of an *almoxarife* of which we have record is that of Diogo Luís Drumond, made by the royal decree of 22 July 1768. The office of clerk (*escrivão*) predates 1556, for in that year Diogo Delgado was appointed to it on the death of his predecessor, Rodrigo Anes. There was also the post of harbour constable (*alcaide do mar*), created well before 1642. We do not know when the Porto Santo customs house ceased to exist.

before: António Alfredo de Santa Catarina Braga, a Franciscan ex-friar (*egresso*), was born in the city of Porto in the last quarter of the 18th century. Around 1820 he left the convent and became a secular priest. In the houses of his order he taught philosophy and theology with distinction, and in his day he was a notable and renowned preacher. Persecuted for his liberal ideas, he was deported to Cape Verde and then went on to Brazil. before: By decree of 7 November 1834 António Alfredo was appointed temporal governor of the diocese of Funchal, a post he held until April 1840; by decree of 25 February of that year he was relieved of it and entrusted with another commission. He was a man of rare talent and wide learning, as his contemporaries testify, as do the speeches, pastoral letters and other occasional writings he left us. Nevertheless, his time at the head of this diocese was not marked by the most austere probity and scrupulous conduct. He became notorious, causing grave scandal, for the showy and solemn act of going in person to the Convent of São Bernardino (St Bernardino of Siena) in Câmara de Lobos at the beginning of June 1835 to forbid the cult paid there to Friar Pedro da Guarda, known as the Holy Servant of God. In his presence he had the statue of the humble friar, which was venerated in a chapel beside the convent, burnt. He then published a pastoral letter condemning and forbidding any cult that anyone might seek to pay to Friar Pedro da Guarda.

before: The old customs and ancient usages of Madeira call for long and careful study, which will receive our particular attention in various articles of this *Elucidário*. Here we shall merely give a brief account of some facts that characterise many of these customs and that show us, above all, the clear traces of the old feudalism which, in some of its nuances, long survived among the old nobility of this archipelago. Our conquests in Morocco and the holding of the cities and strongholds we had taken had a great influence on the customs of our country and on the private lives of its inhabitants. They bred an exaggerated taste for risky enterprises and for unknown and unforeseen adventures, which showed itself in territorial expansion and the enlargement of the overseas dominions, in the quest for unknown regions and ‘seas never sailed before’, in the hallowed phrase of our epic poet. In proportion to its size, no Portuguese land contributed to our struggles in North Africa as much as the Madeiran archipelago. Its donataries organised great expeditions, with fleets of dozens of ships and many hundreds of men and horses, in which a considerable number of noblemen and knights took a very active part. All this was at the expense of the expeditionaries themselves, without the least cost to the mother country, and often lasted for months on end, during which they performed the most valiant deeds, reaching the point of heroism and recklessness. They organised costly military expeditions and sent the richest gifts to monarchs and pontiffs, as Simão Gonçalves da Câmara, the Magnificent, did in the embassy to Leo X, and they appeared at the festivities of the royal palace and at princely weddings with such luxury and display that they dazzled everyone, etc. This excessive love of luxury and grandeur was reflected in the Madeiran nobility, leading it into a useless and idle life spent in Funchal or at court, leaving its lands and manor houses in the care and management of none too scrupulous stewards. Striking examples of this are the games, hunts and cavalcades, the skirmishes, contests and fights, and the showy festivities, typified by the banquet at the wedding of António Gonçalves da Câmara and Isabel de Abreu, etc., etc. Before long a large number of houses were ruined and their revenues mortgaged, reducing many to a shameful and wretched existence. More frequent communication with the mother country and with foreign lands, the growth of trade with many outsiders residing on this island, the departure of countless noblemen and commoners for the wars and adventurous life of India and Brazil, from which they returned with profound changes in their private way of life, the influence of Spanish rule and yet other causes contributed notably to this transformation, which became more marked in the course of the 17th and 18th centuries.

before: Throughout the stay of the king and queen of Portugal on this island there was an unbroken series of festivities and enthusiastic demonstrations in their honour, of which we can give only a brief account. Special mention is due to the gala performance at the Theatre, so brilliantly described by the Count of Arnoso; the solemn session at the town hall; the splendid entertainments given by Luís da Rocha Machado, the Viscount of Cacongo and João Blandy at their *quintas* (country estates) of Monte, Choupana and Palheiro do Ferreiro; the gala dinner at São Lourenço; the open-air Mass in the Praça Académica; the ball at Quinta Vigia; the industrial and agricultural exhibition, etc.

before: It is also asserted that it was the Governor of Brazil, Martim Afonso de Sousa, who requested that these Madeirans go there and, through them, set in motion the first planting of sugar cane. The crises that afflicted Madeira at various times led large waves of emigrants to leave, and the following information, given in one of the annotations to the *Saudades da Terra*, is of interest: ‘By 1676 decline in this archipelago had reached such a point that emigration to Brazil, until then a mere expedient or private speculation, came to be promoted as a measure of government: in that year a royal letter (*carta régia*) was issued, and another in 1747, both recorded in the archive of the Council of Funchal. The first ordered that three hundred to four hundred couples be transported to Brazil at the expense of the state, and the second recommended that the captain-general (capitão-general, military governor of Madeira) give help and favour to this emigration.’

before: He was born in the parish (*freguesia*) of Câmara de Lobos on 24 December 1840 and was a distinguished poet. His verse is scattered through several periodicals of Funchal and of the city of Ponta Delgada, and through the annuals *Novo Almanach de Lembranças Luso-Brasileiro*, *Almanach das Senhoras*, *Almanach Madeirense* and *Almanach de Lembranças Madeirense*. He left in manuscript a book entitled *Espinhos e Flores*, in which many of his poems published in various almanacs and newspapers are said to be collected.

before: He was born in the city of Lisbon on 21 March 1837, the son of Miguel Pinto da Silva Mourão and Dona Joana Marques. He was only three months old when the distinguished physician Dr António da Luz Pita adopted him as his son, at the time when, accompanied by his parents, he was passing through the port of Funchal on his way to Africa. He graduated in medicine from the faculty of Montpellier, defending the thesis *Du Climat de Madère...*, which he published in 1859 in a volume of 262 pp. On the same subject, and under the title *Madère, Station Médicale fixe...*, he published a pamphlet of 101 pp. in Paris in 1889. He was an army doctor, reaching the rank of brigade surgeon, and for many years held the post of clinical director of the Hospício da Princesa Dona Maria Amélia. He served as French consular agent on this island, as representative (*procurador*) to the District General Council (*Junta Geral*), and on other public service commissions. He died in Funchal on 22 May 1906.

before: The island of Porto Santo – so named, according to Frutuoso, because it was there that Gonçalves Zarco and Tristão Vaz Teixeira escaped a violent storm, as already mentioned, which had made them lose ‘all hope of their lives’ – is one of the five islands of the archipelago. It measures 11.4 kilometres in length by 7 in width, and its surface area is calculated at about 50 kilometres. Including its outlying islets, it lies between 32° 59′ 40″ and 33° 7′ 50″ north latitude, and between 16° 16′ 30″ and 16° 24′ 35″ west longitude of Greenwich. Its capital is the town (*vila*) of Baleira, or of Porto Santo, which stands at the head of a vast and beautiful bay, sheltered from the winds from SE round by W to NW (1921).

before: The tamarisk, introduced in 1834 by João António Pedroso, is common on Porto Santo, and the palm, the maritime pine, the tree of heaven, the poplar and the myoporum grow in some parts of the island. before: The numerous soundings made by Vidal in the waters around Porto Santo seem to suggest that the island was once larger than it is today, and in some parts of its territory there are clear signs of uplift caused by volcanic action. Cockerell states that the oldest fossil deposits are Miocene and marine, and that shells and corals mixed with a black volcanic rock, which appears to come from a lower zone, can be found on Ponta da Calheta. Between the peaks of Castelo and Facho there are whitish-grey trachytes, and on the summit of the latter height there is a rather curious dyke.

before: This genus of the Leguminosae family, subfamily Mimosoideae, is represented in Madeira by many species, some with bipinnate leaves, others with the leaves reduced to phyllodes (petioles shaped like leaves). To the first group belong *Acacia dealbata* (white acacia), very common at Monte, Choupana, etc.; *A. Farnesiana* (*aroma amarelo*), grown in gardens and subspontaneous at various places near the coast; *A. Leucocephala* (*aroma branco*), a subspontaneous shrub at Gorgulho and Praia Formosa; and *A. (Albizzia) lophantha*, an almost always shrubby species, naturalised chiefly at Monte. To the second group belong *A. Melanoxylon*, grown in *quintas*, squares and some streets; and *A. retinoides*, *A. Sophorae* and *A. longifolia*, common in the *quintas* and gardens of Madeira. Acacias are native to Australia and the warm regions of America, Asia and Africa, and many other species besides those we have mentioned may be found on the island. *Robinia pseudo Acacia*, wrongly known in Madeira as *acácia*, is a thorny tree belonging to the subfamily Papilionaceae and native to North America; it is easy to recognise by its imparipinnate leaves and its white, fragrant flowers borne in clusters.

Melanoxylon*, grown in *quintas*, squares and some streets; and *A. retinoides*, *A. Sophorae* and *A. longifolia*, common in the *quintas* and gardens of Madeira. Acacias are native to Australia and the warm regions of America, Asia and Africa, and many other species besides those we have mentioned may be found on the island. *Robinia pseudo Acacia*, wrongly known in Madeira as *acácia*, is a thorny tree belonging to the subfamily Papilionaceae and native to North America; it is easy to recognise by its imparipinnate leaves and its white, fragrant flowers borne in clusters.

before: Representative of the American Red Cross, who arrived in Madeira on 6 November 1918 aboard the transport *Lake Forest*. The ship brought to this island 1465 sacks of potatoes (Madeiran *semilha*), 1047 of beans, 3,000 of maize flour and 10,628 of maize grain, sent by that charitable society at the request of Mr Kemper, the American consul in Funchal. before: This name is applied both on Madeira and on Porto Santo to the young of the *goraz* and sometimes of the *besugo* (see those entries). When the first of these fish reaches a certain size it is called *peixe anique*, and only as an adult does it receive the name *goraz*. The adult *goraz* seeks the depths, while the young, the *garapaus*, live close to the coast, where they are caught with hand lines by simple amateurs.

before: ‘Above the town,’ says Frutuoso, ‘a quarter of a *légua* inland, stands the sugar mill (engenho) of the Cabrais; and near it is another belonging to the Doctor of Calheta, a physician named Pedro Berenguer de Lemilhana, *moço fidalgo* (junior nobleman of the Royal Household) and knight of the Order of Christ.’ It is from him that the surname Berenguer derives, and even today a considerable part of the *sesmaria* (royal land grant to settlers on condition of cultivation) lands that Pedro de Berenguer held in Calheta still bears the name Lombo do Doutor. before: The municipality (*concelho*) of Santana has its seat in the parish (*freguesia*) of the same name and was established in 1835. The municipalities of Câmara de Lobos, Santa Cruz, Porto do Moniz and Santana were abolished by the decree of 10 December 1867, but this measure was never fully implemented, because those municipalities were restored shortly afterwards. From its creation the municipality of Santana comprised the parishes of Arco de São Jorge, São Jorge, Santana, Faial, São Roque and Porto da Cruz. before: On 9 December 1761 the Municipal Council (*Câmara Municipal*) of Funchal resolved to hold festivities on the news of the birth of Prince José, in accordance with what had already been decided at the session of 29 October of the same year, in view of an official letter from the governor and captain-general. According to the minute book of the Council’s sessions, the festivities consisted of the following: ‘Three days of public illuminations, with all the inventions of fireworks conducive to and necessary for the said celebration; and on the afternoons of the three days to be appointed, on the first there shall be cavalcades, the arena being prepared with the cleanliness necessary and proper for the occasion; on the second a duck shall be run, and on that afternoon there shall be some music carts and other festivities to fill the same afternoon; and on the third afternoon there shall be a pageant of figures on horseback, representing the four parts of the world, and with them the island of Madeira and all its other towns; and besides this celebration there shall also be ring-tilting (*argolinha*)’.

before: Lieutenant-Colonel Alberto Artur Sarmento published in no. 1983 of the former *Heraldo da Madeira* an interesting article on the Moors in Madeira, from which we transcribe the following passages:
after: Lieutenant-Colonel Alberto Artur Sarmento published in no. 1983 of the former *Heraldo da Madeira* (‘Madeira Herald’) an interesting article on the Moors in Madeira, from which we transcribe the following passages:

before: ‘The Moor was a harder worker than the slave from Guinea and Mina, which is why landowners preferred to import him for their farming estates. This scandalous trade, arranged between the donataries here and the governors of the strongholds in Africa, who ordered raids, provoked the outcry of the chief of the Moors, who complained in a letter to Manuel I of what Azambuja was doing: seizing people indiscriminately, of every class, to send under contract to the captains of Madeira. This is what we find in the “Documentos arabicos copiados dos originaes da Torre do Tombo, 1790.” ‘The Moors formed large communities, gathering in groups or in a separate quarter, as the Mouraria, one of the oldest streets in Funchal, bears witness, and they were heavily traded in the towns, especially in Ponta do Sol and Santa Cruz. In Santa Cruz, until a few years ago, an altarpiece in the parish church could still be seen, depicting Moorish slaves wearing a small funnel-shaped turban with a drooping tip. From this derived the peasant’s *carapuça* (traditional Madeiran cap shaped like an inverted funnel) and the little cloth hanging from the head, old characteristic garments of the Madeiran countrywoman. ‘From the Moors comes the plaintive quality of the songs, though the stamping dance is a movement of the Black people. From the Moors come the rambling rhymes of the hill folk, the popular ones: *lengi lengi* the passing fog, the ant that catches its foot. Amid the mists, enchanted princesses, tales of palaces and hidden treasure, thieves and magic wands are influences and themes of the people, carried over in this current from a distant subject race. ‘From the Moors, too, comes couscous, that granulated paste of wheat flour, so prized by the poorer classes, who eat it only on solemn occasions, with a chunk of pork, at baptisms and weddings, never without the sprig of savory and coriander that crowns the dish and gives it its aroma. ‘“Vae-te p’ra Argel” (Go off to Algiers) is a popular curse that recalls the plundering and captivity in the lands of the Moors. A 15th-century episode is handled by an artist’s hand in one of the chapters of the historical novel “A Filha de Tristam das Damas”, with a vivid colouring of the golden days of the dandyish donatary of Machico. ‘That intelligent and adventurous race gave us a figure in history in the person of the Moor Barque, of Porto Santo, who overthrew the false doctrine of the prophet Fernão Bravo. As in the tale of “the king is naked”, from then on everyone began to see the fraud, and the authorities took charge of the impostor who had deceived a credulous people with his tricks.’

before: Near the Ilhéu da Lapa, off the coast of the parish (*freguesia*) of Campanário, lies a shoal known by that name.

before: Álvaro de Ornelas, who greatly distinguished himself as a navigator and whom his contemporaries called ‘the Great’, held vast lands granted as *sesmaria* (royal land grant to settlers on condition of cultivation) in the parish (*freguesia*) of Caniço. They stretched from the brook of Garajau to the Ribeira do Porto Novo, and from the sea to the uplands. It was there that in 1499 he founded an entailed estate (*morgadio*), whose administration always passed from father to son and whose present representative is Councillor (conselheiro, honorary title of the royal council) Aires de Ornelas e Vasconcelos (1921). The founder laid down as a clause that this entailed house (*casa vinculada*) ‘might be pledged only to ransom the administrator who, in the service of God and the king, should be held captive by the infidels.’ It was around 1591 that Aires de Ornelas e Vasconcelos founded, on lands of this entail (*morgado*), the chapel of Nossa Senhora da Consolação (Our Lady of Consolation), which still exists and belongs to the founder’s family. Together with its adjoining manor house, it became the seat of this entailed foundation (*instituição vincular*, a morgado or capela). It was to this house that the governor and captain-general Sá Pereira exiled in 1774 the holder of the entail, Agostinho António de Ornelas, who died there shortly afterwards, on 5 August of the same year. He was buried in the said chapel, and the marble of his family vault bears this inscription: ‘Tomb of Agostinho António de Ornellas e Vasconcellos, *moço fidalgo* (junior nobleman of the Royal Household) of the Royal Household, ninth lord of this entail. 1718 to 1774.’ This chapel stands in the locality (*sítio*) still called Quinta today, which takes its name from the manor house adjoining the chapel, mentioned above.

before: Beside the road that runs alongside the Levada de Santa Luzia, almost at the point where it meets the Caminho da Torrinha, stands the chapel of Nossa Senhora da Consolação (Our Lady of Consolation). Here, in the summer season, the novenas and the accompanying feast are celebrated with great splendour and draw large crowds. We do not know the year of its construction, but we presume that it dates from the end of the 16th century. It was small, and in 1861 it was suitably rebuilt and enlarged, being blessed in July of that year. The altar front, a fine old mosaic, belonged to the church of the Convent of São Francisco (St Francis of Assisi). This chapel formed part of the parish of Monte before the creation of the parish of Santa Luzia, within whose bounds it now lies.

before: The chapel of Nossa Senhora da Consolação in the parish of Estreito de Câmara de Lobos is more commonly known as the chapel of Foro, because it stands in the locality of that name. It was entailed, and we do not know the year of its construction. On 1 November each year a feast is held there, together with a well-attended *arraial* (open-air popular festival at a church feast) for the people of the surrounding area. Dr Álvaro de Azevedo says that a chapel dedicated to St James once existed in the locality of Foro; we do not know whether it is the same as the one mentioned above or a different one.

before: A bird of the shearwater family (Procellariidae), close to the *boieiro*, from which it differs in its smaller size and in having bluish-grey feet instead of flesh-coloured ones. It lives on all the islands of the archipelago and is common on the Desertas. It is also known as the *pintelho*, from a particular cry it can be heard giving in flight. It is often absent during the hot season, and usually lays a single white egg in rock crevices, generally on the bare ground.
after: A bird of the shearwater family (Procellariidae), close to the *boieiro*, from which it differs in its smaller size and in having bluish-grey feet instead of flesh-coloured ones. It is often absent during the hot season, and usually lays a single white egg in rock crevices, generally on the bare ground.

before: A newspaper of this city reported on 7 May 1922 that the Sindicato Agrícola da Madeira, having been duly approved, had just been installed, and it gave the list of the citizens elected to the syndicate’s general assembly, board of directors and supervisory board. before: Estimates of the surface area of the whole archipelago, and especially of each of the islands that make it up, vary considerably. Dr Álvaro Rodrigues de Azevedo, who dealt with this subject at some length in his notable article in the *Dicionario Universal Portuguez Ilustrado*, says that some authors put the total area of the archipelago at more than a thousand square kilometres, and that it was later accepted that the area was around 800 kilometres. He ends by stating that the most recent calculations, which he considers closest to the truth, give the whole archipelago an area of 560 square kilometres: 500 kilometres for the island of Madeira, 50 for Porto Santo and 10 for the small group of the Desertas.

before: Of the ports of the archipelago, until recently those of Funchal and of the south of the island of Porto Santo were considered good; those of Abra, Machico, Santa Cruz, Câmara de Lobos, Ribeira Brava, Ponta do Sol, Porto do Moniz and Porto da Cruz were regarded as tolerable; and those of Caniçal, Porto Novo, Reis Magos, Oliveira, Campanário, Lugar de Baixo, Madalena do Mar, Anjos, Fajã do Mar, Calheta, Jardim do Mar, Paul do Mar, Pesqueiro, Seixal, Fajã da Areia, Ponta Delgada, Boaventura, São Jorge and Faial as poor. The ports of the parishes of Porto do Moniz and Porto da Cruz are considered good landing places when winds blow from the southern quarter, since all traffic along the whole southern coast of Madeira is then impossible, although this happens only a few times each year. Over the last thirty years, conditions at the ports of these places have improved considerably with the building of small quays and landing places and with extension and repair work on those already existing.

before: He was born in Porto do Moniz on 13 May 1887 and attended the Episcopal Seminary of Funchal (*Seminário Episcopal do Funchal*), being ordained priest (*presbítero*) in 1910. Having assisted the Revd Father Ernesto Schmitz in preparing and identifying the natural history specimens in the Seminary museum, he developed a certain fondness for this kind of work, and for that reason he was later put in charge of the museum when that priest left for Jerusalem. He collected a large number of Madeiran lichens and fungi; the former were studied by Professor Navas and the latter by Professor Torrend. He is a member of the Natural Sciences Society of Zaragoza. Called up to attend the school for militia officers (*oficiais milicianos*) in Lisbon during the state of war between Portugal and Germany, he succeeded in being appointed army chaplain with the rank of second lieutenant (*alferes capelão*) to the Portuguese Expeditionary Corps in France. He left for that country on 23 May 1918 and returned home in June 1919.

before: The *bogangueira* (*cucurbita melanosperma*), native to Asia and introduced from Tenerife in 1836 or 1837, is an extremely common species in both the north and the south of the island. Its leaves are 5-lobed, sometimes somewhat rough, with shallow, rounded lobes; its flowers are yellow and its fruits large and elliptical, without any ridges. Lowe recognised two varieties of this species: the variety *picta*, with fruits speckled green and white, and the variety *lactea*, with entirely white fruits. before: The neighbouring island of Porto Santo has long been recommended as an excellent health resort for the cure of certain diseases. The number of Madeiran visitors who go there is not greater because of the lack of hotels and suitable accommodation, and also because of the complete absence of comfort, speed and safety in the vessels used to carry passengers. There is no one in Madeira who is unaware of this. Dr Nuno Silvestre Teixeira – who was a professor at our Medical School, served as health officer (*delegado de saúde*) of the district and was a distinguished practitioner of the medical sciences through his studies and polished writings, and who had moreover spent long periods on that island – states that a stay on Porto Santo has far more beneficial and wholesome effects than the same length of time spent taking mineral and medicinal waters at the spas where they rise.

before: It was also essential to put the religious affairs of the archipelago on a more satisfactory footing. Madeira belonged to the Order of Christ, which had its seat in Tomar, and it was therefore the Order’s task to oversee matters of ecclesiastical jurisdiction; to this end it had delegated the direction of all religious questions on this island to the vicar of Nossa Senhora do Calhau (Our Lady of Calhau). The creation of an autonomous diocese was thus imperative, headed by a prelate who could perform all acts of worship and freely oversee every matter of church discipline. King Manuel I understood this and requested the creation of the Funchal diocese, which Pope Leo X established by a bull (papal bull) of 12 June 1514, freeing the new bishopric from the jurisdiction of the mastership of the Order of Christ.

before: On page 568 of the *Saudades da Terra* there is the Latin text of a bull, which is described there as the one that created this diocese. This is not correct. It is the bull *Pro excellenti praeeminentia*, cited under this title in various places, that is the papal instrument establishing the bishopric of Funchal. It is transcribed in full on p. 257 of vol. 1 of the *Corpo Diplomatico Portuguez*, edited by Rebêlo da Silva and published in 1862, and it had already appeared, at least in part, in other, older works. Rebêlo da Silva’s edition is a copy taken directly from the Torre do Tombo (National Archives), where the original and authentic record are kept in the Bundle of Bulls (*Maço das Bulas*), under no. 34. This document, which is fairly long, was translated into Portuguese some years ago by Father Ricardo Augusto de Sequeira, a distinguished teacher at our lyceum (state secondary school), and published in several issues of the *Correio do Funchal* in November 1897.

before: The Junta Agrícola was created by the decree of 11 March 1911. This legislative act, which settled the so-called Hinton question (to which its preamble makes special reference), established a new sugar regime (*regímen sacarino*, the legal regime governing sugar and alcohol production). The regime was variously judged and gave rise to conflicting opinions, but it unquestionably contains principles and lays down provisions so useful and wholesome that, if observed, they would contribute greatly to the growth and prosperity of the whole Madeiran archipelago. It must never be forgotten that this decree created the Junta Agrícola and the corresponding expropriation of those laboratories of toxic substances known as spirit (aguardente, distilled from sugar cane or wine) factories.
after: The Agricultural Board (*Junta Agrícola*) was created by the decree of 11 March 1911. It must never be forgotten that this decree created the Agricultural Board and the corresponding expropriation of those laboratories of toxic substances known as spirit (aguardente, distilled from sugar cane or wine) factories.

before: The creation of the Junta Agrícola, says the lucid report that precedes the decree, ‘will contribute in the fullest measure to the economic development of Madeira’. And so it would certainly have done, had the work of this body not at times been hampered by a mistaken approach. In an essentially agricultural country, where most of the population lives by planting and tilling the land, it is easy to judge the notable services that a body of a special technical character, with very substantial resources at its disposal, could render to our agriculture if all the provisions of the said decree had been respected and fully carried out. That did not happen, however. Before the calamitous crisis we are now going through (1921), enormous sums were spent without improving the condition of the Madeiran people by putting into effect certain wholesome measures set out in the decree.

before: The report accompanying the decree of 11 March 1911 refers to the name ‘Island of Spirit’ given to Madeira because of the abundant production of this poison and the excessive use made of it in the archipelago. This name was echoed, and given full currency, by a well-known politician and statesman who, in a public lecture, so ungraciously described the inhabitants of this island as drunkards and alcoholics. He did so after having received here the highest distinctions and the most elevated marks of esteem and regard, which went so far as to confer on him, at a solemn and splendid session of the Funchal Council, the titles and honours of a citizen of Funchal, with the unveiling of his portrait in the great hall of the town hall.

before: Art. 26. A Junta Agrícola da Madeira is hereby created, with the special task of managing the fund formed by the tax on the manufacture of spirit (aguardente, distilled from sugar cane or wine). The revenue of this board shall also include the fines imposed for any infringements of the present decree having the force of law, and whatever is laid down in the respective regulations.
after: Art. 26. An Agricultural Board of Madeira is hereby created, with the special task of managing the fund formed by the tax on the manufacture of spirit (aguardente, distilled from sugar cane or wine). The revenue of this board shall also include the fines imposed for any infringements of the present decree having the force of law, and whatever is laid down in the respective regulations.

before: The creation of the Junta Agrícola da Madeira therefore had the following special and expressly stated aims: 1. the expropriation of the spirit factories; 2. the promotion of Madeira wines abroad; 3. the founding and maintenance of an agricultural station; 4. the transformation, by regrafting, of the grape varieties now in existence, so as to turn them into the traditional types that produce what is called Madeira wine.
after: The creation of the Agricultural Board of Madeira therefore had the following special and expressly stated aims: 1. the expropriation of the spirit factories; 2. the promotion of Madeira wines abroad; 3. the founding and maintenance of an agricultural station; 4. the transformation, by regrafting, of the grape varieties now in existence, so as to turn them into the traditional types that produce what is called Madeira wine.

before: As we have already said, the expropriation of the spirit factories was never even begun (1921). We must now add that the promotion of our wines abroad produced no satisfactory result at all, because of the impractical way in which it was carried out. Nor was the propagation, by grafting, of the varieties that produce traditional Madeira wine undertaken on the desirable scale, even though everyone saw in it the means of restoring to the island one of its oldest and most valuable sources of wealth. The experimental field at Bica da Cana yielded few practical results. Fairness, however, demands that it be said that many useful selected plants came from the nurseries of Louros and Ribeira Brava, especially the latter. The organisation of the services for combating the insects and parasites that attack plants also left nothing to be desired: it was an excellent service to our farmers, sparing them countless losses, above all in fruit trees.

before: It is worth noting that the decree of 15 May 1912, which approved the Regulations for the implementation of the decree having the force of law of 11 March 1911, laid down new provisions on the purposes for which the Junta Agrícola had been created and on its operation, altering the organic and fundamental constitution that a law had assigned and conferred on it. This decree charged the body with afforesting the mountains, establishing an effective rural police and promoting all improvements in roads, sanitation and other matters tending to develop the tourist industry on the island. It was under these provisions that some of the measures we have noted above were carried out.

before: Under these regulations the Junta Agrícola was composed as follows: the district agronomist or the director of the Agricultural Station, three delegates representing the Municipal Councils, two delegates of the District General Council (*Junta Geral*), two delegates of the Commercial Association, one delegate of the Viticulture Commission, and the forestry officer (regente silvícola) serving the General Council.

after: For the proper and regular operation of the Agricultural Board there are three decrees dated 28 December 1912: the first approved the Internal Regulations of the Agricultural Board, the second the Regulations for the expropriation of the spirit distilleries, and the third the Regulations for the collection of the tax on spirit.

before: The second set of regulations completely destroys the most important and most advantageous clause of the law that created the Junta Agrícola, namely the expropriation of the distilleries. It provides that only three years after the sugar regime of 1911 has come into force, and when it is recognised that sugar-cane cultivation has disappeared in some region of the Madeiran archipelago, will the distilleries be expropriated, and even then only when they request it. And so, with a stroke of the pen in a mere set of regulations, the most useful and beneficial provisions of a law are entirely annulled!

before: An annual grass grown in Madeira and Porto Santo. Rye flour, alone or mixed with wheat flour, is used to make a dark but tasty bread, and the straw of the plant is used in hat-making. The archipelago produces around 2,500 hectolitres of rye a year.

before: Dr Balbino do Rego was practising privately as a physician in this city and carrying out his official duties as director of the Bacteriology Laboratory when, towards the end of 1905, a disease of suspicious character appeared here in Madeira. The health authorities were obliged to confine those who had been struck by it in the Gonçalo Aires lazaretto, which had been turned into an isolation hospital, and the director of the Bacteriology and Hygiene Laboratory was placed in charge of that hospital. The sad and regrettable events that followed are briefly narrated in the articles Popular Riots (Volume II, page 404), Bubonic Plague (Volume III, page 77) and Popular Poetry (Volume III, page 87), and we refer readers to them, so as to avoid needless and tedious repetition.

before: Madeira, and some claim that it was the first place of worship built on this island. The legend of Machim, which we shall deal with elsewhere, tells that when the discoverers landed on the beaches of Machico they found the graves of Robert Machim and Anne Arfet, together with a simple epitaph that recounted the adventure of the unhappy lovers and asked that a chapel dedicated to Christ be built on that spot. If we were to believe this romantic legend, the origin of the chapel’s foundation would lie in that ill-fated adventure. In his learned and most interesting notes to the *Saudades da Terra*, Dr Álvaro Rodrigues de Azevedo reduced the Machim affair to its proper proportions, and after this exhaustive study it is no longer permissible to accept the possibility of the legend, as various authors, according to Francisco Manuel de Melo, seek to describe it in poetic terms.

before: The chapel houses the venerated image of Senhor dos Milagres (the Lord of Miracles), the object of a great pilgrimage held on 9 October, to which thousands of people flock from every part of the island. This revered image was swept away by the torrent in the flash flood of 1803 and carried out to the open sea. There it was found by an American full-rigged ship bound for our port, which took it on board; it was later handed over to Funchal Cathedral (Sé Catedral do Funchal). It remained there until 15 April 1813, when it was taken to its small sanctuary in Machico, which had just then been restored.

before: This *tuna*, led by António Correia Caldeira Coelho, then a fifth-year law student, arrived in Funchal on 22 March 1913 and left for Lisbon on 3 April of the same year. It consisted of 45 students who, during their stay in Funchal, were lodged in the building of the former seminary at the start of the Caminho do Monte. The *tuna* was lavishly entertained in this city: on the day it landed, after a short visit to the town hall, it was offered a reception at the residence of the Viscounts of Geraz de Lima. In its honour there were also a ball at the Palácio de São Lourenço (St Lawrence Palace), another at the ‘Grémio dos Empregados do Comércio’, a party at the Quinta da Choupana, and luncheons at the Casino Pavão, the Terreiro da Luta and the Monte Palace Hotel, etc. The students gave two performances at the theatre and visited Portela, Santa Cruz and Machico.

before: He was born in the parish (*freguesia*) of Porto do Moniz on 9 January 1881. After completing his studies at the Diocesan Seminary, he attended the Gregorian University in Rome and was ordained priest in 1904. In 1921 he was appointed canon of Funchal Cathedral (*Sé*). For some years he has been a professor at the seminary of this diocese. He has contributed to various newspapers and is at present (1921) the editor of *Vida Diocesana*. Of his sacred orations, some have been published as pamphlets – *Sermão ao Santíssimo Sacramento*, Funchal, 1912, and *Oração Fúnebre nas exéquias do S. Pontífice Pio X*, Lisbon, 1915 – and others in a volume, *A Aurora da Redenção*. He is the author of the notable works of religious polemic *As Razões do Protestantismo*, *A Existencia de Deus á luz da sciencia e da razão* and *A Igreja e o Protestantismo*. In defence of the return of the building of the Seminary of the Incarnação (*Seminário da Incarnação*; Incarnation) to the Diocesan Worship Commission of Funchal, he wrote the pamphlet *A Legalidade do Decreto n.° 13.514*.

before: António Joaquim dos Santos Pimenta. After various studies and surveys, this commission decided definitively that the rifle range should be built at the locality of Várzea in the parish (*freguesia*) of São Martinho. It never carried out any significant works, however, still less drew up the plans and estimates, because of the obstacles that various local interests then placed in the way of this long-desired improvement. This was in 1909. In June 1911 the Minister of War ordered an urgent study of the construction of the rifle range. A commission was then appointed, made up of Captains Cândido Gomes and Ricardo de Andrade and Lieutenant José Betencourt da Câmara, which at once set to work with the greatest zeal and energy. before: The burning of Madeira’s forests in the time of Zargo, the first donatary (*donatário*) of Funchal, is an event mentioned by João de Barros, Frutuoso, António Cordeiro, Manuel Tomás and other authors, and one that tradition has also kept alive. Ferdinand Denis relates that an early French traveller met an old sailor to whom an eyewitness had described the burning of the island of Madeira. According to the learned annotator of *Saudades da Terra*, the Torre do Tombo (National Archives), in the *Livro das Ilhas*, folio 84, holds a certified copy of an apostolic brief of Pope Paul II, dated 1469, which clearly alludes to this same fire. Gaspar Frutuoso, the historian of the islands, describes the fire in the interior of Madeira in the following terms: ‘Hence the captain (João Gonçalves Zarco) resolved, seeing that the labour of men could not clear so many trees as had stood on this island since the beginning of the world or of its making, that in order to consume them, so that the land might be tilled and put to use, it was necessary to set fire to them. And since, with the great mass of trees and their great age, some lay felled on the ground and some stood dead and dry, the fire took hold in this valley of Funchal in such a way, and was so fierce, that when the wind blew off the land its flames and heat could not be endured, and the people often took refuge on the islets and in the ships until the weather changed. And because the valley was very thick both with much fennel and with trees, the fire was so stoked that it burned for seven years in the trees, and in the trunks and roots below ground, so that it could not be put out. It did great destruction to the timber both in Funchal and in most of the island along the sea on the southern coast, where it had been decided to clear and cultivate the land.’

before: There is no doubt that many forests in the Funchal valley and in other parts of the island’s south coast were destroyed by the fire that João Gonçalves Zargo imprudently ordered to be set in order to clear the land. But to accept that this fire, spreading rapidly and leaping from tree to tree, came to engulf the whole island seems to us a fantasy born of the rich imagination of Manuel Tomás and other early writers. Nothing in the passage from *Saudades da Terra* that we have transcribed suggests that the fire was general. João de Barros, the first historian to record the disaster, confines it to the part of the island of Madeira ‘where it is now called Funchal’, adding, however, ‘that the fire took hold of the clearing and of the rest of the woodland, and that for seven years it burned alive in the wilds of those great forests which nature had raised over so many hundreds of years’.

before: The island cedar is *Juniperus Oxycedrus* subspecies *madeirensis*, a shrub or small tree 4–7 metres tall, with dioecious flowers, drooping branchlets, linear or linear-lanceolate leaves in whorls of three with 2 white stripes on the upper surface, and subglobose galbuli that are usually yellow. This cedar, cultivated on the *quintas* of Monte, Camacha and Santo da Serra but almost extinct in the uplands of Madeira, yields a light, aromatic wood much prized by cabinetmakers. The ceiling of the Cathedral (Sé Catedral) was built of this wood and, if what Manuel Tomás says in the *Insulana* is true, it was also used to build the first two-storey house in Funchal. Oil of cade is produced from *J. Oxycedrus*.

before: We know of this Madeiran through the references to him that we have found in volumes X and XI of Inocêncio’s *Diccionario Bibliographico*. before: A name improperly given to two birds native to Madeira, *Micropus apus* and *M. unicolor*. The first is called *andorinha do mar* (‘sea swallow’), the second *andorinha da serra* (‘mountain swallow’). The true swallows, *Hirundo rustica* and *Chelidonaria urbica*, which visit these islands regularly without breeding, are known on Porto Santo as *andorinhas de fora* (‘swallows from outside’) and in some parishes in the north of Madeira as *andorinhas do Porto Santo* (‘Porto Santo swallows’), perhaps because on reaching the northern coast of Madeira they arrive from the north-east, that is, from the direction of Porto Santo.

before: It owes this name to the fact that its original parish church was larger than the chapel built by João Gonçalves Zarco on the site where the church of Santa Clara (St Clare of Assisi) stands today, both being dedicated to Nossa Senhora da Conceição (Our Lady of the Conception). In former times it was also known as Conceição de Baixo (Lower Conceição), the other being called Conceição de Cima (Upper Conceição). It was likewise called Nossa Senhora do Calhau (Our Lady of Calhau), because it was built not far from the beach; this is the name that has lasted longest among the people, and it is still in use today. This parish became widely known, and still is at present, as the parish of Socorro, a name applied especially to the part of it lying between the parish church and the left bank of the Ribeira de João Gomes. before: The parish (*freguesia*) of Santa Maria Maior has a population of 7,823 inhabitants (1921). It begins at the Ribeira de João Gomes. Its eastern boundary is customarily taken to be the western or left-hand half of the Caminho do Palheiro and the Caminho da Terça, while the eastern or right-hand half belongs to the parish of São Gonçalo. It should be noted, however, that these boundaries do not agree with those marked in the *Mappa Alphabetico* of the city’s streets, approved by the civil governor on 15 December 1863. That map clearly states that the whole of the Rua do Palheiro, from the Quinta do Acciaioly or Quinta do Faial as far as the Rua Bela de São Tiago, belongs to the parish of Santa Maria Maior, and that this parish extends as far as the locality (*sítio*) of Louros; the lane of Olaria, now the Travessa do Lazareto, nevertheless lies in the parish of São Gonçalo. According to the same map, the area between the Rua Bela de São Tiago and the building of Tomás Teodoro, on the Calçada do Socorro, belongs on its northern side to Santa Maria Maior and on its southern side to São Gonçalo. The southern part of the Largo da Forca and of the Caminho do Lazareto, up to the point where the locality of Louros begins, must therefore be considered part of the latter parish.

before: Several officers appeared in the Praça da Constituição, among them Captain Henrique Luís Monteiro, who tried to impose discipline on the troops but was not heeded. Dr Pestana Júnior, municipal administrator (administrador do concelho, the government's representative) of Funchal, then climbed onto a bench in the square. He declared that no officer of the regiment would act against the new political regime, as the captain himself had assured him on his word of honour, and that in these circumstances the men should obey their officers and fall back into line. before: A fishing rig much used by the fishermen of Machico. It consists of a central line or main line (*madre*), which hangs vertically and to which 4 or 5 small rods of quince or osier are fixed horizontally, 3 *palmos* apart; from their ends hang small lines or snoods (*loros*) with their hooks. At its lower end the central line carries a stone sinker (*pandulho*), which makes the rig descend, and at its upper end it is tied to an ordinary fishing line. It is used mainly to catch adult wreckfish (*chernes*), working in depths of 200 and 300 *braças*, where hake, *gata*, *ramudo*, *xara* and other oily fish may also be taken. The rig resembles what in Portugal is called the *barqueira de arame*, and like it is let down vertically until the sinker touches the sea floor. The *cherriola* (vertical multi-hook deep-water line) of the Câmara de Lobos fishermen differs somewhat from the one described above. As to the origin of the term, it is not unreasonable to suppose that the rig, because the arrangement of its rods bears a certain resemblance to the *surriola* booms – which are rigged perpendicular to the side of certain ships and from which ropes hang for mooring the boats – received the name *surriola*, which was corrupted into *cherriola*.

before: The Royal Treasury Board (*Junta da Real Fazenda*) asked the Municipal Council (*Câmara Municipal*) of Funchal ‘to indicate the gentlest means of requiring the inhabitants of this island to contribute to the repair of the damage caused by the flash flood (*aluvião*) of 9 October 1803’. At its meeting of 21 August 1804, having heard the nobility and the people, the latter represented by the House of the Twenty-Four (*Casa dos Vinte e Quatro*, assembly of the craft guilds), the Council resolved ‘that the fairest means, the least burdensome and the most in keeping with the proposed aim of having the island’s inhabitants contribute to the repair of the streams, was that all male inhabitants from the age of 16 to that of 60, without exception of any person, ecclesiastical or secular, native or foreign, *fidalgo* (nobleman of the lesser nobility), noble or commoner, should be obliged to go in rotation to work at clearing and repairing the streams, not more than five times in each year, each without pay, in those of the district of the city or town (*vila*) where he lived and where such work was needed’.

before: Maize has long been grown in Madeira, but it was in 1847 that Laureano da Câmara Falcão, better known as the holder of the entail (*morgado*) of Ilha (a locality in the parish (*freguesia*) of São Jorge), developed its cultivation in the parishes of Santana and São Jorge. For this purpose he brought over from the Azores several farmers, who taught here the growing methods used in that archipelago. The results he obtained from his undertaking were very gratifying, and to encourage maize growing among us the law of 22 July 1853 was passed, exempting local produce from the payment of tithes.

before: At 6 o’clock a salvo of shells announced that the steamer was in sight, at 7 o’clock a *girândola* (wheel of rockets) signalled that she had arrived, and at 8 o’clock the Fort of São Tiago (St James the Greater) fired a 21-gun salute. The landing took place at about half past ten at the Cais da Pontinha, because the sea was quite rough and it was difficult to come alongside the quay opposite the Avenida de Gonçalves Zargo. At the start of this avenue a superb triumphal arch had been raised, covered in box, bearing a double photograph of the President of the Republic and, at the top, the following motto: ‘Supreme incarnation of the Homeland’. Beside it were the *quinas* (the shields of the Portuguese arms) wrapped in green and red.

before: Gaspar Frutuoso says that heaven and earth are full of his ‘heroic deeds and glorious victories, from Japan to China, from Malacca to the Ganges, from the Ganges to the Tagus and from the Tagus to the ends of sea and land’. Many authors have written about Tristão da Veiga, and all are unanimous in extolling his martial valour and the heroic actions he performed; the author of the *Saudades da Terra* devotes fifty long pages to him in the warmest and loftiest panegyric. Yet after so many glorious exploits, which did so much to raise the prestige of the Portuguese name in the East, Tristão Vaz blackened the memory of his deeds. He went over to the enemies of his homeland and basely and treacherously surrendered the fortress of São Julião da Barra, which guarded the entrance to the harbour of Lisbon, thereby hastening the fall of Portugal under the Castilian yoke.

before: Gaspar Frutuoso gives this name to a French corsair who put in at the Port of Funchal (Porto do Funchal) in the time of the donatary Simão Gonçalves da Câmara, Count of Calheta. Two hundred Frenchmen landed from the corsair’s galleons, which numbered seven. They bought provisions in the city and sold many things they had with them, ‘bringing Jaques Soria as their captain to punish them should they get out of hand.’ The ships lay eight days in our port, and during that time ‘Captain Simão Gonçalves da Câmara watched, and had others watch, the city by night with his guard posts, notwithstanding the friendship and peace that the corsair had promised him’.

before: He is the brother of the late ex-Emperor of Austria and ex-King of Hungary, Emperor Charles I. He arrived in Madeira on 17 April 1922 aboard the British steamer *Kenilworth Castle* and went to stay at Monte, in the house of his sister-in-law, the ex-Empress Zita.

before: He began as a typesetter, and his only formal qualification was the primary-school examination. Although he himself regretted the gaps in a broader and more solid education, it is nonetheless certain that in journalism he made up for this original lack with the exuberance of an exceptional talent, with a superficial and fleeting reading of some contemporary prose writers and poets, and with a light study of a few textbooks. In various newspapers, and notably in the *Diário do Commercio*, of which he was principal editor for some years, he revealed his remarkable literary aptitude and his marked qualities as a journalist. The characteristic feature of his writing, to which he always gave an unmistakable note, was biting irony, scathing satire and irreverent mockery. In it, wit, talent, art, literary flavour, perfect metre and pointed phrasing amply redeemed the excesses of thought and the not always pure or praiseworthy intentions of their author. His impulsive, fickle and restless temperament sometimes led him into regrettable excesses, which he was the first to acknowledge once reflection and calm replaced the enthusiasms of his combative and ardent nature. In the *gazetilha* (satirical verse column in a newspaper) Francisco António may be said to have been unsurpassed, and in another setting he would have won well-deserved fame. It is a pity that some of these literary gems have not been collected in a volume.

before: He was born in the parish (*freguesia*) of Calheta in 1770 and died in this city on 4 July 1861. He was ordained priest in 1795 and became a canon of our Cathedral (Sé Catedral), holding high ecclesiastical offices such as those of vicar capitular (administrator of the vacant diocese elected by the chapter) and governor of this bishopric. He was a distinguished and vigorous journalist and, under the pseudonym Estrela do Norte, wrote many articles in the *Patriota Funchalense*, the first newspaper published here in Madeira. He was imprisoned for supporting liberal ideas, but managed to escape from prison and leave for Brazil, where he remained until 1834. He always enjoyed great prestige and influence on this island.

before: An inhabited locality (*sítio*) in the parish (*freguesia*) of Ponta do Sol, where the chapel of Nossa Senhora do Monte (Our Lady of the Mount) stands. It was built by the people in 1751 and enlarged in 1775, and in June 1810 it suffered a serious act of desecration. There was once also a chapel dedicated to São Caetano (St Cajetan), built in 1780 by António de Carvalhal Esmeraldo e Alencastre.

before: Dr José Leite contributed extensively to the Funchal periodical press, notably to *A Lâmpada*, *O Oriente do Funchal*, *A Imprensa Livre* and *O Direito*. Many of his articles became famous for their originality and beauty of form, for the force of their argument and, perhaps even more, for the ardour and vehemence of their language. Had he worked as a journalist in the capital, it can be said without exaggeration that his name would stand alongside those of the great journalists Sampaio, António Enes, Mariano de Carvalho and Emídio Navarro.
