before: The competitive examination he sat, by public trial, for the post of philosophy teacher in the lyceums was a brilliant one. Dr Teófilo Braga, an admirer of Dr Leite Monteiro, travelled from Lisbon to Porto to attend it; one of the other candidates was our distinguished fellow Madeiran Dr Manuel Joaquim Teixeira. He obtained the highest mark and in 1867 was appointed teacher at our lyceum (state secondary school). Despite the brilliant showing he made in that examination and his undeniable competence to hold the chair of philosophy, truth obliges us to say that he lacked the qualities of a true teacher, and that on the whole his pupils gained little from their master’s lessons. Among the public offices he held was that of deputy civil governor; on several occasions he actually exercised this post, to which he was appointed by the decrees of 3 February 1902 and 26 March 1906. He was also a member of the District Council and president of the District General Council (*Junta Geral*) and of the Municipal Council (*Câmara Municipal*) of Funchal. In this last office he showed great interest in the development of the public library. Almost all the foreign works on Madeira held there were acquired during his term of office, and he also sought to create a municipal museum.

before: He belonged to the former Fusionist Party and took part in the Madeiran political struggles of 1868. Later he rendered notable services to the Regenerator Party, chiefly as editor of *Direito*. He was a member of the International Law Association of Berlin, and it is to him and to the late Canon Alfredo César de Oliveira that we owe the publication of *Flores da Madeira*, which brought together many valuable works by Madeiran poets. before: This name is given to two rocks lying near Selvagem Grande. Some seamen call one of them Palheiro de Dentro and the other Palheiro de Fora.

before: He was born at Arco da Calheta on 30 September 1887, the son of Manuel Rocha de Gouveia and Dona Maria Augusta Soares Rocha de Gouveia. He was studying agronomy in Lisbon when he was called up to the army after Germany declared war on Portugal. Commissioned as a second lieutenant, he left for France, where he met his death on 13 October 1917 while on duty in the trenches. It is said that he was chatting carelessly with other officers when he was struck by several shell splinters, which killed him instantly.

before: We have already noted elsewhere that Gaspar Frutuoso, in his brief description, written in 1590, of the most important parishes (*freguesias*) and villages (*lugares*, settlement rank below a town) on the south-west coast of Madeira, refers to the localities of Jardim do Mar and Paul do Mar simply as Jardim and Paul. We do not know whether they were known by these names in the earliest days of colonisation, perhaps without the added designation ‘do Mar’ that they bear today and have long borne. Nor do we know whether the places called Paul da Serra and Jardim da Serra received these names to distinguish them from those localities, the former pair being washed by the ocean and the latter lying in the interior of the island.

before: The lands that make up the present parishes of Paul do Mar, Jardim do Mar and Prazeres once belonged to the parish of Estreito da Calheta. The first to be separated from it was Paul do Mar, created by the royal decree (*alvará*) of 28 December 1676, which then also included the future parish of Jardim do Mar. The curacy (*curato*) of Prazeres was created later, as a dependency of Paul do Mar.
after: The lands that make up the present parishes of Paul do Mar, Jardim do Mar and Prazeres once belonged to the parish of Estreito da Calheta (‘the narrows of Calheta’). The curacy (*curato*) of Prazeres (‘joys’) was created later, as a dependency of Paul do Mar.

before: Paul do Mar, together with the parishes (*freguesias*) of Machico and Câmara de Lobos, forms one of the three most important fishing centres of the archipelago. In Paul some hundreds of people make their living from the toil of fishing. A fish-canning factory was set up there a few years ago and is an important industrial establishment. The salt pans established in this locality did not produce the expected results, as has happened with various attempts made elsewhere on this island. The yield at Paul was always meagre, and the salt pans were abandoned a good many years ago.

before: The so-called town (*vila*) of Câmara de Lobos, seat of the parish (*freguesia*) and municipality (*concelho*) of the same name, faces a cove that is not very large but picturesque. It is bounded by a small beach of rounded pebbles and served by a landing quay, which was built in 1876 and considerably improved in 1903. This landing place sees relatively heavy traffic, because Câmara de Lobos is an important fishing centre, whose industry employs several hundred people. The steamers of the coastal shipping service call here. It lies 4 miles from the Port of Funchal (Porto do Funchal) and 3 from that of Campanário.

before: This family surname was introduced into Madeira in 1476 by João Baptista Lomelino and his brother Urbano Lomelino, both Genoese and descendants of the Lomellini marquises, who were among the twenty-eight families that made up the old Senate (*senado*, the municipal council) of Genoa. They came to this island with the recommendation of the Infanta Dona Beatriz, in a letter written to the Council of Funchal. Urbano Lomelino settled in Santa Cruz, where he acquired a great deal of land. There he married Joana Lopes, with whom he had no children, and he left his property to his nephew Jorge Lomelino, in whose favour he established an entailed estate (*morgadio*) that was among the most important on this island. As we have already said on p. 308 of volume 1, Urbano Lomelino founded the Franciscan convent in the town (*vila*) of Santa Cruz, which Jorge Lomelino completed because Urbano had died in 1518, before the building work was finished. (See Convent of Nossa Senhora da Piedade, p. 308 of vol. 1.) Jorge Lomelino died on 9 December 1548 and was laid to rest in the church of the Santa Cruz convent, of which he was patron. In the chantry (capela) of the Quinta das Cruzes, which belonged to the Lomelino entailed estate, there is a marble burial vault containing bones said to be those of Urbano Lomelino, the founder of that entailed house (*casa vinculada*).

before: On 4 April 1832 Porto Santo was occupied by a constitutional force of 60 artillerymen, who had arrived from the island of Terceira aboard the war brig *Conde de Vila Flor* and the war schooner *Terceira*. The force was commanded by Captain Bento José de Oliveira, who at once had Queen Maria II proclaimed on the island. On the 7th of the same month the frigate *D. Maria II*, returning from the blockade of Madeira, reached Porto Santo. On board were Admiral Sartorius, the future prefect (*prefeito*) Luís da Silva Mousinho de Albuquerque, the dean of Funchal Cathedral (*Sé*), Januário Vicente Camacho, and other constitutionalists. The occupation lasted until 5 May, when the said force and the others who had landed on the island left for the Azores.

before: It was the law of 31 January 1739, recorded on folio 50 of Book 9 of the Archive of the Municipal Council (*Câmara Municipal*) of Funchal, that laid down that the great churchmen should be addressed as *excelência* (‘excellency’). This form was also to be granted to governors holding the rank of captain-general (capitão-general, military governor of Madeira), but only while they were in the districts they governed. No other local authority was granted high honorific forms of address in the same law. This amounts to saying that the *corregedor* (royal district magistrate), the *juiz de fora* (crown-appointed judge from outside the district), the customs judge (*juiz da alfândega*, head of the customs house) and other senior officials in Madeira continued, as before, to receive only the address of *mercê*.

before: At the end of the 18th century the Count of Castelo-Melhor and the Marquis of Valença – the latter *alcaide-mor* (royal governor of a castle and town) of Machico and the former of Funchal – were addressed as *excelência*, since both were grandees of the Kingdom (*reino*, i.e. mainland Portugal), whereas viscounts, barons and *moços fidalgos* were entitled only to *senhoria*. Later this last form was also given to the canons of Funchal Cathedral (*Sé*), under the royal decree (alvará régio) of 15 November 1817, and to colonels commanding troops. All other officers received *mercê*, except marshals, lieutenant-generals and those of equivalent rank, who were entitled to *excelência*.

before: The governors and captains-general Dom Diogo Pereira Forjaz Coutinho and Dom José Manuel da Câmara were in the habit of addressing the Municipal Council of Funchal as *senhoria* (lordship). This was contrary to law and established practice, and the latter was reprimanded for it by the government in mainland Portugal, which pointed out that the Council was entitled only to the form *mercê*. Only from 1834 onwards did the custom take hold – even then without legal authority – of the head of the district addressing the Municipal Councils and all authorities and heads of department (*repartição*) as *senhoria*.

before: The Municipal Council of Funchal began to receive the form *excelência* from the civil governor only after its president was the Count of Carvalhal, a grandee of the realm. The municipal administrators (*administrador do concelho*, the government’s representative), by contrast, were always addressed as *senhoria* by the head of the district for as long as the monarchy lasted in the country. It was around 1872 that the Municipal Council of Funchal began definitively to address the district judges as *excelência*, a form it later extended to the municipal administrator and, later still, to almost everyone.

before: An inhabited locality (*sítio*) in the parish (*freguesia*) of Caniço. There was once a *quinta* (country estate) or country house here, and the chapel of Nossa Senhora da Consolação (Our Lady of Consolation) still stands. Both belonged to the entailed estate (*morgadio*) founded here at the end of the 15th century by Álvaro de Ornelas, which was one of the oldest entails (*instituições vinculares*) in Madeira and whose last representative was Councillor (conselheiro, honorary title of the royal council) Aires de Ornelas (1866-1930). The Consolação chapel was built by Aires de Ornelas e Vasconcelos around 1591 and rebuilt around the middle of the 18th century (see Garajau and Jangão).

before: This convent began as a house for women living in retreat, with no religious character and no observance of canonical rules for its inmates. It was founded in 1654 by Gaspar Berenguer de Andrade and his wife, Dona Isabel de França Andrade. In 1658 the founders turned this house into a religious *recolhimento* (religious retreat house for women), whose residents submitted to a rule or statute modelled on those of certain monastic houses. Finally, by a royal decree (*alvará*) of 1663, confirmed in 1665 by Pope Alexander VII, this *recolhimento* was raised to a monastery of the First Order of St Clare, of severe and strict observance, and so it remained through the ages until the moment of its suppression. We have read somewhere that the founder was granted the right of patronage over this convent, undertaking to endow it with one hundred and sixty thousand *réis* (old Portuguese money of account; 1$000 = 1,000 réis, 1:000$000 = one conto = 1,000,000 réis) every year, an obligation attached to the entailed estate (*morgadio*) of Lombo do Doutor, in the parish (*freguesia*) of Calheta. For the period in which it was made, this endowment seems to us greatly exaggerated; today it would correspond to a very considerable sum.

before: If the monastery of Santa Clara was no model of rigid observance of its rules, it can nevertheless be said that the convent of Mercês gave the most vivid and eloquent example of the practice of all the Christian virtues, carried to the most heroic austerity and to severe and unceasing penance. It was a true cenacle of prayer, seclusion and sacrifice, to which those who went there gave themselves up willingly, seeking, as in a harsh and remote desert, complete withdrawal from the world and from all its coveted and enchanting attractions. Some nuns of this monastery won a reputation for great virtue, notably Mother Brites da Paixão, to whom we shall devote a separate article in its proper place.

before: The small island of Porto Santo, isolated and undefended, was raided and sacked several times by corsairs and pirates. Although they could not hope to find rich and plentiful plunder there, they could at least count on complete impunity and on the hasty flight of the inhabitants to the mountain tops, which left the field clear for the raiders’ rapacity. It was chiefly the summit of Pico do Castelo, difficult to reach and easy to defend against anyone trying to climb it, that served as a refuge for the poor inhabitants of the neighbouring island, who sheltered there from the ferocity of the pirates. The steep mountain gained regular defences, with guns and battlements, only at the beginning of the 18th century. In earlier times the inhabitants relied solely on the sheer slopes of the peak, where plain boulders rolled freely down the sides were enough to repel any assault. The fort of the town (*vila*), which was named São José in honour of King Joseph I, was built in the time of the Marquis of Pombal. We do not know what means of defence Porto Santo had before that time in the event of an attack, but they must have been very weak and useless, for there is no record of any resistance to the various pirate raids (see Preston).

before: Like all similar institutions, this Casa de Saúde has a special religious service, directed by the establishment’s own chaplain. Although their religious work is intended mainly for the patients and the community that works there, the priests of the Brothers of St John of God have taken part in the various acts of worship held in this parish, proving the most excellent and selfless helpers of the parish priests. In their chapel they readily administer the sacraments to the faithful who seek them; they attend the sick in their homes with spiritual comfort, accompany the dead to their last resting place and perform in the Parish Church every service asked of them. The first chaplain was Father José Maria Antunes, who served there from February 1923 to July 1925. In August of the same year he was replaced by Father Lázaro Ribeiro, who is the present chaplain (1928).

before: The history of this model Casa de Saúde, from its foundation to the present day, apart from the ever-growing number of its inmates and the material improvements gradually introduced there, consists simply in this very plain thing, yet admirably beautiful and admirably holy too: always the same spirit of courage, self-denial and sacrifice on the part of the tireless nurses; always the most attentive and affectionate treatment of the patients; always the most devoted care for their material well-being. And this, likewise always, without weakness, without faltering, without discouragement, despite the difficulties, setbacks and struggles that must be faced from time to time.

before: A population centre of some importance had grown up between the parishes of Campanário and Câmara de Lobos, and it had become very difficult to bring spiritual assistance to that settlement. The diocesan bishop, Dom Friar Joaquim de Meneses e Ataíde, therefore decided, by his warrant (*provisão*) of 8 February 1820, to establish a curacy with its seat at the chapel of Nossa Senhora dos Remédios (Our Lady of Remedies). Its area was to take in the 93 households of the localities of Vera-Cruz and Fontainhas, which belonged to Campanário, and the 41 households of the localities of Cama do Bispo and Cadeirinha, which belonged to Câmara de Lobos. In the very month of its creation the curacy was filled by Father Felisberto de Gouveia. Its jurisdiction remained dependent on the parish priests of the two neighbouring parishes, which had given up their land to form this chaplaincy with cure of souls (*capelania-curada*), not yet an autonomous parish. It seems that the parish priest of Campanário always exercised the broader jurisdiction there, and in the end he took over all supervision of the curacy’s religious services.

before: At Quinta Grande stood the chapel of Nossa Senhora dos Remédios, which was the seat of the curacy established in 1880 and also served as the seat of the parish. It was preferred to the chapel of Vera-Cruz because it was more central, and perhaps for other reasons unknown to us. It was built in 1601 and underwent some alterations over time, above all in 1901, when it was considerably enlarged. It is the centre of a well-attended pilgrimage in honour of Nossa Senhora dos Remédios, the patron saint of the parish. The pilgrimage festival takes place on the second Sunday of September each year, drawing enormous crowds from the surrounding parishes.

before: He is the son of Artur Adolfo Sarmento and Dona Margarida Henriques Sarmento, and was born in Funchal on 7 July 1878. before: A native tree of the buckthorn family (Rhamnaceae), now completely extinct in the uplands of Madeira. before: The industries of stearin candles, nails, cheese, chemical fertilisers, paints, cement tiles, biscuits and crackers, and tuna canning are modern on the island. before: The sawing of timber is, like milling, a fairly old industry. Frutuoso refers to it, as does the letter of grant (carta de doação) of the captaincy of Funchal made by Prince Henry the Navigator to João Gonçalves Zarco. According to that chronicler, ‘on the island there was so great a quantity of timber, so fine and hard, that an abundance of boards, beams and masts was carried to many parts, all of which was sawn with engines or water-powered saws, of which there are still many today on the north side of the same island.’ On this subject it is worth reading the pamphlet *Serras de Agua na Ilha da Madeira e Porto Santo*, published in 1937 by Dr Jordão de Freitas.

before: Although rye-straw plaiting for hat-making is carried out in Funchal and Camacha, it is in Estreito de Câmara de Lobos that this industry is most developed and the finest work is done. before: Cheese-making, stagnant for years but now apparently making progress, is carried on in Faial, Estreito de Câmara de Lobos, Ponta do Sol and Canhas. Adolfo Burnay made the first cheeses in Madeira, in a dairy he set up in Santo da Serra in 1895. That attempt was unsuccessful, however, and only fifteen years later did some cheeses begin to appear in the municipality (*concelho*) of Ponta do Sol which, thanks to their pleasant flavour and good preparation, won public favour.

before: Not only the sailing and rowing boats that serve the waters of the archipelago are built in Madeira, but also the small steamer *Vitoria*, which used to sail along the south coast of Madeira. This steamer was built in Machico. More than fifty years ago, to the east of the former Praça Académica, Madeiran workmen built the small but excellent steamer *Queen*, which, after sailing in our waters, went on to serve on the Tagus. In 1920 the yacht *Gonçalves Zargo* was built in the Cabrestante enclosure, and another vessel of greater tonnage than that one – the yacht *Anfitrite*, likewise intended for voyages on the high seas – is now (1921) under construction in the Campo do Almirante Reis.

before: There are three potteries in Funchal, the most important of which is the Funchalense, on the Estrada do Conde de Carvalhal. It is expected that a first-class establishment for the manufacture of glass (see Trachytes) and of roof tiles, bricks, etc. will shortly be set up in the locality (*sítio*) of Gorgulho (1921). The raw materials used in the island’s ceramics are red clay, white sand and saltpetre from Portugal, and *massapez* (heavy ferruginous clay soil) clay from Madeira and Porto Santo; the latter, however, has the drawback of sometimes cracking when not combined with another clay, owing to an excess of ferric oxide. At Estreito da Calheta curved roof tiles, jugs and other objects are made using only the local clay.

before: He was born on this island in the third quarter of the 16th century and died in Valencia, a city in Spain, in 1631. before: A locality (*sítio*) in the parish (*freguesia*) of Câmara de Lobos. before: Anyone leaving Funchal along the Caminho de Santo António will come upon, at the roadside some two kilometres from the city centre, the ruins of an old, dilapidated chapel. From that heap of rubble the ruined façade still rises proudly, as if defying the fury of the centuries. Its pointed-arch doorway reveals its antiquity and the character of the buildings of an age of glory. It is one of the few vestiges of the Manueline style that still survive on this island.

before: This is the chapel of Santa Maria Madalena, which gave its name to the locality (*sítio*), more commonly known by the popular shortened form of Madalena. After Santo Amaro, it is the oldest chapel in the parish (*freguesia*) of Santo António. We lack, however, the precise information needed to determine when it was founded, which does not seem to us to be later than the first quarter of the 16th century. The earliest reference to it that we have found dates from 1593, the year in which it received the grant of a quit-rent (*foro*). After the aforementioned chapel of Santo Amaro, it was also the most important in that parish for its antiquity, its size and its architectural style, and also for the devotion the faithful showed to its patron saint. It even came to own property of its own, of some importance, for the maintenance of its worship, something we are not aware that any other chapel in this parish possessed.

before: In the locality (*sítio*) of Florenças, in the parish (*freguesia*) of Arco da Calheta, there was a chapel of the same dedication, founded by João Portes Homem de El-Rei and his wife Dona Maria de Sousa in the year 1684. The chapel of Santa Maria Madalena in the parish of Porto Moniz is one of the oldest in the north of Madeira. Over the years it has undergone various repairs and additions, and today it is a chapel of no small size. It was enlarged in 1789 and was extended once more only a few years ago. It once held a fine oil painting of its patron saint, which was not properly looked after and has been lost entirely. It may be said to be the seat of the parish’s curacy (*curato*), and beside the chapel stands a residence intended for the assistant priest (*coadjutor*) of the curacy. There is a cemetery close by.

before: ‘João Gonsalves Zargo,’ says Frutuoso, ‘... passing further down to some very high mountains, there laid out another church of the Vera-Cruz...’. The idea of founding this chapel belongs to the discoverer, although it was built only later, in a year that is not known. It is nevertheless one of the oldest chapels in the diocese. Over time it has undergone various transformations, and nothing of the original building, certainly, survives there at present. It originally formed part of the parish of Câmara de Lobos or of Ribeira Brava, and came to belong to the parish (*freguesia*) of Campanário when the latter was created around the middle of the 16th century. Since 1848, when Quinta Grande became an independent parish, the old chapel of the Vera Cruz has belonged to that parish.

before: On 15 October 1835 the old judicial system came to an end, and two *julgados* were set up, both seated in Funchal, each with its own district judge (*juiz de direito*). In 1838 these *julgados* came to be called judicial districts – the eastern and the western. The first comprised four *julgados* and the second five, each of them presided over by an ordinary judge. The eastern judicial district stretched from the parish (*freguesia*) of the Sé, Funchal Cathedral (*Sé*), to that of Arco de São Jorge, and also included the island of Porto Santo. The western judicial district ran from the parish of São Pedro to that of Ponta Delgada and Boaventura, which borders on Arco de São Jorge. On 27 May 1838 the ordinary judges were elected for the newly created *julgados*; the Madeiran newspaper *Chronica*, for the year 1838, records how the parishes were distributed among these *julgados*.

before: Volume I of the Archive of the Municipal Council, and the transcription in the *Saudades da Terra* on p. 325, contain the royal letter (*carta régia*) of Dom Duarte dated 26 September 1433, granting to the Order of Christ ‘for ever and ever all the spiritual jurisdiction of our islands of Madeira and Porto Santo and of the Deserta island...’ Bearing the same date and issued by the same monarch, another letter, included in the work *Alguns documentos do Arquivo Nacional da Torre do Tombo acerca da avançada e conquistas dos portugueses*, bestows the said islands on Prince Henry as a royal grant.
after: Volume I of the Archive of the Municipal Council, and the transcription in ‘Longing for the Homeland’ (*Saudades da Terra*) on p. 325, contain the royal letter (*carta régia*) of Dom Duarte dated 26 September 1433, granting to the Order of Christ (*Ordem de Cristo*) ‘for ever and ever all the spiritual jurisdiction of our islands of Madeira and Porto Santo and of the Deserta island...’ Bearing the same date and issued by the same monarch, another letter, included in the work *Alguns documentos do Arquivo Nacional da Torre do Tombo acerca da avançada e conquistas dos portugueses*, bestows the said islands on Prince Henry as a royal grant.

before: The grant to the Order of Christ should be understood to concern spiritual jurisdiction, and the one made to Dom Henrique the temporal dominion of the archipelago. Since, however, the Prince was Grand Master of the Order, it follows from reading that letter that he would have held the most absolute dominion over the islands of the archipelago; this did not prevent royal interference from sometimes being felt in the administration of the affairs of these islands. ‘It is to be noted, however,’ continues the aforementioned Bernardo de Brito, ‘that the Prince, knowing that after his death the conquests could not be continued with the resources of the Order, and that the arm of the king was needed, divided everything he had discovered in such a way as to leave the Order enlarged and ennobled and the Crown of the Kingdom extended. And so he granted the temporal rule of those islands and of the mainland of Guinea to the kings of Portugal and reserved the spiritual rule for the Order, which is what the kings enjoy today as Masters, for which reason they hold the tithes and the presentations of those churches. Already in the year 1439, when King Duarte was in possession of the temporal rule of the islands of Madeira, Porto Santo and the Desertas, which the Prince had once again granted to him, their spiritual jurisdiction was conceded to the Order by a letter drawn up in Lisbon on 20 May of that year...’ By royal letters of 11 March 1449 and 17 August 1459, Afonso V confirmed the grant made to Prince Henry by King Duarte on 26 September 1433.

And so he granted the temporal rule of those islands and of the mainland of Guinea to the kings of Portugal and reserved the spiritual rule for the Order, which is what the kings enjoy today as Masters, for which reason they hold the tithes and the presentations of those churches. Already in the year 1439, when King Duarte was in possession of the temporal rule of the islands of Madeira, Porto Santo and the Desertas (‘deserted islands’), which the Prince had once again granted to him, their spiritual jurisdiction was conceded to the Order by a letter drawn up in Lisbon on 20 May of that year...’ By royal letters of 11 March 1449 and 17 August 1459, Afonso V confirmed the grant made to Prince Henry by King Duarte on 26 September 1433.

before: The grants had come to an end and Madeira had become Crown land (*realenga*). The document that attests to this, transcribed on p. 479 of the *Saudades da Terra*, is of great interest. It is the royal letter (*carta régia*) of Manuel I, dated 27 April 1497, in which he states that ‘it seems to us a just and necessary thing that the said island, with its lordship, revenues and jurisdiction, should belong solely to our said Crown for ever, and to the kings our heirs and successors... that neither the said island nor any part of it shall ever be given by us or our successors, whether as a favour, for life, in perpetuity or in any other manner whatsoever, to any person of whatever estate, condition and eminence... we swear upon the sign of the cross and upon the holy Gospels, on which we bodily lay our hands, to fulfil and maintain this wholly... and we beg and earnestly charge the kings our heirs and successors, by our blessing and under pain of the curse of God and of ourselves, always so to fulfil and preserve it for ever...’. With the incorporation of the grand mastership of the Order of Christ into the Crown in 1497 and the creation of the diocese of Funchal in 1514, the jurisdiction of that Order in this archipelago became almost nil.

before: The original British cemetery stood where the Largo do Conde do Ribeiro Real now is, at the end of Rua 5 de Junho. The ministerial order (*portaria*) granting British subjects the necessary licence to build a cemetery for burying their dead is dated 3 January 1761, but it was not until 10 September 1767 that land was acquired for the purpose. Before this cemetery was built, the bodies of non-Catholic foreigners who died in Funchal were thrown into the sea. The present British cemetery was built in 1808 and enlarged in 1852 and 1889. The oldest part of this cemetery was acquired for the burial of British soldiers who died in Funchal while Madeira was occupied by British troops, whereas the newest part only began to be used when the Municipal Council of Funchal needed to demolish the original cemetery in order to connect Rua 5 de Junho with Rua da Carreira. The administrators of the British Chapel and Cemetery (*Capela e Cemitério Britânicos*) ceded this old cemetery in August 1888. The Council undertook to make the necessary efforts to facilitate the removal of the remains in that ground to a plot adjoining the present cemetery, which the administrators had until then been unable to use to enlarge the cemetery for lack of the necessary licences. The last burial in the cemetery where the Largo do Conde do Ribeiro Real now stands took place in July 1885.

before: This is a very old family surname here, for it descends from Bartolomeu Perestrelo, the first donatary and settler of Porto Santo. He was the son of Filipone or Felipe Perestrelo, whom the genealogies record as having come to Portugal at the end of the 14th century. Filipone was a native of Piacenza, in Lombardy, and the son of Gabriel Perestrelo, a *fidalgo* (nobleman of the lesser nobility) of lineage whose privileges were recognised in our country. The arms of this family are described thus: ‘shield party per pale; in the first, on a field of gold, a lion purpure armed gules; in the second, on a field of silver, a bend azure charged with three eight-pointed stars between six *tosas* gules, three and three in pale; crest the lion of the shield, with a star on its shoulder’.

He was the son of Filipone or Felipe Perestrelo, whom the genealogies record as having come to Portugal at the end of the 14th century. The arms of this family are described thus: ‘shield party per pale; in the first, on a field of gold, a lion purpure armed gules; in the second, on a field of silver, a bend azure charged with three eight-pointed stars between six *tosas* gules, three and three in pale; crest the lion of the shield, with a star on its shoulder’.

before: In 1662 Diogo da Costa Quintal founded, on land belonging to his entailed estate (*morgadio*), the chapel of Nossa Senhora das Angústias (Our Lady of Sorrows), which gave its name to the street that ran close by and also to the surrounding locality (*sítio*). We cannot say today with certainty whether the chapel of Nossa Senhora das Angústias that stands on the *quinta* (country estate) of the same name (Quinta Lambert) is a reconstruction of the old chapel of the same dedication, nor whether the entailed property of Diogo da Costa Quintal perhaps lay there. We are, however, inclined to think so. It was in this locality of Angústias that the bishop of this diocese, Dom Joaquim de Meneses e Ataíde, while president (provedor) of the Holy House of Mercy (*Santa Casa da Misericórdia*), to which he rendered the most distinguished services, had a small cemetery built in 1818. It was intended exclusively for the burial of the bodies of those who died in the Hospital de Santa Isabel (St Elizabeth of Portugal), and stood on land belonging to João de Carvalhal, who had given it free of charge for this purpose. When a law prohibited burials in churches, the Municipal Council (*Câmara Municipal*) of Funchal obtained from the Holy House of Mercy the transfer of the small Angústias cemetery and asked João de Carvalhal, by then a count, to sell the adjoining land so that the cemetery could be enlarged. This nobleman promptly and generously offered the municipality all the land that might be needed for the planned enlargement, and informed the Council of this in a letter dated 8 July 1836.

before: The church of this convent was the true necropolis of the old Madeiran nobility. Many families had their family vaults there, some of them of fine and costly marble. When the convent and church were demolished in 1865 so that a building intended as the town hall could be put up on the site, the tombstone covering the mortal remains of the founder was removed from inside the church and placed in the Angústias cemetery, and many bones exhumed during that demolition were laid beneath it. In the centre of the tombstone this epitaph was written: ‘Vault of the bones exhumed from the former convent and church of São Francisco (to which the original inscription refers), transferred on 2 May 1865.’ The original inscription carved around the edge of the stone reads: ‘Here lies Lois Álvares da Costa, who founded this house in the year 1473, and his son Francisco Álvares da Costa, first *ouvidor* and overseer of the royal treasury (*vedor da fazenda*) in these islands of Madeira.’ There are many private vaults and mausoleums in this cemetery, the most prominent being the one belonging to the Carvalhal family. When a man took his own life in this city on 4 March 1877, the episcopal authority – at that time the prelate Dom Manuel Agostinho Barreto, who had arrived in Funchal and taken over the government of the diocese only a few days earlier – refused him church burial. Despite the prelate’s ruling, the Municipal Council (*Câmara Municipal*) ordered the suicide to be buried in the section reserved for Catholics, whereupon the diocesan bishop placed the cemetery under interdict by a warrant (*provisão*) of 16 March 1877. The prelate addressed the matter with remarkable boldness from the pulpit of Funchal Cathedral (*Sé*) in a vehement sermon that became memorable. The affair was taken up by the press, which discussed it at length, each paper according to its own opinions. On this subject an interesting pamphlet entitled *A Sepultura Eclesiástica e os Suicidas*, written by Dr Cassiano Neves, was published in Porto; its chief aim was to rebut the claims of the newspaper *A Lei*, then published in Funchal.

before: Within the grounds of this cemetery a fine monument was recently erected to commemorate the barbarous attack by German submarines, which bombarded the city of Funchal. It is dedicated in a very special way to perpetuating the memory of the dozens of victims of German ferocity who rest there, and whom a happy and pious initiative did not wish future generations to forget. On 3 December 1917, the first anniversary of that sorrowful and tragic event, the monument was unveiled after a religious service in the Cathedral. The ceremony was particularly splendid, and several speakers gave eloquent and patriotic speeches on the tribute about to be paid to those poor victims of German barbarity. The monument, which stands to the right of the cemetery entrance, is the work of the chisel of the prize-winning sculptor Francisco Franco and owes its existence to the praiseworthy initiative of the banker Henrique Vieira de Castro. He not only opened the subscription to pay for it with a generous *donativo* (nominally a ‘gift’ to the Crown; a compulsory war levy), but also promoted all the work from the start of construction to its final unveiling. The tomb-monument, which was entrusted to the care and upkeep of the Municipal Council of Funchal, cost approximately two *contos* de réis (*conto*: one million réis) (see Bombardment of Funchal).

before: When the liberal principles of the Porto revolution of 24 August 1820 were proclaimed in Funchal on 28 January 1821, Dr Pita was one of the first to embrace them, and from then on he was always a fierce opponent of the old institutions. Believing that a newspaper was the best means of spreading constitutional ideas among his fellow islanders, he had a printing press brought from Lisbon, and on 2 July 1821 he began publishing the *Patriota Funchalense*. This was the first periodical Madeira ever had, and its contributors included the men best known on the island for their advanced opinions.

before: This small parish lies in the interior of the island, on the floor of the crater of an extinct volcano, as several geologists affirm. To reach this *lugar* (settlement ranking between a town and a parish), one must climb high, steep mountains and descend the sloping ravines that ring the deep valley, which, seen from the mountain peaks, appears to us as a dreadful and fathomless abyss. It is perhaps the spot in Madeira where nature shows itself at its most remarkably grand and most surprising. This is owed to the great height and fanciful shapes of the mountains, the towering, sheer slopes, the gorges and chasms scattered everywhere, and the rugged, wild tone of the landscape. All this gives the whole such an air of grandeur and majesty, and of such extraordinary and enchanting beauty, that the visitor, even the least observant and sensitive, is astonished and entranced on coming upon this scene of so many incomparable wonders. ‘We saw a channel,’ says a distinguished writer, ‘many metres wide and cut almost sheer, a fearsome gulf, an immense hollow around which, except to the south, rise titanic peaks of fantastic outline, and, at the bottom of the abyss... the rustic miniature of a paradise...’ Above Curral das Freiras rise some of the highest peaks in Madeira, foremost among them the well-known Pico Ruivo, which reaches an altitude of approximately two thousand metres above sea level. Numerous Portuguese and foreign works contain extensive references to the Curral, and this *lugar* has been much visited by many illustrious men, among them some who achieved distinction in the fields of science and letters.

before: In 1480 the Curral belonged to Rui Teixeira and his wife Branca Ferreira, who lived in Campanário. On 11 September of that year they signed the deed of sale of this vast property to the second captain-donatary of Funchal, João Gonçalves da Câmara. The estate stretched ‘from the Passo da Cruz and the Ribeirão dos Socorridos up to where it rises, from rocky crest (*arrife*) to rocky crest, on either side’. The purchase price was ‘23,500 réis at five *ceitis* to the *real* (pl. *réis*; old Portuguese money unit, 1,000 réis = 1 milréis) and 50 gold *cruzados*, each worth 380 réis’. The captain-donatary intended this land for the endowment he made to his daughters, Dona Elvira and Dona Joana, when they took their vows at Santa Clara, the convent that he himself had founded in 1492 and which the first nuns entered in 1497. The endowment of the Curral must have been made at some point between 1492 and 1497, and from that time onwards it became known as Curral das Freiras (the Nuns’ Fold).

The captain-donatary intended this land for the endowment he made to his daughters, Dona Elvira and Dona Joana, when they took their vows at the Convent of St Clare (*Santa Clara*), the convent that he himself had founded in 1492 and which the first nuns entered in 1497. The endowment of the Curral must have been made at some point between 1492 and 1497, and from that time onwards it became known as Curral das Freiras (the Nuns’ Fold).

before: In 1560 the city of Funchal was sacked by French Lutheran corsairs, of whom the old Madeiran chronicles speak with such horror. The nuns of Santa Clara were forced to abandon their convent so as not to fall victim to that horde of savages and, as Frutuoso says, ‘they went out through the cane fields and took refuge, and did not stop until they reached their Curral, which lies a good distance from the city, and so they departed without saving any ornament, leaving everything in the convent except the monstrance of the Most Blessed Sacrament...’. The French remained in Funchal, busy with destruction and slaughter, from 3 to 17 October. Soon after they left the island, the nuns left the Curral and returned to their convent in the city. We do not know whether the nuns of Santa Clara had by then already built in the Curral the chapel of Santo António (St Anthony of Padua), which stood there until the middle of the 19th century and belonged to the same convent.

before: Before it was raised to a parish (*freguesia*), Curral das Freiras belonged to the parish of Santo António, from which it was separated in 1790. The Curral nevertheless had its own chaplains, who lived there more or less permanently; in 1678 a chaplain’s licence was issued to Father Cristóvão Vieira. Services were held in the chapel of Santo António. When it was inspected in 1756 by the episcopal visitor (*visitador*, ecclesiastical inspector) Dr António Mendes de Almeida, he ordered, in a visitation decree (*provimento*) recorded in the archive of the parish of Santo António, that the abbess of Santa Clara be told to supply the chapel with the objects needed for worship, as she was obliged to do, on pain (*pena*) of further proceedings.

before: For the building of a new church and a residence for the chaplain – no doubt already with the coming foundation of the parish in view – the convent of Santa Clara, by a deed executed on 24 July 1784, gave the mitre of this diocese six *alqueires* of land, subject only to an annual quit-rent (*foro*) of one pullet, payable on 12 August each year. The buildings were to be for the use of the chaplains and their successors.

before: The learned annotator of the *Saudades da Terra* says that the parish of Curral das Freiras had its seat in the chapel of Santa Quitéria (St Quiteria), founded by Simão de Nóbrega. This is a plain mistake, for that chapel stood in the parish of Santo António, at the locality (*sítio*) that still bears that name today. It is an established fact that the small chapel of Santo António, which stood in the Curral and belonged to the convent of Santa Clara, served as the base and seat of the new parish when it was created by royal decree (alvará régio) of 17 March 1790.
after: The learned annotator of ‘Longing for the Homeland’ (*Saudades da Terra*) says that the parish of Curral das Freiras had its seat in the chapel of Santa Quitéria (St Quiteria), founded by Simão de Nóbrega. It is an established fact that the small chapel of Santo António, which stood in the Curral and belonged to the Convent of St Clare, served as the base and seat of the new parish when it was created by royal decree (alvará régio) of 17 March 1790.

before: The centre of the parish lies 14 kilometres from the parish church of Santo António and 17½ kilometres from the city of Funchal. After crossing the Ribeira de Vasco Gil and climbing the slope of the *lombo* (ridge between valleys) of Dona Isabel, one joins a level road that runs as far as the Eira do Serrado, at an altitude of 1026 metres, from where the whole settlement of the Curral can be seen far below. There begins the steep, winding descent known as the Passo da Chave, which leads to the centre of the parish.

before: On the rugged slopes of this parish rises the Ribeira dos Socorridos, the most important watercourse in the south of the island. The important Levada dos Piornais and Levada Nova do Castelejo (levada: irrigation channel) have their intakes on this stream.

before: The first members of the General Council, thirteen in number, were elected in the Council house on 11 October 1835, in the manner laid down in Article 10 of the decree of 18 July of the same year. The administrative codes of 1836 and 1842 did not change the number of representatives on the General Council, but the code of 1878 raised it to 21, and the elected representatives were to choose the District Committee (Comissão Distrital) at their first session. Direct election of the District General Councils was authorised by the code of 1878; the code of 1842 had laid down that these administrative bodies were to be elected by the municipal councils together with the Municipal Boards (*Conselhos Municipais*).

before: The administrative codes of 1895 and 1896 confirmed the provisions of the decree of 6 August 1892 abolishing the District General Councils. However, the General Council of Funchal was restored by the decree of 8 August 1901, which applied to this district the special organisation granted to the districts of the Azores by the decree of 2 March 1895, as amended by the law of 12 June 1901. With the abolition of the General Councils, a District Committee (Comissão Distrital) remained in existence at the seat of each district. In the mainland districts, the General Councils were not restored until the decree of 13 October 1910.

before: ‘Dom Friar Patrício Xavier de Moura was an Augustinian friar of the Graça, and while a brother (*freire*) of the Order he had been appointed by John VI canon of Bemposta and private chaplain to the Infanta Isabel Maria, after the king had heard the magnificent voice with which he was gifted. Being a legitimist, he withdrew to his native town, preaching from the pulpit until he was sent to serve as priest of the parish (*freguesia*) of Vila Franca de Xira. There he became acquainted with the Viscount of Villa Franca Nova de Ourém, who promised to make him a bishop when he became a minister, a vow that was kept. On leaving for Cape Verde he took with him Dom João de Noronha, already 70 years old, who had been presented as archdeacon, and three servants: Fernandes de Aguiar, who recently died in Cape Verde leaving a fortune of more than 80,000,000 *réis* (old Portuguese money of account; 1$000 = 1,000 réis, 1:000$000 = one conto = 1,000,000 réis); José Silvestre Teixeira, who did not live long; and José Maria Pinto, who at the age of 18 had been appointed to a canon’s place and remained in Cape Verde until 1880, leaving a respected name as a teacher. Dom Patrício, although more inclined to don the helmet and draw the sword than to put on the mitre and grasp the crosier, was a hard-working and zealous prelate. While he would rebuke in public and with asperity a servant who proposed a toast at a festive dinner without asking leave, and would order a priest who sat down in his presence without due reverence to stand up, he generously praised and rewarded those who did their duty and did not take such liberties. Barely restrained in his reprimands, he saw the dean of the Cathedral only once, for the dean never returned there while this prelate remained in the diocese.’ He established his residence on the island of Fogo, but made frequent and lengthy visits to the islands of Brava and Santiago. He fought battles with the governor-general, chiefly over the appointment of acting parish priests (*párocos encomendados*, appointed without tenure), and the government in mainland Portugal confirmed the prelate’s right to make such appointments. When a great food crisis struck the archipelago, he gave up in favour of the starving eighteen *contos* de réis of the mitre’s revenues that were due to him. He administered the bishopric of Cape Verde for about ten years and then, on account of illness, requested his presentation to the See of Funchal.

Being a legitimist, he withdrew to his native town, preaching from the pulpit until he was sent to serve as priest of the parish (*freguesia*) of Vila Franca de Xira. There he became acquainted with the Viscount of Villa Franca Nova de Ourém, who promised to make him a bishop when he became a minister, a vow that was kept. On leaving for Cape Verde he took with him Dom João de Noronha, already 70 years old, who had been presented as archdeacon, and three servants: Fernandes de Aguiar, who recently died in Cape Verde leaving a fortune of more than 80,000,000 *réis* (old Portuguese money of account; 1$000 = 1,000 réis, 1:000$000 = one conto = 1,000,000 réis); José Silvestre Teixeira, who did not live long; and José Maria Pinto, who at the age of 18 had been appointed to a canon’s place and remained in Cape Verde until 1880, leaving a respected name as a teacher. Dom Patrício, although more inclined to don the helmet and draw the sword than to put on the mitre and grasp the crosier, was a hard-working and zealous prelate. While he would rebuke in public and with asperity a servant who proposed a toast at a festive dinner without asking leave, and would order a priest who sat down in his presence without due reverence to stand up, he generously praised and rewarded those who did their duty and did not take such liberties. Barely restrained in his reprimands, he saw the dean of the Cathedral only once, for the dean never returned there while this prelate remained in the diocese.’ He established his residence on the island of Fogo, but made frequent and lengthy visits to the islands of Brava and Santiago. He fought battles with the governor-general, chiefly over the appointment of acting parish priests (*párocos encomendados*, appointed without tenure), and the government in mainland Portugal confirmed the prelate’s right to make such appointments. When a great food crisis struck the archipelago, he gave up in favour of the starving eighteen *contos* de réis of the mitre’s revenues that were due to him. He administered the bishopric of Cape Verde for about ten years and then, on account of illness, requested his presentation to the See of Funchal.

before: González Telmo, more commonly known by the name of Corpo Santo (Holy Body). Worship at this chapel is maintained by the fishing community of Funchal, and it was once the seat of a kind of relief society intended to support seafarers in sickness or disability. It is still not known at present whether the confraternity keeps this charitable character among its members. We shall transcribe what we found on the matter in the *Diccionario Universal Portuguez Illustrado*, which is truly interesting: ‘confraternities... there are two notable ones, both because they date from the time of the first settlement of the archipelago and because they form true mutual-aid associations: the confraternity of Corpo Santo, with its Manueline chapel at the eastern end of Funchal, and that of São Pedro Telmo, in the *lugar* (settlement ranking between a town and a parish) of Câmara de Lobos. Both belong to seafarers and clearly derive from the famous statutes (*compromisso*) of the Algarve seafarers, and, like these, they connect, in religious form, with the nautical institutions of the time of King Denis. The statutes of these two Madeiran confraternities, of which we possess a copy, are, like the Algarve one, precious documents for the history, obscure but glorious, not of princes nor of the navigators in their service, but of the pilots and sailors, the seafaring men properly so called, who had no small share in the discoveries’.

before: The royal decree (*alvará*) of 13 August 1508 laid down that the Council of Funchal should be ‘regida & gobernada por maneyra que se rrege a de Lisboa’ (governed and administered in the manner in which that of Lisbon is governed), that henceforth only noblemen (*fidalgos*) could be councillors (*vereadores*), and that the result of the elections, which were to be held every three years, should be sent to the monarch for his confirmation. Earlier, in 1461, Prince Ferdinand had ordered that the offices of the Council be filled by election and that two ballot balls (*pelouros*) be made each year, one for the judges and the other for the councillors and the representative (*procurador*). The captain-donatary (*capitão-donatário*) was to administer the oath to those elected, but without interfering in the electoral proceedings.

before: John IV, by a decree of 6 July 1654, gave Funchal representation in the Cortes (Portuguese parliament), but a document cited by Dr Azevedo on p. 635 of his notes to the *Saudades da Terra* shows that as early as 1479 Madeira was already sending its own representatives to the Cortes. It should be pointed out, however, that our island is not included in the list of places that supplied representatives in 1535, which is held in the archive of the Torre do Tombo (National Archives) and was published by Mr António de Sousa Júnior in the *Censo da metropole*. before: As regards the local administrative bodies, after the restoration of constitutional government in Madeira the Councils were always elected directly by the municipalities, whereas the District General Council (*Junta Geral*) ceased to be chosen by indirect election only in 1878. As regards the fauna, the collections of birds, fish and shells deserve mention, as do those of corals and of certain groups of insects. As regards the flora, notable for their importance are the collections of mosses and flowering plants made by the late James Yate Johnson, those of lichens and fungi made by Father Jaime de Gouveia Barreto, and the seaweed collection assembled by Father Ernesto Schmitz. before: This parish had its origin in the settled estate (*fazenda povoada*) that Adão Gonçalves Ferreira held there. He was the first man born on this island and the son of Gonçalo Aires Ferreira (see p. 21), the most distinguished companion of Zargo in the discovery of the archipelago. As was generally the case, a small chapel was the centre around which the first settlers gathered: around 1470 Adão Ferreira built a modest chapel there, which seems originally to have been called Nossa Senhora da Incarnação (Our Lady of the Incarnation). It later came to be called Nossa Senhora do Monte, certainly owing to the lie of the land, which fully justified the new and fitting name. Others maintain that it was the miraculous apparition of the image of the Most Holy Virgin, which people at once began to call Nossa Senhora do Monte, that led the chapel to take this name, which passed to the locality and later to the whole parish.

before: The legend of this miraculous apparition is told in the following terms on the back of the engravings depicting the tiny and venerable image: ‘More than 300 years ago, at Terreiro da Luta, about 1 kilometre above the church of Nossa Senhora do Monte, a little Girl played one afternoon with a certain young shepherdess and gave her a snack. Full of joy, the shepherdess told her family of this, but they did not believe her, for it seemed impossible to them that a little Girl should appear in that lonely forest so far from the village. The following afternoon the same thing happened, and the shepherdess told of it again. The next day, at the hour the shepherdess had given, her father secretly went to watch the scene, and he saw on a stone a small Image of Most Holy Mary, and in front of it the innocent shepherdess, who, when her father unexpectedly appeared, declared that this Image was the little Girl she had spoken of. The shepherd, amazed, did not dare to touch the image, and reported the matter to the authorities, who had it placed in the chapel of the Incarnação, near the present church of “Nossa Senhora do Monte”, the name that has been given to that venerable Image ever since.’ This account does not differ in essentials from a manuscript description in our possession dating from the middle of the 18th century, which was itself based on an unbroken oral tradition. That description contains the following interesting detail: ‘On the following day at dawn Our Lady was found outside the Chapel, at the spring close by it, upon a stone on which some ancient characters, barely legible, may still be seen today…’ This most precious stone, says Father Joaquim Plácido Pereira, was buried at the bottom of the Ribeiro de Nossa Senhora (Our Lady’s Stream) when the Municipal Council (*Câmara Municipal*) of Funchal had the Largo da Fonte enlarged in 1896.

before: When the revolution that broke out in Spain in early 1866 failed, many revolutionaries took refuge in Portugal. Seventy of them came to this island – 46 officers and 24 soldiers – arriving here on 1 July of the same year. These Spanish émigrés, some of whom married on the island, left after the triumph of the revolution of 1868, which dethroned Isabella II. They went by night to Praia Formosa to embark, without the authorities learning of their departure.

before: The northern coast of Madeira, generally known as the Costa do Norte (North Coast), stretches from Ponta do Tristão, where it meets the western region of the island, to the tip of the northern slope of Ponta de São Lourenço, which extends along the eastern side. It has been said somewhere, and with every justification, that it is an alpine, craggy coast, forming a line of high rocks like an enormous wall of cliff, its base lashed by the waves and its summit crowned with the luxuriant greenery of a native forest. Because beaches and coves are so rare, and because of the violence of the northerly winds that blow there for most of the year, it is utterly inhospitable to ships and unsafe for boats. It has only two harbours of refuge from bad weather, Porto da Cruz and Porto Moniz, lying roughly at the eastern and western ends of the coast. The coast takes in the parishes of the municipalities (*concelhos*) of Porto Moniz, São Vicente and Santana, as well as the parish of Porto da Cruz and the northern shore of the parish of Caniçal, both of which belong to the municipality of Machico.

before: The outline of the shoreline of the Costa do Norte is described by Luís da Silva Mousinho de Albuquerque in the following terms: ‘From Ponta do Pargo northwards, the coast first runs north-east as far as Ponta do Tristão, where the northern coast of the island begins. It then runs roughly east-south-east as far as São Vicente, and from there east-north-east as far as Ponta de São Jorge, whence it returns to its general south-easterly direction as far as Porto da Cruz, almost at the northern root of Ponta de São Lourenço. This point closes the island at its eastern extremity, stretching out into the sea, very narrow, for roughly three miles, in a west–east direction. Along almost the whole length of this shoreline the sea is deep and free of reefs, with these exceptions only: 1. in the recessed part of this coast, where there are some shoals and isolated rocks, among which the Ilhéu da Ribeira da Janela and the Ilhéu and shoal of Porto Moniz stand out; 2. Ponta do Pargo, where a shoal stretches out into the sea, on which the waves break even in moderate winds, forcing boats to keep well away from the land in order to round it’.

before: The princess, according to trustworthy contemporary witnesses, was of unequalled kindness and aroused the liveliest and most ardent affection in all who saw her or came near her. Her death therefore caused the whole population of Funchal the deepest grief, which endured among us for many years. The empress embarked on her return to Lisbon, accompanying the coffin that held the mortal remains of her daughter, on 6 May 1853. It was an imposing procession, in which not a dry eye was to be seen. From the humblest townsman to the desolate empress, all wept copiously. It seemed as if a great calamity had occurred. This death, as everyone knows, led to the founding of the Hospício da Princesa D. Maria Amélia, of which we shall speak on another occasion. The Empress Dona Amélia died in Lisbon on 26 January 1873.

before: This surname was originally spelt Favela and belongs to an old and noble family that settled on this island at the end of the 15th century. The first to bear it here was Fernão Favela, known as the Elder, who had served valiantly in Africa and had been a nobleman of the Royal Household (*fidalgo da Casa Real*). He married Beatriz Pires in Madeira and founded the entailed estate (*morgadio*) of Piornais, centred on the chapel of Nossa Senhora da Ajuda (Our Lady of Help), which he had founded and where he was buried. He died in 1545, according to Henriques de Noronha, or in 1537, according to the date given by Dr Rodrigues de Azevedo. His son and successor was António Favila, who died in 1601 and lies buried in the Ajuda chapel. Dona Inês Moniz, who was born in 1553 and died in 1589, was the daughter of António Favila. She founded an entailed estate in favour of her niece Dona Isabel Acciaioli de Vasconcelos, with the clause that it should pass in perpetuity to the eldest daughter – an extremely curious circumstance and, we believe, a very rare one, at least here in Madeira.

before: According to Dr José de Arriaga in his *Historia da revolução portuguesa de 1820*, the island of Madeira was one of the first places in Portugal where Freemasonry found a particularly favourable welcome. By 1770 there was already a Masonic lodge in Madeira, whose members included Aires de Ornelas Frasão, Francisco de Alincourt and Bartolomeu Andrieux, as can be seen from an official letter sent by the Governor, João António de Sá Pereira, to the Marquis of Pombal on 3 December of that year. On 14 April 1792 the Governor, Dom Diogo Forjaz Coutinho, complained to Martinho de Melo e Castro that the Frenchman João José de Orquiny had established a Masonic lodge on this island, most of whose members belonged to the nobility and the clergy.

before: The Madeiran poet Francisco Álvares de Nóbrega and the dean of Funchal Cathedral (*Sé*), João Francisco Lopes Rocha, suffered greatly during this persecution. The latter wrote a letter to the minister José de Seabra da Silva, dated 16 October 1793, in which he complained bitterly that the Bishop was keeping him suspended from the exercise of his priestly offices and from the corresponding stipends, in open violation of Portuguese law and of the express instructions of the Queen’s government. This letter, published many years later in volume III of the *Campeão Portuguez* in London, is an important document for the study of Masonic institutions in Madeira.

before: Luiz Cadamosto (Alvise Cadamosto) was a celebrated Venetian navigator in the service of Portugal. He made two voyages to the western coasts of Africa and wrote an account of them, which is regarded as a valuable source for the history of our maritime discoveries. The *Navegações* of Cadamosto were first published in Italian in 1507, and later in Latin. The Portuguese translation was first published in 1812 in the *colecção de noticias para a historia e geographia...* of the Royal Academy of Sciences (*Academia Real das Ciências*). Pinheiro Chagas discusses the worth and importance of these *Navegações* at length. They matter to the history of Madeira because Cadamosto devotes several pages to this archipelago, and his is the oldest account by any of the many navigators who have written about Madeira. The *Heraldo da Madeira* of 5, 9 and 11 January 1906 reproduced the passages of the *Navegações* in which Cadamosto describes his stay on Madeira and Porto Santo. He anchored at the landing place of the latter island on 25 March 1445, and on the 28th of the same month in the bay of Machico. Pinheiro Chagas gives 1455 as the year of the Venetian navigator’s voyage, while Dr Azevedo, in a note to his article ‘Madeira’ in the *Dicc. Port. Univ.* III, adopts the date of 1445 on the basis of arguments that he sets out. Dr Pestana Júnior, in his valuable study on the *Reconhecimento do Arquipelago da Madeira*, places Cadamosto’s voyages in the years 1449 and 1450.

before: This locality (*sítio*) in the parish (*freguesia*) of Canhas takes its name from the chapel of Nossa Senhora dos Anjos (Our Lady of the Angels). The chapel is of considerable age and was built, according to some, by order of the Infanta Dona Beatriz, as guardian of her son, the Grand Master of the Order of Christ, to which Madeira belonged in spiritual matters; according to others, it was built by Martins Afonso in 1508. The image venerated in this chapel was the object of great devotion, and Friar Agostinho de Santa Maria discusses it in vol. X of his *Santuário Mariano*. The locality of Anjos, which is exceptionally fertile and forms the coastal strip of the parish of Canhas, was once part of the parish of Ponta do Sol.

before: Born in Porto do Moniz on 10 February 1873, he attended the lyceum (state secondary school) and the Medical-Surgical School of Funchal (*Escola Médico-Cirúrgica do Funchal*), completing his medical course in 1897. He served as a physician in São Tomé and at Trafaria, and as doctor on the Portuguese steamers of J. M. Andressen, of Porto. He sat on the Administrative Committee (*Comissão Administrativa*) of the Municipal Council (*Câmara Municipal*) of Funchal during the government of Councillor (conselheiro, honorary title of the royal council) João Franco. Later, after the Republic, he became president of the same Council, and it was on his initiative that the gaol building on the Largo da Sé was demolished, a step that the press and the people of Funchal had been demanding for more than half a century. He has been president of the executive committee of the District General Council (*Junta Geral do Distrito*) and was a member of the former Agricultural Board (*Junta Agrícola*); it was owing to a proposal of his that this latter body had the *Flora do Archipelago da Madeira* published in 1914 (1921).

before: He was born in the town (*vila*) of Machico on 7 March 1843, the son of José António de Almada. before: In 1800 the government in Lisbon, in instructions addressed to the governor and captain-general Dom José Manuel da Câmara, recommended the creation of a credit fund in Madeira. On 1 July 1824 the governor and captain-general Dom Manuel de Portugal e Castro sent a petition to the central government asking for a bank to be founded in Funchal. Neither establishment was ever created, and the same happened with other institutions of the same kind that people later sought to found in this city. Issue no. 169 of the *Imparcial*, of 1843, published in full a draft set of regulations for the creation of a bank in Madeira, and issue no. 145 and following of the newspaper *A Ordem*, of 1854, contain the project submitted to the government for the creation of a commercial and agricultural bank on the island.

before: Besides the special conditions that make it a favourite place to spend the summer season, this locality should also be regarded as an excellent health resort. The mildness of a cool, temperate climate, the fine bathing beach and the much-praised São Roque waters (águas de São Roque), with their well-known therapeutic properties, commend it as the most valuable health resort in the archipelago after Porto Santo. Further attractions are the natural beauty of the lovely valley in which the picturesque town (*vila*) lies; the ease of making short excursions to the charming settlement of Santa Cruz and the delightful parish (*freguesia*) of Santo da Serra; boat trips to Caniçal, Prainha and Ponta de São Lourenço; a comfortable hotel open all year; houses to let; and rapid, frequent communications with the city of Funchal, etc. etc.

before: This islet, also known as the Ilhéu da Cal (Lime Islet), lies next to the island of Porto Santo, from which it is separated by a channel, the Boqueirão de Baixo. It stands at the southern tip of the island, at the western end of the wide bay, opposite the locality of Calheta. For centuries all the limestone that supplies the raw material for the lime used in Madeiran building has been quarried on this islet, and it still is. The quarrying follows the seam, forming long galleries with tall columns or pillars to prevent collapses. It is carried out at several points, and each group of workers employed at the various quarrying sites is called a band (*rancho*). The stone is taxed on export to Madeira, the duty being collected at the Funchal customs house, and it is one of the most valuable sources of revenue of the Municipal Council (*Câmara Municipal*) of Porto Santo. The islet is fairly large, and rabbits are still plentiful there, despite the constant poaching of these rodents.

before: Emigration from Madeira was already taking place in the 16th century, for Friar Gaspar da Madre de Deus, in his *Memórias para a Historia da Capitania de S. Vicente do Estado do Brasil*, refers to many married couples from this island going to that captaincy. Emigration to Brazil continued in the 17th and 18th centuries, and among the many Madeirans who went there in search of fortune during Philippine rule (Spanish Habsburg rule over Portugal, 1580–1640) was the celebrated João Fernandes Vieira, the liberator of Pernambuco. before: He was a native of the parish (*freguesia*) of Santa Cruz, and we believe that he belonged to the noble Freitas family, whose founder on this island was Gonçalo de Freitas. We know little of his life, but from the important offices he held we must suppose that he was a man of undeniable merit. He was a monk of the Benedictine order and held the high office of general of Alcobaça Monastery, which at that time was entrusted only to a person distinguished in learning and virtue. Special privileges and prerogatives went with this post, as did jurisdiction over all the religious houses of that order in Portugal. He was a deputy of the Inquisition at Coimbra and wrote several works in Latin and Portuguese, which are listed in the *Bibliotheca Lusitana*. He died in 1654.

before: The common lands (*baldios*), or uncultivated and unused land of Madeira, lie for the most part more than 800 or 900 metres above sea level. Almost all of them are privately owned, although more often than not this ownership cannot be proved by legal title. It is said that the Paul da Serra and a small part of the uplands of São Jorge, Boaventura and Poiso belong to the State, while all the other land in the island’s mountainous region belongs to private owners, except for the Montado do Barreiro, recently acquired by the Municipal Council of Funchal, and the upland commons (montados) bought by the Agricultural Council of Madeira (*Junta Agrícola da Madeira*).

before: In 1770 the vagrant boys of Porto Santo were sent to learn trades in the workshops of this fortress, which included tinsmithing, blacksmithing, tinplate work, gunsmithing and gunstock-making. before: Castelo do Pico (Castle of the Peak), Porto Santo. Repeated pirate raids on the island of Porto Santo led Philip II to see to its resettlement. The worst was the raid of 1619, in which almost the entire population perished or was carried off into captivity, leaving only 18 men and 7 women. He ordered a fortress to be built on the steep, stony Pico that overlooks the town (*vila*), and had residential houses, storehouses and a cistern put up on the small plateau of the knoll. It was a place of refuge rather than of war, although it was suitably armed with artillery.

before: When the governor and captain-general of Madeira, Dom Diogo Forjaz Coutinho, proposed to the botanist Vandelli the creation of large plant nurseries on the island, intended to supply not only the Ajuda botanical garden but also, if need be, the gardens and hothouses of all Europe, the central authorities soon sent the Civil Government of Funchal the authorisation needed to put the project into practice. On 6 May 1799, the said governor having already died, the provisional government ordered the bachelor (*bacharel*, university graduate) José Maria de Afonseca to choose a suitable site for a plant nursery. On 9 August following, the same government stated in an official document that the land intended for growing northern species lay at the Lombada, in the parish (*freguesia*) of Monte, and that the southern species would be grown at whatever sites seemed most suitable until land of their own was assigned to them. Afonseca himself was put in charge of the nursery for northern species; if he was prevented, he could be replaced by José Joaquim de Vasconcelos, who would take charge of the nursery for southern species once it came to be established.

before: By 10 August 1823 the Monte nursery had distributed more than 20,000 trees to various places on Madeira and Porto Santo, according to a report on the work carried out for the benefit of the archipelago’s rural economy, submitted to the competent authorities by José Maria de Afonseca. The Monte nursery was abolished in 1828 by the government of Miguel I, and no one afterwards thought of restoring it. The decree of 4 January 1837 ordered the convent grounds of the former Convent of São Francisco (St Francis of Assisi) to be turned into a plant nursery, but it seems that nothing useful was done there to revive an undertaking that had already given such good results here in Madeira.
after: By 10 August 1823 the Monte nursery had distributed more than 20,000 trees to various places on Madeira and Porto Santo (‘holy harbour’), according to a report on the work carried out for the benefit of the archipelago’s rural economy, submitted to the competent authorities by José Maria de Afonseca. The Monte nursery was abolished in 1828 by the government of Miguel I, and no one afterwards thought of restoring it. The decree of 4 January 1837 ordered the convent grounds of the former Convent of São Francisco (St Francis of Assisi) to be turned into a plant nursery, but it seems that nothing useful was done there to revive an undertaking that had already given such good results here in Madeira.

before: The land where the Monte nursery stood is still known today as the ‘Quinta do Jardim Botânico’. As for the nursery for southern species, we have no record that it was ever created.

before: It does not seem easy to draw an exact and rigorous distinction between the meanings of such terms as *golfo*, *baía*, *enseada*, *angra*, *abra*, *calheta*, etc. Dictionaries and geographical treatises reveal this difficulty, for they disagree when they try to fix the meaning of these words. Differing in part from the classification adopted for Madeira by various authors (Frutuoso, Azevedo, Nóbrega Soares, Sarmento, Loureiro, Meneses etc.), we shall say that, of the inlets along the coast of the whole archipelago, only those of Funchal and Porto Santo deserve in our view the name of bays, and we give the rest the generic name of coves (*enseadas*).

before: Madeira had several charters, but the oldest are known only from mentions in certain later documents and in the *Saudades da Terra* of Dr Gaspar Frutuoso. In the letters granting the captaincies of Funchal and Machico to João Gonçalves Zarco and Tristão Vaz Teixeira, transcribed on pp. 453 and 456 of the notes to Frutuoso’s work, Prince Henry the Navigator refers to the charter (foral) that he had ordered to be drawn up for the island. However, neither this charter nor the one that Afonso V gave in 1452 to what was then the town (*vila*) of Funchal is recorded in the municipal archives.

before: An anonymous manuscript *Miscelânea*, cited by Dr Azevedo and held in the National Library in Lisbon, states that ‘in 1452 Dom Afonso V gave a charter to the town of Funchal with many privileges, exempting the inhabitants of the whole island from paying excise, tolls or any of the levies that existed at that time in the Kingdom’. Dr Gaspar Frutuoso gives 1472 as the year in which this charter was granted, but Dr Azevedo believes this to be an error on the part of either the author of the *Saudades* or the copyist, since several documents recorded in the archive of the Municipal Council (*Câmara Municipal*) of Funchal show that the Funchal municipality already existed before that year.

before: The charter of the city of Funchal (see that entry) and of the towns of Ponta do Sol and Calheta is dated 6 August 1515. A certified copy of it, taken from the *Livro das Ilhas* on 2 May 1736, is kept in a special book in the archive of this city’s Municipal Council. It is a document of interest for many reasons, and Dr Azevedo transcribes it on p. 494 of the notes to the *Saudades da Terra*. Its forty-one chapters set out the taxes to which the people of the captaincy of Funchal were subject, the formalities required for the manufacture, transport and export of sugar, and the fines incurred by gamblers, the excommunicated and persons found carrying or using weapons, etc., etc.

before: The village (*lugar*, settlement rank below a town) of São Vicente was made a town and separated from the jurisdiction of Machico by a royal decree (alvará régio) of 23 August 1743, but whether it was granted a charter we do not know. This decree and the letter of grant (carta de mercê) of 25 August 1744 allowed the *lugares* (settlement ranking between a town and a parish) of Porto do Moniz, Seixal, Ponta Delgada, Arco de São Jorge and São Jorge to be attached to the new town, ‘all of which were far from the town of Machico, for which reason their inhabitants suffered the same oppressions as those of the village of São Vicente’.

before: By a royal decree (*alvará*) of 17 August 1508, Manuel I ordered that the Council of the town (*vila*) of Funchal should be governed in the same way as that of the city of Lisbon. As a result, many provisions of the regulations (*regimento*) of the Lisbon Council were adopted here from the outset. The archive of the Municipal Council (*Câmara Municipal*) of Funchal holds a fairly old book, written by one of the finest calligraphers of the day, containing the regulations and charter of the Municipal Council of Lisbon. Certain changes were gradually introduced into it, some of which appear in notes written in the margins of the book.
