before: As a contribution to the study of Madeiran epigraphy that may one day be undertaken, we record here a number of lapidary inscriptions. Some were already included in the first edition of this work; others we came across in the course of our research into the history of our archipelago. In this way we offer some scattered and still little-known material that may prove useful in preparing that interesting study. All of them belong to relatively recent periods and are of no particular interest for their antiquity, since the history of Madeira began some five hundred years ago and the events recorded can go back no further than the middle of the 15th century. Where the exact dates of events are not known, we have always tried to give the approximate year in which they occurred. João Gonçalves Zarco was buried in the chancel of the church of Conceição de Cima (today Santa Clara), which he had founded. It is stated in some places, though there is no proof of it, that his ashes were moved to the tomb of his son-in-law Martim Mendes de Vasconcelos, which stands beside the choir of the same church. We dealt with this matter at some length in the article Zargo in the first edition of this *Elucidário*, and it is very strange that this church contains no funerary inscription referring to the first captain-donatary (*capitão-donatário*) of Funchal. He must have died around 1467.

before: In 1919 a gravestone was discovered beside the high altar of this church, bearing the following inscription: Tomb of João Gonçalves da Câmara, second captain of the Island. before: Another son-in-law of João Gonçalves Zarco was Diogo Cabral, who died in 1486 and was buried in the chapel of Nossa Senhora da Estrela (Our Lady of the Star), which he had founded in the parish (*freguesia*) of Calheta, at the locality (*sítio*) that still bears that name. Twenty years ago the stone that covered the mortal remains of Diogo Cabral was removed to the parish cemetery and reused for an ordinary grave, after the coat of arms and the epitaph of Zargo’s son-in-law had been scraped off – all of which constitutes an unspeakable abuse.

before: Not far from there, at the locality of Serra de Água in the parish of Arco da Calheta, stood the chapel of Nossa Senhora da Conceição, founded by Gonçalo Fernandes in the first half of the 16th century. About ten years ago a fairly old tombstone was found there with this inscription: Tomb of Gil y Enes, master mason of the Sé. It is now kept in the Funchal Municipal Museum (Museu Municipal do Funchal). According to Henrique Henriques de Noronha, in his highly interesting and respected *Memorias*, Gil Enes was ‘the architect of the whole work’ of Funchal Cathedral (Sé Catedral do Funchal).
after: Not far from there, at the locality of Serra de Água (‘water sawmill’) in the parish of Arco da Calheta (‘arc of Calheta’), stood the chapel of Our Lady of the Immaculate Conception (*Nossa Senhora da Conceição*), founded by Gonçalo Fernandes in the first half of the 16th century. before: As Pedro Vitorino says, such tombs are very rare in our country, and this specimen in the Cathedral (the Sé), the only one in Madeira, therefore deserves the greatest care in its conservation. It has been claimed, without foundation, that the Fleming João Esmeraldo, who died in 1536, and his wife were buried there. The date 1425 is carved on the lintel of the portal of the chapel of Santa Catarina (St Catherine of Alexandria). It is presumably meant to mark the year in which the settlement of Madeira began, and perhaps the year this chapel was built, although one may conjecture that the stone belonged not to the original building but to a rebuilding later than the date shown. It was the first church built in Madeira, and we dealt with it in a detailed article published in the *Jornal* of 27 October 1942.

before: In the Angústias Cemetery there is a marble stone that was formerly in the old Convent of São Francisco (St Francis of Assisi), bearing this epitaph: ‘Here lies Lois Alvares da Costa, who founded this house in the year 1473, and his son Francisco Alvares da Costa, first *ouvidor* (judicial officer of the donatary or the Crown) and overseer of the royal treasury (*vedor da fazenda*) in these islands of Madeira’. When the church of this convent was demolished in 1865 and many of the bones it contained were moved to the Angústias cemetery, the stone was used to cover these mortal remains, and the following words were inscribed on it: ‘Family vault of the bones exhumed from the former convent and church of São Francisco (to which the original inscription refers), transferred on 2 May 1865’.

before: In 1562 Filipe Gentil de Limoges founded a chapel dedicated to St Philip in the parish (*freguesia*) of Santa Maria Maior, at the locality (*sítio*) that still bears the name of this chapel today. In it is a tombstone with this strange inscription: ‘Grave of the innocents who were tyrannically killed at the Achada of this city 1612’. The foundling nurse (*ama dos expostos*) of the time took in newborn children, killed them and buried them at the locality of the Achada. Their bones were gathered some years later and laid beneath the floor of the chapel, where the stone was placed, as described above.

before: More than thirty years ago, during excavations at the barracks of the 25th Infantry Regiment (*infantaria n.º 25*), the former Jesuit College (*Colégio dos Jesuítas*), a large block of dressed stone (*cantaria*) two and a half metres long was found, bearing the following Latin inscription: ‘*Altissimus creavit medicinam de terra et vir prudens non abhorrebit illam*’, which the translator Pereira de Figueiredo renders thus: ‘It is the Most High who has brought forth all medicines from the earth, and the prudent man will not oppose them’. It is verse 4 of chapter XXXVIII of the Book of Ecclesiasticus in the Old Testament, which praises medicine and those who practise that noble and beneficent profession. In the church of the same College of São João Evangelista there are several chapels that served as mausoleums for their founders and descendants, with their tombstones and inscriptions giving the names of the patrons and the dates of their deaths.

before: Until 1759, the year in which they were expelled from this island, secondary education in our archipelago was entrusted chiefly to the members of the Society of Jesus. In their Colégio (College), where the 27th Infantry Regiment (*regimento de infantaria n.º 27*) is quartered today, the Jesuits taught the humanities in the so-called *Aulas do Pátio* ('Courtyard Classes', the public secondary classes held in the former Jesuit college), which formed part of the same College. There, besides a course in theology, they directed the subjects of Portuguese and Latin, philosophy and rhetoric (see Jesuits).

before: We believe that the ten chairs or subjects established by the decree of 17 November 1836 were not all taught in our lyceum from its foundation, and that they were only actually taught in the years immediately following. We cannot trace the various phases through which teaching at the lyceum of this city has passed across the many reforms of secondary education, because that would demand patient research that the shortness of time and the narrow scope of this work do not allow us to undertake. As we have said, the lyceum was installed in the former *Aulas do Pátio* (‘Courtyard Classes’, the public secondary classes held in the former Jesuit college), which were outbuildings of the Jesuit College with access from Rua dos Ferreiros. It remained there for more than 40 years. In January 1881 it was transferred to a house in the same street, a former manor house of the Vasconcelos de Couto Cardoso entail-holders which later belonged to the Barons of São Pedro, and there it began to operate on the 11th of the same month and year. In January 1914 it moved to the former Bishop’s Palace (*Paço Episcopal*), in the old Rua do Bispo, today Rua Gomes Freire, where it is at present (1921) housed; in 1880 it had also spent some time in outbuildings of the Palácio de São Lourenço (St Lawrence Palace).

before: A tree or shrub of the family *Myricaceae*, common in Madeira. It has glabrous leaves, obovate-lanceolate or oblong-lanceolate and usually serrated, dioecious flowers and drupaceous fruits, red at first and later black, gathered in small clusters because the female flowers adhere to one another. The *faia* yields good firewood, and its stems are used for stakes in many places on the north coast. Its bark is rich in tannin, its wood is dull in colour, sometimes tending to pink, and its fruits, apparently many-seeded and granular, taste pleasant when fully ripe. The European beech (*Fagus silvatica*, L.) is grown in some *quintas* in Monte.

before: The line runs from Pombal, where the main station and the Company’s offices are located, to the Terreiro da Luta, its ‘terminus’. This point lies about one thousand five hundred metres from the parish church of Monte, at an altitude of 850 metres above sea level. The whole line is approximately four kilometres long, with several halts along the route and a station at the locality (*sítio*) of Fonte. The Company runs a service of cars to the various stations and halts, which becomes more frequent on certain days when tourists arrive in greater numbers. At the Terreiro da Luta, at the end of the line, which commands one of the most marvellous panoramas, the Railway Company maintains an excellent restaurant, magnificently appointed, which rivals the best of its kind abroad.

before: On 10 September 1919, shortly after 6 p.m., the boiler of one of the Monte Railway’s locomotives exploded violently as the train was passing between Levada and Livramento on its way up. Because of this disaster, journeys to Monte were suspended until 1 February 1920, which did considerable harm to the Company’s interests.

before: There was once in the parish (*freguesia*) of Monte a chapel dedicated to Nossa Senhora da Conceição, founded by Tristão de França Bettencourt in a year unknown to us. In 1906 a chapel with the same patron saint was built in the Largo das Babosas, in the same parish. It was founded to commemorate the jubilee celebrations held in Madeira to mark the fiftieth anniversary of the definition of the dogma of the Immaculate Conception. The main part of these festivities was an imposing and brilliant religious procession that set out from the Cathedral (*Sé Catedral*) and made its way to the Largo da Fonte, in the parish of Monte, where an open-air Mass was celebrated. On that occasion the prelate Dom Manuel Agostinho Barreto delivered one of his most stirring and enthusiastic speeches. It was then that the idea arose of building the Chapel-Monument, which was carried out two years later; the diocesan bishop had first appointed a committee to raise the necessary donations and to direct the construction. Commander João Bernardino Gomes, vice-president of the committee, donated the land for the building of this graceful church and the image of the Virgin that stands on its altar, and there were other generous gifts for the ornamentation and decoration of the chapel. Justice demands that we record here that it was Commander Luís de Bettencourt Miranda who contributed most notably to the construction of the Chapel-Monument. To his diligent and persevering efforts is owed not only the completion of all the work but also the embellishment of the site, which became an exceedingly picturesque spot and an obligatory place to visit for all who go to the enchanting, paradisal resort of Monte. The pamphlet *Nossa Senhora do Monte*, by Father Joaquim Plácido Pereira, contains a detailed account of the jubilee celebrations and the founding of this chapel.

before: On the property he owned in the parish of São Roque, Canon António Lopes de Andrade founded in 1700 a chapel dedicated to Nossa Senhora da Conceição, its deed of endowment being dated 8 July of the same year. before: Around the middle of the 15th century João Gonçalves Zarco donated some land beside the chapel of São Paulo (St Paul the Apostle) for the foundation of a hospital, which was built at the people’s expense around 1469. It was the second charitable institution the archipelago had. This hospital remained there only a few years before it was moved to the parish (*freguesia*) of Santa Maria Maior and placed in the care of the confraternity of the Misericórdia (Holy House of Mercy, a lay charitable brotherhood), which was then founded in this city and later established itself in the towns of Machico, Santa Cruz, Calheta and Porto Santo. We shall deal more fully with the hospital, which later moved to the building it occupies today, and with the Misericórdias of Funchal and of the towns in the article Misericórdias. We have already devoted a separate article in this Elucidário to the hospital of São Lázaro, whose foundation dates from the beginning of the 16th century. The mental hospital, the Manicómio Câmara Pestana, will be dealt with elsewhere in this work.

before: Referring to this chapel, Frutuoso says: ‘... there is a church of Nossa Senhora das Neves (Our Lady of the Snows), within sight of Funchal, on a headland called Garajau, one *légua* before reaching the city.’ It is very old and one of the few 16th-century chapels still standing, although it has undergone some alterations over time. It was founded by João Afonso Mealheiro and his wife Catarina de Sá. Speaking of him, Dr Rodrigues de Azevedo says: ‘... he was one of the first settlers of the island of Madeira, and held a *sesmaria* (royal land grant to settlers on condition of cultivation) at Ribeira Seca, in São Gonçalo, as far as Caniço. before: Bodies of basaltic nature, sometimes rounded, sometimes oblong and tapering at the ends, and almost always marked with parallel longitudinal grooves. They are projectiles hurled into the air long ago by volcanic activity that ceased many centuries ago. They are commonly found, sometimes loose and sometimes embedded, on the slopes of the most recent volcanic cones in the low-lying parts of Madeira and on the other islands of the archipelago. Lodged in the tuffs of these slopes, alongside the volcanic bombs, are other basalt bodies, elongated and twisted like ropes. Although these share the same volcanic origin, they were perhaps formed in a different way from the bombs proper. Characteristic specimens of both appear in many localities, among them Porto do Moniz, São Martinho, Garajau, Caniçal, Porto Santo and Selvagem Grande.

before: A very common shrub on Madeira, which also occurs on the island of Porto Santo. It belongs to the family Leguminosae, subfamily Papilionaceae, and has trifoliate leaves with very small leaflets, yellow flowers and strongly compressed pods, ciliate along the margins. Broom is widely used to manure the land, and its branches are made into baskets, hampers (*gigos*) and other small articles. This craft already existed on the island at the time when the *Saudades da Terra* was written.

before: The great poet Bulhão Pato, writing about Jacinto Sant'Ana in his *Memorias*, refers to the Viscountess of Nogueiras in the following terms: ‘I met Sant'Ana’s mother, the Viscountess of Nogueiras, Dona Matilde, when I was twenty, during some months I spent in Madeira with a childhood friend, the Count of Carvalhal. ‘She was then in the prime of life. Education, character, beauty of face and grace of figure, distinction in everything, and a superior talent made this lady one of the most enchanting beings I have ever known’! ‘She composed verses of admirable delicacy and feeling. She wrote delightful prose. In a wider milieu she would have been a writer of the first rank. Sant'Ana adored his mother, and how often I saw that fearless, impetuous man weeping like a child as he read her letters, which he then kept in a sacred casket with the fervour of the purest love.’ The illustrious lady outlived by one year her son, who died as Portugal’s minister in Washington, but her granddaughters, out of compassion, hid the fatal news from her, and she died without having learnt of it, on 23 December 1888, at the advanced age of 83.

before: From what has been said, it can be seen that from 1924 onwards the hospital services for the mentally ill underwent a remarkable transformation. This was not only because the male patients were housed in the Casa de Saúde do Trapiche, leaving the building of the Manicómio Câmara Pestana reserved solely for female patients, but also because of the great improvement in the treatment of the inmates. In both establishments this treatment became truly exemplary, and it need fear no comparison with similar institutions in our country.

before: The idea of setting up a hospital for the insane in the houses at Trapiche predates the founding of the Manicómio Câmara Pestana. It came from the diocesan bishop, Dom Manuel Agostinho Barreto, who made the most diligent and persistent efforts to bring it about. He persuaded the owner to cede the *quinta* (country estate) intended for that purpose and pressed the Brothers of São João de Deus to take charge of the asylum that was to be founded. His efforts were not successful at the time, for serious difficulties arose that could not be overcome. It should be clearly stressed that he ardently wished to endow this archipelago with a model hospital for the insane, and worked towards that end with the greatest dedication and enthusiasm. This is one more title of glory adding lustre to his eminent qualities as a benefactor and apostolic prelate.

before: The Manicómio Câmara Pestana was created in 1906, and Dom Manuel Barreto still considered the founding of the Trapiche institution necessary, foreseeing that in the near future this further hospital would become absolutely indispensable. Around that time, and perhaps even earlier, some Brothers of São João de Deus, who had come to Madeira more than once to collect alms for the hospitals they maintained on the mainland, recognised how useful and fruitful their work could be on this island. Around that time, and perhaps even earlier, some Brothers of São João de Deus, who had come to Madeira more than once to collect alms for the hospitals they maintained on the mainland, recognised how useful and fruitful their work could be on this island. They had in mind the considerable number of patients who needed to be admitted under the conditions required by science and in keeping with the precepts of true Christian charity.

before: Around 1920 there was talk of handing the management of the Manicómio Câmara Pestana over to the Brothers of São João de Deus, which caused a great outcry in the press and at the sessions of the District General Council (*Junta Geral*). Meanwhile, the old idea of founding the hospital at Trapiche was taking shape. The diocesan prelate, Dom António Manuel Pereira Ribeiro, gave it his most unconditional support, and the dedication and selflessness of Dr João Francisco de Almada, combined with the well-directed efforts of some Brothers of São João de Deus, did the rest. The work would soon be a tangible reality. At the beginning of June 1922 the Brothers of São João de Deus occupied the houses of the Trapiche *quinta*. The installation was more than rudimentary, with difficulties arising on every side and putting the poor brothers’ spirit of self-denial and sacrifice to a severe test. They did not lack courage, and at once took in a few patients from this parish (*freguesia*), none of them insane. Their crusade of good works had begun.

before: In May 1924 the question of transferring the insane from the Manicómio Câmara Pestana to the Casa de Saúde do Trapiche was raised in the General Council. Within that body attention was drawn not only to the inadequate nursing, the cramped premises and the brutal and inhuman treatment given to the patients, but also to scandals of every kind occurring inside that ‘Bastille’, as the asylum at the Quinta do Rochedo was then called. The transfer of the patients to the Trapiche hospital had become absolutely imperative. The chief champion of this idea was Dr Domingos Réis Costa. Supported by the president of the General Council, Dr Vasco Gonçalves Marques, and by other members, he advocated with the greatest enthusiasm, both at the sessions of this administrative body and in the local press, the immediate admission of the asylum’s patients to the Casa de Saúde of the Brothers of São João de Deus. The transfer took place on 21 May 1924, when 38 male insane patients were moved from the Quinta do Rochedo to the Trapiche *quinta*. A great work of humanity had been accomplished.

before: In 1778, aged 13, Pimenta de Aguiar left for Lisbon to enrol at the Colégio dos Nobres; it is not known whether or not he completed his studies there. In 1785 he went to Paris, where for some years he followed the course in arts and sciences. He later abandoned his studies to take his chances in war, taking part in the country’s internal revolts around 1790 or 1791. He always showed great daring and courage, and for this he attained the rank of captain and the Cross of the Legion of Honour. When the war was over and he had obtained his discharge from military service, he returned to his homeland and devoted himself chiefly to study and to his literary interests. In 1816 he published his first tragedy, which he entitled *Virgínia*, and he brought out his last work in 1820. He was remarkably prolific, for in so short a period he printed ten tragedies, all of them of some length. In order of publication, they are entitled *Virginia*, *Os Dois Irmãos Inimigos*, *D. João I*, *Arria*, *Destruição de Jerusalém*, *D. Sebastião em Africa*, *Conquista do Peru*, *Eudoxia Liciana*, *Morte de Socrates* and *Carácter dos Lusitanos*. After 1820, following a period of such literary activity, there is no record of his publishing any further writings, and we do not know to what to attribute this sudden and complete break in his work. We do not know whether he devoted himself to other literary genres besides tragedy; it is recorded only, on the testimony of Inocêncio, that he left some unpublished works. As befits tragedy, and in imitation of the Greek and French tragedians, Pimenta de Aguiar wrote all his compositions in verse, revealing himself as an inspired poet who combined loftiness of thought with beauty of form.

before: It seems that the origin of this parish’s name should be traced to a plant called *tábua*. The names Tabua and Tabuaço were given to places where that plant grew in abundance, and perhaps for the same reason the word Tábua appears several times in Brazilian chorography. Botany knows *Typha angustifolia* and *Typha latifolia*. Although these plants are not found on the island at present, the Madeiran flora has undergone appreciable changes, partly caused by man, so it is reasonable to suppose that in ancient times these plants, or one of them, grew within the area of this parish (*freguesia*). A species of *Typha* is found in the Canary Islands, so it would not be surprising if the genus had been represented in Madeira. In the locality (*sítio*) of Lugar de Baixo and at Tábua there grows a plant, *Cyperus laevigatus*, that is not found anywhere else in Madeira. Might the first settlers have confused this plant with the *tábua*, even though the two belong to species of different families? This too is possible, for it is reasonable to assume that Zarco and his companions were not distinguished for their learning in botanical matters.

before: We do not know where the seat of the parish was established when it was created. We conjecture that a chapel of the Santíssima Trindade (Holy Trinity) already stood there and that the seat of the new parish (*freguesia*) was installed in it, as generally happened throughout the diocese in the early days of colonisation. It was no doubt a chapel of modest proportions, which must have undergone various repairs and perhaps enlargements until a church of more ample dimensions was built. The building that served as the parish church before the present one was destroyed by a flash flood (*aluvião*). It stood opposite the chapel of Nossa Senhora da Conceição (Our Lady of the Immaculate Conception), and traces of the original building can still be seen on the site. An order of the Council of the Treasury (*Conselho da Fazenda*) dated 22 October 1675 decreed that a new church be built. However, it seems that the work either did not begin at once or proceeded very slowly, for on the façade of the church one reads the inscription ‘Rei Dom Pedro – 1696’ (King Dom Pedro), which is certainly the date of the building’s completion.

before: Of this parish, Dr Gaspar Frutuoso wrote in 1590: ‘Half a *légua* from Ribeira Brava lies Ribeira da Tábua, with a parish of almost thirty households (*fogos*, literally ‘hearths’). It once had two sugar mills and has many vineyards, canes and fruits, but its wine is like that of its neighbour Ribeira Brava. From this Ribeira da Tábua come the Medeiros, a noble and honourable people.’ The annotator of the *Saudades* rightly observes that at that time this parish had more than 100 households and not merely 30, as is clearly deduced from the royal decrees concerning the parish stipends which are cited there.

before: This Madeiran laurel was still to be found in many valleys and ravines in the north and centre of the island, and it is cultivated on several *quintas* in Camacha and Santo António da Serra. before: The *barbusano* is found at various points on the north coast of the island between Seixal and Boa Ventura, at São Gonçalo, in Curral das Freiras, on the Levada do Bom Sucesso, etc., and it is the member of the laurel family best suited to the coastal region. Frutuoso mentions it on Porto Santo, where it now seems to be completely extinct. It is widely cultivated in the *quintas* of Funchal and Monte, where it reaches 30 and 35 metres in height, whereas outside these localities it seldom exceeds 20 metres. It flowers from November to March and generally fruits from January to April.

before: The laurel is a species peculiar to Madeira and the Canary Islands; the Azorean tree referred to by Watson and by Meissner as *Laurus canariensis* of Webb is *Persea azorica* of Seubert. The small laurel of Portugal and the Mediterranean region (*Laurus nobilis*) is quite close to the Madeiran tree, which today forms a species distinct from it, owing to geographical isolation and climatic influences, important factors in the separation of systematic forms.

before: This is the tomb said to be that of João Gonçalves Zarco, and it is reproduced as such in engravings in many works, chiefly foreign ones. It is worth mentioning here that the discoverer was buried beside the altar steps of the chancel. An old manuscript states ‘that the work was so arranged that Zarco’s grave lay in the middle of the chancel, with a stone tomb above it so tall that it made it singularly venerable and imposing’. It is said that many years later the nuns obtained the removal of the showy mausoleum, which blocked their view of the altar, and it was perhaps on that occasion that the ashes of the discoverer of Madeira were transferred to the family vault of his son-in-law Martim Mendes de Vasconcelos. It is certain that in March 1919, when the floorboards of the chancel of the church of Santa Clara were lifted, only the tombstones of the second, third and fifth captain-donataries of Funchal were found. Had the mortal remains of Gonçalves Zarco lain there, the gravestone of his tomb would probably have been discovered. But was the transfer really made? And when did it take place? We do not know.

before: He was born in Funchal in 1843, the son of José Figueira da Silva, and attended the lyceum (state secondary school) of this city. He then went to Coimbra, where he enrolled in the faculties of mathematics and philosophy of the University. Having fallen ill after a few months, he returned to Funchal, going back to Coimbra only the following year, not to continue the studies he had begun but to enrol in the Faculty of Law. He did not complete that course either, because his lung complaints worsened in that city. As his native air did not restore his health, he travelled to the United States, where he had an uncle of some means. He got on so well in that country that he decided to stay there, and some time later he enrolled in a school of medicine, completing the course with the highest distinction. For many years he practised his profession in the city of Brooklyn, where he was highly regarded for his learning and tact as a physician. He still lives there, although he gave up practice some years ago. He published various articles in American medical journals, especially in New York, and while he lived in Madeira he contributed to some local newspapers. He was also one of the authors of the *Guyaneida* (see that entry), a mock-heroic poem that was never printed, but of which copies are held by various people in Funchal.

before: She arrived in Madeira with the former Emperor of Austria, Emperor Charles I, on 19 November 1921, at about half past ten in the morning, aboard the British cruiser *Cardiff*. The couple landed at the Pontinha and went from there to the ‘Vila Vitoria’, where they took up residence. In January 1922 the former Empress left the island to fetch her children, who were being educated in Switzerland. She returned on 2 February with the princes Francisco Oto, Adelaide Maria, Roberto Carlos and Carlos Luís, and from the 18th of that month the whole family lived in the parish (*freguesia*) of Monte, at the *quinta* (country estate) of the banker Luís da Rocha Machado.

before: About 10 kilometres from the city and roughly seven from the Parish Church of Monte, but within the bounds of the parish (*freguesia*) of Camacha, stands the finest mountain shelter in our uplands. It is called the Casa do Poiso, because it lies at the well-known locality of the same name. The Poiso is a much-travelled spot, since the road that crosses it links Funchal with several parishes in the north of Madeira. As the place is very exposed and subject to frequent gales, the worthy civil governor José Silvestre Ribeiro had a mountain shelter for travellers built here in 1850. It has rendered the most notable services and saved many of those who passed that way from certain death. The old road across this spot, which connects it with the charming and much-visited locality of Ribeiro Frio and several northern parishes, has been considerably improved, and regular motor-car services have been established between Funchal, the Poiso and Ribeiro Frio. There is also a road, already used by motor cars, between the Poiso and the pleasant resort of Santo da Serra, and it is believed that before long it will be possible to reach the parish of Santana. The Casa de Abrigo do Poiso is equipped with a telephone booth. We have already given a detailed account of the excellent services it provides, and of its foundation, on p. 195 of vol. I of this work.

before: Forty-one native ferns and 4 naturalised ones are known in the Madeira archipelago; these 45 species comprise 1 Cyatheacea, 3 Hymenophyllaceae, 40 Polypodiaceae and 1 Ophioglossacea. Of the 40 Polypodiaceae, 36 are native and 4 naturalised. *Dicksonia culcita*, Herit. (*feto abrum*), is a beautiful Cyatheacea that is common only in the Montado dos Pessegueiros; *Davallia canariensis* (*cabrinha*), *Adiantum reniforme*, *Pteris arguta*, *Pteridium aquilinum* (bracken), *Woodwardia radicans* (*feto de botão*), *Athyrium Filix-foemina*, *Asplenium Adianthum-nigrum*, *Polystichum aculeatum*, *Nephrodium Filix-mas*, etc. etc., are Polypodiaceae common in Madeira. Complete lists of the ferns of the Madeira archipelago are given in the *Flora do Arquipelago da Madeira* by C. A. Meneses (Funchal, 1914) and in *Madeira Ferns* by the same author (Funchal, 1906).

before: Pedro Figueira, a native of the island of Faial and son of João Figueira and Aldonça Fernandes, was one of the first on this island to bear this surname, having settled here around 1500. One of his sons, named Manuel Figueira, founded an entail on this island. Dr Álvaro de Azevedo gives these men the name Figueiró, but in various books of nobility we have found the surname Figueira applied to the individuals mentioned above; the same commentator on the *Saudades* adds that he does not know who first introduced this surname to the island. It is certain that Álvaro Figueira was also one of the first settlers of Madeira and held land by *sesmaria* (royal land grant to settlers on condition of cultivation) in Câmara de Lobos.

before: We have scant information for the biography of this Madeiran. He was a bachelor (*bacharel*, university graduate) in theology and served as acting chaplain of the church of São Tiago Menor (St James the Less), and later as vicar in the town (*vila*) of Santa Cruz. In 1811 he was imprisoned on the orders of the cathedral chapter of Funchal Cathedral (*Sé*), following a complaint brought against him by the ordinary judge (*juiz ordinário*, locally elected lay judge) of the same town. He edited the second newspaper to be published here in Madeira, the *Pregador Imparcial da Verdade, da Justiça e da Lei*, which first appeared in February 1823. Although his political ideas differed from those of José Agostinho de Macedo, he was nonetheless a distinguished disciple of his in the violence of his language and the unruliness of his phrasing, methods he knew how to imitate in the writings he left us. Prominent among these is a pamphlet printed in London in 1825, which is extremely rare and bears the following extravagant title: *O Tramista Descoberto! Converça do cónego Francisco B-r-o, da cidade do Funchal, com o seu moço Simão Caraça, que foi estudante e servio de economo, por alguns anos, em hum beneficio da Igreja da Ponta do Sol da ilha da Madeira, ouvida pelo padre João Vicente do O-v-a no pateo do mesmo cónego*. It is a booklet of 98 pages, riddled with typographical errors, which deals mainly with the governor of Madeira, Sebastião Xavier Botelho. It also contains unflattering references to the author himself, who hides behind anonymity and in this way placed himself further beyond the suspicions that might fall upon him.

before: Because of the intemperate language of his writings, and for other reasons unknown to us, he drew upon himself the hostility of powerful figures in Funchal. This culminated in a sensational incident on 9 February 1822, which caused the greatest scandal here in Madeira and even had wide repercussions in the Kingdom (*reino*, i.e. mainland Portugal). Some officers, cadets and sergeants of the island’s artillery battalion went to the residence of Dr Espínola de Macedo, in the old Rua da Conceição, dragged him violently from it and took him to the pillory (*pelourinho*, stone column symbolising municipal jurisdiction). There, in broad daylight and in view of many people, says a contemporary account, ‘they flogged him, and he was beaten and mocked’. The perpetrators of the assault were arrested and tried, and were sentenced to severe terms of imprisonment and penal exile (degredo). They were saved, however, by the advent of absolutist government, which restored them to liberty.

before: He was born in the parish (*freguesia*) of Ponta do Sol in the first quarter of the 16th century, the son of Dom João Henriques and Dona Filipa de Noronha. He was a close relative of Father Luís Gonçalves da Câmara (see that entry), the celebrated tutor of King Sebastian, and was descended from João Gonçalves Zarco, the illustrious discoverer of Madeira. He studied canon law in Paris and Coimbra, and was the first rector of the University of Évora. He joined the Society of Jesus while its founder was still alive, maintaining close ties of friendship with him and receiving from him directly marks of the highest regard and esteem. Within his order he held the most senior posts, such as rector of the colleges of Coimbra and Évora, provincial, delegate in Rome, etc. For many years he was confessor and counsellor to the Cardinal-King Henrique, with whom he enjoyed great prestige and influence. In his day he was widely renowned as a man of vast learning and extraordinary talent. His biographers dwell particularly on the most generous and ardent charity with which he was endowed, showing the poor and unfortunate the most exquisite displays of affection and tenderness of which the human heart is capable. He died in Lisbon on 8 April 1589.

before: He was governor and captain-general (capitão-general, military governor of Madeira) of this archipelago in the period from 1677 to 1766. The commentator of *Saudades da Terra* calls him the ‘reformer par excellence’, and he also became known as the ‘Madeiran Pombal’, both because he was appointed to this post by the Marquis of Pombal and because of the reforms he carried out in many public services during that statesman’s government. Among his services, one stands out: he went in person to the island of Porto Santo to enforce the famous royal decree (alvará régio) of the fifths and eighths (*quintos e oitavos*: rent of a fifth or an eighth of the produce), which caused the greatest sensation at the time.

before: (Father Fernando Carlos de Meneses). He was born in the parish (*freguesia*) of Santana on 1 February 1884. He studied at the seminary of this diocese and was ordained priest in 1909. He is at present parish priest of the parish of Porto da Cruz. In the *Correio da Madeira* he published some well-crafted articles containing historical information on several parishes in the north of this island. In the parish archive of Faial he recently discovered the birth record of the illustrious Madeiran João Fernandes Vieira, whose native parish had until then been unknown, despite the painstaking research carried out to that end (1921).

before: This body was created by the decree of 13 August 1913. The purpose of its creation and the scope of its remit are set out in Article 1 of its founding law, as follows: ‘The indispensable repair works on the harbour of refuge at Pontinha, on both the inner and the outer side of the cove; the installation on the same mole (breakwater) of loading and unloading machinery; a link with the customs house by means of an electric railway line; warehouses at the terminus of the line, together with the extension and improvement of the quay at the entrance to the city; the construction of a goods quay opposite the customs house; the opening of a seafront avenue between the quay at the entrance to the city and the eastern end of Campo Almirante Reis; the construction of a small dock between the customs quay and the mouth of the Ribeira de Santa Luzia, with the necessary installations for the island’s small-scale coastal shipping; and, finally, all other complementary installations, such as a customs building, the construction of a maritime disinfection station, of a market, a fish market, a building for the Harbour Master’s Office (*Capitania do Porto*) and the health service, and likewise the maintenance, operation and use of all the installations, works and services that it may set up within the limits of its remit’. The Autonomous Harbour Board was made up of the following: the president of the District General Council (*Junta Geral*), the president of the Funchal Council, the president of the Agricultural Board (*Junta Agrícola*), the director of Public Works of the District, the director of the Customs House, the harbour master, the president of the Commercial Association (*Associação Comercial*), a member specially appointed by the Minister of Development (*Ministro do Fomento*), a member elected by the banking houses, a member elected by the trade associations of wholesale and retail merchants, and a member elected by the Councils of the various municipalities (*concelhos*) of the district. The deputies and senators elected for the constituency of Funchal were also members of this body.

before: With the appointment of a technical director for the works to be carried out in the harbour of Funchal, the Junta Autónoma became far more productive. This was soon shown by the reinforcement of the breakwater protecting the mole (breakwater) between the islet and the Pontinha: between April 1930 and March 1931, 239 blocks with a volume of 4,784 m³ were built, at a cost of 590,000 escudos (Portuguese currency from 1911, = 1,000 réis). This improvement had to be carried out at once, because the great storm of 15 December 1926 had caused serious damage to the mole, putting it at risk of imminent and total destruction. Another improvement that local circumstances demanded even more urgently was the extension of the Cais da Entrada da Cidade (City Entrance Quay). A tender for the contract was opened and closed on 30 October 1930, and the construction was awarded to the firm Nederlandsche Maatschappij Voor Havenwerken for the sum of 4,763,000 escudos. The addition to the quay was to be 80 metres long and 16.4 metres wide, and to consist of five large blocks with a total volume of 3,337 cubic metres. The first block was set in place on 25 June 1932 and the fifth and last in January 1933. (See Quays).

before: Aragão is an old and noble surname in Madeira, although the genealogists do not agree about the individuals who first bore it among us. It is said that the first person here to bear the name was António de Aragão e Teive, who settled on this island around 1500 and was married to Dona Helena de Atouguia. The distinguished Madeiran genealogist José Betencourt da Câmara states that ‘there are two branches of Aragão in Madeira: one descends from Henrique Aragão, who settled in Funchal around 1480; the other comes from Dom Afonso de Aragão, a Neapolitan knight whose real name is unknown, and who, either as a fugitive or as a pilgrim, reached this island around 1470. He lived at Calheta, at the locality (*sítio*) that came to be called after him the Volta do Cavaleiro; he went on to the archipelago of the Azores and died there, having directed that the epitaph placed on his tomb should read: “Here lies the troubled Neapolitan”. He came already married, or married in Madeira, Teresa de Lira: his son, Lopo Dias de Lira Varela, knighted in Africa, was a *moço fidalgo* (junior nobleman of the Royal Household) of the royal household in 1515, and a professed knight of the Order of Christ’.

before: Cape Cantin lies on the coast of Morocco, between two well-known points on the littoral: Mazagan to the north and Mogadouro to the south. It is roughly equidistant from these two coastal towns, about 60 miles from each. This is the point of the African continent whose latitude corresponds most closely to that of the island of Madeira. Cape Cantin lies at 32 33’ N and bears some 47 miles SW. ¼ S. of Cabo Branco do Norte. It rises steeply to 60 metres above the sea, and on its summit stands a small chapel. It is also the point on the African coast nearest to our archipelago, from which it is about 350 miles distant.

before: The disaster of Waterloo had forced Napoleon to abdicate and leave French soil. Despite the doubts and hesitations then troubling his mind, it seems that he had at last taken the firm decision to make for the United States. On 16 July 1815 he embarked at Rochefort, voluntarily going aboard the British naval ship *Bellerophon* and placing himself, trusting and resigned, under the noble and generous hospitality of the English. before: On 22 August they sighted the Madeira archipelago. As they passed between Porto Santo and the Desertas, the *Northumberland*’s doctor pointed out to the Count of Las Casas the resemblance he saw between the latter islands and the bare, barren rocks of St Helena. Napoleon, on the ship’s deck, was gazing absorbed at the steep ravines of the Desertas when the count approached him and passed on the ship’s doctor’s remark. The same thought may well have crossed the emperor’s mind. It is also likely that, on seeing the luxuriant vegetation of Madeira, he reflected on the stark contrast between the incomparable beauty and mild climate of this island and the desolate aridity of St Helena and the conditions of so inhospitable a region. Napoleon said nothing to Las Casas, merely giving a faint smile and a disdainful shrug.

before: This last work contains some curious information on certain points of our history. Speaking of the origin of the name Machico, given to a place on the east coast of Madeira, Mr Brito Rebêlo says: In 1894, on the occasion of the 5th centenary of the birth of Prince Henry the Navigator, I discovered the name of a sailor called Machico, captain of the ship of King Ferdinand I, to whom this king gave some houses... The sailor Machico, or one of his descendants, happened to give his name to that part of Madeira (Machico), and this name gave rise to a thousand conjectures, all equally unfounded. With the disclosure of the fact I have just mentioned, it was established that Machico was the name of a sailor, and so all the disputes over the name ceased, after having given rise to numerous dissertations and lectures in foreign geographical societies and in the Lisbon Geographical Society (*Sociedade de Geografia de Lisboa*).

before: Mr Rebelo further declares that what Frutuoso relates on p. 166 of the *Saudades da Terra* about the punishment inflicted on Tristão Barradas, a man held to be a *fidalgo* (nobleman of the lesser nobility), is false. He states that this man was called Diogo, not Tristão, and that he was not shackled with a fetter and set to grind in a flour mill, but seized by the hands and mutilated on the orders of Tristão Vaz, for having abused the hospitality Tristão Vaz had shown him. before: ‘It is known that Madeira lies in the region of the great ocean currents that flow through the liquid part of our planet. From the very beginning, ever since the discovery of Madeira, it was noticed that ships sailing from this island towards the Canaries were imperceptibly carried from N. to W. The current setting towards SSW ran at 12 to 16 miles a day, and was attributed to the action of the wind. On the north coast of Madeira, and especially at Porto da Cruz, the sea sometimes brought unknown fruits, which were supposed to come from the W. The temperature found in the waters seemed to follow persistent laws and phenomena. Since the inhabitants of Madeira included seafarers and men who knew the sea, these facts did not escape them, and it is even believed that Christopher Columbus was led by them to conjecture that there must be lands to the west from which those samples of fruit came.

before: Of the three small islands that make up the Desertas group, the most important and the largest in area is the one called Deserta Grande, or simply Deserta. Running roughly north to south lie the Ilhéu Chão (Flat Islet), the Deserta Grande and the Bugio, separated from one another by narrow channels navigable only by small boats. ‘The Deserta Grande (*Dic. Univ. Port.* II), so called because it is the largest of them, measures seven and a third miles, or thirteen and a half kilometres, in length by one and a third miles, or almost two and a half kilometres, in width. It is separated from each of those two islets by narrow straits or channels through which only boats can pass. All around it... steep rocks rise from the sea, and it is accessible only at a small landing place to the west, from which a narrow, winding gully climbs to the top, which is almost flat. Of the three Desertas, this is the only one that has drinking water, though brackish, and that from a single, meagre spring.’ On this upland there is a small plain, crossed in part by a valley called Pedregal, and there a rise of about 480 m in altitude stands out.

before: Visitors to the Deserta Grande generally land at Porto da Castanheira or to the west of Ponta do Norte. From either of these points it is not difficult to reach the interior of the island, which is more or less flat on top, but where, because of the livestock and the lack of water, no cereals or other useful plants are now grown. before: An inhabited locality (*sítio*) in the parish (*freguesia*) of São Jorge. There was once a small chapel there dedicated to Nossa Senhora da Piedade, built in the last quarter of the 18th century by Father Matias Jorge Jardim. The locality formed part of an entailed estate (*morgadio*) founded by Jorge Pinto in 1559. Its last administrator was the Azorean Laureano da Câmara Falcão, known as the *morgado* of Ilha, who some decades ago sold these lands to their tenant farmers. The locality takes its name from the fact that it is encircled by the stream, which forks and then rejoins itself at a single point.

before: Of the other municipal councils of the archipelago, that of Machico has the richest and most valuable archive, because it was the seat of a captaincy which, in the early days of colonisation, rivalled that of Funchal in importance and prosperity and, according to some, even surpassed it. The first volume of this archive is missing. According to Dr Rodrigues Azevedo it was the most precious, and after being officially requested many years ago by the civil government it never returned to where it came from. It has surely been lost for ever, for it could not be found in that department when the Machico Council reclaimed it, despite the efforts made to that end. The Municipal Council of Calheta also held important documents, among which there would certainly have been the record of the decree raising this place to the status of town (*vila*), whose exact date is unknown. However, a flood there around the middle of the 18th century completely destroyed the whole archive, and so the most precious materials for the history of that town and municipality were lost. We have not had the opportunity to examine the archives of the Councils of Santa Cruz and Ponta do Sol, but we are told that they contain documents worth consulting, of interest not only to the history of those places but to that of the whole archipelago. The archive of the Captaincy of Porto Santo and of its parish must also have been valuable, but the various pirate raids on that island, which more than once set fire to the council house and the parish church, completely destroyed all the documents there. The *Anais* of that municipality (*concelho*) record that the Council’s books were destroyed at the beginning of the 17th century and those of the parish archive in 1690.

before: The archive of the episcopal chamber of this diocese ought to be very important, not only for the history of this bishopric but also for the history of our Church overseas. Funchal was the seat of our first overseas bishopric and also of our first archbishopric, which had four suffragan dioceses and whose jurisdiction extended as far as the Far East. Valuable documents must certainly have been archived there, but a fire in the Bishop’s Palace (*Paço Episcopal*) in the third or last quarter of the 17th century destroyed them entirely.

before: Dr Azevedo described the archive of the Chapter of Funchal Cathedral (Sé do Funchal) as rich, but today it has been stripped of its oldest and most important documents. Some twenty years ago a senior official of the Torre do Tombo (National Archives) removed them to that institution on the orders of the central government. There they lie in a *mare magnum* of thousands of codices and loose documents, with no order or cataloguing whatsoever, and today it is absolutely impossible to consult them. It would have been better had they remained in the archive of the Cathedral, where they had been carefully kept for several hundred years.

before: It remains for us to give a few biographical details of this illustrious fellow countryman of ours. He was born in the parish (*freguesia*) of Santa Maria Maior in this city on 2 April 1820, the son of Francisco João Moniz, a senior official of the Treasury Board (*Junta da Fazenda*), and of Dona Ana Foster Moniz. In 1828, when he was only 8 years old, he went to Rio de Janeiro with his father. His father had been elected deputy for Madeira to the constituent Cortes (Portuguese parliament) that sat from 1821 to 1822 and professed the principles of the Porto revolution, so he was forced to leave the country when Miguel I proclaimed himself absolute king in 1828.

before: The discovery of our archipelago is the great and undying monument that truly marks the auspicious beginning of the wondrous odyssey the Portuguese undertook across unknown seas. It must therefore be especially remembered that the small island of Porto Santo was the first maritime haven at which those daring navigators made landfall, the glorious starting point of one of the most remarkable events in the whole history of our country. This circumstance alone would be enough for the island to be regarded as the firstborn and beloved daughter of Portugal, deserving the most active and valuable protection from the mother country – which, in reality, has not always been forthcoming. As to its discovery, what was set out at some length on pp. 351–356 of vol. I of this *Elucidário*, in the treatment of the discovery of the archipelago, applies in full.

before: The municipality of Ribeira Brava is the most recently created. It has existed for only nine years (1921), for it was created in 1914. Its formal inauguration took place on 2 August of that year. It is made up of the parishes (*freguesia*) of Ribeira Brava, Serra de Água and Tabua, detached from the municipality of Ponta do Sol, and the parish of Campanário, separated from the municipality of Câmara de Lobos. Its population is 12,800 inhabitants. Its arms show the small fort of São Bento, which stands at the entrance to the settlement, on the street leading to the quay.

before: The locality (*sítio*) known as Lugar, being the most populous and busiest in the parish (*freguesia*), adjoining the landing place and in easy and frequent communication with the other localities, could not fail to be chosen as the seat of the new municipality (*concelho*) and the new town (*vila*). The town takes in the said locality of Lugar together with those of Calvário, Bagaceira and Moinhos. Within its area stand the town hall and the other municipal offices, the parish church, two state primary schools, one for each sex, the post and telegraph office and the telephone exchange, the civil registry office, the revenue guard post (*posto fiscal*), the seat of a medical district (*partido médico*, served by a municipal doctor), the parish cemetery, the landing quay, the small fort of São Bento, the ruins of the church of the former convent of Franciscan friars, etc. Some forty years ago the now defunct Agricultural Board (*Junta Agrícola*) set up an experimental agricultural station here; of those established in Madeira at that time, it is perhaps the only one that has been of any practical use. When this district was divided into two primary-education school districts, western and eastern, one of them had its seat at Ribeira Brava. Shortly afterwards the seat was transferred to the city of Funchal, and that district was abolished in 1923.

before: In 1936 the need was recognised to revise the 1914 triangulation, rebuild some destroyed survey markers, triangulate Porto Santo and the Desertas and link the islands of the archipelago, with the immediate aim of a chorographic survey of Porto Santo and the Desertas and a hydrographic survey of the Madeira archipelago. In this new work, carried out in 1936 by the Geographical and Cadastral Institute, some vertices of the old 1914 triangulation were abandoned. At the same time, working in parallel with the Institute, the Hydrographic Mission extended the triangulation to the cliff line and to the landing places where hydrographic plans were surveyed.

before: He was the son of António Soares Felgueiras and Dona Ana de Oliveira, and was born in the parish (*freguesia*) of Porto da Cruz on 23 May 1790. He came to Funchal at a tender age to live in the house of his godfather, Canon Caetano Alberto de Araújo, and in this city he completed his preparatory studies in the humanities and the theology course at the Diocesan Seminary of Funchal (*Seminário Diocesano do Funchal*). He was ordained priest and went straight to Coimbra, where he enrolled in the faculty of law, graduating in 1820 or shortly afterwards. He was practising as a lawyer in Funchal and holding the chair of Latin when, in 1826, he was elected deputy for Madeira. before: Shortly afterwards, when the great parliamentarian António Cândido was Minister of the Kingdom (*reino*, i.e. mainland Portugal), the government decided to send a physician abroad to study the much-vaunted results of Koch’s tuberculin, which had even been called the greatest discovery of recent centuries. Let us see what a newspaper of the time said on the matter: ‘Here, the excitement had spread with an intensity proportional to the large number of consumptives who loom so large in our pathology; and so great and so intense was the stir that it reached even the highest spheres of the state, as a rule indifferent to these petty matters of life or death. It must be said that the emotion of so many people condemned to death could not have found a better conductor to those high spheres than the artistic spirit of the then Minister of the Kingdom. António Cândido was the very negation of the politician, the finest praise that can be given to anyone who has ever taken part in our politics. It had been decided to send someone to Paris or Berlin to establish what was positive in the announced marvel. On the appointment, António Cândido consulted two men eminent for their standing in our medical world and for their worthy and respected characters, Professors Sousa Martins and Ferraz de Macedo. Only one name was put forward: that of Pestana. And despite the friction that arose, in January 1891 Pestana left for Paris, charged with studying bacteriology wherever and however he wished, and with establishing what was known of Koch’s alleged discovery.

before: He was born in Machico on 5 October 1832 and died in Funchal on 1 April 1910. For more than thirty years he served as librarian of the Funchal municipal library, and he was also acting teacher of Portuguese language and literature at the central lyceum (state secondary school) of this city. Although he died almost forgotten, he was a distinguished educator and a man of uncommon talent and great learning. He assisted the distinguished jurist Álvaro Rodrigues de Azevedo (see that entry) in interpreting and correcting Frutuoso’s manuscript entitled *As Saudades da Terra*, and he contributed to several of the island’s newspapers. He left a rich library, which the British subjects W. and A. Reid bought for two thousand escudos (Portuguese currency from 1911, = 1,000 réis) and presented to the Municipal Council (*Câmara Municipal*) of Funchal. The former Rua das Cruzes in Funchal now bears the name of João Joaquim de Freitas. (1921).

before: He was born in Funchal on 21 November 1892, the son of João Isidoro de Araújo Figueira and Dona Virgínia Henriques de Araújo. He completed the course at our lyceum (state secondary school) in 1909 and graduated from the Faculty of Law of the University of Coimbra in 1914. While a student at the University he contributed extensively to various newspapers on the mainland and was one of the founders of the *Imparcial*, published in Coimbra. For some years he was on the editorial board of the *Diário da Madeira*, and he has contributed to other Madeiran newspapers. He practises law and published a pamphlet entitled *Acção de expropriação do Montado do Barreiro requerida pela Câmara Municipal do Funchal contra os proprietários do mesmo Montado*, Funchal, 1917, 19 pp. He is a permanent teacher at the ‘António Augusto de Aguiar’ Industrial and Commercial School and has carried out various public service commissions, being at present (1939) president of the board of the Associação Comercial do Funchal. He was elected deputy for Madeira in 1922 and in successive legislatures, and is a member of the present Chamber of Deputies. In 1928 he published in a volume some of the speeches he had made in Parliament, under the title *Trabalhos Parlamentares*.

before: In the parish (*freguesia*) of Santa Cruz, not far from the town (*vila*) of the same name, lies the Lombada de São Pedro, or Lombada de Santa Cruz. It is crossed by the stream likewise called São Pedro, more commonly known as the Ribeira da Boaventura. In the early 16th century João Escorcio Drumond had a chapel built there, dedicated to the apostle St Peter. The great flash flood (*aluvião*) of 9 October 1803 razed it completely, and shortly afterwards it was rebuilt on a site less exposed to the violence of the current.

before: On 10 April 1864 Prince Ferdinand Maximilian accepted the charge of becoming Emperor of Mexico, and as such he was at once proclaimed and recognised. On the 28th of that month and year he called at Madeira with his wife on the way to that country, aboard the Austrian frigate *Novara*, which was accompanied by the French frigate *Themis*. The emperor and empress were paid the honours due to their high rank, and the illustrious travellers graciously returned them by inviting to dinner aboard the *Novara* the diocesan bishop, Dom Patrício Xavier de Moura, the civil governor, the Count of Farrobo, the Count of Carvalhal, the consul Carlo de Bianchi, Dr Luís Pita, etc.

before: A cirripede crustacean of the family Balanidae, relatively common on the coastal rocks of the islands of Madeira and the Selvagens. It is found in certain spots and lives at the low-tide line, preferring places exposed to the heavy pounding of the waves. Although it very rarely appears in the market, it is edible and is rightly prized as a tasty shellfish. To gather it, people use a striking tool called a *craqueira* (iron tool for prising barnacles off rocks), since the shell that covers it is firmly attached to the rock on which it lives.

before: The annotator of the *Saudades* gives this parish as created by the royal decree (alvará régio) of 4 June 1552. What this decree first created was a chaplaincy with cure of souls (capelania-curada), not yet an autonomous parish, which did not correspond to an autonomous parish. The first chaplain held this post together with that of parish priest of São Jorge. Under the said decree, this curate or chaplain had been allotted 8,000 *réis* (old Portuguese money of account; 1$000 = 1,000 réis, 1:000$000 = one conto = 1,000,000 réis) a year for the parish duties of São Jorge, and a *moio* of wheat and a *pipa* (wine cask and measure, c. 400–500 litres) of wine for his service in Santana. The royal decrees of 16 February 1565, 1 March 1577 and 9 June 1581, which we have found cited in the *Índice Geral* of the Treasury Superintendency (Provedoria da Fazenda), always refer to the curate chaplain (*capelão-curado*) and set his emoluments at 12,000 *réis* in cash and a *moio* of wheat, at 20,000 *réis* and at 25,000 *réis* respectively. In the royal decree of 1 December 1588 the priest who performed the parish duties there is already called *vigário-curado* (curate vicar), and he was assigned an annual stipend (*côngrua*) of thirty *alqueires* of wheat and a quarter of wine. It was perhaps from the date of this decree, or a little before, that Santana began to form a truly independent and autonomous parish.

before: The year in which the original chapel of Santana was built is not known. It was the seat of the chaplaincy with cure of souls (capelania-curada), not yet an autonomous parish, and later of the parish, and it underwent various alterations until it was demolished when the present church was built at the end of the 17th century. About this church we find the following information in an article by Father Fernando de Menezes Vaz, published in the *Correio da Madeira* of 10 April 1923: ‘It was built in 1698, the government spending the sum of 1,193,000 *réis* (old Portuguese money of account; 1$000 = 1,000 réis, 1:000$000 = one conto = 1,000,000 réis), and it was repaired 36 years later. The sacristy, built on the north side, was later rebuilt, in 1745, on the south side, as this was the drier spot and the church furnishings and vestments kept better there. The bell-cote was also put up at that time. In the first quarter of the 19th century the church floor was badly damaged, or rather the church had no floor at all, and the people had to carry in bundles of myrtle, which they spread on the ground so that they could kneel. A committee was then formed, made up of Father Marcelino João da Silva, Carlos Frederico Accioli and Lieutenant Francisco António Jardim, to raise donations so that the floor could be laid anew, as was duly done. In the last few years the church has been re-lined, painted and re-floored, and its churchyard and surroundings have been embellished, thanks to the energy and initiative of its present, zealous parish priest, Joaquim Fernandes’.

before: The municipality (*concelho*) and island of Porto Santo have as their seat, or capital, the town (*vila*) of the same name, which is also known as Vila Baleira. This name is certainly very old, but it seems to have been little used, even in the earliest days of colonisation. From the rare references to it that we have found in old documents, we believe that this strange name gradually fell out of use and so, little by little, sank into complete oblivion. Only now and then, and only in official documents written on the island, does one still come across Vila Baleira, perhaps as a vestige of the ancient lineage of its inhabitants and of the old noble traditions of the descendants of Bartolomeu Perestrelo, the first donatary of Porto Santo.

From the rare references to it that we have found in old documents, we believe that this strange name gradually fell out of use and so, little by little, sank into complete oblivion. Only now and then, and only in official documents written on the island, does one still come across Vila Baleira, perhaps as a vestige of the ancient lineage of its inhabitants and of the old noble traditions of the descendants of Bartolomeu Perestrelo, the first donatary of Porto Santo.

before: What is the origin of this name? We do not know. Dr Rodrigues de Azevedo, in note XII to the *Saudades da Terra*, says the following on the subject, word for word: ‘The name Vila Baleira is of unknown origin: but, reflecting that Baleira has the same root, *bal*, as the first form of the surname Perestrello, and combining this element with the ending *eira*, one readily recognises that Villa Baleira is a name signifying that the town of Porto Sancto was founded by Perestrello: it is as if we were to say Villa de Perestrello. The name of the town kept the letters of the original form, whereas the family surname replaced them in the manner we have already seen when we dealt with Bartholomeu Perestrello (note X, p. 446): and they became so different that they seem words foreign to one another, though they are in fact cognate, as has been said. This is a strong presumption that the said town was founded by Bartholomeu Perestrello.’

before: An old chronicle of this Order states that it was the Order which spiritually discovered this archipelago, because some of its members, who accompanied the discoverers, began to perform religious duties on the very day of the first landing at Machico. There they set up an improvised altar and celebrated the holy sacrifice of the Mass, which is said to have taken place on the feast of the Visitation of Our Lady to St Elizabeth, which the Catholic Church celebrates on the second of July. There is no reason to dispute this statement, since it is certain that in the earliest days of the settlement and colonisation of this island it was the Franciscan friars who exercised all the functions of their ministry here. In the chapels of Santa Catarina (St Catherine of Alexandria), São Paulo (St Paul the Apostle), São Sebastião (St Sebastian) and Conceição de Cima (Upper Conception) they carried out all the parochial religious services, certainly until the time when the priests sent by the Order of Christ, to which the archipelago belonged in spiritual matters, took charge of those same services.

before: An inhabited locality (*sítio*) in the parish (*freguesia*) of Ponta do Sol. before: In 1919, after the monarchist revolution at the beginning of that year, new political prisoners came to Funchal. They arrived on the steamer *Africa*, of the Empresa Nacional de Navegação, which had been commissioned as a troop transport. These prisoners, 289 in number, were accompanied by a naval force and landed on 8 May, three days after the *Africa* arrived. They were housed in the Gonçalo Aires Lazaretto. Among the prisoners were the former minister João de Azevedo Coutinho, the former colonel João de Almeida, the Count of Sucena, the Count of Arrochela, the Viscount of Siqueira and João Moreira de Almeida. A force of 30 naval men and 1 sergeant remained in Funchal to guard the Lazaretto, and an infantry detachment commanded by a second lieutenant joined this force for the same purpose. By order of the harbour master, all vessels were forbidden to pass through or remain in the sea area bounded by the Fort of São Tiago (St James the Greater) and Cabo Garajau.

before: Despite these precautions, on 3 June it was discovered that 8 prisoners had disappeared, among them the Count of Sucena. It later emerged that all of them had reached Las Palmas on the motor launch *Glafiberta*, belonging to the sportsman Humberto dos Passos, who had organised the escape. On how the escape took place, we read the following in a newspaper: ‘One fine afternoon, almost all the political prisoners held in the Funchal Lazaretto left the building on the pretext of taking the air and gathered on the strip of beach immediately below it. The guards merely watched them from the windows of the Lazaretto. For a while they sang, frolicked and cheered, and when the uproar was at its height and the guards were distracted by the merriment, a boat sent from the *Glafiberta* approached the beach and unhurriedly picked up the 8 prisoners... Hours later, the motor launch, towed by the *Milano*, belonging to the Blandy firm (which did not know what kind of service had been asked of its tug), sailed towards the Desertas, and later turned south, on course for the Canary Islands’.

before: From 1828 to 1830, that is, while the notorious José Maria Monteiro, nicknamed ‘the Baize’ (*o Baeta*), governed Madeira, the liberals suffered the harshest persecution. It was enough for someone to be accused of being a *malhado* (derogatory nickname for a liberal under the Miguelist regime) for him to be savagely beaten at once by the Miguelite (supporter of the absolutist King Miguel) mob, with no help from the agents of authority. The constables were then a source of disorder. Egged on by the governor, who often went with them on their night patrols, they committed the worst excesses, arresting and beating every constitutionalist who dared to go out into the street. In 1830 there were also constables in Câmara de Lobos.

before: This small and solitary parish (*freguesia*) lies at the far eastern end of Madeira. It is a village of poor fishermen, set between the sheer cliffs that separate it from Machico and the capriciously indented, rugged ground that forms the point of São Lourenço. It may be said to be cut off from the rest of the island, even though the ocean does not divide it, because communications are so difficult. Only in cases of extreme necessity, and only when the state of the sea rules out the sea route, do people travel to the neighbouring parish of Machico, along a narrow footpath cut into the cliff, which is at times sheer and always strewn with the most hazardous and imminent dangers. The inhabitants spend their lives between the toil of fishing, their chief occupation, and the tilling and cultivation of a few plots of land. They live far below even a modest level of comfort, and when a storm breaks and towering waves lash the coast, preventing work at sea, poverty and hunger enter many households and parade there their whole train of horrors. They are a peaceful and orderly people, accustomed to the happy calm of that isolation and tranquillity. They know nothing of the comforts and conveniences of populous centres and so do not envy the pleasures and attractions that such places, where bustle and pleasure hold sway, offer to fortune’s favoured few.

before: Older than Vasco Martins Moniz, but perhaps still his contemporary, was João Teixeira, third son of the discoverer Tristão Vaz Teixeira, the first donatary of Machico. Of him Gaspar Frutuoso says: ‘... he was a great hunter and fond of the chase, and for that reason he had in the town of Machico a hunting reserve (coutada) of his own at Caniçal, so full of game – rabbits, partridges, peacocks and many wild boar – that it is said to have been the best hunting reserve in all Portugal. This is suggested by a letter which is still kept today in the Council of Machico, written by King Manuel I to its officers, in which he earnestly charges them to keep strict watch over the hunting reserve of the sons of the first captain, and to let no one enter it, because he had been told and assured that, should he happen to come to the island, there were no other lands in which he could hunt and chase game but this one of Caniçal and the fields of Santa Catarina’.

before: The seat of the new parish was established in the chapel of São Sebastião (St Sebastian), founded by Garcia Moniz in the first quarter of the 16th century. Around 1594 the same chapel was enlarged or rebuilt, but the earthquake of 1748 left it in such a state of ruin that a contemporary witness says that *there is no remedy but a new building*. The foundation stone of the new church, the present one, was laid on 9 June 1749, and it was solemnly blessed on 13 December 1750. It was built on a site some distance from that of the first church, which still keeps the name of Sítio da Igreja Velha (Old Church).

before: This parish has the chapel of Nossa Senhora da Piedade (Our Lady of Pity), picturesquely set on top of a hill and leaning out over the waters of the ocean. It was built on Monte Gordo, or Monte da Piedade, 4 kilometres from the parish church. This is the moment to mention the unusual procession that is held every year to this chapel. The religious procession leaves the parish church and heads for the beach, where it boards several brightly decorated boats. Closely followed by a considerable number of small sailing craft, it sails to the foot of the hill, where it lands; then comes the arduous climb up the steep slope, ending finally with entry into the small, solitary chapel.

before: ‘To water the sugar cane in this town (*vila*) (Machico) and for Caniçal, a levada (irrigation channel) was brought from so far away that from the place where the water rises to the town it is four and a half leagues or nearly five, on which more than a hundred thousand *cruzados* were spent, because it comes through great mountains and deep ravines; and they say that in building it two peaks of hard rock were bored through, there being no other remedy. Raphael Catanho, a Genoese, with the great spirit he has, like almost all foreigners and above all those of that nation, was the first to begin bringing this water, and afterwards the King ordered it to be completed: and, because of the great cost it entailed, it is no longer used. To this passage of Frutuoso, Father Fernando Augusto de Pontes adds, in his interesting book *Excursões na Madeira*: “this is the very levada that supplies water to the *quinta* (country estate) of Palheiro Ferreiro”. It seems that in former times this parish was notably wooded, and even today, to the north of it, some woods are found, perhaps remnants of the ancient forests.

before: The great flash flood (*aluvião*) of 9 October 1803, regarded as the greatest calamity ever to strike Madeira, of which we have already given a brief account (I-54 ff.), gave rise to the solemn ‘vow’ to place this island and the city of Funchal under the special protection of the Most Holy Virgin, as recorded in the article Patron saints (III-36 ff.). It should be added that this ‘vow’ included in particular the clause choosing Nossa Senhora do Monte as special protectress of the city of Funchal. This was confirmed by an Apostolic Rescript of Pius VII dated 21 July 1804, and the feast of the Patronage of Nossa Senhora do Monte was then instituted, celebrated on 9 October each year with a solemn procession that went from the Cathedral to the parish church of Santa Maria Maior (St Mary Major). The ninth of October was formerly a holy day of obligation, preceded by its own vigil with fasting.

before: At the capture of Arzila and Tangier, two Flemish noblemen, Martim de Leme and António de Leme, natives of the city of Bruges in the former Flanders, distinguished themselves by their bravery and heroism. Their father, Martim de Leme, had sent them to fight under the orders of the King of Portugal, accompanied by a number of men-at-arms armed and equipped at their own expense. The letters patent and coat of arms of 2 November 1471, granted by Afonso V to António de Leme, who was then a knight of the household of Prince Dom João, made honourable mention of this deed. They conferred and ratified the title of nobility he already held in his native land, and gave him as arms ‘on a field of gold five black blackbirds in saltire, without feet or beaks, and for crest one of the blackbirds within a saltire of gold’.

before: Among other children, António de Leme had Martim de Leme, who seems to have been born, like his father, in Flanders. After serving in Portugal and holding high court offices in his homeland, he came to Madeira around 1483, bringing to the Funchal Council letters of recommendation from Prince Dom Fernando, master of the Order of Christ, to which the island then belonged. He was given lands by *sesmaria* (royal land grant to settlers on condition of cultivation) in the parish of Santo António, which he left to his heirs. He died in Funchal and was buried in the Convent of São Francisco (St Francis of Assisi). Martim de Leme married Dona Maria Adão Ferreira, daughter of Adão Gonçalves Ferreira, the first man born on this island, who was himself the son of Gonçalo Aires Ferreira, companion of Zarco in the discovery of Madeira.

before: Of João Teixeira, the third son of Tristão Vaz Teixeira, the annotator of the *Saudades* says that ‘he was a great huntsman and fond of the chase, and for that reason he had in the town (*vila*) of Machico a hunting reserve (coutada) of his own at Caniçal, with so much game – rabbits, partridges, peacocks and many wild boar – that it is affirmed to have been the best hunting reserve in Portugal.
