before: The new governor of the archipelago, Dom Manuel de Portugal e Castro, arrived in Funchal on 26 August 1823, and on 1 September he at once ordered the destruction and levelling of the foundations of the planned monument to the Constitution, which had been laid 19 months earlier amid the greatest enthusiasm and with uncommon splendour and pomp. Dom Manuel de Portugal e Castro gave the act great solemnity and ceremony, so as to make the Madeirans fully aware that any attempt to restore the principles proclaimed by the Porto revolution would be futile. He reported to the government of mainland Portugal in close detail how he had carried out the complete levelling and destruction of the foundations of the monument that was to have been erected: the foundation stone, the silver casket and what it contained – the corresponding record (*auto*), the commemorative medal and the coins of the time placed there – were all entirely ruined and destroyed. (See Constitution of 1821 and Monuments.)

before: Two years later, on 25 April 1828, Prince Miguel, regent of the Kingdom (*reino*, i.e. mainland Portugal), was proclaimed absolute king after the Cortes (Portuguese parliament) had been dissolved. In Madeira absolute government was not proclaimed at once, because José Lúcio Travassos Valdez, the constitutional governor of this archipelago, remained loyal to the principles he represented and prepared to resist the attempts of the Miguelite (supporter of the absolutist King Miguel) troops who sought to seize the island. The article Occupation of Madeira by the Miguelite troops (p. 6 of vol. III) gives a brief account of this resistance and of its failure to prevent the royalist forces from landing.

before: The premises of the Mercado de D. Pedro V, intended especially for the sale of ‘greens and vegetables’, and of the Praça de São Pedro, where all the fish consumed in the city was sold, were becoming very cramped. These weighty circumstances, together with the pressing need to extend the ‘Avenida do Mar’, made it advisable to build new markets in keeping with the ever-growing population, with the most modern and rigorous rules of hygiene, and with the breadth and spaciousness that these important services required. The Funchal Council ventured upon this undertaking and raised a grand building in which these many services all operated under one roof, though in separate, spacious and independent premises, meeting every condition required for the most perfect organisation of those services. It was even claimed to be the finest installation of its kind in the whole country.

before: Dr Álvaro R. de Azevedo, through an evident slip, places this chapel in the parish of São Martinho, when it has certainly always belonged to the parish of Santo António. The mistake may stem from the fact that its founder owned extensive lands in both these parishes, perhaps adjoining one another, so that at some time in the not-so-recent past the chapel may have been regarded as lying indifferently in one parish or the other. It was built at a spot on the boundary between the two parishes and, moreover, the main entrance of the *quinta* (country estate) that surrounded the chapel opened onto the road separating those parishes. These circumstances could easily have misled him and led him to suppose that the little church of Santo Amaro did not lie within the parish of Santo António.

before: Those even moderately read in the Madeiran chronicles know that four noblemen came to this island from the Kingdom (*reino*, i.e. mainland Portugal) with the express purpose of marrying the daughters of the discoverer of Madeira and first captain-donatary (*capitão-donatário*) of Funchal. The third of them, Dona Catarina da Câmara, married Garcia Homem de Sousa, who was the founder of this chapel. The annotator of the *Saudades da Terra* states verbatim: ‘...Santo Amaro, which was founded by Garcia Homem de Souza, son-in-law of Zargo, in 1460 on the great settled estate (*fazenda povoada*) where he had a castellated dwelling.’ Elsewhere the *Saudades* also say of this same Garcia de Souza: ‘...he built the chapel, or strong or castellated house, to defend himself against his brothers-in-law; he was proud and violent’; and they add finally that ‘having quarrels with his brothers-in-law... he built a tower which stands near the Madre de Deus’.

before: What was the Madre de Deus? The original name of the chapel or locality of Santo Amaro? We cannot say. However, according to tradition, and as the learned annotator of the *Saudades da Terra* affirms, it was at Santo Amaro that Garcia Homem de Sousa built the castellated house mentioned in the old chronicles of this archipelago, to defend himself against his brothers-in-law in the bloody struggles he had with them. Indeed, some ruined houses of quite ancient construction still stand there, which are probably the remains of the fortress-like manor house that the proud and turbulent Garcia de Sousa built to shelter from the assaults of his enemies. A pointed-arch doorway of dressed stone (*cantaria*), still to be seen there and apparently bearing the stamp of Manueline-period buildings, ought to be carefully preserved. Traces of an old cistern also remain, and not many years ago the walls of an old tower could likewise still be seen there, all of it apparently of very early construction (1921).

before: Santo Amaro is one of the most important chapels in this bishopric, for its antiquity and historical traditions, for its size, and also for the crowds of worshippers who attend its patronal feast. It seems to us that little remains of its original structure, which underwent successive alterations over time. With the evident aim of isolating it from the rural and urban property within whose grounds it stood, a high wall was built in front of the façade, three or four metres away from it, and joined to the little church by a porch. All this greatly disfigured the front of the building and also considerably spoilt the beauty of the whole. It was probably from this time, which we cannot determine precisely, that the chapel began to be served exclusively through the present entrance, and the passage that opened onto the road to Tangue and Alecrins was closed off. We presume that the administrators of the chapel had relinquished their duties as patrons and left it to the care and management of the parish vestry, in whose charge it has been for many years, and in this way separated it from the rest of the *quinta* or estate on which it had been built.

before: This chapel always remained in the possession of the successors of Garcia Homem de Sousa, and we know that in 1700 the administrator of the entailed property of Santo Amaro was Filipe de Carvalhal Esmeraldo, captain-major (*capitão-mor*, commander of the local militia) of Câmara de Lobos. His immediate successor was his son, José Joaquim de Carvalhal Esmeraldo, who passed it to his son, also named José Joaquim de Carvalhal Esmeraldo. He was succeeded in this entailed administration by his brother Francisco António de Bettencourt Carvalhal Esmeraldo, whose daughter, Dona Isabel Esmeraldo Barbosa de Matos e Câmara, inherited the property and chapel. She bequeathed it to her sister Dona Júlia Esmeraldo, who died on 14 September 1915.

before: We have read somewhere that there is no plausible explanation for the use of the word Estreito, applied to the parishes (*freguesias*) of Estreito da Calheta and Estreito de Câmara de Lobos. We share this opinion. Even if we give the word the meaning of gorge, valley or *profundidade* (deep, roughly circular mountain basin), as some lexicographers would have it, it does not seem to us that the relief of those parishes, taken as a whole, justifies such a name. It is possible that a small locality (*sítio*) or village (*lugar*, settlement rank below a town), with more or less aptness in the use of the term, originally bore the name Estreito, which then spread to the surrounding land and was later extended to designate an entire parish, as happened with other parishes of Madeira. Moreover, in the earliest days of colonisation the naming of the various localities must have been highly arbitrary. In many cases it would have followed only the whim and preference of the early settlers, without regard to the relief and watercourses of the places, or to any other weighty circumstances that might perhaps have arisen. An event of no importance, and sometimes even a minor episode, was reason enough for the name given to a particular locality or village, as certainly happened with the parishes of Fajã da Ovelha, Campanário, Curral das Freiras, etc.

before: As we have already noted, Calheta was one of the oldest places outside Funchal to be subject to early colonisation and farming. We must suppose that the settlement and clearing of the land that later made up the parish of Estreito did not take long. There were one or more “settled farmsteads” (*fazendas povoadas*) there, which formed the original nucleus of the settlement established in this village.

before: The annotator of the *Saudades*, following the old Madeiran genealogies, says that this parish originated in the settled estate (*fazenda povoada*) begun there by André Gonçalves de França, known as the Pole because he was a native of the kingdom of Poland. He came from there to this island around the middle of the 15th century and obtained a great deal of land by *sesmaria* (royal land grant to settlers on condition of cultivation) in what was then the parish of Calheta, land that later belonged to the future parish of Estreito. It was his son João de França who further enlarged the already vast property and, in the words of Dr Álvaro de Azevedo, ‘enhanced it with fine houses and a chapel’. He had the chapel of Nossa Senhora da Graça (Our Lady of Grace) built, in which the new parish was later created and installed. It was also the seat of the entailed estate (*morgadio*) he founded in 1503, one of the oldest entails (*instituições vinculares*) in Madeira. João de França died around 1511 and was buried in the chapel he had founded.

before: The royal decree of Philip II of 20 October 1602 created a curacy (*curato*) in this parish. The chapel of Nossa Senhora da Graça, later converted into the parish church, was built at the end of the 15th century or the beginning of the 16th, and was enlarged, or rather rebuilt, in a year we cannot state precisely. An order of the Council of the Exchequer (*Conselho de Fazenda*) of 20 July 1690 directed that a new church be built; the works were contracted to Salvador Lopes for the sum of 1,395,000 *réis*. The royal decree of the Infanta Dona Catarina, regent of the Kingdom, of 27 June 1705, approved the transfer of the new church to another site, as ordered by the diocesan bishop, Dom José de Sousa de Castelo Branco. But was the new church actually built at that time? It is certain that the present church was built in 1791 and blessed in 1793. Is it likely that two churches were built within less than a century? We do not think so. Above the portico of the present church is a stone tablet bearing the following inscription: *Mariae Patris Filiae Filii Matri Spiritus Sancti Sponsae hoc templum consecravit Aug. Reg. Maria Prima suae piae liberalitatis regio erario administro. Anno MDCCLXXXXI.* (To Mary, Daughter of the Father, Mother of the Son, Spouse of the Holy Spirit, the August Queen Maria I consecrated this church out of her pious liberality, the royal treasury administering it. In the year 1791.)

before: Describing the exploration of the island made by the discoverers in order to divide it into captaincies, Gaspar Frutuoso says: ‘... João Gonsalves Zarco... reaching a height above Câmara de Lobos, marked out there where a church of the Holy Spirit should be built... and all these heights he took for his heirs.’ This chapel, rebuilt more than once, still exists and is in a good state of repair. It was founded by the discoverer of Madeira himself and served for many years as the parish church when the parish (*freguesia*) of Câmara de Lobos was created in 1430. Around 1720 it was rebuilt because of the advanced state of ruin it was in, and in 1908 major repairs were also carried out on it and on the small house attached to it. Although perhaps nothing remains of the original building, the chapel is nonetheless a small historic monument for the municipality (*concelho*) and parish of Câmara de Lobos, recalling the name of the discoverer of Madeira who had it built, and also because it housed the parish when the parish was created, as already stated. In the locality (*sítio*) of Campo de Baixo on the island of Porto Santo stands the chapel of Espírito Santo (Holy Spirit), which is well preserved and where services are held. It is not of recent construction and was completely restored in the first quarter of the 19th century by Captain Sebastião António Drumond.

before: The illustrious annotator of the *Saudades da Terra* tells us that the first parish (*freguesia*) on this island was established in 1430, with its seat at the locality (*sítio*) of Nossa Senhora da Calheta, in the settlement that had grown up there. This seems to us unlikely if we give that word the meaning of a community of settlers with a life of its own, independent from the social and religious point of view. before: Despite his diligent research, the learned annotator of the *Saudades da Terra* was unable to find the document that raised the early settlement of Funchal to a town. On the strength of the weighty arguments he puts forward, based on various documents, 1451 can nevertheless be given as the year of its creation. The same annotator says he examined a manuscript miscellany in the Public Library of Lisbon, in which he found the following: ‘In 1452 Afonso V gave a charter (foral) to the town of Funchal with many privileges, exempting the inhabitants of the whole island from paying excise (*siza*), tolls, produce dues or any of the taxes then levied in the Kingdom’. This transcription corroborates the conclusions reached by Dr Álvaro Rodrigues de Azevedo.

before: The town and original municipality of Funchal took in the former captaincy of the same name and stretched from Ponta da Oliveira along the south and west coasts of Madeira to Ponta do Tristão. Half a century later this area was greatly reduced by the creation of the towns and municipalities of Ponta do Sol and Calheta, the first in 1501 and the second at roughly the same time, as we have noted elsewhere in this *Elucidário*. A little over 50 years after the town of Funchal was created, it was raised to the rank of city, in 1508.

before: As late as 1834 the municipality of Funchal still stretched from the eastern part of the parish of Ponta do Sol to Caniço; only in 1835 did it acquire its present area. By the royal decree (*alvará*) of the prefect (*prefeito*) of the Province of 20 January 1835, it lost the part of the parish of Ponta do Sol that had been left to it by the letter of King Manuel I of 2 December 1501, in which he made ‘the *lugar* (settlement ranking between a town and a parish) of Ponta do Sol a town’. At the end of that same year, 1835, it lost Caniço, which was annexed to the municipality (*concelho*) of Santa Cruz, together with the parishes of Câmara de Lobos and those that follow it westwards as far as the *lugar* of Ponta do Sol. The old town of Funchal originally covered a very small area. Even at the end of the 15th century it was bounded to the south, by the beach, by a dry-stone wall fitted with small turrets a crossbow shot apart and by a solid wooden stockade; to the west by the São João or São Paulo stream; to the north by the lands of Pico dos Frias and Valverde; and to the east it came close to the right bank of the Santa Luzia stream. The large population centre that had formed from the earliest times on the left bank of the João Gomes stream and near the beach lay outside the area originally called the town, and was later incorporated into it.

before: From its creation this district comprised the ten municipalities (*concelhos*) of Funchal, Machico, Porto Santo, Ponta do Sol, Calheta, Santa Cruz, São Vicente, Câmara de Lobos, Sant’Ana and Porto do Moniz; in 1914 the municipality of Ribeira Brava was created (see Municipalities). before: The Madeiran archipelago, which forms the Administrative District of Funchal, has as its capital the city of that name. It lies on the south coast of Madeira and stretches along the foot of high mountains, climbing rapidly up the slopes from the edge of the ocean to an altitude of roughly two hundred metres. It forms a considerable part of a vast and exceedingly beautiful amphitheatre, spread across a broad valley, which as a whole presents itself as one of the most astonishing wonders the eye is granted to behold. As if serving as a backrest to the city and overlooking it along almost its entire length, there rises an unbroken mountain range of hills and heights, covered with the most opulent and varied vegetation and sprinkled with the most picturesque dwellings, which lend still greater distinction, greater charm and greater splendour to so marvellous a scene. It is no wonder that visitors entering the landing place of Funchal, whether they round Cabo do Garajau or Ponta da Cruz or arrive from the south, should find themselves before a genuine counterpart of the bay and hillsides of the city of Naples, feel their spirits captivated and overwhelmed at the sight of this unequalled panorama, and keep the deepest and most grateful impressions of it for ever. The settlement that served as the nucleus of the future city has existed for five centuries. It was built on very irregular and broken ground, without following any preconceived ideas or plans, in a setting far removed from populous centres, by settlers who came from poor lands and villages and were entirely cut off from what world civilisation could have offered them at that time. The islanders of those days, our ancestors and forebears, left to their own efforts and without effective help from the metropolitan government, gradually built in this isolation of the ocean many settlements, several towns and a city, spurred on above all by the remarkable fertility of the soil and the gentle mildness of the climate. And yet, although the city of Funchal, considered in itself, has no dazzling beauties or charms, it keeps a marked and interesting regional character of its own, and presents distinctive features, shaped by its environmental conditions, that deserve the attentive observer’s notice. It offers the rich produce of its vines, of worldwide reputation, its incomparable embroidery, its fruit and its matchless flowers all year round, its highly original sledges, the typical Monte toboggans, the most enchanting landscape in creation, the mildest and most temperate climate on this planet, etc., etc., and, gilding all of this, an eternal spring and the ever-affectionate hospitality of its inhabitants, which has never been belied.

before: ‘It pleased God to take him,’ says the manuscript already cited, ‘having governed the island.... not as its lord, but as father and companion to all its inhabitants.’ The mortal remains of the discoverer were buried in the church of Conceição de Cima, today the church of Santa Clara (St Clare of Assisi), which he had had built as a family vault for himself and his descendants. Zargo’s tomb lay in the chancel, as was indeed the general custom for the founders and patrons of churches. One reads somewhere ‘that the work was so arranged that the grave.... lay in the middle of the chancel, with a stone tomb above it so tall that it makes it singularly venerable and worthy of respect’. It is said that many years later the nuns succeeded in having the showy mausoleum removed, since it blocked their view of the altar. It was perhaps on that occasion that the ashes of the discoverer of Madeira were transferred to the family vault of his son-in-law Martins Mendes de Vasconcelos.

before: This epitaph makes no reference to the discoverer’s ashes, and, according to what we heard from the person who tried to decipher it, the Gothic inscription does not seem to concern him either. before: The chapel of Santa Catarina (St Catherine of Alexandria), the chapel of São Paulo (St Paul the Apostle), the Quinta das Cruzes and above all the church of Santa Clara are modest but memorable monuments that eloquently recall the discoverer and the discovery of Madeira. These buildings deserve from the public authorities, and especially from the administrative bodies based in Funchal, the respect and veneration that are everywhere paid to objects and things closely bound up with the lives of illustrious men. They have the very grave duty of maintaining these buildings and of protecting them, as far as possible, from the ravages of time. And, as we have already said elsewhere in this book, this is a fitting occasion to make special mention of the two-handed sword (*montante*) of João Gonçalves Zargo. It was always kept in the house at Cruzes, and a constant tradition, handed down from generation to generation within the family that owned it, attributes it beyond doubt to the illustrious discoverer. It was always regarded as such, and the deep veneration paid to that relic there at all times confirms the truth of its origin still further. It is an old weapon, made to be wielded with both hands, and it is not distinguished by fine workmanship. It certainly has no intrinsic or artistic value, but it is worth a great deal for its five hundred and more years of existence and, above all, for having belonged to the great navigator who discovered this archipelago. It is perhaps the sword that Gonçalves Zargo wielded in Morocco in his charges against the Moors, winning fame as a brave and daring knight. This venerable relic is now in this city in the hands of a foreigner, who keeps it with the esteem it truly deserves. It ought, however, to be in the possession of the Municipal Council (*Câmara Municipal*) of this city. It is the duty of this administrative body to arrange its acquisition and to keep it religiously in its archives, until it can take its rightful place in the museum of art and antiquities that must one day be founded in this city (1921).

These buildings deserve from the public authorities, and especially from the administrative bodies based in Funchal, the respect and veneration that are everywhere paid to objects and things closely bound up with the lives of illustrious men. And, as we have already said elsewhere in this book, this is a fitting occasion to make special mention of the two-handed sword (*montante*) of João Gonçalves Zargo. It was always kept in the house at Cruzes, and a constant tradition, handed down from generation to generation within the family that owned it, attributes it beyond doubt to the illustrious discoverer. It was always regarded as such, and the deep veneration paid to that relic there at all times confirms the truth of its origin still further. It is an old weapon, made to be wielded with both hands, and it is not distinguished by fine workmanship. It certainly has no intrinsic or artistic value, but it is worth a great deal for its five hundred and more years of existence and, above all, for having belonged to the great navigator who discovered this archipelago. It is perhaps the sword that Gonçalves Zargo wielded in Morocco in his charges against the Moors, winning fame as a brave and daring knight. This venerable relic is now in this city in the hands of a foreigner, who keeps it with the esteem it truly deserves. It ought, however, to be in the possession of the Municipal Council (*Câmara Municipal*) of this city. It is the duty of this administrative body to arrange its acquisition and to keep it religiously in its archives, until it can take its rightful place in the museum of art and antiquities that must one day be founded in this city (1921).

before: The Madeiran poet Francisco de Paula Medina e Vasconcelos published in Lisbon in 1806 a poem he called *Zargueida*, of which, and of the *Georgeida*, Inocêncio Francisco da Silva says: ‘He sought to sound the epic trumpet, but one sees that this undertaking was far beyond his talent, and so in the two attempts he composed in that genre he never managed to rise above mediocrity. There are, however, in each of them, episodes that do no discredit to his muse and that can be read with pleasure’. Of Medina e Vasconcelos’s compositions, the *Zargueida* brought him the greatest renown, and it is still today the best known of them all. It is an epic poem in *ottava rima*, modelled on the classical forms of the ancient epic. It is divided into ten cantos and contains more than five thousand lines. It deals with the discovery of Madeira by João Gonçalves Zargo, taking the discoverer’s surname for the poem’s title. It contains a series of interesting episodes with some happy poetic digressions, among which the legend of Robert Machin stands out. Only in Canto X is the discovery of this island described. The poem is preceded by a sonnet dedicated to Bocage, to which that eminent poet replies with another sonnet, undoubtedly the finest composition in the volume (1921).

before: It seems that the idea of founding a hospital here arose shortly after the colonisation of this island began. It was the discoverer himself, João Gonçalves Zarco, who by public deed of 25 March 1454 granted some land beside the chapel of São Paulo (St Paul the Apostle) for the building of the new hospital. The building, which was paid for by the people, was not constructed until 1469. The hospital operated there for roughly fifteen years and was transferred to the parish (*freguesia*) of Santa Maria Maior around 1484. The new foundation was built on land belonging to Álvaro Afonso, who gave it for this purpose in 1483 on condition that the hospital should have six beds for poor patients.

before: By virtue of a papal bull obtained from Pope Alexander VI permitting the foundation of a new hospital on this island, King Manuel I ordered, by royal letter (*carta régia*) of 25 May 1507, the construction of a building specially intended for that purpose, on land belonging to one Bartolomeu Malheiro. It is presumed that the old hospital was incorporated into the new foundation and that this was built on the same site, in the street that still bears the name Hospital Velho. However, in an old register of visitation orders (*livro de provimentos*) of the parish church of Nossa Senhora do Calhau (Our Lady of Calhau), we find the following passages, which quite clearly refer to two hospitals, though perhaps housed in adjoining buildings and forming, as it were, a single establishment: ‘The Vicar and Beneficiaries of Nossa Senhora do Calhau shall hold and regard as their parishioners those persons who are taken into the old hospital as incurables, and when they die… shall accompany them to the grave…, and they shall do the same with those who die in the new hospital…’. It is not easy to determine with complete precision when work on the new building was completed, but it cannot have been much after 1515, for in a royal letter of 4 June of that year Manuel I pressed for the works to be finished, ordering the proceeds of the wine tax to be applied to them until they were entirely completed. We read in an old nobiliary (book of noble genealogies) that the bachelor (*bacharel*, university graduate) João Fernandes de Amil was charged by the monarch with directing the foundation and construction of the new hospital. Nothing is known about the running of this establishment in the early years of its existence, particularly as regards the number of patients, its own revenues, the meeting of its expenses, the form of its administration, etc., for no record of any kind on the subject can be found.

before: We are, however, of the opinion that the hospital should be moved to a site and a building whose sanitary conditions fully meet the modern precepts of medical science. For many decades the press has advocated this move, citing the reasons briefly set out above. The lazaretto, Marmeleiros and the former convents of the Incarnação and Santa Clara were put forward as the preferred places for housing the hospital, once the necessary conversion work had been carried out. Among the proposals made, those considered best and most fully suited to the desired purpose were to build new buildings in the convent grounds of the Incarnação and Santa Clara, reusing only some of the materials of the old, ruined monasteries. The authoritative opinion of the doctors confirmed the public’s preference for the site of the convent of Santa Clara (St Clare of Assisi). A committee made up of Drs Nuno Silvestre Teixeira, Fortunato Pita, João Francisco de Almada, José Joaquim de Freitas and José Joaquim Mendes gave its opinion, in a long and well-argued report, that the new hospital building should be erected within the precinct of the convent of Santa Clara, and it rejected the buildings of the lazaretto and Marmeleiros as unsuitable for that purpose. before: He was the first bishop to come to this island. The colonisation of the archipelago had begun more than 80 years earlier, yet no prelate had yet performed episcopal functions there. The Vicar of Tomar (*vigário de Tomar*, head of the Order of Christ's spiritual jurisdiction overseas) – or rather the mastership of the Order of Christ, to which Madeira belonged in spiritual matters – sent Bishop João Lobo in 1508, and he visited all the churches and principal chapels of this island. The bishopric of Funchal was created in 1514, so João Lobo confined his religious mission solely to the exercise of episcopal functions: confirming, ordaining clergy, blessing vestments and liturgical vessels, consecrating churches, etc. He had no part in the administration of ecclesiastical affairs, the observance of canon discipline or the suppression of abuses. These belonged only to the diocesan bishop, who did not yet exist, and that charge therefore fell to the representative of the Order of Christ, who at that time was already Nuno Cão (see I-243), a brother (*freire*) of the Order. The first consecrated church on this island (and few are consecrated, most being merely blessed) was the chapel of the Lombada do Esmeraldo, in the parish (*freguesia*) of Ponta do Sol, and to this day the following inscription can be read on one of the interior walls of the building: ‘This church was consecrated by Dom João Lobo, Bishop of Taiere, on 27 August 1508.’ This prelate returned to Portugal after spending little more than a year on this island. It was after his visit that the need to create a diocese in this archipelago was more fully recognised; it was established only in 1514, as stated above. In Vieira Guimarães’s excellent book *A Ordem de Cristo*, published in 1901, we read the following: ‘As early as 1508, to satisfy the wishes of these petitioners (the creation of the bishopric of Funchal), the Vicar of Tomar sent them the titular bishop (*bispo de anel*) Dom João Lobo, who was awaited on the island by the master, Friar Nuno Cão, with all the clergy, and they held many celebrations for him.’

before: This group consists of three small islands known as Ilhéu Chão (Flat Islet), Deserta Grande, or simply Deserta, and Bugio. They lie in a north-north-west to south-south-east line with the Ponta de São Lourenço, south-east of Madeira, and are closer to that point. To the north of the three islets lies a small islet known as Furilhão, or more properly Farilhão, as Ilhéu or Rocha do Navio, and also as Prego do Mar (see that entry); it is separated from Ilhéu Chão by a narrow channel. Running roughly north to south, Ilhéu Chão is followed by Deserta Grande and that in turn by Bugio, separated from one another by narrow straits navigable only by vessels of very small tonnage. The extreme points of this small group of islands, or tiny archipelago, as it has been called, are: to the north, the said Furilhão islet; to the south, the Ponta das Agulhas, at the southern tip of Bugio; to the east, the same point; and to the west, the Ponta do Pedregal, on the western coast of Deserta Grande. The geographical position of the three islands, taken together, is as follows: they lie between 32° 35′ and 32° 22′ 20″ N and between 16° 27′ 25″ and 16° 32′ W (Greenwich). The group is about eleven miles, or roughly twenty kilometres, from the Ponta de São Lourenço. The Desertas are regarded as belonging to the parish (*freguesia*) of the Sé – Funchal Cathedral (*Sé*) – but it seems that they were once incorporated in the parish of Caniço, and those who died on the islands were generally buried there.

before: At first he confined himself to practising medicine free of charge, in which he soon became renowned, to charity towards the poor and to founding schools. Together with his attractive personal qualities and the prestige of his words, this surrounded his name with an aura of sympathy, esteem and respect among all the social classes of our land. The Municipal Council (*Câmara Municipal*) of Funchal publicly paid him a lofty tribute for his services to education and for his acts of philanthropy towards the unfortunate, and the government in mainland Portugal exempted from duty at the customs house of this city the medicines he imported for treating the poor. The benefactor later turned into a fierce propagandist, and it became clear that in him proselytism outweighed in every respect the disinterested practice of charity. This became even more marked after a journey he made to England, where he stayed from June to September 1845. It is said that the meetings he held there with the leaders of the Bible societies and with important figures interested in anti-Catholic propaganda greatly inflamed his natural sectarian ardour and gave him greater courage and boldness in spreading Protestant ideas.

before: Only from the last quarter of the 19th century did the sanitation of the city of Funchal – particularly the supply of drinking water and the laying of sewers – truly receive from the municipal council sessions the attention that the matter urgently demanded. A ministerial order (*portaria*) of 22 March 1897 instructed the Directorate of District Public Works to carry out the studies needed for the supply of drinking water and the laying of sewers, and the law of 16 September of that year authorised the government to assist with the construction work. These two studies were carried out by the distinguished engineers Adriano Trigo and Aníbal Trigo, and earned the praise and full approval of the higher authorities. The study dealing specifically with the sewers was regarded as a valuable piece of work, and it has been of great help and a useful lesson for the works carried out later. It was published as a pamphlet of 95 pages. These important improvements, which form the chief foundation of public hygiene, have continued to be carried out, as the reputation our land enjoys as a privileged health resort requires. The most recent municipal council sessions have devoted the most careful attention to this important and pressing matter, to the general applause of all the townspeople.

before: In 1910 Judice Fialho set up a tuna trap (*armação*, a fixed trap-net) on Porto Santo, but it produced no results – because, it is said, the waters around that island are very clear. Some time before, in 1903, the late Commanders Manuel Gonçalves and Francisco de Araújo Figueira had tried to establish fixed traps for catching pelagic species, but they too were unsuccessful. This was despite the fact that a specialist and two trap foremen had come to Madeira to study the fishing conditions of our seas, and that a report submitted by the same specialist in October 1903 stated that large-scale fishing in the archipelago, using tuna traps, would be advantageous, naming the Ilhéu de Cima, off Porto Santo, and Machico as the best sites for placing gear for tuna fishing.

before: In 1909 a tuna cannery was established at Ponta da Cruz, and in 1912 another at Paul do Mar. These ventures certainly benefited the fishing industry in Madeira, but they caused the price of tuna to rise, and the fish, formerly plentiful, often became scarce in the market. It should be noted, however, that if tuna has lately sold at 2, 3 and even 4 escudos (Portuguese currency from 1911, = 1,000 réis) a kilo, this is due more to the greed and lack of scruple of the dealers than to the constant demand from the fish-canning industry for the various species of the genus *Thynnus* found in the seas of the archipelago. (1921)

before: We lack reliable and recent data on the activity of this industry here in Madeira. We shall present the statistics for the year 1909 offered by the illustrious engineer Adolfo Loureiro in his important work *Portos Maritimos de Portugal*, which were gathered at the Harbour Master's Office (*Capitania do Porto*) of Funchal. The ports where the fishing industry is carried on are the following: Funchal, Caniço, Porto Novo, Aldonça, Santa Cruz, Seixo, Machico, Caniçal, Porto da Cruz, Faial, São Jorge, Ponta Delgada, São Vicente, Seixal, Porto do Moniz, Ponta do Pargo, Paul do Mar, Jardim do Mar, Calheta, Fajã do Mar, Madalena do Mar, Anjos, Lugar de Baixo, Tabua, Ribeira Brava, Campanário, Câmara de Lobos and Porto Santo. It should be noted, however, that a large number of these ports are fishing centres of little importance, and some of none at all. The total number of fishermen then reached 2,482, of whom 1,566 were over 18 years of age, 726 were between 12 and 18, and 190 were under 10. The ports of Câmara de Lobos, Paul do Mar and Machico are comparatively very busy and the most important of all, with 575, 336 and 244 people respectively employed in the fishing trades. In number of fishermen these are followed by the ports of Funchal with 153, Porto Santo 156, Caniço 95, Caniçal 90, Santa Cruz 88, Calheta 82, etc. The boats engaged in this industry numbered 509, with a capacity of 1,268 tonnes and a value of 29,113,000 *réis* (old Portuguese money of account; 1$000 = 1,000 réis, 1:000$000 = one conto = 1,000,000 réis). The value of the catch was estimated at 126 523$265 *réis*, on which 5,696,572 *réis* was paid in tax.

before: This term is used only as a place name in Madeira. At the eastern end of the island, near Ponta de São Lourenço, between the Abra and Furado points, lies the cove of Abra. Of all the small coves of Madeira it is the widest and the most deeply indented, forming a relatively spacious bay with a good anchorage. During the Pombaline administration there was a plan to build a military port and its arsenal in this cove, and in the first quarter of the 19th century the idea of establishing a small harbour of refuge there was also raised. Besides a beach or pebble beach (calhau), there is a privately owned landing quay. Bounding the cove to the west is a projection of the coastline called Ponta de Abra, and the name Abra is also kept by the locality (*sítio*) which, with its high peaks, curves round the cove and its adjoining landing place.

before: He devoted little time to the practice of medicine, dedicating himself instead almost exclusively to the study of zoology, in which he was an authoritative master. He sat the competitive examination for the chair at the Escola Politécnica where that subject was taught and was appointed to it. He gave zoological studies a wholly new direction in Portugal and is regarded as the true founder of that branch of science in our country, from a rigorously scientific standpoint and in keeping with the advances made by distinguished foreign scholars. He gave these studies an essentially practical character, as the magnificent collections he organised most eloquently prove; that of the natural history cabinet of the Escola Politécnica deserves special mention. His scientific output is vast and valuable: it opened the doors of many foreign academies to him and won him, abroad, the reputation of a most distinguished man of science. We would go too far if we tried to give a detailed account of his scientific works, many of which are mentioned in Inocêncio’s *Diccionario Bibliographico*. Nevertheless, we will say that he wrote and published about 200 works on mammals, birds, reptiles, amphibians, fishes, invertebrates, zoological philosophy, etc., among which the following stand out: *Memória sobre a cabra montez* (*Mem. da Ac. das Sc. de Lisboa*, 1857); *Noticias sobre os Arvicolas de Portugal* (Id., 1864); *Peixes plagiostomos*, Part 1 (Lisbon 1866); *A Ornithologia dos Açores* (*Jorn. da Ac. Sc. Lisboa*, 1866); *Aves das Possessões Portuguesas d'Africa Occidental* (24 lists, Id., 1867 1882); *A Vida Animal nas grandes profundidades do Oceano* (Id., 1870); *Liste des Mammifères et Reptiles observés en Portugal* (*Rev. et Mag. de Zool.*, 1863); *Liste des Antilopes d'Angola* (*Proc. Zool. Soc.*, 1878); *Subsidios para a fauna das Possessões Portuguesas d'Africa Occidental, S. Thomé e Angola* (*Jorn. da Ac. Sc. On our archipelago he wrote only *Noticia sobre uma collecção de conchas das ilhas da Madeira e Porto Santo* (*Ann. das Sc. e Let.*, 1857).

before: Having had the opportunity to examine several samples of wheat gathered in different parts of Madeira in 1904 and 1905, we had no difficulty in recognising that the number of varieties on this island is greater than the number studied by the professors mentioned above. We further found that some of the old types, although similar to certain Portuguese types from which they may perhaps derive, nevertheless differ from them in noteworthy characters. The Madeiran varieties we were able to study all belong to the races *T. vulgare* and *T. turgidum*, known in the trade as soft wheats. We have never found *T. durum*, another race of *T. sativum*, on Madeira or on Porto Santo, and it may well not exist on these islands. The wheats that in Madeira are called ‘hard’ are, in our view, simply sub-races of *T. turgidum*, as can easily be recognised from the shape of their ears and glumes and from the consistency and arched shape of their grains. In true hard or durum wheats the grains are elongated, pointed and almost always vitreous, characters we did not observe in any of the Madeiran varieties.

before: In times now somewhat removed from our own, the images of Senhor dos Passos (Our Lord of the Steps), from the church of Santa Clara (St Clare of Assisi), and of Nossa Senhora da Soledade (Our Lady of Solitude), from the church of the Mercês, were carried in procession on Saturday night: the latter to the Cathedral (the Sé) and the former to the Colégio church (Igreja do Colégio, the Jesuit college church). The image of Our Lord was the first to leave, and the image of Our Lady then joined the cortège. Many boys bearing lighted torches went ahead of the procession, which, after passing the Colégio church, made its way to the Cathedral. The Passos procession (Lenten procession of Christ carrying the Cross) left the Colégio church on Sunday afternoon and went along Rua da Carreira and Rua de São Francisco to visit a station (of the Cross) that stood on the north side of the old Jardim Pequeno. It then proceeded to the Cathedral, where the ceremony of the encounter took place, at first inside the church and later outside it. On that occasion a sermon was preached on the event. The procession, now joined by the confraternity and the image of Nossa Senhora da Soledade, then went on to the church of Santa Maria Maior (St Mary Major), making short halts in front of the Stations of the Passion (*passos*, wayside oratories depicting scenes of Christ's Passion) in Rua do Aljube, at the Pelourinho and in Rua de Santa Maria.

before: The festivities opened with a solemn Te Deum in Funchal Cathedral (*Sé*), which was immensely well attended. The distinguished sacred orator the Revd Father José Marques Jardim went up to the pulpit and delivered a remarkable sermon that pleased everyone present. Among those present were many of the Tenerife visitors (see that entry) who had arrived in Funchal the day before, 28 December, the consular corps, the officers of the destroyer *Guadiana*, several officers of the city garrison, the administrative bodies, the students of Funchal, etc. The ceremony was presided over by the diocesan prelate, Dom António Manuel Pereira Ribeiro, assisted by Canons Manuel A Miranda and Manuel Mendes Teixeira, and the choral music was performed by a large *schola*, accompanied by an excellent orchestra.

before: Seen from the belvedere (*mirante*) built by order of the Public Works Department on the Levada do Juncal, this great valley offers one of the most vast and majestic panoramas of the interior of Madeira. At the head of the valley rise Pico Ruivo and Pico das Torres, the highest peaks on the island, and on its precipitous sides, in many places clothed with trees, grow many of the most beautiful and rare plants of Madeira. The belvedere on the Levada do Juncal is about 15 kilometres from Funchal.

before: The name Pontinha, given to the projection of the coastline that partly bounds our small harbour of refuge, has at times seemed strange. The spot was originally known as Ilhéus (islets), because two isolated rocks washed by the sea once stood there, and the name also covered the immediate surroundings of the locality (*sítio*). Even today the Rua dos Ilhéus, which lies nearby, recalls the original name.

before: The illustrious commentator of *Saudades da Terra*, though somewhat forcedly, offers this explanation of the name Pontinha given to that stretch of the coast: ‘Of these two islets, the one farther out to sea is still now (in 1873) isolated in the waters as before, and so keeps the name of Ilhéu; the other, joined long since to the shore of the island by strong walls, has therefore the name of Pontinha’.

before: This name, which has prevailed over time, is of quite ancient use and may go back to the mid-16th century. The soundest probabilities suggest that the colonisation of Madeira began around 1425. The historian of the islands, describing the first exploration carried out along the coast and referring in particular to the arrival of the first settlers at the locality later called Funchal, tells us that ‘as it was already late, they went to shelter at the Ilhéus, which lie at the end of it (the valley of Funchal)’. This is the earliest known reference to the Ilhéus da Pontinha. The locality and the neighbouring stretch of shore would from then on have been called Ilhéus, the name Pontinha later prevailing, as stated above.

before: In the vicinity of this locality, António Dantas founded in 1622 the chapel of Nossa Senhora da Penha de França (Our Lady of the Peña de Francia), with which several events of considerable interest to the history of Madeira are connected (see Penha de França). Also in the same vicinity, and taking its name from this chapel, a fortress was built in the second quarter of the 17th century. It was rebuilt in 1712 and served as quarters for detachments of English troops in 1801, when they occupied this island.

before: On the islet farther from the coast, the ‘Fortaleza de Nossa Senhora da Conceição do Ilhéu’ was built in 1654. There, in 1682, a small chapel of the same dedication was erected, which had its own chaplain from 1692. In 1866 a tiny red-light lighthouse was installed there, commonly and ironically called ‘the ember of the Islet’ (*a braza do Ilhéu*); in 1931 it was replaced by a proper lighthouse. Until a few years ago a detachment of the Artillery Company quartered in the Fort of São Tiago (St James the Greater) was permanently stationed at this stronghold, chiefly to return the ‘salutes’ of warships entering our harbour. A semaphore station also operated there.

before: Volume I of the *Archivo da Marinha e Ultramar*, published in 1907, cites many documents concerning the works that were to be carried out in the Port of Funchal (Porto do Funchal). before: Around 1872 the construction of the pleasant ‘Estrada da Pontinha’ was planned. Especially since the completion of the works on the small harbour of refuge, this road has rendered the public the most valuable services, which will become greater still as the conditions of the harbour improve. Work did not begin at once and construction was slow; it was declared complete only in 1895, some years after the Pontinha mole. The road contributed greatly to the embellishment of the bay (*baía*), and also eased communications between the busiest part of the city and the western districts of Funchal. On top of the sheer escarpment overlooking this road stand some of the finest *quintas* in Madeira, which enjoy an enviable position with views of the harbour and of the whole amphitheatre of Funchal.

before: Shortly after the drawing class opened, the central government sent, on 10 April 1810, a set of *Instruções* to regulate its operation. These no doubt constituted the class’s founding statute and must have contained the teaching methods or the syllabus of the subjects taught there. We have no knowledge of these *Instruções*, nor do we know where the class was held or how long it lasted. It may have formed part of the group of chairs that made up the so-called *Aulas do Pátio* (‘Courtyard Classes’, the public secondary classes held in the former Jesuit college), but we can state nothing definite on this point. We know only that in 1812 L. Rocha obtained an increase in salary as teacher of the drawing and painting class, and that in 1818 he was still alive and living in this city, for in that year he painted a portrait of the 1st Count of Carvalhal, which hangs in the Palácio de São Pedro (St Peter Palace).

before: Although the Funchal Lyceum, founded in 1837, had a chair of drawing in its curriculum, it was always considered necessary here to have a class in that subject separate from the lyceum (state secondary school). There, workers in particular could acquire the knowledge indispensable to their arts and trades, with teaching geared to the needs of the professions to which they were chiefly devoted. It was in keeping with this aim that the Municipal Council (*Câmara Municipal*) of Funchal created and maintained a chair of drawing. In the last years of its existence its teacher was the head of the Council’s technical department, José Maria Teixeira de Agrela.

before: The decree of 5 October 1893, which brought profound changes to industrial education, raised the António Augusto de Aguiar Industrial Drawing School to the rank of Industrial School, while keeping the same name. Workshops for cabinetmaking and carpentry and for women’s needlework were then created. The decree of 14 December 1897 thoroughly reorganised industrial education in our country, and the Funchal Industrial School benefited from this reform through the creation of three theory classes: Portuguese language, arithmetic and geometry, and principles of physics and chemistry. These posts, with the exception of the last, which was never actually created, were not filled, however, until early December 1901, and they began to operate in the 1902–1903 academic year.

before: ‘To wreak fierce havoc on the Moors!’ (*Ao fazerem nos Mouros bravo estrago!*): in these words the poet refers to the island of Santiago, the principal island of the Cape Verde archipelago, discovered on the first of May in the year 1460. Camões’s mistake is evident, for that island, and likewise the island of Maio in the same archipelago, were found by the Portuguese on the feast of St James the Less, that is, on the first day of May, whereas the lines quoted concern St James the Greater, whose feast the Church celebrates on 25 July. The name given to that island by its discoverers was determined by the fact that it was found on the first of May, the day dedicated to the apostle St James the Less, as stated above.

before: It rises in the mountains of the parish (*freguesia*) of São Vicente and separates that parish from the parish of Seixal before flowing into the ocean. before: He was the penultimate and 26th bishop of this diocese. From what we know of the ecclesiastical chronicles of Madeira, we can state that he was the most illustrious prelate ever to occupy the episcopal throne of Funchal. He was born on 7 December 1835 in the parish (*freguesia*) of Coentral, in the bishopric of Coimbra, the son of José Agostinho Barreto and Dona Maria Barreto. He graduated in theology from the University of Coimbra in 1858, and in 1864 he was appointed a canon of Lamego Cathedral. There he held important offices, among them professor at the Seminary, vicar general, provisor (diocesan judicial and administrative officer) and governor of the diocese (governador do bispado, administering the see in the bishop's absence). Throughout mainland Portugal he enjoyed a reputation as a remarkable preacher, and some of his sermons became memorable. In the diocese of Lamego his name was surrounded by a true aura of veneration and the most respectful esteem, owing to his virtues, austerity of character, talent, learning and ardent zeal in the ecclesiastical duties he performed there for some years.

before: His episcopal consecration took place in the Basílica da Estrela in Lisbon on 4 February 1877. The consecrating bishop was the Archbishop of Mitylene, Dom António José de Freitas Honorato, who had been his professor at Coimbra, and the assisting prelates were Dom José Maria Ferrão de Carvalho Martens, Bishop of Bragança, and Dom José Lino de Oliveira, the retired Bishop of Angola. before: A month after his arrival in this city, a serious conflict arose between the prelate and the Municipal Council (*Câmara Municipal*) of Funchal over the burial of a suicide in the Angústias cemetery, as already mentioned above (see Angústias). He then showed the greatest independence of character, both in the way he settled the question and in the boldness with which he addressed it from the pulpit of the Cathedral in a sermon that became unforgettable. Even so, there were those who described the act as reckless and ill-considered courage, and even as a challenge thrown down to the liberal classes of Madeira. The prelate upheld the canon laws and faced squarely all the consequences of doing his duty.

before: Once that stormy tempest had passed, he devoted himself entirely to the administration of his diocese, which absorbed the whole activity of his mind until the last moments of his long episcopal career, a mind ever filled with the greatest dedication and the purest zeal and solicitude for the welfare of the flock entrusted to him. Seeking a quiet and peaceful refuge, he withdrew to the modest residence of Penha de França, and there he spent 34 years in retirement and work. He left his hermitage only when the unavoidable obligations of his ministry, his official duties or his shaken health forcibly compelled him to do so. Before long, his great qualities as an apostle, his rare administrative tact, his unbending energy in upholding ecclesiastical discipline, his most remarkable reform of the seminary, his unsurpassed zeal in propagating and developing religious feeling, the austerity of his ever modest life, stripped of all pomp, his ardent and proverbial charity, his active and never interrupted evangelisation through the spoken and written word, the founding of schools and of various social works, his frequent pastoral visitations throughout the diocese, etc., etc., won for his name the highest prestige, the loftiest esteem and the deepest respect that few Portuguese prelates can have attained in the last 50 years. If we further add the brilliant oratorical gifts that made him a born orator, his notable learning, his qualities as a writer and the charming conversation that so captivated and attracted, we shall see converging in a single man a series of such rare and extraordinary attributes as we could otherwise find only scattered among many individuals. For all these reasons he was considered the foremost Portuguese bishop of his time.

before: His first and most devoted measures were directed at the diocesan seminary. He arrived in Funchal at the end of February 1877, and by the beginning of the following October a complete course of preparatory studies, which had not previously existed, was already running there. Its boarding facilities were enlarged and its internal organisation completely remodelled, the whole establishment undergoing a radical transformation. Having succeeded in placing Father Ernesto Schmitz at the head of this house of religious instruction and education, he saw this clergyman render the most signal and outstanding services there, not only in the formation and preparation of the future clergy but also in the establishment of a regional zoological museum. This was a truly exemplary creation of its kind, spoken of with high praise by several distinguished foreign naturalists who visited it, and it had an attached physics laboratory for the practical teaching of that science. The greatest ambition of Dom Manuel Agostinho Barreto was to provide the diocese with a building fit to house the seminary, in which the various services of an establishment of this nature would be amply accommodated and could fully serve their purpose. This ardent wish was fulfilled through the inheritance left to him by Dona Maria Leopoldina de Oliveira. On the convent grounds (*cerca*) of the former convent of the Incarnação he had a fine and spacious building erected, on which he spent his entire fortune, both inherited and acquired. Although it was never entirely completed, it had the capacity and the essential requirements to house the diocesan seminary, which operated there for some years until it was abolished by the decree of 20 April 1911, the building passing immediately into the possession of the State. (See Seminary).

before: Dom Manuel Agostinho Barreto died at the residence attached to the chapel of Penha de França on 26 June 1911 and was buried in the Angústias cemetery. Among his last wishes was this humble and pious detail: ‘he asks that, after five years have passed, his bones be moved in a small urn to the churchyard of the Penha chapel, in front of and next to the main door, covered by a plain stone bearing his name and the dates of his birth and death, with a cross at the top and the letters P. N. A. M. at the bottom, to beg the faithful who pass by for a devout *Requiem aeternam*’. Twelve years later, on 26 June 1923, the remains of the eminent prelate were solemnly transferred. They were covered with a small gravestone bearing this modest epitaph: Dom Manuel Agostinho Barreto, Bishop of Funchal. Born on 7 December 1835, died on 26 June 1911, aged 76, in the 34th year of his episcopate. P. A. H. M.

before: There was one in the parish of Canhas, in the locality of Socorro, founded by João Fernandes Linhares in 1665. In the parish of Porto da Cruz there is a chapel with this patron saint, originally known as Nossa Senhora de Belém. We do not know who its founder was, but it belonged to the entailed estate (*morgadio*) established by Captain Manuel Telo Moniz de Meneses, of the house of Lagoa in the same parish, which was later called the Torresão entailed estate. It was built around 1713 and is in a fair state of repair; it is the property of Dona Cristina de Campos Pinto Soares, who lives in Lisbon (1921).

We do not know who its founder was, but it belonged to the entailed estate (*morgadio*) established by Captain Manuel Telo Moniz de Meneses, of the house of Lagoa (‘lake’) in the same parish, which was later called the Torresão entailed estate. It was built around 1713 and is in a fair state of repair; it is the property of Dona Cristina de Campos Pinto Soares, who lives in Lisbon (1921).

before: Of the four native orchids known in Madeira, only one – *Orchis foliosa* – is a truly ornamental plant. It does not flower in Funchal, but in the ravines of the interior it bears small, purple, scentless flowers gathered in spikes that are sometimes elongated. Salep can be extracted from the palmate tubers of this orchid, and this is why it is becoming rare in some parts of the island. Some foreigners who visited our island a few years ago took back to their country all the tubers of *Orchis foliosa* they could gather at Ribeiro Frio!

before: This convent of Franciscan friars stood in the parish (*freguesia*) of Ribeira Brava, a short distance from the parish church. It was built by the Franciscan friars in a year we cannot determine. As recently as ten years ago some ruins of the conventual buildings could still be seen, and the façade and part of the nave of the church, which was of no very modest size, were still standing. Above the portico could be read the date 1730; we do not know whether it represents the year the convent was founded or the year the church was built, which seems to us more probable.

before: The oldest cemetery in Funchal for the burial of Catholics is that of São Roque, built in 1836. Work on the Angústias cemetery also began that year, but was not completed until 1838. The Santa Luzia cemetery dates from 1840 and the São Gonçalo cemetery from 1841. Before cemeteries were established, Catholics were buried in churches or in their churchyards. There was, however, at the locality of Angústias a small plot called the cemetery of the Holy House (*Santa Casa*, the Misericórdia), which received the bodies of those who died in the hospital.

before: In the locality (*sítio*) of Alecrins, in the parish (*freguesia*) of Santo António, stood the chapel of Nossa Senhora da Quietação, of which today not even traces remain. It was better known as the chapel of Alecrins, and in a reference to it made in 1680 it was even called the church of Alecrins, despite its cramped dimensions. The unusual name Quietação comes from the fact that the chapel’s patron saint was the mystery representing the peace and tranquillity that the Most Holy Virgin enjoyed, in the retirement of the house of Nazareth, in the company of the Child Jesus and the patriarch St Joseph.
after: In the locality (*sítio*) of Alecrins (‘rosemary bushes’), in the parish (*freguesia*) of Santo António (‘St Anthony’), stood the chapel of Nossa Senhora da Quietação, of which today not even traces remain. The unusual name Quietação comes from the fact that the chapel’s patron saint was the mystery representing the peace and tranquillity that the Blessed Virgin (*Santíssima Virgem*) enjoyed, in the retirement of the house of Nazaré (‘Nazareth’), in the company of the Child Jesus and the patriarch St Joseph.

before: It was Lourenço de Matos Coutinho and his wife Dona Mariana de Ornelas de Vasconcelos who founded this chapel in 1670, in fulfilment of a vow they had made to the Most Holy Virgin. They built it on the *quinta* (country estate) they owned in the locality of Alecrins, which they had inherited from his father and her father-in-law, the holder of the entail (*morgado*) Bento de Matos Coutinho, who in turn had acquired it by purchase from Simão Gonçalves da Câmara and Jorge da Câmara Esmeraldo. It was on this *quinta* and in this chapel that in 1677 its founder instituted the entailed estate (*morgadio*) of Alecrins. The present representative of this entailed estate is Dr Rui Bettencourt da Câmara (1921).

before: He was born in Funchal on 16 October 1821 and for nearly 60 years taught primary school in this city with great proficiency. On 2 October 1845 he founded his first school in partnership with Augusto Correia de Sampaio, also now deceased. In recognition of his services, the Municipal Council granted him, in the last years of his life, an annual pension of 240,000 *réis* (old Portuguese money of account; 1$000 = 1,000 réis, 1:000$000 = one conto = 1,000,000 réis). He died in Funchal on 9 July 1903.

before: When the civil wars ended in 1834 there were two liberal parties in Portugal: the Cartist party, made up of the entourage of Dom Pedro, and the opposition party, which, while combating the errors and extravagance of the former, nonetheless proclaimed its love of liberty and its devotion to the Constitutional Charter (*Carta Constitucional*). The first of these parties included the Madeirans João de Oliveira, later Count of Tojal, José Ferreira Pestana, Lourenço José Moniz, Sérvulo Drumond de Meneses, Luís Vicente de Afonseca, etc.; the second included António Aluísio Jervis de Atouguia and the members of the former Carmo club, who later figured in the Septembrist party. Yet despite the political differences on the island, the newspaper *A Chronica* stated on 24 March 1838 that the Madeirans had until then ‘marched united and obedient to the principles of legality’, and indeed there is no record that the September Revolution of 1836 gave rise to any noteworthy hostilities between Cartists and Septembrists. *A Flor do Oceano*, which appeared in 1834, was the organ of the Madeiran Cartist party.

before: At that time the Cartist or Cabralist party included Dr Lourenço José Moniz, Dr Luís Vicente de Afonseca, Sérvulo Drumond de Meneses, etc., and the Progressive or Septembrist party included Dr João de Freitas e Almeida, Francisco Correia Heredia, Luís de Ornelas e Vasconcelos, Luís Agostinho de Figueiroa, etc. The last three played an important part in local politics after the uprising of 29 April 1847 and the installation of the Junta Governativa, the governing board (junta governativa) (see that entry), which administered the archipelago until 14 July of the same year. before: The Regeneration of 1851 made it its hallmark to reconcile the parties, since it had drawn the men who then formed the government from both the Cartists and the Progressives. The Cabralist party, however, though reduced, continued to show its vitality, above all while Councillor (conselheiro, honorary title of the royal council) José Silvestre Ribeiro governed the district. In the elections held that year Madeira still sent two Cabralist deputies to parliament, which proves that the policies of the Count of Tomar had admirers here. In the press these policies had two organs, *O Archivista* and later *A Ordem*, edited by the well-known Cabralists Dr António da Luz Pita and Sérvulo de Meneses.

before: The struggles in Madeira between the Fusionist and Popular parties became notorious for the violence committed and for the shameful scenes of which the island was the stage for about a year and a half. The leading figures of Madeiran Fusionist politics were Dr Luís de Freitas Branco, Dr António Gonçalves de Freitas, Jacinto de Santana e Vasconcelos, João de Santana e Vasconcelos and Silvano de Freitas Branco, from the former Regenerator party; António Correia Heredia, Dr Francisco Joaquim Lampreia, Dr João da Câmara Leme, Canon Alfredo César de Oliveira, Pedro José de Ornelas, Dr Manuel José Vieira, Dr José Leite Monteiro and João José Vieira, from the former Historical party; and Dr Joaquim Ricardo da Trindade e Vasconcelos, formerly a Conservative or perhaps a Legitimist. The Popular party, on the other hand, included Dom João da Câmara Leme, who served for a long time as civil governor; Dr Agostinho de Ornelas e Vasconcelos; Canon Filipe José Nunes; Dr Álvaro Rodrigues de Azevedo, Januário Justiniano de Nóbrega and Nuno Dias de Vasconcelos, former Regenerators; Joaquim Coelho de Meireles, once a Miguelite (supporter of the absolutist King Miguel); and the former Cabralist Conservatives Dr António da Luz Pita, Dr Luís Vicente de Afonseca, Caetano Velosa Castelo Branco, the first Popular deputy for the Funchal constituency, and Diogo Berenguer, holder of the entail (*morgado*), in whose house the party committees met. *A Razão*, *O Popular* and *O Direito* were the organs of the Popular party in Madeira, while the *Correio do Funchal*, later replaced by *A Fusão*, *A Voz do Povo* and *A Imprensa Livre* championed the opposing policy.

before: It is curious to note that, although a Historical ministry was in power, in the elections of 1 May 1870 it was not the party supporting the government in Madeira but the opposition that triumphed in most of the polling assemblies. The men killed by the troops in the church at Machico were Popular party voters. Yet it was Popular supporters who, on the Cais da Pontinha, seized the late Dr Ricardo da Trindade e Vasconcelos as he returned from that town and took him to the public garden of Funchal, where they meant to murder him. This shows that they were masters of the situation and free to commit the wildest excesses. It was the lack of energy of the Viscount of Andaluz, then civil governor, and the indulgence he showed towards the opposition, even keeping in office officials who were openly hostile to him, that caused the anarchy and disorder of which Madeira was the stage in May 1870.

before: Dr José Martiniano da Fonseca was now irretrievably lost. After nine months in prison he was tried together with other defendants, and on 9 April 1829 sentence was pronounced, condemning ten of them to the ultimate penalty and others to various punishments. The iniquitous and revolting sentence was carried out on 7 May of that year. Two gallows were erected in the square of the Praça Nova, and there the ten defendants suffered capital punishment, Dr José Martiniano da Fonseca being the eighth to climb the steps of the gallows. To carry out the sentence in full, the victims’ heads were cut off and placed at various points in the city. That of Dr Fonseca was exposed for three days at São João da Foz, and on 12 May the brotherhood of the Misericórdia (the charitable Holy House of Mercy) took it to its chapel and had it buried there together with the mortal remains of the other defendants sacrificed to the ferocity of the Miguelite (supporter of the absolutist King Miguel) government. Seven years later, on 6 February 1836, the ashes of those victims were exhumed; they were all gathered into an urn and reburied in the church of the Misericórdia, awaiting the opportunity of a more fitting and appropriate tomb. It was in 1875 that an elegant mausoleum was raised in the Prado do Repouso Cemetery, within the precinct belonging to the Misericórdia of Porto, to hold the mortal remains of the men executed on 7 May 1829 and of two more who suffered the same penalty on 9 October of the same year. The translation of the last remains of these victims, who became known as the Twelve Martyrs of the Fatherland, was marked by an unusual and most brilliant grandeur. A funeral procession was formed in which thousands of people and the entire Porto garrison took part, making it one of the most splendid and significant processions ever organised in the country, as may be seen in the pamphlet *Memória Descriptiva da trasladação das ossadas dos Doze Martyres da Pátria*, published in 1878.

before: In the early 19th century the government assisted those rebuilding the Teatro Grande by granting them an annual lottery, whose top prize was 3 *contos de réis*. before: On 25 July 1808 the envoy of His Holiness in Lisbon arrived in Madeira by chance, coming from London. He landed at the Pontinha and went straight to the Cathedral, where he heard the ten o’clock Mass. After visiting the church, he got into a sedan chair and went on to the bishop’s palace. He left the island on the 28th. During his short stay he conferred minor orders on some students, since the bishop was not in Funchal, and gave the dean the powers needed to grant certain marriage dispensations. On his departure all the forts of the city fired salutes.

before: The origin of this parish’s name is well known. A family with the surname Canha, which settled there in the earliest days of colonisation, gave its lands the name Canhas. The name later passed to the future parish, of which those same lands were the ancient, original nucleus. Some assert, among them the authoritative commentator of the *Historia Insulana*, that João de Canha, squire to the Duke of Viseu, Dom Diogo, was one of the first settlers of Canhas. He held lands there by *sesmaria* (royal land grant to settlers on condition of cultivation), which he leased on a perpetual tenure to Dona Constança Rodrigues de Almeida, widow of João Gonçalves Zarco; and his son Rui Pires de Canha founded the chantry (capela) of São Tiago, where the seat of the parish was later established. The illustrious annotator of the *Saudades da Terra*, however, holds that Rui Pires de Canha was an earlier settler than João de Canha, without indicating what degree of kinship there may have been between the two men. The more common view, shared by several genealogies we have consulted, is that João de Canha settled there first, and that Rui Pires de Canha was one of his descendants who also acquired various lands within the bounds of this future parish.

Some assert, among them the authoritative commentator of the ‘Island History’ (*Historia Insulana*), that João de Canha, squire to the Diogo, Duke of Viseu, was one of the first settlers of Canhas. He held lands there by *sesmaria* (royal land grant to settlers on condition of cultivation), which he leased on a perpetual tenure to Dona Constança Rodrigues de Almeida, widow of João Gonçalves Zarco; and his son Rui Pires de Canha founded the chantry (capela) of São Tiago, where the seat of the parish was later established. The illustrious annotator of the ‘Longing for the Homeland’ (*Saudades da Terra*), however, holds that Rui Pires de Canha was an earlier settler than João de Canha, without indicating what degree of kinship there may have been between the two men. The more common view, shared by several genealogies we have consulted, is that João de Canha settled there first, and that Rui Pires de Canha was one of his descendants who also acquired various lands within the bounds of this future parish.

before: There is a small landing place there, called the Porto dos Anjos because it lies in the locality of that name, and in this locality stands a chapel known by its dedication to Nossa Senhora dos Anjos. The parish’s trade and passenger traffic pass mainly through the town (*vila*) and landing place of Ponta do Sol. Although it may be considered an inland settlement, since the sea washes only a very insignificant part of its coast, it is nevertheless a manufacturing centre of some importance, far ahead of a great many other coastal parishes. There are four butter factories, one cheese factory, two spirit (*aguardente*, distilled from sugar cane or wine) distilleries, one sawmill and one pasta factory.

before: It was not Melo, however, who invented the story of Machim, for before him, beginning with António Galvão (1563), several writers had referred to it. He sought to give it the standing of historical truth by basing his narrative on a manuscript which he claimed to possess, written by Francisco Alcoforado, one of the companions of João Gonçalves Zarco. Dr Álvaro Rodrigues de Azevedo himself, who treats Dom Francisco Manuel with so little indulgence, admits that he may have been deceived in good faith regarding the existence of this manuscript. Yet there is not the slightest doubt that he gave free rein to his ardent imagination in the account of the discovery of Madeira that he left us in his third *Epanaphora*.

before: The same illustrious annotator also maintains, though with less weighty arguments, that Dom Francisco Manuel de Melo collaborated with Queen Luisa de Guzmán in the plan for that cession by writing his *Epanaphora* and presenting Madeira as discovered by Englishmen, so as to make its handover to England more feasible and less odious to the Portuguese. It is only fair to hear Edgar Prestage, the learned biographer of Dom Francisco Manuel de Melo: ‘… the annotator of the *Saudades da Terra* of Gaspar Frutuoso alleges that Dom Francisco, having received the legend of the island’s discovery by the two English lovers Roberto Machim and Anna de Arfet, turned it into a romance in order to popularise this story and make the handover of Madeira to Charles II of England less hard on Portuguese pride, should that prove necessary. Now in our view this argument is somewhat forced, not to say fantastic, and Mr A. R. de Azevedo, in order to sustain it, has to press the charge further, saying that the *Epanaphora*, which in the printed book is dated from Belas in 1654, was deliberately antedated, having been written after Dom Francisco’s return from Brazil. But he forgets that he has previously stated that the *Epanaphora* shows, on its author’s part, an ignorance of the island’s topography, a circumstance that was natural in 1654 but could hardly have arisen afterwards, since, as we have already related, Dom Francisco stayed there for a month on his way into exile.

before: Rui Gonçalves da Câmara, the second son of the illustrious discoverer of Madeira, was the third captain of the island of São Miguel, having bought that important donatary captaincy (*donataria*) from João Soares. before: Each of the pilgrimage festivals held in Madeira, says the Revd Father Eduardo C. Nunes Pereira, ‘is distinguished by a special attraction for pilgrims, drawn from its general religious motive, its topography or its particular secular character. At Ponta Delgada, Monte and Arco da Calheta it is the vows; at Machico and Santa Cruz the processions on the eve, with burning candles; at Caniço, rosaries of dried pears; at Ribeira Brava, the *império* of offerings and the fisherman’s little boat; at Caniçal, the procession of boats; at Camacha, São Vicente, Porto do Moniz and Curral, the freedom of the countryside and the rustic character of the place’. before: But does settling this point really have any historical importance? Dr Álvaro Rodrigues de Azevedo answers this question in the following terms: ‘...it became important when, in 1868, the Englishman Richard Henry Major, in his work *The Life of Prince Henry of Portugal*, took seriously the false legend of the supposed Englishman Robert Machim and raised to the status of an argument the false etymology that derives Machico from Machim. He concluded that this legend was a real event, and that his Machim discovered the Madeira archipelago many years before Zarco and Tristão Vaz Teixeira landed there at the end of the first quarter of the 15th century. This opinion, which Major developed with artifice, relying on writings of no historical value, may in future be invoked as grounds for leonine claims – all the more plausibly since the Portuguese government and the Royal Academy of Sciences of Lisbon heaped naive honours on the author of this learned but reserved book, the *Life of Prince Henry*, whose aim seems to be none other than, while magnifying our legitimate maritime glories, to claim for England the precedence in the actual discovery of the Madeira archipelago. It is therefore worth unravelling the origin of the name Machico, setting historical probability against the inaccuracy spread by Major’.
