before: We cannot follow Dr Rodrigues de Azevedo in every detail of his long, learned and at times tedious account of the origin of this name. Once it is proved – and Dr Azevedo did so in the most complete and conclusive manner – that the Machim story is nothing but a pure and simple legend, it is also demonstrated that the name Machico cannot derive from the unfortunate Robert Machim, the hapless lover of the ill-fated Anne of Arfet. Dr Azevedo’s argument about this origin merely reinforces the force of his tight reasoning in proving that the legend is baseless, but it is not a new proof of the legend’s falsity. Moreover, the account of the Machim story first appears only a century after the discovery of the Madeiran archipelago, which in itself rules out even the mere probability that the name Machico could derive from Machim.

before: Two years after the publication of the *Saudades*, E. A. Bettencourt writes in his booklet entitled *Memoria sobre a descoberta das ilhas de Porto Santo e Madeira*: ‘Nor, in our view, can the name Machico, given to a place on the island of Madeira, serve as an argument for a stay of Englishmen on that island before the Portuguese arrived there. We shall note in the first place, without however making this our chief objection, that the name Machico may just as well be a corruption of Machim as a diminutive of *macho* [TN: Portuguese for a male mule or male animal]. The popular character of the Portuguese language does not stand in the way of this supposition. Zurara supports it when in his *Chronica* he calls it Machito, as does Melo himself when he names it Machino. For just as in Africa the point where in 1435 the discoverers landed two horses to ride them into the interior of the country came to be called “Angra dos Cavalos”, could not the name Machico, machito or machino likewise have been given to that place on Madeira for a similar reason?’ This opinion is rejected by Pinheiro Chagas and Dr Azevedo.

before: Seventeen years after the controversy between Pinheiro Chagas and Camilo Castelo Branco, General Brito Rebêlo published, in 1894, an interesting document that sheds much light on the subject with which we have been dealing, and to which we have already referred in vol. X of this work, on p. 174. If it is not decisive proof, it is without doubt the most acceptable presumption so far put forward concerning the origin of the word Machico. The document reads as follows: ‘Charter whereby the said lord gave some houses standing in the rua nova of Lisbon, bordering on houses of the captain-major and on Joham piriz canellas, to Machico, master of his barque, to dwell in for as long as it should be his pleasure, etc. At Alenquer, 12 days of April of the year one thousand and 1417 (1379).’ Archive of the Torre do Tombo, Book 2 of Ferdinand I, fol. 42. ‘From this document,’ adds General J. I. de Brito Rebelo, ‘there follows the positive fact of the existence in Portugal, in the year 1379 (1417), of a mariner of important rank named Machico; and once such a name is found, the origin of the name by which a certain spot on the island of Madeira was designated is found. Documents of this nature prove facts with complete evidence. It seems to me, therefore, that the following conjecture may be made: the Machico of whom the document speaks, or some descendant of his, went to the island of Madeira on the first or one of the first voyages; through old age, illness or some other mishap he died at a certain point on the coast; his companions buried him, marking the place with a rough wooden cross. This would be the cross that was placed in the original church when it was founded, and which legend later portrayed as taken from the grave of Machim; and the site would come to be called by the name of the first man who honoured with his remains the land until then uninhabited. However the event came about, in this way or another, a hitherto unknown document now raises from the oblivion of almost five centuries the name of the obscure mariner who, assisting in the enterprise to which Prince Henry the Navigator devoted himself, bequeathed his name to a place in one of the loveliest regions discovered through his zeal, and explains the origin of that name. Let the name of Machico, then, be inscribed on the list of the first discoverers. When, therefore, we cite and extol the names of Gonçalves Zarco and Perestrello, let us never forget that of poor Machico, who was perhaps the one who guided them on their bold and fortunate expedition.’

These lands of Ilha lie in the interior of this parish. before: The new parish took its name from a chapel dedicated to St George, which later became the parish church. This chapel seems to have been built in the last quarter of the 15th century or the early 16th century. The parish church was built in the locality (*sítio*) of Calhau, on one of the banks of the stream; we cannot at present say whether it stood on the same spot as the old chapel. Around 1660 the church was almost entirely destroyed by a flash flood (*aluvião*). It was then decided that the new church should be built on a safer and more sheltered site, one that would also be more convenient for the people, since the homesteads were spreading inland along the left bank of the stream.

before: The visitor’s eye is caught at once by the gilt carved woodwork (*talha dourada*) of the high altar and by the sacristy furniture made to hold the vestments and church furnishings. In several foreign works, especially in a piece by the Marquis Degli Albizzi, we find some references to these works of art. It is worth quoting here the words of Dr Alfredo Leal, recently (1921) published in a magazine of this city: ‘It is certainly one of the most beautiful churches in Madeira, above all for the richness of the gilt carved woodwork of the high altar, which is also the chapel of the Blessed Sacrament. It was in the sacristy, however, that I found an interesting feast for my eyes. The great table and the cupboards in til (*Ocotea foetens*, Madeiran laurel) or Madeira mahogany (vinhático, Persea indica), with turned columns in the style the French call *rococo portugais*, which is found in all the carved woodwork of the 17th and 18th centuries in Portugal, are very artistically executed, without the gilding that has been and still is so abused in Portuguese churches. It is astonishing how, in that sacristy and in some others in Madeira, these lovely carvings have escaped the barbarous brush of the makers of false marble, which imitates bar soap more than marble, as has so unfortunately happened to the slender columns of Funchal Cathedral (*Sé*). In the middle of the cupboards above the sacristy table, facing the place where the priest vests for the sacred mysteries of the altar, is a crucifix in which the body of Christ is perhaps a metre tall. It is one of the most beautiful wooden sculptures I have ever seen. It is a marvel in which anatomy and the expression of the face and gestures unite, producing a feeling that is tenderly grand.’

before: He was born in the parish (*freguesia*) of Câmara de Lobos on 1 March 1667, the son of Pedro Bettencourt Henriques and Dona Maria de Meneses, and succeeded to the entailed house (*casa vinculada*) of his uncle, the holder of the entail (*morgado*) Inácio de Bettencourt e Câmara. He was a highly cultivated mind and devoted himself especially to historical and genealogical studies, in which he had acquired a great wealth of knowledge, and he was regarded as a true authority on matters of Madeiran history. He sent several manuscript works to the Royal Academy of Portuguese History, and was consequently admitted to its membership. Diogo Barbosa Machado in the *Biliotheca Lusitana* and António Caetano de Sousa in the *Historia Genealogica da Casa Real Portuguesa* write approvingly of Henriques de Noronha’s works and refer to him in highly complimentary terms. He is credited with the *Memorias seculares e eclesiásticas para a composição da historia da diocese do Funchal*, mentioned in the *Saudades da Terra* on page 786, which we have also discussed at some length on pp. 389 and 390 of vol. I of this *Elucidário*. He wrote a *Nobiliário Genealógico* of Madeiran families, a nobiliary (book of noble genealogies) of which a three-volume copy exists in the library of the Municipal Council (*Câmara Municipal*) of this municipality (*concelho*), and which is held to be one of the most authoritative writings on the subject (see Nobiliaries).

before: Dr Álvaro Rodrigues de Azevedo calls him Dom Martinho de Aguiar, but in various chronicles and nobiliaries, and in Paiva Manso’s interesting memoir on the *Esquadras de Marrocos*, his name is generally given as Dom Nuno de Aguiar. He is said to have been born in the parish (*freguesia*) of São Martinho, the son of Diogo de Aguiar and grandson of João Gonçalves Zarco, the first captain-donatary (*capitão-donatário*) of Funchal. He was a Cistercian monk and held important ecclesiastical offices. He accompanied King Afonso V to Africa for the conquest of Arzila and Tangier, and when the latter diocese was created he secured his appointment as its prelate. He sought to annex the Madeira archipelago to his bishopric, but this was vigorously opposed by the Infanta Dona Beatriz, as guardian of her son Diogo, Duke of Viseu, Grand Master of the Order of Christ, who was supported by the monarch and by the donataries (*donatário*) of this island. Dom Nuno de Aguiar spent little time in his diocese, and after twenty years as bishop he died in mainland Portugal in 1491.

before: The damage from this flash flood was felt above all in the parish (*freguesia*) of Machico, where 26 people died and more than 80 dwellings collapsed. In the *Anno Histórico*, Father Francisco de Santa Maria, referring to the flood of 1724, says that ‘the island of Madeira suffered a storm and deluge so great that it destroyed the town (*vila*) of Machico, part of that of Santa Cruz and many other places and localities of the same island, and the city of Funchal also suffered great damage and much ruin, both to its walls and to the settlement, from the flooding of the Ribeira do Pinheiro (Santa Luzia) that divides it’.

before: Heavy rain swelled the streams that cross Funchal on this day, destroying the Ponte da Praça and causing considerable damage to other bridges in the city. The waters of the Ribeira da Praça, or Ribeira de João Gomes, swept the Englishman Moita (?) out to sea, and he was never seen again.
after: Heavy rain swelled the streams that cross Funchal on this day, destroying the Ponte da Praça (‘square bridge’) and causing considerable damage to other bridges in the city. The waters of the Ribeira da Praça, or Ribeira de João Gomes (‘João Gomes’s stream’), swept the Englishman Moita (?) out to sea, and he was never seen again.

before: The district of Santa Maria Maior suffered most from the storm. The João Gomes stream, swollen by the abundance and violence of its waters, burst its banks at three different points, forming as many raging currents that caused the greatest damage and claimed several dozen lives. Whole streets and countless dwellings and other buildings were swept into the sea, including the parish church, known as the church of Nossa Senhora do Calhau (Our Lady of Calhau), which stood on the left bank of the stream, between the present Rua de Santa Maria and Rua Nova de Santa Maria. In one house in this street 21 people were buried alive, and in a building on the Pelourinho a British subject and 15 members of his household died. It is estimated that in the district of Santa Maria Maior alone about 200 people perished in the flood.
after: The district of Santa Maria Maior (‘St Mary Major’) suffered most from the storm. Whole streets and countless dwellings and other buildings were swept into the sea, including the parish church, known as the church of Our Lady of Calhau (*Nossa Senhora do Calhau*), which stood on the left bank of the stream, between the present Rua de Santa Maria and Rua Nova de Santa Maria (‘new street of St Mary’). In one house in this street 21 people were buried alive, and in a building on the Pelourinho (‘pillory’) a British subject and 15 members of his household died. It is estimated that in the district of Santa Maria Maior alone about 200 people perished in the flood.

before: The buildings along the Santa Luzia stream also suffered badly. Above the Ponte do Bom Jesus the waters cut new courses along both banks, and caused considerable damage, above all in Rua dos Ferreiros, where several dwellings and shops collapsed. The same happened in Rua dos Tanoeiros and to various buildings on the left bank of that stream which formed Rua Direita; these were swept away by the violence of the current. A contemporary account of the event says: ‘Whole streets disappeared with their inhabitants, and others, flooded with water and mud, left owners and tenants reduced to extreme destitution. A large part of the parish of Santa Maria Maior, together with its church, the oldest in the city, no longer exists, along with a good many of its unfortunate inhabitants; the rest, scattered here and there, flooded and abandoned, presents to the eyes of the feeling man a spectacle of grief, ruin and dismay. The streets called Direita, Tanoeiros, Valverde, Santa Maria, Hospital Velho and others were carried into the sea with an incredible multitude of inhabitants.’

before: Of the town (*vila*) of Machico, the archive of its parish church records the following: ‘…it demolished the wall of the stream, brought down the bridge and invaded the town so that the waters rose to a height of three *côvados* in the church and in all the streets. This flood threatened everyone with death; but an evident miracle saved them all, except fourteen people who perished, swept away by the waters or buried in their houses.’ It also demolished the ancient and historic chapel of Senhor dos Milagres (Lord of Miracles). Its image was found some days later on the high seas by an American full-rigged ship, which had it placed in Funchal Cathedral (Sé do Funchal).

before: The main cause of the harm done by the flood was the lack of channelling of the streams. Belatedly, the government in mainland Portugal resolved to carry out this long-desired improvement, sending to Madeira Brigadier Reinaldo Oudinot to direct the works; he arrived here on 19 February 1804. He showed the greatest competence in the post entrusted to him and worked in it with astonishing energy, managing within a relatively short time to channel the three streams that run through Funchal. In December 1800 he reported to the central government that, despite the great storms and severe winter weather there had been shortly before, the walls had withstood the violent impact of the waters and given clear proof of the solidity of their construction. Oudinot died in this city on 11 February 1807, and in memory of his services his name was given to the street on the left bank of the João Gomes stream, between Campo da Barca and Praça dos Lavradores.

before: One interesting detail: since the chancel of the church of Nossa Senhora do Calhau had been left standing, the royal warrant (*provisão régia*) of 12 March 1805 ordered that it be preserved in the state in which the flash flood had left it, as a reminder for future generations of the event that had been the most calamitous ever to befall the inhabitants of this island. In December 1835 the part of the church that the flash flood had spared was demolished, and the União market was built on the site. The market was recently pulled down to widen the street that runs past it.

before: As had happened on other occasions, it was the raging currents of the streams that caused the greatest damage. Especially at certain points along the banks where there were no walls to contain and direct the flow, the waters burst out of their beds, swept over the adjoining land and cut a new course through streets and houses. They caused not only incalculable damage but also the utmost panic among the inhabitants, some of whom fell victim to the untameable force of the current. This is what happened with the waters of the Ribeira de São João, which, seeking a new course, violently swept away some twenty houses between the Ponte de São Paulo, at the end of Rua da Carreira, and the mouth of the stream.

before: On 11 February 1916 the deputies the Viscount of Ribeira Brava, Dr Carlos Olavo Correia de Azevedo, Captain Américo Olavo Correia de Azevedo and Captain Manuel da Costa Dias introduced in the Cortes (Portuguese parliament) three bills: to grant autonomy to the Agricultural Council (*Junta Agrícola*), to reform the so-called *colonia* contract (Madeiran sharecropping tenancy; produce divided, improvements owned by the tenant), and to sell at public auction the levadas that the State owned on this island, which were by then already in the possession of the Agricultural Council. Such opposition arose in Madeira against these bills that they were never even admitted to parliamentary debate.

before: The importance of this archipelago is set out concisely but strikingly in the following words from the authoritative pen of Dr Álvaro Rodrigues de Azevedo, the learned annotator of the *Saudades da Terra*: ‘This archipelago has been the object of study by learned naturalists, both foreign and Portuguese. It is celebrated, especially the island of Madeira, for the fertility of its soil, its excellent wines, the breathtaking beauty of its landscape and the healthiness of its climate. It is historically notable as the first of the Portuguese discoveries in the 15th century and, afterwards, until the close of the 16th century, as the secular and ecclesiastical metropolis of our overseas dominions and the emporium of our colonial navigation and commerce. For this reason the Madeiran archives, especially those of the Municipal Council (*Câmara Municipal*) of Funchal, of Machico, of the former and now extinct Treasury Board (*Junta da Fazenda*) and of the Civil Government of Funchal, hold precious documents and records, perhaps not to be found elsewhere, for the history of the institutions and government of our possessions beyond the sea’.

before: The archipelago lies between Western Europe, which faces it to the north-east, the Moroccan coast of West Africa, which runs from east to south-east of it, the Azores archipelago to the north-west, and that of the Canary Islands to the south. The nearest point of the Moroccan west coast to the Madeiran archipelago is Cape Cantin, which lies at roughly the same latitude as Madeira and is equidistant, about 60 miles, from the cities of Mazagan to the north and Mogadouro to the south. The archipelago is approximately 500 miles from mainland Portugal and 350 from Cape Cantin, on the west coast of Africa. The relative positions of the islands of Madeira and Porto Santo and the Desertas group form a scalene triangle. Its shortest side is the channel between Ilhéu de Fora, at the eastern tip of Madeira (Ponta de São Lourenço), and the Prego do Mar or Ilhéu do Navio, near Ilhéu Chão (Flat Islet) in the Desertas. The next longest side is formed by the channel (Travessa) running from the said Ilhéu de Fora (Ponta de São Lourenço) to Ilhéu de Baixo or da Cal (Porto Santo). The longest side is the channel stretching from the aforementioned Ilhéu de Baixo or da Cal (Porto Santo) to the Prego do Mar or Ilhéu Chão (Desertas). The channels measure 11, 27 and 32 miles respectively, which are the distances separating Madeira, Porto Santo and the Desertas group from one another.

before: The lands that make up the parish of Boaventura belonged for almost three centuries to the parish of Ponta Delgada, from which they were separated in 1836. Boaventura has borne this name since the middle of the 16th century, and even before that time, and therefore long before the creation of the curacy (*curato*) and before it became an independent parish. In the early days of colonisation, Pedro Gomes Galdo was one of the first settlers to hold extensive lands there by *sesmaria* (royal land grant to settlers on condition of cultivation). He is regarded as one of the earliest colonists of this parish, which at that time, as already stated, belonged to the parish of Ponta Delgada. The foundation of the chantry (capela) of São Cristóvão (St Christopher), in the locality that still bears this name today, is attributed to this Pedro Galdo or to one of his descendants.

before: The parish has several levadas (irrigation channels): the levadas of Achada Grande, built mainly through the efforts of Policarpo José de Abreu and Manuel João de Freitas Galdo; the Levada Grande, whose irrigation extends as far as Ponta Delgada; the Levada das Faias, which owes much of its course to João Pedro de Andrade; the Levada da Achada dos Alves e Pastel, whose construction was begun by the same Policarpo José de Abreu; and also the levada of Achada or of Serrão. All of them rise in the Ribeira dos Moinhos. As we have already said in the article devoted to the parish of Arco de São Jorge, many years ago a levada was planned that would draw its water from the Ribeira do Porco, at the locality (*sítio*) of Falca, and serve to irrigate both parishes; the necessary surveys and estimates were even carried out at the beginning of the last quarter of the 19th century. It never went beyond the planning stage, although Canon Feliciano João Teixeira, deputy for Madeira, championed the idea in parliament during the legislative session of 1890.

before: The Lício family, holders of the entail (*morgado*) of Lagos, had entailed lands (*terras vinculadas*) in this parish, and in the locality (*sítio*) of Silveira they built a large house, which was never entirely finished. It was with the factor (*feitor*) of these holders of the entail and of these lands, who lived in Boaventura, that the following interesting and picturesque incident is said to have occurred. General Beresford had arrived in Madeira in December 1807, in command of the British troops that occupied Madeira for the second time. All the authorities and commissioned officers went to pay their respects to the English general. Colonel Lício, holder of the entail, could be no exception to the rule: he commanded the militia regiment of São Vicente and was then staying on his lands at Boaventura. The factor, who happened to be in Funchal and was the lieutenant adjutant of that regiment, persuaded the lady of the entail (*morgada*), Colonel Lício’s wife, that it would be wise to spare her husband the discomforts of a journey. He put forward the sensible suggestion that he himself should don the colonel’s uniform and present himself to the English general as the commander of the militia regiment of the town (*vila*) of São Vicente! The idea, promptly conceived and accepted without reluctance by the lady of the entail, was put into effect without delay by the good and simple-minded factor. When Beresford learnt that before him stood a raw adjutant disguised as a colonel, he curtly uttered what were perhaps the only words of Portuguese he then knew: ‘Para o Pico’ (To the Pico). And off went our poor lieutenant and factor, led under guard to the Pico fortress (*Fortaleza do Pico*), no doubt cursing the hour he had the unhappy idea of donning the uniform belonging to his chief, the owner of the lands he managed. As he turned his back on General Beresford, however, he came out with a phrase that became famous and, to some extent, immortalised him in local tradition. When he realised the mistake he had made, he let slip, half rueful and half ironic, this inspired remark: ‘I could see straight away this would end in a blunder!’ That was the epilogue to his sad and unfortunate adventure.

before: In the parish (*freguesia*) of Ribeira Brava, a short distance from the parish church, there stood a chapel dedicated to St Joseph which, according to the annotator of *Saudades da Terra*, was founded by Luís Gonçalves da Silva in 1710. Around 1905 it was still standing, though in an advanced state of ruin, and bore the date 1709 above its doorway. On 15 April 1750 a licence was granted for it to be blessed, and its administrator at the time was Second Lieutenant Tomé João Pimentel. Was it only blessed in 1750, or was this a rebuilding? We do not know. It is certain, however, that the licence for the blessing was granted on 15 April 1750, as we were able to verify from an authentic document.

before: In the parish of Calheta there was a chapel dedicated to São José, whose founder and date we cannot determine. We do know, however, that the earthquake of 1748 left it badly damaged and that Francisco Agostinho de Figueiroa e Vasconcelos, its administrator and administrator of the entail attached to it, had it rebuilt in 1776, moving it to a safer site but close to the original building. So that services could be held in it, it was inspected by the ecclesiastical authorities on 3 June 1776.

before: The projection on Madeira’s north coast that juts furthest out to sea is called Ponta de São Jorge and lies on the coast of the parish of the same name. From the tip of this headland, at the spot known as the Vigia, every twist and turn of the coastline can be seen, from the parish of Porto da Cruz to that of Porto do Moniz, and this village (*lugar*, settlement rank below a town) deserves a visit. At the spot known as Ponta Gorda a quay was built between 1904 and 1910; a footpath links it to the main road that connects the parishes of Santana and São Jorge.
after: The projection on Madeira’s north coast that juts furthest out to sea is called Ponta de São Jorge (‘St George Point’) and lies on the coast of the parish of the same name. From the tip of this headland, at the spot known as the Vigia (‘lookout’), every twist and turn of the coastline can be seen, from the parish of Porto da Cruz (‘harbour of the cross’) to that of Porto Moniz (‘Moniz’s harbour’), and this village (*lugar*, settlement rank below a town) deserves a visit. At the spot known as Ponta Gorda (‘broad point’) a quay was built between 1904 and 1910; a footpath links it to the main road that connects the parishes of Santana (‘St Anne’) and São Jorge.

before: The stream rises near Pico Ruivo and crosses the parish of São Jorge, flowing into the sea at the landing place of the same name. Its tributaries are the Canário, Grande and Lombo da Furna brooks.
after: The stream rises near Pico Ruivo (‘russet peak’) and crosses the parish of São Jorge, flowing into the sea at the landing place of the same name. Its tributaries are the Canário, Grande and Lombo da Furna brooks.

before: A small spring near the foot of Pico Ruivo, at about 1870 metres above sea level. In summer it yields very little water. We believe there is no other spring in Madeira situated as high as that of Barreiro. Its water, which we had occasion to drink in the months of July and August, is clear and very cold.

before: It is also known as the Lombada da Ponta do Sol, because it lies in the parish (*freguesia*) of that name. This must have been its original name. Only when it passed to João Esmeraldo and his descendants, as administrators of the entailed estate (*morgadio*) founded there, did it take the name Lombada dos Esmeraldos. To avoid needless repetition, we refer the reader to the article devoted to João Esmeraldo (vol. 1, p. 410), where we have already given a detailed account of this great property, which was and still is the largest on the whole island. We shall add only a few details not mentioned there. In the earliest days of the colonisation, the discoverer João Gonçalves Zarco reserved for himself and his sons several *lombadas* (long ridges between valleys) and extensive tracts of land, almost all of which became important and flourishing entailed houses. Rui Gonçalves da Câmara (see vol. 1, p. 206), the second or third son of Zarco, received the great *lombada* that ran from the sea to the uplands and stretched from the Ribeira da Caixa to the Ribeira da Ponta do Sol. We do not know how long he held this property or what farming he may have carried out on it. Contrary to what is stated in the article on João Esmeraldo, it was in 1473 that Esmeraldo bought, or rather leased, that vast and highly fertile land from Rui Gonçalves da Câmara for the sum of 600,000 *réis* (old Portuguese money of account; 1$000 = 1,000 réis, 1:000$000 = one conto = 1,000,000 réis) and a life annuity of 150,000 *réis*. This was the year before Rui Gonçalves went to settle in the Azores, for the chronicles of that archipelago give as certain his departure for the island of São Miguel in 1474.

Rui Gonçalves da Câmara (see vol. 1, p. 206), the second or third son of Zarco, received the great *lombada* that ran from the sea to the uplands and stretched from the Ribeira da Caixa to the Ribeira da Ponta do Sol. We do not know how long he held this property or what farming he may have carried out on it. Contrary to what is stated in the article on João Esmeraldo, it was in 1473 that Esmeraldo bought, or rather leased, that vast and highly fertile land from Rui Gonçalves da Câmara for the sum of 600,000 *réis* (old Portuguese money of account; 1$000 = 1,000 réis, 1:000$000 = one conto = 1,000,000 réis) and a life annuity of 150,000 *réis*. This was the year before Rui Gonçalves went to settle in the Azores, for the chronicles of that archipelago give as certain his departure for the island of São Miguel in 1474.

before: João Soares de Albergaria, 2nd captain and donatary of São Miguel, accompanied his wife to Madeira, where she died. Father António Cordeiro, in the *Historia Insulana*, says that, wishing to thank Rui Gonçalves da Câmara for ‘the great hospitality he had shown him’, he decided to sell him his donatary captaincy (*donataria*), and at so low a price, adds Gaspar Frutuoso, ‘that he ceded it for eight hundred thousand *réis* in cash and four thousand *arrobas* of sugar’. It is said that the sale, or rather the emphyteutic lease (*aforamento*, perpetual lease for an annual quit-rent), of the *lombada* of Ponta do Sol was intended to fund the purchase of the donatary captaincy of the island of São Miguel, which seems very likely.

before: As already outlined in the articles cited, João Esmeraldo married twice, and in 1522 he founded two entailed estates (*morgadio*) in favour of the two sons born of these marriages. The entailed estate of Vale da Bica comprised the eastern half of the *lombada* (long ridge between valleys); that of Santo Espírito comprised the western half. The dividing line ran from Pico das Pedras, near the Paul da Serra, down the municipality (*concelho*) road to the crown of Pico da Amendoeira, and from there to the sea. Once the division had been made, lots were drawn: the entail (*morgado*) of Vale da Bica fell to João Esmeraldo de Vasconcelos, son of the first marriage, and that of Santo Espírito to Cristóvão Esmeraldo, son of the second. Doubts arose over this division, and long lawsuits followed which, with intervals, were renewed over the years; these seemingly interminable legal disputes lasted for more than a century. They gave rise to curious episodes and incidents, which Councillor (conselheiro, honorary title of the royal council) Agostinho de Ornelas, the last holder of the entailed estate of Vale da Bica, briefly describes in an interesting article published in no. 237 of the newspaper *A Verdade* of 16 October 1897.

before: There Esmeraldo built a chapel dedicated to the Espírito Santo (Holy Spirit), also called the chapel of the Conceição, which was consecrated by Bishop João Lobo in 1508 and became the seat of this entailed estate. The present church is a rebuilding from the first half of the 18th century, and it is the largest, most elegant and richest chapel in the whole diocese. Worthy of admiration and esteem is the dado of *azulejos* (painted glazed tiles) lining the lower part of the chapel’s interior walls, which depicts in symbolic figures the Gifts and the Fruits of the Holy Spirit. It has five altars and contains several exquisitely carved images. Nearby stands the vast, ruined manor house, once the most splendid country house in Madeira, rebuilt around 1679 by Luís Esmeraldo de Atouguia, holder of the entail. The last representative of this entailed foundation (*instituição vincular*, a morgado or capela) was the 2nd Count of Carvalhal, who displayed there the brilliance and magnificence with which he used to adorn his dazzling and lavish festivities. In this locality (*sítio*), at the place called Passo, are one of the two parish cemeteries and the ruins of an old chapel dedicated to Santo Amaro (St Maurus), whose construction is likewise attributed to João Esmeraldo. See *A Lombada dos Esmeraldos na Ilha da Madeira* by Father Fernando A. Silva.

before: The law of 27 July 1893, which authorised the government to subsidise a regular steam navigation service between Lisbon and the Adjacent Islands (*Ilhas Adjacentes*), also allowed support for a similar service between the islands of each of the two archipelagos. Under a provisional contract of 30 November of that year, concluded between the government and the trading firm Bensaúde & C.ª, regular sailings were established between Madeira and Porto Santo, made by the small steamer *Falcão*, belonging to the Blandy house of Funchal. Towards the end of 1897 this firm began a coastal navigation service between Funchal and various landing places on the south and north coasts of Madeira. It was one of the most notable benefits ever conferred on the principal settlements of the whole island.

before: He was born in the parish (*freguesia*) of Ponta Delgada on 5 December 1827, the son of Captain António Joaquim Gonçalves de Freitas and Eulália Cândida de Freitas, and died in Lisbon on 14 July 1875. He graduated in law from the University of Coimbra (*Universidade de Coimbra*) in 1848, having earned several distinctions and shown himself a highly talented and diligent student. From 1852 to 1860 he practised as a lawyer in Funchal and devoted himself to politics and journalism. He was deputy for Madeira in the three legislatures from 1860 to 1865. Settling in the capital, he held several public offices there, among them that of director-general of direct taxation. He was regarded as a great authority on the administration of public finance, in which he specialised. More than once he was invited to take a ministerial portfolio, at a time when not everyone could aspire to one, but he always refused to accept a post of such great responsibility. He enjoyed great prestige in Lisbon, not only for his intellectual gifts and acknowledged competence but also for the austere qualities of character that ennobled his spirit. He was one of the most distinguished Madeirans of the 19th century.

before: This locality was first called Ponta do Tristão, a name which then covered the land corresponding to the present parishes of Seixal, Ribeira da Janela, Porto Moniz, Achadas da Cruz, and perhaps also part of Ponta do Pargo. Once the chapel of Nossa Senhora da Conceição (Our Lady of the Immaculate Conception) had been founded, the place took the name of that chapel with the addition ‘da Ponta do Tristão’; the learned annotator of the *Saudades* states that the parish is so named in the royal letter (*carta régia*) of 12 March 1574. Dr Álvaro de Azevedo also says that in the letter of 1 March 1577 it is already given the name of Porto do Moniz, which is the one that prevailed and endured. Francisco Moniz was of noble descent and a native of the Algarve. Some genealogists say that he married, on this island, Filipa da Câmara, daughter of Garcia Rodrigues da Câmara, who was the natural son of the discoverer João Gonçalves Zarco. As we said in the article devoted to the parish of Achadas da Cruz, Garcia da Câmara owned a great deal of *sesmaria* land at Ponta do Tristão, granted to him by his father, and it is not unreasonable to conjecture that Francisco Moniz shared, by inheritance, in the ownership of those lands. The approximate period in which Francisco Moniz made his first settlement in this locality is unknown; Dr Rodrigues de Azevedo first gives 1535 as the year of his death, and later 1533.

before: Since Francisco Moniz died in 1533 or 1535, the chapel of Nossa Senhora da Conceição (Our Lady of the Conception), which he founded, must predate that year, but the year of its construction is unknown. The chapel underwent several alterations and was demolished after the new church was built on a different site. It is said in some source, and local tradition held, that the move was made to place the church in greater safety from the raids of the corsairs who at times infested those waters. Work on the new building began in 1660, but it was only in 1668 that it was declared entirely finished. It is of simple architecture and bare of any works of art. It should be noted, however, that the chapel of the Blessed Sacrament, built later, shows good artistic taste and contrasts with the other decorations of the church. This chapel is owed to Captain Manuel Rodrigues Ferreira Ferro, who died in 1717 and was buried in it as its founder.

before: Referring in 1590 to the parish we are discussing, Gaspar Frutuoso says the following: ‘Half a league from Seixal lies Magdalena, which is a parish of thirty households, with much growing of grain and plenty of water. This parish lies inland, nearly half a league, at Ponta do Tristão...’ These few words contain several inaccuracies. The parish is not that of Magdalena but of Porto do Moniz, the former name referring to a locality that has an old chapel dedicated to Santa Maria Madalena. Porto do Moniz is not merely half a league from Seixal, nor does it lie half a league inland at Ponta do Tristão for someone coming from the Seixal side, as the author describes. The royal decrees that regulated the stipend (*côngrua*) of parish priests show that Porto Moniz could not have had only thirty households (*fogos*, literally ‘hearths’) at that time, but approximately a hundred or even more. In 1611, that is, twenty-one years later, Achadas da Cruz alone already had about twenty households.

before: We mentioned above that, according to tradition, the site for the parish church was chosen because it placed the church in a better position to escape the raids of corsairs, which is not hard to believe. The Moors of the Moroccan coast at times attacked the island of Porto Santo and some settlements on the Madeiran coast. It may be presumed that Porto do Moniz did not escape the corsairs’ plunder, since it was one of the places in Madeira closest to their point of departure, although we have no reliable record of these raids by Moroccan pirates. We have read somewhere (1921) that at the top of the town, in the place called Pedra Mole, one can still see today the remains of caves dug into the clay, where the wealthier inhabitants are said to have hidden their church furnishings and valuables whenever the corsairs approached the coast. To prevent these incursions and drive off the raiding ships, a fort was built in this parish; according to the annotator of the *Saudades*, it was the best on the north coast. It was Captain Manuel Rodrigues Ferreira Ferro, already referred to, who paid all the costs of building this fort, the State contributing only the guns and the rest of its artillery equipment. It bore the name of São João Baptista (St John the Baptist), and we are told that the stone tablet bearing the inscription recording the date and the founder of this small fort is kept in one of the military offices housed in the Palácio de São Lourenço (St Lawrence Palace).

before: In the parish of Caniço, the disturbances provoked by the supposed meeting of the parish council (*junta de paróquia*) also reached the gravest proportions, with the most tragic consequences. On 22 November 1887 a considerable number of the parish’s inhabitants invaded the parish priest’s house, on the pretext that the parish council was meeting there. before: Everyone knows that our Cathedral (Sé Catedral) was honoured as a metropolitan see and that it was the seat of an archdiocese. Its existence, however, was short-lived. Created in 1533, it had already been abolished by 1551. Our ever-growing colonial and maritime expansion from the beginning of the 15th century, together with the settlement and exploitation of the newly discovered lands, led first to the establishment of the bishopric of Funchal in 1514 and, twenty years later, to the creation of the dioceses of Angra, Cape Verde, São Tomé and Goa. Before these latter bishoprics were created, the idea arose of establishing an archdiocese to serve as the seat of an ecclesiastical province, with those dioceses, and any others that might later be created, as its suffragans. Funchal, as the first bishopric established outside mainland Portugal, was chosen as the seat of the new archdiocese, which comprised the aforementioned dioceses of Angra, Cape Verde, São Tomé and Goa. The Archbishop of Funchal extended his spiritual jurisdiction from the Madeiran archipelago to the farthest reaches of the East.

before: We do not know the date of the papal bull creating the archdiocese. In the *Corpo Diplomático Português* we find the consistorial schedules of 31 January and 11 February 1533: the first communicates to John III the establishment of the archdiocese, and the second concerns the appointment of the first archbishop, who was Dom Martinho de Portugal. The bull of creation is not included there. However, since the consistorial schedules announcing such an event generally bore the date of the creation itself, we shall not stray far from the truth in stating that the archdiocese was established by a bull of 31 January 1533 and that Dom Martinho de Portugal was appointed archbishop by a bull of 11 February of the same year.

before: The four ‘maces’ that, even today, are carried by clerics before the prelate at great ceremonies in our Funchal Cathedral (*Sé*) are the only trace that the archdiocese has left here. These ‘maces’ symbolised the four suffragan bishoprics that belonged to the archbishopric of Funchal. Once the archdiocese was abolished, Funchal reverted to the simple status of a bishopric. To its jurisdiction over the Madeira archipelago was added the castle of Arguin, on the coast of Senegal, which some years later ceased to belong to this diocese.

before: – Funchal Cathedral (Sé Catedral do Funchal) was the only building regarded as a National Monument (*monumento nacional*), although there were other buildings that ought to have been included in that category. The *Diário do Governo* of 24 September 1940 and of 18 August 1943 published the complete lists of the buildings classified as National Monuments and as ‘properties of public interest’ throughout our country. As regards this district, the following were declared National Monuments in addition to the Cathedral: the Palácio de São Lourenço (St Lawrence Palace), the church and outbuildings of the convent of Santa Clara, the church of São Evangelista (the Colégio) and the Customs House (*Casa da Alfândega*).
after: – Funchal Cathedral (the Sé) (*Sé do Funchal*) was the only building regarded as a National Monument (*monumento nacional*), although there were other buildings that ought to have been included in that category. As regards this district, the following were declared National Monuments in addition to the Cathedral (*Sé Catedral*): the São Lourenço Palace (‘St Lawrence’), the church and outbuildings of the Convent of St Clare (*Santa Clara*), the church of São Evangelista (the College) and the Customs House (*Casa da Alfândega*).

before: In the national assembly, where he sat as a deputy for many years, he brilliantly upheld the reputation as a distinguished jurist and orator that had preceded him. It was perhaps, however, as a member of various parliamentary committees and as rapporteur of countless bills that he revealed his qualities as a distinguished parliamentarian. He would several times have held a ministerial portfolio had he not always sought to avoid joining any cabinet. The work of his law office, which frequently handled cases of great importance, some of them notoriously celebrated, his regular attendance at the sessions of the Higher Council of Instruction and his work on parliamentary committees systematically kept him away from the grave concerns and heavy responsibilities that a minister’s portfolio would have brought him. ‘It was for this reason,’ we read somewhere, ‘that in Justino de Freitas, besides remarkable talent, served by an uncommon learning in forensic matters, there was something like the artistic inspiration of advocacy; and in the last years of his life, more than the interests of that honourable and glorious profession, it was a fanatical love of the practice of jurisprudence that kept him at the advocate’s bench.’

before: In 1803 the flash flood (*aluvião*) swept the chantry (capela) of the Misericórdia and the adjoining house into the sea, and with them its archive, so that we lack the essential material for writing a historical account of this institution. We can nevertheless say, from some data provided by the *Anais do Município*, that its functioning was governed by the statutes (*compromisso*) of the Misericórdia of Lisbon. Its administration seems always to have left much to be desired, and the benefits it gave the poor were not great. It is certain, however, that besides the president (provedor) and board member it came to have two clerks, two collectors, a keeper of the strongbox, two procurators of the poor and two informants. This bureaucratic apparatus, though perhaps unpaid, did not prevent many quit-rents and properties from being lost, especially after their title deeds were destroyed by the flood at the beginning of the 19th century.

before: Originally it had no hospital, only a chantry that served as the seat of the brotherhood, which we have already discussed at some length (vol. 1, p. 332) and to which we shall return in the article Capela de Cristo. The beneficed cleric (*beneficiado*) of the collegiate church of Machico, Father Inácio Barbosa da Silva, by public deed of 20 May 1748, bequeathed to the confraternity some houses he owned in the locality of Banda de Além, so that a hospital could be set up in them and they could serve as the Misericórdia’s building, since the confraternity had no building intended for that purpose. We can give no information on the running of the hospital; the said *Anais* state that those houses passed into the possession of the Confraternity of the Santíssimo Sacramento of the parish (*freguesia*) of Caniço, for reasons unknown. In 1856 the Misericórdia leased a property to house a hospital, which played an important role during the cholera epidemic and was closed around 1862.
after: Originally it had no hospital, only a chantry that served as the seat of the brotherhood, which we have already discussed at some length (vol. 1, p. 332) and to which we shall return in the article chapel of Christ (*Cristo*). The beneficed cleric (*beneficiado*) of the collegiate church of Machico, Father Inácio Barbosa da Silva, by public deed of 20 May 1748, bequeathed to the confraternity some houses he owned in the locality of Banda de Além (‘the far side’), so that a hospital could be set up in them and they could serve as the Misericórdia’s building, since the confraternity had no building intended for that purpose. We can give no information on the running of the hospital; the said ‘Annals of the Municipality’ state that those houses passed into the possession of the Confraternity of the Blessed Sacrament (*Santíssimo Sacramento*) of the parish (*freguesia*) of Caniço (‘reed’), for reasons unknown. In 1856 the Misericórdia leased a property to house a hospital, which played an important role during the cholera epidemic and was closed around 1862.

before: One of the most zealous presidents of the Misericórdia of Machico was Captain Cristóvão Esmeraldo, elected to that office in 1810. Besides his good service in running the brotherhood, he did much to rebuild the chapel, which the flash flood of 9 October 1803 had destroyed. Another president who rendered no less notable service to this institution was the vicar of that town, Father Manuel José da Paixão. He obtained several certificates for properties and quit-rents and returned to the Misericórdia’s possession some assets already considered lost by then.

before: At Rabaçal, the locality (*sítio*) that travellers explore so enthusiastically for the superb scenery it offers, the damage was not total, and the houses suffered nothing, thanks to the effort and dedication devoted to saving them. At Monte and São Roque the fire took on truly frightening proportions, covering an area of several kilometres and threatening to destroy a great number of dwellings. At Bica da Cana, on the Paul da Serra, the plantations laid out there by the Agricultural Board (*Junta Agrícola*) were badly damaged.

before: In the Ribeiro do Meio, in the valley of São Jorge, at about 300 metres above sea level, two seams or deposits of impure lignite have been known for many years. This lignite is associated with various layers of tuff and clay, in one of which fossil leaves of dicotyledons and ferns were found in abundance. Since a thick layer of basalt and scoria, more than 300 metres high, rests on top of the deposits, it seems evident that abundant land vegetation once existed at the spot, long before the volcanic formations that now cover it.

before: As we say elsewhere, two tombstones were recently found in the chancel of the church of Santa Clara (St Clare of Assisi). The one in the middle of the chancel bears the epitaph of the 2nd captain-donatary of Funchal, and the one on the Epistle side carries two funerary inscriptions relating to the 3rd and 5th donataries (*donatário*), with some struck-through lines between them whose letters are completely illegible. It is very strange that, although the 4th captain-donatary died in Funchal and was buried in the church of Santa Clara, the family vault of the captains-donatary, the stone that should cover his grave is not to be found there, nor can his epitaph be read on the tombstones of his father and grandfather.

before: Besides contributing to various newspapers, in both prose and verse, he has published the short poems *A Escola*, Coimbra, 1893; *A Consciência*, Funchal 1897; *Versos da Mocidade*, Funchal, 1903, 127 pp.; *Versos para meus filhos*, Funchal, 1910, 118 pp.; *Collar de Vidrilhos*, Funchal, 1911, 54 pp.; *Canção das lágrimas*; and *Sonetos*, Lisbon, 1916.
